The study used only female patients as it was related to ovarian metastases. 195 patients were included in the study and the median age when diagnosed with CRC was 49 years. The under expression of SMAD4 resulted in a reduced OS(HR=27.69, CI 4.98-154.02, p=0.0001).

Of a set of 338 pediatric brain tumors, Gielen et al identified the K27M mutation in 35 of 129 glioblastomas (27.1%) and in 5 of 28 (17.9%) anaplastic astrocytomas. The authors state that H3F3A K27M could potentially be used as a molecular diagnostic marker for these tumors, as it has a sensitivity of 25.5% and specificity of 100% for diffuse malignant astrocytic tumors (ie, GBM and AA).

Wu et al analyzed 127 pediatric HGGs, including diffuse intrinsic pontine gliomas (DIPGs) and non-brainstem HGGs (NBS-HGGs) by whole genome, whole exome, and/or transcriptome sequencing. In addition to ACVR1, they identified 41 recurrent K27M mutations in H3F3A (H3.3, 41/112 = 36.6%), and in 14 HIST1H3B (H3.1, 14/112, 12.5%) in NBS-HGGs and DIPGs. The authors focus on ACVR1 mutations, as H3F3A and HIST1H3A mutations in pediatric gliomas have previously been reported. However, this evidence helps confirm potential diagnostic utility of H3F3A K27M mutations.

Sequence analysis between normal vs. tumor samples showed the presence of 4 missense mutations and a somatic 12–base pair deletion in 16% of the 31 colorectal cancer (CRC) patients. The results of this research confirmed the role of SMAD4 as a tumor-suppressor gene in CRC patients, although, the frequency of alterations was quite low at 16.7% (5 of 31 colorectal cancers) compared to 75% who had allelic loss where the SMAD4 gene is located.

One of the goals of this study was to find the local failure rates in tumors for patients with Prostate Cancer. The failure rates for the first and second year for patients who lost SMAD4 expression were 19% and 29% and for patients whose SMAD4 expression stayed intact there rates for the first and second year were 8% and 13% respectively(P = 0.015). SMAD4 loss is strongly related with increased chance of local failure(HR, 2.37; 95% CI,1.10–5.11; P = 0.027). SMAD4 loss was also associated with higher rates of DF(HR, 1.45; 95% CI, 0.91–2.31;P = 0.11). Patients with a loss of SMAD4 are at a greater risk for local failure.

Whole genome sequencing (WGS) was performed on the diffuse intrinsic pontine gliomas (DIPGs) and matched germline DNA of 7 pediatric patients. Targeted sequencing was performed on an additional 43 DIPGs and 36 non-brainstem pediatric glioblastomas (non-BS-PGs). Authors identified K27M mutations in 30/50 (60%) of pediatric DIPGs (including 4/7 WGS samples) and 7/36 (19%) pediatric non-brainstem glioblastomas. The authors comment that the K27M mutation appeared exclusive to pediatric high grade gliomas, with H3F3A p.K27M mutation in one of 9 pediatric anaplastic astrocytomas (Grade III), but no histone H3 mutations found in any other pediatric brain tumors including 7 low-grade brainstem gliomas, 15 low-grade non-brainstem gliomas, 38 medulloblastomas, and 22 ependymomas. H3 K27M was not found in an additional 170 non-central nervous system pediatric tumors.

Only 12/118(10.2%) of patients with type I papillary renal cell carcinoma expressed FGFR2 whereas 37/96 (38.5%) patients with type II papillary renal cell carcinoma(P=0.001). In addition, FGFR2 expression was correlated with a number of metastatic sites (2+ sites vs. 0-1) and lower nucleolar grade(P=0.001).Patients with FGFR2 overexpression also had significantly shorter survival rates and progression free survival rates in first line therapy (P<0.05). On multivariate analysis, FGFR2 expression, MSKCC risk group and type of pRCC were found to be independent predictors of survival.

The correlation between FGFR2/SPRY2 and clinicopathologic factors was analyzed by Chi-square to screen the FGFR2/SPRY2-relevant factors. SPRY2 low expression was demonstrated to be significantly associated with positive lymphatic invasion (P = 0.007), Lauren subtype (P = 0.031) and higher FGFR2 expression (P = 0.029). Additionally, low expression of SPRY2(P = 0.031, 5-year survival rate: 52.2% vs. 35.9%) was a biomarker of poor prognosis.

Patients with high FGFR2 expression had an overall survival rate of 72.2,40.6% at 1,3 years (p<0.05) and those with low FGFR2 expression had a 1,3 year survival rate of 92.0,82.8% (p<0.05). The disease free survival rates for 1,3 years were 53.3,20% for patients with high FGFR2 expression and 75.8,47.5%, for those with low expression of FGFR2 (p<0.05). In addition, multiple or distant metastases were more frequent in those with high FGFR2 expression than low expression (p<0.05).

Treatment of cell lines harboring FGFR2 mutations with dovitinib 0.5 mmol/L for 72 hours resulted in a significant decrease in cell viability of AN3CA (37.80%) and MFE-296 (53.14%). Conversely, in cell lines expressing wild-type FGFR2 the effects of dovitinib were nearly indiscernible after treatment. Dovitinib and drugs were used alone or in combination. Using a MTT assay it was observed that combination of inhibitors caused a clear decrease in cell viability in FGFR2-mutated ECC lines. The combination therapy was especially effective in limiting growth of cell lines with FGFR2 mutations as opposed to those without mutation. (P<0.05)

Among 80 patients, FGFR2 amplification was observed in seven cases (11.5%). Patients with FGFR2 amplification had significantly shorter overall survival (OS) than did those without FGFR2 amplification (9.1 vs. 16.5 months; p=0.037). In multivariate analysis, disease status and number of metastatic sites were associated with worse OS (p=0.015 and p=0.009, respectively). And since FGFR2 amplification was also associated with more metastatic sites, FGFR2 amplification tended to be correlated with a poorer outcome (p=0.080) but this was not statistically significant.

FGFR2 over-expression was observed in 75.9 % (n = 107)of the 141 eligible patients and was correlated with perineural invasion (P = 0.005) and inferior tumor regression grading (TRG) (P = 0.009). On univariate analysis, FGFR2 over-expression was significantly associated with worse rectal cancer-specific survival (RCSS) (P = 0.005) and disease-free survival (DFS) (P = 0.035). FGFR2 over-expression did not independently influence patient outcome but FGFR2 over-expression was associated with worse prognosis and inferior TRG.

FGFR1, -2, -3, and -4 were expressed in 5.3%, 11.1%, 3.8%, and 52.7% of HCCs, respectively. Among the development set of 153 patients, FGFR2 positivity in HCC was associated with a significantly shorter overall survival (5-year survival rate, 35.3% vs. 61.8%; P=0.02). FGFR2 expression in HCC was an independent predictor of a poor postsurgical prognosis (hazard ratio, 2.10; P=0.02) in the development set. However, the corresponding findings were not statistically significant in the validation set.

Statistical analysis showed that the inverse relationship between COUP-TF II and SMAD4 expression was shown in 112 different patients with Colorectal Cancer(CRC)(45 COUP-TF II-positive/SMAD4-negative tumors and 24 COUP-TF II-negative/SMAD4-positive tumors (rs=-0.221, P=0.019)). The log-rank test found that over expression of COUP-TF II in patients was related to poor survival and adverse clinical outcome. COUP-TF II positive/SMAD4 negative status is an important prognostic factor for patients with CRC.

The under expression of SMAD4 resulted in a higher Gleason score and a higher level of preoperative prostate specific antigen (PSA). It is considered for low levels of PSA to be normal. Patients with an under expression of SMAD4 has a much shorter biochemical recurrence (BCR) -free time compared to patients with an over expression of SMAD4. In multivariate analysis the results showed that the under expression of SMAD4, higher Gleason score, angiolymphatic invasion, and seminal vesicle invasion were independent predictors of shorter BCR-free survival.

Behjati et al identified K36M mutations in a set of 77 chondroblastomas. Chondroblastoma is a typically a pediatric or early adult cancer. Of the 77, 5 had K36M mutations in H3F3A, 68 had K36M in H3F3B and 4 were WT. Of the 77, 65 of the cases were 25 years old or less. Of those, 3 had K36M in H3F3A and 59 had K36M in H3F3B with 3 being WT (See Supplementary Table 1). Thus, 59/65 (90.7%) cases at age 25 or less had K36M mutations in H3F3B. Behjati et al screened over 268 other bone and cartilage tumor types, and identified only 1 K36M H3F3B mutation (a clear cell chondrosarcoma). The authors conclude discussing the remarkable specificity of these mutations and implications for immediate diagnostic utility.

This study shows that KRAS mutations such as G12D, G13D and KRAS amplification are frequent drivers of acquired resistance to cetuximab in colorectal cancers. KRAS mutant clones can be detected through non invasive procedures months before radiographic progression of the disease. This study also shows preliminary results on how MEK inhibitors can be used to delay or reverse acquired resistance to cetuximab.

Three major drug resistance mutations, namely L718Q, L844V, and C797S were identified in EGFR and caused resistance to both WZ4002 and CO-1686. In contrast, only EGFR C797S caused AZD9291 resistance. Cells containing EGFR-sensitizing mutations such as exon 19 deletion or L858R substitution, in conjunction with L718Q, L844V, or C797S retained sensitivity to EGFR inhibitors, gefitinib and afatinib. The C797S mutation, in the presence of exon 19 deletion or L858R substitution and T790M substitution, causes resistance to all current EGFR inhibitors. However, EGFR L858R/T790M/C797S mutations remain partially sensitive to cetuximab which leads to disruption of EGFR dimerization.

It is clear that patients with FGFR2/Plcγ1/Grb2 relative concentrations as: high/high/low have the poorest prognosis whilst those having FGFR2/Plcγ1/Grb2 as: low/low/high drastically enhances the prognosis. There was also a correlation observed by staining cancerous cell lines with FGFR2, Grb2 and Plcγ1 antibodies, observing that FGFR2 and Plcγ1 staining intensity is higher in lung adenocarcinoma compared to normal lung tissue while it is lower for Grb2.

VHL patients were screened for mutations by single-strand conformational polymorphism analysis and DNA sequencing. Restriction fragment length polymorphism confirmed a familial frameshift mutation (c.462delA) of the VHL gene in a proband and his two sons. This caused splicing abnormalities in the gene as well. Phenotypes of the patients are unknown.

evidence_statement: A 33 year old Asian male patient presented with advanced bilateral multicentric renal carcinoma. Genetic testing confirmed a de novo missense variant at c.194C>G of the VHL gene. The patient was diagnosed with an epididymal cyst at age 23, bilateral retinal angiomatosis at age 26, and bilateral clear cell renal cell carcinoma at age 33. ACMG codes:PM1; PM5; and PP4.

phenotypes: Late onset,Juvenile onset,Middle age onset,Young adult onset
evidence_statement: In this study, the authors analyzed 53 cases of giant cell tumour of bone using capillary sequencing and massively parallel sequencing. They identified histone 3.3 mutations in 49/53 cases (92%). All variants were located in the H3F3A gene and involved substitutions at glycine 34, comprising 48 G34W mutations and 1 G34L mutation. The authors additionally screened 268 other bone and cartilage tumours for mutations in H3F3A and H3F3B. G34W mutations were not identified in these other tumour types, although one osteosarcoma harboured a G34R variant. The study states that histone 3.3 mutations show tumour-type specificity and notes that these findings may have diagnostic utility, particularly in cases where tumour classification is uncertain.

Plasma concentrations of Th1 and Th2 cytokines were analyzed using the Bio-Plex multiplex suspension array system in 34 homozygotes VHL patients, 4 heterozygous VHL patients, and 32 VHL wild-type participants from Chuvashia. RFLP confirmed a missense mutation at c.598C > T in all 38 patients. All patients presented with Chuvash polcythemia. Family history is unknown.

Thirty-eight subjects from three unrelated Taiwanese families (F01, F02 and F03) were enrolled from those attending the Department of Surgery, Cathay General Hospital. All enrolled members were genetically tested. The age range that firstly examined these patients to contract VHL disease is 34.4 – 49.4 years. A complete VHL deletion was found in family F01. 31 members of the F01 family were enrolled and 10 were confirmed with the mutation: Pt. 16 was a female presenting with CNS hemangioblastoma, Pt 18 was a male presenting with CNS hemangioblastoma and pancreatic cysts, Pt 21 was a female presenting with CNS hemangioblastoma, Pt 33 was a female presenting with CNS hemangioblastoma. Pt 19, 28, 31, 37, and 38 were carriers. Pt. 5 and 13 were not enrolled in the study but they are suspected to have VHL disease.

Thirty-eight subjects from three unrelated Taiwanese families (F01, F02 and F03) were enrolled from those attending the Department of Surgery, Cathay General Hospital. All enrolled members had their blood genetically tested. The age range that firstly examined these patients to contract VHL disease is 34.4 – 49.4 years. This deletion in the VHL gene was found in family F02, with 2 enrolled members: Pt 3 was a female with CNS hemangioblastoma and Pt. 4 was a carrier.

Nagasubramanian et al reports on a case of refractory infantile fibrosarcoma (IFS) with constitutive activation of the tropomyosin‐related kinase (TRK) signaling pathway from an ETS variant gene 6–neurotrophin 3 receptor gene (ETV6–NTRK3) gene fusion. The patient was diagnosed with IFS at 6 months of age. At 16 months the patient enrolled in a pediatric Phase 1 trial of LOXO‐101 (Larotrectinib, ARRY-470), an experimental, highly selective inhibitor of TRK. The patient experienced a rapid, radiographic response, demonstrating the potential for LOXO‐101 to provide benefit for IFS harboring NTRK gene fusions.

Prasad et al queried the histopathology of 28 Papillary Thyroid Carcinomas (PTCs) from patients ages 6-18 years (20 females, 8 males). None had significant exposure to radiation. 5 / 27 PTCs (18.5%) had NTRK3-ETV6 fusion oncogenes. The authors compare NTRK3-ETV6 (and include 2 other NTRK fusion samples) to PTCs with BRAF(V) (600E) and find they are associated with large size (mean, 2.2 cm vs 1.5 cm, respectively; P = .05), solid and diffuse variants (11 of 13 vs 0 of 13 tumors, respectively; P < .001), and lymphovascular invasion (12 of 13 vs 6 of 13 tumors, respectively; P = .02); The authors conclude that NTRK fusion oncogene PTC presents with more extensive disease and aggressive pathology than BRAF(V) (600E) PTC in the pediatric population.

Shukla et al report on a remarkable case study of a 14 year old pediatric patient with refractory secretory breast carcinoma first presenting as a fibroadenoma at 8 yo. Over the next years, she experienced recurrence, multiple rounds of chemotherapy and metastasis -- until her case was presented at a virtual multidisciplinary tumor board organized by the Global Cancer Institute which recommended testing for ETV6-NTRK3 fusion. This fusion was confirmed by RNA-seq, targeted DNA and WGS sequencing as well as immunohistochemistry staining with a TRK antibody. The patient was treated with LOXO-101 (larotrectinib) in a single patient use protocol. Within two months, she experienced near complete resolution of a 10.4 × 8.5 cm fungating chest mass with multiple satellite lesions (See Figure 2). The authors note that TERT promoter mutation and a reciprocal inversion including CDKN2A were also identified, but given what is known about LOXO-101 and ETV6-NTRK3, they infer ETV6-NTRK3 fusion as the primary mitogenic driver in this patient.

Thirty-eight subjects from three unrelated Taiwanese families (F01, F02 and F03) were enrolled from those attending the Department of Surgery, Cathay General Hospital. All enrolled members were genetically tested. The age range that firstly examined these patients to contract VHL disease is 34.4 – 49.4 years. 5 sibilings in the F03 family were enrolled. This deletion was found in the blood of Pt 5, who had CNS hemangioblastoma, pancreatic cysts, and bilateral renal cell carcinoma. This mutation was also confirmed in the a somatic brain hemangioblastoma sample from Pt5. The other siblings had no VHL manifestations and did not carry the mutation.

Case studies of three familes affected by VHL and their children was described. This missense mutation was found in Family 1 of 5 members. The father was 48Y when he was found to have renal cell carcinoma and bilateral pheochromocytoma. He died one year after diagnosis despite chemotherapy treatments. His son was diagnosed with and treated for bilateral pheochromocytoma at 13Y and endolymphatic sac tumours at 19Y. The son had a sister who tested postive for the mutation although her phenotype is not described. It is unclear whether the mother and the second son were negative for the mutation or were not tested.

Tissue specimens were retrieved from the archives of the Department of Pathology of the Erasmus MC (Rotterdam, The Netherlands), The University Medical Center St Radboud (Nijmegen, The Netherlands), and the University Hospital Zürich (Zürich, Switzerland). The mutation analysis of pheochromocytoma tissue samples showed two patients, 31Y and 24Y males, with R64P germline mutations in exon 1 of the VHL tumor suppressor gene and both had no metastasis. These patients belonged to the same family. Besides bilateral pheochromocytoma, the paper does not provide any other phenotypic information.

Ninety VHL R200W homozygotes and 52 controls with normal VHL alleles from Chuvashia, Russia, were studied under basal circumstances. 52 participants were female and 38 were male. The participants were on average 43 years old. They presented with Chuvash polycythemia. Genetice testing confirmed a missense mutation at c.598C>T of the VHL gene. Family history of participants is unknown.

Patients with erythrocytosis from 4 families of Asian and Western European ancestry were genetically screened. This confirmed a missense mutation at c.598C > T of the VHL gene. The sample included 6 males and 7 females, of which nine were homozygous mutations and four were heterozygous mutations. Homozygous mutants presented with Chuvash polycythemia while heterzygous mutants were asymptomatic.

A family containing an unknown number of members had one member present with pancreatic cysts. Genetic analysis revealed a germline mutation involving the deletion of exon 1 in the VHL gene. The family was taken from the Freiburg VHL registry. No other demographic information was available.

In the 746 metastatic breast tumors analyzed,KMT2C mutations were found in 9.8% of tumors, making it one of the most commonly mutated genes in breast cancer. Analysis of the 818 cases in the TCGA dataset demonstrated the majority of KMT2C mutations to be frameshift, truncation, or missense mutations that occur in all breast cancer subtypes with a relatively even distribution. In 283 metastatic breast cancer cases that underwent single agent aromatase therapy, 18 had deletions or truncations of KMTC2C and these 18 patients demonstrated worse progression free survival (PFS 6.6 months; p=.036) than KMT2C wildtype patients (n=260; PFS 12.1 months).

A 12 year old white male child presented with polycythemia. Genetic testing confirmed a germline missense mutation found at c.571C>G (p.His191Asp) in the VHL gene. This is the only other case of a homozygous VHL germline mutation causing polycythemia other than 598C>T.

An asymptomatic 47-year-old woman was diagnosed as an obligate carrier of a mutant von Hippel-Lindau gene. The diagnosis of von Hippel-Lindau disease in her daughter had led to her retrospective diagnosis and that of her son. The patient was screened and found with metastic renal cell carcinoma and extra-adrenal pheochromocytoma. The VHL mutation in the family is c.257C>T (p.Pro86Leu). The patient died 31 months after being diagnosed and phenotype of her children is unknown.

A family study indicated the presence of VHL mutation in a Kuwaiti family with Arab parentage. 10 family members were recruited, of which 1 was clinically diagnosed with VHL disease. Four children in family (2 males, 1 female), 1 of which was the patient, were shown to have the same mutation in the splice donor site of the first intron. The mutation was identified as IVS1 + 1 G-->T3. Additional phenotypic information was not described.

A mutation in one of the alleles in the exon 3 region was seen in Duke VHL family 1393. Sequences of this region were obtained from exon 3 PCR products. The VHL 1393 samples included five affected and five unaffected individuals. This mutation was found in the VHL 1393 affected samples. No phenotypic or demographic information was provided.

A 65Y male patient of Japanese ethnicity presented with hypertension, pheochromocytoma, and bilateral adrenal tumors. A mutation c.460C>T (p.Pro154Ser) was confirmed in the VHL gene. His 35Y son had the same mutation and presented with pheochromocytoma.

evidence_statement: A 20Y male patient presented with pheochromocytoma and genetic analysis confirmed a germline mutation c.311G>T (p.Gly104Val) in the VHL gene. This mutation was confirmed in the patient's 48Y father who presented with a T1 vertebral body hemangioma, multiple bilateral renal cysts, left adrenal nodularity, and an indeterminate right kidney midpole lesion. The paternal first cousin once removed died due to complications from clear cell renal cell carcinoma at 50Y, although genotype for the cousin is not provided.

A 27 year old pregnant woman, the index patient, was referred to the obstetric department of our University Medical Centre with hypertension and pre-eclampsia at 26 weeks. She was found to have bilateral pheochromocytoma and a germline mutation c.277G>A (p.Gly93Ser) in the VHL gene. Her father was also confirmed for this mutation and had pheochromocytoma right adrenal gland which was resected at age 48, epididymal cysts on the left side, and bilateral renal cysts. The patient's newborn daughter was confirmed with the mutations. The patient's paternal grandmother and grandmother's brother both died due to cerebral vascular incident a 42Y and 57Y respectively.

A 68Y male patient presented with CNS haemangioblastoma, retinal haemangioblastoma, renal cell carcinoma, and serous cystadenoma. At 74Y he developed phaeochromocytoma. Genetic testing confirmed a mutation c.245G>C (p.Arg82Pro) in the VHL gene which was confirmed in 3 other family members. One was his grandson which was asymptomatic, his son that had renal cell carcinoma and pancreatic cysts or serous cystadenoma, and a distant relative had CNS hemangioblastoma, RCC, symptomatic phaeochromocytoma, and pancreatic cysts/serous cystadenoma. 4 other relatives had CHS hemangioblastoma but were not confirmed for the mutation.

3-year-old white male child presented with renal cell carcinoma. Genetic testing confirmed 2 mutations: a translocation between chromosome X and 1 t(X;1)(p11.2; p34.3). A germline missense mutation was found c.562C>G (p.Leu188Val) in the VHL gene. Family history is unknown.

16 members in a Japenese family were analyzed and the same mutation VHL mutation was detected in 8 individuals c.482G>A (p.Arg161Gln). The 18Y F proband, the 19Y female cousin, and the 20Y brother were asymptomatic. There were 5 affected family members: brother had a twin who had unilateral pheochromocytoma, the aunt had a pancreatic neuroendorcine tumour, the uncle had a bilateral adrenal tumour, a cousin had bilateral pheochromocytoma and the father had unilateral pheochromocytoma and paraganglia.

A VHL disease family has been previously identified (Huang et al., 2007). An updated reported revealed a new affected patient (patient #43) with a ~250.9 kb deletion encompassing the VHL gene as other family members and CNS hemangioblastoma. His daughter (patient #48) presented as a carrier of the same identical deletion. The exact age of the patients is unknown although it is described that the father's age is between 36-56 and the daughter is between 13-16 years old.

Western blots were done with 50 5-μm sections (approximately 10 mg) cut from five frozen phaeochromocytoma tissue samples from patients with germline mutations in SDHB (EX3del), SDHD (p.Asp92Tyr), RET (p.Cys634Arg), VHL (c.191G>C; p.Arg64Pro), and NF1 (clinically determined).

A germline translocation t(1;3)(q32;q13.3) was identified by karyotyping in five members of the family including all three RCC cases tested: 56Y male with bilateral ccRCC, his 62Y male cousin with ccRCC, his 79Y aunt with left ccRCC and multiple lung metastases, and his mom and daughter who were both carriers. There were two other family members who died from non-renal cancer. III.5 died of gastric cancer at the age of 49 and III.7 died of exocrine pancreatic cancer at the age of 60. Genotyping was not available for either. Genotyping was not available for his uncle and aunt, who had ccRCC and was expected to be a VHL mutation carrier, respectively.

A case report revealed a 34-year-old, Caucasian male diagnosed with bilateral pheochromocytoma. Genetic testing revealed a c.500G>A (p.Arg167Gln) mutation in the VHL gene. The paper did not explicitly state whether the genetic testing was done from a tumour tissue or blood sample, so the variant origin was left as unknown. There was no family history of endocrine neoplasms or early cerebral or cardiovascular disease.

A case report showed that a 7-year-old girl presented with decreased vision in both eyes for 1 month. Examination showed visual acuity of 20/50 and 20/60, no afferent pupillary defect, cecocentral scotomas, and bilateral optic disc edema with extensive peripapillary and macular exudates. Magnetic resonance imaging showed multiple cortical and subcortical white matter lesions. The patient was lost to follow-up until age 18 when she developed shortness of breath and was found to have multiple pulmonary metastases identified as pheochromocytoma by biopsy. Genetic testing identified a 3p25-26 (c.482 G>A) VHL gene chromosomal mutation consistent with von Hippel-Lindau disease genotype. Multiple peripheral retinal vascular dilations and small retinal capillary hemangioblastomas were also found. Her past medical history and family history were negative for eye disease, renal cell carcinoma, or neurologic syndromes.

A 12Y male African-American patient was found with multiple bilateral pheochromocytoma, in addition to congenital microcephaly, developmental delay and cryptorchidism. Genetic anaylsis confirmed a c.238A>G (p.Ser80Gly) mutation in the VHL gene, but this mutation was not confirmed in the parents suggesting a de novo mutation.

Data was collected from 82 VHL mutation carriers in the Dutch VHL surveillance program. One patient age 20Y at the last follow-up had retinal hemangioblastoma and a germline c.208G>A (p.Glu70Lys) mutation in the VHL gene. Family history was not described.

evidence_statement: A male patient born to consanguineous parents was found with a c.256C>G (p.Pro86Ala) mutation in the VHL gene at 10 years old. He went on to develop bilateral retinal capillary hemangioblastomas and multiple pancreatic cysts. He also presented with weakness, muscular algias, and myoblobinurina which is consistent with a homozygous c.338C>T(p.Ser113Leu) mutation found in his CPT2 gene. Genetic analysis revealed the VHL mutation in other family members, but not the CPT2 mutation. Patient's mother, maternal grandmother, 2 maternal aunts, brother, and cousin were confirmed for the VHL mutation. The cousin was found to be an asymptomatic carrier. Mother presented with CNS hemangioblastoma, renal cysts, pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour, and retinal capillary hemangioblastoma. Maternal grandmother presented with CNS hemangioblastoma, renal cysts, pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour, and tympanic paraganglioma. One maternal aunt had CNS hemangioblastoma, retinal capillary hemabgioblastoma, and a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour, and the other aunt had CNS hemangioblastoma, renal cysts, pancreatic cysts, pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour, retinal capillary hemangioblastoma and a endolymphatic sac tumor. Finally, the patient's brother presented with pheochromocytoma and epididymal cysts.

Thirty-two surgically resected HB specimens from 28 patients treated at the University of Tokyo Hospital between 1995 and 2012 were analyzed retrospectively. Of the 32 specimens, 11 were VHL-related HBs from 7 patients. Two brothers (22Y and 30Y) identified as hemangioblastoma patients were confirmed with a germline c.216delC deletion in the VHL gene. The 22Y brother had hemangioblastoma in the cerebellum at 22Y and then again at 24Y, and the 30Y brother had a hemangioblastoma in the brainstem. No other phenotypic information was available.

evidence_statement: A 45Y male patient presenting with bilateral retinal angiomas, multifocal cerebellar hemangioblastomas, and bilateral RCC was found to have a c.473T>A (p.Leu158Glu) germline mutation in the VHL gene. His 30Y nephew was confirmed with this mutation and had a similar phenotype indicating VHL 1 disease. 2 of the patient's brothers also presented with VHL 1, although their exact phenotype was not described and their genotype was not confirmed.

A 41Y male patient presented with right cerebellar hemangioblastoma and bilateral adrenal pheochromocytoma. A mutation c.499C>T (p.Arg167Trp) was confirmed in the VHL gene. The patient's brother and sister were also confirmed for the mutation, although the sister was asymptomatic and the brother had a nodule in the left cerebellar tonsil with a size of ~9.0×10.5 mm, which indicated the presence of a hemangioblastoma, astrocytoma or ependymoma. However, the diagnosis for the brother could not be confirmed. The patient had 2 other siblings that were negative for the mutation. The mother exhibited a brain tumor and coronary heart disease and has since passed.

A 38Y male patient presented with right clear cell RCC and multiple small cystic lesions in the left and right kidneys and pancreas. A mutation c.500G>A (p.Arg167Gln) was confirmed in the VHL gene. Familial genetic screening revealed the same mutation in his 2 sons, who had no abnormalities in the abdomen but refused MRI brain scanning. The patient's mother passed due to pancreatic cancer and genotypic information on the mother is not available.

PRKCB was mutated in 33% of ATLL cases. 93% of these mutations were within the catalytic domain at Asp427. This gene has not been reported to be significantly mutated in any other cancers. Indeed this is the first known example in any cancer that appears to involve activation by the PKC gene family. Nearly all occurrences of this mutation in COSMIC correspond to ATLL.

This evidence supports AMCG code 'PM2' - Absent from controls (i.e. gnomAD).

Both in vivo and in vitro models demonstrated Larotrectinib was an effective treatment against cells harboring ETV6-NTRK3. In YFP-luciferase PDX mice from a 16-year-old with Ph-like B-ALL, flow cytometry indicated the absence of leukemic cells in the bone marrow (p<.0001), peripheral blood (p=.0018), and spleen (p=.0001) after 6 weeks of Larotrectinib (n=10) compared to vehicle treated mice (n=10). Treated mice also had lower splenic weight (p<.001) and the absence of leukemia burden in the bone marrow and central nervous system as determined by histopathology. In 2 mice, leukemic burden increased while Larotrectinib was paused from weeks 6-25. Upon the reintroduction of treatment for 4 weeks, leukemic burden was lowered. Conditional knock-in Etv6-NTRK CD19-Cre cells isolated from bone marrow and cultured ex vivo were highly sensitive to serial dilutions of Larotrectinib. After 48 hours of Larotrectinib exposure, Ba/F3 cells stably expressing ETV6-NTRK3 demonstrated a response with an IC50 of 17.0nM (viability measured by CellTiter blue). Finally, Larotrectinib was 1000x more potent against 3 human cancer cell lines with an NTRK fusion versus the 76 with other alterations. The most sensitive was an AML cell line (M0-91) with an ETV6-NTRK3 fusion.

Cancer-associated mutation of PTPN12 or reduced PTPN12 protein leads to aberrant activity of several tyrosine kinase receptors (MET, PDGFRβ, EGFR, and others). Restoring PTPN12 protein levels restrained signaling from RTKs, including PDGFRβ and MET, and impaired TNBC survival. In contrast with single agents, combined inhibitors targeting the PDGFRβ and MET receptors induced the apoptosis in TNBC cells in vitro and in vivo. This therapeutic strategy resulted in tumor regressions in chemo-refractory patient-derived TNBC models. Notably, response correlated with PTPN12 deficiency, suggesting that impaired receptor feedback may establish a combined addiction to these proto-oncogenic receptors.

The study showed association of the ABL1 fusions with partner genes other than BCR with a specific molecular/genetic subtype of B-lymphoblastic leukemia characterized by the expression signature similar to the one of the BCR-ABL1 (Ph)-positive B-ALL. This subtype is known as BCR-ABL1 like (of Philadelphia (Ph)-like). According to this study, the presence of non-BCR ABL1 fusion in B-ALL is diagnostic for BCR-ABL1 subtype, which is recognized in the 2017 WHO classification as a provisional entity. In this study by Roberts et al., 264 out of 1725 precursor B-cell ALL cases (15.3%) were identified as being Ph-like based on the expression signature. The prevalence of Ph-like ALL significantly increased with age, from 10% among children with standard-risk ALL and 13% among those with high-risk ALL to 21% among adolescents with ALL and 27% among young adults with ALL. In this Phase III trial (NCT01584648 COMBI-d), 423 previously untreated patients with unresectable stage IIIC or IV BRAF V600E or V600K mutant melanoma received dabrafenib and trametinib or dabrafenib alone with primary endpoint of progression free survival with secondary endpoints including disease response. The hazard ratio for progression or death in the dabrafenib–trametinib group was 0.75 (95% confidence interval, 0.57 to 0.99; P=0.03). Of 210 patients in the dabrafenib + trametinib group, 67% of patients had a response, which was 16 percentage points higher than in the dabrafenib-alone group (95% CI, 6 to 25; P=0.002).

After progressing on 6 multi-kinase inhibitor (MKI) regimens (including sorafenib , vandetanib, cabozantinib, MGCD-516, RXDX-105, and vandetanib plus everolimus ), a metastatic medullary thyroid cancer patient with a RET M918T mutation was found to have acquired a gatekeeper RET mutation V804M in addition to the M918T mutation. Upon treatment with the selective RET inhibitor selpercatinib (LOXO-292), the patient had a significant response with reductions in tumor volume, calcitonin, and carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) levels as well as resolution of painful hepatomegaly and tumor-related diarrhea. Detection of RET M918T and RET V804M in cell-free DNA decreased in the first 8 weeks and remained suppressed. The patient remained on therapy for more than 7 months as of the time of publication. The study showed that in B-ALL the the presence of ABL2 fusions with different partner genes is diagnostic for the so-called BCR-ABL1-like (or Philadelphia (Ph)-like) molecular subtype of B-ALL. Ph-like ALL is recognized as a separate (provisional) entity in the 2017 WHO classification of hematologic malignancies. BCR-ABL1-like B-ALLs have similar expression profiles as BCR-ABL1-positive cases. In this study, 264 of 1725 precursor B-cell ALL cases (15.3%) were identified as Ph-like; of those, seven were found to have ABL2 fusions with different partner genes. The specific ABL2 fusions observed were: PAG1-ABL2, RCSD1-ABL2 and ZC3HAV1-ABL2.

evidence_statement: In this study, 264 of 1725 precursor B-lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL) cases were identified as BCR::ABL1 (Ph)-like based on the expression signature similar to the BCR::ABL1 positive B-ALL; of those 264 cases,19 were found to have JAK2 fusions with different partner genes resulting in JAK2 over-expression. Expression analysis showed activated kinase and cytokine receptor signaling, confirming association of JAK2 fusions with the Ph-like B-ALL expression signature. The specific JAK2 fusions observed were: ATF7IP::JAK2, BCR::JAK2, EBF1::JAK2, ETV6::JAK2, PAX5::JAK2, PPFIBP1::JAK2, SSBP2::JAK2, STRN3::JAK2, TERF2::JAK2, TPR::JAK2. Functional studies were performed for one of the detected JAK2 fusions, PAX5::JAK2. The fusion was found to confer cytokine independent proliferation in cell lines, and JAK2 inhibitor ruxolitinib attenuated phosphorylated STAT5 in cells expressing the PAX5::JAK2 fusion. The findings support that JAK2 fusions with different partner genes are defining primary drivers in Ph-like molecular subtype of B-ALL.

In this Phase 1b study, 129 patients with unresectable or metastatic melanoma were verified for BRAF V600 mutation using the cobas 4800 mutation test were selected who had progressed on vemurafenib (66 patients) or never received BRAF inhibitor (63 patients). We identified missense mutations in PTPN11 in 21 of 62 individuals with JMML but without Noonan syndrome (34%; 95% confidence interval (c.i.) = 22–47%), with nine different molecular defects in exon 3 and one in exon 13 (Table 1). The most common mutations, each accounting for 25% of the total number, were a G→T transversion at position 181 and a G→A transition at position 226, predicting D61Y and E76K substitutions within the N-SH2 domain, respectively.

Five of the 11 somatic mutations were non–RAS pathway mutations, involving SETBP1 (3 p.Asp868Asn alterations), JAK3 (1 p.Arg657Gln alteration) and SH3BP1 (1 p.Ser277Leu alteration), which had not been reported in JMML cases. SETBP1 was originally isolated as a 170-kDa nuclear protein that interacts with SET, a small protein inhibitor of the putative tumor suppressors PP2A and NM23-H1 (ref. 6). Several lines of recent evidence suggest that SETBP1 has a role in leukemogenesis (Supplementary Fig. 4)7,8,9,10,11. SETBP1 participates in translocations that result in an aberrant fusion gene (NUP98-SETBP1) and overexpression of SETBP1 in T cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) and acute myeloid leukemia (AML), respectively12,13. SETBP1 is one of the downstream targets induced by the Evi-1 oncoprotein14 and, together with EVI1 and its homolog PRDM16 (also known as MEL1), was reported to be activated through retrovirus integration. SETBP1 is also known to augment the recovery of granulopoiesis after gene therapies for chronic granulomatous disease15. SETBP1 overexpression is found in more than 27% of adult AML cases and is associated with poor survival13. The discovery of recurrent hotspot mutations of SETBP1 provides unequivocal evidence for the leukemogenic role of deregulated SETBP1 function.

However, the authors identify Y253H, E255K/V, and F359C/V variants as resistant as they had an IC50 of >150nM. In patients with F359C and/or F359V mutations prior to nilotinib treatment, complete hematological responses were achieved in 3 of 10 patients, a major cytogenetic response in 1 of 11 patients, a complete cytogenetic response in 0 of 11 patients, and major molecular response in 0 of 10 patients. After a median follow-up of 15.5 months, 9 of 11 patients with this mutation progressed or died. The F359C mutation was present in 1 patient at baseline and newly emerged in 1 patient at progression. The F359V mutation was present in 4 patients at baseline and newly emerged in 1 patient at progression.

Ph-like ALL is a provisional entity in the 2017 WHO classification. A patient with metastatic colon cancer who was previously treated with more than 3rd line cytotoxic chemotherapy was found to have FLT3 amplification and then received regorafenib showing partial response. In two PDC cell lines with FLT3 amplification, FLT3 mRNA expression was increased, however, the growth of tumor cells was not significantly inhibited by either regorafenib or sorafenib which is known to block the activity FLT3.

Treatment with sorafenib of a patient with metastatic colorectal cancer and FLT3 translocation who had previously been heavily treated showed significant symptomatic and laboratory improvement with sorafenib treatment.

Retrospective analysis of thyroid carcinoma patients from a single institution identified 33/58 patients with follicular carcinomas had any RAS mutations (NRAS, KRAS, or HRAS at codons 12 or 61), 22 of which were NRAS Q61. NRAS Q61 was associated with aggressive disease in the form of distant metastases. Patients with RAS mutations had significantly shorter overall survival than those without (P=0.034, Kaplan-Meier). However, NRAS Q61 alone was not significantly associated with death (P=0.36, Chi-squared).

Screening of 1,039 CRC samples to assess the prevalence of KRAS amplification and the role of this genetic alteration on the sensitivity to anti EGFR therapies. KRAS amplification was mutually exclusive with KRAS mutations. Tumors or cell lines harboring this genetic lesion are not responsive to anti-EGFR inhibitors. Although KRAS amplification is an infrequent event in CRC, it might be responsible for precluding response to anti-EGFR treatment in a small proportion of patients.

Human mutant V143A p53 was stably transfected into the murine fibroblast (10)3 and human osteosarcoma SAOS-2 cell lines, which lack endogenous p53 expression, resulting in viable cells. In contrast, permanent expression of wildtype p53 did not result in viable (10)3 or SAOS-2 cells. Injection of parental (10)3 cells in nude mice resulted in 0 tumors in 10 inoculated mice, and 0 of 9 inoculations for three vector control cell lines resulted in tumors. In contrast, 3/3 (10)3 cell lines with V143A p53 resulted in tumors. SAOS-2 cells with V143A were not able to form colonies in soft agar and did not show tumorigenicity in mice. The authors conclude these results suggest tumorigenic GOF in V143A p53 over cells with no p53.

Human mutant R175H p53 was stably transfected into the murine fibroblast (10)3 and human osteosarcoma SAOS-2 cell lines, which lack endogenous p53 expression, resulting in viable cells. SAOS-2 cells with R175H gained ability to form colonies in soft agar over controls, but did not show tumorigenicity in mice. The authors conclude these results suggest tumorigenic GOF in R175H p53 over cells with no p53.

The Ml myeloblastic cell line subclone designated M1/2 cells lacks endogenous p53, and undergoes rapid apoptosis after growth factor deprivation with p53 transduction. M1/2 cells were stably transduced with temperature sensitive mutant V134A p53, which takes on a mutant conformation at 37 degrees celsius but wildtype at 32 degrees. Wildtype p53 expressing and V135A cells grown at 37.5 degrees were subjected to growth factor deprivation, inducing apoptosis in wiltype p53 cells, while V134A cells showed reduced cell death, indicating loss of apoptotic apoptotic function with p53 V135A.

FISH was used to detect HEY1-NCOA2 fusions in 10 paraffin embedded samples from patients diagnosed with mesenchymal chondrosarcoma. HEY1 and NCOA2 are located on the same chromosome but generate distinct FISH signals, whereas the HEY1-NCOA2 fusion appears as a single fused dot. Specimens were considered positive for fusion when FISH showed overlapping signals of HEY1 and NCOA2 in greater than 20% of the cells. Overlap signal of over 20% was seen in 8/10 patients. The two patients with no overlap signal were also negative for FISH staining, suggesting insufficient or damaged material for FISH.

Meningeal hemangiopericytoma (HPC) and mesenchymal chondrosarcoma (MC) are aggressive neoplasms with overlapping clinical presentations and morphology. Thirteen FFPE samples of MC (9 females, 4 males) from ages 19 to 54 and Eighteen cases of meningeal HPC (8 females, 10 males) from ages from 24 to 73 years were tested using RT-PCR for the presence of HEY1-NCOA2 fusion. Of cases with evaluable RNA, 6/6 MC cases were positive for the fusion, but 0/11 meningeal HPC cases were fusion positive.

Whole transcriptome RNA-seq was performed in pediatric patients with cytogenetically normal acute myeloid leukemia. Identified a recurrent cryptic inversion of chromosome 16, that gives rise to an inframe CBFA2T3-GLIS2 fusion transcript. Two recurring breakpoints linking exon 11 of CBFA2T3 and exon 3 of GLIS2, and CBFA2T3 exon 10 fused to exon 2 of GLIS2. Fusions confirmed by RT-PCR and Sanger sequencing. Fusion found in 20 of 237 cases (8.4%) with cytogenetically normal-AML. 10/20 fusion carriers belonged to the M7 FAB subgroup. The 5-year event-free survival (EFS) of the 20 patients with the CBFA2T3-GLIS2 fusion gene was significantly worse than that of the 217 pediatric CN-AML patients not harboring the translocation (27.4%, standard error [SE] 10.5 vs 59.6%, SE 3.6; P = .01). This was independent of patient classified as M7 FAB. Overall publication provides good evidence of existence of fusion transcript in cn-AML, and poorer patient outcomes with fusion compared to without fusion.

EBF1-PDGFRB fusion was detected in leukemia cells of a 6 year old male who presented with B-ALL and an initial WBC of 244,400. He received 4-drug induction chemotherapy but failed to enter remission with day 29 marrow showing 44% blasts. Cytogenetics were normal, however FISH was positive for PDGFRB break apart and EBF1-PDGFRB fusion confirmed by RT-PCR. Imatinib was commenced with 3 courses of intensified salvage therapy. (MRD 0.38%). Patient received matched sibling donor HSC transplant and switched to dasatinib with 0.08% MRD at day 30 post-transplant, and negative MRD day 191 post-transplant

The EBF1-PDGFRB fusion was detected in leukemia cells of a 7 year old Latino boy who presented with B-ALL and initial WBC of 600,000. He failed to enter remission with 4 drug induction (90% blasts at day 23), and showed testicular involvement. SNP array showed deletion of IKZF1 deletion and gains in 5q32 and 5q33.3 that interrupted the PDGFRB and EBF1 loci, respectively. FISH studies demonstrated an extra PDGFRB signal with suspect EBF1-PDGFRB that needs molecular confirmation. Imatinib, cyclophosphamide and etoposide were commenced with MRD 4.3% after 1 month. Imatinib dose was increased with MRD 0.44% after additional month of treatment. MRD was 0.0226% after two months of dasatinib treatment, and the patient proceeded to matched unrelated donor hematopoietic stem cell transplantation.

A 14 month old female with normal karyotype B-ALL was found to have an atypical ATF7IP-PDGFRB fusion. At day 19 of VDLP induction, she achieved partial remission with 6.5% lymphoblasts, and a 40 mg/day dose of dasatinib was added to her regimen. She achieved complete remission at day 49 and was MRD negative by flow cytometry but not by RT-PCR. At day 125, flow cytometry and RT-PCR were negative for the ATF7IP-PDGFRB fusion and MRD was negative by FACS.

phenotypes: Renal cyst,Pancreatic cysts,Clear cell renal cell carcinoma
evidence_statement: A 27 year old woman with a confirmed germline VHL mutation (c.-77_-32del) presented with ccRCC, pancreatic cysts, and renal masses. Her father was diagnosed with a renal mass and pancreatic cysts at 45 years of age. He also presented with ccRCC. His brother was also diagnosed with ccRCC at 38 years of age. Her relatives were not confirmed with the mutation.

phenotypes: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma,Renal cyst
evidence_statement: A 53 year old male confirmed with the germline VHL mutation (c.-61_-51dup11) presented with ccRCC, a renal cyst, and pancreatic nodules. He had mild hearing loss, possibly indicating the presence of an endolymphatic sac tumour. His 24 year old daughter was also confirmed with the mutation, but had no symptoms of VHL.

• A 53 year old Puerto-Rican male presented with bilateral adrenal pheochromocytomas and a paracaval lymph node with a paraganglioma. He had a history of morbid obesity, obstructive sleep apnea, diabetes, hypertension, and smoking. Due to a family history of cancer (sister with unknown genitourinary cancer), peripheral blood was drawn and next generation targeted gene sequencing of 12 hereditary pheochromocytoma genes revealed the heterozygous Y175C (c.524A>G) in VHL. The presence of the variant was confirmed by Sanger. In vitro overexpression of Y175C and WT VHL demonstrated similar function based on HIFa levels in both normoxic and hypoxic conditions. This information classifies the variant as a Type 2C VHL mutant. ACMG codes: Missense variant in a gene that has a low rate of benign missense variation and in which missense variants are a common mechanism of disease (PP2).

A healthy 21 year old woman presented with high blood pressure. She noted palpitations ongoing for 6 months prior. Her adrenal galnds were found to be normal via CT scan. A 2cm x 1.8cm x 1.5cm lesion close to costovertebral angle of third right thoracic vertebra was found via PET scan were histological findings found this to be consistent with paraganglioma. Blood samples for genomic DNA analysis were taken and screening for mutations in SDHA, SDHB, SDHC, SDHD, RET, SDHAF2, TMEM127, MAX, NF1, FH, MDH2, and EPAS1 genes was negative but she was positive for a heterozygous mutation in the VHL gene, c.311G > T (p.Gly104Val). This same variant was found in her 17 year-old sister and her mother but not in her father. Her mother refused a complete staging. The probands sister presented with a small retinal hemangioblastoma at this time. ACMG evidence codes: 'PM2' since this variant is absent from controls (gnomAD), 'PP1' since there is cosegregation with disease in multiple affected family members, 'PP2' since we have a missense variant in a gene where missense variants are a common mechanism of disease, 'PP4' since the patient presents phenotypes highly specific for a disease with a single genetic etiology.

From a cohort of 944 patients with myelodysplastic syndrome, 311 patients harboring SF3B1 mutations were identified. In univariate analysis of 875 patients with sufficient clinical outcomes data, SF3B1 was the only gene identified to be significantly associated with improved overall survival (P<0.05, HR=0.52).

Since significant ALK and MET expression was only detected in ARMS samples, the effect of crizotinib, an ATP competitive, MET and ALK inhibitor, was evaluated on the growth of RH4 and RH30 ARMS cell lines. Cells were exposed for 72 h to increasing concentrations of the drug, with values ranging from 0 to 5 μM. Cell growth and viability were clearly inhibited in a dose-dependent manner, with IC50 values of about 1.5 μM (Fig. 2a), which are within the range of clinical relevance [25]. Direct counting for living cells using the trypan blue dye exclusion test confirmed that crizotinib induced a significant reduction in cell number (Fig. 2b).

Indeed, cell lines expressing the highest levels of FGFR4 (above a relative level of six) were the most sensitive to ponatinib (Figure 1C, p = 0.0344). These results, therefore, suggest that increased expression of FGFR4 confers sensitivity to ponatinib. - Given our findings, we believe that targeting FGFR4 will be most effective in ERMS with high expression (due to amplification) or mutation of FGFR4 or in alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma (ARMS) where the PAX3/7-FOXO1 fusion gene found in ARMS directly increases expression of FGFR4. Future studies regarding this observation are being actively pursued using in vivo studies of human rhabdomyosarcoma cell lines.

Analysis of the antiproliferative effects of pharmacologic CDK4/6 inhibitors provided initial evidence of this notion, as lowest CDK4- expressing Rh28 cells showed the highest sensitivity to both LEE011 and PD0332991, while highest CDK4-expressing Rh30 cells exhibited the lowest sensitivity. Moreover, rescue of cell viability upon overexpression of CDK4 in Rh41 and Rh28 cells treated with LEE011 indicated that elevated CDK4 expression confers decreased sensitivity to CDK4/6 inhibition. Our in vivo results of robust LEE011 activity in Rh28-derived xenograft tumors compared to more modest, albeit statistically significant, antitumor effects in Rh30-derived xenografts further support this finding.

The angiosarcoma harbored amplifications of VEGFR2 (KDR) of 8 copies and VEGFR3 (FLT4) of 16 copies. The patient was initially treated with sorafenib, an inhibitor of VEGFR2, and developed progressive disease. The patient then received pazopanib, an inhibitor of VEGFR2 and VEGFR3 and experienced a potent antitumor response resulting in clinically stable disease for 6 months.

phenotypes: Spinal hemangioblastoma,Renal cell carcinoma,Adenocarcinoma of the colon
evidence_statement: A 74 year old man confirmed with the germline mutation (c.208G>A) presented with colorectal adenocarcinoma, spinal hemangioblastoma, and lesions in bilateral cerebellar hemispheres, suggesting cerebellar hemangioblastoma. After one month, he was also diagnosed with renal cell carcinoma. The patient's mother was diagnosed with a brain tumour of unconfirmed pathology. Both his brothers were confirmed with the mutation and presented with renal cell carcinoma. The patient's 44 year old son was confirmed with the mutation, but was asymptomatic. The paper found that early detection and appropriate intervention are crucial to optimize prognosis of VHL disease.

A 12 year old Japanese female confirmed with the germline VHL mutation (c.482G>A) presented with pheochromocytoma. It was found that neither of her parents harboured this variation, confirming that she had a de novo mutation. The paper concluded that weight loss could be indicative of pheochromocytoma.

A 24 year old woman was confirmed with a germline VHL mutation (c.499C>T). She was diagnosed with bilateral pheochromocytomas and a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour. Her aunt also had a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour, but was not confirmed with the variation. This paper investigated the effectiveness of Somatostatin Analog Therapy and found that it may delay the need for surgical intervention in patients with VHL-related pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours.

A 17 year old female confirmed with a germline VHL mutation (c.337C>T) presented with cerebellar and spinal hemangioblastomas. Six months later, she was diagnosed with retinal hemangioblastomas. After failing to attend follow-up appointments, the patient presented with several CNS and retinal hemangioblastomas. The patient's mother died of colon cancer at 36 years of age. Her maternal grandmother died of a brain tumour at 50 years of age and her aunt died of a brain tumour at 18 years of age. Her maternal grandfather died of colon cancer (age unknown). No one in her family was tested for the mutation. The case report found multiple drop-metastases like spinal lesions, which researchers believe are associated with hemangioblastoma.

Authors report the ALK inactivation in ALK-positive ALCL induces an increase in BCL2 levels, which could contribute to therapeutic failures of current ALK targeted therapies. Their data strongly suggest that the BCL2 protein, acting at the crossroads between different forms of cell death, is the key-stone of an escape mechanism in therapeutically-challenged ALK-positive ALCL. Therefore, BCL2 downregulation in combination with crizotinib treatment could significantly improve the clinical outcome in ALK-positive ALCL patients.

A phase II trial assessed if nilotinib demonstrated response in a subset of 42 melanoma patients (acral and mucosal subtypes) harboring KIT gene mutations and/or amplification. Overall, 25 (59.5%) had KIT mutations, 15 (35.7%) had KIT amplifications, and 2 (4.8%) patients had both mutations and amplifications. Of these 42 patients, 1 achieved complete response, 6 achieved partial response, and 17 achieved stable disease. Of the 7 responders 1 had KIT amplification and 6 had KIT mutations. Overall response rate was 16.7% (95%CI 5.4-28.0) and disease control rate was 57.1% (95%CI 42.1-72.1). The median duration of response was 34 weeks (range of 5-55 weeks).

JMML is characterized by hypersensitivity to granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF). CBL linker and RING finger mutants, such as Y371H, lead to enhanced GM-CSF signaling due to elevated kinase expression.

Three patients displayed variable developmental conditions with predisposition to JMML. All cases included a copy neutral loss of heterozygosity of the 11q23 chromosomal region, encompassing the CBL locus. A heterozygous germline CBL p.Y371H substitution was found in each of them and was inherited from the father in one patient.

Genetic alterations in pilocytic astrocytoma (PA) were evaluated. Whole-genome sequencing of normal (blood) and tumor samples (n=96) was performed along with corresponding RNA-Seq (n=73) and mate-pair (MP) sequencing (n=68). Several known events activating the MAPK pathway were identified with KIAA1549-BRAF fusion being the most frequent variants (70 of 96 cases, 73%). Importantly, all but one of the cerebellar PA harbored a BRAF fusion (47 of 48 samples, 98%) with this one exception having a KRAS alteration.

Genetic alterations in 96 patients with pilocytic astrocytoma (PA) were evaluated. In addition to KIAA1549-BRAF fusions, other BRAF mutations and fusions were identified. Known MAPK activating events including FM131B-BRAF fusion (n=1), BRAFV600E mutation (n=4), and BRAFins599T (n=1) were found. In addition, four new BRAF fusions— RNF130-BRAF fusion derived from t(5;7)(q35;34) chromosomal translocation (n=2) and single cases identified of CLCN6-BRAF, MKRN1-BRAF, and GNAI1-BRAF fusion, and one new BRAF alteration (p.R506_insVLR, n=1) were also recognized. Of note, the BRAF-insVLR mutant was shown in vitro to increase the MAPK pathway (ERK phosphorylation) as effectively as the BRAF-V600E mutant.
Genetic alterations in 96 patients with pilocytic astrocytoma (PA) were evaluated. Two new alterations with double KRAS mutations (p.[Glu63Lys]+[Arg73Met] and p.[Leu19Phe]+[Gln22Lys] ) were observed.

Genetic alterations in pilocytic astrocytoma (PA) were evaluated. Two new NTRK2 fusion events were identified in this study. These two NTRK2 fusion events, namely QKI-NTRK2 (2 of 96 samples) and NACC2-NTRK2 (1 of 96 samples), were both involved in the region encoding the kinase domain of NTRK2. Moreover, both 5’ partners contained regions encoding dimerization domains, suggesting that these fusion events could induce ligand-independent dimerization. Of note, mutations in NTRK2 and alterations in RAF and RAS were mutually exclusive.

Two new recurrent alterations within the kinase domain of FGFR1 in Pilocytic Astrocytoma (PA) were identified. The p.Asn546Lys variant (3 of 96 samples) had been shown in another study to increase kinase activity and transforming potential via altered autophosphorylation. The p.Lys656Glu (2 of 96 samples) was shown previously to have transformation capacity in vitro. Gene expression analysis further showed increased mRNA expression of FGF2 ligand (aka bFGF) in PA samples (n=118) compared with other astrocytic tumors (n=157) or normal tissues (n=362) (p<0.001 for each comparison, two-sided t-test). Of note, mutations in FGFR and alterations in RAF and RAS were mutually exclusive.

Genetic alterations in pilocytic astrocytoma (PA) were evaluated. Two alterations were found in the PTPN11 (aka SHP-2) gene, encoding a RAS-MAPK-related adaptor protein and phosphatase. Both alterations (p.Glu69Lys, p.Glu76Ala; 1 of 96 for each alteration). Notably, these alterations were found in FGFR1-mutant tumors; however, they did not affect FGFR1 mutant-induced phospho-ERK levels. Additionally, mRNA expression of PTPN11 was higher in PA (n=118) compared with other astrocytomas (n=157) or normal tissues (n=362) (p<0.001 for each comparison, two-sided t-test). Of note, mutations in PTPN11 and alterations in RAF and RAS were mutually exclusive.

Inactivating mutations in SMARCA4 underlie small cell carcinoma of the ovary, hypercalcemic type (SCCOHT). The authors show that loss of SMARCA4 leads to downregulation of Cyclin D1 and deficient cells (by RNAi) show to be highly sensitive to CDK4/6 inhibitors in SCCOHT cells, proficient of Rb/p16.

Preclinical evidence showing that SMARCA4 inactivation results in downregulation of Cyclin D1 in NSCLC cells and confers sensitivity of such to CDK4/6 inhibitors. SMARCA4 loss is synthetic letha with CDK4/6 inhibition.

Patients with completely resected colorectal adenocarcinoma (Stage II-III) were treated with fluorouracil and leucovorin +/- ironotecan. Of the 1,307 FFPE samples tested, V600E was observed in 31 Stage II samples (7.6%) and 72 Stage III samples (7.9%). V600E was prognostic for overall survival, but not for relapse-free survival, in patients with stages II and III combined, and in stage III alone. For all MSI low and stable tumors, BRAF V600E positive samples had a hazard ratio (HR) of 2.19 (95% CI, 1.43 to 3.37, P=0.00034). For all samples in the cohort (MSI-H and MSI-L) BRAF V600E positive samples had a 1.66 HR (95% CI, 1.15 to 2.40, P=0.0069). The authors note prognostic value for BRAF V600E, especially in non-MSI high tumors. The authors present this as a prognostic result for BRAF V600E in the patent population, but also note that the patient population was all given standard chemotherapy.

The CRYSTAL Phase III Trial evaluated efficacy of irinotecan, fluorouracil, and leucovorin (FOLFIRI) with or without Cetuximab for colorectal cancer patients who presented with unresectable metastatic disease. BRAF mutation status (V600E) was analyzed via LightMix BRAF V600E Kit. V600E mutations were detected in 60/999 tumor samples (6%), 59 of which were wild-type for KRAS. When comparing patients with wildtype KRAS (n=625), BRAF V600E tumors had worse outcomes relative to BRAF wildtype. For patients with BRAF V600E tumors (n=566), median overall survival (OS) was 25.1 months with cetuximab and 21.6 months without cetuximab. For patients with wildtype BRAF (n=59), median OS was 14.1 months with cetuximab and 10.3 months without cetuximab.

In the Medical Research Council (MRC) COIN trial, ISRCTN27286448, patients who presented with advanced colorectal cancer were randomly assigned to chemotherapy (oxaliplatin and fluoropyrimidine; arm A), or chemotherapy plus cetuximab (arm B). Median overall survival was found to differ by mutation, regardless of treatment. Median overall survival was 8.8 months (IQR 4.5-27) for patients with BRAF variants, 14.4 months (IQR 8.5-24.0) for patients with KRAS variants, and 20.1 months (IQR 11.5-31.7) for wildtype patients. BRAF mutations were found in 102/1291 samples (7.90%), and of these, 12 were D594G and 90 V600E.

A meta analysis was performed using data from 21 published studies (n = 9885 patients) to assess prognostic value of BRAF mutations in colorectal cancer. When evaluating 14 studies (n = 7778 patients), the odds ratio (OR) of a proximal lesion, which is associated with greater mortality in colon cancer, was increased for patients with BRAF mutations (OR 5.222, 95% CI 3.801–7.174, P < 0.001). When evaluating 4 studies (n = 1526 patients), the odds ratio of T4 tumors, which indicates tumor growth past bowel lining, was increased for patients with BRAF mutations (OR 1.761, 95% CI 1.164–2.663, P = 0.007). When evaluating 8 studies (n = 2786 patients), the odds ratio of poor tumor differentiation was increased in patients with BRAF mutations (OR 3.816, 95% CI 2.714–5.365, P < 0.001). These results support that BRAF mutations indicate poor prognosis for patients with colorectal cancer.

Eleven of 15 (73.3%) patients with intact Smad4 had a local dominant disease; 10 of 14 (71.4%) with Smad4 loss showed distant dominant progression (p=0.16). disease: Head And Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma
evidence_statement: In this retrospective study, the impact of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAID) on survival in PIK3CA-altered HNSCC patients (N=266) was assessed. 37 of 266 (14%) patients harbored a mutation, 29 of 266 (11%) had only amplification, and 9 patients had both. Among patients with a PIK3CA mutation or amplification, regular NSAID use was significantly associated with disease-specific (HR 0.23, p=0.0032) and overall survival (HR 0.31, p=0.0043). These findings were recreated in a panel of six patient-derived xenograft models, where treatment with NSAIDs (sulindac, Celecoxib or Aspirin) significantly reduced growth rates in PIK3CA mutant, but not wild-type models.

The aim of this Chinese study was to identify prognostic biomarkers for pediatric low-grade gliomas (PLGG). Approximately 300 patients were included. Using Sanger sequencing, mutations at TERT promoter (TERTp) regions were identified (C228T: 3/278; C250T: 4/278). The median age of patients with TERTp mutations was 15 years. There were 5 males and 2 females. Six patients had diffuse astrocytoma and one had pilocytic astrocytoma. Tumors were found in the midline of four patients, the hemisphere of two, and the cerebellum of one. Kaplan-Meier survival analysis showed that TERTp mutations were associated with shorter progression-free survival and overall survival [mt (n=6) vs wt (n=205); p<0.0001 for both OS and PFS]. However, the association of TERTp mutations with OS and PFS was no longer statistically significant after adjusting for age, grade, histology, tumor location, and extent of resection in multivariate analysis.

Using Sanger sequencing, H3F3A mutations in patients with pediatric low-grade gliomas (PLGGs) were identified (K27M: 13/280; G34R: 5/280). Kaplan-Meier survival analysis showed that H3F3A mutations were associated with shorter progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) [15 cases with H3F3A mutation (n=15) vs wt (n=197); p<0.0001 for both OS and PFS]. A further multivariate analysis indicated H3F3A mutation as an independent, unfavorable prognosis marker for both PFS [HR 2.76 (95% CI 1.10–6.94); p = 0.031] and OS [HR 3.96 (95% CI 1.36–11.53); p = 0.012].

Loss of ATRX was identified in 12 of 247 patients with PLGGs using immunohistochemistry. Survival analysis showed that ATRX loss was associated with adverse overall survival (p<0.0001) and progression-free survival (p=0.0002) [mt (n=10) vs wt (n=175)]. In a multivariate analysis taking into account age, grade, histology, tumour location, and extent of resection, ATRX was still an independent prognosticator of PFS [HR 3.85 (95% CI 1.27–11.65); p = 0.017], and OS [HR 3.53 (95% CI 1.02–12.24); p = 0.047].

Using Sanger sequencing, BRAFV600E mutations were identified in 21 of 285 patients with PLGGs (7.4%). This mutation was enriched in hemispheric tumors (p<0.007) and was associated with shorter progression-free survival (p=0.011) and overall survival (p=0.032) [mt (n=18) vs wt (n=166)].

CDKN2A deletion was identified in 24 of 273 patients with PLGGs using FISH analysis. An association between this alteration and BRAFV600E was detected (p=0.0001). Hemispheric tumors with CDKN2A deletion were associated with shorter progression-free survival (p=0.0073) but did not affect overall survival (p=0.5) [mt (n=10) vs wt (n=59)]. CDKN2A deletion remained an independent prognostic factor in multivariate analysis for PFS [HR 4.38 (95% CI 1.05–18.23); p = 0.043]. CDKN2A deletion was not a prognostic factor in midline or cerebellar tumors.

KIAA1549-BRAF fusion was identified in 87 of 272 patients with PLGGs using Fluorescence In situ hybridization (FISH) analysis. This mutation was strongly associated with a greater progression-free survival (p=0.0017) and overall survival (p=0.0029) [fusion-positive (n=64) vs fusion-negative (n=141)].

MYB amplification was detected in 28 of 263 patients with PLGGs using Fluorescence In situ hybridization (FISH) analysis. The amplification of MYB was strongly associated with greater progression-free survival (p=0.04) but did not affect overall survival (p=0.13) [amplified (n=19) vs not amplified (n=177)]. MYB amplification was not an independent prognostic factor in multivariate analysis.

In a study of 44 signet ring cell colorectal cancer cases, 25% were found to carry a KIT M541L mutation. The authors speculate that this relatively high frequency of KIT mutations (actionable in other cancer types) suggests that imatinib would be a good candidate genomic targeted therapy for this rare cancer subtype.

Cells transduced with ATF7IP-PDGFRB showed hyperphosphorylation of the AKT/MAPK pathway and IL-3 independent proliferation was MEK dependent in these cells. Importantly, cells transduced with ATF7IP-PDGFRB showed sensitivity to TKIs (imatinib, dasatinib, nilotinib, ponatinib, bafetinib, and rebastinib) in cell culture as evidenced by reduced cell number and, in the case of imatinib, reduced phosphorylation of key targets.

This preclinical study proposed to use a combination therapy of an MEK inhibitor (e.g. trametinib) and an mTOR inhibitor (e.g. everolimus) for the treatment of pediatric low-grade gliomas (PLGGs) with BRAF fusions to evade acquired resistance to MEK targeted therapy. The PI3K/Akt/mTOR pathway was identified as a resistance mechanism to MEKi treatment based on RNASeq and GSEA analysis. Using flank xenograft model, mice were injected with NIH3T3 cells expressing FAM131B-BRAF fusions and treated daily with trametinib, everolimus either alone or combined with each other (n=~10 for each treatment arm). Combination therapy (Trametinib 1mg/kg+ Everolimus 10mg/kg) resulted in better suppression in tumor growth than single-agent treatment.

Hawkins et al. (2011) retrospectively studied 70 consecutive patient with incompletely resected pediatric low-grade astrocytomas (PLGA). KIAA1549-BRAF fusion was identified in 60% of cases in this cohort. Multi-variant analysis suggested that KIAA1549-BRAF fusion was the most significant favorable prognosis factor in incompletely resected PLGA and was independent of location, pathology, and age. Five-year PFS of fusion positive and fusion negative patients were 61% +/- 8% and 18% +/- 8% (P=0.0004), respectively. These results suggested that KIAA1549-BRAF fusion confers a less aggressive clinical phenotype on PLGA and may explain their tendency to growth arrest.

This GWAS study identified a structural variant of FGFR1. Duplication of the tyrosine kinase domain (TKD) of FGFR1 was found in 11 of 149 patients (13/151 tumor samples, including 2 recurrent tumors, aged 1-17) with pediatric low-grade gliomas (PLGGs) and related low-grade glioneuronal tumors (LGGNTs). This alteration resulted in autophosphorylation of FGFR1 and subsequent activation of downstream PI3K and MAPK/ERK pathways. Also, transfection of Tp53-null astrocytes with TDK duplicated FGFR1 and implantation into the brains of nude mice results in high-grade astrocytic tumours with short latency and complete penetrance. Of note, this variant was present in 24% (8 of 34) of grade II diffuse cerebral gliomas.

Activated BRAF protein kinase mutations are characteristic of pediatric astrocytomas with KIAA1549-BRAF fusion commonly observed in low-grade astrocytomas. Sievert et al. (2013) generated BRAF fusion cell lines to characterize KIAA1549-BRAF fusion targeting by BRAF inhibitors. Cells expressing KIAA1549-BRAF fusions display resistance and an associated enhanced paradoxical activation in response to first-generation BRAF inhibitors, including PLX4720 and vemurafenib. In contrast, the KIAA1549-BRAF fusion appears to be responsive to second-generation selective BRAF inhibitors, such as PLX PB-3, that do not induce activation of wild-type BRAF.

evidence_statement: The manuscripts describes a small case series (6 patients) with the t(14;19)(q32;p13.1) involving the EPOR locus in 19p13.1 and the IGH locus in 14q32, which is predicted to result in EPOR overexpression. All patients received aggressive multiagent chemotherapy. . Four of six patients achieved an initial complete remission, but all relapsed. At the last follow-up, five of six patients had died of disease. The authors conclude that the t(14;19)(q32;p13.1) involving IGH and EPOR, is a rare, recurrent cytogenetic abnormality in B-ALL. It appears to occur more frequently in young adults (the median age for the patients described in this report was 39 years) and has a highly aggressive clinical course.

EPOR overexpression in B-ALL is associated with the Philadelphia-like subtype of the disease (although high EPOR expression can also be observed in B-ALL with t(12;21)-ETV6-RUNX1). In this study, EPOR-rearrangement was detected in 8.9% of Ph-like ALL cases. The authors describe four types of chromosomal rearrangements resulting in EPOR overexpression: 1)insertion of the EPOR locus distal to the immunoglobulin heavy chain (IGH) locus enhancer (most common), not detectable by karyotype analysis or FISH; 2) insertion of EPOR into the immunoglobulin kappa chain (IGK) locus, not detectable by karyotype or FISH; 3)a reciprocal t(14;19)(q32;p13) rearrangement of IGH to EPOR (detectable) ; 4) an intrachromosomal inversion of chromosome 19 that juxtaposes EPOR to the upstream region of LAIR1 (leukocyte-associated immunoglobulin-like receptor 1) at chromosome 19q13 (not detectable by karyotype). EPOR rearrangements truncate the C-terminus of EPOR leading to its increased stability and activity. The authors showed that the truncated EPOR was hypersensitive to EPOR stimulation. Expression of truncated EPOR in mouse B-cell progenitors induced ALL in vivo (in mice). Human leukemic cells with EPOR rearrangements were sensitive to JAK-STAT inhibitors (ruxolitinib and others) in model cell lines, engineered mouse leukemias and human xenografts (ex vivo and in vivo). A 15-year-old girl with B-cell precursor ALL was placed into the very high risk group after showing corticoid resistance on treatment day 8, and induction failure on day 35 (MRD >0.01). During this relapse, SNP microarray was performed on the diagnostic sample and identified amplification of 9q34 flanked by the NUP214 and ABL1 genes. Follow-up molecular studies confirmed a NUP214-ABL1 fusion gene. The patient was then started on dasatinib in combination with vincristine and dexamethasone. The patient achieved a second CR, and continued on dasatinib until her disease relapsed 2 months later.

Acute basophilic leukemia is a very rare subtype of acute myeloid leukemia. This study reports 4 cases of ABL with a t(X;6)(p11;q23) translocation occurring in male infants. Authors performed multiple in-depth FISH studies showing evidence of complex rearrangements resulting in der(X) carrying MYB-GATA1 fusion. Performed RACE to confirm presence of MYB-GATA1 fusion transcripts. Ectopic expression of MYB-GATA1 in mouse lineage-negative cells committed them to the granulocyte lineage and blocked at an early stage of differentiation. Cells also had increased colony replating capacity highlighting elevated proliferation. Fusion appears to be oncogenic and diagnostic of Acute Basophilic Leukemia.

EZH2 (enhancer of zeste homolog 2) is a critical enzymatic subunit of the polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2), which trimethylates histone H3 (H3K27) to mediate gene repression. Somatic mutations, overexpression and hyperactivation of EZH2 have been implicated in the pathogenesis of several forms of cancer. In particular, recurrent gain-of-function mutations targeting EZH2 Y641 occur most frequently in follicular lymphoma and aggressive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and are associated with H3K27me3 hyperactivation, which contributes to lymphoma pathogenesis. However, the post-translational mechanisms of EZH2 regulation are not completely understood. Here we show that EZH2 is a novel interactor and substrate of the SCF E3 ubiquitin ligase β-TrCP (FBXW1). β-TrCP ubiquitinates EZH2 and Jak2-mediated phosphorylation on Y641 directs β-TrCP-mediated EZH2 degradation. RNA interference-mediated silencing of β-TrCP or inhibition of Jak2 results in EZH2 stabilization with attendant increase in H3K27 trimethylation activity. Importantly, the EZH2(Y641) mutants recurrently implicated in lymphoma pathogenesis are unable to bind β-TrCP. Further, endogenous EZH2(Y641) mutants in lymphoma cells exhibit increased EZH2 stability and H3K27me3 hyperactivity. Our studies demonstrate that β-TrCP has an important role in controlling H3K27 trimethylation activity and lymphoma pathogenesis by targeting EZH2 for degradation.

evidence_statement: This study examined outcomes of 240 rectum cancer patients treated with total mesorectal excision therapy. Tumor samples were obtained at the time of surgery and genotyped for PIK3CA mutations in exons 10 and 21 (listed as exons 9 and 20 in the source, as it was common to exclude non-coding exon 1). PIK3CA mutations were identified in 19 cases (12 in exon 10 and 7 in exon 21). PIK3CA mutations were associated with a 3-fold increase in risk of recurrence of rectal tumors (5-year risk: 27.8% vs 9.4%, p = 0.008). Furthermore, patients with PIK3CA mutations experienced a shorter time to recurrence compared to those with WT PIK3CA (median: 7.9 vs 19.6 months, p = 0.07). Patients with concomitant PIK3CA and KRAS mutations had a similar local reoccurrence rate to patients with PIK3CA mutations only. In multivariate analysis, PIK3A mutation was an independent predictor for the development of local recurrences (HR: 3.4, P =0.017).

Multilevel analysis demonstrated a tight correlation between high reactive-oxygen exposure, chromosomal damage, high proliferation, and in parallel, a transition from multiclonal indolent primary PCa to monoclonal aggressive disease. The EphB2 gene has been implicated as a tumor suppressor gene somatically altered in both prostate cancer (PC) and colorectal cancer. A set of 341 single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) encompassing the EphB2 locus, including known and novel coding and noncoding variants, in 490 African American sporadic PC cases and 567 matched controls were genotyped. Single marker-based logistical regression analyses revealed seven EphB2 SNPs showing statistically significant association with prostate cancer risk . The most significant association was achieved for a novel synonymous coding SNP, TGen-624, (Odds Ratio (OR) = 0.22; 95% Confidence Interval (CI) 0.08–0.66, p = 1×10−5). Two other SNPs also showed significant associations toward a protective effect rs10465543 and rs12090415 (p = 1×10−4), OR = 0.49 and 0.7, respectively. Two additional SNPs revealed trends towards an increase in risk of prostate cancer, rs4612601 and rs4263970 (p = 0.001), OR = 1.35 and 1.31, respectively. Furthermore, haplotype analysis revealed low levels of linkage disequilibrium within the region, with two blocks being associated with prostate cancer risk among this population. These data suggest that genetic variation at the EphB2 locus may increase risk of sporadic PC among African American Men.

Authors found that RB1 carriers were more likely to have the non-wildtype CA genotype for rs1801270 than healthy controls (p=0.0117), and the chance of developing retinoblastoma increased 1.98 fold with the CA genotype compared to the wildtype CC genotype (OR: 1.98, 95% CI: 1.16-3.37).
