Researchers calculated Spearman rank correlation coefficients for each gene vs proliferation rate and platinum drug sensitivity in 14 ovarian cancer cell lines. STAT1 expression was found to be highly correlated with resistance to cisplatin and AMD473 (r=0.65 and 0.76, respectively). STAT1 transfection into drug sensitive ovarian cancer cells caused increased resistance to cisplatin and AMD473 in STAT1 expressing clones.

Study of FGFR1 inhibitor AZD4547 in NSCLC xenograft models. FGFR1-amplified models that overexpress FGFR1 (detected by IHC) were strongly inhibited by 25mg/kg AZH4547 (P≤0.0001). Another FGFR1-amplified model that had low FGFR1 protein expression was not inhibited as strongly by AZH4547 (P=0.01). A model with normal FGFR1 copy number on undetectable expression was minimally inhibited (P=0.25).

Xenograft models of SNU-16 human gastric cancer cell lines with FGFR2 amplifications were treated with JNJ-42756493 (erdafitinib). A dose dependent reduction in tumor volume was observed with treatment of 10 and 30 mg/kg causing TGI of 37.8% and 59.4%, respectively.

JNJ-42756493 (erdafitinib) inhibitory effect was tested across a broad panel of lung cancer cell lines. Increased inhibit was associated with FGFR1 amplification. However, not all FGFR1-amplified cell lines were sensitive to JNJ-42756493. It was found that many cell lines not sensitive to JNJ-42756493 had an oncogenic mutation in the EGFR/KRAS pathway.

Patients with breast cancer had their tumor samples analyzed by Foundation Medicine in order to determine an appropriate clinical trial with targeted therapy or retrospectively to correlate with response to therapy. One patient had a FGFR3 amplification and was treated with pazopanib; no response to therapy was observed.
Treatment with bazedoxifene inhibited cell colony formation in rhabdomyosarcoma cell lines RH30 and RD. Addition of excess IL6 reduced the inhibitory effect of bazedoxifene on colony formation.

A patient derived Ph-like B-ALL Xenograft (V) harboring the JAK1 S646F mutation was treated with ruxolitinib. Compared to vehicle, the ruxolitinib treated Xenograft had lower peripheral and splenic blast counts (P<0.05). Additionally, pJAK levels were found to be lower in the ruxolitinib treated mice.

Mouse xenograft models using NIH3T3 cells stably expressing MET H1112L were established to test the efficiency of the MET inhibitor EMD1214063 (Tepotinib). The MET H1112L xenograft tumours showed complete regression after only five days of treatment with 50mg/kg/d EMD1214063. MET H1112L expressing cells also showed strong sensitivity to EMD1214063 in terms of pMET and pERK reduction, cell-cycle arrest, and reduction of anchorage-independent growth.
Vandetanib in Combination With Metformin is tested in Phase II trial in People With HLRCC or SDH-Associated Kidney Cancer or Sporadic Papillary Renal Cell Carcinoma

disease: Small-cell Carcinoma Of The Ovary Of Hypercalcemic Type
evidence_statement: IHC analysis of tissue microarrays or slides demonstrated loss of SMARCA4 expression in 42/46 (91%) SCCOHT primary tumors, 2/2 SCCOHT (100%) patient-derived xenografts, and 2/2 (100%) SCCOHT derived cell lines. SMARCA4 expression was only lost in 15/2324 (.65%) primary ovarian, epithelial, sex cord-stromal, and germ cell tumors. All tumor types in the same histological differential diagnosis group of SCCOHT retained SMARC4 expression. Additionally, only 3/630 (.48%) primary uterine tumors displayed no SMARC4 expression. SMACRA4 expression was retained in 44 extra-ovarian, non-gynecological tumors that histologically resemble SCCOHT. Overall, specificity of 99% for SMARCA4 loss in SCCOHT tumors was observed. Of the 45 SCCOHT tumors, 43 lacked SMARCA4 expression and 2 lacked SMARCB1 expression (both members of the SWI/SNF complex). Notably, 45/45 of the SCCOHT primary tumors also displayed loss of SMARCA2 expression.

Siblings (brother and sister) each were diagnosed with multiple primary lung cancer at the age of 60, along with various other cancers in their lifetimes. Homozygosity mapping revealed their parents (who also had cancer) had a consanguineous union. Each sibling was homozygous for CHEK2 R474C. The brother also had a son who died of neuroblastoma at 22 months of age. Amino acid R474 is highly conserved (98%) and forms a salt bridge in both the inactive and active CHEK2 homodimer. Modeling reveals R474C likely negatively affects the saltbridge and destabilizes the protein. Calcium phosphate DNA precipitation to overexpress CHEK2 WT or R474C in NIH3T3 cells revealed limited expression of R474C and limited activation through phosphorylation after UV exposure compared to the WT CHEK2 controls. ACMG codes as follows: Mutation in critical and well established functional domain (saltbridge) (PM1). Absent from control databases (ESP, dnSNP) except 1000 genomes with 1/2503 cases (.02%)(PM2). Predicted deleterious/damaging by multiple (4; SIFT, PolyPhen, MutationTaster2, Align GCGD) in silico algorithms (PP3).

This study showed that patients with TP53 mutated medulloblastoma (8/49, 16%) exhibited worse prognosis compared to those with wildtype medulloblastoma (41/49, 84%). A 5-year overall survival of 0% was reported in mutated medulloblasoma, compared to 74% (± 8%) in non-mutated disease (p < 0.0001). Multivariate analysis supported mutated TP53 as an adverse prognosis biomarker (hazard ratio = 9.5; 95% CI, 2.1 to 43; P=0.003).

This study examined the prognostic implication of TP53 mutation status in different molecular subgroups of medulloblastoma. A discovery cohort of 397 patients and a validation cohort of 156 cases were included. In the discovery cohort, 5-year overall survival rates for patients with SHH pathway medulloblastomas with wild-type (105 of 133) and mutated TP53 (28 of 133) tumors were 81% ± 5% vs. 41% ± 9% (OS ± SE), respectively (p < 0.001). In contrast, 5-year overall survival is not significantly different in WNT medulloblastomas with (7 of 35) and without TP53 (28 of 35) mutations (mutations: 90% ± 9% vs. wild-type: 97% ± 3% (OS ± SE), p = 0.21). Similar results were observed in the validation cohort. Multivariate analysis revealed that TP53 mutations correlate with poor survival in SHH medulloblastomas (HR = 4.39%; 95% CI, 1.7 to 11.29; p < 0.002) but have no implication in WNT subgroup.

A series of 72 pediatric medulloblastomas were evaluated for CTNNB1 mutations (by direct sequencing), copy number alterations (by array-comparative genomic hybridization), and beta-catenin protein expression (by immunohistochemistry). CTNNB1 mutations were detected in all six cases with extensive (>50% of the tumor cells) nuclear staining of beta-catenin. Remarkably, five out of these six tumors demonstrated a loss of chromosome 6, a cytogenetic event that is absent in CTNNB1-wildtype tumors (p <0.0001, Fisher’s exact test).

In a study of 109 pediatric medulloblastomas, children with medulloblastomas that showed a nucleopositive beta-catenin immunophenotype (27 of 109; 25%) had significantly better overall (OS) and event-free (EFS) survivals than children with tumors that showed either membranous/cytoplasmic beta-catenin immunoreactivity or no immunoreactivity. For beta-catenin nucleopositive and nucleonegative medulloblastomas, 5-year OS was 92.3% (95% CI, 82% to 100%) versus 65.3% (95% CI, 54.8 to 75.7%), and 5-year EFS was 88.9% (95% CI, 77% to 100%) versus 59.5% (95% CI, 48.8 to 70.2%), respectively. Mutations in CTNNB1 were found exclusively among medulloblastomas that demonstrated nuclear beta-catenin immunoreactivity.

A total of 51 medulloblastomas from two independent cohorts (19 and 32 cases) were assessed for evidence of Wnt/Wg pathway activation, alongside a genome-wide analysis of associated copy-number aberrations. Cases displaying evidence of Wnt/Wg activation (CTNNB1 mutation and/or beta-catenin nuclear stabilization) were exclusively associated with a distinct genomic signature involving loss of an entire copy of chromosome 6 but few other aberrations. Loss of chromosome 6 was exclusively observed in Wnt/Wg-activated medulloblastoma, as evidenced by 3 of 3 cases with nuclear immune-positivity for b-catenin in the first cohort (19 cases). In the second cohort (32 cases), loss of chromosome 6 is observed in Wnt/Wg-active tumors and absence in Wnt/Wg-negative cases (8/13 vs. 0/19; p=0.0001).

Patients with mutations at TERT promoter region of -124 and -146 of ATG showed poor survival in the absence but not in the presence of the variant allele of a common polymorphism with ID of rs2853669 located within 120 - 140 bp of the mutation sites. The mutations in the absence of the variant allele were highly associated with the disease recurrence in patients with Tis, Ta, and T1 tumors.
ARQ 087 exhibited inhibitory effects biochemically, in cell line and cell cycle study of FGFR2 functions.

Four of six heavily pretreated, high-risk CLL patients with a 17p deletion from the phase 2 trial M13-9824 with continuous venetoclax treatment, who were treated with venetoclax for a period longer than 3 years, developed progressive CLL. Targeted sequencing found G101V in refractory CLL tissues in 3 out of 4 of the patients, but not in sequencing performed before venetoclax treatment. Indepth sequencing performed on one of the patients showed the variant allele fraction of G101V increasing from 9% to 16% during disease progression. Sequencing of 546 venetoclax-naive CLL patients was reported, and none had BCL2 G101V. The variant was also not observed in four patients who relapsed after time-limited venetoclax therapy. The authors suggest that time-restricted venetoclax treatment in combination with a second drug may lower risk of developing resistance variants.

A familial platelet disease with propensity to acute myeloid leukemia (FPD/AML) pedigree (A) of 2 generations with 6 individuals was evaluated by sequencing as more than 1 first degree relative had MDS or AML. Exons 1, 3-6, 7b, and 8 of RUNX1 were sequenced in 4/6 members and revealed all 4 subjects in the second generation harbored a frameshift and ultimate truncating mutation within the transactivation domain of RUNX1. Of these four individuals ii1 had thrombocytopenia, ii2 had MDS at age 37, ii3 had thrombocytopenia, and ii4 had childhood ALL. No samples were available for sequencing from the first generation where the father was unaffected and the mother had thrombocytopenia and MDS followed by AML. ACMG codes: Protein length decrease (PM4)

A familial platelet disease with propensity to acute myeloid leukemia (FPD/AML) pedigree (B) of 4 generations with 15 individuals was evaluated by sequencing as more than 1 first degree relative had MDS or AML. Exons 1, 3-6, 7b, and 8 of RUNX1 were sequenced in 3/15 members and revealed all 3 subjects harbored a frameshift and ultimate truncating mutation within the RUNT domain. Overall 10/15 subjects presented with thrombocytopenia. Two of the sequenced subjects (ii5 and iii4) had AML. No samples were available for sequencing from the 5 unaffected indivuals or the other 2 subjects with AML. ACMG codes: Protein length decrease (PM4)

A familial platelet disease with propensity to acute myeloid leukemia (FPD/AML) pedigree (C) of 3 generations with 7 individuals was evaluated by sequencing as more than 1 first degree relative had MDS or AML. Exons 1, 3-6, 7b, and 8 of RUNX1 were sequenced in 5/7 members and revealed all 4 subjects with at least thrombocytopenia harbored RUNX1 D96H, which occurs prior to the RUNT domain. Both second generation subjects had MDS. The unaffected first-generation female (mother) did not harbor D96H. No sample was sequenced from the first generation father, though he had AML. ACMG codes: Cosegregation of disease in multiple family members (PP1)

Exons 1, 3-6, 7b, and 8 of RUNX1 were sequenced in 1/7 members and revealed a RUNX1 K90fsX101 in the RUNT domain. The sequenced subject (ii1) had thrombocytopenia, her mother (i2) had thrombocytopenia and MDS, her uncle (i3) had AML, and her cousin (ii3) had thrombocytopenia and MDS followed by AML. No samples were available for sequencing from unaffected subjects. ACMG codes: Protein length decrease (PM4)

A familial platelet disease with propensity to acute myeloid leukemia (FPD/AML) pedigree (E) of 2 generations with 5 individuals was evaluated by sequencing as more than 1 first degree relative had MDS or AML. Exons 1, 3-6, 7b, and 8 of RUNX1 were sequenced in 3/5 members and revealed RUNX1 R292X in the first generation proband with thrombocytopenia and MDS. In the second generation, the mutation was not seen in either offspring, but one child (ii2) had childhood AML and received a HSC transplant from the other child (i1). The authors theorize ii2 is negative for R292X because the tissues tested (peripheral blood and saliva) were of ii1 origin. ACMG codes: Protein length decrease (PM4)

In a trial of 68 glioblastoma patients treated with either temozolomide or semustine, 24 patients were found to have TP53 mutations at codons 175, 248, or 273. Patients with TP53 mutation were found to have worse overall survival than those with wild-type TP53 (p=0.001).

In a trial of 68 glioblastoma patients treated with either temozolomide or semustine, MGMT expression was found to be inversely correlated with survival. Patients in the MGMT high expression group (n=25) had significantly worse OS (p=0.001) than those in the MGMT low group (n=43). In addition, Cox proportional hazards regression models showed that MGMT expression had a hazard ratio of 2.194 (p=0.004).

In a trial of 68 glioblastoma patients treated with either temozolomide or semustine, 24 patients were found to have TP53 mutations at codons 175, 248, or 273. Kaplan-Meier analysis of the 35 patients treated with temozolomide showed that those with TP53 mutation (n=12) had worse overall survival than those with wild-type TP53 (n=23) (p=0.006), suggesting TP53 mutation induces resistance to temozolomide.

The glioblastoma T98G cell line possesses a TP53 M237I variant. This cell line initially exhibited resistance to temozolomide treatment, but a five-fold increase in chemosensitivity (IC50 112.15 ug/ml vs. 575.32 ug/ml) was seen following siRNA knockdown of mutant TP53. In addition, knockdown of mutant TP53 was associated with a drastic decrease in MGMT expression, suggesting that the mechanism of chemoresistance is through mutant TP53 induced MGMT expression.

The glioblastoma U138 cell line possesses a TP53 R273H variant. This cell line initially exhibited resistance to temozolomide treatment, but a four-fold increase in chemosensitivity (IC50 127.79 ug/ml vs. 510.79 ug/ml) was seen following siRNA knockdown of mutant TP53. In addition, knockdown of mutant TP53 was associated with a drastic decrease in MGMT expression, suggesting that the mechanism of chemoresistance is through mutant TP53 induced MGMT expression.

Both RT-PCR and PCR were used to detect and confirm the presence of fusion transcripts in RNA extracted from the surgical resections of 74 liposarcomas and 98 lipomas. FUS-DDIT3 (TLS-CHOP) was found in 22/74 (30%) liposarcomas, but not detected in any of the 98 noncancerous lipomas. Within the liposarcomas FUS-DDIT3 was found in 1/12 (8%) well-differentiated, 1/4 (25%) de-differentiated, 1/17 (6%) unclassified, and 19/41 (46%) myxoid subtypes. The results demonstrate the specificity of FUS-DDIT3 fusions to liposarcomas.

Both RT-PCR and PCR were used to detect and confirm the presence of fusion transcripts in RNA extracted from the surgical resections of 74 liposarcomas and 98 lipomas. EWSR1-DDIT3 (EWS-CHOP) was found in 3/74 (4%) liposarcomas, but not detected in any of the 98 noncancerous lipomas. Within the liposarcomas FUS-DDIT3 was found in 0/12 well-differentiated, 1/4 (25%) de-differentiated, 0/17 unclassified, and 2/41 (2%) myxoid subtypes. The results demonstrate the specificity of EWRS1-DDIT3 fusions to liposarcomas.

Both RT-PCR and PCR were used to detect and confirm the presence of fusion transcripts in RNA extracted from the surgical resections of 74 liposarcomas and 98 lipomas. LPP-HMGA2 or HMGA2-LPP fusions were found in 22/98 (22.4%) lipomas, but not detected in any liposarcoma. The results demonstrate the specificity of HMGA2-LPP and LPP-HMGA2-LPP fusions to lipomas.

A total of thirteen studies including 2857 patients were combined in a meta-analysis. Combined HRs suggested that CDKN2A/B deletions were poor prognostic factors for both overall survival (OS) (HR = 2.15, 95% CI 1.82-2.54) and event-free survival (EFS)/disease-free survival (DFS)/relapse-free survival (RFS) (HR = 2.16, 95% CI 1.73-2.69).

Phase 2 trial of adult hepatocellular patients treated with sunitinib analyzed how baseline concentration of different soluble VEGF proteins predict overall survival (OS) and time to progression (TTP). Only in VEGF-C did baseline higher concentration predict greater TTP (P=0.0096) and OS (P=0.0165). Baseline VEGF-C was also the strongest predictor of disease control (PR or SD > 12 weeks) versus PD, with an accuracy of 0.82 and relative risk of 4.71 (P = 0.0012).

A high-throughput screen of 637 cancer cell lines revealed 2 to be sensitive to the multiple tyrosine kinase inhibitor, sunitinib. The most highly sensitive line was A-204, a rhabdomyosarcoma cell line. A-204 was then compared to a panel of 6 other rhabdomyosarcoma cell lines and was the only one of the 7 with detectable PDGFRA protein (Western) and to demonstrate sensitivity to sunitinib. In A-204, no PDGFRA gene amplification was detected by FISH, but qPCR revealed a an increased PDGFRA mRNA expression. Reduction of PDFGRA expression by shRNA decreased cell number similarly to sunitinib treatment. Additionally, targeting the PDGFRA ligand, PDGFC, with shRNA or antibody decreased cell number similarly to sunitinib treatment.

Cell line NCI-H1703 is PDGFRA amplified and KIT wild-type. NCI-H1703 was treated with a PDGFRA inhibitor, imatinib or sunitinib. The IC50 of imatinib or sunitinib was lower in PDGFRA amplified NCI-H1703 when compared to a non-amplified squamous cell carcinoma cell line, HCC15.

A 47-year-old man was diagnosed with pre-B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia. FISH and nested PCR revealed the patient had a t(4;22)(q12;11) translocation that created an in-frame BCR-PDGFRA fusion. The constitutively activating coiled-coil domain and serine/threonine kinase encoded by BCR exon 1 fused with exon 13 of PDGFRA, which retained both tyrosine kinase domains. During initial therapy, intensification, and consolidation, hyperleukocytosis persisted. Based on the presence of the BCR-PDGFRA fusion, single agent imatinib (Glivec) was administered. A complete hematological response was observed within 6 weeks as the presence of t(4;22) in the bone marrow went from a 70% down to 15%. However, the patient had a relapse in the central nervous system. Continued treatment with imatinib along with intrathecal chemotherapy achieved a meningeal remission after 2 weeks. According to the authors, this patient’s response implicates PDGFRA as a clinically actionable imatinib target.

A 37-year-old man presented with dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans (DFSP). Post resection, multiple nodular metastases were found in both lungs and the disease progressed following treatments with cytotoxic agents and microwave ablation. Overexpression of PDGFRB was detected by IHC and a COL1A1-PDGFB fusion was detected by RT-PCR. Increased PDGFRB is activated by the COL1A1-PDGFB fusion product, which promotes the overactivation of downstream PDGFRB signaling pathways. Imatinib treatment failed as stable disease was followed by disease spread and progression. The patient was then treated with a daily oral dose of sunitinib (a multi-tyrosine kinase inhibitor) for 4 consecutive weeks, followed by a 2-week rest period. After 2 months on sunitinib, the patient experienced overall shrinkage of the body’s tumor mass (reduction of tumor in arm and partial response in lung and pancreas metastases). Sunitinib resulted in 9 months of progression free survival and improved quality of life. Ultimately, the disease progressed and the patient died 46 months after diagnosis.

Case report of a 61-year-old man with B-ALL. An initial analysis detected the ETV6-NTRK3 fusion and a NRASGly12Asp mutation. Initial therapies included chemotherapy and CAR-T infusion. Relapse 6 weeks after initial complete response to these therapies found a large increase in fusion transcripts and NTRK3 rearrangements were detectable by FISH in 50/50 blast nuclei whereas NRAS mutations were no longer detectable. The patient was treated with oral monotherapy larotrectinib (100mg twice per day). After 4 days on treatment peripheral blood blasts became undetectable; after 6 days on treatment lymphadenopathy and leukemia cutis resolved and a biopsy revealed an ablated bone marrow with only a few scattered blasts. The patient experienced clinical benefit with no apparent side effects during 42 days of larotrectinib treatment, however, patient eventually succumbed to multifocal angioinvasive aspergillosis because of insufficient recovery of normal hematopoiesis. Later sequencing of the NTRK3 kinase domain did not detect any larotrectinib resistance mutations (p.G623R, p.G696A).

Two AML cell lines, IMS-M2 and M0-91, with the ETV6-NTRK3 fusion were treated with entrectinib. Sequencing of these cell lines found no other driver mutations in 265 other cancer genes suggesting the ETV6-NTRK3 fusion is the oncogenic driver. The IC50 for the IMS-M2 and M0-91 cell lines was 0.47 and 0.65 nmol/L, respectively. Mouse xenografts treated with entrectinib at 10 or 30 mg/kg had complete remission while treatment with 3 mg/kg caused significant reduction in tumor growth. Testing of the bone marrow of IMS-M2 xenografts after 3 weeks of treatment found no human CD45-positive cells in the 3, 10, and 30 mg/kg treatment groups; all vehicle treated mice had some human CD45-positive cells in their bone marrow. Zebrafish xenotransplantation of M0-91 cells were sensitive to entrectinib treatment.

In B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma (B-ALL), the presence of this fusion is associated with so-called BCR/ABL1 like (Ph-like) subtype of the disease. The SMU1-JAK2 fusion is rare; in this study involving 798 B-ALL patients of which 194 had clinical characteristics of Ph-like ALL, only one case with the SMU1-JAK2 fusion was observed. SMU1 was detected as a novel JAK2 partner in Ph-like B-ALL. There is pre-clinical and case-study evidence that the presence of JAK2 fusions in B-ALL predicts sensitivity to JAK2 inhibitors; clinical trials are ongoing to evaluate efficacy of adding JAK2 inhibitors to treatment of Ph-like B-ALL cases with JAK2 fusions (Clinicaltrials.gov Identifier: NCT02723994).

To identify potentially druggable kinase fusions, this study of 278 B-ALL patients (all BCR-ABL1 negative), 34 (12.2%) harbored an IKZF1 deletion as determined by MLPA. Sufficient RNA from 16/34 of these IKZF1 deleted patients underwent mRNA sequencing and detected fusions were validated with RT-PCR and Sanger. Seven patients with clinical characteristics of Ph-like ALL were confirmed to harbor kinase fusions. The novel in-frame OFD1-JAK2 fusion (Exon 22 to Exon 13) was detected in an 11-year-old boy with hyperleukocytosis (185.8e9/l), no response to prednisolone therapy, and classified as NCI high risk. The authors hypothesize this fusion could constitutively activate the JAK-STAT pathway.

High expression of miR-21 was shown to be associated with worse OS (p<0.001) and PFS (p<0.001) in a Kaplan-Meier analysis of TCGA glioma dataset (n=641). Multivariate Cox regression analysis also showed that miR-21 overexpression was a potential independent prognostic biomarker of worse OS (HR 1.27, 95% CI 1.01-1.59, p=0.042) and PFS (HR 1.46, 95% CI 1.17-1.82, p<0.001).

The expression of a set of miRNAs was evaluated by qRT-PCR in 124 astrocytoma (grade I-IV) samples and 60 adjacent normal tissue samples in order to determine miRNAs with altered expression in astrocytomas. miR21 was found to be up-regulated by a factor of 2.33 in tumour relative to normal tissue. High miR21 expression was shown to be associated with worse prognosis in Kaplan-Meier survival analysis (p=0.029), and this result was even more pronounced when considering only grade III/IV astrocytoma patients (p<0.001). Elevated miR21 expression was also found to be associated with susrvival in a univariate (HR 1.84, 95% CI 1.051–3.222, p=0.033) and multivariate (HR 1.882, 95% CI 1.07–3.308, p=0.028) Cox proportional hazard regression analysis.

Prior to dasatinib treatment, one imatinib-resistant patients with chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) in myeloid blast crisis had the BCR-ABL1 fusion with F359V, F359V/Q252R, and L273M secondary variants in 9/12, 1/12, and 2/12 clones, respectively. Clones were generated using peripheral blood RNA. The patient had complete best cytogenetic and no evidence of leukemia best hematologic responses to dasatinib which were better outcomes in comparison to those seen in patients with unmutated BCR-ABL in this phase.

IL33 expression was assessed by qRT-PCR, IHC, and western blot in 86 glioma (grade I-IV) tissue samples and 16 normal controls. IL33 expression was consistently shown to be elevated in glioma tissues relative to normal control brain tissue, and levels were significantly higher in high-grade than low-grade glioma. Kaplan-Meier survival analysis showed that high IL33 expression was associated with worse OS (p<0.001) and PFS (p<0.001) in high grade gliomas. In addition, IL33 overexpression was an independent predictive factor of worse OS (univariate HR 6.443, 95% CI 3.665–11.327, p<0.0001; multivariate HR 5.319, 95% CI 2.849–9.931, p<0.0001) and PFS (univariate HR 13.003, 95% CI 6.209–27.229 p<0.0001; multivariate HR 5.319, 95% CI 2.849–9.931, p<0.0001).

Expression of WDR12 was found to be significantly higher in tumour than normal tissue from TCGA LGG and GBM datasets. Kaplan-Meier analysis showed high WDR12 expression to be significantly associated with shorter OS (p=9.5e-09) and disease-free survival (p=0.0014). In addition, knock-down of WDR12 with shRNA in GBM cells showed increased apoptosis, reduced cellular proliferation, and reduced tumour growth when implanted in mice.
Kaplan-Meier analysis of PLK1 gene expression showed that elevated expression is significantly associated with shorter disease-free survival in GBM (p=9.1e-11).
Kaplan-Meier analysis of EZH2 gene expression showed that elevated expression is significantly associated with shorter disease-free survival in GBM (p=1.3e-12).

Expression level of RRM1 was evaluated in 61 NSCLC samples with RT-qPCR. Low expression of RRM1 was associated with longer median survival time (13.9 versus 10.9 months, P = 0.039). However, RRM1 expression was not found to be an independent prognostic indicator by multivariate analysis (HR 3.25 , 95% CI 0.38–27.71, P=0.2287)

Expression level of ERCC1 was evaluated in 61 NSCLC samples with RT-qPCR. Kaplan-Meier analysis showed that low expression of ERCC1 was associated with longer median survival time (17.3 versus 10.9 months, log-rank 8.69, P = 0.0032). A multivariate regression analysis found ERCC1 expression to be an independent prognostic factor of survival (HR 3.43, 95% CI 1.71–6.86, P=0.0003)

In this retrospective circulating biomarker study, in two cohorts of osteosarcoma patients, the cytokine in blood samples was measured by Luminex assay. The cutoff values for cytokine was determined by the discovery cohort (n = 37) and was applied to the validation group (n = 233). The high level of CXCL10 was showed significant correlation with lower overall survival (HR = 1.94, P = 0.0007) and decreased event-free survival (HR = 1.77, P = 0.0013). Also, high level of FLT3LG showed a significant correlation with lower overall survival (HR = 1.75, P = 0.0046) and event-free survival (HR = 1.69, P = 0.0041). A multivariate model that combined CXCL10, FLT3LG expression with metastatic status was able to stratify the validation cohort to 4 risk groups: low risk, intermediate risk, high risk, and very high risk. The relative 5-year overall survival rates were 77%, 54%, 47%, and 10%, respectively, while the 5-year EFS rates were 64%, 47%, 27%, and 0%, respectively. This model had a greater prognostic significance compared to the metastatic status alone. (P =1.6 x 10^-8)

The expression of CTGF (CCN2) is significantly higher in TCGA LGG and GBM cohorts compared to non-tumour tissue (P<0.05). Levels of CTGF mRNA and protein were found to be higher in glioma than non-tumour tissue samples by RT-PCR and Western blot, respectively. The median OS of patients with high and low CTGF expression was 35.4 and 63.3 months in TCGA dataset (P=0.0012), and 26.97 and 55.1 months in the CGGA dataset (P=0.0059). In addition, knock-down of CTGF expression with siRNAs in two high-grade glioma cell lines resulted in suppressed cell invasion, proliferation, and migration.

Third generation EGFR inhibitor osimertinib can overcome the T790M resistance mutation on L858R or exon 19 del background. Drug screening of Ba/F3 cells expressing EGFR triple mutant (C797S/T790M/del19 or C797S/T790M/L858R) found brigatinib to be the most potent candidate. Addition of anti-EGFR antibody cetuximab or panitumumab with brigatinib resulted in a synergistic inhibitory effect. In vivo experiments showed that both drug combinations reduced tumour volume, inhibited downstream pathway activation, and improved survival in xenografts created from lung cancer cell lines. Similar synergistic effects were seen in vitro in Ba/F3 and lung cancer cells expressing EGFR triple mutants.

Meta-analysis of 275 T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia (T-PLL) patients from 10 different studies. Sequencing data from each study (Sanger sequencing, targeted amplicon sequencing, whole exome sequencing, whole genome sequencing) was collected. WES and WGS were reanalyzed and assessed for mutations in JAK/STAT genes (includes JAK1, JAK2, JAK3, TYK2, STAT1, STAT2, STAT3, STAT4, STAT5A, STAT5B, and STAT6). Germline mutations were filtered using matched tissue when available. Of patients with WES/WGS data, 62.1% (n = 54/87) carried at least one mutation in a JAK/STAT gene. When including Sanger and targeted amplicon sequencing, STAT5B was mutated in a hotspot region in 18.8% of cases (n = 38/202). When assessing overall survival (OS), no difference in OS was observed between T-PLL patients with or without a mutation in any JAK/STAT gene. But, a difference in OS was noted for patients with the STAT5B Y665F mutations (p = 0.06), however, only a limited group of patients carry this mutation (n = 5).

Novel BRAF gene fusion in Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis lesions results in constitutive ERK activation that is responsive to second-generation BRAF and MEK inhibitors, but not to a BRAF-V600E inhibitor.

Jens Neumann et al analyzed 1018 cases of metastatic colorectal cancer. They focused on KRAS mutation of codons 12 and 13. Direct genomic sequencing was applied to detect the KRAS mutation. After the investigation of all cases, they found that 60.7%(618) cases showed a wild-type sequence, and 39.3%(400) showed mutation in exon 2 codons 12 and 13 of the KRAS proto-oncogene. The most common mutation was glycine to aspartate on codon 12, that is variant G12D. This mutation accounts for 36% of mutated tumors, which is 144 out of 1018. The following most common mutations are glycine to valine on codon 12( pG12V, 21.8%), and glycine to aspartate on codon 13 (p.G13D, 18.8%).

The paper showed that PCNA (p.K164R) inhibits the ubiquitination of PCNA and the variant can render cells sensitive to DNA-damaging agents and reduce activation-induced single-nucleotide substitutions in the immunoglobulin light-chain locus. This may demonstrate the necessity of reducing PCNA-ubiquitin pathway for immunoglobulin hypermutation in neuroblastoma treatment.

Ghosh et al. provide compelling evidence that thyroid cancers with a BRAFV600E mutation are sensitive to combined PLX4720 and Ponatinib treatment. They predicted a synergistic effect using HTS of active drugs and validated this prediction both in vitro and in vivo. The treatment combination significantly inhibited the growth of BRAFV600E mutant cancer cell lines, as well as reduced tumor growth, decreased metastases, and increased survival in a thyroid cancer mouse model. The authors recommend that this combination be tested in clinical trials.

This clinical trial used a cohort of 32 pediatric low grade glioma (pLGG) patients. The primary endpoint of this study was objective response rate (ORR). In this study, an ORR of 44% and a 1-year progression free survival rate of 85% was reported. Approximately half of the patients had an ongoing treatment response at the end of the study, while only two had progressive disease. Although the study cohort was on the smaller side, this provides evidence that treatment BRAF V600-mutant pLGG patients with Dabrafenib could be beneficial. Being a clinical trial, the study was not well controlled.

Using mouse models, the authors demonstrated that Acvr1G328V arrested the differentiation of oligodendroglial lineage cells to generate high-grade diffuse gliomas. Using a cellular NanoBRET target engagement assay, they identified the binding between E6201 and ACVR1 with half maximal inhibitory concen- tration [IC50] ≈ 0.25 mM). Furthermore, in primary brainstem glial cells, they demonstrated that E6201 had a larger suppressive effect on BMP signaling pathway activation induced by mutant ACVR1 than by wild-type ACVR1. In addition, to obtain mechanistic insights into the inhibitory effect of E6201 on ACVR1, they solved the 1.5-A ̊ structure of ACVR1 in complex with its interacting partner E6201 by X-ray crystallography. And they showed that E6201 occupied the ATP-binding pocket of ACVR1 with a binding position similar to that in the equivalent MEK1 complex.

Based on the ability of a Brca2 construct with P655R to rescue the lethality of Brca2-deficient mES cells and its effects on sensitivity to DNA-damaging agents, homologous recombination and genomic integrity, the authors classified P655R as not pathogenic.

While evidence from multiple clinical studies establishing a strong association between loss of function mutations in APC and response to 5-fluorouracil is lacking, some studies suggest APC mutations may be associated with poor prognosis on 5-fluorouracil therapy. Evidence from a clinical study has shown that in colorectal cancer (CRC) patients treated with 5- fluorouracil, those with APC mutation positive tumors had a significantly increased risk for cancer related death (HR=6.9), compared to patients without APC mutations (HR=0.34). Preclinical studies have also shown that APC-mutant CRC cells display a limited response to 5-fluorouracil induced apoptosis, when compared to cells with wild-type APC.

The resistance to novel drugs targeting the G12C KRAS variant is caused by RAS pathway reactivation. Ryan et al showed that SHP2, which delivers signals from RTKs to RAS, is critical for RAS pathway activation. They showed in both a panel of cell lines and mouse xenograft models that combining the SHP2 inhibitors and KRAS inhibitors was able to block feedback reactivation. They suggested that this combination therapy is a promising candidate for future clinical trials.

Both in vitro and in vivo models in Kebebew et al. provide evidence that a combinatorial treatment of PLX4720 (a BRAF inhibitor) and ponatinib (a multi targeting tyrosine kinase inhibitor) shows potential efficacy for treatment of thyroid cancer harboring a BRAF V600E mutation. The authors use in vitro data to show that combinatorial therapy of PLX4720 + ponatinib causes less colony formation, increased apoptosis, and reduced MEK and ERK phosphorylation in thyroid cancer cell lines containing a BRAF V600E mutation when compared to the single agents alone and DMSO control as well as compared to WT BRAF thyroid cancer lines. The authors' in vivo model suggests that a combinatorial therapy reduces tumor burden of BRAF V600E thyroid cancer tumors without a significant loss of body weight. They also show that at 6 weeks of treatment, significantly more mice are surviving on the combinatorial treatment when compared to the single agents alone and the control. Lastly, the authors show that in a BRAF inhibitor resistant cell line model, they also find less colony formation capability, increased apoptosis, and reduced MEK and ERK phosphorylation with the combination therapy. Both the in vitro and in vivo data is convincing. However, the in vivo data would be more convincing if the authors had followed the progression of the mice past 6 weeks of treatment and if they had used a WT BRAF model as an additional control. The authors claim that PLX4720 and ponatinib ought to be considered for a clinical trial and their data seems to suggest a similar conclusion and thus validates this claim.

The authors demonstrated that in contrast to the K-RasG12D or K-RasG12V mouse models, mice that express the K-RasV14I mutation at postnatal stages, either in all cells or only in the lungs, did not develop tumours. Moreover, no other solid tumours were found when the K-RasV14I mutation was expressed from adult stages in all cells. These results suggest that K-RasV14I does not have enough oncogenic potential.

A healthy 12 year old with right neck mass was found to have heterogeneous solid mass originating from the right thyroid lobe. Total thyroidectomy confirmed papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) with multiple involved lymph nodes. Following radioactive iodine treatment and further resection after relapse, the patient was found to have multiple pulmonary nodules. Genome and transcriptome sequencing were performed on debulked tissue and archival sample revealing a fusion between TPM3 exon 8 and NTRK1 exon 9, which was validated by PCR. In addition, NTRK1 had extremely high expression relative to TCGA thyroid cancer samples and Illumina BodyMap normal thyroid tissue. The patient received larotrectinib on a phase I/II study (NCT02637687), showing improvement on CT scans after just two cycles of therapy, and remains on therapy after 10 months with almost complete resolution of pulmonary modules and excellent performance status.

These authors demonstrated that cyclin-dependent kinase 5 (CDK5) is instrumental in metastasis of melanomas and that inhibition of this kinase impairs melanoma metastasis. CDK5 phosphorylates the intermediate filament vimentin. A genetic knock out of CDK5 in a mouse model of melanoma inhibited metastatic spread. Further evidence is presented with similar effect, chemical inhibition of CDK5 in a mouse xenograft model impaired the metastatic spread of melanoma.

T315I is an unfavorable mutation in the BCR-ABL1translocation leading to Chronic Myeloid Leukemia. In this article, experts review and compile the literature regarding the use of Ponatinib (a tyrosine kinase inhibitor) in CML therapy. This review presents several studies and clinical trials, demonstrating an improved prognostic outcome for use of Ponatinib in T315I BCR-ABL1 CML.

UK Caucasians were enrolled in a large-scale GWAS study looking for loci associated with lung cancer susceptibility (1529 cases and 2707 controls). Of 64 nonsynonymous, single nucleotide polymorphisms identified as significant (adjusted P-value 0.01) through the set association procedure, rs2602141 (K1136Q) and rs560191 (D353E), map to the tumor protein p53 binding protein 1 (TP53BP1) and display strong linkage disequilibrium (LD).

Primarily based on the results from the phase III ExteNET clinical trial (Study 3004, NCT00878709), on July 17, 2017, the FDA approved neratinib (NERLYNX, HKI-272) for extended adjuvant therapy of adult early stage HER2 positive (overexpressed/amplified) Breast Cancer post adjuvant trastuzumab. Over a 2 year period, Neratinib treatment safely and significantly improved invasive disease free survival (iDFS) compared to the placebo group.

A phase III clinical trial (NALA, NCT01808573) with a randomized parallel design of 621 patients evaluated the combination therapy of Neratinib plus capecitabine (N+C) (307 pts.) vs. Lapatinib plus capecitabine (L+C) (314 pts.) as a treatment for adult stage IV HER2 positive metastatic breast cancer patients that had previously received 2 or more HER2-directed regimens. The co-primary end points were progression free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS). The N+C group demonstrated a 24% reduction in risk of disease progression or death versus the L+C group (Hazard ratio: .76; p=.006). Improvements in 6 / 12 month PFS (47.2 / 28.8% vs. 37.8 / 14.8%) and OS (90.2 / 72.5% vs. 87.5 / 66.7%) were observed in N+C compared to L+C, respectively. N+C also delayed intervention for symptomatic central nervous systems metastases.

evidence_statement: The initial 2 year follow-up of the Phase III clinical trial (exteNET, NCT00878709) where early stage HER2 positive breast cancer patients underwent adjuvant trastuzumab therapy and then either received Neratinib (NERLYNX, HKI-272) or a placebo for one year, demonstrated Neratinib significantly improved the primary endpoint of invasive disease free survival (iDFS) versus the placebo (stratified hazard ratio (HR): .67, 95% CI .5-.91, p=.0091). This 5 year follow-up showed the Neratinib group maintained significantly fewer iDFS events (116 vs. 163; HR .73, 95% CI .57-.92, p.=.0083) versus the placebo group. The iDFS rates were 90.2% in the Neratinib treated group and 87.7% for the placebo. A reduction in distant and local reoccurrences was observed in the Neratinib group. Neratinib was more effective in the subset of patients that started treatment within 1 year of completing adjuvant trastuzumab compared to those that began over 1 year post trastuzumab. Additionally, Neratinib led to improvement in 5 year iDFS in hormone receptor positive patients whereas iDFS improvements were not maintained after the completion of Neratinib in hormone receptor negative patients. Overall, 1 year of Neratinib therapy after adjuvant trastuzmab improved iDFS in patients without a significant risk of toxicity.

A Phase II clinical trial (NCT00741260 ) assessed the safety and efficacy of Neratinib plus capecitabine in the treatment of HER2 positive breast cancer patients. Of the 72 patients in this study, 65 were lapatinib naive and 7 had previously received lapatinib. All 72 patients had completed adjuvant trastuzumab therapy. The primary end point, objective response rate (ORR), was 64% (95% CI 51-76%) in lapatinib naive patients and 57% (95% CI 18-90%) in patients previously receiving lapatinib. Additionally, neratinib plus capecitabine treatment resulted in complete response (CR) in 12% of lapatinib naive patients and 14% of the lapatnib treated patients achieved CR. Median progression free survival (PFS) was 40 weeks in the no lapatinib group and 36 weeks in the prior-lapatinib group. These results were more favorable than a trial of neratinib monotherapy and a trial of lapatinib plus capecitabine. The authors concluded that combination therapy of neratinib and capecitabine was associated with acceptable tolerability and substantial clinical activity. A phase III trial (NALA) was initiated as a result of these findings.

Mutation of ARID2 in Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC) is often seen. There is about 6/16 of the truncated mutations found at the C2H2 domain (zinc finger) and about 16/24 mutations show that this domain has been mutated. Indicating the significance of C2H2 of ARID2 in Hepatocellular Carcinoma metastasis. In this study, they used cells derived from portal vein tumor tissues (PVTT) of patients and found that this mutation (R1273* (c.3817C>T), a truncated mutation of C2H2) is positively associated with the metastasis of this tumor. In this study, the authors created C3817T mutants from the ARID2 WT cells. Using molecular methods, they noticed that C3817T truncated mutant interfered with the interaction between ARID2 and DNMT1; and a weakened association of DNMT1 at the Snail promoter, leading to a decrease in the methylation on Snail by DNMT1. R1273* truncated mutant was found to show a decrease in the function of ARID2 to inhibit the migration and invasion of the HCC cells.

A 62 year old patient with 4 pack-year smoking history with back and flank pain was found to have metastatic lung adenocarcinoma by CT and MRI. Targeted NGS sequencing discovered an EGFR L858R mutation and the patient started 80mg osimertinib treatment with excellent response of all disease sites, including brain metastases. The patient had continued response until 8.5 months after treatment initiation when a new liver lesion was found. NGS sequencing of a repeat biopsy detected the original EGFR L858R mutation as well as L718V and L718Q mutations. Afatinib treatment led to a partial response for 4.5 months, at which time disease progression occurred. Biopsy of a progressing liver lesion showed acquired EGFR T790M mutation as well as increase and decrease of L718V and L718Q mutation frequencies, respectively.

This patient originally presented in the clinic with an ER+, PR-, and HER2- mass on the left breast and bone metastasis. Family history showed negative germline mutations in BRCA1/2. Patient responded well with original clinical and radiologicial response. The cancer metastasized to the liver and was identified to be HER2-, ER-, and PR- breast cancer metastasis by IHC (data not shown). Next generation sequencing identified HER2 L755S mutation (data not shown). This mutation is known to produce resistance to the drug lapatinib while being highly sensitive to neratinib. Patient was treated daily with neratinib for 11 months and had a partial response. Clinical worsening occurred and patient began treatment with neratinib and capecitabine and a similar partial response was observed as with neratinib alone treatment.

In vitro and in vivo studies that demonstrate that RAC1-P29S is capable of promoting cell survival and resistance to treatment, specifically BRAF inhibition. The authors expressed both a 4-hydroxytamoxifen activated RAC1-P29S and endogenous RAC1-P29S in an immortalized breast epithelial cell line. In both cases, there was no increased cell proliferation, but there was increased cell survival in absence of growth factors or anchorage (suppression of apoptosis). Activation of genes involved in epithelial mesenchymal transition (EMT) was also observed in both cases. Inhibition of the downstream effectors of these genes in presence of RAC1-P29S reversed the EMT phenotype. When RAC1-P29S was expressed in mice, melanoma formation was not observed. However, from genomic data analysis, the authors were able to find that RAC1-P29S usually co-occurs with driver mutations in BRAF, NRAS or NF1. RAC1-P29S was seen to have tumor-promoting effects in the context of a BRAF-V600E mutation and the authors reported these double mutant mice to always develop melanoma and have a higher number of tumors per mouse when compared to only BRAF-V600E mice. Moreover, treatment of the BRAF-V600E/RAC1-P29S mice with a BRAF inhibitor, the tumors were still able to grow, while those in the treated BRAF-V600E/WT-RAC1 mice were stable or regressed. Mouse melanoma cell cultures with RAC1-P29S treated with the inhibitor also showed less apoptosis than those with the WT-RAC1.

A genetically engineered mouse model of lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) was created expressing human EGFR L858R transgene. Mice were treated with either daily 5mg/kg, followed by 25mg/kg after tumour recurrence, or 25mg/kg only osimertinib 5 days/week and monitored by MRI for treatment-resistant tumours. Osimertinib-resistant tumours emerged after an average of 5.3 months and 7.8 months, respectively. In the two mouse cohorts EGFR L797S was found in 5/17 and 14/54 tumours, EGFR L718Q was in 0/17 and 7/54 tumours, EGFR L718V was found in 5/17 and 3/54 tumours, while the remaining 7 and 30 tumours had no secondary EGFR resistance mutations. Osimertinib treatment of 293T cells transiently transfected with C797S in combination with EGFR L858R cDNA showed reduced suppression of pEGFR relative to EGFR L858R, suggesting resistance to osimertinib. CRISPR/Cas9 was used to model subclonal population dynamics of L718V or L718Q mutations in three human LUAD cell lines, PC9 (EGFR Del19), PC9-VanR (EGFR Del19+T790M), and II-18 (EGFR L858R) in the presence or absence of osimertinib. Cell lines with L718V or L718Q showed increased proliferation in the presence of osimertinib relative to controls, and amplicon sequencing showed these mutations to be enriched in all cell lines.

In a panel of 14 cell lines representing multiple tumor types (endometrial, bladder, gastric, breast, lung, and colon) and containing FGFRs dysregulated by a variety of mechanisms, ponatinib inhibited FGFR-mediated signaling with IC(50) values <40 nmol/L and inhibited cell growth with GI(50) (concentration needed to reduce the growth of treated cells to half that of untreated cells) values of 7 to 181 nmol/L. Daily oral dosing of ponatinib (10-30 mg/kg) to mice reduced tumor growth and inhibited signaling in all three tumor models examined.

Among 32 colorectal cancer patients with acquired resistance (PFS > 12 weeks) to cetuximab, one was determined to have V955I mutation. evidence_statement: Performed Sanger sequencing and immunohistochemistry of SMARCA4 in 12 SCCOHT (Small cell carcinoma of the ovary, hypercalcemic type) tumors. When complementing this data with data previous data from other 12 tumors, found that 19 of the 24 tumors have mutations in SMARCA4 and that 16 of 19 stained tumors have lost SMARCA4 protein. Most of these mutations are truncating, frameshift, deletion and splice-site mutations. SMARCA4 is a tumor suppressor which is inactivated in most of the SCCOHT tumors.
Single strand conformation polymorphism and sequencing was used on human tumors to determine tumor NF2 genotype. This is a nonsense mutation.

Blood or tumor specimens of 37 unrelated adult patients with ependymomas related to neurofibromatosis Type 2 (NF2) underwent sequencing of the NF2 gene to reveal germline variants. Overall, 64% were found to harbor truncating mutations of NF2, which the authors conclude supports previous reports of truncating mutations in NF2 associate with more severe phenotypes. Three unrelated patients harbored NF2 R466* (c.1396C>T). It's unclear whether these three patients were symptomatic, but none of them underwent surgical resection of the ependymomas during the study period.

In preclinical analyses, treatment with AMG 510 led to the regression of KRASG12C tumours and improved the anti-tumour efficacy of chemotherapy and targeted agents. In immune-competent mice, treatment with AMG 510 resulted in a pro-inflammatory tumour microenvironment and produced durable cures alone as well as in combination with immune-checkpoint inhibitors. Cured mice rejected the growth of isogenic KRASG12D tumours, which suggests adaptive immunity against shared antigens. Furthermore, in clinical trials, AMG 510 demonstrated anti-tumour activity in the first dosing cohorts and represents a potentially transformative therapy for patients for whom effective treatments are lacking.

Preclinical models of osimertinib-resistant EGFR mutants were treated with erlotinib or afatinib. Treatment with erlotinib suppressed phosphorylation of EGFR L858R+C797S but did not decrease phosphorylation in the EGFR L858R+L718V mutant to the same extent as the EGFR L858R cell line. Mice with EGFR L858R osimertinib-resistant tumours were treated with erlotinib or afatinib. Of 16 osimertinib-resistant tumours that were also resistant to erlotinib, 3 had the L718V mutation. These tumours showed a brief transient response to erlotinib before becoming resistant.

Preclinical models of osimertinib-resistant EGFR mutants were treated with erlotinib or afatinib. Treatment with afatinib suppressed EGFR phosphorylation of L858R+C797S, and caused complete inhibition of phosphorylation of L858R+L718V and L858R+L718Q EGFR mutants. Mice with EGFR L858R osimertinib-resistant tumours were treated with erlotinib or afatinib. Of twelve osimertinib-resistant tumours that responded to afatinib treatment, 7 had the C797S mutation and 4 had the L718Q mutation. Comparison of growth rates before and after being switched to erlotinib or afatinib treatment showed that both C797S and L718Q mutant tumours had a negative growth rate when treated with afatinib, suggesting sensitivity.

A panel of HER2 positive breast cancer cell lines (n=12) displayed greater sensitivity to Neratinib (HKI-272) compared to triple negative breast cancer cell lines (n=15, p=.0002) and luminal breast cancer cell lines (n=9, p=.0055) based on IC50s generated from cell proliferation assays. As demonstrated by Western blot, Neratinib inhibited the activation of HER2 and downstream pathways in a dose dependent manner in the tested HER2 positive breast cancer cell lines. In the 11 neratinib-sensitive HER2 positive breast cancer cell lines, higher baselines levels of HER2 and pHER2 significantly correlated with increased neratinib response.

Two HER2 positive breast cancer cells lines were 480-times more sensitive to Neratinib (HKI-272) compared to a HER2 negative breast cancer cell line (MDA-MB-435) as indicated by decreased proliferation. Additionally, overexpressing HER2 in mouse fibroblast 3T3 cells resulted in sensitivity 230-fold below the parental unmodified 3T3 line after Neratinib treatment. Neratinib inhibited tumor growth in mouse xenografts from HER2 positive breast cancer cells (BT474), but had limited impact mouse xenografts from HER2 low breast cancer lines (MCF-7 & MX1). Neratinib irreversibly inhibited HER2 activation as demonstrated by pHER2 reduction and subsequent downstream inhibition of MAPK and AKT phosphorylation and led to cell cycle arrest . Overall, the data indicate neratinib negatively impacts growth through the direct inhibition of the HER2 kinase through irreversible covalent bonding, which subsequently blocks downstream pathway activation.

Treatment with erlotinib suppressed phosphorylation of EGFR L858R+C797S and to a lesser extent EGFR L858R+L718V, while the EGFR L858R+L718Q mutant was not inhibited. Mice with EGFR L858R osimertinib-resistant tumours were treated with erlotinib or afatinib. None of the osimertinib-resistant tumours sensitive to erlotinib had the L718Q mutation, while three of the resistant tumours possessed this mutation. Comparison of growth rates before and after being switched to erlotinib or afatinib treatment showed that L718Q mutant tumours grew rapidly when treated with erlotinib, suggesting resistance to this therapy. In addition, molecular dynamics suggest weaker binding of erlotinib due to L718 substitutions as a result of L718 being a direct contact in EGFR/erlotinib crystal structures.

Lentiviral-mediated overexpression of NT5C2 R238W (a relapse specific variant) in Reh cells resulted in resistance against thiopurines (mercaptopurine and thioguanine) compared to NT5C2 wildtype overexpression cells and empty vector control cells, as indicated by cytotoxicity assays. This result implies a gain-of-function mechanism of drug resistance.

A genetically engineered mouse model of lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) was created expressing human EGFR L858R+T790M transgene. Twenty of 49 mice treated with osimertinib developed treatment-resistant tumours at an average of 8 months. Of 27 tumours examined, one contained C797G. The C797G mutation was never seen in the EGFR L858R background that lacked T790M, suggesting this resistance mutation arises more frequently in the presence of T790M.

In addition, growth rates were assessed before and after combination treatment and C797S tumours showed negative growth rates.

Isogenic WT TP53 (p53WT) and null TP53 (p53NULL) A549 human lung carcinoma cell lines were induced with WT, P278A and luciferase, and treated with Nutlin-3 to inhibit MDM2 function, releasing p53 activity. In p53NULL cells, p53 WT expression reduced cell growth in viability assays in comparison to both p53 P278A and luciferase control cells, which showed comparable viability to each other, indicating that P278A was equivalent to a null (luciferase) allele.

In p53WT cells, p53 WT expression and control luciferase expression both equivalently reduced cell growth in viability assays in comparison to p53 P278A. This result suggests that P278A interferes with WT p53 function, indicating a dominant negative effect.

Continuous exposure to oxaliplatin was used to produce an oxaliplatin resistant HCT116 cell line (HCT116/OXA), that showed significantly higher IC50 (145.5 ± 3.52 μM vs. 7.53 ± 0.63 μM) than the parental HCT116 cells. The HCT116/OXA cells had increased proliferation, migration, and invasion, and reduced apoptotic rate relative to parental HCT116 cells. FOXC2 had significantly up-regulated mRNA (p<0.001) and protein (p<0.05) levels in HCT116/OXA cells. Over-expression of FOXC2 in chemosensitive HCT116 cells inhibited oxaliplatin sensitivity, while FOXC2 knock-down in HCT116/OXA cells increased oxaliplatin sensitivity in vitro and in vivo.

In a cohort of 118 CC patients, ZEB1 had high expression in 66.9% and low expression in 33.1% of patients by IHC. Median OS was longer in the ZEB1 low expression group (14.0 months, 95% CI 11.63-14.97) than the ZEB1 high group (9.34 months, 95% CI 8.34-11.04; p=0.0064). Median PFS was also longer in the ZEB1 low expression group (11.6 months, 95% CI 9.34-11.91) than ZEB1 high expression group (7.23 months, 95% CI 7.10-9.18; p=0.0222). In addition, a multivariable Cox proportional hazards model found that ZEB1 expression was an independent prognostic factor for PFS (HR=1.542, p=0.023) and OS (hazard ratio [HR]=1.588, p=0.016) in CC patients.

The oxaliplatin resistant HCT116/OXA cell line shows increased EMT phenotype, as well as cell invasion and migration ability compared to parental HCT116 cells. The EMT-associated transcription factor ZEB1 was found to be highly up-regulated in HCT116/OXA relative to HCT116 cells. Knock-down of ZEB1 reduced the IC50 of oxaliplatin in HCT116/OXA cells, as well as attenuating the EMT phenotype and promoting apoptosis. ZEB1 knock-down also reduced oxaliplatin resistance in vivo, with subcutaneous xenografts showing reduced tumour size, EMT phenotype, and increased apoptotic rate, relative to control cells.

The expression of CUL7 was found to be significantly higher in glioma samples than normal brain tissue, and increased with tumour grade. The prognostic value of CUL7 was examined in TCGA LGG (n=457) and GBM (n=141) datasets. Kaplan-Meier analysis showed that patients with high expression of CUL7 had shorter overall survival (OS) than those with low expression (63.51 vs 95.51 months, p < 0.001 in LGG, 11.73 vs 15.11 months, p < 0.05 in GBM). These results were validated in an independent dataset (CGGA; n = 285).

In this study, patients on imatinib monotherapy were monitored for ABL1 kinase domain variants in BCR-ABL1 fusions amplified from peripheral blood RNA. An acute-phase patient achieved complete hematologic response but progressed to chronic phase with detection of the E355G mutation and then to accelerated phase. After allograft, this patient relapsed into chronic phase and the E355G mutation was again detected in 100% of transcripts.

An accelerate-phase patient had a complete cytogenetic response until progressing to major cytogenetic response (MCyR) at month 17 and then losing MCyR at month 24 despite dose escalation. At month 9, the F486S variant was found in ~25% of transcripts increasing to ~50% at month 16 and then remaining at a stable proportion.

A late-chronic phase (CP) patient had a complete hematologic response but acquired resistance 7 months after treatment initiation. At month 11, the L248V, G250E, S417Y, and E459K variants were present in approximately 25, 25, 25, and 50% of transcripts, respectively. The patient died in accelerated phase at month 14.

In this study, patients on imatinib monotherapy were monitored for ABL1 kinase domain variants in BCR-ABL1 fusions amplified from peripheral blood RNA. A chronic-phase patient had a partial hematologic response with the Q252H and M351T variants present. The patient progressed to myeloid blast crisis (MBC) and was then negative for secondary variants. However, they had cytogenetic evidence of double Ph-chromosomes and later died. In this study involving 574 pediatric B-ALL patients (from a Dutch/German cohort), 77 were shown to be Ph-like cases identified by hierarchical clustering of gene expression data. In one male patient with Ph-like disease, an in-frame BCR-JAK2 fusion involving exon 1 of BCR and exon 17 of JAK2 was identified. In this study involving 373 high risk pediatric B-ALL cases with no recurrent fusions, 29 were kinase-fusion positive as determined by mRNA-seq or mRT-PCR and validated by RT-PCR and Sanger. Gilteritinib inhibited the cell growth of Ba/F3 cells expressing D835Y (IC50 1.6 nM; 95% CI: 1.1–2.4 nM) compared to controls (IC50 420nM; 95% CI: 350–500 nM). Additionally, immunoblots showed gliteritinib reduced phosphorylation of FLT3 and downstream targets in Ba/F3 D835Y cells in a dose dependent manner. Furthermore, in nude mice xenografted with Ba/F3 cells expressing D835Y, gilteritinib showed antitumor efficacy at 10 mg/kg and 30 mg/kg, and induced tumor regression at 30 mg/k. Computational modelling demonstrated that gilteritinib interacts with activated FLT3 at the ATP-binding site, which is distant from the D835 containing activation loop. K356dup was observed in an imatinib resistant CML. After switch to dasatinib, the patient regained deep molecular response. Therefore, K356dup seems to be resistant to imatinib and susceptible to dasatinib treatments.

A 35 year-old male patient (AML4) presented with a FLT3-ITD mutation at diagnosis and was refractory to induction and salvage chemotherapy. He then received quizartinib and underwent allogenic transplant, but relapsed after 6 months. He then responded to sorafenib, but had disease progression with a FLT3-D835Y mutation. MIR21 expression was assessed in 58 NSCLC patient samples by real-time PCR. There was a significant association between MIR21 expression and platinum sensitivity (p=0.007). MIR21 expression was significantly increased in treatment resistant patients compared to treatment sensitive patients, with a median MIR21 expression ratio of 5.798 between the two groups (p=0.000). In vitro experiments using cisplatin sensitive and resistant lung cancer cell lines showed that MIR21-associated cisplatin resistance is likely mediated through it's regulation of PTEN and Bcl-2.

MIR21 expression was assessed in 58 NSCLC patient samples by real-time PCR and a significant association between MIR21 expression and platinum sensitivity was found (p=0.007). To directly test the role of MIR21 in platinum therapy resistance, cisplatin sensitive and resistant A549 and A549/CDDP lung cancer cell lines were used. MIR21 was found to have 1.61 fold higher expression in the A549/CDDP cisplatin resistant cell line than the parental A549 line. Knock-down of MIR21 expression in A549/CDDP resulted in increased cisplatin sensitivity as determined by decreased IC50 (p<0.05), while overexpression of MIR21 in A549 cells resulted in increased resistance shown by increased IC50 (p<0.05). Overexpression of MIR21 in A549 cells results in decreased PTEN expression and increased Bcl-2 expression, while knock-down of MIR21 in A549/CDDP cells has the inverse effect. These results suggest that MIR21-associated cisplatin resistance are mediated through regulation of PTEN and Bcl-2.

Second level inhibitor FF-10101 was used to measure the inhibition of FLT3 kinase activity due to the potential for patients with the D835Y mutation to have a relapse in AML after first-generation monotherapy treatment. Cervical cancer cell lines were treated with 1uM cisplatin followed by 1-6Gy ionizing radiation (IR). CaSki cells with PIK3CA E545K mutation show resistance to cisplatin plus IR when compared with HeLa or SiHa cells that express only wild-type PIK3CA. Transfection of HeLa cells with PIK3CA E545K resulted in resistance to cisplatin plus IR compared to cells expressing only wild-type PIK3CA or with PIK3CA depleted.

Reverse phase protein array (RPPA) revealed upregulation of CCND1 at diagnosis in B-ALL relapse patients (n=27) versus patients that did not relapse (n=86, p>.01). 5-year cumulative incidence of relapse analysis showed B-ALL patients within this cohort with CCND1 expression at diagnosis above the 75th percentile had a higher incidence of relapse versus those below the 75th percentile. CCND1 upregulation appears to impact relapse 500 days post initial diagnosis.

Six members of a family were analyzed for germline VHL mutations. Three members, including the proband (III-1), and two paternal uncles (II-1 and II-4) were found to carry the heterozygous missense variant A to T, c.269 in VHL exon 1 determined through Sanger sequencing. The proband, a 25 year-old male, was admitted with an occipital headache for 1 month and a cerebellar hemangioblastoma was found via MRI (solid‐cystic mass in the vermis cerebelli and left cerebellar hemisphere 30mm in diameter). 3 years later, MRI showed no recurrence and a CT scan showed no neoplasms. He had a definite family history of VHL disease whereby his uncle and aunt (deceased) were both diagnosed with CH, and his father (deceased), uncle, and father's elder brother were all diagnosed with RCCC. ACMG evidence codes: 'PP1' since there is cosegregation with disease in multiple affected family members, 'PP4' since the patients present phenotypes highly specific for a disease with a single genetic etiology.

A comparison of tyrosine kinase inhibitors that target glioma tumour cells directly or the tumour microenvironment were tested on a PDGF-B-driven glioma genetically engineered mouse model (PDG). PDG mice with tumours <=40mm3 in size were treated for 7 days with PLX3397, vatalinib, dovitinib, or vehicle, and tumour volume was assessed by MRI. PLX3397 treated tumours showed regression or slowed growth from -40% to 140% compared to all vehicle treated tumours that progressed with tumour size increases of 150% to 930% over 7 days. When tumours were allowed to grow to a larger size (>40mm3) before treatment, PLX3397 reduced tumour growth by 97.5% compared to controls (P<0.0001). Immunoblots of tumour protein fractions showed the PLX3397 potently inhibited CSF-1R phosphorylation while vatalinib and dovitinib had modest effect. The effect of these inhibitors on cell viability was tested directly on PDGC23 and U-87MG glioma cells, as well as mouse bone-marrow derived macrophages (BMDMs) and human monocyte-derived macrophages (MDMs). PLX3397 had no effect on the survival of glioma cells but efficiently decreased viability of BMDM and MDM cells. Histological analysis of tumours after 7 days of treatment showed that PLX3397 decreased tumour nuclear density. Blinded histological analysis showed 90% of PLX3397 treated tumours being classified as grade II and 10% as grade III, compared to 100% scored as grade IV in the control group (P<0.0001). PLX3397 also significantly decreased proliferating cells and increased apoptotic cells relative to controls (P<0.0001). Further functional experiments show that PLX3397 treatment led to depolarization of M2-like TAMs and impaired the pro-tumourigenic functions of TAMs.

A comparison of tyrosine kinase inhibitors that target glioma tumour cells directly or the tumour microenvironment were tested on a PDGF-B-driven glioma genetically engineered mouse model (PDG). The CSF-1R inhibitor PLX3397 depolarized M2-like TAMs and caused reduced glioma tumour growth. In order to test whether PLX3397-induced changes in the glioma microenvironment affect sensitivity to the multi-tyrosine kinase inhibitors vatalanib and dovitinib in vivo, combination treatment with PLX3397 was administered to PDG mice for 7 days. Combination therapy caused greater tumour regression than PLX3397 alone in most tumours. Greater than 30% reduction in tumour volume was seen in 58.8% of the PLX3397 and vatalanib group and 76.5% of the PLX3397 and dovitinib group, but only 3.7% of mice treated with PLX3397 monotherapy. Both combination therapies induced significant tumour volume reduction when compared to PLX3397 alone (P<0.05 and P<0.001), as well as abolishing tumour cell proliferation and inducing apoptosis at similar or greater levels than PLX3397 alone. These results show the improved therapeutic efficacy of targeting glioma cells and TAMs concurrently.

This study identified G101V mutation in BCL2 emerged in 7 out of 15 patients with CLL progression treated with Venetoclax. In addition, this study demonstrated that the G101V mutation impairs binding of venetoclax to BCL2, confers resistance to venetoclax in both patient leukemia cells and engineered cell lines, thus provides a selective growth advantage over WT cells when maintained in the presence of the drug in vitro.

A novel seven amino acid deletion (p.K227_T233del) in the RARA region was detected in a refractory APL patient. The PML-RARA mutant was transduced into HL-60 cells and these in-vitro PML-RARA expressing cells were treated with all trans retinoic acid (ATRA) and tamibarotene. Findings indicated significantly lower CD11b expression and infrequent or impaired formation of PML nuclear bodies in mutant cells after treatment with ATRA when compared to the control. Frequency of the p.K227_T233del mutation also increased after re-induction therapy, pointing to resistance to ATRA.

In this retrospective study of 66 GBM patients treated with PD-1 inhibitors (nivolumab or pembrolizumab) at recurrence, mutations in PTEN were frequently found among non-responders. Of 45 IDH1 wild-type tumours there were PTEN mutations in 23 of 32 non-responders and only 3 among 13 responders (Fisher p = 0.0063, odds ratio = 8.5, FDR corrected p < 0.05). Compared to the background PTEN mutation rate of 33% from TCGA GBM cohort, PTEN mutations were more frequent than expected among non-responders (Fisher p = 0.0018, odds ratio = 3.3, false discovery rate (FDR) corrected p < 0.05). PTEN mutations were associated with immunosuppressive gene expression signatures, lower tumour purity, and increased levels of tumour-associated macrophages.

Five point mutations were identified in the PML B2 domain of PML-RARA transcripts in 9 patients diagnosed with APL and resistant to arsenic. DNA from these 9 patients was cloned into flag-tagged pCag expression vectors. Immunoblotting analyses demonstrated that after the addition of arsenic, the A216V, S214L, and A216T mutants experienced no change in expression or degradation when compared to wild type cells, indicating that these mutants were not inhibited by arsenic and demonstrate resistance. Immunofluorescent measurements indicated arsenic treatment did not alter the nuclear localization pattern of mutants A216V, S214L, or A216T, but had an effect on the localization of other mutants as well as wild type cells.

Patient-derived GBM brain tumour stem cells (BTSCs) were used to test the efficacy of the EGFR inhibitor afatinib in vitro and in vivo. Afatinib inhibited the growth and sphere-forming ability of BTSCs but not normal astrocytes. EGFR vIII mutant BTSCs (1.45-6.95 nM) showed higher sensitivity to afatinib than EGFR wt BTSCs (21.1-746 nM) in cell viability assays. Immunoblots showed decreased phosphorylation of EGFR and MAPK following afatinib treatment. Intracranial xenografts were established using EGFR wt (BT67) and EGFR vIII (BT73 and BT147) BTSCs and were treated with 15mg/kg afatinib or vehicle for 5 days. Afatinib treatment did not improve survival of BT67 xenografted mice, while a significant survival advantage was seen for both EGFR vIII mutant xenografted mice (P<0.0006 and P<0.0003; log-rank test) compared to controls.

Patient-derived GBM brain tumour stem cells (BTSCs) were used to test the efficacy of the EGFR inhibitor afatinib and JAK2 inhibitor pacritinib in vitro and in vivo. Combination treatment with suboptimal doses of afatinib and pacritinib resulted in significantly decreased cell viability and sphere-formation ability, and increased cell death in BTSCs. Multiple combinations of afatinib and pacritinib were tested at different concentrations and showed that combined treatment is synergistic in inhibiting BTSC growth. Immunohistochemistry showed decreased phosphorylation of EGFR and STAT3 following combination treatment compared to afatinib or pacritinib alone. Intracranial xenografts were established using EGFR vIII (BT73) BTSCs. Xenografts were treated with vehicle or 15mg/kg afatinib and/or 100mg/kg pacritinib for 3 weeks and tumour burden was measured by MRI. Both the afatinib and combination treatment groups showed decreased tumour growth with the combination treatment having a significantly greater effect (P<0.0021; t-test). Survival analysis could not be performed on the combination treatment group due to symptoms of toxicity. The authors noted a 5-fold increase in brain concentrations of pacritinib when administered with afatinib, which could be associated with the toxicity seen.

This study evaluated forty-nine cases of rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS) (17 cases of alveolar RMS, 10 of embryonal RMS, 21 of spindle cell and sclerosing RMS, and a single case of a pleomorphic RMS) for MYOD1 (L122R), PIK3CA (H1047), and PIK3CA (E542/E545) variants. All 10 cases that were positive for the MYOD1 (L122R) variant were either the spindle cell (3/12) or the sclerosing (7/9) subtypes of RMS, while all 10 cases of the embryonal subtype of RMS were negative for the MYOD1 (L122R) variant. The study suggests that the MYOD1 L122R variant is specific for spindle cell and sclerosing subtype of RMS (where it was detected in 10/21 cases or 48%). The study also confirmed the positive relationship between the spindle cell and the sclerosing subtypes of RMS, which both can have the same molecular abnormality (MYOD1 L122R variant) and are now considered to be the same subtype. Finally, the study confirmed the negative correlation between the aforementioned subtypes with the embryonal subtype of rhabdomyosarcoma.

This study evaluated forty-nine cases of rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS) (17 cases of alveolar RMS, 10 of embryonal RMS, 21 of spindle cell and sclerosing RMS, and a single case of a pleomorphic RMS) for MYOD1 (L122R), PIK3CA (H1047), and PIK3CA (E542/E545) mutations. 10/49 cases were positive for the MYOD1 (L122R) variant, and all the positive cases belonged to either spindle cell or sclerosing RMS subtype. None of the embryonal RMS cases was positive for the MYOD1 L122R variant. All cases were treated with surgical resection and either adjuvant chemotherapy, adjuvant radiotherapy, or both. On patient follow-up, the alive-with-disease ratio was higher in the adult than in the pediatric population. Furthermore, the patients positive for MYOD1 mutation showed a higher number of disease-positive states on follow-up, while the patients negative for MYOD1 mutation showed a higher number of disease-free states on follow-up. This suggests that the MYOD1 L122R variant is associated with a more aggressive clinical course, although the difference did not reach statistical significance (P=0.34).

evidence_statement: A 61-year old patient with KIF5B-RET fusion positive NSCLC received clinical benefit from selpercatinib treatment initially. ctDNA surveillance showed the emergence of RET G810S 3 months after the start of treatment. After 4 months, RET G810S and KIF5B-RET fusion increased in abundance in the plasma, and additional solvent front mutations emerged. Imaging after 6 months found progressive disease. Post-mortem analysis showed RET G810R in post-treatment liver lesions but not pre-treatment sample, and presence of G810S/C/R at varying allele frequencies in the plasma. ctDNA analysis also uncovered RET solvent front mutations in other patients, where the frequency of founder RET mutation increased together with the resistance mutation in patients. In silico modeling, xenograft and cell line experiments also support the notion that RET G810C/S/R mutations confer resistance to selpercatinib.
In two out of three patients with MTC treated in a phase1/2 trial, the RET G810 mutation emerged in ctDNA together with an acquired resistance after initial response to selpercatinib.

evidence_statement: This study was conducted to evaluate morbidity, specific clinical risk profile, and mortality among a series of 125 VHL c.292T>C mutation carriers (legend nomenclature c.505 T>C used is paper). Frequently observed lesions were phaeochromocytoma (47%), retinal angiomas (36%), haemangioblastoma of the spine (36%), and haemangioblastoma of the brain (16%). Four patients developed renal cell carcinoma. VHL was symptomatic in 47% of subjects; 30% were asymptomatic despite the presence of at least one VHL related tumour and 23% of the carriers had no detectable VHL lesion. Of the 19 patients who had died (15%), 10 died of symptomatic VHL lesions. Overall penetrance by cumulative incidence functions is estimated at 48% by 35 years and 88% by 70 years.

evidence_statement: A case report on a 31Y female with bilateral multiple renal cysts on US misdiagnosed as autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease. The patient passed away from metastatic malignancy from an unknown origin. 2 years later, her daughter 18Y was diagnosed with cerebellar and retinal hemangioblastoma. Based on the clinical features and family history, VHL disease was suspected. Southern blot hybridization using the restriction enzymes PvulI, BglII, EcoRI, and BamHI was used to detect a deletion within the VHL gene in Exon 1. Patient-derived GBM brain tumour stem cells (BTSCs) were used to test the efficacy of EGFR inhibitors in vitro. Two EGFR G598V mutant BTSC lines showed higher sensitivity to afatinib (78.9 and 0.186 nM) than most EGFR wt BTSCs (21.1-746 nM) in cell viability assays. Similar results were seen with erlotinib (3.2 and 0.14 nM) and AZD9291 (0.92 and 0.076 nM), compared to EGFR wt BTSCs (erlotinib: 0.29-17.8 nM; AZD9291: 0.193-3.4 nM).

A 9 year old girl with B-lymphoblastic leukemia/ lymphoma (2016 WHO) relapsed 15 months post-maintenance chemotherapy. FISH and genomic analysis detected the EBF1-PDGFRB fusion (exon 11 with Exon14). The patient was treated with induction [fludarabine, idarubicin and cytarabine] therapy followed by additional chemotherapy (cyclophosphamide, adriamycin, vincristine, and dexamethasone followed by high-dose methotrexate and cytarabine) plus tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI, imatinib). Imatinib was stopped 10 days before cord blood transplant (CBT) with reduced intensity conditional and re-initiated on day 47 until 12 months post-transplant. The EBF1-PDGFRB transcript level measured using reverse-transcriptase polymerase chain reaction remained below detection limit (<2.5x102 copies/ microgram RNA) for 36 months post CBT. Furthermore, the patient maintained molecular remission during the 24 months post-CBT and the 12 months following completion of TKI administration, based on minimal residual disease (MRD) testing conducted every 6 months.

evidence_statement: In a cohort of 84 de novo AML patients with a CBFB/MYH11 rearrangement and in 36 patients with a RUNX1/RUNX1T1 rearrangement, the FLT3 N676K mutation was identified in 5 and 1 patients, respectively (5 [6%] of 84; 1 [3%] of 36).
