In a phase 2 trial, a total of 364 patients with non-small cell lung cancer and MET alterations were assigned to cohorts based on prior treatment and type of MET alteration. A total of 97 patients, from cohorts 4 (pretreated) and 5b (no previous treatment), had MET exon 14 skipping mutations. Among pretreated (1-2 lines of therapy) patients with NSCLC with a MET exon 14 skipping mutation, overall response was observed in 41% (95% confidence interval [CI], 29 to 53) of 69 patients. Overall response rate was 68% (95% CI, 48 to 84) of 28 patients who had not received treatment previously. The median duration of response was 9.7 months (95% CI, 5.6 to 13.0) for cohort 4 and 12.6 months (95% CI, 5.6 to could not be estimated) for cohort 5b.

In this open-label phase 2 trial, MET inhibitor tepotinib was administered to patients with non-small cell lung cancer and MET exon 14 skipping mutation found in either liquid and/or tissue biopsy. A total of 152 patients were enrolled, with an efficacy population consisting of 99 patients who had at least nine months of follow-up. The response rate by independent review was 46% (95% confidence interval [CI], 36 to 57), with a median duration of response of 11.1 months (95% CI, 7.2 to could not be estimated) in the combined-biopsy group. The investigator-assessed response rate was 56% (95% CI, 45 to 66). Response rates were consistent between liquid-biopsy and tissue-biopsy groups and regardless of the number of previous lines of therapy.

In a phase 2 trial, a total of 364 patients with non-small cell lung cancer and MET alterations received the MET inhibitor Capmatinib after assignment to cohorts based on prior treatment and type of MET alteration. Among previously treated patients with MET amplification who had a gene copy number of less than 10 an overall response rate was reached in 7 to 12% of patients. Among patients with MET amplification and a gene copy number of 10 or higher, overall response was observed in 29% (95% CI, 19 to 41) of previously treated patients and in 40% (95% CI, 16 to 68) of those who had not received treatment previously.

Patients with RET-fusion positive non-small cell lung cancer were enrolled in this phase 1-2 trial of RET inhibitor selpercatinib. Among 105 consecutively enrolled patients who had previously received at least platinum-based chemotherapy, the percentage with an objective response was 64% (95% confidence interval [CI], 54 to 73). The median duration of response was 17.5 months (95% CI, 12.0 to could not be evaluated), and 63% of the responses were ongoing at a median follow-up of 12.1 months. Among 39 previously untreated patients, the percentage with an objective response was 85% (95% CI, 70 to 94), and 90% of the responses were ongoing at 6 months. Among 11 patients with measurable central nervous system metastasis at enrollment, the percentage with an objective intracranial response was 91% (95% CI, 59 to 100).

In this international phase 1/2 trial (NCT03157128), 55 RET-mutant medullary thyroid cancer patients who had previously received the multi-kinase inhibitors vandetanib and/or cabozantinib received the highly selective RET-inhibitor selpercatinib. Response in this previously treated population was 69% (95% CI, 55 to 81) with 5 complete responses (CR) and 33 partial responses (PR). The 1-year progression-free survival was 82% (95% CI, 69 to 90). In 88 patients with RET-mutant medullary thyroid cancer who had not previously received vandetanib or cabozantinib, the response rate was 73% (95% CI, 62 to 82) with 10 CR and 54 PR. The 1-year progression-free survival was 92% (95% CI, 82 to 97). The most frequent RET mutations overall included RET M918T (57%)in the kinase domain, RET mutations in extracellular cysteines residues at positions 609, 611, 618, 620, 630, and 634 (19%), and the RET V804M/L (7.6%) gatekeeper mutation. Responses were seen across all qualifying RET mutations including the V804M/L gatekeeper which is an acquired resistance mechanism seen with vandetanib and cabozantinib treatment.

In this phase 1/2 trial (NCT03157128), patients with RET altered thyroid cancers were enrolled to receive the highly selective RET inhibitor selpercatinib. Among 19 patients with previously treated RET fusion positive thyroid cancer, the percentage who had a response was 79% (95% CI, 54 to 94), and 1-year progression-free survival was 64% (95% CI, 37 to 82). Responses included 8 of 11 (73%) papillary thyroid cancers, 2 of 3 poorly differentiated thyroid cancers, 1 of 2 anaplastic thyroid cancers, and 1 of 1 Hurthle-cell thyroid cancer. The most common fusions were CCDC6::RET and NCOA4::RET seen in 47% and 32% of fusion cases respectively.

In contrast to controls (empty vector and FGFR3 wild-type overexpression NIH-3T3 cell lines), the stable transfection of NIH-3T3 cells with FGFR3b-S249C led to ligand-independent phosphorylation of FGFR3 and the acquisition of elongated, refractile spindle-shaped morphology like transformed cells. Using a thymidine incorporation assay, S249C-expressing cells were shown to lose contact inhibition and grew 3x to 4x more rapidly than controls. Soft agar assays demonstrated increased colony formation and anchorage-independent growth in S249C-expressing cells versus controls. All nude mice subcutaneously injected with S249C cells rapidly formed tumors, but no tumors were observed in empty vector-injected mice. The authors concluded mutated FGFR3b-S249C has transforming properties attributed to oncogenes.

Forster Resonance Energy Transfer (FRET)-based technique acquired quantitative measurement of the effect of S249C on unliganded mutant FGFR3 dimer stability and structure in plasma membrane vesicles from CHO cells. Dimer stability was modestly increased by S249C (-3.7 kcal/mol) versus wildtype FGFR3 (-3.4 kcal/mol). Intrinsic FRET demonstrated S249C dimers were significantly closer together (45 A) than the wildtype dimer (53 A). The substitution of cysteine was expected to lead to strong covalent bonds, but the authors conclude their data demonstrates S249C does not induce constitutive FGFR3 dimerization, but induces dimer structural modifications.

Compared to controls (empty vector, FGFR3 wildtype, and S249C-Kinase dead cell lines), stable expression of S249C in NIH-3T3 cells resulted in a transformed spindle-like morphology, a 3-fold proliferation increase (p=.004) and a 20-fold increase (p=.05) in colony formation on soft agar, enhanced receptor phosphorylation and activation of downstream targets as shown by Western blot. At confluence, Human TERT-NHUC cells stably expressing S249C displayed a multilayered appearance, reduced cell-cell adhesion, formed ridges, and increased saturation density compared to controls. Additionally, cell cycle analysis demonstrated S249C cells were significantly more viable (p<.001) at confluence and fewer S249C cells were in G0/G1 than controls. Western blots also showed confluent S249C had increased levels of cell cycle and cell survival proteins. Unlike wildtype FGFR3, S249C displayed constitutive activation independent from the presence of ligand.

In this case series, 7 elderly patients with secondary AML (sAML) not eligible for intensive chemotherapy and refractory to HMA (including 1 patient with antecedent myeloproliferative neoplasm) were treated with venetoclax monotherapy. Three of 7 patients showed response. Of these: 2 patients achieved complete remission (1 of which was mutated for IDH2). One patient with IDH1 mutation showed PB blast clearance (derived anti-leukemic benefit) but BM was not performed to evaluate response. Venetoclax responders had high BCL‐2 and/or BIM expression levels in myeloblasts, and the response was significantly associated with OS. BCL-2 and BIM expression levels can potentially identifer venetoclax responders.

Expression of the N841I variant in murine BaF3 cell line resulted in constitutive autophosphorylation of FLT3 and the amount of autophosphorylated FLT3 was decreased with exposure to the FLT3 inhibitor, midostaurin (PKC412). These results were performed using three independent polyclonal BaF3 cell lines. The quantitation was done using western blots. Treatment of cell lines expressing the N841I mutation with the PKC412 showed decreased growth and was more sensitive with a IC50 of 10nm compared to the WT cell line IC50 of 30nm. The sensitivity and specificity of the N841I to PKC412 was supported by reversal of growth inhibition by stimulation of the cell line with IL-3. The N841I expressing cell lines showed phosphorylation of the STAT5 and ERK in the absence of IL-3. Exposure of the cell lines to PKC412 decreased the amount of STAT5 and ERK phosphorylation. Treatment with imatinib was used as a control and did not have an effect on level of FLT3, STAT5, and ERK phosphorylation, suggesting that the effect of PKC412 is specific to the FLT3 N841I. The authors conclude that the N841I mutation results in a constitutively active FLT3 kinase that leads to downstream STAT5 and ERK activation and that this mutation is sensitive to the drug midostaurin.

Based on histopathological evaluation of the bladder after 20 weeks following the start of carcinogen treatment (N-butyl-N-(4-hydroxybutyl)-nitrosamine (OH-BBN)), transgenic mice expressing FGFR3 S249C (9/29 with tumor) in the urothelium demonstrated more advanced bladder tumor pathogenesis (p=.0454) and increased invasion properties (p=.0239) compared to treated wildtype mice (6/47 with tumor). The urothelium of treated S249C mice displayed increased lobulated basement membrane (p=.0073) and squamous cell transformation plus keratinisation (p<.0001) compared to wildtype mice. The time course of neutrophil infiltration was delayed in S249C mice compared to wildtype, but by 20 weeks tumors in S249C mice exhibited a more prominent inflammatory response than the controls.

In this multicentre phase II study of ALK-positive NSCLC patients that progressed on crizotinib, the safety and efficacy of 225mg daily ensartinib was assessed. Objective responses were seen in 76 (52% [95% CI 43-60]) of 147 response evaluable patients. Disease control rate was 93% (95% CI 88-97). Patients harboring ALK C1156Y had an objective response rate of 71% (5/7) and disease control rate of 100%.The most common treatment related AEs were rash, increased alanine aminotransferase, and increased aspartate aminotransferase, mostly of grade 1-2.

53 pediatric tumors consisting of 20 AT/RT, 10 PNET, and 23 other central nervous system tumors were classified using microscopic diagnosis, and then tested for expression of the SMARCB1 gene product INI1. In the 20 cases of AT/RT, expression of INI1 was not detected in tumor cells using the BAF47/SNF5 monoclonal INI1 antibody. Expression of INI1 was detected in 31 out of the 33 remaining tumors, with one Oligodendroglioma showing no expression, and one pituitary adenoma showing weak expression. The authors conclude that immunohistochemical staining with an INI1 antibody may be useful in confirming histologic diagnosis of AT/RT.

Atypical teratoid/rhabdoid tumor (AT/RT) is now defined by WHO guidelines by alterations of either INI1 (SMARCB1) or BRG1 (SMARCA4; rarely mutated) which result in loss of tumor nuclear expression of the protein, as evaluated by immunohistochemistry. Tumors with histological features of AT/RT but lacking these diagnostic genetic alterations are only eligible for the descriptive diagnosis of CNS embryonal tumor with rhabdoid features.

In a pediatric phase 1 trial (NCT02637687), a 2 year old with infantile fibrosarcoma of the shoulder harbored the SQSTM1-NTRK1 fusion. After two surgical resections and multiple rounds of chemotherapy, Larotrectinib treatment resulted in 93% tumour reduction. An R1 resection was performed followed by adjuvant Larotrectinib. The patient remained on Larotrectinib without evidence of disease progression at the time of last follow-up.

Whole exome sequencing of 4 low grade gliomas (LGGs) and targeted sequencing of 28 LGGs revealed ATRX variants are found exclusively in a subset of IDH1-mutant, 1p/19q intact LGGs. Paired blood samples were sequenced in all cases and mutations were confirmed by Sanger. IDH1mutation was found in 28/32 LGGs and of these 12 possessed an ATRX mutation (~43%). In all 12 ATRX mutated cases 1p/19q was intact (correlation p=0.0003), and ATRX variants were not observed in the 12 1p/19q codeleted cases. Additionally, multiplex mRNA profiling of 28 astrocytic tumors with subclasses assigned based on 75 gene signatures demonstrated ATRX mutations were associated (p=.0044) with the early progenitor-like subclass (EPL) (11/13 EPL cases harbored ATRX mutants).

We suspect that the variant origin is germline, although we were not able to confirm this based on the paper alone. ACMG PP4 phenotypes consistent with VHL disease.

Six patients with classic VHL disease (VHL patients) and 6 healthy control participants took part in the study. The patients were free from any associated neoplasia at the time of the study and had no other medical disorders. VHL patients were recruited through their respective physicians. Control participants were recruited through advertisement and were chosen to match VHL patients for sex, age, height, weight, and body mass index. One 53Y female VHL patient and a 27Y male VHL patient with unknown phenotypes were described to have this VHL mutation. We suspect that the variant origin is germline, although we were not able to confirm this based on the paper alone. Unclear ACMG.

A case report presented a 8Y boy with an isolated benign phaeochromocytoma of the left adrenal. Three years later a second adrenal phaeochromocytoma was diagnosed on the right side and removed. Genetic analysis found a de novo germline missense mutation in the VHL gene (reported by the authors as nucleotide 695 G to A (legacy notation)). His family history was negative and both parents had wildtype VHL copies. At 18 years, the patient did not reveal any other manifestations of VHL disease. ACMG PP4: phenotypes consistent with VHL disease, PM6: de novo mutation with no paternity described.

evidence_statement: A 44-year-old man presented with a generalized epileptic attack. Diagnostic workup revealed a cystic left cerebellar tumor, which on histologic examination proved to be a hemangioblastoma. Identification of a VHL germline mutation (Ser65Leu) in a blood sample of the patient confirmed the diagnosis.The patient also had retinal hemangioblastomas, and renal cell carcinoma. Family history was positive for VHL disease. The patient died 10 years later at 54Y from mets to the heart and autopsy also confirmed pheochromocytoma and pancreatic endocrine tumour. ACMG PP4 phenotypes and family history consistent with VHL disease.

A retrospective analysis of 164 patients waiting for surgery for hemangioblastomas at Freiburg University Medical Center, Freiburg, Germany was conducted. Two patients were found with germline VHL exon 1 deletions: patient #1 (male, 54Y) with spinal hemangioblastoma and patient #14 (female, 41 Y) with supratentorial hemangioblastoma. Family history was not described. ACMG: PP4 phenotype consistent with VHL disease.

A retrospective analysis of 164 patients waiting for surgery for hemangioblastomas at Freiburg University Medical Center, Freiburg, Germany was conducted. Patient #2 (male, 53Y) was found with germline VHL point nonsense mutation (c.548C>A, p.Ser183*) and with cerebellar hemangioblastoma and renal cysts. Family history was not described. ACMG: PP4 phenotype consistent with VHL disease.

A mass found at birth in a patient’s left arm became enlarged at age 2 and was resected and characterized as a high-grade spindle cell sarcoma. FISH and RT-PCR did not detect any common sarcoma translocations. A recurrence and a new mass formed after 4 months of therapy, so amputation was performed. Metastatic high-grade sarcoma appeared in the lungs 4 months later followed by multiple recurrences 10 months after treatment. Whole exome and transcriptome sequencing of diagnosis and normal samples were performed and the in-frame LMNA-NTRK1 fusion (exon 2 & exon 10) with the kinase domain intact was discovered. Treatment with Crizotinib was started and a chest CT after 2 months revealed partial response. After 22 months of therapy, chest CT revealed a complete response of lung nodules, which has been sustained >18 months beyond the conclusion of treatment at 31 months.

Using site-directed mutagenesis, the authors investigated the phenotypic and signaling consequences of three FGFR3 mutations, S249C, Y373C (in the paper described as Y375C), and K652E, in immortalized normal human urothelial cells (TERT-NHUC) and mouse fibroblasts (NIH-3T3). In the NIH-3T3 cells, expression of Y373C resulted in a transformed spindle-like morphology, higher proliferation rate, and colony formation in soft agar. Expression Y373C in NIH-3T3 resulted in auto-phosphorylation and increased phosphorylation of downstream targets (not seen in wild type expressing cells). TERT-NHUC expressing Y373C cells reached 16% higher cell numbers than controls (for S249C it was 20%), but still statistically significant at confluence (due to increased proliferation and viability), acquired different morphology at confluence such as reduced cell-cell adhesion, formed ridges and acquired a multi-layered appearance and had fewer cells in the G0/G1 phase of the cell cycle at confluence (compared to controls, though not statistically significant). Confluent TERT-NHUC expressing Y373C exhibited changes in cell cycle-related proteins (RB expression was switched off in control cells at confluence, but 373C mutant cells retained RB expression and the protein was hyper-phosphorylated (less than S249C); increased expression of CDK1, BCL2 were up-regulated in Y373C expressing cells. Ligand independence experiments suggests partial independence for Y373C, whereas cells expressing having S249C have complete ligand independence. These findings support the proliferative and survival advantages conferred by Y373C to urothelial cells. It should be noted that these effects are less pronounced than S249C, but still significant.

The authors identified a bladder cancer cell line (MGH-U3) with a homozygous Y373C mutation. With immunoprecipitation (IP), and immunoblotting (IB) experiments, they demonstrated constitutional phosphorylation of FGFR3 Y373C protein. Then with SU5492 (an FGFR3 TKI) and FGFR3 siRNA, they also demonstrate that constitutional phosphorylation of the FGFR3 Y373C can be inhibited. Furthermore, cells treated with SU5492 (for inhibition) and FGFR3 siRNA (for depletion) of the mutant FGFR3 Y373C protein show inhibition of cell proliferation and anchorage independent growth. These studies suggest potentially oncogenic properties for the Y373C mutation.

The Y373C variant was introduced into full-length FGFR3 constructs and co-transfected into NIH3T3 cells with a reporter under the control of the Fos promoter. FGFR3 Y373C resulted in a ligand-independent 5-10 fold increase in reporter expression over wild type FGFR3. FGFR3 Y373C was also transfected into COS cells and radiolabeled protein isolated by immunoprecipitation. Ligand-independent formation of FGFR3 dimers were detected by electrophoresis under non-reducing conditions, while dimers were absent in wild type controls.
Transfection with constructs expressing FGFR3 Y373C induced transformation of NIH3T3 cells in a colony formation assay, while wild type FGFR3 did not.

The FGFR3 Y373C variant is present in the KMS-11multiple myeloma cell line, on the background of a 4;14 translocation. This cell line shows ligand independent phosphorylation of FGFR3, in contrast to another multiple myeloma cell line carrying the FGFR3 G382D mutation. Transfection of FGFR3 Y373C into a different multiple myeloma cell line that does not express endogenous FGFR3 (U266) also resulted in ligand-independent FGFR3 phosphorylation , while transfection of wt FGFR3 did not. Introduction of FGFR3 Y373C into NIH3T3 cells resulted in ligand-independent phosphorylation of Mapk, Stat1 and Stat3, and in transformation in a colony formation assay, while introduction of wt FGFR3 did not.

In a cohort of 171 uniformly treated pediatric rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS) patients, 78 patients had alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma (ARMS). Of ARMS patients, 55% harbored a PAX3-FOXO1 fusion, 22% harbored a PAX7-FOXO1 fusion, and 23% were fusion negative. Authors found a trend toward worse overall survival (OS) for PAX3-FOXO1 positive ARMS compared to PAX7-FOXO1 ARMS (4 year survival 52% vs 77%, p=0.08); fusion-negative ARMS had an intermediate OS. Among patients with metastatic disease, the PAX3-FOXO1 fusions were associated with significantly worse OS (4-year survival: 8% vs 75% for PAX7-FOXO1 ARMS, p = 0.002). In multivariate analysis, PAX3-FOXO1 fusion was independently associated with failure or death compared to loco-regional embryonal RMS (P=0.033), and among metastatic fusion positive ARMS (for failure: p=0.025, for death: p=0.019). The authors concluded that PAX3-FOXO1 fusion is an independent indicator of poor outcome.

Of ARMS patients, 55% harbored a PAX3-FOXO1 fusion, 22% harbored a PAX7-FOXO1 fusion, and 23% were fusion negative. Authors found a trend toward better overall survival (OS) for PAX7-FOXO1 positive ARMS compared to PAX3-FOXO1 ARMS (4 year survival 77% vs 52%, p=0.08); fusion-negative ARMS had an intermediate OS. Among patients with metastatic disease, the PAX7-FOXO1 fusions were associated with significantly better OS (4-year survival: 75% vs 8% for PAX3-FOXO1 ARMS, p = 0.002). In multivariate analysis, among metastatic fusion positive ARMS, PAX7-FOXO1 fusion was not significantly associated with increased risk of failure or death. Further, among PAX7-FOXO1 fusion patients, there was little difference in outcome whether patients presented with loco-regional or metastatic disease, in striking contrast with PAX3-FOXO1 fusion positive patients. The authors concluded that PAX7-FOXO1 fusion is an independent indicator of favorable outcome in metastatic ARMS.

molecular_profile: ALK G1269A AND EML4::ALK e6::e19 AND ALK Amplification
evidence_statement: This study analyzed patients with non small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) who were positive for EML4-ALK fusions (ALK+) and progressed on crizotinib monotherapy. One ALK+ patient had a novel fusion between EML4 exon 6 and ALK exon 19 (E6;A19, typical fusions involve ALK exon 20) and ALK G1269A co-mutation in post-crizotinib progression biopsies. This patient's tumor also demonstrated a 5-fold increase in rearranged ALK copy number between pre- and post- crizotinib biopsies as measured by FISH. The presence of ALK G1269A pre-crizotinib could not be evaluated. This patient was a 62 year old non-smoking female with adenocarcinoma, wt for KRAS and EGFR, who experienced crizotinib as a 2nd line therapy. The patient experienced partial response and was on crizotinib for 197 days. In vitro, Ba/F3 cell line expressing EML4-ALK fusion (E6a;A20, a known sensitizing alteration to crizotinib) and an ALK G1269A co-mutation, demonstrated resistance to crizotinib treatment (341 nmol/L vs. 22 nmol/L) compared to Ba/F3 cells expressing EML4-ALK fusion. Resistance was determined by assessing cell viability and colony formation. Levels of phosphorylation of ALK, ERK, STAT3, and AKT were higher in ALK+ G1269A mutant cells than ALK+ controls, by western blot. The authors note that ALK G1269A likely induces resistance by preventing crizotinib from accessing its binding pocket in the ALK kinase domain.

In this retrospective analysis of 7 diagnostic specimens from patients with AML-Normal Karyotype (AML-NK), which also included 2 remission specimens and 1 relapse specimen (n =10), described a targeted DNA capture with cRNA baits followed by deep sequencing method that enabled the simultaneous identification of mutations in 24 AML genes (NRAS; DNMT3A; SF3B1; IDH1; KIT; TET2; CSF1R; NPM1; EZH2; JAK2; PTEN; WT1; MLL (KMT2A); CBL; KRAS; PTPN11; FLT3; IDH2; TP53; NF1; CEBPA; ASXL1; RUNX1; KDM6A), including the 10 most frequently mutated in AML–NK, without a normal constitutional DNA specimen. Mutations in the dominant leukemic clone were validated using capillary sequencing, demonstrating 100% specificity for both open source software and their in-house mutation caller—Mutation Identification and Analysis Software (MIDAS). Following analysis of putative leukemic subclones (with as few as 1% of cells), they identified the FLT3-N676K mutation in a single sample (P4). This proband was a 43F, who carried a NPM1-L287fs* and IDH2-R140Q in the dominant AML clone at diagnosis; at relapse, she carried a TP53-G374fs*8. The authors concluded that although most diagnostic laboratories use allele-specific technologies to identify mutations in genes such as NPM1 and FLT3, which have validated prognostic and therapeutic significance—there are further mutations present at diagnosis that may be missed on these platforms. Instead, the authors suggest that sequencing that also allows for the analysis of subclone mutation(s) present at diagnosis, could identify aberrations that may be differentially sensitive to chemotherapy and can expand to become the dominant clone at the time of disease relapse, making their identification at the time of diagnosis important.

PDGFRA mutations (exon 12, 14, 18) were assessed in 351 melanoma patient samples. 18 different mutations were detected in 4.6% of samples (all without chronic sun-induced damage and mainly in acral and mucosal melanoma, mutually exclusive with KIT). 12 novel missense mutations were tested for functional significance (western blot of autophosphorylation in transduced 293T cell line). PDGFRA V658A was detected in one sample of mucosal melanoma. In vitro, PDGFRA V658A expressed in IL-3 dependent Ba/F3 cells resulted in strong autophosphorylation of PDGFRA and cell growth independent of the presence of IL-3. Treatment with imatinib did not substantially reduce p-PDGFRA or reduce cell proliferation. Authors concluded that PDGFRA V658A is resistant to imatinib.

This study analyzed patients with non small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) who were positive for EML4-ALK fusions (ALK+) and progressed on crizotinib monotherapy. One patient harbored KRAS G12V co-mutation in post- crizotinib tumor cells but not pre-treatment cells. This patient was a 45 year old non-smoking female who had adenocarcinoma and had undergone one line of therapy prior. The patient's best response was partial response and was on crizotinib for 244 days. In an in vitro study, H3122 cells expressing EML4-ALK fusion and KRAS G12V did not demonstrate resistance to crizotinib treatment compared to H3122 cells expressing EML4-ALK fusion and wild-type KRAS (IC50: 117 vs. 111 nmol/L). Resistance was determined by assessing cell viability. The authors suggest that KRAS G12V may induce resistance, though the results are unclear.

We describe a novel RBPMS-MET driver fusion in association with a locally aggressive IFS-like tumor. MET functions as an oncogene and, when associated with the RNA binding protein RBPMS, forms an in-frame fusion product that retains the MET kinase domain. This fusion is associated with aberrant cell signaling pathway expression and subsequent malignancy. We describe treatment with cabozantinib in a patient with an IFS-like neoplasm.

Proliferation of Ba/F3 cells with FLT3 double mutations was studied for the activity of ponatinib. Compared to control cells with native FLT3-ITD mutant (IC50: 3.0nM), cells with double mutants (FLT3-ITD/F691I) showed similar sensitivity to ponatinib treatment ((IC50: 4.2nM). Cells with double mutants (FLT3-ITD/F691L) showed mild resistance but were still sensitive to ponatinib ((IC50: 52nM). Immunoblots revealed ponatinib could inhibit phosphorylation of FLT3 and downstream targets in Ba/F3 cells with FLT3-ITD or double mutants (ITD/F691I or ITD/F691L) in a dose dependent manner (10-500nM).

Proliferation of Ba/F3 cells with FLT3 double mutations was studied for the activity of ponatinib. Compared to control cells with native FLT3-ITD mutant (IC50: 3.0nM), cells with double mutants, FLT3-ITD and a secondary point mutation at the activation loop residue D835 (D835V/Y/F/H), were resistance to ponatinib ((IC50: 211-349nM). Immunoblots also demonstrated this resistance to ponatinib by evaluating phosphorylation of FLT3 and its downstream targets.

Proliferation of Ba/F3 cells with FLT3 double mutations was studied for the activity of ponatinib and sorafenib. Compared to control cells with native FLT3-ITD mutant (IC50: 3.0nM), cells with double mutants as FLT3-ITD plus Y842C, a secondary point mutation at the activation loop, were resistance to ponatinib (IC50: 229nM), as well as to sorafenib (IC50: 469nM). Immunoblots also confirmed this resistance to ponatinib by evaluating phosphorylation of FLT3 and its downstream targets.

Proliferation of Ba/F3 cells with FLT3 double mutations was studied. Compared to control cells with native FLT3-ITD mutant (IC50: 0.13-3.0nM), cells with double mutants (FLT3-ITD/D839G) were sensitive to AC220/quizartinib (IC50: 1.9nM), resistance to sorafenib (IC50: 112nM), and mild resistance to ponatinib (IC50: 54nM). Immunoblots confirmed the mild resistance to ponatinib by evaluating phosphorylation of FLT3 and its downstream target (STAT5).

Compared to control cells with native FLT3-ITD mutant (IC50: 0.13-3.0nM), cells with double mutants (FLT3-ITD/D839G) were sensitive to AC220/quizartinib (IC50: 1.9nM), resistance to sorafenib (IC50: 112nM), and mild resistance to ponatinib (IC50: 54nM). Immunoblots confirmed the mild resistance to ponatinib by evaluating phosphorylation of FLT3 and its downstream target (STAT5).

Using in vitro proliferation assay in Ba/F3 cells, it was found that the cells with FLT3-ITD G697S exhibited potent resistance to Gilteritinib. Similar resistance was found in cells bearing FLT3-ITD F691L or FLT3-ITD D698N as well. Molecular modeling reveals that G697S variant caused loss of interaction and a steric clash with the phenyl ring of Gilteritinib, which may explain the reduced of inhibitory activity. The authors also noted G697S has never been identified clinically.

The study screened for mutations in the second tyrosine kinase domain of FLT3 (TK2) in 172 untreated patient with de novo AML. Nonisotopic RNase cleavage assay was used to identify samples that did not match the WT cDNA in the TK2 region. This identified 16 samples (9.3%), reproduced by running the assay twice, that did not match the WT sequence. A restriction digest assay to detect the known D835 mutation in the 16 positive samples. 15 out of the 16 had a D835 mutation, leaving one sample with a novel mutation in the TK2. This sample was sequenced and was determined to be a N841K substitution. The sample that harbors the N841K mutation also had a t(8;21) translocation. The authors conjecture that this is may be an activating mutation given that a c-KIT activating mutation N822K is orthologous to the N841K residue in FLT3. They also comment on the N841I mutations that was shown experimentally to be activating.

After disease progression with no objective response to therapy, a 75-year-old with metastatic colorectal cancer that spread to the liver displayed elevated NTRK1 expression in both primary tumor and liver metastasis as measured by immunohistochemistry. FISH of the tumor and patient derived xenograft indicated NTRK1 involvement. 5’RACE PCR discovered a novel LMNA-NTRK1 fusion (exon 11 & exon 10), which resulted in the expression of two different fusion splice transcripts (exons 1-10 with exons 10-16 and exons 1-11 with exons 10-16). Fusion expression of both transcripts was confirmed by western blot, and Sanger sequencing revealed the fusion to be in-frame with the kinase domain intact. After 4 weeks of treatment with Entrectinib, CT scan revealed the patient showed a partial response with a 30% reduction of target lesions. This response was maintained for 5 months.

FISH of the tumor and patient derived xenograft of a 75-year-old with metastatic colorectal cancer that spread to the liver indicated NTRK1 involvement. 5’RACE PCR discovered a novel LMNA-NTRK1 fusion (exon 10 & exon 10), which resulted in the expression of two different fusion splice transcripts (exons 1-10 with exons 10-16 and exons 1-11 with exons 10-16). Expression was confirmed by Western and Sanger sequencing revealed the fusion to be in-frame with the kinase domain intact. Western blot of the tumor also indicated constitutive activation of the fusion based on phosphorylation of the fusion. Additionally, downstream kinase targets (PLCγ1, AKT, and MAPK) were also phosphorylated in the tumor, similar to levels observed in the TPM3-NTRK1 containing KM12 colorectal cancer cell line.

A 40-year-old patient with a left calf mass revealed by biopsy to be a low grade myxoid spindle cell carcinoma underwent surgery and radiotherapy. Over a 5-year period, the patient experienced 3 lung metastases, which were all resected. At year 6, unresectable metastases were found in the lungs and lymph nodes. FISH and targeted next generation RNA sequencing of an earlier lung metastasis revealed and confirmed an in-frame LMNA-NTRK1 fusion (exon 2 & exon 10) with the kinase domain intact. TRK inhibitor was administered and PET-CT scan revealed near complete response and no new lesions 1 year later.

The in-frame LMNA-NTRK1 fusion (exon 2 & exon 11) with intact kinase domain was found and confirmed by next generation sequencing, RT-PCR, FISH, and/or immunohistochemistry in 3 Spitz neoplasm cases. Compared to controls (wildtype NTRK1 overexpression and GFP), lentiviral mediated overexpression of LMNA-NTRK1 in mouse melanocyte cells (melan-a) displayed increased phosphorylation of the fusion and downstream kinase targets, as assessed by Western Blot. Treatment with the NTRK1 inhibitor, AZ-23, quenched fusion and pathway activation. Additionally, injection of LMNA-NTRK1 melan-a cells into immunocompromised mice resulted in the rapid growth of tumors at the injection site within 40 days. Similar results were observed in mice injected with melan-a cells overexpressing NRAS G12V or HRAS G12V, but no tumors were observed in mice injected with GFP control melan-a cells.

A total of 140 Spitzoid neoplasm cases were analyzed by FISH and/or targeted DNA and RNA sequencing (n=38). Mutually exclusive kinase fusions were found in 72 cases. NTRK1 fusions were observed in 23 cases (8/75 Spitz naevi; 8/32 atypical Spitz tumors; 7/33 Spitzoid melanomas) and their expression was confirmed by immunohistochemistry. NTRK1 expression was absent in cases without a NTRK1 rearrangement. A 743kb deletion leading to the in-frame LMNA-NTRK1 fusion (exon 2 & exon 11) with the kinase domain intact was found in 3/38 NGS analyzed cases (1 nevus, 1 atypical, 1Spitzoid) and was verified by RT-PCR.
Identification of an oncogenic mutation in FGFR4 in a human gastric tumour that leads to constitutive activation and sensitivity to ASP5878.

therapies: FGF/VEGF Receptor Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitor, PD173074
evidence_statement: FGFR4 tyrosine kinase domain mutations were found among 7 of 94 (7.5%) primary human RMS tumors. The mutants K535 and E550 increased autophosphorylation, Stat3 signaling, tumor proliferation, and metastatic potential when expressed in a murine RMS cell line. These mutants also transformed NIH 3T3 cells and led to an enhanced metastatic phenotype. Finally, murine RMS cell lines expressing the K535 and E550 FGFR4 mutants were substantially more susceptible to apoptosis in the presence of a pharmacologic FGFR inhibitor than the control cell lines expressing the empty vector or wild-type FGFR4.

This is a case report about an adult patient with acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) who had relapse in a testicle prior to systemic relapse of APL. Retrospective analysis of the preserved samples from the initial diagnosis and throughout the course of the disease identified recurrent FLT3 p.D839G and WT1 p.R458P variants. The information about the correlation between these genetic alterations and extramedullary relapse of APL is limited.

Murine pro-B lymphocyte lines Ba/F3 cells with FLT3-ITD were exposed to sorafenib with increasing low doses (i.e., 1-5 nmol/L) of sorafenib for up to 3 months, and further exposed for an additional 3 weeks to serial dilutions (5-50 nmol/L) of sorafanib. Sorafenib-resistant clones were collected for mutational analysis, of which a D651G mutation was identified in the tyrosine kinase domain 1 (TKD1). Similarly, samples from FLT3-ITD-mutated patients with AML who relapsed while on sorafenib also have acquired FLT3 point mutation in D651G. Ba/F3-ITD cells were engineered with D651G (Ba/F3-ITD+651) and evaluated for in vitro activity of sorafanib. Compared to control cells with only FLT3-ITD (EC50: 0.006 umol/L), cells with double mutation FLT3-ITD+D651G, demonstrated greater resistance to sorafanib-induced apoptosis (EC50: 0.69 umol/L). These results suggested that a mutation in TKD was sufficient to provide resistance to sorafenib-induced apoptosis.

Ba/F3-ITD cells were engineered with Y842C (Ba/F3-ITD+842) and evaluated for in vitro activity of sorefanib. Compared to control cells with only FLT3-ITD (EC50: 0.006 umol/L), cells with double mutation FLT3-ITD and Y842C demonstrated greater resistance to sorafenib-induced apoptosis (EC50: 2.6 umol/L). Although mutation in either TKD was sufficient to provide resistance to sorafenib-induced apoptosis, mutation in TKD2 (Y842C) was more important to the acquired resistance compared to alteration in TKD1 (D651G, N676D, I687F). Furthermore, FLT3-ITD cells containing compound mutations in both TKDs (D676D and Y842C in Ba/F3-ITD+676/842 cells) displayed greatest resistance to sorafenib-induced apoptosis (EC50: 6.6 umol/L). Cells harboring TKD2 mutations (Ba/F3-ITD+842 and Ba/F3+676/842) were least sensitive to the inhibitory effects of sorafenib, and maintained persistent phosphorylation of FLT3 and its downstream effectors ERK, AKT, Stat5, and S6K after exposure to sorafenib. Increased level of phosphorylated ERK was observed in ITD and Y842C cells (Ba/F3-ITD+842), and persistent phosphorylated-AKT, -Stat5, and -S6K in ITD and compound N676D/Y842C cells (Ba/F3-ITD+676/842). These results suggested FLT3 gene point mutations in TKD2 may result in conformational change that interfere with binding ability (i.e., accessibilty) of sorafenib more than mutations occurring in TKD1, and eluded to a bypass/feedback regulation could be an effective approach in the modulation of FLT3 downstream signaling.

The Ba/F3-ITD-Res cells contain both N676D and Y842C mutations in tyrosine kinase domain (TKD) 1 and TKD2, respectively. Compared to control cells with only FLT3-ITD (EC50: 0.006 umol/L), sorafenib-resistant cells demonstrated resistance to sorafenib-induced apoptosis (EC50: 4.2 umol/L). These results suggested that a mutation in TKD was sufficient to provide resistance to sorafenib-induced apoptosis.

The phase 2 EUCROSS trial (NCT02183870) examined the safety and efficacy of 250mg crizotinib twice daily in European ROS1-rearranged NSCLC patients. ROS1 status was assessed by break-apart FISH or both FISH and panel sequencing. Of 35 patients recruited, 34 were included in the safety population and 30 were evaluated for treatment response. The objective response rate was 73.3% (95% CI, 54.1-87.7) by independent review, all of which were partial responses. Disease control rate was 83.3% (95% CI, 65.3-94.4), and median progression-free survival was 20.0 months (95% CI, 9.6-NR). While safety and toxicity profiles were similar to previous crizotinib trials, there were more dose reductions observed. Adverse events were noted in 97% of patients, with just 1 (3%) patient experiencing a grade 4 or 5 AE.

All lines of conventional therapy (including allogeneic HSCT, blinatumomab, and CAR T cells) were inefficient for a 6-year-old boy with B-cell ALL and CNS infiltration (National Cancer Institute high risk). Conventional cytogenetics, FISH, and an Abbott break-apart probe of a peripheral blood sample collected at diagnosis revealed an unbalance translocation of the ETV6 locus. The patient relapsed twice and RNA sequencing of the initial diagnosis sample revealed a cytogenetically cryptic ETV6-NTRK3 fusion. Treatment with larotrectinib was initiated in combination with etoposide and methotrexate resulted in molecular remission in 66 days in bone marrow and CNS. A third relapse occurred 45 days after Larotrectinib was paused for CAR-T infusions. Larotrectinib was resumed with a dosage increase and again achieved sustained undetectable minimal residual disease after 66 days, and displayed molecular remission through 39 days. The authors suggest larotrectinib as a potential effective treatment for B-cell ALL patients harboring ETV6-NTRK3, including those with CNS infiltration.

Cell-free DNA was analysed in a patient with RET-mutant (M918T and V804M) medullary thyroid cancer and another patient with CCDC6-RET fusion positive non-small cell lung cancer who had developed acquired resistance to the RET inhibitor selpercatinib after initial response. The RET G810C/S and RET Y806C/N mutations were identified in cfDNA in the MTC patient and RET G810C mutation was the only identified mutation in the NSCLC patient. Cell line analyses using random mutation libraries identified four selpercatinib-resistant mutations and generation of selpercatinib-resistant cell lines by stepwise drug increase identified another RET mutation, thus identifying 5 selpercatinib-resistant RET mutations that were shown to also confer resistance to pralsetinib: RET V738A, RET Y806C/N, RET G810C/S. These mutations were shown to be non-gatekeeper mutations.

This study was designed to test the efficacy of FLT3 inhibitors in vitro against FLT3-ITD and other TKD variants clinically observed. IC50s were determined from immunoblots quantifying FLT3 phosphorylation in endogenous (Molm14) or ectopic expression FLT3-ITD cell lines (TF-1, Ba/F3) and the endogenous wildtype FLT3 SEMK2 cell line after gilteritinib treatment. IC50 values ranged from 1.4 to 1.8 nM in the three FLT3-ITD lines compared to 5nM in wildtype cells, suggesting increased sensitivity to the inhibitor. As measured by MTT assay, primary cultures from two AML patients with high allelic FLT3-ITD showed cytotoxic response to gilteritinib. Additionally, plasma taken from 3 patients receiving 120mg of gilteritinib daily was able to inhibit FLT3 phosphorylation in Molm14 cells.

In vitro gilteritinib treatment of MV4-11 and MOLM-13 cells, which endogenously express FLT3-ITD, showed growth suppression based on CellTiter GLO cytotoxicity assays with IC50 values of 0.92 nM (95% CI: 0.23–3.6 nM) and 2.9 nM (95% CI: 1.4–5.8 nM), respectively. Phosphorylation of FLT3 and its downstream targets were rapidly inhibited in MV4-11 cells relative to control treatment (DMSO). In a mouse xenograft model using MV4-11 cells, increasing doses of gilteritinib further reduced tumor size and growth and inhibited phosphorylation of both FLT3 and STAT5 (N=6, p<0.05 at lowest dose). Gilteritinib inhibited growth in vitro of Ba/F3 cells expressing FLT3-ITD (IC50 1.8nM; 95% CI: 1.0-3.0 nM) and in vivo as tumor maintenance or shrinkage was also significant in mice xenografted with Ba/F3 FLT3-ITD cells (N=5, p<0.001). Mice receiving an intra-bone marrow injection of MV4-11 cells labelled with luciferase began gilteritinib treatment on day 15. Gilteritinib treated mice showed significantly less widespread disease at day 42 than control counterparts (N=10, p<0.001) and significantly improved survival (log-rank, p<0.001).

In this study, records of 69 FLT3 mutated AML patients treated with different FLT3 inhibitors were analyzed for emergence of new mutations. Before the start of therapy with a FLT3 inhibitor, 60 (87%) of the 69 patients had a FLT3 ITD mutation, 4 (6%) had a D835/I836 kinase domain mutation, and 5 (7%) had combined ITD and D835/I836 mutations. It was observed that none of the patients with D835/I836, whether alone or concomitant with FLT3 ITD achieved a response. Mutational assessment at the time FLT3 inhibitor treatment was discontinued showed that 68% of patients were unchanged, 10% had become undetectable, and 22% of patients progressed from a single ITD to have combined ITD+D835/I836 mutations. In those patients with unchanged FLT3 mutation at progression the median survival was 5 months, while in those with undetectable and with combined ITD-D835/I836 mutations the median survival was 7 months respectively

In this study, 162 pediatric ALL patients (50 infants younger than 11 months and 112 children older than 1 year (93 B-cell precursors, 19 T-cell phenotypes)—in addition to 81 healthy donors were analyzed. 44 out of the 50 infants had CD10- early pre-B cell ALL with MLL rearrangements. Out of these 44 infants, one infant had an I836M mutation and 2 infants has the I836del. All the mutations were heterozygous, and the open reading frame was conserved. Ile836del has also been shown to have strong autophosphorylation, suggesting an association with the proliferation of leukemic cells because these mutations were detected in adult AML and tended to reduce disease-free survival. However, this difference was statistically not significant. 6 of 8 patients with the FLT3 TKD mutations died, and the overall survival rate in the patients with the mutations was lower than that in the patients with wild-type FLT3, though the difference was not significant (P = .42)

Single strand polymorphism targeting FLT3 in addition to RUNX1, KIT, CEBPA, PTPN11, and NRAS was carried out to identify novel recurring gene mutations in an acute myeloid leukemia cohort comprised of 175 samples stratified by French-American-British type (excluding FAB type M3). Out of these samples, D839G was measured to be present in 2 of these patients. Unlike other variants in this study, there was remission data available for these specific variants in the study. The frequency of this variant in the cohort was noted to reflect the frequency of this variant in the AML population. Overall, this was a variant discovery paper that only measured the frequency of variants in the cohort, rather than a mechanistic paper with follow-up studies, so no further data was provided.

Conventional cytogenetics, FISH, and an Abbott break-apart probe of a peripheral blood sample collected at diagnosis of a 6-year-old boy with B-cell ALL and CNS infiltration (National Cancer Institute high risk) revealed an unbalance translocation of the ETV6 locus. RNA sequencing of detected a cytogenetically cryptic ETV6-NTRK3 fusion. Larotrectinib therapy achieved remission of the patient’s two separate relapses. Patient derived xenografts injected into mice and treated with Larotrectinib demonstrated significant reductions in spleen volume, blasts in spleen, and blast in bone marrow (p < .0001) compared to controls 25 days after injection. Larotrectinib treatment was effective regardless of the day of initiation post xenograft injection (1 day or 8 days after).

The tyrosine kinase domain of NTRK3 was inserted into exon 6 of Etv6 to create conditional knock-in Etv6-NTRK3 mice . Expression was induced in pre-b cells during lymphoid development by CD19-Cre. Fusion expression in the bone marrow was confirmed by RT-PCR. Etv6-NTRK3/+ CD19-Cre mice developed aggressive lymphoid leukemia. Compared to controls (Etv6-NTRK3/+; n=28), Etv6-NTRK3/+ CD19-Cre mice (n=27) displayed worse overall survival (p<.0001), decreased body weight (p<.0001), increased spleen weights (p<.05), and increased circulating CD19+/B220+ cells (p=.0008). Over 60% of Etv6-NTRK3 CD19-Cre mice demonstrated extramedullary tumors and over 50% presented with central nervous system infiltration. RNA-sequencing indicated upregulation of the AP1 complex in the Etv6-NTRK3 CD19-Cre mice. The authors conclude this ETV6-NTRK3 Cre-19 mouse model mimics human B-ALL.

A novel mutation (FLT3 Y842C) was detected in 2 AML patients (n = 110). Ex vivo PKC412 treatment of primary blasts resulted in suppression of constitutive FLT3 and STAT-5 activation (Figure 1D). Cell cycle analysis showed that PKC412 caused significant apoptotic cell death (Figure 2B), suggesting that FLT3 Y842C is sensitive to the FLT3 kinase inhibitor PKC412 at the cellular level in vitro.

FLT3-Y842C demonstrated constitutive activation of FLT3 and of the downstream molecule STAT-5 in 32D cells overexpressing FLT3-Y842C and in primary AML blasts from an AML patient, suggesting the functional significance of this novel mutation in AML.

This study evaluates the genetic features of melanotic schwannoma (MS). Twelve cases of MS were examined. A hybrid capture-based next-generation sequencing (NGS) assay screened the coding exons for mutations in 341 key cancer-associated genes. Single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP)-array was done to analyze copy number variations. The cases of MS are categorized as one PRKAR1A mutation with monosomy, one PRKAR1A mutation coupled with a loss of heterozygosity of chromosome 17q, and two mutations of the PRKAR1A gene. Five of the cases have chromosome 17 monosomy with one PRKAR1A mutation. Four of the cases have copy neutral loss of heterozygosity of chromosome 17q with one mutation in PRKAR1A. Three cases have two different mutations in the PRKAR1A gene. Thus, the authors conclude that PRKAR1A gene acts as a tumor suppressor in melanocytic schwannoma, follows the Knudson hypothesis, and is shown to be involved in the pathogenesis of melanotic schwannoma.

Authors note that inhibitory effects were more pronounced in cells treated with trametinib than cells treated with selumetinib.

44 archival FFPE samples from confirmed cases of Wilms tumor with mean age 3 years 2 months, and taken from the most histologically aggressive parts of each tumor, were stained with p53 monoclonal antibody and the corresponding patient clinical data was analyzed. 24 samples were p53 positive, and did not correlate with age or sex. All tumors with unfavorable histology were p53 positive, in contrast to 13 of 33 tumors with favorable histology, with weak-moderate p53 signal (p<0.001). 2 year overall survival rate was 89.2% in p53 negative, and 55.7% for p53 positive cases (P = .01), and mean survival was 46 months in p53 negative and 26 months in p53 positive cases (P = .02). Compared with p53 negative, tumors with week to moderate p53 signal had HR 3.75 (P = .05), and high signal had HR 8.61 (P = .01). No significant correlation was seen between tumor clinicopathological stage and p53 expression.

In BaF3 cells, the R248C mutant was shown to fully activate FGFR3 with complete independence of the ligand presence. Ligand independent activation was determined by proliferation, phosphorylation, and dimerization assays (via the formation of an intermolecular disulfide bond).

Prostate cancer cell lines over-expressing TSPYL1 P62S had similar levels of cell proliferation as control cells normally expressing TSPYL1 wildtype when treated with abiraterone. Authors note that TSPYL1 P62S abolished TSPYL1 regulation of the abiraterone metabolizing enzyme CYP3A4, and concluded that TSPYL1 P62S may be a marker for abiraterone response in prostate cancer patients.

Nine patients with BRAF V600R mutated metastatic melanoma were given dabrafenib (n=7) or vemurafenib (n=2) monotherapy as part of a compassionate access program. Five out of six radiographically assessed patients had achieved partial response, and one patient progressed. Median PFS for the six patients was 3.6 months (2.1-10.4 months). Four out of five responders were still alive at time of reporting, all of whom had taken dabrafenib. One responder was treated with vemurafenib and had an overall survival of 9.6 months. Two additional patients who had not been radiographically assessed at time of reporting experienced rapid clinical response (reduction in size of subcutaneous metastases and resolution of neurological symptoms). The authors concluded that dabrafenib and vemurafenib can be effective treatments for BRAF V600R mutated metastatic melanoma.

A 74 year old male patient was diagnosed with metastatic melanoma following histological assessment of multiple brain and lung tumors. One tumor harbored BRAF V600E and the patient began dabrafenib monotherapy as part of a compassionate access program. Partial response was confirmed after 8 weeks of therapy with substantial decrease in tumor size and stable intracranial disease. Disease progression within the brain was observed at 10 months, and the patient was treated with whole brain radiotherapy. The patient continued on dabrafenib and was alive at the time of reporting (12 months after dabrafenib initiation).

293 adult cases of low grade gliomas (LGGs) underwent a variety of analyses, including but not limited to exome sequencing (289 samples), copy number profiling (285), mRNA sequencing (277) and sequencing of the TERT promoter region (287). In IDH-mutant LGGs with no 1p/19q codeletion (i.e. astrocytomas), inactivating ATRX alterations were found in 86% of cases. The majority of alterations were somatic mutations (SNV/indels - 79%), high deletions (3%), gene fusions (2%) or a combination (2%). Concomitant reduced mRNA expression of ATRX was observed. Gene fusion partners for ATRX included ZNF304, DDX11L1 and BCL2. TP53 mutations also typified the IDH-mutant/non-1p/19q codeleted group, occuring in 94% of cases. In IDH-mutant LGGs with 1p/19q codeletion (i.e. oligodendrogliomas), ATRX mutations were rare. TERT promoter mutations were frequent in this group, occuring in 96% of cases. By contrast, TERT promoter mutations occured in 4% of non-1p/19q codeleted cases, where ATRX mutations were frequent. ATRX mutations therefore appeared mutually exclusive with TERT promoter mutations.

evidence_statement: A case report of a 51Y male patient presenting with headaches and a family history of VHL disease revealed multiple CNS hemangioblastomas, bilateral clear cell renal cell carcinomas (ccRCC), pheochromocytoma, and a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor. A germline mutation of VHL p.Arg167Trp was confirmed. The patient underwent resection of the largest cerebellar lesion, total right and partial left sided nephrectomy, and adrenalectomy. Pazopanib monotherapy was initiated for treatment of metastatic RCC. The patient experienced shrinkage of some but not all spinal hemangiolastomas. After 21 months on pazopanib, the patient was placed on a drug holiday, and many of the CNS hemangioblastomas grew slightly.

evidence_statement: A study reports a 58Y male patient with macrohematuria and a history of nephrectomy due to renal cell carcinoma. The patient showed retinal angiomatosis, cerebellar hemangioblastomas, multiple pancreatic cysts, right kidney with polycystic features plus two RCC. The patient's three children, two females and one male, showed VHL lesions: retinal angiomatosis, cerebellar hemangioblastomas and polycystic kidney disease. The affected family members were screened for mutations in the VHL gene and were found with a deletion encompassing exon 1 of the VHL gene. ACMG: PP4

evidence_statement: Between 1976 and 1997, nine RCC patients from three VHL families were evaluated and treated in the University Hospital of Utrecht. Patients 1–7 were from one large family with a p.Val170Asp mutation in the VHL gene. All 7 patients were genetically confirmed with the mutation. Patient 1 (II-5) was a male diagnosed with their first VHL phenotype (RCC) at 42Y. He also had retinal capillary angioma; hemangioblastoma; pheochromocytoma; renal cyst and his last known age is 64Y old in 1997. Patient 2 (II-7) was a female diagnosed with their first VHL phenotype (RCC + PHEO) at 40Y. She also had CNS hemangioblastoma; renal cyst and her last known age is 58Y old in 1997. Patient 3 (III-11) was a male diagnosed with their first VHL phenotype (RCC + retinal angioma) at 26Y. He also had CNS hemangioblastoma; renal cyst and his last known age is 35Y old in 1997. Patient 4 (III-12) was a male diagnosed with their first VHL phenotype (renal cyst) at 28Y. He also had renal cell carcinoma and his last known age is 33Y old in 1997. Patient 5 (III-8) was a female diagnosed with their first VHL phenotype (RCC) at 24Y. She also had pheochromocytoma and her last known age is 30Y old in 1997. Patient 6 (III-13) was a female diagnosed with their first VHL phenotype (hemangioblastoma) at 20Y. She also had renal cell carcinoma; retinal capillary angioma; and her last known age is 30Y old in 1997. Patient 7 (III-4) was a male diagnosed with their first VHL phenotype (RCC and retinal angioma) at 24Y. He also had hemangioblastoma; pheochromocytoma and his last known age is 41Y old in 1997. 6 other family A members were not available for genotype analysis but had VHL related symptoms. Family member I-1 was a female with renal cell carcinoma and died at 55Y. Member II-3 was male with cerebellar hemangioblastoma and died at 39Y. Member II-11 was male with pheochromocytoma; cerebellar hemangioblastoma and died at 33Y. The cases of fifty-four Black African patients presenting with pheochromocytoma between 1980 and 2009 were reviewed. Two patients had VHL syndrome. In one patient, the diagnosis was based on the presence of a symptomatic cerebellar hemangioblastoma and a mildly symptomatic adrenal pheochromocytoma which were successfully removed. Genetic testing revealed a missense mutation VHL P86S (c.256C>T). Further investigation revealed bilateral renal cell carcinoma. The patient had family history of brain tumors (father). The patient's daughter was positive for the VHL variant. Although the daughter is clinically well, she had evidence on MRI of brain and spinal cord hemangioblastomas. ACMG: PM1 (P86 is an established germline hotspot), PP4.

Patients' records in a tertiary care university hospital were reviewed. Fifty-four Black patients presenting with phaeochromocytoma between 1980 and 2009 were included. Two patients had VHL syndrome (submitted for publication). The second diagnosis of VHL syndrome was made in the pregnant woman (Case 9) who had bilateral adrenal phaeochromocytomas. There were no clinical features of VHL syndrome; however, MRI showed a haemangioblastoma in the cervical spine. Genetic testing revealed a missense mutation (c.499C>T) in the VHL gene, located on chromosome 3p26-p25. Her 6-year-old daughter screened positive for the mutation; her 8-year-old son was negative. Both mother and daughter will be investigated further and monitored long-term. ACMG PP4

High expression of ACTL6A has been shown to be associated with resistance to cisplatin in multiple cancer types. In vitro experiments using A549 and H1299 lung cancer cell lines showed that overexpression of ACTL6A resulted in significantly increased cell survival following cisplatin treatment, while shRNA knockdown restored cisplatin sensitivity. Similarly, xenografts overexpressing ACTL6A showed significantly higher tumour volume and weight after cisplatin treatment when compared with control xenografts. Further experiments demonstrated that ACTL6A regulates the repair of cisplatin-induced damage by maintaining SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complex integrity.

ACTL6A plays a role in DNA damage repair by maintaining integrity of the SWI/SNF complex, and is associated with resistance to cisplatin. Results from cell viability and survival assays showed that treatment with the pan-HDAC inhibitor panobinostat re-sensitized ACTL6A overexpressing lung cancer cells to cisplatin. Similarly, combination treatment had synergistic effect on inhibiting the growth of lung cancer xenografts. Further experiments showed that panobinostat blocked the interaction between ACTL6A and other SWI/SNF components and inhibited the enhanced clearance of cisplatin-DNA adducts normally seen in ACTL6A overexpressing cells.

A preclinical study investigated the sensitivity of PARP inhibitors in Neuroblastoma with MYCN-amplified (IMR-32) cells and found a decrease in cellular viability in comparison to the non-MYCN amplified expressing SHEPP-1 cells (Student’s t-test p<0.001 at 5 μM olaparib, p<0.01 at 5 nM talazoparib and p<0.05 at 5 μM veliparib). Sensitivity to PARP inhibitors of all cell lines showed to be dependent on MYCN expression with the GI50 values being lower in MYCN expressing cells than non-expressing cell lines and average GI50 value for cell lines showing intermediate MYCN expression (p<0.05 for both olaparib (AZD-2281) and niraparib (MK-4827)). These data suggest that MYCN expression can be indicative of response and sensitivity to PARP inhibitors. MYCN expressing mice treated with olaparib (n=8) showed significantly prolonged survival (log-rank p<0.05) as well as significantly decreased tumor growth (Student’s t-test p<0.01) compared to vehicle-treated animals (n=9).

In a subprotocol of the NCI-MATCH Trial (EAY131-Y Nonrandomized Trial), 35 patients with AKT E17K Mutant Tumors progressive after Standard therapy received Treatment with capivasertib. Among the patients, breast (18 patients total; among which 15 with hormone receptor (HR)-positive/ERBB2-negative and 3 with triple-negative disease) and gynecologic (n=11) cancers were the most frequent. The primary end point, ORR rate was 28.6% (95% CI, 15%-46%). One patient with endometrioid endometrial adenocarcinoma achieved a CR (35.6 months on therapy). Partial responses were reported in: 7 HR-positive/ERBB2-negative breast cancer, 1 uterine leiomyosarcoma, and 1 oncocytic parotid gland carcinoma. Sixteen patients (46%) had stable disease as the best response, 2 (6%) had progressive disease, and 7 (20%) were not evaluable. With a median follow-up of 28.4 months, the overall 6-month PFS rate was 50% (95% CI, 35%-71%).

Within a preclinical trial, 37 patients with metastatic melanoma showed a limited number of cases that responded to anti-PD-1 antibodies in correlation to higher immunohistochemical PD-L1 expression. Of the 37 patients enrolled, only 18 had pretreatment tumor specimens available for PD-L1 staining. Those with PD-L1 positive immunostaining (1% cutoff value) attained an overall response rate (ORR) of 20% (2 of 10 patients) and a disease control rate (DCR) of 80% (8 of 10 patients) while the negative PD-L1 group’s ORR was 12.5% (1 of 8 patients) of patients and DCR of 37.5% (3 of 8 patients). The median progression-free survival (PFS) was 6.2 months for the PD-L1 positive group and 1.6 months in the PD-L1 negative group (p=0.137). Although the positive PD-L1 group had a better ORR and median PFS than negative PD-L1 these findings were not statistically significant.

Within a phase one clinical trial, the response to atezolizumab from 938 patients with non-small cell carcinoma indicated high PD-L1 expression corresponded independently to response to atezolizumab on tumor cells (TC) and or infiltrating immune cells (IC).PD-L1 high expression cell types had an overall objective response rate including TC3 with an ORR of 40% and IC3 with an ORR of 22%, while PD-L1-negative tumors response rates were 8%. For PD-L1 positive tumors TC3 patients showed a median progression-free survival of 11 months (95% CI) and IC3 patients 4.7 mo (95% CI, 2.8–5.8) with in comparison to PD-L1 negative (TC0 and IC0) 2.8 mo (95% CI, 1.5–4.2). Moreover, the fastest median time of response recorded correlated to the patients expressing PD-L1 the highest within both subgroups of TC and IC. This suggests the possible associative durable clinical efficacy of atezolizumab with patients expressing PD-L1 in their TC or IC.

In a Clinic Phase 2 Consortium, 44 patients with metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma had an overall response rate (ORR) to nivolumab of 20.5%; 1 complete response lasting over 12 months; 8 partial responses with a median duration of response 9.3 months; 15 had stable disease (SD) with 3 having SD for over 12 months; 18 has disease progression; and two patients were not evaluated for response. In addition to analysis of ORR, the plasma-based biomarkers were also investigated and found in a descriptive analysis that 6 patients of 18 (33%) with PD-L1 positive tumors (1% expression) responded while only 3 of 23 patients (13%) with PD-L1 negative tumors responded to nivolumab. However, these results were not statistically significant and indicate the need to further perform studies on biomarkers within a larger cohort to confirm the trend.

This study consists of a cohort of 42 pediatric and adult patients with sarcomas that were classified as undifferentiated. Six of the forty two patients had BCOR::CCNB3 fusions detected by whole transcriptome paired-end RNA sequencing. The BCOR::CCNB3 fusion occurred between exon 15 of BCOR and exon 5 of CCNB3. The fusion-positive tumors were found in male patients between the ages of 7 and 13; these tumors were equally distributed in the axial and extra-axial locations. Reverse-transcriptase PCR was performed on the six cases and revealed the fusion transcript in all six cases with high sensitivity and specificity. In five of the six cases, pre-treatment CCNB3 nuclear staining was strongly positive. This study illustrates that the BCOR::CCNB3 fusion can be used as a marker for classification of undifferentiated or unclassified sarcomas into the novel genetic subgroup of BCOR sarcomas.

This study consists of a cohort of 115 patients with a class of sarcomas that had similar morphology to Ewing sarcoma. The presence of a CIC rearrangement was detected in all the cases by FISH. Previously, it was unclear whether this class of sarcomas should be classified as a separate entity or be classified as a variant of Ewing sarcoma. CIC-rearranged sarcomas showed a male predominance with an average age of 32 years old. A CIC::DUX4 fusion was found by additional FISH testing for DUX4 loci in 57% of the cases, with either a translocation between chromosomes 4 and 19 or between chromosomes 10 and 19. 57 patients were followed clinically and showed a 5-year survival rate of 43%, which was significantly lower than the 77% 5-year survival rate of Ewing sarcoma patients (p=0.002). In histologic evaluation, stromal myxoid change was a common finding in CIC-positive tumors, while this is not usually found in Ewing sarcoma. CIC-positive tumors showed a diffuse CD99 immunohistochemical staining pattern in only 23% of the cases, in contrast to that found in Ewing sarcoma, which showed a diffuse CD99 staining pattern in almost all of the cases. Therefore, this study provides evidence that sarcomas that contain CIC::DUX4 fusion should be considered a separate entity, distinct from Ewing sarcoma.

This retrospective study evaluated 72 pediatric medulloblastoma patients for CTNNB1 mutations (by direct sequencing), copy number alterations (by array-comparative genomic hybridization), and beta-catenin protein expression (by immunohistochemistry). CTNNB1 mutations were detected in six tumors (D32Y [n=1], S33F [n=3], G34R [n=1], I35K [n=1]). All six cases of extensive beta-catenin nuclear staining (>50% of tumor cells) were CTNNB1 mutated, and 5/6 harbored a complete chromosome 6 loss. All six patients with CTNNB1 mutated tumors had classic histology. CTNNB1 mutated medulloblastomas were associated with higher mean age at diagnosis (127.7 months vs 85.1months, p = 0.01), lack of metastatic disease (0/6 vs 20/56), and greater mean 5-year overall survival (OS; 100% vs 53.7%, p =0.047) compared to wildtype CTNNB1 tumors. All six patients were in first complete remission at the time of last follow-up. When OS of the 6 CTNNB1-mt patients was compared to 19 patients with similar characteristics (>3 years at diagnosis, classic histology, absence of metastatic disease), a trend toward longer survival for CTNNB-1 mutated patients was evident. All three patients with focal beta-catenin nucleopositivity (<10% of tumor cells) died within 3 years of diagnosis. Authors conclude that CTNNB1 mutations are associated with favorable outcome in pediatric medulloblastomas.

Based on the results of this patient and other CTNNB1 mutated patients in the larger cohort, authors concluded that CTNNB1 mutants are prognostic for favorable outcome in pediatric medulloblastoma.

Open label phase 2 (Clinical Level B) trial including patients from across the globe (USA, Italy, and the Netherlands) investigating sensitivity to Vemurafenib in patients that have BRAF V600E-positive papillary thyroid cancer that have become resistant to radioactive iodine (the standard treatment). There were 116 patients identified for this trial, 51 of which met the conditions to be included. These 51 patients were split into two cohorts: 1) patients that had never been treated with a multikinase inhibitor targeting VEGFR and 2) patients that have previously been treated with a VEGFR multikinase inhibitor. In cohort 1, ten of 26 patients had best overall response. Best overall response was defined as the proportion of patients with a complete or partial response, however these ten patients were all partial response. In the same cohort 1, nine had achieved stable disease control for at least six months; therefore, 19 patients achieved disease control (73% of total cohort 1, 95% CI 52-88). In cohort 2, of 23 eligible patients, six had a partial response as best overall response and six had stable disease control for at least six months; therefore, 12 patients achieved disease control. (55% of total cohort 2, 95% CI 32-76). The authors conclude that vemurafenib is a potential treatment option for late-stage BRAF V600E-positive papillary thyroid cancer for treatment in patients naïve to a multikinase inhibitor (Cohort 1) and to patients that have been previously treated with a multikinase inhibitor (Cohort 2).

The non-randomized, sequential phase II ICEBERG trial evaluated the efficacy and safety of olaparib monotherapy in 54 patients (2 cohorts of 27 patients, treated with 400mg or 100 mg twice daily) with a germline BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation and metastatic or locally advanced breast cancer. 34 patients had mutations in only BRCA1, 11 of which had triple negative breast cancer. One patient had in the 100mg cohort had mutations in both BRCA1 and BRCA2 (Q563X and C1573Y). The objective response rate within the 400mg cohort was 50% (1 complete response, 8 partial response, 7 stable disease, 2 progressive disease), and it was 19% within the 100mg cohort (3 PR, 9 SD, 4 PD). Authors conclude their results provide proof of concept for the utility of treating breast cancer patients harboring germline BRCA1 mutations with olaparib.

Gilteritinib is the first FLT3 inhibitor approved by the Food and Drug administration (FDA) as monotherapy in adult refractory/relapse acute myeloid leukemia (R/R AML) patients with FLT3-ITD and/or tyrosine kinase domain (TKD) D835/I836 mutations. The noncanonical TKD mutation G697S was identified as a gilteritinib resistance-conferring mutation through in vitro mutagenesis screen, present in resistant clones of FLT3-ITD/D835V-expressing Ba/F3 cells under the selection of 20nm gilteritinib. Further in vitro assays showed that noncanonical TKD mutations F691L, Y693C/N, G697S and D698N conferred a moderate degree of gilteritinib resistance in vitro in either ITD or ITD/D835V background, with G697S demonstrating the highest degree of resistance with an IC50 of ~100nM, ~40X higher than that of FLT3-ITD (for reference, 200-2000X resistance was seen in the most resistant FLT3-ITD/D835V substitutions to type II FLT3 inhibitors in vitro). Of note, G697S was not seen in resistant clones under the selection of 40nM gilteritinib in vitro, a concentration below the steady-state concentration achieved in patients stabilized on the FDA-approved dose of 120mg. It was also not detected in 240 patients before the initiation of gilteritinib therapy nor in the 5 patients acquiring additional FLT3 TKD mutations during therapy in the CHRYSAMLIS gilteritinib phase 1/2 study in R/R AML. Computer modeling showed that G697S lacked 1 Cα-H atom for the CH-π interaction with gilteritinib and its side chain would have a steric clash with the phenyl ring of gilteritinib, providing a structural basis for gilteritinib resistance.

Through the analysis of 10 patient-derived glioblastoma cells, AMG232 was found to have increased sensitivity in comparison to RG7112 with the average IC50 of 76nM vs. 720nM; thus indicating a 9.5 fold increase of effectiveness in TP53 wild-type cells in response to AMG232. Significantly, 464T stem cells possessing MDM2 gene amplification were found to be highly sensitive in response to AMG232 with an IC50 of 5.3 nM. Overall these findings suggest TP53 wild-type patient-derived glioblastoma cells to be increasingly more responsive and sensitive to AMG232.

Within a preclinical study 15 patient samples with adenoid cystic carcinoma MYB-NFIB fusion activation loop can be modulated through AKT-dependent signaling induced by IGF1R overexpression and downregulated through IGF-R1-inhibition (% expression of control ± SD = 27.2 ± 1.3, P < .001). Out of the fifteen patient samples all had overexpression of IGF1R as well as EGFR and MET compared to normal salivary gland tissue (P=.004). Mouse model xenograft inhibition of IGF-R1, MET and EGFR using a combination of linsitinib, crizotinib and gefitinib showed significant interference of growth (ACCX5M1, P = .006; ACCX6, P = .04). Additionally, siRNA knockdown of IGF1R decreased MYB-NFIB mRNA by 50% to 60% as well as lowered cell proliferation (mean ± SD, P < .001). As a result of these findings it can be inferred that regulation of IGF-R1 and other predominantly overexpressed genes in ACC can directly influence MYB-NFIB fusion loop activation.
