A 52-year-old Caucasian male with second relapsed B-ALL following chemotherapy and blinatumomab (NCT02013167). BMA obtained at study entry on the INOVATE trial (NCT01564784) was analyzed by RNA-seq and showed a novel chimeric fusion that juxtaposed exon 7 of G3BP2 to exon 11 of KIT and encoded a fusion protein retaining the nuclear transport factor 2 domain (NTF2) of G3BP2 and the entire kinase domain of KIT. Of note, the patient was not treated with tyrosine kinase inhibitors, and primary leukemia cells were not available for functional studies. The B-ALL sample was predicted as Ph-like B-ALL using Prediction analysis of microarrays (PAM) and clustered with Ph-like B-ALL. To investigate the oncogenic role of this fusion: G3BP2-KIT fusion transcript, truncated KIT or empty viral vector were cloned and expressed in IL-3–dependent Ba/F3 and in IL-7–dependent ARF null pre-B cells. Only the cells expressing G3BP2-KIT sustained cytokine independent proliferation, suggesting that the 5’ G3BP1 is necessary to confer oncogenic properties to truncated KIT, likely by promoting KIT dimerization. Both Ba/F3 and ARF null pre-B cells expressing G3BP2-KIT but not those transduced with empty vector, showed phosphorylation of KIT and activation of JAK-STAT signaling pathway. Transplantation of ARF null pre-B cells expressing G3BP2-KIT in C57BL6 sublethally irradiated mice resulted in the development of B-ALL. WES did not detect pathogenetic cooperating driver sequence mutations or copy number changes supporting the fact that G3BP2-KIT is a necessary and sufficient oncogenic driver alteration.

Family history was not described for the patient.

Three recurrent CTCF mutations found in endometrial carcinoma were expressed in Ishikawa cells and compared to expression of wild-type CTCF. The K365T mutation did not demonstrate altered localization or anti-proliferative effects but a protective effect against UV-incuded apoptosis was observed.

Phase II trial of sunitinib in 40 patients with first recurrence of primary glioblastoma. Median PFS 2.2 mo, median OS 9.2 mo, 5 stable disease >=6 months, no objective responses, so primary study endpoint was not met. However, IHC of multiple receptor kinases was performed, and protein expression of KIT in vascular endothelial cells was associated with longer PFS (P = .017; HR, 2.564; 95% CI, 1.180–5.570). All 5 with stable disease were KIT+ in vascular endothelial cells. Note KIT staining was not observed in tumour cells. No association with OS.

Analysis of 5 uterine serous carcinoma (USC) primary cell lines in vitro indicated enhanced sensitivity to CDK2/9 inhibitor CYC065 in cell lines overexpressing cyclin E1 (CCNE1) in comparison to low CCNE1-expressing cell lines (p=0.0003). Combination of CYC065 and taselisib in the primary tumor models of CCNE1 amplified cell lines USC-ARK-1 and USC-ARK-2, potentiated the inhibition of tumor growth than either single agent alone (USC-ARK-1 p<0.05 and USC-ARK-2 p<0.05). In vivo combination of CYC065 and Taselisib in SCID mice bearing USC-ARK-1-derived xenografts inhibited tumor growth more effectively than the single agents alone (p<0.03). In vivo USC-ARK-1- derived xenografts treated with single agent CYC065 (22.5 mg kg−1) demonstrated significant reduction in tumor growth when compared to the vehicle treated mice (p=0.012). Given this data, a single agent of CYC065 may induce tumor inhibition in vitro and in vivo however, combination with taselisib enhances inhibition in CCNE1-amplified USC cells.

Breast cancer cell lines derived from T-47D (vector control, overexpress cyclin E1, overexpress cyclin E2) were treated with CDK4/6 inhibitor PD0332991 and CDK2 inhibitor SNS-032 as single agents and in combination. Single agent treatment with PD0332991 in cyclin E1- or cyclin E2–overexpressing cells showed to be ineffective at reducing the relative cell number and bromodeoxyuridine (BrdU) incorporation assay in comparison to the vector control cells; thus indicating resistance to CDK4/6 inhibitor PD033299. However, combination of PD0332991 and SNS-032 reduced BrdURd incorporation and relative cell number compared to single agents. This effect of combinational therapies suggests CDK4 inhibitor resistance due to overexpression of cyclin E1 or E2, can be overcome by combining CDK2 inhibitors such as SNS-032.

In a study of 114 unrelated VHL families, 85 germline mutations were found. VHL mutations were detected in affected family members, but not in unaffected family members or 96 normal individuals. 18 families were listed with deletions in the VHL gene (family IDs: 2447, 3625, 3968, 4411, 2092, 3764, 3102, 1678, 3183, 4383, 3978, 3567, 1970, 2875, 3106, 3222, 3512 and 3103). This was detailed as a large deletion (4-380 Kb) detected by Southern blotting or pulsed-field gel electrophoresis. No further mutation information was provided specified to each family. Familial specific information provided is as follows: family 2447 consisted of 15 members and 9 of these members had CNS hemangioblastomas. Family 3625 had 10 members, 5 of which has CNS hemangioblastomas and 1 has renal cell carcinoma. Family 3968 had 6 members, all with CNS hemangioblastoma and 1 with renal cell carcinoma. Family 4411 consisted of just one member with renal cell carcinoma. Family 2092 had 8 members, 5 had retinal capillary angiomas, 5 with CNS hemangioblastomas, and 4 with renal cell carcinoma. Family 3764 had 8 members, 4 retinal capillary angiomas, had 6 had CNS hemangioblastomas and 5 had renal cell carcinoma. Family 3102 had 6 members 3 retinal capillary angiomas, had 2 had CNS hemangioblastomas and 4 had renal cell carcinoma. Family 1678 had 5 members, all of which had renal cell carcinomas, 3 had retinal capillary angiomas, and 3 had CNS hemangioblastomas. Family 3183 had 8 members, all of which had retinal capillary angiomas, 6 had CNS hemangioblastomas, and 1 had renal cell carcinoma. Family 4383 consisted of 2 members, both of which had retinal and CNS hemangioblastomas, and 1 had renal cell carcinoma. Family 3978 was one individual with retinal and CNS hemangioblastomas. Family 3567 had 2 total members each with renal cell carcinoma, and one of which had a CNS hemangioblastoma. Family 1970 had 2 members both with retinal capillary angiomas and renal cell carcinoma. Family 2875 had 8 members, of which, 5 had retinal capillary angiomas, 6 had CNS hemangioblastomas and 6 had renal cell carcinoma. Family 3106 had 8 members, 4 had retinal capillary angiomas, 4 had CNS hemangioblastomas and 4 had renal cell carcinoma. Family 3222 consisted of 2 members, both with CNS hemangioblastomas and 1 with renal cell carcinoma. Family 3512 was one member with retinal and CNS hemangioblastomas, and renal cell carcinoma. Lastly, family 3103 had 20 members, 7 of which had retinal angioma (hemangiomas), 9 had hemangioblastomas, 8 had renal cell carcinoma, and 1 had pheochromocytoma.

Case studies of three families affected by VHL and their children were described. Families 2 and 3 were found to have a germline exon 3 variant (unspecified) in VHL. Proband of family 2 presented with: right pheochromocytoma (8Y), brain hemangioblastoma (17Y), retinal haemangiomas (18Y), recurrent cerebellar hemangioblastoma (21Y) and left pheochromocytoma (21Y). Her daughter had this mutation and presented with pheochromocytoma (12Y). Proband of family 3 presented with: pheochromocytoma and retinal capillary hemangioma (22Y). Two of his sons were positive for this genetic mutation. One son was asymptomatic and the other presented with pheochromocytoma (13Y). Probands of families 2 and 3 were siblings whose father was positive for this mutation and presented with pheochromocytoma and stomach carcinoma.

An update on the genetic findings pertaining to a previously published (pmids: 8239848, 21713522) large familial pheochromocytoma Pennsylvania kindred. The family is comprised of: 18 living individuals with only pheochromocytoma; 7 living individuals with only retinal angioma; 6 living individuals with both; 51 other first-degree relatives; 5 additional relatives with pheochromocytomas, including a 69Y woman and her 42Y son described previously as non-penetrant individuals (pmid 8239848). Family classified as a VHL Type 2A (pheochromocytoma, retinal angioma, CNS hemangioblastoma, and little to no RCC). All 31 individuals (including 6 archival specimens) with a diagnosis of pheochromocytoma, retinal angioma or both had the identical T547C (legacy nomenclature) germline mutation determined through PCR, single-strand conformational polymorphism analysis and direct sequencing.

A large scale tumor genome analysis identified p190RhoGAP-encoding gene ARHGAP35 to be frequently mutated in endometrial tumours. Mutant and wild-type HA-tagged ARHGAP35 constructs were created and expressed in Huh7 cells for functional analysis. Mutations affecting the PLS domain (including S866F) demonstrated increased GAP activity and altered localization compared to wild type . The authors concluded these mutations are gain of function and allow cancer cells to migrate randomly.

Phase II study of pasireotide in metastatic neuroendocrine tumours enrolled 29 patients. Overall median PFS was 11 months (95% CI, 7.6–16 months). High SSTR5 expression (seen in 17/22 samples measured) was associated with prolonged PFS (P=0.0068). Median PFS for low-SSTR5 tumours was 2.8 months (95% CI, 2.3–12.1 months) vs high tumours 19.9 months (95% CI, 7.7–29.1 months).

Clear cell RCC tumors from patients with von Hippel-Lindau disease were investigated for HIF expression. Tumours were from 4 patients with confirmed germline partial VHL deletions (patient 4 had 2 tumors, and patients 3 and 6 each had 1 tumor. All patients had hereditary renal carcinoma syndrome. Germline genetic testing was confirmed in the families of all patients included in this study. Other phenotypes and demographics were not described.

The BACH2 variant E788K was found in a father and daughter displaying inflammation of the bowel, pulmonary disease, bronchiectasis, and fibrosis. Functional analysis showed that BACH2 wild-type protein was evenly distributed in the cytoplasm and nucleus, while protein containing the E788K mutation was aggregated in the cytoplasm suggesting an impairment in protein localization.

A female with infancy-onset colitis who later presented with non-infectious fever, splenomegaly and pancytopenia was found to have a BACH2 L24P mutation by whole exome sequencing. Expression of the wild-type BTB domain of BACH2 resulted in soluble protein that formed dimers, whereas the L24P mutant was insoluble, likely misfolded, and formed multiple aggregates, suggesting that this mutation causes defects in protein stability.

The deubiquitinating enzyme BAP1 was overexpressed in MCF10A and MCF12A cells to assess the effects on cell growth. Expression of the C91S mutant inhibited cell growth while wild-type BAP1 did not. BAP1 C91S was also shown to increase ubiquitination of it's interaction partner HCF-1N, relative to wild-type, likely due to a dominant negative effect of the mutant protein by interfering with wild-type BAP1 function.

In a screen for TGF-beta signaling pathway alterations in colorectal cancer cell lines, the SMAD3 missense mutation R373H was discovered in SNU-769A cells. SMAD3 R373H was expressed in Mv1Lu cells to assess protein localization and showed that this mutation inhibited translocation to the nucleus. The R373H mutant also showed reduced TGF-beta induced transcriptional activation in a reporter assay, with 50% less reporter activity than wild-type controls. These results suggest that R373H causes SMAD3 loss of function.

Analysis of the U2AF small subunit (U2AF23) in fission yeast, U2AF35 in humans, found that mutation I24T is at the interface between the zinc finger motifs and results in a threefold RNA-binding activity decrease compared to wild-type.

Two Swedish families with von Hippel-Lindau disease (VHL) were analyzed. Family B consists of 4 members across 2 generations. Functional analysis of TSC2 variants showed that D1734E did not cause changes in the function of the TSC1-TSC2 complex, as measured by levels of TSC1, TSC2, S6K and phospho-S6K in an immunoblot assay. In addition, the SIFT algorithm predicted this amino acid change to be tolerated.

Exome sequencing of a panel of HNSCC-derived cell lines identified three lines with SMAD4 alterations, two with truncating mutations and one (UM-SCC-2) with the missense mutation H132Y. H132Y was predicted to be deleterious by the variant effect prediction software PROVEAN. In vitro experiments showed that TGF-beta treatment induced phosphorylation of SMAD2 in all cells except CAL27, while SMAD3 phosphorylation was absent in both CAL27 and UM-SCC-2 cells. Despite activation of SMAD2 in UM-SCC-2 cells, TGF-beta treatment did not result in expression induction of downstream transcriptional target SMAD7. A functional rescue experiment was performed by transfecting cells with an inducible wild-type copy of SMAD4. Upon induction of the wild-type SMAD4 and in the presence of TGF-beta some cell lines showed recovery of SMAD7 expression, but UM-SCC-2 cells did not. The authors suggest that H132Y in UM-SCC-2 cells behaves as a dominant negative mutation, preventing SMAD2/3-mediated transcription.

Tumor-derived mutations in SMAD2 and SMAD4 were examined in vitro for their effect on heterocomplex formation, which is important for TGF-B/SMAD signaling. Mutant proteins were purified, checked for proper folding and solution properties, and examined for heterodimer formation in a size exclusion chromatography interaction assay. The SMAD4 D493H mutation was shown to disrupt the formation of a heterodimer with SMAD2, and therefore likely represents a loss of function.

A fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET) assay was used to assess the interaction between the Nrf2 (NFE2L2) ETGE motif and the Keap1 Kelch binding domain. A peptide containing the E79Q mutation showed reduced affinity for the Kelch domain compared to wild-type, as measured by the FRET assay. This result suggests that E79Q causes a loss of binding between Nrf2 and it's negative regulator Keap1, which would result in activation of Nrf2.

evidence_statement: This paper reports on 4 Chinese kindreds with VHL. The VHL gene was screened using direct DNA sequencing and MLPA in 44 volunteers among the 4 families. The exon 1 deletion mutation was found in 1 kindred; 18 members were tested and 5 were found to harbour the mutation. The 13 members without a mutation and 1 carrier were asymptomatic, while 4 of the 5 carriers had manifestations. In addition to the 4 carriers, there were 2 additional members who displayed manifestations, but died before testing could be performed. It should be noted that these family members also harboured a concurrent homozygous deletion of IRAK2. Clinical manifestations in this kindred included: CNS and cerebellar hemangioblastoma, pancreatic cysts, renal cell carcinoma, and a neoplasm of the liver. ACMG evidence codes: 'PP1' because of segregation results, 'PP4' because the patient's phenotypes or family history are highly specific for a disease with single genetic etiology, 'PVS1' because they observe a single exon deletion variant in a gene where loss of function is a known mechanism of disease.

This study described the genomic landscape of sporadic schwannomas. Among the 125 cases, 12 (10%) of them were identified to bear in-frame SH3PXD2A-HTRA1 fusion with RNA-seq. An 18-month-old female patient presented with a history of an enlarging, subcutaneous mass in her right lower extremity since birth. A biopsy was performed and the findings were typical of Dermatofibrosarcoma Protuberans (DFSP). Dual color fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) in paraffin sections was performed and showed that the DFSP cells had an unbalanced rearrangement of the PDGFB locus. Infantile fibrosarcoma was excluded upon performing RT-PCR as t(12;15) result was negative. Imatinib mesylate was chosen as a therapeutic intervention instead of surgery to avoid functional and cosmetic defects. An initial dose of 400 mg/m2 was administered once a day. Clinical improvement started after one week of the drug administration. After 4 weeks, there was no palpable mass. Radiological improvement started to be evident at week 23 as an MRI showed reduction in the subcutaneous thickness of the mass (from 9.8 X 8.1 mm to 5.2 X6.2 mm). The halt of tumor progression allowed limb growth and a smaller volume of tissue to be resected. In this case study, the authors report the first pediatric patient with DFSP who has exhibited a positive response to imatinib mesylate without signs of toxicity or adverse reactions

Phase 3 trial of 146 patients randomized to either IDH1 inhibitor ivosidenib and azacitidine or azacitidine and placebo revealed significantly longer event-free survival in the ivosidenib-group. Patients with newly diagnosed IDH1-mutation positive (assessed by Abbott RealTime IDH1 in vitro polymerase-chain-reaction (PCR) assay) acute myeloid leukemia, ineligible for intensive induction chemotherapy were randomized to IDH1-inhibitor ivosidenib and azacitidine or azacitidine and placebo. Primary end point was event-free survival (time from randomization until treatment failure, relapse, or death from any cause, whichever occurred first). 146 patients were randomized (72 ivosidenib and azacitidine and 74 placebo and azacitidine). At a median follow-up of 12.4 months, event-free survival was significantly longer with ivosidenib and azacitidine than with placebo and azacitidine (hazard ratio 0.33; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.16 to 0.69; P=0.002).

In this study, 57 cases of dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans (DFSP) were evaluated. The COL1A1-PDGFB fusion was detected in 42 (74%) out of the 57 sample after performing targeted PCR amplification and direct sequencing. The 42 samples were then evaluated for PDGFB and PDGFRB gene amplification using qPCR. SYBR green assay was also used to evaluate PDGFB gene amplification in comparison with a reference gene and a normal tissue. PDGFB mRNA expression was detected in all analyzed samples and was significantly higher in tumor cells compared to adjacent normal tissue; as amplification levels (copy number of PDGFB/ copy number of reference gene) varied from 0.6. to 8.3 (mean 2.4) in 42 tumor samples, and from 0.4 to 3.0 (mean 1.2) in 20 adjacent normal tissue samples (P = 0.0002). Moreover, the mRNA expression levels of PDGFB and PDGFRB showed a significant correlation (P < 0.0001). The authors of this study conclude that these results demonstrate the generation of the COL1A1-PDGFB fusion transcript that functions as a ligand for PDGFRB which subsequently activates the downstream PDGFB/PDGFRB signaling pathway involved in tumorigenesis of DFSP.

A cohort of 28 patients with malignant melanoma, with previously excised high-risk lesions were evaluated for STAT1 and STAT2 expression prior to treatment with v. interferon-alpha 2b (IFN-a2b). Staining intensity of either STAT1 or STAT2 was not correlated with disease recurrence after IFN-a2b treatment (P=0.61 for STAT1; P=0.52 for STAT2). Location of expression of STAT1 or STAT2 in either the nucleus or cytoplasm was also found not to be indicative if a patient experienced recurrent disease (P=0.94 for STAT1; P=0.85). Although STAT1 staining was strong in 11 out of 26 patients (>60% positive) and STAT2 staining in 18 out of 24 patients, prognostic outcomes were not associated with expression of STAT1 and STAT2 genes.

The H1862L mutation resulted in similar levels of growth compared to wild-type in the complementation assay and a corrected IC50 value similar to wild-type in the cisplatin-sensitivity assay, and therefore was classified as neutral.

A retrospective analysis of 164 patients waiting for surgery for hemangioblastomas at Freiburg University Medical Center, Freiburg, Germany was conducted. Patient #6 (male, 35Y) was found with a 2 kb partial deletion of the VHL gene and with spinal hemangioblastoma. Family history was not described.

A retrospective analysis of 164 patients waiting for surgery for hemangioblastomas at Freiburg University Medical Center, Freiburg, Germany was conducted. Patient #20 (female, 28Y) was found with a 10 kb partial deletion of the VHL gene and with spinal hemangioblastoma. Family history was not described.

Retrospective analysis of patients with ALK-fusion positive gastrointestinal cancers. 13 patients were identified (5 pancreas, 3 right-sided colon, 1 gastric, 1 duodenal, 1 rectal, 1 left-sided colon, 1 biliary). 7 patients were treated with alectinib, 5 with crizotinib and 1 with entrectinib. 5/12 evaluable patients achieved a partial response, 2 had progressive disease. Median PFS was 5 months, median OS was 9.3 months.

Case report of a 32-year old male patient with pilocytic astrocytoma. Genomic profiling (FoundationOne) revealed a FGFR1 N546K mutation. The patient was enrolled in a phase I/II trial of pemigatinib and achieved a partial response lasting 18 months.

Case report of a 27-year old female patient with spindle cell sarcoma. Initial treatment consisted of eight cycles of alternating vincristine-doxorubicin-cyclophosphamide and ifosfamide-etoposide plus definitive radiation for suspected Ewing's sarcoma. An Archer panel revealed a QKI-RAF1 gene fusion, no EWSR1 and SS18 gene rearrangement were identified and a diagnosis of spindle cell tumor (S100 and CD34 coexpression with recurrent gene fusion) was made. Three months after end of treatment a relapse was diagnosed which progressed under temozolomide-irinotecan. Third-line therapy with trametinib was started which led to a complete metabolic response. The patient died 10months later from septic shock. No tumor progression was noted.

Case report of a 62-year old male patient diagnosed with pancreatic acinar cell carcinoma. Liver metastases were diagnosed and treatment was started with gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel regimen. After disease progression, patient received chemotherapy with fluorouracil, leucovorin, and irinotecan for 6 months followed by disease progression and third-line fluorouracil, leucovorin, and oxaliplatin again followed by disease-progression. Sequencing using the FoundationOne CDxF1CDx assay revealed ASXL1 R596fs*107 and BCORL1 V937fs*10 mutations as well as a KANK4-ALK gene fusion, which was confirmed by FISH. Treatment with alectinib was started and partial response was ongoing 4 months from the start of therapy.

Five colorectal cancer (CRC) cell lines with BRAF V600E mutation were resistant to treatment with the BRAF inhibitor vemurafenib. An RNAi screen in the WiDr cell line (a V600E CRC line) identified EGFR as an enhancer for survival when exposed to vemurafenib. Treatment with vemurafenib and an EGFR inhibitor (cetuximab or gefitinib) in V600E CRC cells (WiDr, VACO432 and KM20) showed inhibited growth as well as induction of the cleaved PARP apoptotic marker.

Five colorectal cancer (CRC) cell lines (VACO432, HT29, SNU-C5, KM20, WiDr) with BRAF V600E mutation were resistant to treatment with the BRAF inhibitor vemurafenib. An RNAi screen in the WiDr cell line (a V600E CRC line) identified EGFR as an enhancer for survival when exposed to vemurafenib. Treatment with vemurafenib and an EGFR inhibitor (cetuximab or gefitinib) in V600E CRC cells (WiDr, VACO432 and KM20) showed inhibited growth as well as induction of the cleaved PARP apoptotic marker. Xenografts of WiDr and VACO432 cell lines showed similar tumour growth when treated with vemurafenib or control treatment, suggesting resistance to vemurafenib in vivo.

In this retrospective study, two patients with locally advanced Dermatofibrosarcoma Protuberans (DFSP) and two patients with recurrent DFSP received imatinib treatment prior to undergoing Mohs surgery. The two patients with recurrent DFSP were given a daily dose of 800 mg while the other two patients with primary DFSP received a dose of 300 mg and 600 mg. The treatment duration lasted for almost three months except for one of the patients with recurrent DFSP who was put on treatment for 7 months. The duration of the treatment was determined based on initial response and/or stable reduction in tumor size. All patients responded well to the treatment as tumor lesions were reduced in size by an average of 36.9% (varied between 18.9% and 61.6%). Furthermore, histopathological findings post treatment showed 100% reduction in cellularity along with significant production of hyalinized material. Following Mohs surgery, 3 of the patients achieved clear margins whereas the fourth patient who initially had recurrent DFSP had to undergo further resection but ended up achieving clear margins. After 1.5 to 4 years of follow-up, patients were reported to be tumor free. Some adverse effects were reported but no reduction or alteration in the dosage took place as patients eventually managed to tolerate the dosage. The authors of this study highlight imatinib as a safe and well-tolerated therapy that offers patients with primary or recurrent/challenging DFSP the possibility of reducing their tumor size significantly before surgery, thereby resulting in a smaller postsurgical defect and a less complicated repair.

TERT promoter mutations are activating and commonly found at two hotspots within the TERT promoter region which occur 124 and 146 base pairs (hg19) upstream of the translation start site. These hotspots, termed C228T and C250T are observed in many cancer types and have a particularly high prevalence in glioblastoma (83%), melanoma (71%), bladder cancer (66%) and hepatocelluar carcinoma (HCC) (47%). The two mutations are usually heterozygous and mutually exclusive and result in an increased similarity to an ETS binding domain and may act as a binding site to an ETS transcription factor. These mutations are thought to be early events in tumorgenesis and aid in cellular immortality. Decreased overall survival in patients with these mutations have been observed in medulloblastoma, thyroid cancer, urogenital cancer, melanoma, and laryngeal tumors. The presence of these mutations has also been shown to be predictive of malignant/premalignant nodules in HCC and meningiomas.

Ten patients with Dermatofibrosarcoma Protuberans (DFSP) were enrolled in phase II study to investigate the response to imatinib in locally advanced or metastatic DFSP. Eight of the ten patients had locally advanced DFSP, in which COL1A1-PDGFB t(17;22) was detected through karyotyping and/or FISH. Only one of the two patients with metastatic DFSP had evidence of t(17;22) along other complex aberrations. All patients were treated with an imatinib dose of 400 mg twice a day, in which all reported well tolerated responses except for one patient where the dose had to be reduced to 600 mg a day. Tumor tissues were examined for expression and activation of PDGFRA and PDGFRB by western blot prior to therapy. PDGFRB activation was at least 10-fold lower in 5 evaluated patients when compared to gastrointestinal stromal tumors with oncogenic mutation. The response to imatinib was complete in 4 patients and partial (≥50% decrease from baseline in the sum of products of perpendicular diameters of all measurable lesions) in the other 4 patients with locally advanced DFSP and in the patient with t(17;22) metastatic DFSP. Tumor biopsies were obtained before and 28 days after the initiation of treatment, where histopathological findings showed reduced cellularity and presence of hyalinization post treatment. The authors suggest that imatinib may assist in disease control in patients with locally advanced or metastatic disease. Furthermore, authors revealed that patients who were followed-up with after surgical resection were rendered free of disease and had no evidence of progression.

In this case report, a 36-year-old male is presented with an advanced and recurrent Dermatofibrosarcoma Protuberans (DFSP) lesion. Following the third relapse and a round of radiotherapy, he was put on a 400 mg/ day dose of Imatinib that rendered him free of DFSP for two years. Yet, the lesions progressed and he was put on 800 mg/ day dose of Imatinib with no positive response nor regression. At this point, the patient was left with multiple untreated lesions and CT scan also revealed large mediastinal masses and post obstructive pneumopathy on the left bronchus. The patient was put on a 800 mg/ day dose of Sorafenib which led to significant improvements days following the treatment as shown through radiological and clinical observations. The treatment lasted for 5 months with no recurrence or progression of DFSP. The dose was well tolerated and the patient had only reported moderate fatigue and dehiscence of previous surgical wounds. However, the patient passed away after one week of discontinuing the drug as a result of recurrent pulmonary infection that caused a septic shock. The authors state this case report as the only one of DFSP treated with Sorafenib after failure of Imatinib at the time of publishing. Furthermore, the authors highlight Sorafenib as a therapeutic alternative in such cases of DFSP.

In this study, DFSP-transformed cell lines (4A and 5A) were used in-vitro and in-vivo to investigate the possibility of blocking the autocrine loop that forms as a result of the t(17;22) COL1A1-PDGFB rearrangement, as well to study the effect of STI571 drug on DFSP growth and morphology. Cell culture of transformed 5A cells conducted with different concentrations of serum showed that tumor proliferation requires the presence of other factors. Addition of STI571 to media with different serum concentrations produced a significant (> 60%) reduction of cell proliferation. Furthermore, STI571 toxic effects induced morphological changes in a dose-dependent fashion. These morphological changes were reversible as cells went back to their flattened shape once the drug was discontinued. Moreover, no apoptosis was detected through TUNEL assay. Analysis of PDGFRB activation by western blot demonstrated that tyrosine phosphorylation in 5A treated cells was reduced in a dose-dependent fashion. The in-vivo results mirrored those observed in-vitro; nude mice were injected subcutaneously with 4A and 5A cell lines and were treated intraperitoneally or orally on day 1 and day 7 of transformation (50 and 200 mg/kg of body weight, twice/day for 5 days/week for 3 weeks). The tumor latency of clone 4A was longer than that of clone 5A (11 vs. 7 days). No lethal toxicity was observed after STI571 oral administration, but one mouse from each cell line group died due to toxicity after intraperitoneally treatment. Similar to the in-vitro observations, the tumor growth restarted when STI571 administration was discontinued. STI571 was also administered according to a more frequent and continuous treatment; mice were treated orally with 160 mg/kg, 3 times/day for 11 days. In the early tumor group, the continuous treatment was slightly more efficient than the discontinuous one (90% vs. 80% inhibition). On the other hand, the late tumor group showed 80% inhibition of tumor weight vs 50% inhibition in the 5A and 4A groups, respectively. Finally, in-vivo analysis of PDGFRB activation by western blot on treated 5A cell line showed STI571-induced PDGFRB inactivation lasts only for 6 hours; as PDGFRB phosphorylation was detectable after 2 hours of treatment and reached its lowest level by the 5th or 6th hour, but started to increase after the 7th and 8th hour, suggesting that frequent administration may be required to maintain PDGFRB inactivation. The authors conclude that STI571 anti-tumor effect can be improved by increasing the number of administrations per day.

In this study, NIH3T3 cell lines were used to characterize the COLIA1/PDGFB fusion protein functionally and structurally in Dermatofibrosarcoma Protuberans (DFSP). The cell lines B5/5 (COLIA1/PDGFB transfectant) and CNEG-1 (negative control) were used following the isolation of a COLIA1/PDGFB cosmid and establishment of COLIA1/PDGFB-expressing NIH3T3 cell lines. Upon cell culturing, only B5/5 cells grew in a disorganized manner and displayed a spindle-shaped morphology. Addition of the tyrosine kinase inhibitor, CGP57148B dramatically altered the morphology of B5/5 cells to a phenotype resembling the control cells and significantly reduced the growth rate. The presence of activated PDGF β-receptors in B5/5 cells in the absence or presence of CGP57148B was observed following immunoprecipitation and blotting. The inhibitory effect of CGP57148B on PDGF receptor activation was demonstrated by the dramatically reduced tyrosine phosphorylation of PDGF receptors after treatment. Furthermore, pulse-chase studies showed that the fusion protein forms a disulfide-linked precursor dimer that is processed to mature PDGFBB. Regarding the in-vivo studies, B5/5 cells and CNEG-1 cells were injected subcutaneously into nude mice. The B5/5 cells formed tumors of measurable size within 2 weeks. Half of the mice in each group were given 50 mg/kg/day CGP57148B in 200 μl of PBS orally, and the other half were given 200 μl of PBS only. Treatment started on the day following injection of tumor cells and CGP57148B significantly reduced the growth of B5/5 derived tumors. Finally, sections of tumors derived from COLIA1/PDGFB-expressing cells were analyzed histologically and have displayed a malignant phenotype similar to human sarcomas. The authors conclude that the COLIA1/PDGFB fusion associated with DFSP contributes to tumor development through ectopic production of PDGF-BB and the formation of an autocrine loop. They also highlight the potential use of kinase inhibitors, such as CGP57148B, on primary cultures of DFSP tumors and for treatment.

In this non-controlled phase 2 clinical trial, 25 patients with primary or recurrent Dermatofibrosarcoma Protuberans (DFSP) were recruited. Only 21 had the t(17;22) COL1A-PDGFB fusion as detected through FISH or karyotyping. Patients were given a dose of Imatinib as 600 mg/ day orally. Clinical response to Imatinib was investigated after two months of drug administration; the total response rate was 36.0% (IC 95%, 18.0-57.5), and the relative decrease in tumor size was 48.5% as estimated using ultrasound vs 21.6% as estimated using MRI. However, these results were not in agreement with the clinical observations; as ultrasound overestimated the relative tumor decrease by 20% as compared with clinical evaluation (P = 0.03). Among the 21 patients with the COL1A1-PDGFB fusion, 8 achieved partial or complete response, 12 were nonresponders, and 1 discontinued Imatinib due to toxicity. A modification of extracellular components was noted in 19 of 25 patients with varying degrees of hyalinization. Tumor density decreased in 9 of 25 patients. This decrease was statistically associated with clinical response (P = 0.022). TUNEL assay was performed on samples from 8 patients, in which 50% to 75% of cells were apoptotic in five patients, and less than 5% apoptotic cells were detected for the other 3 patients. The drug was well tolerated with some adverse effects, including edema, diarrhea, anemia, fatigue, nausea..etc. Although, three patients suffered from severe toxic effects that required discontinuation of Imatinib. The authors indicate that this is the second study that investigates Imatinib’s response in patients with DFSP and note this study as the first to perform a systematic analysis of the effect of Imatinib on histologic parameters and apoptosis. Finally, they highlight Imatinib as a well-targeted drug for DFSP that could be used as a neoadjuvant therapy in locally advanced or recurrent DFSP.

Molecular analysis of 30 Ewing tumors (designated as Ewing's sarcomas and primitive neuroectodermal tumors (PNET) in this 1994 paper) from patients with well-documented clinical course was performed. RT-PCR revealed fusion transcripts in 28 of 30 cases (93%) with EWSR1::FLI1 found in 93% (26 of 28) and EWSR1::ERG in 7% (2 of 28). Of note, these fusions were not identified in 7 tumors of other diagnoses. 19 of 28 (67%) were EWSR1 ex7::FLI1 ex6 (type I), 4 of 28 (14%) were EWSR1 ex7::FLI1 ex5 (type II) and there was 1 each of EWSR1 ex7:: FLI1 ex7, EWSR1 ex 10::FLI1 ex 5, and EWSR1 ex 9::FLI1 ex4. This last tumor (EWSR1 ex 9::FLI1 ex4) had evidence of an additional 4 splicing variants corresponding to EWSR1 exon 7 to FLI1 exons 4, 6, 8 and 9. Two tumors had EWSR1::ERG with breakpoints between exon 7 of EWSR1 and exon 6 of ERG. Of note, karyotyping only revealed a chromosome 22 rearrangement in 18 out of 27 cases tested (67%), however this was thought to be due to failure to obtain mitotic figures (5 of 9) and insufficient material (4 of 9). Authors conclude RT-PCR is better than karyotyping for identifying these EWSR1 rearranged tumors. In this small study, EWSR::FLI1 type I fusion predominated over type II in localized Ewing's and were more abundant in tumors affecting the long bones (9 versus 0), however no correlations between different EWSR1 transcripts and any other clinical parameters could be identified.

Molecular analysis of 30 Ewing tumors (designated as Ewing's sarcomas and primitive neuroectodermal tumors (PNET) in this 1994 paper) from patients with well-documented clinical course was performed. RT-PCR revealed fusion transcripts in 28 of 30 cases (93%) with EWSR1::FLI1 found in 93% (26 of 28) and EWSR1::ERG in 7% (2 of 28). Of note, these fusions were not identified in 7 tumors of other diagnoses. The two tumors with EWSR1::ERG had breakpoints between exon 7 of EWSR1 and exon 6 of ERG with a t(2;22) rearrangement detected in 1 of these 2 cases by karyotyping. Authors conclude RT-PCR is a sensitive method for identifying these EWSR1 rearranged tumors.

DDX41 p.G530D (NM_016222.2) was detected in the germline of 5 family members. Family H's pedigree can be seen in Fig. 1H - which includes: 1) III.6 (proband) was diagnosed with AML at 50 (CBC parameters available 2 months before diagnosis and at diagnosis), 2) III.5 (sister) was unaffected at 63/64 (CBC parameters available), 3) II.5 (deceased father) was an obligate carrier who was diagnosed with AML at 53, 4) II.6 (deceased paternal uncle was an obligate carrier who was diagnosed with AML at 44, and 5) III.8 (II.6's daughter) was unaffected at 59/60 (CBC parameters available) - but there is even more of an extensive family history of AML plus one family member with MDS.

This study profiled DDX41 variants in 1529 patients with myeloid neoplasms, including MDS, AML, MPN, and MDS/MPN, using targeted next-generation sequencing of 114 hematologic malignancy-associated genes with confirmation of potential germline variants through matched oral epithelial cell testing and Sanger sequencing. DDX41 p.G530D was identified in 2 patients: Patient No. 9, a 76-year-old male with karyotypically normal MDS-EB2 who harbored germline DDX41 p.S217Ifs*4 together with somatic DDX41 p.G530D (VAF=7%), and Patient No. 42, a 72-year-old male with cytogenetically normal AML who harbored somatic DDX41 p.M620Hfs*22 together with somatic DDX41 p.G530D (VAF=30.5%). The authors reported that myeloid neoplasms with DDX41 variants were characterized by older age, male predominance, normal karyotype, frequent advanced MDS/AML, favorable prognosis, and high response rates to hypomethylating therapy.

Three patients in this French study acquired DDX41 G530D in their myeloid neoplasm. 1. 59yo French male (Patient #9) with aplastic anemia (bone marrow dysplasia and 2% BM blasts) that evolved into cytogenetically-normal MDS-EB1 by age 60 carried DDX41 G173R in the germline and acquired G530D at VAF=7%; he only had a prior history of laryngeal cancer at 56 and family history was negative. 2. 69yo female (Patient #30) with AML M0 (trisomy 8) carried DDX41 c.799-2T>A and acquired G530D at a VAF=12%; family history was negative. 3. 88yo French male (Patient #6) with CN-AML M2 carried H315fs in the germline and acquired G530D at a VAF=11%; family history was negative. Note: VAF of acquired G530D were obtained from PMID: 34349893 (Supplemental Table 2).

In a cohort of 5,801 patients with hematologic malignancies evaluated using next-generation sequencing (NGS)–based myeloid panels, 90 patients were identified with at least one DDX41 alteration at >40% VAF and 33 were confirmed to carry germline DDX41 variants by skin fibroblast testing. One 60-year-old male with cytogenetically normal acute myeloid leukemia and a prior history of leukopenia and thrombocytopenia carried germline DDX41 Q41* and acquired somatic DDX41 G530D (VAF 8.7%). The authors concluded that recurrent somatic DDX41 mutations identified through NGS frequently occur in the setting of germline DDX41-associated myeloid neoplasms and support the use of systematic DDX41 testing in myeloid malignancies.

Patient with an unspecified myeloid neoplasm had DDX41 c.232_233insAA/p.P78Qfs*3 (VAF=47%) and DDX41 c.1589G>A/p.G530D (VAF=5%), as well as SRSF2 c.284C>A/p.P95H (VAF=4%); germline/somatic origin could only be assessed in 8 patients who had non-tumoral tissue samples, but this patient (UPN4) was not one of them and so origin was inferred from VAFs.

A case study revealed an 8Y boy, presenting with a profound sensorineural hearing loss and intermittent vertigo. He was found to have an endolymphatic sac tumor, discovered by high-resolution computed tomographic imaging. Genetic analysis revealed a missense VHL mutation c.388G>C/p.V130L (originally written in paper as legacy notation AF010238.1, c.601G>C). Family history was not described.

Pro-B Ba/F3 cells transfected with wild type FGFR3 resulted in Il-3 independence with FGF1 dependence for growth. Monoclonal antibody R3Mab treatment in addition to FGF1 resulted in suppression of proliferation of Ba/F3 cells with wild type FGFR3.

Ba/F3 cells transfected with wild type FGFR3 or common bladder carcinoma variant FGFR3 G372C both resulted in IL-3 independence with FGF1 dependence for growth. Monoclonal antibody R3Mab treatment with FGF1 suppressed proliferation of Ba/F3 FGFR3 G372C cells. Wildtype FGFR3 overexpression in Ba/F3 cells as well as bladder cancer cell lines RT112 and RT4 (who both have normal levels of endogenously expressed wildtype FGFR3), were similarly sensitive to R3Mab treatment, therefore mutation G372C did not change that responsiveness.

Pro-B Ba/F3 cells transfected with wild type FGFR3 resulted in IL-3 independence with FGF1 dependence for growth. Cell transfected FGFR3 with mutation Y375C also resulted in IL-3 independence and FGF1 dependence. Monoclonal antibody R3Mab treatment along with FGF1 resulted in suppression of proliferation of Ba/F3 cells with FGFR3 Y375C. Wild type FGFR3 overexpression in Ba/F3 cells with FGF1 was sensitive to monoclonal antibody R3Mab treatment, and mutation Y375C did not change that responsiveness.

Ba/F3 cells transfected with wildtype FGFR3 resulted in IL-3 independence with FGF1 dependence for growth, whereas cells transfected with common bladder carcinoma variant FGFR3 K652E resulted in IL-3 independence, weak ligand-independent proliferation and a strong growth response to FGF1. Monoclonal antibody R3Mab treatment with FGF1 suppressed proliferation of Ba/F3 FGFR3 K652E cells. Wildtype FGFR3 overexpression in Ba/F3 cells as well as bladder cancer cell lines RT112 and RT4 (who both have normal levels of endogenously expressed wildtype FGFR3), were similarly sensitive to R3Mab treatment, therefore mutation K652E did not change that responsiveness.

A 50-year-old male patient was admitted with abdominal pain. CT found a tumor of the right kidney found to be clear cell renal cell carcinoma through histological findings. Chromosome analysis of the peripheral blood lymphocytes of the patient revealed a reciprocal translocation between chromosomes 3 and 12 (t(3;12)(q13.2;q24.1)). The patient had no siblings and his father was deceased. Cytogenetic analysis of the blood lymphocytes of the probands' mother revealed a normal karyotype. This patient was also published in PMID 20633763.

In a Thai cohort of 81 patients with cholangiocarcinoma, 17 patients harbored EGFR variants, 9 of which were T790M. EGFR T790M variants were associated with longer overall survival than patients with other EGFR variants (18.84 vs 4.08 months, HR=0.26 [0.08-0.93], P=0.038) and lower Ki-67 staining. However, patients with EGFR T790M variants did not show significantly longer survival when compared to patients without EGFR variants (N=64, 11.52 months, HR=0.55 [0.22-1.37], P=0.199).

In a study of 137 biliary tract carcinomas, 13 patients were identified to have EGFR variants in exons 18-21 (no other exons were evaluated). EGFR variants were associated with worse survival in univariate (6 vs 37 months, P=<0.00001) and multivariate analysis (HR=5.655[95% CI 2.72-11.74], P<0.0001).

An MRI in a previously healthy 6-year-old boy now presenting with neurologic abnormalities and seizures revealed a mass obstructing the foramen of Monro and diffuse leptomeningeal dissemination. The primary tumor was resected and subsequent radiation therapy resulted in moderate cognitive and motor improvements. Seven months later, an MRI detected a recurrence, which led to tumor molecular profiling of patient DNA and RNA. RNA analysis discovered and confirmed an in-frame KANK1::NTRK2 e3::ex16 fusion, which was predicted to preserve NTRK2’s tyrosine kinase domain. The patient was started on larotrectinib and within 2 weeks demonstrated cognitive and motor improvements. After 2 months of therapy, an MRI showed significant tumor response and by 4 months cognition and memory were near-baseline. Overall, larotrectinib resulted in both sustained clinical and radiographic response through 10 months of treatment with no related toxicity.

An MRI of 26-year-old man presenting with motor weakness and language difficultly revealed a lesion in the left frontal lobe that extended across the corpus callosum. Histologic analysis of the biopsy characterized the lesion as a glioblastoma wildtype for IDH and was negative for EGFR and MET amplification based on FISH. The biopsy material was analyzed with a DNA based genotyping panel and RNA-based NGS assay. The latter detected a KANK1::NTRK2 e4::e16 fusion that was confirmed by FISH. Following the partial resection of the tumor and six weeks of concurrent temozolomide and radiation therapy, an MRI revealed enhancement of the remaining tumor with no significant disease progression. Larotrectinib (100mg) was administered and after 49 days an MRI displayed significant treatment response as the lesion shrunk (25mm to <10mm) and the patient demonstrated slight motor improvements. By day 106 of Larotrectinib treatment, disease progression was evident. However, molecular analysis of a rebiopsy revealed KANK1::NTRK2 was no longer detectable, but a minor subclone at diagnosis with PDGFRA amplification was driving disease progression. Therefore, the authors conclude the KANK1::NTRK2 clones were effectively targeted by Larotrectinib treatment over several months resulting in a robust clinical response.

In a further investigation of non-traditional sarcoma cases, a 41-year-old man was thought to have a malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor (MPNST) in the neck and spinal cord, but large rhabdoid/epithelioid cell morphology and retained H3K27Me3. Metastatic lesions were found in the lung and spine. Pan-TRK immunostain was positive and RNA NGS detected a KANK1::NTRK2 fusion. The authors state this is the first report of a KANK1::NTRK2 fusion in a sarcoma, which seems to forecast high-grade morphology and behavior.

Pro-B Ba/F3 cells transfected with wild type FGFR3 resulted in Il-3 independence with FGF1 dependence for growth. Monoclonal antibody R3Mab treatment in addition to FGF1 resulted in suppression of proliferation of Ba/F3 cells with wild type FGFR3. R3Mab was then tested on t(4;14)-positive multiple myeloma cell line UTMC-2 which has wild type FGFR3. R3Mab stopped proliferation of UMTC-2 cells but did not attenuate multiple myeloma cell line KMS11 with FGFR3 Y373C. KMS11 cells were xenografted into nude mice in which R3Mab treatment abolished tumor growth. When R3Mab's Fc-region (which binds to immune effector cells) was modified with D265A/N297A (DANA), R3Mab no longer inhibited tumor growth of KMS11 xenograft tumors. Further testing also showed that multiple myeloma cells expressed 5 to 6 fold more cell surface FGFR3 than bladder cancer cell lines. The authors to conclude that in addition to ligand blocking and preventing dimerization, R3Mab can induce antibody-depedent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC) in cells expressing high wild type or mutant FGFR3 cell surface levels.

In culture, monoclonal antibody R3Mab treatment inhibited the growth of multiple myeloma cell line UTMC-2 which has wild type FGFR3 but did not affect proliferation of multiple myeloma cell line KMS11 with FGFR3 Y373C. Since UTMC-2 cells do not form tumors in mice, OPM2 and KMS11 were xenografted into nude mice. R3Mab abolished xenograft tumor growth in both cell lines. Another experiment was conducted to test R3Mab's mechanism of action where R3Mab's Fc region, which binds to immune effector cells, was modified with D265A/N297A (DANA). The DANA mutation did not affect R3Mab's ability to bind to FGFR3 nor did it affect R3Mab's antitumor activity against bladder cancer cell line xenografts (UMUC-14 and RT112). However, the tumors of xenografted cell lines OPM2 and KMS11 were resistant to DANA R3Mab. Further testing also showed that multiple myeloma cells expressed 5 to 6 fold more cell surface FGFR3 than bladder cancer cell lines. All this information led the authors to conclude that in addition to ligand blocking and preventing dimerization, R3Mab can induce antibody-depedent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC) in cells expressing high FGFR3 cell surface levels. This conclusion applied to both wild type and mutant FGFR3.

A targeted sequencing study of 135 relapsed/refractory DLBCL patients identified an association between missense mutations in MS4A1 and acquired resistance to R-CHOP.

G380R mutation was created in the transmembrane region of murine FGFR3 to study its effect. An in vitro kinase assay using 293 human cells found the mutant FGFR3 to be expressed at levels similar or slightly higher than the control. The mutant receptor was then expressed in L6 rat cells, in which the degree of phosphorylation was found to be lower in fibroblasts but relatively higher than the control. Also, in the presence of the ligand FGF-1, the mutant receptor became much more phosphorylated; which indicates that the mutant receptor acts as constitutively activated receptor. In transformed NIH3t3 cells, only with the presence of a ligand did the mutant receptor show morphological transformation of cells, and this effect kept increasing with the increased ligand’s concentration. Finally, upon transfecting the C2-7 myoblast cell line, the mutant receptor was completely resistant to differentiation. The authors conclude that the G380R variant in FGFR3 causes constitutive activation/autophosphorylation of the receptor in the absence of ligand, which could be possible due to receptor dimerization, and they highlight the variant as an oncogene based on the observed results.

In this study, authors investigated a K650M variant in FGFR3, which occurs within the receptor tyrosine kinase domain activation loop. The variant was found in four unrelated patients, whose clinical and radiographic features fit as severe achondroplasia, with developmental delay and acanthosis nigricans. The K650M was not found in more than 150 tested normal chromosomes which led the authors to exclude the possibility of being a casual polymorphism. A significant increase in the mutant receptor’s autophosphorylation activity was observed upon transfection of NIH3T3 cells with the K650M variant and performing in vitro kinase assay. Furthermore, the authors highlight the severity of clinical outcome and degree of long-bone dysplasia observed in these patients in comparison to patients harboring different substitution at or near the same position. Finally, the authors propose the possibility of increased amounts of FGFR3 tyrosine kinase activity that leads to this outcome as a result of either inappropriate cell cycle arrest or increased intensity/ duration of FGFR3 signaling by the K650M that might cause activation or inhibition of other signaling pathways controlling endochondral bone growth.

Authors of this paper aimed to investigate the role of the FGFR3 K650E variant in transforming cells in vivo and in vitro. After 3-4 weeks of transducing mice’s bone marrow (BM) with the mutant receptor, leukemic blood profile with leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia, and reticulocytes with polychromasia were developed. Fragile bones, splenomegaly, enlarged lymphs and nodes were also observed in postmortem mice. Passage of FGFR3 mutant mice was done serially up to four generations, in which, within 6-8 weeks, moribund mice showed hematopoietic tumors infiltrating major organs. Furthermore, cultured cells with mutant FGFR3 showed increased B-cells colonies with predominant B220+ cells. When attempting to test the progenitor target cells in vivo, transplanted mice developed pre-B cells within 2 weeks. Finally, initial cell expansions were polyclonal whereas tumors in later passages exhibited either clonal B- or T-cell receptor gene rearrangements, predominantly JH configuration. The authors state that their results support that mutant FGFR3 is capable of transforming cells to much greater extent than the wild type, and that mutant FGFR3, subsequent to translocation into the IgH locus in multiple myeloma, would appear to have devastating consequences.

Patient samples were sequenced before and after progression on venetoclax. A patient (CLL10) with richter transformation showed increased frequency of PLCG2 N571S at relapse after 6 months on venetoclax.

Phase I dose-escalation cohort (NCT01703481) of patients with advanced solid tumors in which antineoplastic therapy was no longer effective using pan-FGFR inhibitor erdafitinib (JNJ-42756493). 1 cholangiocarcinoma patient with an FGFR2 mutation receiving 10 mg intermittently (7d on/7d off) showed a partial response (PR) of approximately 60% maximal reduction of the sum of diameters of targeted lesions and had progression-free survival (PFS) of about 7 months. Cholangiocarcinoma patients with FGFR mutations or fusions receiving 10 mg intermittently had an objective response rate (ORR) of 30%. The Lys650Glu variant was investigated in terms of its ability to activate the receptor kinase FGFR3. Upon NIH3T3 cells transfection, the kinase assay showed a significant increase in the ligand-independent kinase activity of the Lys650Glu mutant receptor compared with the wild-type receptor (~100-fold). This variant is known to cause thanatophoric dysplasia type 2 (TD2), and occurs within the receptor tyrosine kinase domain activation loop. Another variant that was discussed thoroughly in the study also occurs at the same position and was found in the examined patients; however, the patients were presented with markedly different phenotypes than those observed in TD2 patients. The authors highlight the striking and unexplained difference between the recruited patients and those with TD2 in regards to occurrence of severe craniosynostosis in TD2 and propose a possibility of threshold effect and that craniosynostosis does not occur if there is too much or too little constitutive activation of the FGFR3 kinase.

Five patients from four families suffering from skeletal dysplasia were found to harbor a novel heterozygous K650N variant in FGFR3. The variant cosegregated in two patients from one family (a father and his daughter), whereas it occurred sporadically in the others. NIH3T3 cells were transfected with the variant construct followed by kinase activity assay that showed increased activity by ~ 4 folds compared to the wild type. The authors suggest that this variant, although showing lower activation levels than other known variants responsible for severe skeletal dysplasia forms, is responsible for the milder skeletal dysplasia form seen in those patients (mild hypochondroplasia phenotype), and they further highlight the significance of Lys650 site in the active domain loop of the receptor.

A patient suffering from skeletal dysplasia was found to harbor a novel heterozygous K650Q variant in FGFR3. NIH3T3 cells were transfected with the variant construct followed by kinase activity assay that showed increased activity by 4.9 folds compared to the wild type. The authors suggest that this variant, although showing lower activation levels than other known variants responsible for severe skeletal dysplasia forms, is responsible for the milder skeletal dysplasia form seen in those patients (mild hypochondroplasia phenotype), and they further highlight the significance of Lys650 site in the active domain loop of the receptor.

A novel EML4::NTRK3 fusion was identified in a 9-month-old male with a recurrent congenital fibrosarcoma. The in-frame fusion transcript contained exons 1-2 of EML4 fused to exon 14 of NTRK3 which is predicted to include the entire intact NTRK3 kinase domain. The fusion transcript was cloned through RT-PCR from the patient’s pulmonary tissue and stably transduced with lentivirus into NIH-3T3 cells. These fusion expressing cells demonstrated in vitro anchorage independent growth in a soft agar assay after 21 days. These cell lines also generated large tumors when injected subcutaneously into the flanks of mice after 18 days with tumors exhibiting histology similar to congenital fibrosarcoma. NIH-3T3 cells with only empty vector generated no colonies in the soft agar assay and no tumors in mice.

The K650M variant in FGFR3 is known to be responsible for the severe skeletal dysplasia forms seen in thanatophoric dysplasia type 1 / severe achondroplasia with developmental delay and acanthosis nigricans (TD1/SADDAN), and therefore was used as positive control in an autophosphorylation assay. FGFR3 cDNA construct with the K650M variant was synthesized and transfected into NIH3T3 cells. The K650M variant receptor had 18.1-fold greater kinase activity compared to the wild type receptor.

The FGFR3 variant K650E is known to be responsible for thanatophoric dysplasia type 2 (TDII), a severe form of skeletal dysplasia. The mutant receptor was tested for comparison between other variants discussed in this paper. FGFR3 cDNA construct with the K650E variant was synthesized and transfected into NIH3T3 cells. The K650E variant receptor had a 9.6-fold greater kinase activity compared to the wild type receptor.

FGFR3 cDNA construct with the K650T variant was synthesized and transfected into NIH3T3 cells. The K650T variant receptor had a 3.1-fold greater kinase activity compared to the wild type receptor in an autophosphorylation assay.
Xenografts of multiple myeloma cell line OPM2 (FGFR3 K650E) into nude mice resulted in tumor growth.

In CFK2 chondrocytic cell line model, cells with the G380R variant in FGFR3 showed growth retardation in comparison to the cells expressing the wild type receptor. Cells with the mutant receptor grew slower, failed to differentiate properly, had less incorporated 3H-thymidine, cell numbers and total protein content; both in the absence and in the presence of a ligand (FGF-1). The reduced proliferation rate was also accompanied by altered/reduced apoptotic cell property. The authors suggest that the signaling pathway downstream of the mutated FGFR3 may have been modified in some way.

Ba/F3 cells transfected with wild type FGFR3 or common bladder carcinoma variant FGFR3 Y375C both resulted in IL-3 independence with FGF1 dependence for growth. However, tumors grew when multiple myeloma cell line KMS11 (FGFR3 Y373C) cells were xenografted into nude mice.

FGFR3 S249C promoted FGF1 and IL-3 independent cell proliferation when transduced into Ba/F3 cells, whereas Ba/F3 cells with wildtype FGFR3 were IL-3 independent, but FGF1 dependent. R3Mab (monclonal antibody) treatment inhibited growth of S249C Ba/F3 cells and prevented FGFR3 dimerization in the UMUC-14 bladder cancer cell line, which harbors FGFR3 S249C. Therefore, S249C was determined to undergo ligand-independent dimerization leading to constitutive activation and phosphorylation. UMUC-14 cell xenografts and Ba/F3 S249C allografts into nude mice both resulted in tumor growth.
FGFR3 R248C promoted FGF1 and IL-3 independent cell proliferation when transduced into Ba/F3 cells whereas Ba/F3 cells with wildtype FGFR3 were IL-3 independent, but FGF1 dependent.

Protein co-chaperone Cdc37 is required in FGFR3 remodeling for recognition by chaperone protein Hsp90. Cdc37 must partially deactivate the kinase and present it in a particular orientation to Hsp90. Size-exclusion chromatography showed FGFR3 N540K occupied nearly 6 fold more space in the ternary complex than wildtype FGFR3. Isothermal titration calorimetry of I538F showed strong binding to Cdc37 with a Kd value of 1.8uM, whereas wildtype binding affinity to Cdc37 was too weak to be detected. The lower melting temperature of I538F indicates this variant to to be far more unstable than wildtype. Since Cdc37 must partially deactivate FGFR3 to couple Hsp90, variant and wildtype FGFR3 autophosphorylation was measured. I538F had more pronounced inhibition of auto-phosphorylation compared to the wildtype in-line with the variant's stronger binding to Cdc37. The authors concluded that due to the instability of I538F, the variant binds more tightly to Cdc37, which allows for greater incorporation with Hsp90.

FGFR3 N540K exhibited increased kinase activity compared to wild-type FGFR3, as reported in prior characterization of the mutation. In this study, FGFR3 N540K demonstrated enhanced incorporation into binary and ternary complexes with Cdc37 and Hsp90 relative to wild-type FGFR3. Size-exclusion chromatography and pull-down assays showed higher complex occupancy for N540K, consistent with stronger interaction with the chaperone system. Based on comparative analyses, the binding affinity of FGFR3 N540K to Cdc37 was estimated to be in the range of 1–2 μM, whereas binding of wild-type FGFR3 was too weak to be detected. Thermal stability assays indicated that FGFR3 N540K has reduced stability compared to wild-type FGFR3. These findings are consistent with increased association of FGFR3 N540K with the Cdc37/Hsp90 complex.

Protein co-chaperone Cdc37 is required in FGFR3 remodeling for recognition by chaperone protein Hsp90. Cdc37 must partially deactivate the kinase and present it in a particular orientation to Hsp90. Size-exclusion chromatography showed FGFR3 E466K occupied nearly 6 fold more space in the ternary complex than wildtype FGFR3. Comparative ITC experimentation of another variant I538F showed strong binding to Cdc37 with a Kd value of 1.8uM, which lead the authors to estimate a 1-2 uM Kd value for E466K to Cdc37, due to similar space occupancy in the ternary complex. Wildtype binding affinity to Cdc37 was too weak to be detected by ITC so N540K was a strong client for Cdc37. The lower melting temperature of E466K indicates this variant to to be far more unstable than wildtype. Since Cdc37 must partially deactivate FGFR3 to couple Hsp90, variant and wildtype FGFR3 autophosphorylation was measured. Variants with stronger binding to Cdc37 like E466K had more pronounced inhibition of auto-phosphorylation compared to the wildtype. The authors concluded that due to the instability of E466F, the variant binds more tightly to Cdc37, which allows for greater incorporation with Hsp90.

Protein co-chaperone Cdc37 is required in FGFR3 remodeling for recognition by chaperone protein Hsp90. Cdc37 must partially deactivate the kinase and present it in a particular orientation to Hsp90. A SEC experiment showed that hotspot mutation FGFR3 K650E occupied a similar amount of space as wildtype FGFR3 in the ternary complex. Melting point analysis and antibody testing showed that K650E had similar thermal stability and antibody recognition as the wildtype. ITC experimentation showed K650E bound very weakly to Cdc37 similar to the wildtype. The authors concluded that due to K650E's instability, it bound weakly to Cdc37 and had lower incorporation with Hsp90 like wildtype FGFR3.

A pooled analysis of three phase 1/2 clinical trials investigating the efficacy and safety of larotrectinib in 159 NTRK fusion positive solid tumor patients (1 month - 84 years old) confirmed larotrectinib to be effective and safe in these patients. NTRK2 fusions were found in 4 of the 159 patients. Two cases NTRK2 fusion cases were shown to have reduction in tumor size with another tumor showing only minor growth.

NIH 3T3 cells were transfected with wild-type and mutant K650E FGFR3. Immunoprecipitation measuring kinase activity showed FGFR3 K650E had 100-fold greater autophosphorylation than wildtype. The authors concluded that the position and charge of K650E lead to its constitutive activation.

Ezh2 Y641F (EZH2 Y641F) was conditionally expressed in mouse B-cells and caused high-penetrance lymphoma that was further accelerated by Bcl2 overexpression or p53 loss (but not c-Myc overexpression). Expression of Ezh2 Y641F increased global abundance of H3K27 trimethylation (H3K27me3) and also caused widespread redistribution of H3K27me3 leading to widespread transciptional changes. Overall, these results suggest that Ezh2 Y641F induces B-cell lymphoma through widespread reorganization of chromatin structure.

While receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) like FGFR3 form both homodimers and heterodimers (often in the same family), heterodimerization of RTKs is considered to be a method of greater receptor activation and diversification. The authors measured dimer stability and conformation via imaging and statistical analysis of FRET data. FGFR3 A391E greatly stabilized wildtype/mutant FGFR3 dimers similarly to mutant/mutant FGFR3 homodimers, however the mutation had weaker stabilizing effects on FGFR1 and FGFR2 heterodimers. This variant also had significant effects on the conformation and increased the distance between the receptors following dimerization. The authors concluded that this variant stabilizes FGFR3 heterodimers more than wildype homodimers and that A391E has equally dominant effects on both the mutant/wildtype heterodimer and mutant/mutant homodimer of FGFR3.

Phase I dose-escalation cohort (NCT01703481) of patients with advanced solid tumors in which antineoplastic therapy was no longer effective using pan-FGFR inhibitor JNJ-42756493. All 16 patients with urothelial carcinoma who had FGFR3 mutations responded, with 8 patients receiving 9 mg daily, 5 of which showed partial responses (PR), 1 showing stable disease (SD), and two showing progressive disease (PD). Another 8 patients received 10 mg intermittently (7d on/7d off), with 3 showing PRs, 3 showing PD, 1 showing SD, and 1 non-evaluable patient (NE). In patients with urothelial carcinoma who were positive for an FGFR mutation or fusion receiving 9 mg daily, the objective response rate (ORR) was 70%, while patients receiving 10 mg intermittently (7d on/7d off) had an ORR of 33%. The total ORR among patients with urothelial carcinoma who were positive for an FGFR mutation or fusion was 46%.

Phase I dose-escalation cohort (NCT01703481) of patients with advanced solid tumors in which antineoplastic therapy was no longer effective using pan-FGFR inhibitor JNJ-42756493. 2 cholangiocarcinoma patients with FGFR3 mutations received 10 mg intermittently (7d on/7d off) and displayed progressive disease (PD). One patient saw a ~20% maximal increase of the sum of diameters of targeted lesions and had progression-free survival (PFS) of approximately 2 months. The other patient had a ~10% maximal increase in the sum of targeted tumor diameters and a PFS of about 2 months. Cholangiocarcinoma patients with FGFR mutations or fusions receiving 10 mg for 7 days on and then 7 days off had an objective response rate (ORR) of 30%. The total ORR for FGFR mutation or fusion-positive cholangiocarcinoma patients was 27%.

A case series reports 5 famiies with pheochromocytoma. In family 4, the proband was a female who had a bilateral pheochromocytoma at the age of 46Y that recurred locally with liver metastases, melanoma, bilateral renal cysts. Her brother had a monolateral benign pheochromocytoma, but no VHL mutation was tested for, so it is unclear if the brother was also confirmed with a germline VHL splice mutation. Molecular analysis of the proband using on PCR–SSCP blood, showed the following sequence variants: VHL: c.463+43A>G, RET c.2071G>A p.G691S, SDHD c.34G>A p.G12S, IVS2-29A>G, c.204C>T p.S68S, and IVS3-32T>C.

NIH 3T3 cells were transfected with wild-type and mutant FGFR3 K650D. Immunoprecipitation measuring kinase activity showed FGFR3 K650D had similar autophosphorylation through constitutive action to FGFR3 K650E, which had 100-fold greater autophosphorylation than wildtype. The authors concluded that for constitutive FGFR3 activation, an acidic residue at position 650 is beneficial but not required.

NIH 3T3 cells were transfected with wild-type and mutant FGFR3 K650Q. Immunoprecipitation measuring kinase activity showed FGFR3 K650Q had much lower autophosphorylation to FGFR3 K650E, which had 100-fold greater autophosphorylation than wildtype, but that FGFR K650Q still had higher autophosphorylation driven by constitutive action than wildtype. The authors concluded that for constitutive FGFR3 activation, an acidic residue at position 650 is beneficial but not required.

NIH 3T3 cells were transfected with wild-type and mutant FGFR3 K650L. Immunoprecipitation measuring kinase activity showed FGFR3 K650L had much lower autophosphorylation than FGFR3 K650E, which had 100-fold greater autophosphorylation than wildtype but had higher autophosphorylation driven by constitutive action than wildtype. The authors concluded that for constitutive FGFR3 activation, an acidic residue at position 650 is beneficial but not required.

The G380R variant of FGFR3 was studied in the context of being a known genetic cause for achondroplasia (dwarfism). The authors performed Western blots using HEK 293 cells and antibodies capable of detecting both phosphorylated and un-phosphorylated FGFR3 and found that the G380R mutant version of FGFR3 had increased phosphorylation compared to the wild type protein. Based on this observation and data comparing FGFR3 without and without ligand and dimerization assays, the authors conclude that an increase in FGFR3 activation associated with this variant is related to increased phosphorylation of unliganded FGFR3 dimers.

PKC412 inhibited the growth of FGFR3 K650E-transformed Ba/F3 cells. Researchers introduced an N540D mutation to FGFR3-transformed Ba/F3 cells, which reduces inhibition of the FGFR3 K650E-transformed cells, confirming that FGFR3 mutants are the critical targets for PKC412-mediated cytotoxicity. t(4;14) positive multiple myeloma cell line OPM-1 expressing FGFR3 K650E were inhibited by PKC412, with relative viability dropping to 0.9/1.0 at 100 nM, 0.8/1.0 at 200 nM, 0.58/1.0 at 400 nM, 0.25/1.0 at 1000 nM with a sudden spike upwards at 0.9/1.0 at 2000 and 5000 nM. Mice were transplanted with bone marrow cells expressing FGFR3 K650E and split into a placebo and treatment group. Mine in the placebo group were all killed by day 25, while the PKC412-treated group continued treatment for an extra week, with 7/8 mice surviving to the endpoint of the study at 32 days. PKC412's efficacy was also confirmed through histopathologic examination that showed a reduction of lymphoid disease in bone marrow, spleen, and liver in the drug-treated mice. These findings were confirmed by flow cytometry of bone marrow cells, as immature B-cells only made up 1% of the population when treated with PKC412, as compared to the placebo which left 73% of the population as immature B-cells. This confirmed PKC412's efficacy in treating immature B-cell lymphoid disease.

t(4;14) positive multiple myeloma cell line OPM-1 and KMS11 expressing FGFR3 Y373C were inhibited by PKC412, with relative viability dropping to 0.9/1.0 at 100 nM, 0.8/1.0 to 200 nM, 0.58/1.0 at 400 nM, and 0.25/1.0 at 1000 nM, with a spike upwards to 0.9/1.0 at 2000 and 5000 nM in the OPM-1 line. In KMS11 cells, relative viability dropped to 0.8/1/0 at 100 nM, 0.7/1.0 at 200 nM, and 0.4/1.0 at 400 nM.

PKC412 inhibited the growth of TEL-FGFR3 fusion-transformed Ba/F3 cells by 25% at 100 nM, 45% at 200 nM, and 85% at nM in the absence of interleukin 3. The N540D mutation in the context of FGFR3 was introduced to the Ba/F3 cells and reduced inhibition of TEL-FGFR3-transformed cells, confirming FGFR3 mutants as the critical targets for PKC412-mediated cytotoxicity. Mice received bone marrow transplantation of cells containing TEL-FGFR fusion and were split into a placebo and treatment group. The placebo-receiving group died on day 16, while the PKC412 treated group lived on past day 20. Histopathologic examination of the TEL-FGFR-transplanted mice showed loss of white pulp and expansion of red pulp in the spleen by a population of myeloid forms. In PKC412 treated mice, the mice had increased prolongation of survival and showed a reduction in spleen and peripheral white blood cell counts. Flow cytometry of bone marrow samples showed elevated numbers of mature neutrophils that were positive for late myeloid markers Gr-1 and Mac-1 in spleen samples from TEL-FGFR-transplanted animals. The authors concluded that PKC412 successfully treated myeloproliferative disease as 18% of the population was Gr-1/Mac-1 double-positive neutrophils in the PKC412 group compared to 43% of the population in the placebo-treated group.

Cell line LP1 expressing FGFR3 F384L was treated with small molecule inhibitor PKC412, with relative viability rising above 1.1/1.0 at both 50 nM and 100 nM. Relative viability dropped to 0.96/1.0 at 200 nM, 0.6/1.0 at 400 nM, 0.5/1.0 at 1000 nM, 0.3/1.0 at 2000 nM, and 0.2/1.0 at 5000 nM. The authors concluded that this difference in sensitivity to the OPM-1 cell line, which displayed increasingly lower relative viability as the concentration increased, may be due to the FGFR3 F384L having lower expression levels of FGFR3 protein as compared to cell line OPM-1 which overexpresses FGFR3 mutant.

Ba/F3 cells transformed with FGFR3 K650E or TEL-FGFR3 had mutation FGFR3 N540D introduced to determine whether the FGFR3 mutants were the critical targets for PKC412-mediated cytotoxicity. The cells transformed with N540D displayed resistance to PKC412, as cells were tested for growth with PKC412 treatment and showed little growth inhibition. The authors concluded that N540D confers resistance to PKC412 and that the FGFR3 mutants are the targets for PKC41-mediated cytotoxicity.

Genomic DNA was extracted from peripheral blood leukocytes using the DNA isolation kit formammalian blood and mutation analysis was performed using direct sequencing of the PCR-amplified DNA, and strand conformation polymorphism analysis (PCR-SSCP). Of the 41 patients with phaeochromocytomas, one (patient 9) was reported as having the CGG167CAG (Arg to Gly) mutation of the VHL gene. This can be deduced as p.R167Q (c.500G>A): with the correction from lift over that “Arg to Gly” should be rather “Arg to Gln”. This patient was 20 years old when they were diagnosed with VHL disease. They presented with an adrenal mass indicated as a diagnosis of pheochromocytoma, and were also found with cerebellar hemangioblastoma and retinal angioma manifestations. No family information was provided. ACMG evidence codes: 'PP4' since the patient presents phenotypes highly specific for a disease with a single genetic etiology.

39 common nonepidermolytic, nonorganoid keratinocyte epidermal nevi were sampled from 33 patients and analyzed using a SNaPshot assay. FGFR3 R248C was found in 15/39 samples and 9/33 patients. The two subtypes presented in the R248C samples were the common soft and common hard subtypes. 4 patients with FGFR3 R248C in the epidermal nevus had biopsies of clinically and histologically normal epidermis adjacent to the nevus. SNaPshot analysis of the biopsies showed that the normal skin displayed a wildtype codon 248, while the FGFR3 R248C sample displayed the R248C peak underneath a smaller wildtype 248 peak. The authors concluded that these results suggested an epidermal mosaic of the FGFR3 mutation and a strong genotype-phenotype correlation.

A patient's biopsy, which was the common soft subtype of keratinocytic epidermal nevi, displayed a double mutation of both FGFR3 G372C (aka G370C) and G382R (aka G380R). The nevus from which the biopsy was taken displayed no histopathological abnormalities. It is unknown whether the G372C mutation, which activates FGFR3 more strongly than G382R, caused the epidermal nevus or if both mutations were necessary for its growth. The authors concluded that the nevus being caused primarily by G372C was unlikely, as achondroplasia, a disease associated with G372C, usually does not develop acanthosis nigricans, as opposed to thanatophoric dysplasia, a disease associated with G382R, which has been shown to develop benign skin lesions such as seborrheic keratosis.

Achondroplasia associated FGFR3 mutant G380R (ACH), K650E (TDII), and wildtype (WT) FGFR3 constructs were cloned and transfected into NIH3T3 cells, and immunopercipitated with anti-FGFR3. In vitro kinase assays were performed and G380R was found to have activity between WT and K650E, which had approximately 100 fold increase over WT.

To determine if EML4::NTRK3 fusions were recurrent in tumors types known to harbor ETV6::NTRK3 fusions, the authors screened 63 cases with varying diagnoses (infantile fibrosarcoma, congenital mesoblastic nephroma, mammary analog secretory carcinoma and secretory breast carcinoma). A novel NTRK3 break-apart probe set detected an NTRK3 rearrangement in 34/58 cases tested, including 25/26 infantile fibrosarcomas. In 46 cases tested, a novel EML4::NTRK3 dual fusion FISH probe set detected the fusion in 1 infantile fibrosarcoma case (case 58; 1 years old) known to harbor the EML4::NTRK3 fusion and a new case (case 3; 7 months), both with histology typical for what is observed in ETV6::NTRK3 infantile fibrosarcoma. The probe did not detect the fusion in any case known to have an ETV6::NTRK3 fusion.
