A 33-year-old Han Chinese woman has been associated with an NTRK fusion cervical sarcoma which was positive for Pan-TRK by immunohistochemistry (IHC) analysis. However, FISH for NTRK1 was negative. The tumor resection was performed by hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, pelvic lymph node dissection, and partial vaginal resection. No evidence of lymph node metastasis was noted. Patient underwent 6 course adjuvant chemotherapy. On a follow-up visit after two months from her last follow up a mass in the right trigeminal nerve area was detected. This was morphologically confirmed as spindle cell sarcoma. NGS and IHC on this tumor specimen confirmed EML4-NTRK3 (e2-e14) fusion and pan-TRK positive, respectively. Tumor recurrence and invasion was noted one month later with a mass protruding from the vaginal external orifice. The mass was resected, and this specimen was positive for Pan-TRK by IHC. The patient passed away (14 months after diagnosis) before being enrolled in the TRK inhibitor clinical trial. The authors of this paper reported this as a first cervical sarcoma case with TRK fusion from a Chinese institution.

Whole genome sequencing and RNAseq were performed on 400 patients with resected or locally advanced/metastatic Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma (PDAC). Immunohistochemistry (IHC) analysis was performed in a subset of these patients. Two adult cases of PDAC were identified with an in-frame EML4::NTRK3 (e6-e14) fusion. This fusion was further confirmed by RT-PCR and Sanger sequencing. Pan-Trk IHC was positive for this fusion. In one case, the fusion was found postmortem.

Targeted mutation analysis on the FGFR3 gene in 297 bladder cancer patients was conducted, where 177 patients were found to harbor FGFR3 mutations. One patient was found to harbor a novel G380R mutation that affects the transmembrane domain and results in the replacement of a glycine by an arginine residue in exon 10 of FGFR3 . This mutation is identical to a germinal activating mutation associated with the most common form of genetic dwarfism, achondroplasia. Furthermore, another patient had a compound heterozygous mutation and displayed a S249C mutation in FGFR3. The authors suggest that the presence of this variant in bladder carcinoma might have higher risk to develop bladder cancer than the general population.

A construct of PDGF and FGFR3 was created as a chimeric receptor to study the effect of the K650E variant on downstream signaling pathways. Transfecting PC12 cells showed continuous ligand-independent activity of the chimeric mutant receptor with the presence of an inducer alone (zinc) but not the ligand; PDFG. Upon addition of PDGF, further activation was also observed. Conversely, control cells showed activity only with the addition of both ligand and zinc. Gene expression profiling showed P21 gene was expressed at a higher level (1.7 folds) in mutant receptor cells, providing evidence of ERK1/2 and STAT1/3 activation. The mutant receptor produced a highly sustained ERK1/2 activation even after 1 hour of PDGF treatment, whereas wild-type expressing cells showed a decrease in ERK1/2 activity. Lastly, cells only expressing the variant K650E receptor were able to phosphorylate tyrosine in STAT1, and tyrosine, along with serine, in a ligand-independent manner in STAT3. Authors confirm that mutant FGFR3 activates ERK1/2 and STAT1/3 in a ligand-independent manner and maintains this activation over longer periods of time when treated with ligand than does the wild-type receptor.

A novel and recurrent t(12;15)(p13;q25) translocation was identified in all three cases of congenital fibrosarcoma (CFS) studied. Molecular cloning of the breakpoints revealed that this translocation creates a gene fusion, joining the 5' region of the ETV6 (TEL) gene on chromosome 12 to the 3' region of the NTRK3 (TRKC) gene on chromosome 15. Reverse transcriptase-PCR (RT-PCR) analysis confirmed the expression of the resulting ETV6-NTRK3 chimeric transcript in all CFS tumors, but not in histologically similar control cases of adult-type fibrosarcoma or infantile fibromatosis. The in-frame fusion transcript encodes a chimeric protein composed of the helix-loop-helix (HLH) dimerization domain from ETV6 fused to the entire protein tyrosine kinase (PTK) catalytic domain of NTRK3. The authors conclude that this ETV6-NTRK3 fusion protein likely functions as a constitutively active tyrosine kinase, driving oncogenesis in CFS through the dysregulation of NTRK3 signal transduction pathways.

A 6-year-old female had invasive breast adenocarcinoma with the histopathologic features of a secretory breast carcinoma (SBC). FISH and RT-PCR on frozen tumor tissue found ETV6::NTRK3 fusion. 11 of 12 breast cancer cases, ranging from 19 to 75 years, where SBC was the predominant or only histologic component were found to have ETV6::NTRK3 fusion. 50 typical IDC cases were tested, and 49/50 did not host the fusion. Authors state the positive case may have originated from SBC. Authors conclude that ETV6::NTRK3 is a nonrandom rearrangement and that SBC is characterized by expression of the ETV6-NTRK3.

A 6-year-old female was diagnosed with secretory breast carcinoma (SBC), a rare invasive breast adenocarcinoma. Analysis of the tumor revealed a genetic driver: an ETV6::NTRK3 gene fusion. This fusion was confirmed through FISH and RT-PCR, and sequencing showed it contained the full SAM dimerization and tyrosine kinase domains, with ETV6 exon 5 fused directly to NTRK3 exon 13 (skipping NTRK3 exon 16). Immunoprecipitation and western blotting verified that the chimeric oncoprotein was expressed and tyrosine-phosphorylated in the tumor cells. To confirm the fusion's transformative potential, researchers expressed ETV6::NTRK3 in two murine mammary epithelial cell lines: Eph4 (epithelial phenotype) and Scg6 (mesenchymal phenotype). The engineered cells exhibited a transformed morphology and, when injected into nude mice, readily formed tumors. In contrast, control cells with an empty vector did not form any tumors, demonstrating that the ETV6::NTRK3 fusion is a potent driver of oncogenesis.

In a study of 426 unrelated VHL patients, 111 were discovered to have alterations in the VHL gene. 18 novel variants were identified in VHL patients, but none were present in 200 unaffected control individuals. DNA samples from peripheral blood leukocytes underwent polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplification, denaturing high-performance liquid chromatography (DHPLC), and direct sequence analysis of the entire coding sequence and intron-exon boundaries. The P76del (c.227_229del) germline mutation of the VHL gene was found in a 25 yr old VHL patient with hemangioblastomas of the central nervous system and pancreatic cyst or tumor (index case 280). No family information is provided.

FRET was used to compare the structural changes in FGFR dimers when FGF1 and FGF2 bind, and found that FGF2 bound dimers were much closer to each other than FGF1. The authors also looked at FGFR3 phosphorylation using western blot analysis and found that FGF2-bound dimers had increased FGFR3 phosphorylation. Therefore it was concluded that the FGF1 bound dimer is the inactive state, while the FGF2 bound dimer is the active state. Common bladder cancer and Crouzon syndrome with acanthosis nigricans variant FGFR3 A391E dimerization and phosphorylation were measured via FRET and western blot assays respectively. The A391E substitution was shown to activate FGFR3 through ligand-independent dimerization similar to the FGF2 bound state. Thus the authors concluded that the A391E mutation traps FGF3R in its most active state.

93 families examined at the Clinical Center of the National Institutes of Health (Bethesda, MD) underwent genetic testing for germline mutations of the VHL gene. Whole blood was extracted and genomic DNA was amplified by PCR and products were sequences using a cycle sequencing kit with dye-labeled terminators and automatically sequenced. VHL Family 12 was found to have the c.553G>C (G114R) germline variant of the VHL gene. The number of family members included in this study is not specified. This family was diagnosed with VHL Type 2 (with pheochromocytoma). Other phenotypes of family details were not provided. Only supporting evidence for pathogenicity because the patient's phenotype is highly specific for a disease with a single genetic etiology (ACMG code: PP4).

Yeast strain yIG397 was cultured to express both wild-type (WT) and mutant R175H originally identified in anaplastic astrocytoma. Should the mutant be dominant-negative (DN), TP53 will not bind and transactivate the ADE2 protein, resulting in red/pink colonies. If the mutant is recessive, then WT function is not blocked and ADE2 protein is expressed through TP53 transactivation, resulting in white colonies. Western blot analysis showed that yeast lysates showed expression of both WT and mutant alleles. Yeast expressing p53 variant and WT p53 produced red/pink colonies, demonstrating that R175H displays transdominance. Authors reported that all of the DN mutants affected the amino acids essential to the upkeep of DNA binding surfaces according to crystallographic structure.

Authors reported that all of the DN mutants affected the amino acids essential to the upkeep of DNA binding surfaces according to crystallographic structure.

In this study, 91 patients with diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma (DIPG) underwent stereotactic biopsy and were analyzed using histone H3 mutation testing, immunohistochemistry, gene expression profiling, and copy number analysis. Diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma (DIPG) patients harboring a H3.3 K27M mutation have a proneural/oligodendroglial phenotype and a prometastatic gene expression with PDGFRA activation. These mutation carriers were resistant to radiotherapy and relapsed significantly earlier with more metastatic recurrences. H3.3-K27M mutations confirmed by sanger sequencing from the corresponding biopsy core were mostly localized in midline pediatric high-grade glioma (pHGG). Gene expression microarray profiling of H3.3-K27M tumors showed a strong enrichment for the proneural-glioblastoma multiforme, oligodendrocytic or neural signatures. H3.3-K27M DIPG was frequently associated with oligodendroglial differentiation when assessed histologically. H3.3-K27M tumors are associated with a significant downregulation of genes inhibited in metastases (N=26) involving extracellular matrix receptor interaction (KEGG pathway) and cell-matrix adhesion pathways (GO:0007160). Comparative genome hybridization showed frequent loss of cytoband 14q24 and 17p13.1 in H3.3-K27M tumors. TP53 accumulation detected by IHC was significant in H3.3-K27M tumors. This study results support H3.3-K27M is a driving event in DIPG oncogenesis. H3.3-K27M samples showed metastatic evolution of the disease, and had poor overall survival compared with H3.1-K27M tumors.

This retrospective study analyzed 91 biopsy-confirmed diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma (DIPG) patients using systematic stereotactic or surgical biopsy at diagnosis. Histone H3 alterations were assessed using Sanger sequencing of H3F3A, HIST1H3B/C, and HIST2H3C, together with immunohistochemistry for H3K27 trimethylation (H3K27me3) and H3-K27M mutant protein, complemented by gene expression microarrays, array comparative genomic hybridization (aCGH), and radiologic correlation. Among 62 DIPG samples evaluated by IHC, 59/62 (~95%) demonstrated loss of H3K27me3, and most tumors harbored either an H3-K27M mutation or associated loss of this epigenetic mark. H3.3-K27M tumors demonstrated distinct molecular and clinical features compared with H3.1-K27M tumors, including proneural and oligodendroglial gene expression signatures, PDGFRA pathway activation, increased metastatic progression, earlier relapse, and reduced overall survival. These findings support molecular subclassification of diffuse midline glioma based on H3 K27M histone variants and identify H3.3-K27M tumors as a clinically aggressive molecular subgroup.

evidence_statement: This manuscript is a study of 37 TFEB-altered tumors, 15 of which are associated with TFEB amplification at 6p21.1 and 22 of which are associated with TFEB-rearrangement. Previous literature had indicated that renal tumors with the TFEB amplification showed a worse prognosis than those with the TFEB rearrangement. In the 22 TFEB-rearranged cases, two of the seven cases that were available for follow-up show the presence of metastases. In the 15 TFEB amplification cases, seven of the eight cases that were available for follow-up demonstrate the presence of metastases. Furthermore, digital droplet PCR in this study is used to quantify the expression of TFEB mRNA in both the TFEB amplified and the TFEB-rearranged tumors. The TFEB expression from digital droplet PCR reveals a mean of 51.2% in tumors with TFEB amplification and a mean of 224.7% in tumors with the TFEB rearrangement (p=0.06). The results reveal an unexpectedly higher TFEB expression in the TFEB-rearranged tumors as compared to that of the TFEB amplified tumors. However, it has been shown that the biphasic morphology is present in the TFEB-rearranged tumors, which is notably absent in the tumors with TFEB amplification. The TFEB expression from digital droplet PCR reveals a mean of 401.7% in the tumors with biphasic morphology as opposed to the mean of 58.7% in the tumors without biphasic morphology (p=0.00004). This shows that the increased TFEB mRNA expression could be associated with the biphasic morphology in the tumors with TFEB rearrangement. In addition, there is the presence of a less consistent and more diffuse expression of downstream markers of TFEB activation (cathepsin K, Melan A, HMB45) seen in the TFEB amplified tumors. Moreover, there are previously identified additional oncogenic drivers at the 6p21.1 locus (VEGFA and CCND3) that could contribute to the aggressive behavior of the tumors with TFEB amplification at 6p21.1. Therefore, this study indicates that the increased aggressive behavior of the TFEB amplified tumors in comparison with the TFE¬B-rearranged tumors could have stronger correlation with the oncogenic drivers at the 6p21.1 locus and less with the TFEB expression.

Of 351 primary thyroid carcinoma patients assessed by targeted gene rearrangement next-generation assay, 11 cases (3.1%) had NTRK rearrangement. Only one case of EML4::NTRK3 fusion (e2,e13) with an intact kinase domain was detected in an intracranial metastatic thyroid carcinoma. This patient underwent a total thyroidectomy and radioactive iodine (RAI) treatment at initial diagnosis. However, disease persisted and after three decades brain metastasis occurred. NTRK inhibitor therapy was given which showed a 69.7% decrease in disease burden following 34 cycles of entrectinib (400 mg daily) with mild side effects. pTERT C228T mutation and the frameshift MEN1 deletion cooccurred with EML4::NTRK3 fusion and both did not confer to entrectinib resistance.

Molecular effects of EML4::NTRK3 fusion gene was assessed using HEK293T cells or NIH-3T3-A14 cells transfected with pBABE constructs containing fusion gene and co-transfected with constructs encoding either MYC-tagged ERK1 or GFP-tagged AKT. Rare germline and somatic cancer variant FGFR3 K650E crystal structure was compared to phosphorylated and unphosphorylated FGF1 and FGF2 via superimposition. This comparison showed that K650E (located in the A-loop of FGFR3) was in the active state in the absence of a ligand. A-loop tyrosine phosphorylation of FGFR3 leads to activation of the receptor and the location is generally a hotspot for pathogenic gain-of-function mutations. The authors also showed that the K650E mutation circumvents the requirement of A-loop tyrosine phosphorylation for FGFR3 activation by comparing the kinase activity of K650E versus wildtype FGFR3 and K650E with other A-loop mutations at locations (Y647,Y648) considered to be essential for A-loop activation/phosphorylation. The K650E mutation had far greater activity than the wildtype, but nearly the same activation levels compared to K650E with other "essential" A-loop mutations. This confers that K650E is a ligand-independent constitutively active mutation which is activated independently of A-loop phosphorylation via mimicry.

Crouzon syndrome with acanthosis nigricans mutation FGFR3 A391E activation was tested in the presence of ligand fgf1 via Western blots as well as testing dimerization, phosphorylation and ligand binding levels. HEK cells were transfected with wildtype and A391E FGFR3 after which the cells were incubated with different levels of fgf1. Although the cells expressed different levels of FGR3 for wildtype vs A391E, the mutation increased receptor activation at every ligand concentration level. Dimerization levels were measured by calculating the fraction of crosslinked receptors via the intensities of monomeric and dimeric bands on a Western blot. The authors concluded that the A391E mutation increases activation both in the presence and absence of ligand due to increased dimerization.

evidence_statement: A study describing phenotypic and genotypic characteristics of VHL in an Indian population of 31 subjects, from 15 families diagnosed with VHL. Genomic DNA was amplified with PCR and sequenced and large deletions in the VHL gene were investigated with MLPA. Multi-cystic pancreas and CNS hemangioblastomas were the most common manifestations in this population. The G114D (c.340+1G>A) germline variant of the VHL gene was found in 8 members of a family (ID AD). Patients 7, 8, 9, 11, 12, 13 and 14 presented with multi-cystic pancreatic lesions. Patients 10, 11, 12 and 14 presented with CNS hemangioblastomas. Patient 10 presented with retinal angioma. Patients 11, 13 and 14 present with renal cell carcinoma. Demographic information is as follows (ID, age of onset, sex): 7, 27, M; 8, 34, F; 9, 38, F; 10, 17, M; 11, 40, M; 12, 50, F; 13, 50, M; 14, 50, F. Patients 10 and 14 were also found to have the c.340+5G>C germline variant of the VHL gene. ACMG: PM6, PM4.

A study of 419 patients with liver metastases of colorectal cancer identified 12 with A146 mutations. Compared to KRAS G12 tumors, patients with A146 positive tumors exhibited higher ctDNA levels. Patients harboring a KRAS A146 mutations also had larger tumors and inferior overall survival (median 10.7 v 26.4 months; hazard ratio = 2.5; P = .003).

This study screened for VHL and RET mutations in a group of patients taken from the European-American Pheochromocytoma-Paraganglioma and German von Hippel-Lindau Disease Registries. The patients were genotyped using PCR and restriction digest and underwent germline mutation analyses for exons 10–11 and 13–16 of RET and all exons of the VHL, SDHB, SDHC, and SDHD (SDHx) genes. The proband of family 3 (II.1) was found to have c.241C>T mutation (p.P81S) alongside a large exon 1-3 deletion. The proband presented with hemangioblastoma (age 50) and pancreatic cysts. Family history screening showed the P81S variant was inherited from a healthy father (I.1), while the large deletion was de novo. This family may have been previously published in 11106358 and/or 7563486.

evidence_statement: The patient cohort consisted of 57 patients (26 male and 31 female) from Southern Italy, most of whom (55 of 57) presented with solitary HGB of the CNS: 6 were syndromic and 51 were apparently sporadic. 8 patients had germline VHL mutations. Both peripheral blood and tumor tissue samples were sequenced using Big Dye Terminator Ready Reaction mix v.1.1 (Life Technologies, Foster City, CA). Sequencing reactions were loaded on an ABI 3100 capillary sequencer (Life Technologies) and analyzed using the Sequencing Analysis software v.3.7 (PE Applied Biosystems, Grand Island, NY). A 61 year old Italian male patient (Case ID HGB-25) was found to harbor two somatic mutations, a c.375insA was found in tumor sample 2 and a c.163delG was found in sample 1a. He was diagnosed at age 53 with cerebellar hemangioblastoma. He was also found to have one germline missense mutation (c.74C>T; p.Pro25Leu) in the VHL gene.The patient has positive family history for VHL disease.

The authors evaluated a family of five VHL c.241C>T (p.Pro81Ser) carriers, as well as the clinical characteristics of all the p.Pro81Ser carriers reported in the literature. Five members of one family were investigated and their blood samples were taken and sequencing using sanger sequencing of exons and exon-intron boundaries. The proband (age 31), presented with renal cell carcinoma at age 29 and had a germline VHL mutation (p.P2P) in addition to the germline (p.Pro81Ser)mutation. The proband had one son who was asymptomatic and only carried the p.P2P mutation. The proband had one brother (age 32) and one-half brother (age 36) who carried the p.Pro81Ser mutation but were asymptomatic. The proband's mother (age 52), harbored the p.Pro81Ser mutation and had breast cancer at age 34. The proband's maternal grandmother (age 71) also harbored the p.Pro81Ser mutation but was asymptomatic. Although the mutation was maternally inherited, the proband’s paternal uncle died from metastasizing renal cell carcinoma at 46 years of age, and the proband’s father died from urosepsis in relation to bladder cancer in situ at the age of 56. Neither of these men were able to undergo genetic testing.

The authors evaluated a family of five VHL c.6C>G (p.Pro2Pro) carriers. Five members of one family were investigated and their blood samples were taken and sequencing using sanger sequencing of exons and exon-intron boundaries. The proband (age 31), presented with renal cell carcinoma at age 29, the P2= germline mutation and had an additional VHL mutation (p.P81S). The proband had one son who was asymptomatic and only carried the p.P2P mutation. The proband's two brothers, mother, and maternal grandmother were all found to carry the other VHL mutation (p.P81S). The proband’s paternal uncle died from metastasizing renal cell carcinoma at 46 years of age, and the proband’s father died from urosepsis in relation to bladder cancer in situ at the age of 56. Neither of these men were able to undergo genetic testing.

The authors identify a new VHL cryptic exon (termed E1') deep in intron 1 that is naturally expressed in many tissues. Mutations in E1' are identified in 7 families with erythrocytosis and in 1 large family with typical VHL disease but without any alteration in the other VHL exons. Whole blood was isolated from patients and sequenced using sanger sequencing and whole-genome sequencing performed at the clinically accredited Molecular Diagnostics Laboratory at the John Radcliffe Hospital using the Hi-Sequation 4000 platform (Illumina Inc., San Diego, CA) in high-throughput mode. As well, paired-end sequencing was carried out in a single lane on the HiSeq 2500 system (Illumina).In this study, the authors show that the mutations in E1' induced dysregulation of VHL splicing with excessive retention of E1' and were associated with a downregulation of VHL protein expression. Three patients were found with both the c.598C>T germline VHL mutation and the c.340+770T>C mutation resulting in p.Ser179Pro mutation on potential X1 protein encoded by E1' exon. In family 2, II.1 was the only person who had both of these mutations. In family 3, brothers II.1 and II.2 had these two mutations. Biological material from the parents of these three children were not available but Chuvash core haplotype analysis demonstrated that all patients were compound heterozygous with one mutation being inherited from each parent. All three cases described above had erythrocytosis.

This paper analyzed VHL sequences in the renal cell carcinomas of patients exposed to high, cumulative doses of trichloroethylene. Whole blood and tumour tissues were isolated and mutations were identified, respectively, by direct sequencing of purified PCR products. For fast analysis of the presence of a frequent mutation at nt 454 (C>T), a restriction endonuclease-based assay (enzyme AciI based assay) was used. Patient 1654 presented with renal cell carcinoma and was diagnosed at age 59. This patient was found to have the germline P81S (c. 241C>T) (denoted as nt454 C>T mutation in the paper) VHL mutation in DNA isolated from tumor-adjacent normal kidney parenchyma (germline) and a somatic c.260_263del VHL mutation.

Mutations at codon K385 are specific to glial and glioneuronal tumors. In addition, tumors with these mutations do not typically have other pathogenic mutations in other typical brain-cancer-associated genes and consequently are a separate entity from other gliomas with well-described associated variants.

PDGFRA K385L (6) or K385I (2) mutations were identified as the sole somatic pathogenic alteration in 8 patients with low-grade glioneuronal tumors; furthering defining "Myxoid glioneuronal tumor, PDGFRA p.K385‐mutant" as a distinct CNS entity. All 8 patients were treated with initial resection. Three patients experienced disease progression/recurrence and all were treated with either a second resection or drug therapy; and all remained stable at last clinical followup. To date PDGFRA mutations at this residue have not been found in any other tumor entity.

A 15-year-old Indian male presented in 2017 with a history of acute-onset painless vision loss of both eyes. He also had intermittent history of headache, which was not severe before the onset of vision loss for about 3 months and was treated as a case of optic neuritis. 2 months later he presented with episodes of headache, palpitation, chest pain, and persisting low visual acuity and high blood pressure. He was evaluated for endocrine causes of hypertension and a CT scan of abdomen revealed bilateral pheochromocytoma, which was more likely considering his young age and presenting symptoms of episodic headache and hypertension. He was given antihypertensive medications to control blood pressure and was taken up for adrenalectomy, following which his blood pressure stabilized. At his 1 year follow up, his visual acuity was more improved in both eyes. Due to his bilateral pheochromocytoma, genetic testing was performed and was found to have the c.482G>A VHL mutation consistent with VHL disease. Further follow up showed no novel tumors, no family history and his relatives have been advised to get screened for the mutation. ACMG codes: N/A.

A large Hungarian VHL type 2 family involving 32 members underwent mutational analysis of their peripheral blood and had exons 1, 2, and 3 of the VHL gene sequenced using direct sequencing of PCR-amplified DNA. Only oatient II-1, a 70-year-old asymptomatic compound heterozygote, had two germline mutations, c.74C>T and c.239G>A (wrongly described as S80I in the paper). Her daughter the proband (III-1) did not carry the Pro25Leu mutation but carried the Ser80Ile mutation and presented with a bilateral RCC (40Y), brain hemangioblastoma (42Y) and pheochromocytoma (34Y). The probands maternal aunt died of bilateral RCC. A male maternal cousin was diagnosed with both retina (18Y) and brain (37Y) hemangioblastomas. The probands female maternal cousin once removed showed brain hemangioblastomas (22Y), renal cysts (20Y) and retina hemangioblastoma (23Y). Her male maternal cousin once removed presented bilateral pheochromocytoma (10Y) and a retina hemangioblastoma (26Y). Her male maternal cousin presented retina (29Y) and brain (38Y) hemangioblastomas as well as pheochromocytoma (39Y).

Germline mutations were found in 20 Brazilian, VHL probands and their families. Peripheral blood samples were taken and genomic DNA was sequenced using PCR and Southern Blotting. The three exons of the VHL gene were amplified by PCR, sequenced in both strands with Big Dye terminators (Applied Biosystems), and collected and analysed on an ABI Prism 377 (Applied Biosystems). Germline rearrangements involving part or the entire VHL gene were detected by quantitative Southern blotting using g7 cDNA11 and a β globin probe. This mutation, H115Pfs*44 (c.344delA) , was found in a VHL type 1 family of 3 affected individuals (VHL family 9). This mutation caused a frameshift to occur leading to the protein terminating at residue 157. One had hemangioblastomas of the central nervous system, one with retinal angiomas, and one with renal carcinoma. Within this family a second mutation was also discovered in the VHL gene, P61= (183C>G), which was assumed to not be deleterious. ACMG codes as follows: A frameshift mutation in a gene where loss-of-function is a known mechanism of disease (PVS1). Cosegregation with disease in multiple affected family members in a gene definitively known to cause the disease (PP1).

41 non-related patients with retinal capillary hemangioma presenting in the Benjamin Franklin University Eye Clinic between 1988 to 1999 Germany were evaluated for the presence of other VHL lesions. VHL disease was diagnosed in 33 patients based on the presence of other severe VHL lesions (spinal hemangioblastoma, cerebellar hemangioblastoma, renal cysts, pancreatic cyst, renal carcinoma, and pheochromocytoma), molecular genetic testing, and/or family history. VHL germline mutations were identified in 27 out of 29 VHL families screened with molecular genetics. Blood samples were genetically tested using PCR-SSCP sequencing. One patient with VHL-related retinal capillary hemangioma was found to have a 2kb deletion in the VHL gene. It's unclear which other VHL-related lesions were identified in this patient. ACMG evidence codes: 'PP4' because the patients' phenotypes are highly specific for a disease with single genetic etiology.

Eight children with a history of polycythemia and elevated serum erythropoietin level were evaluated. Three germline mutations were identified in 4 patients while, mutations were not detected for other 4 patients. Peripheral blood samples were taken and PCR products of either each VHL exon or the cDNA were purified and sequenced using a DNA sequencing kit (BigDye Terminator Cycle Sequencing Ready Reaction; Applied Biosystems, Foster City, CA). The sequencing reaction was performed in the Peltier Model P200 thermocycler. The products were then analyzed on the ABI Prism 377 DNA Sequencer (Applied Biosystems) according to the manufacturer's protocol. Clonality was determined by a transcriptional assay of exonic polymorphisms in 5 X-linked genes. An in vitro assay of erythroid progenitors' sensitivity to Epo was also performed. Patient 8, a 5 year old boy with polycythemia, was found to be a compound heterozygote harboring two germline VHL variants; c. 598C>T and c.388G>C. The patient was found to have inherited the c.598C>T mutation from his mother and the c.388G>C from his father. Both him and his parents had normal sensitivity of erythroid progenitors to Epo.

Twelve patients with hereditary non-SDHx head and neck paragangliomas were analyzed. Eleven of the 12 patients were found to carry germline mutations in the VHL gene. Blood was used for molecular genetic analyses and the NM_000551.2 reference sequence was used. The paper includes 3 additional VHL patients: case 22, 23, 27. Case 22 is a male who was found to harbour the p.V166F (c.496G>T) mutation of the VHL gene. He presented with a head/neck paraganglioma, as well as pheochromocytoma and CNS hemangioblastoma. A negative family history was described.

Complete molecular analysis of the VHL gene on genomic DNA was conducted on 4 patients and some of their relatives. Peripheral blood lymphocytes were collected and the VHL gene dosage was evaluated by quantitative Southern blot or real-time quantitative PCR analysis. The coding region was studied via direct sequencing. One patient (4), a 16 year old female, was found to harbour a polymorphic variant on the 3' UTR of the VHL gene (c.1149 A>G) AND the promoter region mutation c.–65_–55dup11 of the VHL gene. She presented with an isolated retinal angioma and an unremarkable family history, although the dup11 variant was inherited from an nonsymptomatic parent. ACMG evidence codes: 'PP4' since the patient presents phenotypes highly specific for a disease with a single genetic etiology.

Tumor samples from 3 unrelated patients with germline deletion of VHL gene were analyzed for genetic changes in the second copy of the VHL gene. The germline deletions were demonstrated through blood lymphocytes of all 3 patients and fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) using genomic probes P1, c3, c11 and g7 cDNA for the VHL gene. Case 1, 2, and 3 each had VHL germline deletions: paitent 1 had a germline deletion of the VHL gene demonstrated by loss of one open-reading frame signal detected by g7 cDNA probe, and patients 2 and 3 had germline deletions on chromosome 3 (>35kb, <90kb). No familial relations were discussed. Patient 1 also had a missense somatic mutation I151S(c.452T>G) in the second copy of VHL gene, observed in the renal cell carcinoma sample of this patient. ACMG: 'PP4' because the patients' phenotypes is highly specific for a disease with single genetic etiology.

Case 1, 2, and 3 each had VHL germline deletions: paitent 1 had a germline deletion of the VHL gene demonstrated by loss of one open-reading frame signal detected by g7 cDNA probe, and patients 2 and 3 had germline deletions on chromosome 3 (>35kb, <90kb). No familial relations were discussed. Patient 3 also had a missense somatic mutation R69C(c.205C>T) in the second copy of VHL gene, observed in the renal cell carcinoma sample of this patient. ACMG: 'PP4' because the patients' phenotypes is highly specific for a disease with single genetic etiology.

A 37-year-old woman was admitted for adrenal diseases with bilateral adrenal tumors and multiple hepatic and pulmonary lesions for surgery. She was first diagnosed with VHL disease in 2000 due to a heterozygous c.292T>C mutation in exon 1 of the VHL gene. Her father was also diagnosed with a VHL gene mutation. She lost 4-5-kg in 4 months, had increased daytime fatigue, and anxiety, and revealed occasional past nicotine abuse. CT scan of chest, abdomen and pelvis revealed bilateral adrenal tumors, multiple partially calcified hepatic lesions, and multiple bilateral partially calcified pulmonary lesions and nodules. An MRI revealed bilateral adrenal tumors. Due to these CT and MRI findings, a diagnostic hypothesis of metastatic pheochromocytoma or adrenocortical carcinoma was made. Bilateral partial adrenalectomy, liver biopsy, and thoracoscopic atypical left lung excision were performed. Histopathologic examination confirmed bilateral pheochromocytomas and hepatic epithelioid hemangioendothelioma with pulmonary metastases. ACMG code: PP4

A patient with recurrent metastatic salivary secretory carcinoma and ETV6-NTRK3 fusion was treated with entrectinib and achieved durable ongoing response. The patient had partial response after 4 weeks and mass was no longer identifiable after 19 weeks. Pulmonary nodules are either no longer apparent or stable on CT at 46 months followup.

41 non-related patients with retinal capillary hemangioma presenting in the Benjamin Franklin University Eye Clinic between 1988 to 1999 Germany were evaluated for the presence of other VHL lesions. VHL disease was diagnosed in 33 patients based on the presence of other severe VHL lesions (spinal hemangioblastoma, cerebellar hemangioblastoma, renal cysts, pancreatic cyst, renal carcinoma, and pheochromocytoma), molecular genetic testing, and/or family history. VHL germline mutations were identified in 27 out of 29 VHL families screened with molecular genetics. Blood samples were genetically tested using PCR-SSCP sequencing. One patient with VHL-related retinal angiomatosis was found to have germline missense mutation (c.465G>C) mutation in the VHL gene. This variant was reported as c.677+1G>C/Codon 155 but was assumed to be intended to be c.678G>C given the codon provided (AF010238.1) and was mapped to p.V155= (c.465G>C) (NM_000551.3).

evidence_statement: Patient 1 and Patient 2 are Arab brothers who were both diagnosed with VHL disease type 1 at age 44 and 45, respectively. The two brothers had very similar VHL clinical manifestations including cerebellar hemangioblastomas, renal cell carcinoma, and cysts in the pancreas. However, patient 1 also had testicular and epididymal cysts, as well as lesions in the spine, which were absent in Patient 2. No other family history was noted. Genomic DNA was isolated from peripheral blood from either patient and PCR was performed to amplify the coding exons of the VHL gene. Sanger sequencing revealed a recurrent germline in-frame p.Phe76del(c.227_229delTCT) VHL deletion in both brothers. Immediate family members were recommended to genetically test for the relevant variant or monitor for VHL-related symptoms. ACMG code: PP4

evidence_statement: At 63 years of age, patient 3 displayed multiple cysts in the pancreas and right kidney, and possessed a lesion in the right kidney. Due to renal cell carcinoma, she had a left radical nephrectomy. Four years later, at the age of 67 years, she was found to have hemangioblastomas in the left cerebellum and spine, renal cell carcinoma, as well as cysts in kidneys and pancreas, revealing a diagnosis of VHL disease. Two years later, a right partial nephrectomy was done for renal cell carcinoma. At the time, her pancreas was covered with cysts. She had no family history of VHL disease. Genomic DNA was isolated from peripheral blood and PCR was performed to amplify the coding exons of the VHL gene. Sanger sequencing revealed a recurrent germline missense I151T(c.452T>C) mutation in the VHL gene. Immediate family members were recommended to genetically test for the relevant variant or monitor for VHL-related symptoms. ACMG: PP4

evidence_statement: At 40Y, patient 4 was diagnosed with cerebellar and spinal hemangioblastomas. He had multiple cysts in the kidneys and pancreas, as well as kidney stones, leading to a diagnosis of VHL disease type 1. Three years later, a renal cyst and kidney stones were discovered again. The following year, hemangioblastomas of the spine were found, as well as kidney stones. A year later, a lesion in the left and right cerebellum were detected. Patient 4 also had cysts in both kidneys and pancreas, as well as more kidney stones. Genomic DNA was isolated from peripheral blood and PCR was performed to amplify the coding exons of the VHL gene. A 4-year-old boy exhibited hypertension and was diagnosed with bilateral pheochromocytoma. Patient 5 underwent bilateral adrenalectomy, which completely removed the tumor on the right side and partially removed the tumor on the left side. His hypertension continued. 9 years later, a tumor was removed from the left side. Genomic DNA was isolated from peripheral blood and PCR was performed to amplify the coding exons of the VHL gene. Sanger sequencing revealed a novel germline 18bp in-frame P59_R64del(c.174_191del) deletion in the VHL gene. No mutations were found in the coding regions of the RET, SDHB, and SDHD genes. The presence of two pheochromocytomas and a mutation in the VHL gene were used to diagnose this patient with VHL type 2C disease. The patient had no family history and no genetic testing was performed on family members. Due to the absence of family history, the authors denote that appears to be a sporadic case of the disease with a de novo occurrence. ACMG code: PP4

evidence_statement: A retrospective cohort study describes phenotypic variability within families with von Hippel-Lindau disease. Patients with genetically confirmed VHL were identified, although methods were not stated. 27 patients belonging to 5 families were discussed. Spitzoid tumors from 49 patients were analyzed by RNA-seq and 33% of cases had either a MAP3K8 fusion or C-terminal deletion. All fusion and truncated transcripts contained MAP3K8 exons 1-8 but were missing exon 9 which contains an autoinhibitory domain. Phosphorylated MEK1/2 was expressed more highly in a case with MAP3K8-GNG2 fusion than with a normal skin control. Truncated MAP3K8 (missing exon 9) was shown to be oncogenic in a colony-forming assay with NIH 3T3 cells.

25 tumors from individuals with lung adca who have <= 10 pack-year smoking history underwent whole exome sequencing and RNA-seq. 5 tumors did not identify an established oncogenic driver. In one (tumor 9), RNA-seq identified an OCLN-RASGRF1 fusion. RASGRF1 expression was 8.7 fold higher in this tumor than the mean of RASGRF1 expression in the other 24 tumors. Two additional RASGRF1 fusions (SLC4A4- and IQGAP1-) were identified through database searches. All three fusions were transfected into HEK 293T cells and showed increased levels of GTP-RAS expression. RAF-MEK-ERK signaling was also upregulated in the transfected cells. OCLN-RASGRF1 and SLC4A4-RASGRF1 fusions induced anchorage-indepdendent proliferation in NIH3T3 cells. IQGAP1-RASGRF1 did not induce anchorage-independent proliferation but did induce loss of contact inhibition. All three tested fusions activated the RAF-MEK-ERK and PI3K pathways in NIH3T3 cells. OLCN-RASGRF1 induced IL3-independent proliferation in Ba/F3 cells; and all three tested fusions formed tumors when NIH3T3 cells were implanted into immune-deficient mice. Ba/F3 cells with OCLN-RASGRF1 were sensitive to trametinib.

This case report describes a male infant with a recurrent (post-resection) infantile fibrosarcoma (IFS) with lymph node involvement and ETV6-NTRK3 fusion. The tumor did not respond to chemotherapy but had a rapid response to larotrectinib. After 4 days parents reported that the tumor was visibly smaller and softer. On day 56, MRI showed a complete response by Response Evaluation Criteria In Solid Tumors version 1.1 (RECIST v1.1). On day 112, the target lymph node was deemed normal. Disease remained in remission after 16 months at last followup.

FOXL2 p.C134W acquires the ability to bind SMAD4; forming an aberrant complex which binds to new hybrid sites in the genome to activate transcription. A yeast two-hybrid luciferase assay showed 20-fold higher luciferase activity for p.C134W compared to wt. SMAD4 and SMAD2/3 were strongly enriched at FOXL2 binding sites where the mutant signal exceeded the wt signal. p.C134W promotes transcription at these hybrid sites by inducing an enhancer-like chromatin state. p.C134W was found to upregulate genes involved in epithelial-mesenchymal transition; as well as genes known to be markers of granulosa cell tumors. Similar effects were observed in primary granulosa tumor tissues.

This report studied the prevalence of germline variants in Japanese PPGL patients. Of the 370 PPGL original Japanese probands, this cohort consisted of 15 patients with pheochromocytoma and/or paragangliomas with germline VHL variants. Blood samples were used to examine 7 genes: MAX, SDHB, SDHC, SDHD, TMEM127, VHL, and RET, using Sanger sequencing. Of these 15 VHL patients: 10 had bilateral PCC, 4 had PCC with abdominal/thoracic PGL, and one had metastatic PPGL. The variant R64P (c.191G>C) was one of the 15 found in a patient with PPGL. Their family history or further manifestations were not detailed.

K356dup was observed in an imatinib resistant CML. After switch to dasatinib, the patient regained deep molecular response. Therefore, K356dup seems to be resistant to imatinib and susceptible to dasatinib treatments.

Two patients and their families were presented in this paper with PKD1 and PKD2 mutations. Case 2, with 3 familial generations ADPKD, was diagnosed soon after birth with multiple small cortical cysts in both kidneys. The 4 year old male inherited a PKD1 and PKD2 mutation from each parent: c.7288C>T p.(Arg2430*), and c.124_125ins52bp p.(Ala42fs66*). A heterozygous variant in the VHL gene (NM_000551.3 (c.556G>A p.[Glu186Lys]) was additionally identified in this individual through a gene panel based Next Generation Sequencing approach.

A genomic analysis of this Chinese cohort of clear cell renal cell carcinoma was conducted. Whole blood was collected from 106 sporadic patients diagnosed with ccRCC at Qilu Hospital of Shandong University from January 2017 to November 2019. ID#022 was a 34Y patient with the VHL mutation: H115Q (c.345C>G). Relevant family history involved the grandmother, although no further details were presented.

Whole-exome sequencing of 151 HNSCC tumours found a high frequency of mutations in PI3K pathway genes. Four novel mutation were found, including PIK3CA p.G363A. Stable transformation of HNSCC cell lines with PIK3CA p.G363A was found to confer increased pathway activation shown by elevated AKT phosphorylation, supporting a gain of function role for this variant.

In a robotic adrenalectomy case report, a 13-year-old male pediatric case was noted with intermittent tachycardic and hypertensiveity during hospitalization for a pneumonia episode. He found to have a 6cm right adrenal mass. It was resected and he remains disease-free at 19 months of post-operative follow-up. Patient’s father has VLHd, and had undergone bilateral adrenalectomy for pheochromocytoma and bilateral nephrectomy for renal cell carcinoma. A pathogenic VHL mutation (c.583C>T, p.Q195*) was found in the patient and his father.

Targeted sequencing of 164 genes was performed on germline and somatic DNA derived from the blood and tissue samples of 50 Saudi Arabia breast cancer patients. From sample BCB-D-59, 3 germline mutations were found. 2 heterozygous mutations: TP53: c.241C>T p.R81X and MLH1: c.208-1G>C, and one homozygous VHL: c.154G>T p.E52X mutation. Mutations in E1' are identified in 7 families with erythrocytosis and in 1 large family with typical VHL disease but without any alteration in the other VHL exons. In this study, the authors show that the mutations in E1' induced a dysregulation of VHL splicing with excessive retention of E1' and were associated with a downregulation of VHL protein expression. A variant in the CHEK2 gene (considered a moderate breast cancer gene) was observed in this case study of a man with 5 different cancers. The man was under investigations of a possible VHL syndrome diagnosis, although this was negative as no variant was detected in him. This report studied the prevalence of germline variants in Japanese PPGL patients. Of the 370 PPGL original Japanese probands, this cohort consisted of 15 patients with pheochromocytoma and/or paragangliomas with germline VHL varaints. Blood samples were used to examine 7 genes: MAX, SDHB, SDHC, SDHD, TMEM127, VHL, and RET, using Sanger sequencing. Of these 15 VHL patients: 10 had bilateral PCC, 4 had PCC with abdominal/thoracic PGL, and one had metastatic PPGL. The variant F136C (c.407T>G) was one of the 15 found in a patient with PPGL. evidence_statement: A case report of a 43Y female is presented. She was screened for germline mutations associated with renal cancer development due to her gross hematuria and renal colic. A CT showed small kidney stones and a left 14mm renal mass, along with bilateral renal cell carcinoma. SNPs were genotyped sequencing a panel of five genes: VHL, MET, SDHB, SDHD, and FLCN. A total of 12 variants were found in the patient. The VHL mutation c.340+384G>C was described as a likely benign intronic variant. 2 years later, she underwent 3 right partial nephrectomies, revealing clear cell carcinoma in each tumor. Months later she also underwent 2 partial left nephrectomies revealing papillary-type renal carcinomas. The patient had no familial background.

evidence_statement: The authors generated genome-wide DNA methylation profiles of 323 tumors with an institutional diagnosis of ‘primitive neuroectodermal tumors of the central nervous system (CNS-PNETs)’, which are highly aggressive, poorly differentiated embryonal tumors occurring predominantly in young children but also affecting adolescents and adults. Four novel methylation profiles were identified. One of those profiles was exhibited by 10/323 (3 %) cases, and all these tumors were found to have a duplicated region in exon 15 of BCOR [BCOR internal tandem duplication (ITD)] by DNA/RNA sequencing, identical to that of the BCOR ITD in other tumor types including clear cell sarcomas of the kidney, undifferentiated round cell sarcomas in infants, and primitive myxoid mesenchymal tumour of infancy. The authors compared DNA methylation pattern of the BCOR-ITD positive cases with an in-house collection of > 10,000 methylation profiles from a broad variety of pediatric and adult CNS tumors. Additional tumors with variety of histologies showed the same methylation profile as BCOR-ITD positive cases, and were also found to have BCOR-ITD. The authors proposed that BCOR-ITD defines a specific molecular subtype of CNS tumors.

BCOR internal tandem duplications (ITDs) were found frequently in cases of clear cell sarcoma of kidney (CCSK), a rare pediatric renal cancer. The study initially evaluated 3 CCSK samples by whole exome sequencing and whole transcriptome sequencing. All 3 samples demonstrated BCOR ITD by RNA sequencing. This was further validated by targeted DNA sequencing of a validation institutional cohort of 11 primary and 2 matched metastatic CCSK cases, and an additional external cohort of 13 CCSK samples. Overall, BCOR ITDs were found in 85% (23/27 cases). No BCOR ITDs were found in neither matched normal kidney/blood, nor other childhood renal cancers. Upregulation of mutant BCOR transcripts and protein expression by immunoblotting and immunohistochemistry was shown.

27 cases of CCSK were profiled by whole exome sequencing and whole transcriptomics, identifying BCOR ITDs in the majority (23/27, 85%). BCOR encodes a key constituent of a variant polycomb repressive complex (PRC). Similar to BCOR::CCNB3-related tumors, transcriptome analysis revealed enrichment of PRC2-associated target genes including those associated with H3 K28 trimethylation. Disruption of polycomb repressive complex signaling likely plays a role in the pathogenesis of CCSK.
16 of 30 high-grade gliomas (HGG) were found to harbor K27M mutations. The frequency of mutations was similar between adults and children (52% vs 54%).

disease: Central Nervous System Tumor With BCOR Internal Tandem Duplication
evidence_statement: 10/323 studied high-grade primitive neuroectodermal tumors of the central nervous system (CNS-HGPNETs) clustered together based on their unique methylation profile. 10/10 of those tumors exhibited in-frame internal tandem duplications in the BCOR gene. The duplicated region was identical with that of the BCOR ITDs described in clear cell sarcoma of the kidney. 1 additional tumor harbored a BCOR intragenic in-frame deletion, and two additional tumors had BCOR frameshift mutations. Gene expression of BCOR was higher in CNS HG PNET BCOR-ITD positive tumors than in other CNS tumor types, suggesting different mechanism from BCOR loss-of-function mutations reported in other malignancies,. The results are consistent with BCOR-ITDs acting as primary oncogenic drivers in a unique type of CNS HG PNETs.

This study investigated the effectiveness of whole exome sequencing (WES) and an in-house hybridization based gene panel (ENDOGENE Panel v2.0) at detecting mutations in pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma (PPGL) related genes. The ENDOGENE panel included EGLN1, EPAS1, FH, KIF1B, MAX, MEN1, NF1, RET, SDHA, SDHB, SDHC, SDHD, SDHAF2, TMEM127, VHL, GOT2, MDH2 and SLC25A11. WES and the ENDOGENE panel were tested on 37 samples with known variants. After optimization of the bioinformatic pipeline, 61 additional samples were tested prospectively. phenotypes: Mucinous cystic neoplasm of the pancreas,Renal cell carcinoma,Cerebellar hemangioblastoma
evidence_statement: A 35-year old woman was diagnosed with VHL due to clinical presentation of pancreatic serous cystic neoplasm and renal cell carcinoma at age 35, and cerebellar hemangioblastomas that were surgically removed at age 21. She had no family history. Genetic testing performed for her previous case report (PMID: 21673464) revealed a N78I (c.233A>T) missense mutation in the VHL gene. The patient had previously underwent total pancreatectomy and right nephrectomy for pancreatic serous cystic neoplasm (SCN) and renal cell carcinoma (RCC), respectively. Since her surgery, she had follow-up examinations performed every 6 months. At the 4th year follow up, tumors in the liver were detected by CT scan and radiographically diagnosed as metastases of the pancreatic SCN or RCC. 53 months after the initial surgery, partial resections of the liver were performed. Immunohistochemical findings of the resected liver tumour were similar to the primary pancreatic SCN, and not the RCC. Thus, the liver tumors were pathologically diagnosed as liver metastases of the pancreatic SCN. After the second surgery, follow up examinations continued to be performed every 6 months. At the first follow-up, 3 tumors in the liver were detected by CT and MRI. After 6 months, no increase in the number of tumours were detected. Anterior segmentectomy and partial resection of segment III of the liver were done 66 months after 1st surgery and 13 months after second surgery, respectively. Again, morphology and immunohistochemical findings of the resected tumors again were similar to the primary pancreatic SCN, thus diagnosed as multiple metachronous liver metastases of pancreatic SCN. Since then the patient has remained disease-free without any recurrence after the third operation for 6.5 years until the last follow-up.

314 Chinese patients with Pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma (PPGL) from Peking Union Medical College Hospital, China, were included in this study for germline profiling. The majority of patients underwent surgery and were histopathologically diagnosed with PPGL. For patients who had an unresectable or metastatic tumor, PPGL diagnosis was determined based on clinical features (headache, palpitations, sweating, etc). Genomic DNA was extracted from peripheral blood of all 314 PPGL patients, and detect potential variants in 12 known genes associated with hereditary PPGL (SDHA, SDHB, SDHC, SDHD, SDHAF2, FH, VHL, RET, NF1, MAX, TMEM127, and KIF1B) using next-generation and Sanger sequencing. Germline variants were detected in 29% of the 314 PPGL patients. Germline genetic testing revealed a missense R167Q(c.500G>A) variant in exon 3 of the VHL gene of 2 patients. Patient #93 is a 22Y male PPGL patient who first presented with pheochromocytoma at age 10 and was diagnosed at age 13. Patient 93 has a family history of PPGL. Patient #94 is a 45Y male PPGL patient who first presented with pheochromocytoma at age 14 and was also diagnosed at age 14. He does not have a family history of PPGL.

A patient with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) and a somatic PALB2 mutation (NM_024675.4: c.3350+1G>T) experienced disease progression after 10 cycles of FOFIRINOX and 2 cycles of gemcitabine. She was switched to talazoparib and achieved a complete clinical response after 25 months. The patient is still alive three years after induction of talazoparib with no clinical or radiological signs of disease progress and no therapy-related toxicities. Of note, the patient also had a nonsense mutation in BLM (NM_000057.4: p.Gln548Ter) and a KRAS G12C mutation. The BLM mutation was confirmed to be germline.

disease: Head And Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma
evidence_statement: Concurrent inhibition of both AURKB (and AURKA) and PI3K is synergistic in NOTCH1-wild type and NOTCH-1 mutant head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) cell lines. In NOTCH1-wt cell lines, the combination index (CI) was <1 in 46/56 (82%) of cell lines at an effect size of 0.5 and 49/56 (88%) of cell lines at an effect size of 0.75. In the NOTCH1-mut cell lines, the CI was <1 in 13/13 (100%) of cell lines at an effect size of 0.75. Additional inhibitors were tested and all in vitro testing suggested that the combined inhibition induced apoptosis of NOTCH1-mut cell lines and sensitized NOTCH1-wt cell lines. A xenograft model was tested using copanlisib (PI3K inhibitor) and alisertib or barasertib for 21 days. Mice receiving copanlisib or alisertib alone demonstrated significantly smaller tumor volumes compared to baseline; whereas the combined drugs led to tumor regression. Similar results were seen for copanlisib and barasertib both alone and in combination. Alisertib was better tolerated than barasertib and mice initially treated with copanlisib + alisertib underwent a second cycle and showed prolonged and durable tumor regression.

From a series of 71 oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) samples, 44 showed FGFR3 exon 17 band shift and when sequenced showed G2128T resulting in missense G697C was observed. Blood in 12 of the FGFR3 mutant patients showed normal sequence. OSCC cells with G697C had strong FGFR2b cell membrane expression in contrast to tumor cells without the mutation. In Sf9 (fly) cell lysates, G697C FGFR3 showed strong phospho-tyrosine signal in western blots in comparison to lysates with wildtype FGFR3. The authors conclude that the mutation may be involved in the progression of OSCC. This evidence gives support for ClinGen/CGC/VICC evidence code OS2 for laboratory evidence supporting variant oncogenicity.

In human skin grafts, FGFR3, R248C, and S249C, but not G697C induced MAPK activation and hyperproliferation. The authors conclude that G697C is likely not an oncodriver and may be a geographically associated variant with high frequency in certain populations and not widely associated with tumor pathogenesis. This evidence provides support for ClinGen/CGC/VICC benign code SBS2, indicating that this variant has no oncogenic effect in tumor formation.

Purified proteins of 26 FGFR3 kinase domain variants were used to directly compare the impact of different mutations on FGFR3 auto-phosphorylation. While known hotspot mutations K650E and N540K resulted in approximately 45 fold autophsphorylation over wildtype, G697C showed no increase over wildtype phosphorylation. To test if G697C could impact FGFR3 function in a way that can only be detected in a cellular setting NIH3T3 was stably transfected with G697C along with positive K650E, N540K, and negative wildtype controls. In contrast to positive controls, G697C did not show transformation, anchorage independent growth or downstream phosphorylation. The authors conclude that they have not been able to provide supporting evidence for an activating Role of G697C, and note that other studies demonstrating such a role may be cell type specific. This evidence supports an SBS2 benign Code for G697C resulting from in vitro assays.

A 23 month old (at the time of report) male was diagnosed prenatally with Stage II cellular mesoblastic nephroma (MN) on the right kidney, which was surgically removed on the sixth day of life. ETV6::NTRK was found by FISH. At 12 months a lesion on the distal tibia developed. The patient entered the larotrectinib pediatric study NCT02637687 and received eight cycles of therapy without any grade 2 or greater toxicities so far. After this the patient had a full range of motion in the lower extremity and the there was a complete disappearance of the soft-tissue component and a near-complete reconstitution of the cortex of the distal right tibial metastatic focus.

A frequent genetic alteration in congenital mesoblastic nephroma is the translocation t(12;15) resulting in a fusion of the ETV6 gene on 12p13 and the NTRK3 gene on 15p15 that occurs almost exclusively in cellular mesoblastic nephroma subtype. In a group of 111 mesoblastic nephroma (MN) samples, 79 were were evaluable by FISH, which consisted of 38 classical MN, 29 cellular MN, and 12 mixed MN samples. 16 of 29 cellular type MN had ETV6::NTRK3 via break apart FISH, while 0/38 classical and 0/12 mixed types were positive.

In a group of 111 mesoblastic nephroma (MN) samples, 79 were were evaluable by FISH, which consisted of 38 classical MN, 29 cellular MN, and 12 mixed MN samples. 5 year relapse free survival (RFS) was reported for the groups of patients. Classic MN had 98% +/- 2% RFS, mixed MN had 80% +/- 10% RFS. ETV6::NTRK3 negative cellular MN patients had 73% +/- 13% RFS, while ETV6::NTRK3 positive cellular MN patients had 100% RFS. The authors suggest the fusion positive MN is a genetically distinct subgroup for cellular MN, and has a tendency for better outcome in comparison to other cellular MN cases.

Analysing whole transcriptome data from 185 GBM samples from TCGA, EGFR fusion events were found in 7.6% (14) of the cohort. In 6 of 14 cases, in-frame EGFR::SEPT14 (e24:e10) fusions were detected (3.2%), resulting in the fusion of the EGFR tyrosine kinase domain to the coiled-coil domain from Septin14. All EGFR::SEPT14 fusions occurred within amplified regions of the fusion genes. In GBM-derived sphere cultures, the presence of EGFR::SEPT14 was associated with increasd proliferation, enhanced migratory capacity and upregulated gene expression of genes related to an inflammatory/immune response.

At 12 years old, a female patient presented with fever and headache with high blood pressure. Upon a CT scan, a right adrenal tumor was detected and tumor resection was performed, revealing a pathological diagnosis of pheochromocytoma. She presented with the same symptoms 5 years later and multiple round nodular shadows were found in left adrenal and paraganglion region zones upon another CT scan. She was diagnosed with pheochromocytoma (PCC) and paraganglioma (PGL). A lung puncture revealed a carcinoid and a pancreatic puncture indicates a neuroendocrine tumor. Left adrenalectomy and PPGL resection was performed and diagnosis was pathologically confirmed. Patient is on life long hormonal replacement therapy and Octreotide and microspheres therapy. The diagnosis was an atypical VHL type 2 due to the lung carcinoid and neuroendocrine tumor of the pancreas. Genetic analysis was performed on peripheral blood and screened for potential mutations in the following genes: SDHAF2, SDHB, SDHC, SDHD, MAX, NF1, RET, and VHL using Target Capture-Based Deep Sequencing. A case study on a 35 year old female of Indian (South Asian) descent was presented. She presented 6 years prior (2006) with severe abdominal pain prompting an abdominal ultrasound. Imaging revealed a left renal mass measuring 3.5 × 4.0 × 3.5cm (biopsy consistent with papillary renal cell carcinoma). Final pathology revealed a 3.2cm low-grade primary renal carcinoid (neuroendocrine neoplasm of the kidney) with two of four lymph nodes involved with metastatic disease. She currently remains disease free after 31 months. A clear cell renal cell carcinoma tissue sample removed surgically from a patient with VHL detected a germline VHL mutation: R167Q (c.500G>A), which was used as a positive control. This was described in the paper was c.713G>A due to a difference in transcript reference used.

phenotypes: Squamous cell carcinoma,Non-small cell lung carcinoma,Hepatocellular carcinoma,Lung adenocarcinoma
evidence_statement: A 63-year-old male without family history presented with cough, 20-pound weight loss, and right lower lung infiltrate on chest X-ray. A CT of the chest confirmed a mass in the right lower lobe, and biopsy revealed a differentiated adenocarcinoma. Surgery was attempted but resulted in a right lung pneumonectomy. Tumor molecular profiling revealed an EGFR exon 19 deletion (pE746_T751delinsVA). Systemic targeted therapy was started with osimertinib, and 10 months later, surveillance imaging revealed a hepatic mass in the right lobe of the liver that was found to be Hepatocellular cell carcinoma. 2 months after liver resection MRI revealed a new lesion in the sternum consistent with squamous cell carcinoma. Tumor profiling revealed a mutation ATM [p.R2832H]. 10 days later, severe pain in his knee led to the diagnosis of squamous cell carcinoma of the femur. Tumor profiling of the femur lesion revealed an EGFR mutation identical to the lung tumor. Molecular profiling also revealed an identical VHL mutation in exon 3 in all 3 tumors p.L188V(c.562C>G), confirmed to be a heterozygous germline mutation through analysis of a blood sample. The patient had 5 other germline mutations in the following genes: KIAA1549, BCL11B, AXIN1, ASXL1, CAMTA1, along with various other somatic mutations from femur, lung, and liver tissue. None of which were associated with VHL-tumor-suspect genes.

phenotypes: Breast carcinoma,Clear cell renal cell carcinoma
evidence_statement: 3 unrelated patients with unexpected or non-syndromic phenotypes, accompanied by a VHL component tumor received germline gene panel testing as part of the PROACTIVE study at the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, each detected with a low penetrant variant. At age 52, patient 1 (male) presented with worsening lower abdominal discomfort. A CT scan and histopatholoy revealed a right renal solid mass consistent with renal cell carcinoma, which required a right radical nephrectomy. A year later, CT imaging, MRI and pathological examination revealed metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) and spindle cell lipoma. 3 years later, progression in the liver and pancreas was noted. Somatic next generation sequencing testing revealed mutations in VHL and several copy number losses. As part of the PROACTIVE study, peripheral blood was collected. Sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis of 133 genes (including MAX/NF1/RET/TMEM127/SDHA SHDB SHDC SDHD SDHAF2) revealed a heterozygous germline VHL L188V(c.562C>G) variant. A somatic VHL, c.445G>A (p.Ala149Thr) was also found. The patient's two sons have not been tested for the variant, however both have skin cancer. After genetic counselling, patient reported that his sister tested positive for the same mutation. She was diagnosed with metastatic lobular breast carcinoma at age 52 following pathological examination of the tumor specimen. Previous germline genetic testing using an 88-gene cancer panel revealed the heterozygous germline VHL L188V(c.562C>G) variant, further confirmed by testing a second blood sample. Both of her children had no VHL variants, but daughter has papillary thyroid cancer. She had no features of VHL until her death at age 61 from breast cancer. Similarly, other than ccRCC, patient 1 had no other features of VHL. Finally, their parents each had cancer: father with lung cancer, mother with skin cancer, as well as 8 other family members. No genetic make up was discussed in these members. ACMG: PP4

Patient 2 died from cancer at age 82, a few months after receiving her genetic results. ACMG: PP4

3 unrelated patients with unexpected or non-syndromic phenotypes, accompanied by a VHL component tumor received germline gene panel testing as part of the PROACTIVE study at the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, each detected with a low penetrant variant. At age 32, patient 3 (female) presented with posterior headaches, which a CT scan and MRI revealed to be a cerebellar hemangioblastoma. Treatment involved a gross total resection of the lesion. Somatic testing of a left cerebellar mass revealed a somatic VHL variant: p.Leu63fs*4 (c.188_188T>TG). Single gene testing of VHL revealed a heterozygous germline VHL p.Pro81Ser (c.241C>T) variant. Her mother (age 72) and two of her three siblings (ages 38 and 36) carry the same VHL p.Pro81Ser variant, but have been negative for hemangioblastoma or any other VHL component tumor. ACMG: PP4

phenotypes: Retinal capillary hemangioma,Spinal cord lesion,Abnormality of the adrenal glands,Pheochromocytoma,Cerebellar hemangioblastoma
evidence_statement: A 52-year-old Iranian man was hospitalized because of headache, vertigo, and gait problems for the past two months. Medical history was positive for bilateral pheochromocytoma diagnosed at 30Y which had been operated on at 50Y. Familial history was positive for BL-PCC in his son and daughters and for retinal hemangioblastoma and BL-PCC in his siblings. Furthermore, the patient’s family history revealed that there have been multiple cases of PCC, brain tumor and retinal tumors in 10 first and second-degree relatives of the patient. A total of 43 members of the kindred (24 males and 19 females, aged 2-77 years) were reached for evaluation. DNA was extracted from peripheral white blood cells of all the members of the kindred. PCR was used to amplify a 292bp fragment for Exon 3 of the VHL gene and sequenced. Gene sequencing revealed a R167Q(c.500G>A) mutation in exon 3 of VHL in the proband and all affected individuals. Gene sequencing also revealed four asymptomatic members of the kindred with the same mutation (nephew, niece, and second degree relatives). Further evaluation and imaging revealed a mass in the left adrenal gland of the nephew, and multiple brain and spinal cord tumors in the second degree relative. A total of 14 members of the kindred had the VHL mutation confirmed, with 3 symptomatic diseased patients assumed, and the remainder were mutation negative.

Genetic and clinical data from 63 patients with hereditary Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (GpNET) and 145 with sporadic PNET (SpNET) were collected from two Polish endocrine departments from January 2004 to February 2020. Genomic DNA was extracted from peripheral blood leukocytes and the VHL and MEN1 genes were analyzed. The VHL gene was analyzed by Sanger sequencing and targeted next-generation sequencing (NGS), while the MEN1 gene was analyzed by by High-Resolution Melting, Sanger sequencing, Multiplex-ligation dependent probe amplification (MLPA), and targeted NGS. Only patients with confirmed germline mutations were included in the the GpNET cohort. Out of 53 patients with VHL, only five were diagnosed with GpNET. Patient 3 had this hereditary PNET with the confirmed germline mutation: R167Q (c.500G>A). Comparison of the two cohorts revealed that patients with GpNET are diagnosed earlier, have longer overall survival, less frequent metastases, and their tumors are smaller and often multifocal compared to the SpNET group. ACMG: 'PP4' because the patients' phenotypes or family history are highly specific for a disease with single genetic etiology.

molecular_profile: PALB2 Oncogenic Mutations (loss of function alterations)
evidence_statement: In a Phase II trial, the efficacy of talazoparib was evaluated in patients with pretreated advanced HER2-negative breast cancer or other solid tumors with mutations in homologous recombination pathway genes other than BRCA1 and BRCA2. Among the 6 patients (breast cancer (n=5) and pancreatic cancer (n=1)) with germline pathogenic or likely pathogenic mutations in PALB2, the overall response rate was 50%. All responders had breast cancer. All 6 patients showed tumor shrinkage. A patient with pancreatic cancer had co-mutation in BRIP1.

A 12-year-old boy presented with vision loss, headache and dizziness. MRI revealed a large irregular mass located in the suprasellar region, which was removed after craniotomy and microsurgical treatment. The pathological diagnosis was left optic nerve hemangioblastoma and the patient lost vision completely in the left eye after surgery. The proband's mother previously underwent surgery for HGB in the CNS and had pheochromocytoma and pancreatic cysts. She was diagnosed with VHL disease, but refused genetic sequencing. Therefore, patient was examined for VHL disease before surgery. Sequencing of exon 1 of the VHL gene revealed a familial germline p.Pro86Leu (c.257C>T) mutation. ACMG: PP4

Seventeen patients (age range 3–73) with VHL, including 12 probands and 5 relatives, that were observed between 2005 and 2020 were recruited for a retrospective analysis in relation to pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (PanNETs). A total of 13/17 patients had PanNETs. In 4 patients, PanNETs were found at VHL diagnosis and in 9 patients they were found during follow-up after a median time of 12 years. Six of these patients underwent surgery and seven were conservatively treated. Four of these patients had lymph node metastases and a tumordiameter significantly larger than the nonmetastatic PanNETs. Five patients who underwent surgery had stable disease after a 3 year follow up, while one patient showed liver metastases. Similarly, six non-resected PanNETs were stable after a 2 year, while one patient developed a novel small PanNET and slight growth of the pre-existing PanNET. Genomic DNA from blood was extracted and high-coverage sequencing for VHL gene was performed using an AmpliSeq custom panel that targets all exons, as well as intron–exon junctions of genes that are frequently mutated in PanNETs (VHL; RET; MEN1). A total of nine different VHL mutations were identified. Three patients were found to be de novo, but authors did not specify who. Two families presented with the germline missense variant R167Q (c.500G>A) in exon 3 of the VHL gene, Patients 15 and 16. The first proband (ID:15) presented with Paraganglioma and Metastatic PanNET. The second (ID:16) presented with CNS/Retinal Hemangioblastoma and PanNET. ACMG: PP4

molecular_profile: VHL Exon 3 Deletion AND VHL S139C (c.416C>G)
evidence_statement: A 9-year-and-5-month old male patient was diagnosed with polyglobulia after an accident at 8 years of age. Proband's mother reported that the patient displayed fatigue and peripheral cyanosis during exercise. The physical exam showed a tumor in the right testicle. This was confirmed to be a cyst in the right epididymis was identified by a testicular ultrasound. Due to family history of VHL disease (4 generations, 12 patients with VHLd), genetic testing was performed on the mother, where an exon 3 deletion in the VHL gene was identified. The mother died due to complications of a CNS hemangioblastoma at 30Y. A peripheral blood sample was then obtained from the patient, where the same exon 3 deletion was identified by MLPA. Complete VHL gene sequencing was then performed on the proband's sample which identified a new S139C(c.416C>G) missense mutation, revealing that the patient was a compound heterozygote. This missense mutation was not previously reported. There was also no information on the proband's father; thus it is not confirmed whether the missense mutation was paternally inherited or de novo. Prediction tools such as PolyPhen2, Mutationassesor, Provean, and SIFT suggests it is deleterious. Due to the clinical presentation and molecular biology studies, the patient was diagnosed with both familial erythrocytosis type 2 and VHL disease. ACMG: PP1_moderate (~11 segregations), PP3, PP4

The medical records of 78 Korean patients with pheochromocytoma (PCC) and paragangliomas (PGL) were examined, 61 patients were diagnosed with PCC and the other 17 patients with PGL. 57 patients were included in the study. After excluding patients, 57 patients underwent sequencing. 14 patients received Sanger sequencing in pre-NGS period, while the other 43 patients underwent genetic testing by either direct sequencing (n=2) or targeted NGS (n=41) in the post-NGS period. 28 patients were found to have germline mutations in 7 PPGL-related genes (SDHB, RET, VHL, NF1, MAX, SDHA, and SDHD). Out of the 28 patients, 6 patients had germline mutations in VHL (5 presented with Pheochromocytoma and 1 with Paraganglioma). This patient was diagnosed with PCC due to bilateral adrenal mass and was found to have a R161Q(c.482G>A) missense variant in the VHL gene, which was detected by targeted NGS. ACMG: PP4
