evidence_statement: A 40-year-old male was admitted to the hospital in 2018 with headache and dizziness that has been ongoing for 2 months. In 2015, 5 years prior, this patient had surgical resection for cerebellar hemangioblastomas. In 2018 he showed multiple lesions again in the cerebellum, and he underwent the operative resection for a second time. A CT scan demonstrated multiple cysts in the pancreas and kidneys in the patient. After 2 years (42Y), he was stable with no recurrence. Five of his family members from three generations also had undergone surgical resections for CNS-related HGBs. Another 4 were asymptomatic. Genomic DNA was extracted from peripheral blood for genetic analysis. Three coding exons were directly sequenced to screen missense and splicing mutations. Genetic testing revealed a a heterozygous germline c.464-1G>C mutation in the splice site in intron 2 of VHL in the patient and 8 of his family members. Only the mother of the male patient was diagnosed with renal cell carcinoma and underwent left nephrectomy. ACMG: PVS1, PP1, PP4

A 58-year-old female was admitted to the hospital with headache and dizziness. MRI showed multiple hemangioblastomas (HGBs) in the cerebellum. An abdominal CT scan revealed renal cell cancer and multiple renal and pancreatic cysts. She underwent surgical resection for HGBs and her symptoms improved. Her condition was stable with no recurrence at the two-year follow up. Genomic DNA was extracted from peripheral blood for genetic analysis. Three coding exons were directly sequenced to screen missense and splicing mutations. Genetic testing revealed a a heterozygous germline c.464-2A>G mutation in the splice site in intron 2 of VHL, but none of her family members showed any abnormal changes in VHL. ACMG: PVS1, PP4

Phase 3 trial compared ipatasertib plus abiraterone and prednisolone or placebo plus abiraterone and prednisolone for patients with castration resistant prostate cancer. Primary endpoint was radiographical progression free survival (rPFS) in PTEN loss by immunohistochemistry (IHC) population and in the intention to treat (ITT) population. rPFS was improved moderately in PTEN loss by IHC population (hazard ratio (HR) 0.77 [95%CI 0.61-0.98]; p=0.034; significant at α=0.04). rPFS was not improved in ITT population (HR 0.84 [95%CI 0.71-0.99]; p=0.043; not significant at α=0.01). In exploratory analysis, addition of ipatasertinib seemed to be more effective in patients with PTEN loss by next-generation sequencing (HR 0.65 [95%CI 0.45-0.95]).

A 19-year-old female patient was referred to a psychiatric inpatient service due to a suspicion of anorexia nervosa (AN) following severe weight loss, low food intake, and a lack of a menstrual cycle for at least 1 year. The patient is the second child of a non-consanguineous relationship and there were no abnormalities in developmental milestones, but her weight never exceeded 35 kg. Apart from weight loss and weakness, physical and neurological examinations showed no alterations. The patient frequently complained of epigastric burning sensation, nocturnal headaches, postural hypotension and difficulty swallowing. The patient did not meet the necessary criteria for a diagnosis of AN or another psychiatric disorder. The patient experienced episodes of nausea during fasting after waking up, followed by unprovoked vomiting, which is highly uncommon in AN. Blood tests, urinalysis and chest X-ray were all normal. Abdominal CT scan revealed cystic lesions throughout the parenchymatous portion of the pancreas, suggestive of VHL. After 3 weeks of hospitalization, the patient progressively developed gait abnormality and bilateral dysmetria, which was worse on the left side. A brain MRI examination revealed a massive lesion suggestive of a hemangioblastoma (HB) in the fourth ventricle causing hypertensive hydrocephalus. HB and pancreatic cysts support the diagnosis for VHL. Whole blood was obtained for sanger sequencing of all 3 exons of the VHL gene, revealing a nonsense mutation in the VHL gene (c.481C>T; p.Arg161*) that results in a truncated protein. In silico analyses by mutation analyzer 2.0.28 suggests a pathogenic variant. Surgery inserting a ventriculoperitoneal shunt to relieve the hypertensive hydrocephalus only temporarily relieved her appetite; yet she no longer had fasting nausea and vomiting, or nocturnal headaches. Fractionated radiotherapy did not improve appetite or nausea but was successful in controlling tumor growth as an MRI revealed no significant alterations in the size of the lesion six months post-radiotherapy. ACMG: PVS1, PP4

VHL germline mutation carriers who had an ophthalmologic examination at the Erasmus Medical Centre or the Rotterdam Eye Hospital between 1984 and 2017, and were diagnosed with retinal hemangioblastoma (RH) were included in this study. A diagnosis of RH was based on the clinical appearance of a vasoproliferative retinal tumour. Peripheral blood samples from every member that had clinically suspected VHL disease of each family were collected for VHL mutation analysis. A total of 21 patients from 10 families were included on the basis of both a VHL germline mutation and ocular manifestations. Copy number analyses were carried out by multiplex ligation dependent probe amplification (MLPA) and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH). Mutations were described as one of the following two groups: truncating (complete deletion, partial deletion, nonsense mutation, splice site mutation, duplication and insertion) or missense. Ocular manifestations were not reported on an individual level, but rather were broken down based on the two groups. From Pedigree (family) 3, one individual was suspected of VHL disease and mutational analysis revealed an in-frame germline P76del deletion. This individual had RH development.

A 17-year-old girl was referred to the Department of Endocrinology at La Rabta University Hospital for the investigation of a newly diagnosed diabetes mellitus and a severe arterial hypertension. The patient is the first child of consanguineous parents and has a family history of type 2 diabetes and dyslipidemia, but no conditions that may suspect VHL disease. Blood tests disclosed hypercalcemia and abdominal computed tomography showed bilateral adrenal tumors. A clinical diagnosis of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2a (MEN2A) was originally suspected but genetic analysis (not further detailed) revealed the missense mutation c.191G > C (p.Arg64Pro) in exon 1 of the VHL gene. The authors concluded that the presence of pheochromocytomas and the missense mutation in VHL gene suggests type 2 VHL disease. She was further diagnosed with dyslipidemia and primary hyperparathyroidism. The patient underwent a bilateral adrenalectomy marked by normalization of blood pressure, blood glucose, calcium, and PTH levels. ACMG: 'PP4' because the patients' phenotypes or family history are highly specific for a disease with single genetic etiology. 'PM2' because variant absent from controls in gnomAD.

The LEOPARD syndrome associated mutation A461T is found in the protein-tyrosine phosphatase domain of Shp2 (encoded by PTPN11) and is predicted to affect catalysis. An assay to assess catalytic activity showed that WT Shp2, as well as activating mutants common in Noonan syndrome result in increased basal and ligand-activated catalytic activity, while A461T was inactive even in the presence of activating ligand. Examination of crystal structure suggests that the change from alanine to threonine at amino acid 461 would alter the catalytic site and interfere with substrate binding. To assess the possibility of a dominant negative effect, WT and mutant Shp2 were transfected into 293T cells and either starved or stimulated with EGF and assessed for ERK activation. Cells expression Shp2 A461T showed significantly lower ERK activation than cells with WT Shp2 or other known activating mutations. Similar results were seen with FGF or PDGF stimulation, A461T inhibits receptor tyrosine kinase signaling and is therefore a dominant negative mutation.

The multicenter randomized double-blind phase 3 study included patients with IDH1-mutant cholangiocarcinoma who had progressed on previous therapy. Patients were randomly assigned to Ivosidenib or placebo. Placebo to Ivosidenib crossover was permitted on radiological progression. The primary endpoint was progression-free survival by independent central review. Progression-free survival was significantly improved with Ivosidenib compared with the placebo (median 2.7, vs 1.4 months; hazard ratio 0.37; 95% CI 0.25-0.54; one-side p<0.0001). Median overall survival was 10.8 months for the Ivosidenib group versus 9.7 months for the placebo group (HR 0.69 [95% CI 0.44-1.10]; p=0.060) in which 35 patients were crossover from the placebo group. In a prespecified exploratory analysis, the rank-preserving structural failure time (RPSFT) method was used to reconstruct the survival curve for patients receiving a placebo as if crossover had never occurred. RPSFT assumes that the treatment effect is the same for all patients, regardless of when the treatment is given. The RPSFT-adjusted median overall survival was 6.0 months for the placebo group (HR 0.46 [95% CI 0.28-0.75]; p=0.0008).

evidence_statement: 10 cases of high-grade neuroepithelial tumor (HGNET) with BCOR exon 15 ITD were studied. In addition, 25 previously reported and published patients were included in survival analyses. These tumors are newly proposed to belong to a separate entity with a distinct methylation profile and a characteristic genetic alteration. The authors further describe their clinical, pathologic, radiographic, and genetic features. Shared histologic characteristics included predominantly solid growth, glioma‐like fibrillarity, perivascular pseudorosettes, and palisading necrosis, but absence of microvascular proliferation. Immunohistochemistry testing showed absent GFAP expression, no synaptophysin expression, variable OLIG2 and NeuN positivity, and diffuse strong BCOR nuclear positivity. In 6 of 10 cases, BCOR ex15 ITD was the only pathogenic alteration seen, while other cases showed additional genetic abnormalities including CDKN2A/B homozygous deletion, TERT amplification or promoter hotspot mutation, and damaging mutations in TP53, BCORL1, EP300, SMARCA2 and STAG2. The authors conclude that their findings further support inclusion of HG NET with BCOR ex15 ITD as a distinct CNS tumor entity.

"Classical" glioblastoma patients (referred to as group IGS-18) exhibited overexpression of EGFR and showed improved survival with combination therapy of bevacizumab and lomustine with a median OS 11.9 months compared to 7.9 (lomustine alone) and 8.3 months (lomustine alone) (p =0.09). A significant benefit was also observed in PFS - 4.2 months with combination therapy compared to 1.4 months (lomustine alone) and 2.9 months (bevacizumab alone) (p = 0.0004). This trend did not hold when grouping all samples not assigned to IGS-18 due to too few individuals assigned to certain other GBM subtypes.

A patient was initially diagnosed with stage IIIA lung adenocarcinoma with EGFR L858R and was treated with lobectomy and adjuvant pemetrexed and cisplatin. 20 months later the patient had recurrent disease in the liver, lung, and bone, and the patient was started on icotinib and a partial response was observed. After icotinib treatment a VOPP1::EGFR fusion consisting of VOPP1 exons 3-5 and EGFR exon 28, along with EGFR T790M, were detected in pericardial effusion and blood samples. The EGFR Fusion break point was between exon 27 and exon 28. Patient progressed after 6 months on icotinib and was then switched to osimertinib and experienced more than 11 months of PFS. Given that the fusion and T790M were not present until after icotinib treatment; the authors suggest that the fusion is also a resistance mechanism along with the well-known T790M resistance mutation.

From a retrospective review of 38,095 tumor samples from 33,997 patients that underwent fusion screening at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, 87 tumors were found to be positive for an NTRK1, NTRK2, or NTRK3 fusion. One positive patient with Glioblastoma Multiforme had an in-frame KANK1::NTRK2 (e11::e14) fusion that was not detected by MSK-IMPACT, but was found with the RNA Archer screen. Detection of this fusion was positive in the cytoplasm by Pan-Trk immunohistochemical staining.

Of the 4854 Breast Cancer patients analyzed by Memorial Sloan Kettering-IMPACT targeted DNA sequencing and MSK-Fusion targeted RNA-seq, fusions were detected in 27 patients. One of these patients was a 49 year-old that harbored the SCP2::NTRK1 e13::e11 fusion with the NTRK tyrosine kinase domain intact in their lymph node metastasis that arose post endocrine therapy (tamoxifen and letrozole), which was detected by MSK-IMPACT and MSK-Fusion. The patient’s diagnosis sample was negative for the fusion as determined by negative FISH and Pan-TRK immunohistochemical staining.

A breast cancer patient harbored the SCP2::NTRK1 fusion. This report demonstrated positive pan-tyrosine receptor kinase (TRK) immunohistochemical staining in a core-needle biopsy taken from the patient post-endocrine therapy. The fusion contained the tyrosine kinase domain of NTRK1.

Case report describing a patient with NSCLC and EGFR(ex25)::Intergenic Region of SEC61G(breakpoint 32 aa downstream of SEC61G) fusion and concurrent EGFR amplification with treatment response to a combination of gefitinib with cetuximab, which according to RECIST guidelines was considered as partial response. A post-treatment biopsy of a 1.3 cm adenocarcinoma revealed no EGFR fusion or gene amplification, suggestive of treatment response.

Between 1985 and 2017, the clinical materials of patients with VHL disease were collected from 3 different families. Peripheral blood was obtained from each patient for genetic analysis. The VHL gene was amplified by PCR and mutations were confirmed by bi-directional sequencing. Of 22 patients from 3 VHL pedigrees, 10 exhibited VHL gene mutations (3 genotypes) at the germline level. The genotypes of each of the three families were p.R161Q (c.482G>A), p.N78S (c.233A>G), and p.R167Q (c.500G>A), respectively. Family 1: Female proband was admitted to the Lishui People's Hospital at age 50 due to headache, palpitation and hyperhidrosis. Ultrasound and CT results revealed a mass on the right side of the adrenal gland, consistent with a diagnosis of right pheochromocytoma (PHEO). Proband's son (III6) was admitted to the Lishui People's Hospital at age 9 and 17, with masses on both sides of the adrenal gland; pathology confirmed bilateral PHEO. Proband's niece (III2) was admitted to the Lishui People's Hospital at age 28 due to a headache and hypertension, revealing a mass on the right and left side of the adrenal gland - resected and postoperative pathology confirmed bilateral PHEO. The father of this patient died from hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage at the age of 38. These 3 symptomatic members carried the VHL mutation: R161Q (c.482G>A). ACMG: PP4

The brother's daughter (5Y) was noted to be a germline carrier without any symptoms. ACMG: PP4

evidence_statement: Between 1985 and 2017, the clinical materials of patients with VHL disease were collected from 3 different families. Peripheral blood was obtained from each patient for genetic analysis. The VHL gene was amplified by PCR and mutations were confirmed by bi-directional sequencing. Of 22 patients from 3 VHL pedigrees, 10 exhibited VHL gene mutations (3 genotypes) at the germline level. The genotypes of each of the three families were p.R161Q (c.482G>A), p.N78S (c.233A>G), and p.R167Q (c.500G>A), respectively. Family 3: Male proband admitted to the First People's Hospital of Wenling City at age 34 due to dizziness and headaches that lasted 1 month. Cranial MRI revealed masses that were considered to be cerebellar and central nervous system hemangioblastomas (CNS-HB). Cranial gamma knife radiotherapy was performed, which remained stable after 5 years of follow-up. Proband's elder sister was admitted to the First People's Hospital of Wenling City at the age of 45 due to dizziness lasting 3 months. A brain MRI revealed a cerebellar mass that was excised via surgery. Proband's father The patient was hospitalized in the First People's Hospital of Wenling City at the age of 66 due to cough and expectoration with low fever for 2 months. Ultrasound/CT revealed a mass on the right side of the adrenal gland, multiple solid lesions of both kidneys with multiple small cysts and pancreatic head lesions. The adrenal and kidney tumors were resected. Postoperative pathology results revealed right PHEO and right RCC. Lastly, a young man (proband’s son; III1; age 21Y) was germline positive for the mutation, although not yet symptomatic. ACMG: PP4

A 23-year-old Indian woman presented to the hospital due to right flank pain, fever and recurrent UTIs. A CT scan and MRI of the abdomen were performed and revealed a mass adjacent to the liver, which was suspicious of and determined to be a paraganglioma (PGL) once resected. When questioned for relevant symptoms, she reported a history of night sweats but denied palpitations, headache, diaphoresis, or hypertension. With regards to family history, her 36-year-old first cousin was recently diagnosed with a PGL. Due to personal and family history, she was referred for genetic testing which revealed a germline L163F(c.487C>T) mutation in VHL. Surveillance for other tumors associated with VHL are negative so far. Her cousin, nor other first-degree family members have undergone genetic testing despite recommendations to do so. ACMG: PP4

A 41-year-old asymptomatic caucasian male presented to his family doctor for VHL genetic testing due to family history of pheochromocytoma (PHEO). His sister was diagnosed with VHL disease after experiencing multiple tumors including paraganglioma of left carotid, spinal neuroma, bilateral adrenal PHEO and a skull based tumor with intracranial extension. His father, paternal grandmother and paternal great grandfather all had clinical history of PHEO. Genetic testing revealed a heterozygous synonymous mutation P138P(c.414A>G) in the VHL gene, the same one as his sister. 6 years later, he remained asymptomatic but decided to take an MRI, revealing a PHEO in the left adrenal gland and hemangioblastomas in the spine and brain. An adrenalectomy was performed, as well as radiotherapy with a craniotomy and resection. The family received VHL testing, where the wife was found to have wildtype VHL. Out of their 3 children, the 2 fraternal twin daughters inherited the mutation and were diagnosed at age 4. They both presented with retinal hemangioblastomas without PHEO at age 7, where one twin needed four laser treatments. To examine the mechanism of how the synonymous mutation causes VHL, primary skin fibroblasts carrying the heterozygous mutation or wild type VHL were established from skin biopsies of the 5 individuals of the proband's family. To examine whether this mutation affects splicing and gene expression, RT-PCR was performed with Sanger sequencing. Mutant fibroblasts downregulated full length VHL mRNA and protein, and upregulated the short VHL mRNA isoform at the mRNA level, but not at the protein level. Despite being synonymous, the mutation is not functionally silent because it causes aberrant splicing by skipping exon 2. This highlights the need to include splicing-altering synonymous mutations into the screening for VHL disease. This is the first report on detecting and validating a synonymous VHL mutation using patient-derived fibroblasts. ACMG: PVS1, PS3, PM2, PP4.

Recently, Lenglet et al., 2018 identified a new VHL cryptic exon termed E1' deep in intron 1 that is naturally expressed in many tissues, and found E1' mutations in eight families with either erythrocytosis or VHL disease. The goal of this study was to determine the prevalence of E1' germline mutations from two cohorts, 221 patients with a single or multiple tumours, suggestive of VHL disease, and 946 patients with a Pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma (PPGL) but without an identified mutation in the three VHL exons or in the main PPGL susceptibility genes. They identified a rare germline genetic variant (maf <1%) in the E1’ VHL cryptic exon in 1% of patients (12/1167). Patient 1 was diagnosed at the age of 47 with follow up of a 5 year duration due to a Carotid body paraganglioma (PGL) and was found to have a germline c.340+563C>T E1' variant. Tumor analysis was performed for patient 1 since there was a paraffin embedded sample. Patient 1 did not have loss of heterozygosity, but the mutated allele was lost in the tumor. Immunostaining was negative for detection of CA9 expression. CA9 is a protein reported to influence regulation cell proliferation and tumor progression and is known to be expressed at the membrane of tumour cells in the case of VHL inactivation. ACMG: PM2_Supporting, PP4

phenotypes: Hemangioblastoma,Retinal capillary hemangioma,Renal cell carcinoma,Pancreatic cysts,Spinal hemangioblastoma
evidence_statement: A 49-year-old woman had episodes of vertigo 12 years ago and abdominal pain 10 years ago. Ultrasonography and abdominal MRI revealed the presence of pancreatic cysts. Seven years ago, an abdominal computed tomography scan showed a solid mass in the right kidney. A right partial nephrectomy was performed and pathological examination revealed renal cell carcinoma of the right kidney. That same year, the patient complained of altered visual acuity and a CT scan of the skull and orbit revealed thickening of the left optic nerve and the right optic nerve had a conserved aspect. These results were suggestive of a hemangioblastoma (Hb) in the optic nerve of the left eye. Peripheral blood was sampled to extract genomic DNA for VHL gene sequencing and the detection of VHL copy number variants using multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification (MPLA). A heterozygous W88* (c.263G>A) nonsense variant was identified in the VHL gene. The patient's family history revealed siblings with VHL manifestations. The patient's mother was the index case and died at age 63 of clear cell renal carcinoma. The patient has one child, who is 27-years-old and complains of recurrent headaches, but refuses to undergo VHL screening. The patient's 5-year-old grandson does not have symptoms. The patient has five brothers and two sisters. One sister underwent partial nephrectomy due to carcinoma in the right kidney, another sister was operated on due to CNS Hb and had pancreatic cysts, and one brother had two Hbs removed that were detected in the brain and spine. One of the patient's nephews was diagnosed with a CNS Hb at age 12 and died 4 years later due to complications with the brain tumor that was not removed. Another niece was diagnosed at age 21 of cerebral Hb, and had the tumor resected. Upon follow-up, the patient still possesses pancreatic and renal cysts, but without renal tumor recurrence or metastases. The right optic nerve is intact, and there are no CNS lesions. She has slight decrease in visual acuity in the left eye due to the optic nerve Hb. Genetic testing of any of the patient's family members was not reported. ACMG: PP1, PP4

A 48-year-old female, who was diagnosed with VHL at age 25, presented with pain in her left arm. Genetic testing of genomic DNA extracted from peripheral blood revealed a R167Q(c.500G>A) missense mutation in the VHL gene. Her medical VHL history included surgery for central nervous system hemangioblastomas at age 26, 28, 39 and 45, as well as a retinal hemangioma for which she underwent a coagulation procedure at age 26. Imaging studies following complaint of arm pain suggested a lesion in the left distal ulna. A biopsy was taken that suggested clear cell chondrosarcoma, which was confirmed upon surgical resection of the complete tumor. DNA was isolated and the PCR amplified VHL gene was analyzed by Sanger sequencing. Gene panel analysis confirmed the VHL gene mutation in the tumor and no other mutations were found. However, loss of heterozygosity was noted for VHL, confirmed by a SNP array. To determine the effect of the loss of the wild type VHL allele on pVHL expression, immunohistochemistry was performed and revealed significantly lower levels of pVHL in the tumor cells compared to neighbouring cells. These results suggest that a second genetic hit occurred in trans during tumor development, leading to the loss of pVHL. No family history for this patient was discussed. ACMG: PP4

Case report describing a 63-year-old patient with colorectal adenocarcinoma. He started treatment with XELOX and bevacizumab. After findings of disease progression, they changed to bevacizumab and FOLFIRI. They detected EGFR::SEPT14 fusion (exon 24 & exon 10) and EGFR amplification by NGS on a paraffin sample after discontinuing the treatment due to complications. The tumor was microsatellite stable. The patient started treatment with erlotinib with signs of partial response (CT scan) 20 days later. A couple months later the patient showed signs of progressive disease, but a new variant, EGFRvIII (deletion of Exons 2-7), was detected in the mediastinal lymph nodes sample tested that likely contributed to erolotinib resistance.

Case report of a 62-year-old woman with lung adenocarcinoma. She underwent treatment with liposome-paclitaxel and carboplatin. They detected EGFR-SEPT14 fusion (N-terminal amino acids of EGFR and C-terminal amino acid of SEPTIN14) by NGS on a tumor sample. The patient started oral treatment with icotinib and demonstrated a partial response (RECIST). Thus far, the disease is stable and she is continuing treatment with icotinib.

This study was designed to characterize the endothelium of VHL patients through transcriptomic analysis of blood outgrowth endothelial cells (BOECs). BOECs were derived from peripheral blood of 5 VHL patient volunteers and non-VHL controls. Patient 1 was found to have a R167Q(c.500G>A) missense variant in exon 3 of the VHL gene. The patient's VHL-related clinical manifestations were a CNS hemangioblastoma, as well as renal cell carcinoma. Confocal staining shows pVHL distribution is likely in endoplasmic reticulum cysts. No family information was reported on. ACMG: PP4

BOECs were derived from peripheral blood of 5 VHL patient volunteers and non-VHL controls. Patient 5 was found to have a R64P(c.191G>C) missense variant in exon 1 of the VHL gene. The patient did not have any tumours. However, patient 5 had an additional disease and was also found heterozygous for the CLN5 protein in the neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis rare disease. The authors hypothesized that the CLN5 mutation in this patient may confer a protective effect, preventing tumor development in tissues that may potentially have a second VHL mutation. No family information was reported on.

17 patients from 10 families affected with VHL syndrome, particularly with retinal capillary hemangioblastomas (RCHs) were examined. 24-year-old woman had her first retinal examination due to the detection of a cerebellar hemangioblastoma. Her vision was 20/20 in both eyes, but a peripheral retinal capillary hemangioblastoma (RCH) was present in the left eye. Laser was performed on the retina surrounding the lesion. During the follow-up in 2019, the tumor was stable in size and there was no development of RCHs in the right eye. Genomic DNA was extracted from whole blood for sanger sequencing of the VHL gene and multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification was performed to identify genomic rearrangements. A novel frameshift P154Qfs4*(c.461delC) mutation was identified in exon 2 of the VHL gene. The parents of patient 1 were molecularly tested and neither possessed the mutation; thus, the mutation was identified as de novo. The parents nor the sister of patient 1 had VHL syndrome characterized by RCHs.

17 patients from 10 families affected with VHL syndrome, particularly with retinal capillary hemangioblastomas (RCHs) were examined. A 42-year-old woman was referred to the Eye Clinic due to a lesion in her left eye. The right eye was normal and her vision was 20/25. A peripheral RCH was observed. The tumor was treated using laser photocoagulation over several treatment sessions. The pseudohole progressed into a full-thickness macular hole one week after the first laser session. Visual acuity worsened to 20/63 in 2012, and pars plana vitrectomy was successfully performed. During a follow-up in 2014, a retinal tear was detected and was treated using laser. The last follow-up in 2019 revealed a good macular profile, RCH regression, and visual acuity in the left eye was 20/25, with no lesions development. Genomic DNA was extracted from whole blood for sanger sequencing of the VHL gene and multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification was performed to identify genomic rearrangements. A novel missense P192L(c.575C>T) mutation was identified in exon 3 of the VHL gene. Both the mother and daughter of patient 2 were found to have the same mutation. Neither the 61-year-old mother nor the 6-year-old daughter had RCHs. The mother had other tumours, which were not specified.

evidence_statement: 17 patients from 10 families affected with VHL syndrome, particularly with retinal capillary hemangioblastomas (RCHs) were examined. A 32-year-old man had an ophthalmic emergency service in 2010. His visual acuity was 20/32 in the right eye, but fundoscopic examination revealed three peripheral RCHs with retinal detachment. Moreover, two small retinal lesions were detected in the left eye, yet the visual acuity of this eye was 20/20. The patient underwent retinal surgery in the left eye and lesions in both eyes were treated with multiple laser sessions. CNS imaging revealed multiple cerebellar and spinal hemangioblastomas. In 2012, cataract surgery was performed in the right eye. In 2019, visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes and all the RCHs regressed. Genomic DNA was extracted from whole blood for sanger sequencing of the VHL gene and multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification was performed to identify genomic rearrangements. A nonsense R161*(c.481C>T) mutation was identified in exon 3 of the VHL gene. Both the son and daughter of patient 5 were found to have the same mutation. Neither the 10-year-old daughter (patient 6), nor the 7-year-old son (patient 7) had RCHs or any other tumors.

evidence_statement: 17 patients from 10 families affected with VHL syndrome, particularly with retinal capillary hemangioblastomas (RCHs) were examined. In 2019, a 14-year-old boy (patient 8) from family 4 was diagnosed with visual impairment, due to visual acuity of 20/20 in the right eye and 20/640 in the left eye. Four peripheral RCHs were detected in the right eye. The visual impairment of the left eye was due to the severe exudative process involving the macula. Moreover, numerous microhemangioblastomas were revealed by fluorescein angiography. Laser therapy was performed in both eyes, but vitreous hemorrhage occurred in the left eye. Bevacizumab was given three times, as well simultaneous cryotherapies were performed under general anesthesia. Many laser sessions were performed for regression of the RCHs to occur. Further testing revealed a cerebellar hemangioblastoma. Genomic DNA was extracted from whole blood for sanger sequencing of the VHL gene and multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification was performed to identify genomic rearrangements. A nonsense R113*(c.337C>T) mutation was identified in exon1 of the VHL gene. The parents of patient 8 were molecularly tested and neither possessed the mutation; thus, the mutation was identified as de novo. Neither parent had VHL syndrome characterized by RCHs. A 32-year-old woman (patient 9) from family 5 had been diagnosed in 2000 with multiple cerebellar and spinal hemangioblastomas. In 2005, she was examined at the eye clinic, and were visual acuity was 20/20 and 20/25 in the right and left eye, respectively. No abnormalities were found in the right eye, but a peripheral RCH that was already partially treated with laser was observed in the left eye. Many tiny RCHs that surrounded the major lesion were also detected in this eye. Further laser treatments were scheduled, but the patient did not follow up and instead came to the ophthalmic emergency service three years later. Visual acuity of the left eye worsened to 20/640, and she presented with retinal detachment. The partially treated RCH of the left eye worsened and more tiny RCHs were detected. Cryotherapy was performed in the left eye but retinal detachment was still present at follow-up. On follow-up, no RCHs were detected in the right eye, and vision loss developed in both eyes. The same nonsense R113*(c.337C>T) mutation was identified in exon1 of the VHL gene in this patient. Neither parent of patient 9 had VHL syndrome characterized by RCHs.

evidence_statement: 17 patients from 10 families affected with VHL syndrome, particularly with retinal capillary hemangioblastomas (RCHs) were examined. A 37-year-old man (patient 10) from family 6 accessed emergency eye service in 2009, and a nasal retinal detachment was detected in the right eye. Multiple RCHs were detected. Visual acuity was 20/400, due to the tumours and the presence of macular scars. CNS imaging detected several cerebellar and bulbar hemangioblastomas. Nasal scleral buckle, cryotherapy, and several laser photocoagulation sessions were performed. In 2012, the patient developed a new retinal detachment in the right eye. Visual acuity of OD worsened showing no light detection. At the last follow-up in 2019, no RCHs were detected in the left eye. Genomic DNA was extracted from whole blood for sanger sequencing of the VHL gene and multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification was performed to identify genomic rearrangements. MLPA revealed an intragenic c.341+1_341–1(463*1_?) deletion spanning exons 1-3 of the VHL gene. Both parents were molecularly examined and did not have the mutation or VHL syndrome. The mutation was identified as de novo, but passed onto both sons of patient 10, as they had the same deletion. The 14-year-old son (patient 11) was asymptomatic, while the 10-year-old son (patient 12) had CNS hemangioblastoma. Neither son had RCHs.

evidence_statement: A 54-year-old man (case 1) was hospitalized in 2009 due to headaches that were diagnosed as a cerebellar lesion via MRI. In 2011, he presented with dysfunction of the lower extremities and an MRI revealed several large cysts in the bilateral cerebellum. In 2014, a CT scan showed multiple renal cysts in both kidneys, and underwent symptomatic treatment. In 2017, the patient presented with dizziness and severe weight loss. CT scans revealed infarctions in the basal ganglia, cerebellar hemangioblastomas, polycystic kidney disease, and many hepatic cysts and pulmonary nodules. The patient was initially diagnosed with renal carcinoma that metastasized to the lungs. After a full analysis, the patient was believed to have VHL syndrome. Genomic DNA from the patient’s peripheral blood was extracted and VHL gene coding sequence analysis was performed by direct sequencing of PCR-amplified products. Sanger sequencing revealed an R177Tfs*23(c.530_536del) frameshift deletion in exon 3 of the VHL gene. Despite the increase in the size of the renal tumors and lung metastatic lesions in August 2017, the patient discontinued treatments and died in 2018. The patient's daughter possesses the same R177Tfs*23(c.530_536del) mutation. The daughter (case 2) was a 31-year-old patient who was diagnosed with seronegative arthritis at 12 years old, along with pain in the extremities. At 29 years old, she was diagnosed with ankylosing spondylitis. Symptomatic treatment was not effective and joint deformation was identified at the extremities. She cannot walk independently. In 2018, CT scans revealed multiple renal and pancreatic cysts, but none in the brain. Due to genetic testing results and family history, patient 2 was diagnosed with VHL.

21 patients from different pedigrees of 12 Chinese provinces enrolled in this study based on a clinical and genetic diagnosis of VHL syndrome. Genetic testing was performed on genomic DNA isolated from peripheral blood. All three VHL coding exons and flanking intronic regions were directly sequenced to identify missense and splicing mutations. Multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification (MLPA) was performed to detect large exon deletions, further confirmed by quantitative PCR. All patients were divided into two groups based on mutation type: the missense group (9 individuals) and the partial deletion group (12 individuals). A total of 30 CNS hemangioblastomas from these patients were studied to identify correlations between differentially expressed mRNA and proteins, as well as histological grading and tumor burden amongst the two groups. Patients had 5.5 ± 3.1 tumors/patient on average. Due to the high number of tumors, most patients underwent surgery. 20/21 patients recovered well post-operatively and were discharged 1 week later. One patient died from aspiration after surgery. It was not indicated whether this one patient was amongst the partial deletion or missense group. No family information was provided.

RNAseq data of 162 glioblastoma patients identified NTRK1 fusions with both NFASC and BCABN. By analyzing exome and RNA data, the NFASC-NTRK1 fusion was found to retain NTRK1's kinase and transmembrane domains. Transfection of the NFASC-NTRK1 fusion into NIH 3T3 cells showed increased cell proliferation, soft agar colony formation, and tumor formation in mouse xenografts (using BALC/c nude mice). In addition, three shRNAs targeting the fusion transcripts were able to reduce proliferation in the transfected cells; however commercial TrkA inhibitors were not able to do so.

A 3 year old patient was initially diagnosed with a high grade glioma at 5 months of age. She was treated with 13 cycles of chemotherapy. 4 months after completing initial treatment, she showed progressive disease and was treated with further tumor debulking. After 6 months she experienced disease progression again and was treated with resection and focal radiation. 3 months post radiation she showed progressive disease again. Whole genome sequencing identified an ETV6-NTRK3 fusion. The patient was started on larotrectinib. After 4 weeks, symptoms improved. After 8 weeks of treatment, an MRI showed improvement or resolution of all masses and nodules. At 5 months after start of treatment, MRI confirmed the response. As of publication, patient remains on larotrectinib and has had no adverse effects for 9 months.

A patient with a recurrent, metastatic uterine myxoid neoplasm and a DCTN1-ALK fusion experienced both clinical and radiographic improvement with crizotinib and pazopanib. The patient was initially diagnosed with a smooth muscle tumor of uncertain malignant potential (STUMP) but after multiple recurrences and genomic profiling, was upgraded to inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor (IMT) with myxoid features; due to identification of a DCTN1-ALK fusion. The patient was started on a combination of crizotinib and pazopanib. After 2 cycles, the patient showed a partial response by RECIST 1.1 criteria. At time of publication, the patient continued to have a reponse for >6 months and is in confirmed partial remission.

SEC61G::EGFR (5'UTR::e14) (5'-UTR of SEC61G and 3'-UTR of EGFR) was detected in ependymoma as a change sensitive to gefitinib (also confirmed by mice xenografts model). Screening of 16 ependymoma patients by RT-PCR sequencing identified this change in 1. Precise frequency of this variant in ependymoma is unclear. This fusion creates two products (EGFRdeltaN566/EGFRdeltaN599) which resemble EGFRvIII which lacks part of the extracellular domain, is constitutively phosphorylated.

SEC61G::EGFR fusion identified in 4 out of 164 (2.4%) glioblastoma tumors (TCGA GBM working group, patient samples with pathobiology data). Fusion transcripts were confirmed by RNA-seq and were frequently part of a focal gain, suggesting a complex rearrangement. No functional data.

TCGA pan-cancer data analysis of 9,624 tumors across 33 tumor types identified 25,664 fusions. Significantly associated gene fusion and increased expression level (by RNAseq compared to samples without fusions) was shown for EGFR fusions in LGG (by Fisher exact analysis).

A 13-year-old boy was screened for a VHL mutation at 7-years-old upon identification of a missense V170G(c.509T>G) variant in the patient's father. Genetic screening of the patient also revealed that he was a carrier of the same mutation as his father, but without expression of the disease at diagnosis. The father had been operated on for a bilateral pheochromocytoma at age 12. Upon diagnosis, annual follow-ups were performed on the patient and appeared normal. At 13-years-old, the patient was rushed to the hospital due to polyuria, headache, flushes, and abnormal perspiration. Abdominal ultrasonography revealed an adrenal gland tumor. His vitals were monitored and high blood pressure was treated with antihypertensive bitherapy combining an α- and β-blocker (labetalol) with a calcium antagonist (nicardipine). An MRI confirmed that the adrenal gland tumour was compatible with a pheochromocytoma. Adrenalectomy was performed, followed by slowly weaning the patient of the medications. At the last follow-up 2 years after surgery, there has been no recurrence.

phenotypes: Pancreatic endocrine tumor,Spinal hemangioblastoma,Retinal capillary hemangioma,Cerebellar hemangioblastoma,Renal cell carcinoma,Pheochromocytoma,Dermoid cyst
evidence_statement: Two patients, a mother, and daughter developed relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (MS) in the background of VHL disease. Their family history was significant for multiple cancers in prior generations. The mother is a 51-year-old woman who was diagnosed with VHL (C.500G > A, p.Arg167Gln) in 2007 with hemangioblastomas in the spinal cord and cerebellum, renal cell carcinoma, pancreatic neoplasm, and a left ovarian dermoid cyst. She also exhibited vision loss in 1993 which recovered after 4-5 months. She was neurologically asymptomatic until 2010 but started developing left lower extremity muscle weakness, which was partially resolved by a nephrectomy. The limb weakness worsened in 2012 and decreased vision for 2 months, which raised a diagnosis of MS. Since then, treatment with corticosteroids showed a partial response of symptoms, and Copaxone was then initiated for treating MS. The patient’s daughter is a 36-year-old woman diagnosed with VHLD (C.500G > A, p.Arg167Glu) in 2008 with retinal and cerebellar hemangioblastomas, pheochromocytoma, pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor, and recurrent renal cell carcinoma. In 2020, she started exhibiting numbness in her limbs which was treated with corticosteroids. She similarly developed vision loss and MRI was consistent with optic neuritis, reinforcing an MS diagnosis.

ATRX deficient glioblastoma model cell lines were created using CRISPR-based gene editing to knock-out ATRX in immortalized astrocytes. The ATRX knock-out cells were found to be particularly sensitive to treatment with the G-quadruplex stabilizer pyridostatin in a clonogenic survival assay.

ATRX deficient glioblastoma model cell lines were created using CRISPR-based gene editing to knock-out ATRX in immortalized astrocytes. ATRX knock-out cells were found to be sensitive (IC50 0.012 uM) to treatment with wee1 inhibitor MK1775 (adavosertib) in a short term viability assay.

ATRX deficient glioblastoma model cell lines were created using CRISPR-based gene editing to knock-out ATRX in immortalized astrocytes. ATRX knock-out cells were found to be more sensitive than wild-type cells to treatment with PARP inhibitors olaparib (IC50 7.4uM vs 35.4uM) and talazoparib (IC50 0.61 uM vs 2.3uM) in a short term viability assay. In addition, U251 glioblastoma cells with ATRX knock-down via shRNA showed sensitivity to olaparib and talazoparib.

A 21-year-old male presented with long-standing poor vision in the right eye. He was found to have a large exudative retinal detachment (ERD) in the right eye with multiple retinal capillary hemangioblastoma (RCH) in both eyes. Next generation sequencing revealed a heterozygous N131*(c.390dupT) mutation in the VHL gene. Intravitreal triamcinolone acetonide injection resulted in near total resolution of the ERD. Retinal flattening made RCH accessible for laser photocoagulation. Following multiple focal lasers, the lesions were regressed with the flat retina, leading to stable vision. There was no definite family history for this patient.

A 11-year-old girl with a history of bronchial asthma presented to the hospital with a an acute onset of breathlessness, chest discomfort, pallor and sweatiness and elevated blood pressure secondary to an adrenal tumour, which is consistent with a catecholamine crisis. She was given nebulised salbutamol at the emergency department and then referred to the paediatric team for hypertension. She started prazosin for initial control of her blood pressure. She had unexpectedly normal urinary metanephrine and catecholamine results, which placed doubt in an initial suspicion of pheochromocytoma. She improved spontaneously and underwent surgery later . Post-operatively, praozin was weaned off. Histopathological examination confirmed a pheochromocytoma with large central necrosis. However, while pheochromocytoma should still be suspected, other causes of adrenal mass associated with hypertension should be considered. Genetic testing revealed a heterozygous VHL c.467A>G(p.Tyr156Cys) mutation. The sample used was not mentioned, but patient's father has the same gene mutation, suggesting a germline variant. Although, patient had no family history of malignancy. An abdominal ultrasound repeated in 6 weeks showed a reduction in the size of the lesion with no further intervention and remained asymptomatic on follow-up.

85 VHL patients from 34 pedigrees in 16 Chinese provinces who underwent 121 operations for Central nervous system (CNS) hemangioblastomas (HGBs) were enrolled. Surgery was performed on patients who had tumors with obvious mass effects on MRI. The mean age at first operation in these patients was 33.9 ± 13.6 years and the male-to-female ratio was 43:42. Genetic analysis using DNA extracted from peripheral blood. Three coding exons and their flanking intronic regions were amplified by polymerase chain reaction. Direct sequencing was used to detect missense and splicing mutations. Large exon deletions were detected using multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification (MLPA) and confirmed by real-time quantitative PCR. All patients were divided into the following 5 groups based on their genetic results: partial deletion group, large deletion group, frameshift group, missense group, and splicing site mutation group. There were 3 families (12 HGB patients total) in the large deletion group. The biological parents of most patients were deceased and not available for genetic testing, but de novo status was confirmed in 8 patients out of the 33 remaining patients

A 5-year-old male presented to a urology clinic in 2009 for adrenal pheochromocytoma screening due to a known VHL heterozygous V170G(c.509.T>G) missense variant in the VHL gene, despite unremarkable medical history. The patient's mother was the index case in this VHL family, as she was diagnosed with bilateral pheochromocytoma at age 23 and underwent bilateral adrenalectomy. Genetic screening of the mother revealed the V170G(c.509.T>G) variants, which also prompted the screening of family members. DNA sequencing from the blood of consenting family members confirmed the presence of the VHL variant in seven family members (three generations from the maternal side). This included the mother (index case), the patient, his brother, maternal grandmother, uncle, and two cousins. The patient remained asymptomatic on routine annual visits until nine months after his yearly visit at age 7. He was admitted to the hospital due to 3-months of flushing, night sweats, heat intolerance, and headaches. An abdominal ultrasound and MRI showed a left suprarenal mass. A total adrenalectomy was performed since the mass was too big for partial adrenalectomy. Pathology confirmed a left pheochromocytoma. At age 10, a routine ultrasound revealed a new mass in the right adrenal gland measuring 2 cm, confirmed by MRI. Right adrenalectomy was delayed 3 months, but pathology confirmed a pheochromocytoma. Six years after his second surgery he is asymptomatic with no clinical evidence of recurrence. He remains on fludrocortisone and hydrocortisone as hormone replacement therapy. The brother, who was 3 years younger, similarly underwent routine screenings. At 11 years old, MRI revealed an adrenal mass, which required total adrenalectomy. Pathology confirmed it to be a right pheochromocytoma. The brother remains well 2.5 years later. Regarding the other family members, the uncle developed hemangioblastoma, multiple bilateral renal cell carcinomas, and bilateral pheochromocytomas, and succumbed to his disease at age 45. The uncle's two daughters both had the mutation. One of his daughters was found to have pheochromocytoma at age 15 due to routine screening. The other 8-year-old daughter has not had any manifestations. No phenotype was noted for the grandmother.

Mice carrying the p.L1363P variant (the equivalent of human p.L1407P) were created using a CRISPR/Cas9 protocol. Heterozygous mice were viable without any apparent aberrant phenotypes. Homozygous mice die during embryonic development. Partial rescue of embryonic lethality occurred when TP53 was also knocked out (heterozygous and homozygous both rescued but in slightly different ways). The p.L1363P variant was found to disrupt BRCA1-PALB2 binding as measured by co-immunoprecipitation in both heterozygous and homozygous mutant MEFs. Ionizing radiation-induced foci of RAD51 were decreased in BRCA1 mutant homozygous / TP53 knockout mice; and this was correlated with an increased sensitivity to cisplatin and PARP1 inhibition. In addition, a conditional mutant was created to induce the BRCA1 p.L1363P mutation in epithelial cells. In this model BRCA p.L1363P causes similar tumor formation latency in TP53-deficient tumors as complete BRCA1 loss. Heteozygous knockout and heterozygous L1363P mice also showed similar tumor latency. The tumors observed with L1363P showed an epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) phenotype and low genomic instability. The sensitivity to cisplatin and the PARP inhibitor AZD2461 as observed in MEFS was recapitulated in mice with orthotopic tumor transplants. Overall this paper shows that L1363P disrupts BRCA1 function and causes sensitivity to cisplatin and PARP inhibitors.

phenotypes: Clear cell renal cell carcinoma,Papillary cystadenoma of the epididymis
evidence_statement: A 42-year-old man came to the emergency department with progressive dyspnea on exertion for 1 month. An X-ray revealed pleural effusion, thus a thoracocentesis was performed. CT scan revealed a mass consistent with clear cell renal cell carcinoma, confirmed by a renal biopsy. He received palliative treatment with pazopanib. He previously had bilateral scrotal masses that were identified as benign cysts and surgically removed. Ultrasonography of both testes revealed bilateral papillary cystadenomas of the epididymis (PCEs). Bilateral PCEs is a characteristic hallmark of Von Hippel-Lindau disease (VHL). The patient was previously diagnosed with diabetes mellitus (DM) at age 25. It was noted that the cause of insulin-dependent DM may be chronic pancreatitis, rather than type 1 DM. His family history revealed an intracranial tumor in his brother, father, and grandfather. A genetic test for the VHL gene reported a heterozygous nonsense mutation of c.263G>A (p.Trp88Stop) in exon 1 of the VHL gene.

phenotypes: Edema of the dorsum of hands,Nocturia,Pheochromocytoma,Renal artery stenosis
evidence_statement: A healthy 10-year-old girl presented with occasional high routine blood pressure. She noted mild hand edema over the past few days and reported recent nocturia. Physical examination appeared normal other than the elevated blood pressure of 139/113 mm Hg. Urine tests showed moderate albuminuria (albumin-creatinine ratio of 50 mg/g), as well as high levels of noradrenaline and normetanephrine, suggestive of benign pheochromocytoma. Ultrasound showed normal kidney size and parenchyma, but color duplex sonography revealed an increased flow rate of the left renal artery. This finding suggests renal artery stenosis. Magnetic Resonance Angiography of the kidney vessels showed a solid tumor that had cystic features. Tumor resection normalized blood pressure and pathologic examination of the removed tumor confirmed pheochromocytoma. The patient was diagnosed with secondary hypertension due to compression of renal vessels and catecholamine production by VHL-associated pheochromocytoma. Antihypertensive therapy with phenoxybenzamine as α blockade was initiated, along with the subsequent expansion of the therapy with a β-blocker. Gene panel analysis identified a recurrent sequence variant c.311G>T [p.Gly104Val] in VHL that occurred de novo. The authors mention that the patient is in complete remission with no other manifestations of VHL disease and is receiving close follow-up.

To characterize germline gene mutations associated with hereditary tumors, the authors designed a custom gene panel that targets 23 genes selected according to the ACMG recommendations for reporting of incidental findings. The panel excludes any genes not related to hereditary tumors. Samples were obtained from 12 patients previously diagnosed as having hereditary tumors via Sanger sequencing. The custom gene panel successfully identified all variants previously detected by Sanger sequencing, but also identified previously unrecognized variants that either confirmed the disease or even revised the diagnosis. Genomic DNA was extracted from peripheral blood and all coding exons of the 23 genes were amplified and sequenced. This proband presented with bilateral pheochromocytoma (PHEO) and a pancreatic endocrine tumor. When the unilateral PHEO first developed at age 23, the RET gene was ruled out by Sanger sequencing, but screening of mutations in SDHN and SDHD identified a p.V111I mutation in SDHD. Although the classification of the SDHD variant was uncertain, the patient's 3rd son also developed pheochromocytoma. SDHD-related diseases are characterized by maternal imprinting and thus the children of female patients should not develop such tumors. The proband was also diagnosed with thyroid medullary carcinoma at age 52. Her sister also had PHEO and thyroid medullary carcinoma, and her 2nd son was also diagnosed with thyroid medullary carcinoma. Due to inherited pheochromocytoma, pancreatic endocrine tumor, and suspected hemangioblastoma, it was concluded to be sporadic VHL rather than an SDHD-related disease. Genetic testing confirmed a heterozygous p.V166F (c.496G>T) mutation in the VHL gene and a heterozygous c.1249+7G>C mutation in WT1 with uncertain significance.

Although date of onset of RH, as well as data on central nervous system haemangioblastomas (CNSH), pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma (PPGL), clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) and pancreatic neuroendocrine neoplasm (PNEN) were collected, it was not reported on a per patient basis and therefore could not be discussed per variant. There was 1 patient reported with the c.493del (p.V165Lfs*5) mutation. This member presented with retinal hemangiomas. No family information was provided.

A 35-year-old African-American male diagnosed with VHL syndrome presented with increased nasal congestion and epistaxis. He has a history of multiple benign CNS and visceral tumors and is known to have an R161P (c.482G>C) germline missense mutation in exon 3 of the VHL gene. CT imaging and MRI showed a right-sided nasal mass and MRI. A nasal endoscopic biopsy revealed a proliferation of follicles and immunohistochemistry confirmed the diagnosis of Sinonasal renal cell-like adenocarcinoma. CT of the abdomen and whole body PET showed local disease only. Surgical resection using an endoscopic endonasal approach was performed. The patient had adjuvant radiotherapy, with no recurrence one year after diagnosis. This VHL variant was also detected somatically. Other somatic mutations include P623A in the MSH6 gene, V772M in the MST1R gene, and H660R in the PIK3C2B gene.

Three siblings with a genetic diagnosis of VHL were referred for routine audiometric surveillance upon detecting a heterozygous exon 1-3 deletion in the VHL gene in all 3 siblings and their mother. All three children underwent peripheral audiological assessment. None of the siblings had audiovestibular symptoms and all their brain/spine MRIs were regular. However, both 9-year-old twins showed either absence (twin 2) or left asymmetry (twin 1) in the assessment of vestibular function that monitors an individual's sense of balance and spatial orientation. These results suggest weakness in saccule/inferior vestibular nerve function. The vestibular test results of the 16-year-old sibling also showed right asymmetry and ear canal weakness. Since in all 3 cases the vestibular system showed partial weakness, this could suggest intra-vestibular endothelial abnormalities, such as tiny cysts or hemangiomas associated with VHL, or early signs of endolymphatic sac tumors.
