evidence_statement: A16-year-old female patient came for genetic consultation in 2008 because genetic testing indicated the deletion of the entire VHL gene. Genetic testing was performed following the detection of multiple renal cysts on ultrasound examination, thus the patient was clinically and molecularly diagnosed with VHL. After five years of following up on the renal cysts, a tumour was detected in the left kidney. Contrast-enhanced computer tomography (CECT) detected six tumours in the kidneys – three in each kidney, and multiple renal cysts on both sides. A biopsy and cryoablation of the largest tumours were performed. Pathology revealed clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC). A long-term ureteric stent was placed in the left ureter to prevent stenosis and was removed two months later due to fever. After one year, CECT showed no signs of local recurrence, but a new tumour in the left kidney was found. After two years, an abdominal MRI was performed and showed one tumour in the left kidney and three in the right one. Cryoablation was performed on the tumours. Few years later, control CECT showed an enlarging tumour in the right kidney, as well as several new tumours in both kidneys. Four years later, four enlarging tumours in the kidneys were found on CECT and cryoablastion was performed on three of them. In addition to the renal tumours, a cerebellar hemangioblastoma was detected and removed by posterior trepanation. MRI revealed more cerebellar hemangioblastomas, as well as a spinal hemagioblastoma. The patient was treated with radiotherapy and not surgery due to the high risk of surgical complications. During a subsequent scan, an ovarian cyst was found and right ovarian endometrioid cyst was confirmed after laparoscopic cystectomy.

A metastatic lung adenocarcinoma (bone and brain) was diagnosed in a 42-year-old woman (patient 3). The primary adenocarcinoma was found in left lower lobe (LLL). Her initial treatment with whole-brain radiotherapy and platinum-based chemotherapy resulted in a partial response. During her chemotherapy, the tumor biopsy sample was sent for NGS testing and found to harbor an EGFR rearrangement at the exon 25, resulting in the formation of a fusion gene between EGFR and PURB genes. She was treated with erlotinib, resulting in a 48% decrease in the LLL index lesion, ongoing for 20 months.

By transcriptome sequencing, they identified the fusion variant EGFR::PPARGC1A in around 30% (31 out of 102) of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC). They found that the lesions harboring the fusion variant tended to be located in long-term sun-exposed areas. Their hypothesis is EGFR::PPARGC1A protein causes constitutive tyrosine phosphorylation, and induces the phosphorylation of wild-type full-length epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) by dimerization.

phenotypes: Epididymal cyst,Renal cyst,Renal neoplasm,Cerebellar hemangioblastoma,Pancreatic cysts
evidence_statement: A case report of a male patient in his 20s with features consistent with a clinical diagnosis of VHL was seen at the Urologic Oncology Branch at the National Cancer Institute. He had multiple cerebellar haemangioblastomas, bilateral epididymal cysts, pancreatic cysts, and bilateral renal tumors and cysts. The patient had no family history of VHL and was negative previously found for germline VHL mutation by standard genetic testing. Blood, saliva, and skin samples were obtained from the patient to test for germline mosaicism, yet no VHL alterations were found. Further karyotype analysis revealed a translocation between chromosomes 1 and 3. Whole genome sequencing followed by Sanger sequencing indicated a balanced germline translocation t(1;3)(p36.3;p25) with a breakpoint on chromosome 3 within the second intron of the VHL gene. The break in chromosome 1 did not occur within a gene. The germline alteration in intron 2 of VHL is expected to result in a truncated VHL protein or no protein produced by this allele. This report showcases a germline translocation not detectable by standard genetic testing that results in VHL gene loss.

In this preclinical study, EZH2 inhibitor, EPZ-6438, was tested for its antitumoral efficacy and potency using WSU-DLCL2 lymphoma cell line and mice harboring Y646F mutation. In-vitro cell treatment showed global reduction in H3K27Me3 levels, inhibition of cell proliferation through cell-cycle arrest and induction of apoptosis (with more than 90% reduction in global methylation and significant proliferation inhibition by the fourth day of treatment). In-vivo treatment of xenograft mice model showed both dose-dependent significant tumor growth inhibition and reduction of H3K27Me3 levels. These results support the potential therapeutic use of EZH2 inhibitors for lymphoma treatment in lymphoma patients with EZH2 Y646F mutation.

In this preclinical study, authors aimed to study the effect of combining glucocorticoid receptor agonists with the EZP-6438 inhibitor in NHL. WSU-DLCL2 lymphoma cells harboring the Y646F mutation were treated with EPZ-6438 alone for 4 days and then with glucocorticoid receptor agonists; CHOP components (Cyclophosphamide, Hydroxyldaunomycin, Oncovin and Prednisone), one by one. Results showed improved efficacy of cell growth with variant degrees depending on the agent. Global H3K27 trimethylation was not found to be altered when combining EZH2 with glucocorticoid receptor agonists. Finally, EZH2 mutant lymphoma xenograft model showed the maximum tumor growth inhibition when combining EPZ-6438 doses in comparison to using CHOP alone (71% vs 45%, respectively, p<0.001). This study highlights the efficacy and potency of EPZ-6438 inhibitor, alone or with combination with CHOP agents in treating NHL harboring the Y646F mutation.

Three families with VHL syndrome were enrolled in this study in 2012 to identify variants and whole exome sequencing (WES) was performed on members (3 generations) with VHL syndrome of all three families. The three families included 9 patients with confirmed VHL syndrome, but according to family history and clinical diagnosis, some members of all 3 families had VHL syndrome. 9 patients were found to have CNS Hemangioblastomas (Hbs), but not all of them had VHL gene mutations. This means CNS Hb in VHL syndrome is not only related to VHL gene mutations. Therefore, mutations in CNS HB-related genes were examined and a total of 34 mutations in the following 21 genes were found: BCLAF1, CACNA1B, CROCC, FRG1, KCNJ12, MAP2K3, MUC4, MUC5B, MUC6, OR4C3, OR4 M2, OR9G1, POTEC, PRIM2, PRSS1, SLC25A5, SLC9B1, SUSD2, TAS2R19, TAS2R31, and TUBA3E. In family C (pedigree B), the WES results showed a large fragment deletion ATATCACACTGCCA>T in exon 2 of the VHL gene in all patients (Ca01, Cb01, Cc01, Cd01) and their offsprings (Ca001, Cb001, Cc001). Proband Ca01 had CNS Hb; proband Cb01 has retinoblastoma, pheochromocytoma, and pancreas cystic disease; and Cc01 has hemangioblastoma, kidney disease, and pancreatic cystic disease. None of the offspring (Ca001, Cb001, Cc001) had any recorded symptoms. Variant reported as GRCh37 chr3:10188300ATATCACACTGCCA>T in the paper.

Analysing whole transcriptome data from 185 GBM samples from TCGA, EGFR fusion events were found in 7.6% (14) of the cohort. In 6 of 14 cases, in-frame EGFR::SEPT14 (e24:e10) fusions were detected (3.2%). In vivo testing of patient derived GBM cell lines with EGFR inhibitor, lapatinib, was conducted. Cells harbouring EGFR::SEPT14 fusions demonstrated sensitivity to lapatinib. This was reproduced in a patient derived xenograft model of GBM with EGFR::SEPT14, where treatment with lapatinib and erlotinib resulted in delayed tumor growth.

A case report of a 49 year old female with gastric signet ring cell carcinoma, in whom a genomic screen of cf tumour DNA revealed an EGFR::SEPT14 fusion at a VAF of 45.3%. The fusion was confirmed by complementary DNA sequencing (via cell free tumour RNA), in which the genomic event was confirmed as an in-frame fusion of exon 24 of EGFR to exon 10 of SEPT14. As the patient refused further therapy, targeted treatment was not trialed in this case.

170 cases of IDH-wildtype GBM were screened using whole genome SNP arrays for chromothripsis. 66 cases of 170 demonstrated chromothripsis, of which 52 had adequate RNA available for RNA sequencing. From this subset of 52 cases, five EGFR fusion events were recorded, of which two harboured EGFR::SEPT14 (3.8%, 2/52). EGFR::SEPT14 was found to have the same breakpoint in EGFR as EGFR::VOPP1 (also found in IDHwt GBMs), encoding the N-terminal portion of EGFR including the tyrosine kinase domain. The bioinformatic tool Oncoscore was used to assess potential oncogenic fusion partners. SEPT14 scored above the minimum threshold, providing further evidence for EGFR::SEPT14 oncogenicity.

A case report of a 56 year old male with metastatic lung adenocarcinoma to the leptomeninges, in whom two rare EGFR::SEPT14 fusions were identified. On second recurrence, NGS was performed on the CSF, in which one fusion (EGFR exon 25::SEPT14 exon 7) occurred at a VAF of 57% and the other (EGFR exon 24::SEPT14 exon 10) occured at a VAF of 0.1%. The patient was on a targted therapy (osimertinib) prior to the second recurrence and the detection of the EGFR::SEPT14 fusions. The addition of intrathecal permetrexed resulted in complete remission at 6 months.

phenotypes: Pancreatic cysts,Clear cell renal cell carcinoma,Hemangioblastoma
evidence_statement: Three families with VHL syndrome were enrolled in this study in 2012 to identify variants. Whole exome sequencing (WES) was performed on members (3 generations) with VHL syndrome of all three families. The three families included 9 patients with confirmed VHL syndrome, but according to family history and clinical diagnosis, some members of all 3 families had VHL syndrome. 9 patients were found to have CNS Hemangioblastomas (Hbs), but not all of them had VHL gene mutations. This means CNS Hb in VHL syndrome is not only related to VHL gene mutations. Therefore, mutations in CNS HB-related genes were examined and a total of 34 mutations in the following 21 genes were found: BCLAF1, CACNA1B, CROCC, FRG1, KCNJ12, MAP2K3, MUC4, MUC5B, MUC6, OR4C3, OR4 M2, OR9G1, POTEC, PRIM2, PRSS1, SLC25A5, SLC9B1, SUSD2, TAS2R19, TAS2R31, and TUBA3E. In family 1 (A), the WES results showed a homozygous P86S(c.256C>T) missense variant in exon 1 of the VHL gene in proband A01 and offspring A002. Proband A01 had CNS Hb, clear cell renal cell carcinoma, and pancreatic cystic disease, while the daughter has no disease. Proband's mother, two uncles, and aunt-in-law had hemangioblastomas and are no longer alive. Proband's cousin also had a hemangioblastoma.

MPL S204P was identified somatically in 2 individuals with PMF and ET. Using a luciferase reporter assay in JAK2- deficient gamma 2A cells, S204P and other identified MPL variants (T119I, S204F, E230G, R321W,V285E,Y591D) were able to induce ligand-independent JAK-STAT signaling, similar to other established pathogenic variants such as S505N and W515; however, detection of activity required longer times (48 hours) than for the usual pathogenic variants W515K or S505N, which exhibit constitutive activity at 24 hours post transfection. The authors suggest that the variants have a milder gain of function effect compared with the common W515K mutant. To further study the functional consequence of these identified MPL variants, we MPL wild-type or variants were expressed in the interleukin-3 (IL-3)- dependent murine cell line Ba/F3. None of the variants conferred cytokine-independent growth of Ba/F3 cells or hypersensitivity to IL-3, except for the W515K which was used as a positive control.

Comprehensive genomic characterization was undertaken in a total of 2035 patients including 1321 patients with essential thrombocythemia, 356 with polycythemia vera, 309 with myelofibrosis, and 49 with other diagnoses of myeloproliferative neoplasms. Targeted sequencing for the full coding sequence of 69 genes and genome wide copy-number information was undertaken in 1887 patients, and 148 patients underwent whole-exome sequencing. The term “myelofibrosis” (MF) was used to encompass both primary myelofibrosis and myelofibrosis that evolved from essential thrombocythemia (ET) or polycythemia vera. The authors characterized distinct genetic subgroups and provided a classification of myeloproliferative neoplasms on the basis of causal biologic mechanisms. The mutational profile of this cohort is included in table S4. MPL S204P was seen in 5 patients (#524, #659, #715, #1242, #1367), of which 4 with MF and 1 with ET. MPL S204P was also reported in patient #1363 with MF along with additional mutations in CALR, SF3B1 and CBL. The authors report that MPL S204P co-occurred with loss of heterozygosity (LOH) at chromosome 1p, which in their opinion suggests a clonal advantage to acquired homozygosity for this variant.

Seventeen patients diagnosed as triple-negative ETs namely negative for any JAK2V617F, MPLW515K/L, and CALR exon 9 mutations were studied via WES on paired granulocyte and T-cell samples (considered as the tumoral and control cells, respectively). Two patients carried an MPL S204P variants (table 1, patient 14 and 24). The effects of MPL S204P on cell proliferation was studied. MPL S204P did not induce cytokine-independent growth nor render cells hypersensitive to TPO or GM-CSF hypersensitivity. In addition, there was no difference in apoptosis in the presence or absence of TPO or in cell cycle at different TPO doses. No constitutive activation in STAT3, STAT5, and AKT was observed in UT7 cells expressing MPLS204P. To investigate whether the MPL S204P was able to support TPO-independent JAK/ STAT signaling like MPL W515K, a luciferase reporter assay for STAT5 activation induced via MPL in the JAK2-deficient g2A cells was used. Expression of MPL S204P supported TPO-independent JAK2/STAT5 signaling, albeit to lower levels than MPL W515K . However, although MPL W515K-induced JAK2/ STAT5 activation was evident at 24 to 30 hours after transfection, a longer period was necessary for MPL S204P (40 hours). This indicates that the MPLS204P variant signals are weaker than those induced by MPL W515K. Also the authors show that MPL S204P could induce prolonged signaling in UT7 cells after stimulation with TPO and culture without cytokine for 3 hours. A sustained phosphorylation of STAT5 and AKT was observed for the mutant cells. Altogether, the results demonstrate that MPL S204P is a gain-of- function mutant.

DLBCL cell line carrying the EZH2 Y641F mutation (WSU-DLCL2 ) was used to study the effect of a selective EZH2 inhibitor (EI1) on these cells. Immunoblot assay showed an increase in baseline H3K27me3 and H3K27me2 levels in comparison to lymphoma cell line with wild type EZH2. Upon treating cells with EI1, WSU-DLCL2 cells showed a significant inhibition of H3K27me3 and H3K27me2 levels and activation of EZH2 target gene, p16. These results indicate that the Y641F mutation causes activation of EZH2 which in turn increases methylation of H3K27me3 levels and represses targeted genes.

DLBCL cell lines carrying the EZH2 Y641N mutation (SU-DHL6 and Karpas422) were used to study the effect of EI1, a selective EZH2 inhibitor that functions by competing with the methyl group donor S-Adenosyl methionine (SAM). Immunoblot assays demonstrated an increase in baseline H3K27me3 and a decrease in baseline H3K27me2 levels in the SU-DHL6 mutated cell line compared to wild-type EZH2 cells. Upon treating cells with EI1, SU-DHL6 cells showed a significant reduction in H3K27me3 and H3K27me2 levels. Gene expression changes in treated Karpas422 cells showed that the early response to EZH2 inhibition is primarily gene up-regulation, consistent with EZH2’s role in transcriptional repression. Ultimately, EI1 treatment led to the down-regulation of a proliferation gene signature and the up-regulation of a memory B-cell signature.

A selective EZH2 inhibitor (EI1) and siRNA were used to inhibit EZH2 Y641F mutation in DLBCL mutated cell line (WSU-DLCL2). Two independent siRNAs knocked down EZH2 mRNA by almost 80% and inhibited cell proliferation in the mutated cell line. EI1 also showed a significant inhibition of proliferation in the mutated lymphoma in comparison to treated EZH2 wild-type (wt) DLBCL cells. EI1 treatment showed a decrease in the number and size of colony formation in mutated cells but not the wt cell line. Finally, WSU-DLCL2 cells were treated with EI1 and examined for DNA synthesis and cell cycle progression where significant decrease of BrdU+ cells and cells in G2/M was detected along with a significant decrease in cyclin A and B1 levels. These results suggest that Y641F mutation causes cellular proliferation and cell cycle progression in DLBCL mutated cells.

A selective EZH2 inhibitor (EI1) was used to target the EZH2 Y641N mutation in DLBCL cell lines. EI1 treatment significantly inhibited proliferation in EZH2-mutated cells compared to lymphoma cells with wild-type EZH2. When mutated cells were treated with EI1 and examined for DNA synthesis and cell cycle progression, a significant decrease in BrdU+ cells and cells in G2/M was detected, alongside a decrease in cyclin A and B1 levels. Additionally, EI1-treated Karpas422 and SU-DHL6 mutant cells showed a mild increase in the sub-G1 population, and apoptosis was further confirmed in SU-DHL6 cells by the detection of elevated cleaved caspase-3 by western blot. Notably, EZH2 wild-type DLBCL cell lines (such as OCI-LY19, GA10, and Toledo) showed no significant changes in DNA synthesis or cell cycle distribution upon EI1 treatment. These results suggest the Y641N mutation specifically drives cellular proliferation and cell cycle progression in mutated DLBCL cells.

phenotypes: Spinal hemangioblastoma,Adrenal pheochromocytoma,Abnormal lung morphology,Abnormality of the liver,Clear cell renal cell carcinoma
evidence_statement: A 55-year-old male presented to the emergency room due to shortness of breath, chest pain, and coughing. A chest X-ray and CT scan found a perihilar mass on the left lung, as well as a left renal lesion. A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a mass on the left kidney and right adrenal gland. A biopsy showed that the left kidney mass was a renal cell carcinoma. The patient had a left-sided radical nephrectomy and right-sided adrenalectomy. Pathology confirmed clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) and pheochromocytoma. Two pieces of lung tissue were orally expelled and examination supported metastatic ccRCC. Spinal MRI and chest CT identified both bone metastases and two spinal lesions consistent with spinal hemangioblastomas. Histology also confirmed liver metastases from the ccRCC. 10 months after his initial presentation, the patient succumbed to his disease 10 months. The patient had no family history of VHL and no other VHL-associated manifestations. The patient was clinical diagnosis with Type 2B VHL. Germline DNA from peripheral blood leukocytes was isolated and sent for gene panel genetic testing targeting known hereditary renal cell cancer and hereditary paraganglioma-pheochromocytoma genes. The gene panel targeted FH, FLCN, MET, MITF, MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2, PTEN, SDHA, SDHB, SDHC, SDHD, TP53, TSC1, TSC2, MAX, MEN1, NF1, RET, SDHAF2, TMEM127, and VHL. The patient tested negative for both single nucleotide or copy number variants in any of the genes. The variant allele threshold for this germline panel was >10%. Subsequent sequencing analysis of all four postmortem tumor tissues revealed an L198P(c.593T>C) missense VHL mutation at varying allele fractions (range: 10–55%) in all four tissues. Both of the patient's daughters underwent germline genetic analysis of VHL and were negative. However, due to family history, both daughters underwent full VHL screening including ophthalmologic assessment, brain, spine, and abdominal MRI. They have no VHL manifestations at the ages of 25 and 30. The germline genetic testing results of the proband's blood sample were re-analyzed and the VHL missense variant was detected at 6% variant allele frequency (below the standard 10% threshold), strongly suggesting that this case is a result of somatic mosaicism.

The paper reports three patients (P1, P2 and P4) with Stage IV lung adenocarcinoma with metastasis, harboring the EGFR::RAD51 fusion detected by hybrid capture NGS (FoundationOne). Breakpoints were in intron 24 of EGFR and intron3 of RAD51. These patients were not amenable to systemic chemotherapy due to disseminated intravascular coagulation or DIC (P1 and P2) or showed disease progression following chemotherapy (P4), and were subsequently treated with the EGFR inhibitor Erlotinib. Noticeable clinical and functional improvements were seen, including regression of miliary nodules, reduction in tumor size and resolution of DIC.

Expression of EGFR::RAD51 via retroviral transfection in IL-3 dependent murine Ba/F3 cells results in activation of Pi3K/AKT pathway (Fig. 2C, increased levels of pAKT), and IL-3 independent proliferation of these cells (Fig. 2B) when compared to experimental controls and Ba/F3 cells expressing wild type EGFR. Further, these oncogenic effects of EGFR::RAD51 are comparable to the known oncogenic mutant EGFR L858R (Fig2B and 2C). IL-3 independent proliferation of Ba/F3 is a known transforming event in other tyrosine kinases as well (Ref11, provided in the paper). Expression of EGFR::RAD51 in NR6 cells significantly increased colony formation in soft agar compared to controls or wild type EGFR (Supplementary Fig S5). EGFR::RAD51 fusion protein retains the critical EGFR tumorigenic Tyrosine 845 phosphorylation site in its kinase domain. These findings indicate that the EGFR::RAD51 fusion is oncogenic.

Response to Erlotinib was assessed by measuring viability of Ba/F3 cells expressing the EGFR::RAD51 variant 72 hours after treatment with Erlotinib (10-1000 nmol/L). Viabilty was measured using the CellTiter Blue Assay (Promega). Progressive decrease in viabilty was observed in EGFR::RAD51 population compared to control (Fig3A). This was also associated with decreasing levels of pAKT and pERK. (Fig 3B). These observations were comparable to a known target of TKIs, EGFR L858R (Fig 3A and 3B).

Retrospective analysis of a phase 2 trial of imatinib in desmoid tumors. Among 33 evaluable patients,CTNBB1 T41A mutations were identified in 30,3%, S45 mutations were identified in 48.5 %, whereas CTNNB1 wild-type status was found in 21.2 %. The Progression Arrest Rate at 6 months was 70, 81, and 43 %. There was a statistically significant difference comparing patients with S45F mutations (85 % PAR) versus wild-type status (p = 0.05).

Response to Afatinib was assessed by measuring viability of Ba/F3 cells expressing the EGFR::RAD51 variant 72 hours after treatment with Afatinib (10-1000 nmol/L). Viability was measured using the CellTiter Blue Assay (Promega). Progressive decrease in cell viability was observed in the EGFR::RAD51 population compared to control (Fig3A) and associated with decreasing levels of pAKT and pERK. (Fig 3B). These observations were comparable to the EGFR L858R variant (Fig 3A and 3B), which is a known target for the drug.

This study, involving 20 pediatric patients, looked at molecular alterations in Lipofibromatosis. RNA sequencing detected EGFR::BRAF fusion in Patient 19 (6-year-old male). The fusion was picked up by one of the two algorithms implemented. Fusion breakpoints were in exon 27 of EGFR and exon 10 of BRAF. The kinase domains of EGFR and BRAF are predicted to be retained in the fusion product.

Case report of a 30-year-old male with lung adenocarcinoma and metastasis to several organs, including several lesions in the brain. NGS assay (Foundation One CDX panel) detected the EGRF::RAD51 fusion. He was treated with platinum-based agents and palliative radiation therapy to the spine. Once the disease was stable as per RECIST guidelines, treatment was switched to Osimertinib. Marked improvement was seen within two weeks with reduction in lymph node metastases and reduction in back pain. Dramatic reductions in brain lesions were observed after 2 months of treatment. The patient was followed up for 9 months during which significant improvement was seen in his clinical status, and he remained on therapy at the time of publication. The authors have also noted that osimertinib fared better in improving his CNS symptoms compared to his earlier chemotherapy treatment.

In neuroblastoma, high FGFR1 expression is associated with metastatic and relapsed tumors and inferior relapse-free survival, suggesting its role in promoting disease progression and recurrence. In vitro data show that FGFR1 silencing in neuroblastoma cells impairs cell proliferation, cell invasion and cell growth while in cells overexpressing FGFR1 wild-type protein cell proliferation, cell invasion and cell colonigenicity increases. These results suggest a potential oncogenic role of FGFR1 in neuroblastoma. Morever, in vitro experiments demonstrate that the aggressive phenotype, resulting from FGFR1 overexpression, is rescued by the treatmet with its inhibitor AZD4547.

FGFR1 N546K mutation affects the conformational dynamics of the tyrosine kinase domain, resulting in gain-of-function and ligand-independent constitutive activation. In vitro data show that FGFR1 N546K overxpression increases cell proliferation, cell invasion and cell colonigenicity in neuroblastoma cell lines, enhancing the receptor kinase activity and resulting in higher FGFR1 auto-phosphorylation. FGFR1 N546K overexpressing cells failure to respond to treatment with FGFR1 inhibitor (AZD4547) by activating ERK, STAT3 and AKT pathways. These signaling cascades enhanced by N546K mutation can be suppressed using AZD4547 and FGFR1 downstream pathways inhibitors (i.e. GDC0941).

phenotypes: Spinal hemangioblastoma,Cerebellar hemangioblastoma,Renal cell carcinoma,Retinal capillary hemangioma,Renal cyst
evidence_statement: Data was collected from 82 VHL mutation carriers in the Dutch VHL surveillance program. One patient was found with this mutation in the VHL gene c.235C>T, p.Arg79Cys (stated as c.235 CAG-TAG in the paper and updated to this presumed nomenclature). The patient was 63Y at the last follow-up and presented with: retinal hemangioblastoma, cerebellar hemangioblastoma, spinal cord hemangioblastoma, renal cell carcinoma, and renal cysts. Family history was not described, nor any further individual information.

In this preclinical study, authors aimed to study EZH2 inhibition effect on PRAME in DLBCL. IμBcl6 EZH2-Y646F Cγ1-Cre mice were used for in vivo experiment using a vehicle or EZH2 inhibitor, EPZ011989. Mice treated with EPZ011989 maintained a stable disease and had induced PRAME expression and T cells in contrast to the control group. This effect was sustained after three months without the treatment. Authors highlight EZH2 inhibitor's potential significance in upregulating PRAME and other immune cells that are silenced by mutant EZH2 in DLBCL cells.

Case report of a 50-year-old male with Stage 1 Lung adenocarcinoma. NGS detected the presence of KIF5B::EGFR fusion (exon 15 and exon 18). The patient received two cycles of chemotherapy but experienced disease progression to lymph nodes and left rib after 13 months. The lymph nodes showed both squamous cell carcinoma and adenocarcinoma. He was then treated with afatinib and showed progression-free survival for 11 months, after which intracranial metastasis was observed, and treatment with afatinib was discontinued. Following a whole brain radiation therapy, the patient was treated with Osimertinib for 4 months due to the detection of a known resistance marker T790M, however only a limited benefit was seen and the treatment was discontinued. The authors conclude the detection of the novel KIF5B-EGFR fusion in advanced NSCLC was a good indicator of response to afatinib.

Several splicing factors known to drive myeloid neoplasms (including SRSF2) require phosphorylation by CLK family kinases for nuclear translocation. The authors describe development of an inhibiter of a CLK family kinase called CTX-712 and evaluate its efficacy in cell line and murine models. CTX-712 efficacy was confirmed in MDS/AML-derived xenografts (PDX). One PDX model with an SRSF2 P95L variant exhibited significant reduction in tumor volume 2 weeks after CTX-712 high dose treatment compared to vehicle (P=0.0162, N=6). CTX-712 treatment also improved survival in the SRSF2 P95L-mutated model (P=0.0030, N=6 mice).

Several splicing factors known to drive myeloid neoplasms (including SRSF2) require phosphorylation by CLK family kinases for nuclear translocation. The authors describe development of an inhibiter of a CLK family kinase called CTX-712 and evaluate its efficacy in cell line and murine models. CTX-712 efficacy was confirmed in MDS/AML-derived xenografts (PDX). One PDX model with an SRSF2 P95H variant showed a significant response to CTX-712 in a dose-dependent manner. 4 out of 5 mice receiving a high dose protocol achieved complete remission. CLK inhibition also induced aberrant splicing events including skipped exons and this effect was more prevalent in the SRSF2-mutated model.

The cooperation of IDH1 R132H and CIC R201W mutations were evaluated in HOG and HEK cell lines transfected with wildtype and mutant forms. In the IDH1-R132H background, 2KG metabolite levels were increased in cells co-expressing F-CIC-R201W (p<0.0001). CIC was shown to interact with ACLY by reciprocal IP, and influence ACLY phosphorylation; cells transfected with CIC R201W showed reduction in pACLY (p<0.016) compared to wild type CIC.

Wild-type and mutant (D418N, E419K, E419Q) KLF5 were infected into HEK293T cells and DNA binding specificity evaluated by ChIP-Seq. The binding motif for wild-type KLF5 has a C or T at the 5th nucleotide, while E419K binds preferentially to guanine (G) at the 5th nucleotide of the DNA motif, while E419Q binds preferentially to adenine (A) at that position.

The binding motif for wild-type KLF5 has a C or T at the 5th nucleotide, E419K binds preferentially to guanine (G) at the 5th nucleotide of the DNA motif, and E419Q binds preferentially to adenine (A) at that position.

Case study of a 2-year-old male with a slowly enlarging mass and gradual loss of function in right hand. First considered to be a vascular malformation. Tumor involved soft tissue spaces around and between fingers. Tumor was low grade infiltrative deep soft tissue sarcoma in the hand with prominent-vascularity, myopericytoid/lipofibromatosis-like ovoid cells, and collagenized stroma. Cells from tumor were equivocally SMA positive, focally CD34 positive, and negative for S100 protein. Immunostaining was not positive for NTRK but positive for ALK. ERC1::ALK fusion was identified and patient was treated with pediatric dose liquid crizotinib. After 5 months hand motion improved and amputation was avoided. Patient remains on crizotinib with barely detectable disease.

Analysis of a single patient is reported from a phase II trial (NCT02952573) testing erdafitinib in relapsed/refractory myeloma patients with or without FGFR3 mutations. The single patient (52 year old female) with t(4;14) multiple myeloma received induction chemotherapy, autologous stem cell transplantation, consolidation and maintenance chemotherapy. Disease progress occurred within one year and the patient received additional chemotherapy. At this stage, sequencing was performed and revealed a stop-loss, in-frame 30bp deletion in FGFR3 (p.G802_X807del). Sequencing also confirmed the presence of IGHA1::FGFR3 fusion transcripts indicative of t(4;14). The patient was enrolled on the erdafitinib clinical trial at this point, received the drug for two months and succumbed to disease one month later. scRNA profiling of bone marrow samples obtained before and after 28 days of erdafitinib revealed cells expressing the p.G802_X807del variant (4 cells total) were detectable in the pre-treatment sample but not the post-treatment sample. These cells appeared to correspond to a sub-cluster of tumor cells defined by single cell expression signatures. The authors suggest that clearance of a sub-clone harboring G802_X807del indicates sensitivity of this variant to erdafitinib.

An array of KDM6 deficient AMP cells showed increased sensitivity to PARP inhibition. In a mouse model xenotransplant with a KDM6A loss of function AMP cell line increased susceptibility to PARP blockade was seen.
FLT3-ITD positive AML cells with lower KDM6A expression showed sensitivity to olaparib.

KDM6A repression was reported to sensitize AML cells to venetoclax. In addition, attenuation of KDM6 was reported to increase mitochondrial activity and intracellular ROS levels and de-reporessed BCL2 expression, which is a target of venetoclax. KDM6 loss also resulted in transcriptional repression of BCL2A1 which the authors note has bee associated with venetoclax resistance.

Dual targeting of PARP (olipartinib) and BCL2 (venetoclax) was reported to be superior to either PARP or BCL2 inhibition alone in inducing primary AML cell apoptosis, and loss of KDM6A further enhanced the synergistic effect. The authors conclude that KDM6A is a central regulator for susceptibility of AML to PARP and BCL2 inhibition, suggesting potential for effective clinical combination therapy.

phenotypes: Early young adult onset,Childhood onset,Juvenile onset
evidence_statement: Whole genome sequencing (WGS) was performed on the diffuse intrinsic pontine gliomas (DIPGs) and matched germline DNA of 7 pediatric patients. Targeted sequencing was performed on an additional 43 DIPGs and 36 non-brainstem pediatric glioblastomas (non-BS-PGs). Authors identified H3-3A K27M mutations in 30/50 (60%) of pediatric DIPGs (including 4/7 WGS samples) and 7/36 (19%) pediatric non-brainstem glioblastomas. The authors comment that the K27M mutation appeared exclusive to pediatric high grade gliomas, with H3F3A p.K27M mutation in one of 9 pediatric anaplastic astrocytomas (Grade III), but no histone H3 mutations found in any other pediatric brain tumors including 7 low-grade brainstem gliomas, 15 low-grade non-brainstem gliomas, 38 medulloblastomas, and 22 ependymomas. H3 K27M was not found in an additional 170 non-central nervous system pediatric tumors.

SMAD2 S276L mutations were observed in 3/744 cases of colorectal cancer. This mutation was introduced by site-directed mutagenesis and transfected into HEK293T cells. The interaction of wildtype and mutant SMAD2 with SMAD4 was evaluated by immunoprecipitation, where SMAD2 mutant proteins were pulled down in lower amounts than wild-type (p < 0.01) by FLAG-tagged SMAD4, suggesting a reduced ability to complex with SMAD4.

POLE mutations observed in CRC or endometrial cancer were introduced by site-directed mutagenesis. Each mutation dramatically reduced 3′-5′ exonuclease activity relative to the wild-type POLE in in vitro reactions. L424I had exonuclease activity 17% of wild-type (SEM +/- 5.5, figure 3). The effects on replication fidelity (mutation rate) were evaluated by a lacZ forward mutation assay. The mutant POLE variants all increased the mutation frequency over the wild-type POLE; L424I had a mutation frequency 7.1x that of wild-type (supplementary figure 3).

POLE mutations observed in CRC or endometrial cancer were introduced by site-directed mutagenesis. Each mutation dramatically reduced 3′-5′ exonuclease activity relative to the wild-type POLE in in vitro reactions. P286H had exonuclease activity 12% of wild-type (SEM +/- 3.2, figure 3). SMARCA2 mutations K755R and R1159Q are seen in Nicolaides-Barraitser syndrome (NCBRS) (PMID: 22366787). To evaluate the effects of these mutations, CRISPR/Cas9 was used to introduce heterozygous K755R or R1159Q SMARCA2 mutations into the H9 hESC line. SMARCA2 K755R or R1159Q mutants had reduced staining for neural progenitor markers PAX6 and SOX2 (p<0.05), and reduced staining for proliferation marker Ki67 (p<0.05), indicating these SMARCA2 mutations affect self-renewal and neural differentiation. ATAC-seq indicated changes in overall chromatin binding, with an increase from <100 peaks in wild-type SMARCA2 to 54,920 (K755R) and 34,362 (R1159Q) peaks, respectively, suggesting a global gain in SMARCA2 binding to chromatin.

RAF1 (CRAF) R391W was observed in a melanoma patient from which cell line M375 was derived (wild-type for BRAF and NRAS). KARPAS-422 cell line also showed an increase in apoptosis in response to tazemetostat treatment, whereas the wild type cell line showed none. Lastly, EZH2 inhibition resulted in induced B-cell maturation along an increase in tumor suppressor genes in the mutated cell line.

Authors of this study identified and detailed the role of USP47, a novel deubiquitinase (DUB), that stabilizes mutated EZH2 in cancers and prevents the protein’s degradation by ubiquitination. Degradation of mutated EZH2 protein by targeting USP47 was performed using two DUB inhibitors in DLBCL cell line-SU-DHL6- harboring the EZH2 y646N mutation. The two inhibitors, P22077 and 1247825-37-1, were able to degrade mutant EZH2 protein by increasing mutated EZH2 ubiquitination, inhibit cell growth and selectively kill mutant EZH2-expressing transformed cells over wt EZH2. In vivo mice experiment also showed that targeting of USP47 leads to EZH2-Y641N-positive cell death and significant tumor growth inhibition in comparison to the vehicle. These results propose the effective and beneficial use of DUB inhibitors for DLBCL and other hematological malignancies, independently of highly activated EZH2 mutations, EZH2 methylation activity or potential acquired EZH2 resistant mutations.

1,404 Formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue blocks were prospectively screened from patients over 18 with stage II or III adenocarcinoma of the colon completely resected. Patient samples were screened for KRAS mutations in codon 12 (12D, G12A, G12V, G12C, G12S, G12R) and 13 (G13D). KRAS mutations were found in 36.0% in stage II and 37.5% in stage III disease cases. KRAS mutations did not have major prognostic value for relapse-free survival or overall survival in univariate or multivariate analysis. No correlation of KRAS status to relapse free survival was seen when patients were stratified by disease stage or unstratified. The authors conclude that In stage II-III colon cancer, the KRAS mutation status does not have major prognostic value.

The Medical Research Council (MRC) COIN trial consisted of patients with histologically confirmed adenocarcinoma of the colon or rectum, inoperable metastatic or locoregional measurable disease, and who had not received chemotherapy for metastatic disease. In arm A patients were given oxaliplatin plus capecitabine or fluorouracil with folinic acid. In arm B patients were given the same chemotherapy with additional cetuximab. 110 patients had G13D, and HR for effect of cetuximab on progression-free survival was 1·11 (95% CI 0·76–1·63, p=0·60) The authors conclude that in contrast to a different report, they do not see a sensitizing effect for KRAS G13N when cetuximab is added to chemotherapy.

A comprehensive genomic analysis was conducted on 172 cases of pediatric low-grade gliomas (PLGGs) across various histologic subtypes, utilizing whole-genome sequencing (WGS) and/or RNA sequencing. The study identified recurrent somatic alterations in 154 tumors (90%), encompassing all 140 tumors subjected to WGS. Among the seven angiocentric gliomas (AGs) examined, six displayed intrachromosomal deletions leading to MYB::QKI rearrangements, and the remaining one contained a MYB::ESR1 rearrangement. To validate these findings, 12 additional AGs with only formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue were analyzed using fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) (n=9) or whole-exome sequencing (WES) and/or array comparative genomic hybridization (aCGH) (n=3). All tested cases were confirmed to harbor MYB rearrangement or deletion, though the specific gene partners were not determined. Functional studies both in vitro and in vivo demonstrated that MYB::QKI rearrangements facilitate tumorigenesis through activating MYB through truncation of a 3' region, driving aberrant MYB::QKI expression through enhancer translocation, and losing a single copy of the QKI tumor suppressor gene. The research concluded that MYB::QKI represents a novel recurrent fusion defining AGs diagnostically.

TKI effectiveness was measured using phospho-FLT3 western blot at variants TKI concentrations. The TKIs Midostaurin, Lestaurtinib, Linifanib, Quizartinib, Sunitinib, Sorafenib, TTT-3002, KW2449, and Ponatinib had IC50s below 200 nM, which met the author's criteria for sensitivity.

In some cancers such as infant ALL, B-lineage ALL and AML samples with the highest levels of wild-type FLT3, constitutive FLT3 phosphorylation is seen from paracrine or autocrine activation from FLT3 ligand FL (FLT3L gene). The authors tested 13 tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) in Ba/F3 cells expressing FLT3, where FL was added to the culture medium to mimic FLT3L autocrine/paracrine activation loops. Crenolanib, R406 and AG1295 were not effective at inhibiting wildtype FLT3 phosphorylation by the author's criteria, having IC50 values greater or equal to 200 nM, which were determined by phospho-FLT3 western blots done at multiple TKI concentrations.

The authors characterized the occurrence of SMARCB1 gene loss in epithelioid sarcomas. SMARCB1 immunohistochemistry staining demonstrated 19/21 patient samples were negative. Multiplex ligation dependent probe amplification (MLPA) of the 12 epitheliod sarcoma patients with available DNA showed 10/12 to have homozygous deletion of SMARCB1. The other two cases had heterozygous exon 1-9 deletion of SMARCB1. The authors concluded both proximal and classical epithelioid sarcomas contain homozygous deletions of SMARCB1; therefore, somatic SMARB1 deletion alone is not sufficient to differentiate epithelioid sarcoma from malignant rhabdoid tumor.

D835N was originally identified from an AML patient. Transfection of D835N into Ba/F3 cells led to IL3 independent growth, indicating an oncogenic driver effect for the variant in these cells. This evidence gives support for ClinGen/CGC/VICC oncogenicity code OS2

D835G was originally identified from an AML patient. Transfection of D835G into Ba/F3 cells led to IL3 independent growth, indicating an oncogenic driver effect for the variant in these cells. This evidence gives support for ClinGen/CGC/VICC oncogenicity code OS2

A panel of 13 FLT3 tyrosine kinase inhibitors was tested against Ba/F3 cells transfected with FLT3 D593del using MTT growth/survival assay, and results were compared to Ba/F3 cells transfected with FLT3-ITD. IC50 for Midostaurin, Lestaurtinib, TTT-3002, and Crenolanib against D593del were all within 2x the IC50 for ITD. FLT3-ITD was considered responsive by the authors to each of the TKIs tested. Authors also note that Lestaurtinib, midostaurin, and TTT-3002 inhibited all 10 FLT3 activation loop mutants they tested with similar or even greater strength compared to the FLT3-ITD cells.

A panel of 13 FLT3 tyrosine kinase inhibitors was tested against Ba/F3 cells transfected with FLT3 D593del using MTT growth/survival assay, and results were compared to Ba/F3 cells transfected with FLT3-ITD. Linifanib, Quizartinib, Sunitinib, and Sorafenib all had IC50 against D593del approximately 20x of what it was against FLT3-ITD, which the authors suggest as a cutoff for a valuation of sensitivity for the TKI against the variant.

Ba/F3 cells with FLT3 D835Y were transplanted into mice. The cells were stably transfected with luciferase and this was used to monitor disease progression with luciferin injections to visualize bioluminescence. After 5 days mice were treated with lestaurtinib, and at 9 days this resulted in greatly reduced leukemic burden in comparison to vehicle controls.

Ba/F3 cells with FLT3 D835Y were transplanted into mice. The cells were stably transfected with luciferase and this was used to monitor disease progression with luciferin injections to visualize bioluminescence. After 5 days mice were treated with sorafenib, and at 9 days there was no reduction in leukemic burden in comparison to vehicle controls.

To investigate the therapeutic potential of JAK inhibitors in pediatric B-ALL, the authors examined the efficacy of rapamycin in murine xenograft models of 8 pediatric B-ALL cases. Five xenografts (I to IV (Ph-like) and VI (B-ALL)) harbored CRLF2 rearrangements (P2RY8::CRLF2 (n=1) or IGH::CRLF2 (n=4)). Rapamycin treatment yielded significantly lower peripheral blast counts (P<.01) and lower splenic blast counts (P<.05) compared with vehicle in all 5 CRLF2 rearranged xenografts. This pre-clinical study demonstrated the efficacy of rapamycin in B-ALL xenografts with CRLF2 rearrangements.

molecular_profile: BRAF V600E AND EGFR L858R AND EGFR T790M
evidence_statement: A 42 year old man with non-smoking history presented with EGFR L858R positive lung adenocarcinoma. He was given various treatments including erlotinib and gefitinib and progressed four years later. biopsy revealed EGFR T790M mutation, and osimertinib treatment was given. Partial response was seen, and progression occurred after 13 months. BRAF V600E mutation was found in progressed tumor cells, but was not reported before osimertinib resistance.

A 45-year-old non-smoking female patient was diagnosed with a stage IV lung adenocarcinoma and magnetic resonance imaging showed multiple brain metastases. Targeted NGS analysis on the pleural biopsy using the Oncomine Comprehensive Assay v3 panel identified the EML4::NTRK3 (e2::e14) fusion. This fusion was confirmed by both fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) analysis, using NTRK3 and EML4 Dual Color Break Apart probes and panTRK antibody IHC staining. Entrectinib was started and two months later PET scan and brain MR revealed partial response. After 5 months of treatment, complete response was observed in the lungs and brain. As of publication, the patient was still being treated with entrectinib, and their most recent PET and MR scan taken 1 year and 5 months into treatment demonstrated maintained complete response in the brain and lungs.

A 7 month old male had a large cystic mass in his brain surgically resected. Pathological analysis determined the mass to be an infantile high-grade glioma and transcriptome sequencing of the tumor RNA found the tumor harbored an EML4::NTRK3 fusion. The patient then went through four cycles of chemotherapy, but imaging taken two months later revealed no change in tumor size. The patient was treated with Larotrectinib (100 mg/m2/dose BID) and an MRI two months later demonstrated a significant decrease of his tumor. The patient (now 17 months old) continues on twice daily larotrectinib and shows no signs of progression after 10 months of treatment.

EGFR::VSTM2A was identified by RNA-seq in tumor sample derived from 1/78 recurrent glioblastoma patients who benefited from combined beva/CCNU (bevacizumab in combination with lomustine) in the BELOB clinical trial. The GBM tumor from this 58yo female patient belonged to subtype IGS-18 and patient displayed 10.8 months overall survival and 3.9 months progression-free survival on beva/CCNU combination therapy. Authors demonstrate that "classical" GBMs assigned to class IGS-18 trend toward improved survival from beva/CCNU therapy. EGFR::VSTM2A breakpoints were EGFR g.55268105 and VSTM2A g.54636701 (e24::e5). See Supplementary Tables S3 and S6.

170 cases of IDH-wildtype GBM were screened using whole genome SNP arrays for chromothipsis. 66 cases of 170 demonstrated chromothripsis, of which 52 had adequate RNA available for RNA sequencing. RNA-seq identified EGFR::VSTM2A in 2/52 tumor samples from IDH-wild-type glioblastoma patients with chromothripsis (CT) features. Fusions were validated by RT-PCR followed by Sanger sequencing. EGFR::VSTM2A breakpoints are EGFR 7:55087058 (GRCh38) and VSTM2A 7:54544622 (GRCh38) (i1::e2) and EGFR 7:55087058 (GRCh38) and VSTM2A 7:54612315 (GRCh38) (i1::3'UTR). The bioinformatic tool Oncoscore was used to assess potential oncogenic fusion partners.

Using NGS, genomic profiling from tumor/plasma biopsies from 17,442 Chinese lung cancer patients was performed. EGFR::VSTM2A reported in 2/1053 recurrent kinase fusions in lung cancer (NSCLC, adenocarcinoma subtype). Breakpoints not provided, however, only kinase fusions retaining an intact kinase domain were included in this study. See Figure 2.

EGFR::WIF1 was identified by RNA-seq in a tumor sample derived from 1/78 recurrent glioblastoma patients in the BELOB clinical trial. The IDH-wildtype GBM tumor from this 59yo female patient belonged to prognostically unfavorable subtypes IGS-18 and IGS-23 and patient displayed 9.3 months overall survival and 1.2 months progression-free survival on bevacizumab therapy. EGFR::WIF1 breakpoints were EGFR 7:55268105 and WIF1 12:65445249 (e24::e10). See Supplementary Tables S3 and S6.

EZH2 inhibitor, GSK126, showed high potency against DLBCL cell line, KARPAS-422, which harbors the variant Y646N, and resulted in cellular proliferation inhibition after six days (growth IC50 = 232 nM). Consistent with this, mice xenografts from the cell line were treated for 10 days and showed both tumor and H3K27me3 reduction, along with gene expression increase in a dose-dependent manner. These observations highlight EZH2 inhibitors positive role in treating lymphomas, such as DLBCL.

EZH2 inhibitor, GSK126, showed high potency against DLBCL cell lines, WSU-DLCL2 and SU-DHL-10, harboring the Y646F variant. Cell proliferation inhibition was measured after six days at growth IC50= 134 nM and 448 nM, respectively. The inhibitor also induced transcriptional activation and reduction in H3K27me3 levels upon treatment of the cell lines. These observations highlight EZH2 inhibitors positive role in treating lymphomas, such as DLBCL.

In this phase I study, four Japanese patients with follicular lymphoma were recruited to test the efficacy of EZH2 inhibitor-Tazemetostat. Patients were screened for presence of EZH2 mutations and only one patient had an activating mutation in EZH2. The patients were treated with Tazemetostat at a dose of 800 mg twice a day. Three of the four patients had partial response (including the one with the activating mutation), while one had a stable disease status after the treatment cycle. The authors highlight the treatment's acceptable safety profile and promising antitumor activity in relapsed or refractory B-cell lymphomas.

disease: Diffuse Large B-cell Lymphoma Germinal Center B-cell Type
evidence_statement: In this phase I study (clinical trial NCT03009344), one patient with germinal center B‐cell‐like (GCB) DLBCL and two with non-GCB DLBCL types were recruited to test the efficacy of EZH2 inhibitor-Tazemetostat in Japanese patients with refractory/relapsed B-cell lymphomas. The patients were treated with a dose of 800 mg twice a day and an objective response was reached only in the patient with the GCB-DLBCL type (complete response), while the other two had progressive disease status. Since EZH2 is known to be expressed in GC and have a role in cellular proliferation and differentiation, the authors speculate that the the cellular origin of DLBCL might be a key in predicting the efficacy of Tazemetostat.

molecular_profile: EZH2 Y646S OR EZH2 Y646F OR EZH2 Y646H OR EZH2 Y646C OR EZH2 Y646N OR EZH2 A692V OR EZH2 A682G
evidence_statement: In this study, Koji Izutsu et al. conducted a multicenter, open-label phase II clinical trial to evaluate the efficacy and safety of the EZH2 inhibitor tazemetostat in Japanese patients with relapsed or refractory B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma harboring activating EZH2 mutations (as detected through the Cobas EZH2 mutations test). Tumor EZH2 mutation status was confirmed using a molecular diagnostic assay (Cobas EZH2 Mutation Test), and patients received oral tazemetostat at 800 mg twice daily in continuous 28-day cycles. The results demonstrated a high level of clinical activity in the follicular lymphoma cohort (n=17), with an objective response rate (ORR) of 76.5%, including 35.3% complete responses and 41.2% partial responses, while the remaining patients had stable disease. Additionally, progression-free survival (PFS) was not reached at a median follow-up of 12.9 months, indicating durable responses. The estimated PFS rate at 12 and 15 months was 94.1% and 73.2%, respectively. In two patients, grade 3 treatment‐emergent adverse event (TEAE) of lymphopenia was seen. While Grade 4 TEAE included hypertriglyceridemia and pneumonia aspiration in one patient, which authors say were not related to tazemetostat. The authors claim treatment was generally well tolerated, with manageable adverse events and no unexpected safety signals. The authors concluded that tazemetostat shows encouraging and durable clinical efficacy with an acceptable safety profile in patients with EZH2-mutant relapsed/refractory follicular lymphoma, supporting its use as a targeted therapy for tumors driven by activating EZH2 mutations.

molecular_profile: EZH2 Y646S OR EZH2 Y646F OR EZH2 Y646H OR EZH2 Y646C OR EZH2 Y646N OR EZH2 A692V OR EZH2 A682G
evidence_statement: This phase II study evaluated the efficacy and safety of the EZH2 inhibitor tazemetostat in Japanese adults with relapsed or refractory B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma harboring EZH2-activating mutations assessed with the cobas EZH2 Mutation Test. Three patients with DLBCL—including two with transformed follicular lymphoma (FL)—who had previously received chemotherapy without available standard therapy, were treated with tazemetostat 800 mg twice daily in 28-day cycles. All three patients achieved an objective response with reduction in tumors from -60 to -80 precent, reaching partial response (PR), although one patient discontinued treatment due to adverse events. In the broader study, 17 patients with relapsed/refractory FL also demonstrated favorable outcomes, with a high objective response rate and manageable safety profile. These results support the clinical activity and tolerability of tazemetostat in EZH2-mutant DLBCL and FL.

molecular_profile: EZH2 Y646S OR EZH2 Y646F OR EZH2 Y646H OR EZH2 Y646C OR EZH2 Y646N OR EZH2 A692V OR EZH2 A682G
evidence_statement: In this large cohort study, 366 patients with follicular lymphoma (FL) were recruited to investigate the incidence and distribution of EZH2 mutations. NGS and Sanger detected EZH2 positive mutations in 101 patients (27.5%). In total, 106 mutations were detected in 101 patients, which included 87 mutations at codon Y646 (Y646N=36, Y646F=27, Y646S=12, Y646H=9, Y646C=3), 9 A682G, and 7 A692V mutations (mean VAF=21.6%). There were 3 novel variants (K634E, V637A and V679M). There was no difference in the mutation frequency at diagnosis (29%; n = 70/237) and relapse (24%; n = 31/129). EZH2 VAFs were compared to other mutation targets to test clonality. Out of the 43 FL tested cases, 81% (35/43) represented true clonal events, while 19% (8/43) were subclonal. For the 33 paired FL and transformed FL (tFL) cases, 8 carried Y646 mutations, and the mutation was maintained in both biopsies in 6 of those cases. Despite no significant association between the mutation status and overall survival of FL patients, authors stress the need to evaluate EZH2 targeted therapy considering the high incidence of EZH2 mutations and their stability during disease progression and/or transformation (tFL).

43 DLBCL patients were recruited for this phase Ib study to evaluate the safety and efficacy of combining both EZH2 inhibitor, tazemetostat, and PDL1 blocker, atezolizumab. Tazemetostat was administered orally at 800 mg twice daily for 21 days in combination with atezolizumab (dose of 1200 mg on the first say of each cycle). The combination regimen was safe and well tolerated but resulted in modest anti-tumor efficacy (ORR, 16.3%; median DOR, 7.4 months) when compared with tazemetostat alone. The EZH2 mutation status was assessed only for 28 patients, of which, only two patients had Y646N mutation and were responsive to treatment (one patient had the Y646C mutation at but the response is not recorded). This suggests that tazemetostat treatment is effective only in patients with EZH2 mutations, however, the poor prognosis of the patients along the small number of mutated EZH2 cases make it difficult to confirm this.

molecular_profile: EML4::ALK Fusion AND ALK I1171N AND ALK L1196M
evidence_statement: This case report describes a 33 year-old non-smoker with no known exposure to asbestos who was diagnosed with stage IIIB malignant pleural mesothelioma. Panel next generation sequencing (NGS) of 520 genes revealed an EML4::ALK fusion and the patient was subsequently treated with alectinib. After 1 month of therapy the patient showed clinical improvement, and plasma NGS revealed a decrease in EML4::ALK allele fraction (AF) from 24.21% to 8.22%. Progressive disease was confirmed after 4.5 months of alectinib therapy at which time plasma NGS revealed the emergence of two acquired resistance mutations, I1171N (AF=4.24%) and L1196M (AF=0.33). He then received lorlatinib and achieved a PR within one month with 34% tumour shrinkage, suggesting lorlatinib sensitivity despite compound I1171N and L1196M acquired mutations. He began showing signs of progression after 3.6 months of lorlatinib treatment and plasma NGS at that time identified a third concurrent acquired resistance mutation G1202R (AF=3.07%) in cis with L1196M.

molecular_profile: EML4::ALK Fusion AND ALK I1171N AND ALK L1196M
evidence_statement: A 33 year old male with no smoking history or known exposure to asbestos was diagnosed with malignant pleural mesothelioma (MPM). EML4::ALK was found using a panel of 520 genes in NGS, and the patient responded to alectinib treatment. At 3.5 months, symptoms worsened, cough returned and blood tumor markers including NSE, SCC, and CA-125 were increased. Progressive disease was confirmed after 4.5 months of alectinib. NGS of plasma showed ALK kinase domain mutations I1171N (allelic fraction 4.24%) and L1196M (allelic fraction 0.33%).

Case report describing a 63-year-old patient with colorectal adenocarcinoma with disease progression after treatment with XELOX-bevacizumab and bevacizumab-FOLFIRI. After the detection of EGFR aberrations after discontinuing treatment [EGFR::SEPT14 fusion (exon 24 & exon 10) and EGFR amplification] he was treated with erlotinib with partial response (CT scan). A couple of months later, the patient showed signs of progressive disease. A new variant, EGFRvIII (deletion of Exons 2-7), was detected in the mediastinal lymph nodes that likely contributed to erolotinib resistance in the patient.

BA/F3 cells transfected with ZMIZ1-ABL1 fusion were able to proliferate in the absence of IL3 by multiple orders of magnitude over 8 days, while cells transduced with empty vector failed to proliferate.

An 11 year old female (46,XX) had B-ALL. The patient received a 4-drug induction and end induction day 29 MRD was 5.4%. LDA card was used to analyze the patient and the leukemia was determined to be Ph-like. RT-PCR showed ZMIZ1-ABL1 fusion. Dasatinib was added to chemotherapy during consolidation due to the poor prior response to therapy. After 3 weeks of dasatinib MRD was 0.88%. At 6 months after initial diagnosis, the patient continued to receive chemotherapy and dasatinib. The study also reports three other patients with ZMIZ1-ABL1 who were not given dasatinib, and who were younger in age with lower white blood cell count.

IL3 indépendant Ba/F3 cells transduced with ZMIZ1-ABL1 driver fusion were treated with dasatinib. ZMIZ1-ABL1 cells had IC50 of 1-2 nM, whereas cells transduced with the driver PAX5-JAK2 were not responsive. The authors also report the cells were responsive to imatinib with IC50 135 to 900 nM.

The phase III ALTA-1L open-label randomized trial examined 275 NSCLC patients given brigatinib (137 patients) vs crizotinib (138 patients). Patients were ALK fusion positive by an FDA-approved diagnostic test and had not previously received ALK inhibitors. Brigatinib showed superior PFS compared to crizotinib (HR 0.49 [95% CI, 0.35 to 0.68]; log-rank P < .0001; median, 24.0 v 11.0 months). Initial results from this trial were previously reported in 2018 (PMID: 30280657).

9 patients with ALK-positive inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour (IMT) enrolled in the PROFILE 1013 (NCT01121588) phase 1b single-arm, open-label, multi-centre study received crizotinib. ORR was 67% for IMT (95% CI, 30–93), with 1 CR, 5 PRs, and 3 SDs. PFS at 2 years was 66.7% (95% CI, 28.2–87.8). Note that ALK positive included ALK mutations, but the mutation vs. fusion status for the patients in the IMT group was not specified.

Describes a meta-analysis of three separate phase I or II trials: ALKA-372-001, STARTRK-1, and STARTRK-2. All of these evaluate entrectinib in ROS-1 fusion-positive NSCLC (locally advanced or metastatic, no previous ROS1 tyrosine kinase inhibitors). 41/53 patients had objective response (77%; 95% CI 64—88). Median duration of response was 24·6 months (95% CI 11·4–34·8) with median follow-up of 15·5 months (IQR 13·4–20·2). Fusions included: CD74-ROS1 (21), SLC34A2-ROS1 (7), SDC4-ROS1 (6), EZR-ROS1 (5), TPM3-ROS1 (2), and unknown partner because results were only from FISH (12).

Describes a meta-analysis of three separate phase I or II trials: ALKA-372-001, STARTRK-1, and STARTRK-2. All of these evaluate entrectinib in NTRK fusion-positive solid tumours. 31/54 had objective response (57%; 95% CI 43·2–70·8), including 4 CR and 27 PR. 9 had SD. Response by NTRK gene type: 13/22 NTRK1 fusions [59%; 95% CI 36·4–79·3], 18/31 NTRK3 fusions [58%; 39·1–75·5], and 0/1 NTRK2 fusion. Most frequent tumour types were sarcoma, NSCLC, salivary, breast, thyroid, colorectal. Most common fusions were ETV6-NTRK3 (25), TPM3-NTRK1 (4) and TPR-NTRK1 (4).

A set of 117 BRCA1 missense variants in the essential BRCT domain of BRCA1 that have been identified in individuals with a family history of breast or ovarian cancer were assessed for functional and structural defects. A proteolysis assay was used to assess protein folding stability, a phosphopeptide pull-down assay to assess the ability of each of the variants to specifically interact with a known functional target, and a transcriptional assay to assess the ability of each variant to act as a transcriptional activation domain in human cells. BRCA1 S1841N showed severe folding defect in the proteolysis assay, compromised binding activity and specificity in the pull-down assay, and compromised activation ability in the transcriptional assay. This variant was classified by the authors as having a strong functional effect.

Combined meta-analysis of Study 10 (NCT01482715, phase I/II) and ARIEL2 (NCT01891344, phase II), both multi-centre, open-label, single-arm trials evaluating rucaparib in ovarian cancer with BRCA1 or BRCA2 deleterious germline or somatic mutations. Mutation status was determined by local testing or by central Foundation Medicine sequencing. Of 106 patients, OR was 53.8% (95% CI, 43.8-63.5); 8.5% and 45.3% of patients achieved complete and partial responses, respectively. Median duration of response was 9.2 months (95% CI, 6.6-11.6). Response rates by gene/mutation: BRCA1/2 germline (n=88, OR 53.4); BRCA1/2 somatic (n=18, OR 55.6); BRCA1 (n=67, OR 53.7); BRCA2 (n=39, OR 53.8).

Seminal paper presenting the original analysis of the TCGA Glioblastoma dataset, of over 500 glioblastoma genomes. EFGR::SEPT14 fusion was found in 6 cases by WGS and confirmed by RNASeq. The fusion is associated with EGFR amplification, indicating a complex rearrangement involving 7p11 locus.

The study utilises a targeted gene fusion RNASeq panel to screen 356 diffuse gliomas for fusion events. Of these, 155 cases were IDH-wildtype glioblastomas, of which 2 harboured an EGFR::SEPT14 fusion. One of these cases also harboured a concurrent EGFRvIII (exon 2-7 deletion), whilst the other harboured an EGFR exon 5-6 deletion. A relationship between EGFR fusions overall (including EGFR fusions with fusion partners other than SEPT14) and prognosis was not found.

The study presents a new fusion detection algorithm, CICERO ("CICERO Is Clipping Extended for RNA Optimization"). The authors compare their pipeline to gene fusions reported by TCGA network, using the TCGA Glioblastoma dataset, comprised of 167 adult GBM samples. The authors identify the EGFR::SEPT14 fusion, also identified by TCGA network, in addition to other novel EGFR fusions in other GBM samples.

evidence_statement: RNASeq data from 161 primary GBM samples and 24 glioma spheroids were analysed for gene fusion events. EGFR::SEPT14 was found to be the most common fusion event, after the well-documented FGFR3::TACC3, occurring in nine of 185 samples. Accompanying EGFR amplification was found in all nine cases, with EGFR vIII found in seven of nine cases harbouring EGFR::SEPT14 fusion. With regards to gene expression subtype of GBM, eight of nine cases with EGFR::SEPT14 clustered into the classical / mesenchymal subtypes. On lentiviral transduction of glioma spheroids, glioma cells expressing EGFR::SEPT14 were found to maintain growth and self-renewal, proliferate at a higher rate and have increased migratory capacity, as compared to EGFR wildtype cells. Similar findings were made in those cells alternatively expressing EGFR vIII.

The primary aim of the study was the characterisation of fusion events in 185 GBM samples. As part of this study, a GBM xenograft with EGFR::SEPT14 fusion, derived from a heavily pre-treated patient, demonstrated that both erlotinib and lapatinib delayed tumor growth, with lapatinib displaying stronger anti-tumour effects. A patient derived GBM xenograft without EGFR::SEPT14 fusion showed no response when treated with either EGFR TKI.

The authors examined data from the database of Origimed (a precision medicine platform based in China) and identified EGFR fusions in 1.1% of Chinese patients with lung adenocarcinoma (11/989). Of these 11 cases, one harboured the EGFR::ZNF713 fusion event. Further functional analysis or correlation with clinicopathologic parameters were not detailed.

In this open-label phase II study, 20 patients with systemic mastocytosis (SM) were recruited between 2003 and 2005. Seven of 20 patients were KIT D816V mutation-negative. Among these, one patient with KIT D816V-negative and FIP1L1-PDGFRA-negative SM-HES achieved a complete response with resolution of signs and symptoms, normalization of bone marrow and blood abnormalities, and normalization of tryptase levels. The patient remained in complete remission after more than 44 months. Four additional KIT D816V-negative patients reported symptomatic improvement without achieving a complete response. Two of 13 KIT D816V-positive patients also reported symptomatic improvement. These data support imatinib use in selected patients with KIT D816V-negative systemic mastocytosis.
An EGFR::YAP1 fusion was reported in a patient with non-small cell lung cancer. The breakpoint in EGFR is given as exon 26. Breakpoint in YAP1 is not specified.

In this open-label phase II study, 20 patients with systemic mastocytosis (SM) were enrolled between 2003 and 2005 and treated with imatinib mesylate. Thirteen of the 20 patients were positive for the KIT D816V mutation. Among these patients, no objective clinical responses were observed. Two patients with the KIT D816V mutation reported symptomatic improvement, including improvement in fatigue in one patient and diarrhea in another; however, no measurable changes in bone marrow mast cell involvement or consistent reductions in serum tryptase levels were documented in this subgroup. Overall, only one patient in the study achieved a complete response, and this patient was negative for the KIT D816V mutation. The remaining patients, including those with KIT D816V mutation, showed no significant clinical benefit from imatinib therapy.

evidence_statement: In this preclinical study, two subclones of human mast cell leukemia line were used to investigate cellular response to KIT inhibitor STI571. HMC1.1 cell line expressing only the KIT V560G mutation and HMC1.2, expressing both V560G mutation and D816V mutations were used. STI571 inhibited the phosphorylation of wild-type KIT induced by its natural ligand and inhibited phosphorylation of KIT caused by the V560G alone. In contrast, the inhibitor failed to inhibit phosphorylation of KIT containing the cell line with D816V mutation. Moreover, apoptosis was only observed in HMC1.1 cell line. Interestingly, two variants found rarely in systemic mastocytosis (D816F/D816Y) resulted in high spontaneous phosphorylation of KIT that was later inhibited when treated with STI571. These observations support D816V is resistance to KIT inhibitors but response of other KIT mutations (or wildtype status) in systemic mastocystosis. This further highlights the need to identify KIT status in patients for accurate therapy selection.

evidence_statement: In this phase IV clinical trial, ten patients with systemic mastocystosis (SM) were recruited to test efficacy and safety of imatinib. Nine patients fulfilled criteria for well-differentiated SM (WDSM), as three were diagnosed with mast cell (MC) leukemia, three with indolent SM and three with cutaneous mastocytosis. The 10th patient had SM associated with a clonal haematological non-MC disease. All patients lacked the KIT D816V mutation (or any other mutation in the 17th exon). Germline K509I mutation in exon 9 was detected in the 3 patients (two sisters and their father). Objective responses were obtained in 5/10 patients including; one patient who had a partial response and four patients had complete response (among which were the family members with the mutation in exon 9, follow-up for 72 months after therapy initiation). These results highlights the importance of KIT mutational status in selecting SM patients for treatment with imatinib.

In this case report, a 56 y/o female patient with normal karyotyping and no KIT mutation was diagnosed with systemic mastocytosis associated with MDS/MPN . Treatment with imatinib was initiated at a dose of 400 mg/daily. Significant improvements in symptoms, bone marrow and hematological parameters were recorded after three months. This case adds up to the reports of successful imatinib treatment in MS patients lacking the KIT D816V mutation.

In a retrospective analysis of 20 patients with renal medullary carcinoma, all patients had loss of SMARCB1 staining by IHC. FISH revealed 11 (55%) had a SMARCB1 translocation with loss of the second allele, 6 (30%) had biallelic SMARCB1 loss, and 3 (15%) did not have structural or copy number alteration detected. Of these 3, one had a somatic SMARCB1 mutation (H68Qfs*).

Of 10 tumors analyzed by FISH, SMARCB1 gene translocations with concurrent loss of heterozygosity were detected in 8 and biallelic SMARCB1 loss was detected in 2. Of 6 patients analyzed by NGS, none had SMARCB1 mutations.

All 7 of 7 poorly differentiated chordomas exhibited loss of SMARCB1 expression while SMARCB1 expression was retained in 14 conventional chordomas. Copy number profiling revealed loss of chromosome 22q including the SMARCB1 locus as the only recurrent alteration in 7 of 7 poorly differentiated chordomas. FISH or MLPA was used to confirm heterozygous or homozygous deletions of SMARCB1 in 6 of 7 cases. No SMARCB1 point mutations were identified. This supports loss of SMARCB1 as a diagnostic marker of poorly differentiated chordoma.

All chordomas including 14 conventional chordomas and 7 poorly differentiated chordomas exhibited nuclear expression of brachyury (TBXT) by IHC whereas only 2 of 30 atypical teratoid/rhabdoid tumors were positive for TBXT. This supports TBXT expression as a diagnostic marker aiding in the diagnosis of chordoma.

evidence_statement: In a pediatric phase 2 trial of the MEK inhibitor selumetinib (NCT01362803), partial responses were seen in 70% (35 of 50) children with neurofibromatosis type 1 and symptomatic inoperable plexiform neurofibromas. 28 of these children had durable responses lasting greater than 1 year. Clinically meaningful improvements were seen regarding interference of pain in daily functioning, overall health-related quality of life, as well as in functional outcomes of strength and range of motion. Age range of children in this study was 3.5 to 17.4 years old. This study led to FDA approval of selumetinib for pediatric patients with NF1.

evidence_statement: 325 ATRTs underwent methylation profiling, revealing three methylation distinct clusters - ATRT-TYR, ATRT-SHH and ATRT-MYC. In the ATRT-TYR subgroup, the characteristic pattern of SMARCB1 loss was of biallelic inactivation of SMARCB1, via whole or partial loss of chromosome 22, accompanied by an inactivating mutation in the other allele. In the ATRT-SHH subgroup, compound heterozygous point mutations were more common as opposed to hetero- or homozygous deletions involving SMARCB1. In the ATRT-MYC subgroup, loss of SMARB1 inactivation occurred by homozygous broad deletions of involving SMARCB1 (42/74 cases).

In the dose expansion of phase I pediatric trial (NCT02601937) of the EZH2 inhibitor tazemetostat, 2 of 6 patients with SMARCB1-deficient poorly differentiated chordoma had a partial response and 1 of 6 had stable disease, as reported at the ASCO 2022 Annual Meeting.

In the dose expansion of phase I pediatric trial (NCT02601937) of the EZH2 inhibitor tazemetostat, the overall response in 21 patients with SMARCB1-deficient atypical teratoid rhabdoid tumors (ATRT) was 24%, with 1 complete response, 4 partial responses, and 2 stable diseases (ASCO 2022 Annual Meeting).
