In a phase 3 trial (ASCEND-4, NCT01828099), a comparison of the selective ALK inhibitor ceritinib (750 mg daily) to chemotherapy (cisplatin or carboplatin plus pemetrexed) in 376 untreated ALK-fusion positive, non-squamous NSCLC patients demonstrated superiority of ceritinib as a first line treatment. The overall response rate was 73% with ceritinib treatment with 1% CR and 72% PR compared to an ORR of 27% with chemotherapy (all PR). Median progression-free survival was 16.6 months (95% CI 12.6-27.2) in the ceritinib group and 8.1 months (5.8-11.1) in the chemotherapy group. In patients with brain metastasis, the overall intracranial response rate was 57% compared with 22% in the chemotherapy group. This study demonstrated that first-line ceritinib had a statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvement in progression-free survival versus chemotherapy in patients with advanced ALK-rearranged NSCLC and superior activity in brain metastases.

In a phase 3 trial (CROWN, NCT03052608), a comparison of the selective third generation ALK inhibitor lorlatinib to the first generation ALK inhibitor crizotinib in 296 untreated ALK-fusion positive NSCLC patients demonstrated superiority of lorlatinib as a first line treatment. In the interim analysis, progression free survival at 12 months was 78% (95% CI, 70 to 84) in the lorlatinib-treated patients compared with 39% (95% CI, 30 to 48) in the crizotinib group. An objective response occurred in 76% (113 of 149 patients) of the lorlatinib group versus 58% (85 of 147 patients) in the crizotinib group. Of those with measurable brain metastases, 82% (14 of 17) of those on lorlatinib responded, with 71% of these being an intracranial complete response. Only 23% (3 of 13) of crizotinib-treated patient with brain metastases responded. This study supports use of lorlatinib in ALK-fusion positive NSCLC and in patients with brain metastasis.

In a post hoc analysis of the phase 3 trial (CROWN, NCT03052608) comparing the selective third generation ALK inhibitor lorlatinib to the first generation ALK inhibitor crizotinib in ALK-fusion positive NSCLC patients, lorlatinib was demonstrated superior for intracranial efficacy. In patients with brain metastases at baseline, the 12-month PFS was 78% with loratinib treatment versus 22% with crizotinib. Lorlatinib was associated with lower 12-month cumulative incidence of CNS progression versus crizotinib in patients with (7% v 72%) and without (1% v 18%) brain metastases at baseline.

Analysis of somatic copy number alterations (SCNAs) in 1087 medulloblastoma tumours identified a recurrent tandem duplication of SNCAIP that was restricted to Group 4 medulloblastoma. SNCAIP duplications were found to be mutually exclusive of other potential driver SCNAs, including amplification of MYCN and CDK6.

In a phase 1 study (NCT02073994), 21 patients with advanced IDH-mutant chondrosarcoma received the IDH1-mutant specific inhibitor ivosidenib. Plasma levels of the 2-HG oncometabolite decreased to normal levels in all patients indicating target inhibition. Median progression free survival was 5.6 months (95% CI, 1.9 to 7.4 months). Eleven (52%) of 21 patients experienced stable disease. 4 patients had a durable disease control for > 2.5 years. PFS rates were higher in patients without dedifferentiated histology suggesting that ivosidenib is more effective in conventional chondrosarcoma. Given that the drug had minimal toxicity, significant target inhibition, and durable disease control in a disease with no known effective systemic therapy, the authors recommend further evaluation of ivosidenib as a monotherapy or in rational combinations.

Conditional knock-in of IDH1 R132Q in chondrocytes of weaned mice resulted in the development of multiple enchondroma-like lesions. Enchondromas are benign cartilage tumors and precursors to malignant chondrosarcomas. This supports IDH1 mutations as an initiator in the development of chondrosarcomas.

Approximately 1200 mesechymal tumors were screened for IDH1 R132 mutations by Sequenom mass spectrometry, including 220 cartilaginous tumors, 222 osteosarcomas and another 750 bone and soft tissue tumors. Cartilaginous tumors and chondroblastic osteosarcomas lacking IDH1 R132 mutations were analysed for IDH2 R172 and IDH2 R140 mutations. Heterozygous somatic IDH1/IDH2 mutations were only identified in central and periosteal cartilaginous tumors and found in at least 56% of these. 40% of the mutations were R132C and the ratio of IDH1:IDH2 mutation was 10.6:1. Mutations were detected in enchondromas through to conventional central and dedifferentiated chondrosarcomas but none were found in peripheral chondrosarcomas and osteochondromas.

A patient with Clear cell renal cell carcinoma previously treated with sorafenib, axitinib, and everolimus was found to harbor a BAP1 frameshift mutation described as c.799_800del (p.Q267fs). Based on this observation the patient was given the PARP inhibitor Niraparib (nilapanib) in followed by CyberKnife radiosurgery to treat a brain metastasis. A partial response was reported based on imaging of the renal tumor. LDH and CEA markers also appeared to reduce on Niraparib treatment though the authors acknowledge that these are not specific markers for ccRCC.

The PALOMA-3 trial compared palbociclib plus fulvestrant vs placebo plus fulvestrant and evaluated molecular correlates of response in 302 patients with metastatic breast cancer. mRNA expression levels of CDK6, as measured by targeted capture and sequencing, were not predictive of response to palbociclib in Cox PH models based on splitting high and low expressors at the median (p=0.515, n=302).

Report of OlympiA (NCT02032823), a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of 1836 patients with HER2-negative breast cancer with germline pathogenic or likely pathogenic mutations in BRCA1 or BRCA2. Patients were early stage but had completed chemotherapy; ER/PR+ patients could also have concurrent hormone therapy. 82% of patients were triple negative. 72% of patients had BRCA1 germline mutations, 27% had BRCA2, and 0.4% both. 921 patients received olaparib and 915 placebo. Invasive disease-free survival (IDFS) showed improvement with olaparib treatment (86% vs 77%, HR 0.58 [0.41 to 0.82], P<0.001). For overall survival, deaths in the olaparib arm were lower (59 vs 86, HR 0.68 [0.44 to 1.05], P=0.02). The IDFS benefit was independent of whether mutation was in BRCA1 (HR=0.52, 0.39-0.70) or BRCA2 (HR 0.52, 0.30-0.86).

This randomized, open-label, phase 3 trial evaluated the PARP inhibitor olaparib in 387 men with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) who had disease progression while receiving a new hormonal agent (e.g., enzalutamide or abiraterone). The study found that in men with mCRPC who had somatic or germline deleterious alterations (irrespective of zygosity) in any of the following HRR genes (BRCA1, BRCA2, ATM, BRIP1, BARD1, CDK12, CHEK1, CHEK2, FANCL, PALB2, PPP2R2A, RAD51B, RAD51C, RAD51D, and RAD54L), olaparib was associated with longer progression-free survival and better measures of response and patient-reported end points than either enzalutamide or abiraterone (PFS HR 0.49 [0.38, 0.63]). For 15 patients with BRCA1 mutations specifically, PFS HR 0.41 [0.13-1.39]. . Based on the results of this study, on May 19, 2020, the Food and Drug Administration approved olaparib (LYNPARZA) for adult patients with deleterious or suspected deleterious germline or somatic HRR gene-mutated mCRPC, who have progressed following prior treatment with enzalutamide or abiraterone.

Case report describing a 34-year-old female patient without a family history of breast cancer. After a radical mastectomy, histopathology revealed an invasive ductal carcinoma HER2 positive (FISH). She started treatment with six cycles of adjuvant chemotherapy and trastuzumab therapy for one year. After a year, she was diagnosed with metastatic breast cancer (multiple metastases in the lung and sternum), positive for HER2. Lapatinib was used and combined with chemotherapy. After six cycles, a CT scan showed metastases in the lumbar spine and right lobe of the liver. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed multiple metastases in the brain (RECIST: progressing disease). Circulating tumor DNA assays showed a novel EGFR::ZNF880 fusion and EGFR E114K mutations. They changed the treatment to pyrotinib with chemotherapy. Two months later, the metastases of the lung, sternum, lumbar spine and right lobe of the liver disappeared, the size of the brain metastases reduced and bone metastases were relieved (RECIST: partial response). Following the results of circulating tumor DNA assays, HER2 amplification, EGFR::ZNF880 fusion, and EGFR E114K mutations disappeared. A small lesion was present in the brain so the patient was subjected to radiotherapy. After nine months of treatment with pyrotinib, enhanced CT indicated that tumors in the breast, liver, lungs, brain, and bone were under control. The author suggests, based on this case study alone, that when lapatinib fails, pyrotinib therapy could be considered. The patient continually received oral pyrotinib, however, a new brain lesion appeared six months later.

Report of OlympiA (NCT02032823), a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of 1836 patients with HER2-negative breast cancer with germline pathogenic or likely pathogenic mutations in BRCA1 or BRCA2. Patients were early stage but had completed chemotherapy; ER/PR+ patients could also have concurrent hormone therapy. 82% of patients were triple negative. 72% of patients had BRCA1 germline mutations, 27% had BRCA2, and 0.4% both. 921 patients received olaparib and 915 placebo. Invasive disease-free survival (IDFS) showed improvement with olaparib treatment (86% vs 77%, HR 0.58 [0.41 to 0.82], P<0.001). For overall survival, deaths in the olaparib arm were lower (59 vs 86, HR 0.68 [0.44 to 1.05], P=0.02). The IDFS benefit was independent of whether mutation was in BRCA1 (HR=0.52, 0.39-0.70) or BRCA2 (HR 0.52, 0.30-0.86).

This trial enrolled 26 patients with anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALCL). The groups received twice daily crizotinib at doses of either 165 or 280 mg/m2. 83% of the 165 mg/m2 ALCL patients had a complete response with a median treatment time of 2.79 years versus 80% of the 280 mg/m2 group with a median treatment time of 0.4 years. The most common drug-related adverse event was a decrease in neutrophil count in 33% of the patients dosed at 165 mg/m2 and 70% of the patients dosed at 290 mg/m2.

molecular_profile: EGFR L858R OR EGFR Exon 19 Deletion
evidence_statement: In this phase 3, double-blind trial, 682 patients were randomly assigned 1:1 to either osimertinib (80 mg once daily) or placebo for 3 years following complete resection of EGFR mutation positive (exon 19 deletion or L858R) non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). At two years, 90% of the patients with stage II to IIIA disease in the osimertinib group (95% CI, 84 to 93) and 44% of those in the placebo group (95% CI, 37 to 51) were alive and disease-free (HR for disease recurrence or death, 0.17; 99.06% CI, 0.11 to 0.26; P < 0.001). Including all patients, 89% in the osimertinib group (95% CI, 85 to 92) and 52% of those in the placebo group (95% CI, 46 to 58) were alive and disease-free at two years (HR for disease recurrence or death, 0.20; 99.12% CI, 0.14 to 0.30; P < 0.001). In total, 29 patients died (9 in the osimertinib group and 20 in the placebo group), and grade 3 adverse events occurred in 20% of the osimertinib group versus 13% of the placebo group while 16% of the osimertinib group experienced serious adverse events versus 12% in the placebo group.

molecular_profile: EZH2 Y646S OR EZH2 Y646F OR EZH2 Y646H OR EZH2 Y646C OR EZH2 Y646N OR EZH2 A692V OR EZH2 A682G
evidence_statement: In a multicentre, open-label, phase 1 trial, tazemetostat was evaluated in 64 adult patients (≥18 years) with relapsed or refractory B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma (n=21) or advanced solid tumours (n=43). Patients received oral tazemetostat in continuous 28-day cycles, with doses ranging from 100 mg to 1600 mg twice daily. The primary objective was to determine the maximum tolerated dose and recommended phase 2 dose, which was established as 800 mg twice daily. Among patients with B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma, 8 of 21 (38%; 95% CI: 18.1–61.6) achieved an objective response, with a median time to first response of 3.5 months (IQR: 2.6–6.5). The median duration of response—defined as time until disease progression or death from any cause—was 12.4 months (IQR: 3.5 to >18.3). Tazemetostat was generally well tolerated, with most adverse events being grade 1–2, and dose-limiting toxicities were observed at the highest doses. These results support the clinical activity of tazemetostat in genetically defined populations, including patients with EZH2-activating mutations in B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma and SWI/SNF-deficient advanced solid tumours, providing a foundation for further clinical evaluation in phase 2 studies.

A homozygous splice site point mutation at the donor site of Met Exon 14 (G>T at +1 position; Figure 1A, and Figure S1a) was identified in the H596 lung cancer cell line. RT-PCR of RNA demonstrated skipping of exon 14 in the presence of this variant (Figure 1B). Compared to MET wild type cells, H596 cells showed increased and sustained phospho-Met and phospho-MAPK levels (Figure 3A). H596 cells exhibited the highest proliferative potential following stimulation by the MET ligand HGF (compared to a panel of 27 lung cancer cell lines; Figure 4a). When HGF stimulated H596 cells were treated with the HGF-competitive anti-Met OA-5D5 antibody, dose dependent reduction in Met, MAPK, and Akt phosphorylation and proliferation were observed (Figure 6).

54 patients aged 18 or older with metastatic or locally advanced NTRK-fusion positive solid tumours (including ten tumour types and 19 unique histologies) were enrolled in one of three phase 1 or 2 trials (ALKA-372–001, STARTRK-1, and STARTRK-2). The patients were administered a 600 mg dose of entrectinib orally daily, with the primary endpoints being the proportion of patient with an objective response and the median duration of response. 31 of the 54 patients had an objective response (95% CI: 43.2–70.8), four of which were complete responses. The median duration of the response was 10 months (95% CI: 7.1 to not estimable). The most common fusions were ETV6-NTRK3 (n = 25), TPM3-NTRK1 (n = 4) and TPR-NTRK1 (n = 4), and only one patient had an NRTK2 fusion (SQSTM1-NTRK2)

233 patients aged 18 or older who had Ph+ CML and were previously treated with two or more tyrosine kinase inhibitors were recruited to an open-label, multicentre phase 3 trial. The patients were randomized 2:1 to receive either 40 mg twice daily or bosutinib 500 mg once daily. At 24 weeks, the major molecular response rate was 25% (95% CI: 19 - 33) in patients treated with asciminib compared to 13% (95% CI: 6.5 - 23; p = 0.029) in those receiving bosutinib. 89.7% of patients receiving asciminib experienced an adverse effect, with 50.6% experiencing a grade 3 or higher adverse event compared to 99.1% and 60.5% respectively for bosutinib.

536 patients with CML, 487 of which were Philadelphia chromosome-positive were enlisted to a multicentre, open-label phase 3 trial assessing the efficacy and safety of bosutinib. The patients were randomized 1:1 to receive (starting dose) bosutinib or imatinib 400 mg once daily. The primary endpoint was the major molecular response (MMR) of a BCR::ABL1 ≤ 0.1% on the international scale at 12 months. The median duration of treatment was 55 months for both groups. MMR rate by 5 years was greater with bosutinib (73.9%) versus imatinib (64.6%; OR, 1.57 [95% CI: 1.08 – 2.28]). Any grade treatment-emergent adverse effects occurred in 98.9% (grade 3/4: 73.5%) of bosutinib-treated patients versus 98.9% (grade 3/4: 57.0%) of imatinib-treated patients.

In phase 1, dose-escalation trial 141 patients with chronic-phase chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) and 9 patients with accelerated-phase CML who had previously taken at least two ATP-competitive tyrosine kinase inhibitors with unacceptable side effects or resistance to treatment. The goal of the trial was to determine the maximum tolerated dose and/or the recommended dose of asciminib. Dosing was done once to twice daily at doses of 10-200 mg. 45 patients in the trial had Philadelphia chromosome-positive CML with the T315I mutation. The efficacy of 200 mg twice daily asciminib in the 45 patients was measured by the major molecular response (MMR) at 24 weeks. MMR was achieved by 24 weeks in 42% (95% CI: 28% - 58%) of the patients. MMR was achieved by 96 weeks in 49% (95% CI: 34% - 64%) of the patients. The median duration of treatment was 108 weeks with a range of 2 to 215 weeks).

In a phase 2, dose-reduction trial, 282 patients were enrolled who had previously been treated with at least 2 prior TKIs or had a T315I mutation. Efficacy was assessed on an interim analysis based on the rate of the molecular response of ≤1% BCR-ABL1IS (MR2) at 12 months in the modified intent-to-treat population of 261 patients, with 88, 86, and 87 patients in the 45, 30, and 15 mg groups, respectively. The rate of ≤1% BCR-ABL1IS (98.3% CI) at 12 months was 44.1% (31.7 - 57.0) in the 45-mg group, 29.0% (18.4 - 41.6) in the 30-mg group, and 23.1% (13.4 - 35.3) in the 15-mg group. The median time to response was 6.0 (2.9 - 18.0), 3.0 (2.9 - 15.3), and 6.0 (2.9 - 31.9) months in the 45, 30, and 15-mg groups, respectively. Cumulative responses increased over time in all groups with the 45 mg group showing the largest increase. The estimated probability of 24-month progress-free survival was 80%, 76%, and 78% in the 45, 30, and 15-mg groups, respectively.

In this phase 1, open-label, dose-escalation trial, 81 patients with NSCLC involving an EGFR exon 20 insertion in phase 2 of the study were administered 1,050 mg amivantamab (1,400 mg if > 80 kg) given once weekly for the first month and then once every two weeks starting at week five based of phase 1 of the trial determining the recommended dose. The overall response rate was 40% (95% CI: 29 - 51), including three complete responses. The median duration of response of 11.1 months (95% CI: 6.9 - not reached) and the median progression-free survival was 8.3 months (95% CI: 6.5 - 10.9).

In this open-label phase1/2 trial, 114 patients with EGFR exon 20 insertion NSCLC who were previously treated with platinum received 160 mg mobocertinib once daily. The primary endpoint was confirmed objective response rate (ORR). The median follow-up period was 14.2 months, with a confirmed ORR of 28% (95% CI: 20% - 37%) by independent review committee (IRC) assessment and 35% (95% CI: 26% - 45%) by investigator assessment. The median duration of response was 17.5 months (95% CI: 7.4 - 20.3) by IRC assessment. Further, the median progression-free survival was 7.3 months (95% CI: 5.5 - 9.2) by IRC assessment. Lastly, the median overall survival was 24.0 months (95% CI: 14.6 - 28.8). 19 of 114 patients discontinued treatment because of adverse effects, dose reductions due to an adverse effect occurred in 29 of 114 patients, and response rates were greater in the 85 patients without dose reduction.

molecular_profile: EGFR S768I OR EGFR G719A OR EGFR L861Q
evidence_statement: In a phase 2 trial, 129 patients with lung adenocarcinoma with EGFR mutations including mutations other than exon 19 deletions or exon 21 L858R substitutions who had no more than one previous chemotherapy regimen for advanced disease or an EGFR tyrosine-kinase inhibitor. 99 patients started with a dose of 50 mg and the other 30 patients with a starting dose of 40 mg. 79 of 129 patients had an objective response (two complete responses, 77 partial responses). 70 of the 106 patients with exon 19 deletion or exon 21 L858R EGFR mutations had an objective response, as did nine of 23 patients with the less common mutations. Median progression-free survival was 10.1 months (95% CI: 8.12 – 13.80, however, median progression-free survival was shorter for patients with the uncommon mutations. The median overall survival was 24.8 months (95% CI: 21.98 – 38.74), and the median overall survival for patients with the less common mutations was again shorter. Grade 3 adverse events were more common in patients receiving the higher 50 mg starting dose, and there was one possible drug-related death secondary to interstitial lung disease.

This open-label phase 2 trial included 122 patients with histologically or cytologically confirmed, locally advanced or metastatic cholangiocarcinoma, 108 of whom had an FGFR2 fusion or rearrangement. Each patient received 125 mg of oral infigratinib once daily for 21 days of 28-day cycles and this was continued until there was disease progression, intolerance, withdrawal of consent, or death. Median follow-up of 10.6 months (IQR: 6.2 – 15.6) and the objective response rate was 23.1% (95% CI: 15.6 – 32.2), with one confirmed complete response and 24 partial responses. The median progression-free survival was 7.3 months (95% CI: 5.6 – 7.6) and the median overall survival was 12.2 months (95% CI: 10.7 – 14.9). There were 61 grade 3 adverse events, and 9 grade 4 adverse events, however, there were no treatment-related deaths.

Variant found by RNA screening analysis in a UBC (urothelial bladder cancer) cell line (VM-CUBIII). The variant is located in the signal domain. In regards to the response to lapatinib, after three days of treatment in RT112 cell lines, L15F did not show significant sensitivity to lapatinib according to the IC50 in comparison with other variants tested (Figure 5). The variant was in de I (resistant) Cluster according to Figure 5 C. There were no conclusions by the author for this variant.

Variant found by RNA screening analysis in a UBC (urothelial bladder cancer) cell line (VM-CUBIII). The variant is located in the signal domain. RT112 cells infected with lentiviral vectors containing the variant did not show significant phosphorylation and downstream target effects compared to WT and no evidence of “mini-foci” formation (Figure 2; A-B). There were no conclusions by the author for this variant.

In an open-label, phase 1/2 trial on 87 patients with NSCLC including RET-fusion were given 400 mg once-daily oral pralsetinib, with the outcome measured as overall response rate. Overall responses were seen in 53 patients (95% CI: 50 – 71),nicluding five patients with a complete response. Further, 80% of the patients had responses lasting at least 6 months. Lastly, the median progression-free survival was 17.1 months (95% CI: 8.3 – 22.1).

In a phase 1/2, open-label trial, 122 patients with RET-mutant medullary cancer and 20 with RET-fusion positive thyroid cancer were administered 400 mg daily oral pralsetinib. The overall response rates (ORR) were 15/21 in patients with treatment-naive RET-mutant medullary thyroid cancer (95% CI: 48 - 89) and 33 of 55 who had previously received cabozantinib or vandetanib, or both (95% CI: 46 - 73), and 8/9 in patients with RET fusion-positive thyroid cancer (95% CI: 52 - 100). For the 8/9 patients with RET fusion-positive thyroid cancer, all had responses lasting 6 months or longer.

In a phase 2, open-label trial, a cohort of 78 patients with BCR-ABL positive ALL received 60 mg/m2 of dasatinib daily for up to 24 months in combination with chemotherapy (AIEOP-BFM ALL 2000 multi-agent chemotherapy protocol). The efficacy was assessed on the 3-year event-free survival (EFS). The 3-year EFS rate in the cohort was 64.1% (95% CI: 52.4 - 74.7). At the end of the induction phase, 75 patients had bone marrow with < 5% lymphoblasts and 76 patients achieved bone marrow with < 5% lymphoblasts by the end of the consolidation phase.

In a phase 2, open-label trial, 449 patients with either CML or Philadelphia chromosome-positive ALL or has a BCR-ABL T315I mutation were enrolled and administered once daily 45 mg ponatinib. In the 32 patients with Philadelphia chromosome-positive ALL, 41% (95% CI: 24 - 59) had a major hematologic response, 47% had a major cytogenetic response, and 38% had a complete cytogenetic response. The median time to a major hematologic response in these patients was 2.9 weeks (1.6 – 24 weeks), the duration was 2 - 14 months or more (median of 3 months), and the estimated sustained response rate of at least 12 months was 8%.

In this histology-independent, phase 2, open-label study, 26 patients (22 with Erdheim-Chester disease (ECD) and 4 Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH)) were administered 960 mg, twice daily doses of vemufarfenib. The primary end point was confirmed objective response rate (ORR). The ORR was 61.5% (95% CI: 40.6% - 79.8%) in total and 54.5% (95% CI: 32.2% - 75.6%) in patients with ECD. The 2-year preogression free survival was 86% (95% CI: 72% - 100%), and 2-year overall survival was 96% (95% CI: 87% - 100%).

In this phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 514 patients with unresectable stage IIIc–IV, BRAFV600 mutation-positive melanoma were randomly assigned to either 28-day cycles of the atezolizumab, vemurafenib, and cobimetinib group or atezolizumab placebo, vemurafenib, and cobimetinib control group on a 1:1 basis. The trials primary outcome was progression-free survival. It was discovered at the median follow-up of 18.9 months (IQR: 10·4 – 23·8), that progression-free survival was significantly prolonged with atezolizumab versus control (15.1 vs 10.6 months; hazard ratio: 0.78; 95% CI: 0·63 – 0·97; p = 0·025). 13% of patients in the treatment cohort and 16% in the control cohort stopped all treatment due to adverse events.

molecular_profile: EGFR L858R OR EGFR Exon 19 Deletion
evidence_statement: In this phase 3, open-label, randomized trial, 452 patients with EGFR mutation-positive non-small cell lung cancer including exon 19 deletions and exon 21 L858R point mutations were randomized into cohorts receive either oral dacomitinib 45 mg/day or oral gefitinib 250 mg/day, both in 28-day cycles. The median duration for follow-up for progression-free survival was 22.1 months (95% CI: 20.3 – 23.9), and the median progression-free was 14.7 months (95% CI: 11.1 – 16.6) in the dacomitinib cohort versus 9.2 months (9.1 – 11.0) in the gefitinib group (hazard ratio: 0·59, 95% CI: 0·47 – 0·74; p < 0.0001). Treatment-related serious adverse events were observed in 21 patients given dacomitinib and in ten patients given gefitinib. Further, two treatment-related deaths occurred in the dacomitinib group and one in the gefitinib.

molecular_profile: EGFR L858R OR EGFR Exon 19 Deletion
evidence_statement: In this phase 3, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 449 patients stage IV NSCLC with EGFR exon 19 deletions or exon 21 (L858R) mutations. Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to receive oral erlotinib (150 mg/day) plus either intravenous ramucirumab (10 mg/kg) or matching placebo once every 2 weeks. The primary endpoint was investigator-assessed progression-free survival. The median duration of follow-up was 20.7 months (IQR: 15.8–27.2), and the progression-free survival was found to be significantly longer in the ramucirumab plus erlotinib group 19.4 months (95% CI: 15.4 – 21.6) than in the placebo plus erlotinib group at 12.4 months (11.0 – 13.5), with a hazard ratio of 0.59 (95% CI: 0.46 – 0·76; p < 0·0001). Lastly, grade 3/4 adverse events were reported in 159 of 221 patients in the ramucirumab plus erlotinib group versus 121 of 225 in the placebo plus erlotinib group, and one death was recorded in the ramucirumab plus erlotinib group.

molecular_profile: EGFR L858R OR EGFR Exon 19 Deletion
evidence_statement: In this phase-IV, open-label, single-arm study, 106 patients with NSCLC and EGFR mutations including exon 19 deletion and exon 21 L858R point mutations were administered 250 mg daily doses of gefitinib with the primary endpoint being objective response rate (ORR). The objective response rate was 69.8% (95% CI: 60.5 – 77.7), with a median progression-free survival of 9.7 months (95% CI: 8.5 – 11.0), and a median overall survival of 19.2 months (95% CI:17.0 – not calculable).

In this phase 2 study, 129 patients with NSCLC, including those with less common, non-resistant EGFR mutations such as S768I, L861Q, and/or G719X, were treated with afatinib in two cohorts: 99 with a starting dose of 50 mg and 30 with a starting dose of 40 mg. 79 of 129 patients had an objective response (two complete responses, 77 partial responses), and included in that is nine of the 23 patients harbouring the less common mutations. Similar proportions of patients had an objective response when the starting dose was accounted for (18/30 patients at 40 mg versus 61/99 patients at 50 mg). Both progression-free survival and overall survival was higher for the common mutation group versus the less common mutations.

In a randomized, double-blind, phase 3 trial, 553 patients with ovarian cancer, fallopian tube cancer, or primary peritoneal cancer with predominantly high-grade serous histologic features were enrolled. Of the 553 enrolled, 203 had germline BRCA1/2 mutations and 350 had non-germline BRCA1/2 mutations (including both somatic mutant and wildtype BRCA1/2); BRCA1/2 mutation status was determined via BRACAnalysis testing (Myriad Genetics). The patients were randomized in a 2:1 ratio to receive niraparib 300 mg or placebo once daily. Patients in the niraparib group had a significantly longer median duration of progression-free survival than the placebo group: 21.0 vs. 5.5 months in the gBRCA cohort (hazard ratio, 0.27; 95% CI: 0.17 - 0.41; p < 0.001) and 9.3 months vs. 3.9 months in the overall non-gBRCA cohort (hazard ratio, 0.45; 95% CI: 0.34 - 0.61; p < 0.001).

In an open-label, phase 3 randomized trial, 250 patients with either previously untreated, stage IV or unresectable stage III BRAF V600E mutation-positive melanoma were randomly assigned (3:1) to receive dabrafenib 150 mg twice daily, orally or dacarbazine 1000 mg/m(2) intravenously every 3 weeks. The median progression-free survival was 5.1 months for dabrafenib and 2.7 months for dacarbazine, with a hazard ratio of 0.30 (95% CI: 0.18 – 0.51; p < 0.0001). Treatment-related adverse events of grade 2 or greater occurred in 100/187 patients who received dabrafenib and in 26/59 patients who received dacarbazine.

disease: Fallopian Tube, Ovarian Cancer, And Peritoneal Serous Carcinoma
evidence_statement: In an integrated analysis of Study 10 (NCT01482715) and ARIEL2 (NCT01891344) trials, 106 patients with either germline or somatic BRCA1 or BRCA2 who received a starting dose of oral rucaparib 600mg twice daily were studied, with the primary endpoint being objective response rate (ORR), and secondary endpoints including duration of response (DOR) and progression-free survival (PFS). The ORR was 53.8% (95% CI: 43.8 - 63.5), with 8.5% and 45.3% of patients achieving complete and partial responses, respectively. The median DOR was 9.2 months (95% CI: 6.6 - 11.6). Lastly, PFS in the 10.0 months (range, 0.0–22.1 months; 95% CI: 7.3 – 12.5 months). 47.2% of patients had not progressed at the time of the visit cut-off, and the PFS rate at 6 and 12 months was 79.0% and 41.0% respectively.

In a phase III, randomized, open-label trial, 408 women with HER2-positive, locally advanced or metastatic breast cancer that, after treatment with regimens that included an anthracycline, a taxane, and trastuzumab, still had progression were randomly assigned to receive either combination therapy consisting of lapatinib dosed at 1250 mg per day continuously plus capecitabine dosed at 2000 mg per square meter of the body-surface area on days 1 through 14 of a 21-day cycle or monotherapy consisting of capecitabine dosed at 2500 mg per square meter on days 1 through 14 of a 21-day cycle. With the primary endpoint of time to progression, the study found that the hazard ratio for time to progression was 0.49 (95% CI: 0.34 - 0.71; p < 0.001), with 49 events in the combination-therapy group and 72 events in the monotherapy group. The median time to progression was 8.4 months in the combination group as compared with 4.4 months in the monotherapy group, without an increase in toxic effects or cardiac complications.

In a phase III, randomized, double-blind, controlled trial, 219 post-menopausal women with HER2-positive, histologically confirmed stage IIIB/IIIC or IV estrogen receptor-positive and/or progesterone receptor-positive metastatic breast cancer were randomly assigned to daily letrozole 2.5 mg orally plus lapatinib 1,500 mg orally or letrozole 2.5 mg orally and placebo. The study's primary endpoint was progression-free survival (PFS). The study found that the addition of lapatinib significantly reduced the risk of disease progression versus placebo (HR = 0.71; 95% CI: 0.53 - 0.96; p = .019). Further, the median PFS was 8.2 versus 3.0 months, respectively. The clinical benefit, defined as responsive or stable disease for 6 months or greater, was significantly higher for lapatinib versus placebo (48% versus 29%, respectively; OR = 0.4; 95% CI: 0.2 - 0.8; p = .003).

In this phase III, randomized, open-label trial, 536 patients with HER2-positive breast cancer who have received two or more prior anti-HER2 regimens, with at least one being for metastatic disease. The patients were randomized 1:1 to margetuximab 15 mg/kg or trastuzumab 6 mg/kg (loading dose of 8 mg/kg), each in 3-week cycles. The primary endpoints were progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS). The study found that margetuximab improved primary PFS over trastuzumab (HR, 0.76; 95% CI: 0.59 - 0.98; p = .03; median, 5.8 [95% CI: 5.5 - 7.0] months versus 4.9 [95% CI: 4.2 - 5.6] months). At the second interim analysis of 270 deaths, the median OS was 21.6 months for margetuximab versus 19.8 months with trastuzumab (HR, 0.89; 95% CI: 0.69 - 1.13; p = .33, and PFS showed relative risk reduction favouring margetuximab (HR, 0.71; 95% CI: 0.58 - 0.86; p < .001; median, 5.7 versus 4.4 months). Margetuximab improved ORR over trastuzumab at both times of analysis on October 10th, 2018, and September 10th, 2019: 22% vs 16% (p = .06;) and 25% vs 14% (p < .001) respectively.

In this phase II, randomized, double-blinded, controlled study, 612 patients with HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer previously treated with trastuzumab, pertuzumab, and trastuzumab emtansine. The primary endpoint was progression-free survival (PFS) in the first 480 patients who were randomized. Patients were randomly assigned in a 2:1 ratio to receive either 300 mg oral, twice daily tucatinib or oral, twice daily placebo, with both regimens in combination with 6 mg/kg of body weight, intravenous trastuzumab once every 21 days, with an initial loading dose of 8 mg/kg and 1000 mg per square meter of body-surface area, oral, twice daily capecitabine on days 1 to 14 of each 21-day cycle. The 1 year PFS was 33.1% in the tucatinib-combination group and 12.3% in the placebo-combination group (HR, 0.54; 95% CI: 0.42 - 0.71; p < 0.001), and the median duration of PFS was 7.8 months and 5.6 months, respectively. Overall survival at 2 years was 44.9% in the tucatinib-combination group and 26.6% in the placebo-combination group (HR, 0.66; 95% CI: 0.50 - 0.88; p = 0.005), and the median overall survival was 21.9 months and 17.4 months, respectively.

In this randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, Phase III trial, 264 patients were enrolled with histologically or cytologically confirmed diagnoses of previously untreated, locally advanced, unresectable or metastatic HER2-positive gastric or GEJ adenocarcinoma. The patients in the study were randomly assigned 1:1 to receive pembrolizumab 200 mg or placebo with trastuzumab (8 mg/kg loading dose; 6 mg/kg thereafter) by intravenous infusion every 3 weeks and investigator’s choice of chemotherapy regimen, either 5-fluorouracil dosed at 800 mg per m2 of body-surface area administered IV on days 1–5 of each 3-week cycle and cisplatin dosed at 80 mg per m2 administered IV once every 3 weeks or capecitabine dosed at 1,000 mg per m2 administered orally twice daily on days 1–14 of each 3-week cycle and oxaliplatin dosed at 130 mg per m2 administered intravenously once every 3 weeks. The overall response rate was 74% (95% CI: 66 - 82) in the pembrolizumab cohort and 52% (95% CI: 43 - 61) in the placebo cohort (one-sided p-value < 0.0001). The median duration of response was 10.6 months (range: 1.1 - 16.5) in the pembrolizumab cohort and 9.5 months (range 1.4 - 15.4) in the placebo cohort.

In this randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, Phase III trial, 264 patients were enrolled with histologically or cytologically confirmed diagnoses of previously untreated, locally advanced, unresectable or metastatic HER2-positive gastric or GEJ adenocarcinoma. The patients in the study were randomly assigned 1:1 to receive pembrolizumab 200 mg or placebo with trastuzumab (8 mg/kg loading dose; 6 mg/kg thereafter) by intravenous infusion every 3 weeks and investigator’s choice of chemotherapy regimen, either 5-fluorouracil dosed at 800 mg per m2 of body-surface area administered IV on days 1–5 of each 3-week cycle and cisplatin dosed at 80 mg per m2 administered IV once every 3 weeks or capecitabine dosed at 1,000 mg per m2 administered orally twice daily on days 1–14 of each 3-week cycle and oxaliplatin dosed at 130 mg per m2 administered intravenously once every 3 weeks. The overall response rate was 74% (95% CI: 66 - 82) in the pembrolizumab cohort and 52% (95% CI: 43 - 61) in the placebo cohort (one-sided p-value < 0.0001). The median duration of response was 10.6 months (range: 1.1 - 16.5) in the pembrolizumab cohort and 9.5 months (range 1.4 - 15.4) in the placebo cohort.

In this open-label, randomized, phase II trial, 187 patients with HER2-positive gastric or gastroesophageal junction (GEJ) adenocarcinoma that had progressed while they were receiving at least two previous therapies, including trastuzumab, were randomized in a 2:1 to receive trastuzumab deruxtecan (6.4 mg/kg body weight every 3 weeks) or the physician’s choice of chemotherapy (55 received irinotecan and 7 paclitaxel). 51% of patients in the trastuzumab deruxtecan cohort had an objective response, compared to 14% in the chemotherapy cohort (p < 0.001). Overall survival was longer with trastuzumab deruxtecan cohort compared to the chemotherapy cohort (median, 12.5 versus 8.4 months; HR, 0.59; 95% CI: 0.39 - 0.88; p = 0.01). The median progression-free survival was 5.6 months (95% CI: 4.3 - 6.9) in the trastuzumab deruxtecan cohort versus 3.5 months (95% CI: 2.0 - 4.3) in the chemotherapy cohort (HR, 0.47; 95% CI: 0.31 - 0.71).

In this open-label, randomized, phase II trial, 187 patients with HER2-positive gastric or gastroesophageal junction (GEJ) adenocarcinoma that had progressed while they were receiving at least two previous therapies, including trastuzumab, were randomized in a 2:1 to receive trastuzumab deruxtecan (6.4 mg/kg body weight every 3 weeks) or the physician’s choice of chemotherapy (55 received irinotecan and 7 paclitaxel). 51% of patients in the trastuzumab deruxtecan cohort had an objective response, compared to 14% in the chemotherapy cohort (p < 0.001). Overall survival was longer with trastuzumab deruxtecan cohort compared to the chemotherapy cohort (median, 12.5 versus 8.4 months; HR, 0.59; 95% CI: 0.39 - 0.88; p = 0.01). The median progression-free survival was 5.6 months (95% CI: 4.3 - 6.9) in the trastuzumab deruxtecan cohort versus 3.5 months (95% CI: 2.0 - 4.3) in the chemotherapy cohort (HR, 0.47; 95% CI: 0.31 - 0.71).

In this phase 3, open-label, randomized controlled trial, 594 patients (584 in the primary analysis) with HER2-positive amplification or overexpression gastric or gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma were enrolled and randomly assigned in 1:1 to receive a chemotherapy regimen consisting of capecitabine dosed at 1000 mg/m² orally twice a day for 14 days followed by a week off with cisplatin dosed at 80 mg/m² on day 1 by IV infusion, or fluorouracil dosed at 800 mg/m² per day given by continuous IV infusion on days 1–5 of each cycle with the same dosing of cisplatin in combination with trastuzumab dosed at 8 mg/kg loading dose, followed by 6 mg/kg every 3 weeks, versus chemotherapy alone. The median overall survival was 13.8 months (95% CI: 12 - 16) in the trastuzumab plus chemotherapy cohort versus 11.1 months (95% CI: 10 - 13) in the chemotherapy cohort (HR, 0.74; 95% CI: 0.60 – 0.91; p = 0∙0046). The median progression-free survival was 6.7 months (95% CI: 6 - 8) in the trastuzumab plus chemotherapy cohort versus 5.5 months (95% CI: 5 - 6) in the chemotherapy cohort (HR, 0.71; 95% CI: 0.59 - 0.85; p = 0.0002).

In this phase 3, open-label, randomized controlled trial, 594 patients (584 in the primary analysis) with HER2-positive amplification or overexpression gastric or gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma were enrolled and randomly assigned in 1:1 to receive a chemotherapy regimen consisting of capecitabine dosed at 1000 mg/m² orally twice a day for 14 days followed by a week off with cisplatin dosed at 80 mg/m² on day 1 by IV infusion, or fluorouracil dosed at 800 mg/m² per day given by continuous IV infusion on days 1–5 of each cycle with the same dosing of cisplatin in combination with trastuzumab dosed at 8 mg/kg loading dose, followed by 6 mg/kg every 3 weeks, versus chemotherapy alone. The median overall survival was 13.8 months (95% CI: 12 - 16) in the trastuzumab plus chemotherapy cohort versus 11.1 months (95% CI: 10 - 13) in the chemotherapy cohort (HR, 0.74; 95% CI: 0.60 – 0.91; p = 0∙0046). The median progression-free survival was 6.7 months (95% CI: 6 - 8) in the trastuzumab plus chemotherapy cohort versus 5.5 months (95% CI: 5 - 6) in the chemotherapy cohort (HR, 0.71; 95% CI: 0.59 - 0.85; p = 0.0002).

In this open-label, phase II trial, 99 patients with locally advanced and unresectable or metastatic urothelial carcinoma with various FGFR alterations who had a history of disease progression during or after at least one course of chemotherapy or within one year after neoadjuvant/adjuvant chemotherapy. The overall response rate was 40% (95% CI: 31 - 50) and the median duration of response was 5.6 months (95% CI: 4.2 - 7.2). Further, at the median follow-up of 11.2 months, the median duration of progression-free survival was 5.5 months (95% CI: 4.2 - 6.0). Lastly, 46% of the patients reported adverse event of grade 3 or higher that was treatment-related.

In this open-label, phase II trial, 99 patients with locally advanced and unresectable or metastatic urothelial carcinoma with various FGFR alterations who had a history of disease progression during or after at least one course of chemotherapy or within one year after neoadjuvant/adjuvant chemotherapy. The overall response rate was 40% (95% CI: 31 - 50) and the median duration of response was 5.6 months (95% CI: 4.2 - 7.2). Further, at the median follow-up of 11.2 months, the median duration of progression-free survival was 5.5 months (95% CI: 4.2 - 6.0). Lastly, 46% of the patients reported adverse event of grade 3 or higher that was treatment-related.

molecular_profile: FLT3 ITD AND FLT3 D835 AND FLT3 I836
evidence_statement: In this phase III, randomized trial, 371 patients with Relapsed or Refractory FLT3-Mutated AML were randomized 2:1 to receive either gilteritinib (at a dose of 120 mg per day) or salvage chemotherapy. The median overall survival in the gilteritinib cohort was significantly longer than that in the chemotherapy cohort (9.3 months vs. 5.6 months; HR, 0.64; 95% CI: 0.49 - 0.83; p < 0.001). The percentage of patients who had complete remission with full or partial hematologic recovery was 34.0% in the gilteritinib cohort and 15.3% in the chemotherapy cohort (95% CI: 9.8 - 27.4) and the percentages with complete remission were 21.1% and 10.5%, respectively (95% CI: 2.8 - 18.4). The median event-free survival was 2.8 months in the gilteritinib cohort and 0.7 months in the chemotherapy cohort (HR, 0.79; 95% CI: 0.58 - 1.09). It was also found that grade 3 or higher adverse events were more frequent in the chemotherapy cohort.

molecular_profile: FLT3 ITD OR FLT3 D835 OR FLT3 I836
evidence_statement: In this phase III randomized, double-blind placebo-controlled trial, 717 patients with FLT3 mutations (tested for ITD or 835 or 836) underwent randomization 1:1 such that 360 were assigned to the midostaurin cohort, and 357 to the placebo cohort. Treatment consisted of daunorubicin dosed at 60 mg per square meter of body-surface area per day and cytarabine dosed at 200 mg per square meter with midostaurin or placebo, administered at a dose of 50 mg orally twice daily, on days 8 through 21. Overall survival was longer in the midostaurin cohort versus the placebo cohort (HR, 0.78; 95% CI: 0.63 – 0.96; one-sided p = 0.009), as was event-free survival (HR, 0.78; 95% CI: 0.66 – 0.93; one-sided p = 0.002).

In this open-label, randomized, controlled, phase III trial, 1,198 patients with histologically confirmed adenocarcinoma of the colon or rectum and immunohistochemical evidence of tumour EGFR expression were randomized 1:1 to receive cetuximab plus FOLFIRI and FOLFIRI alone. The FOLFIRI regimen was dosed as follows: 30- to 90-minute infusion of irinotecan at a dose of 180 mg per square meter of body-surface area; an infusion, for 120 minutes, of racemic leucovorin or L-leucovorin at a dose of 400 or 200 mg, respectively, per square meter of body-surface area; fluorouracil in a bolus of 400 mg per square meter of body-surface area and then continuous infusion for 46 hours of 2400 mg per square meter of body-surface area. Cetuximab was dosed at an initial 120-minute infusion on day 1 of 400 mg per square meter of body-surface area, followed by 60-minute infusions of cetuximab at a dose of 250 mg per square meter of body-surface area, once weekly. The hazard ratio for progression-free survival in the cetuximab cohort compared to the FOLFIRI cohort was 0.85 (95% CI: 0.72 - 0.99; p = 0.048). Further, the two treatment regimens had no significant difference in overall survival (HR, 0.93; 95% CI: 0.81 - 1.07; p = 0.31). There was a significant interaction between the treatment group and KRAS mutation status for tumour response (p = 0.03) but not for progression-free survival (PFS) (p = 0.07) or overall survival (p = 0.44). Lastly, the hazard ratio for PFS among patients with wild-type KRAS tumours was 0.68 (95% CI: 0.50 - 0.94), in favour of the cetuximab cohort.

In the phase 1/2 clinical trial NCT03037385, one arm assessed the therapeutic benefit of the selective RET inhibitor pralsetinib across a range RET fusion positive solid tumors, excluding NSCLC and thyroid cancer. 26% of these harbored CCDC6 as the fusion partner. 5 of 6 cancers harboring RET::CCDC6 fusions yielded an overall response to pralsetinib including 1 pancreatic, 2 cholangiocarcinoma, 1 neuroendocrine, and 1 sarcoma. One patient with RET::CCDC6 colorectal cancer had a best response of stable disease (SD).

In this randomized, phase III trial, 1,183 patients with previously untreated metastatic adenocarcinoma of the colon or rectum, were randomized 1:1 to receive panitumumab-FOLFOX4 versus FOLFOX4. Panitumumab was administered IV over 1 hour at 6 mg/kg every 2 weeks on day 1 before FOLFOX4 chemotherapy. If tolerated, later infusions could be administered over 30 minutes. FOLFOX4 was administered every 2 weeks and dosed as follows: oxaliplatin 85 mg/m2 IV infusion on day 1 and leucovorin 200 mg/m2 (or equivalent) IV infusion followed by fluorouracil 400 mg/m2 IV bolus and 600 mg/m2 22-hour continuous infusion on days 1 and 2. For patients with a wild-type KRAS, panitumumab-FOLFOX4 significantly improved progression-free survival compared with FOLFOX4 alone (median PFS of 9.6 versus 8.0 months, respectively; HR, 0.80; 95% CI: 0.66 - 0.97; p = .02). In terms of overall survival, a nonsignificant increase was observed for panitumumab-FOLFOX4 versus FOLFOX4 (median OS, 23.9 versus 19.7 months, respectively; HR, 0.83; 95% CI: 0.67 - 1.02; p = .072). For patients with mutant KRAS PFS was significantly reduced in the panitumumab-FOLFOX4 cohort versus the FOLFOX4 cohort (HR, 1.29; 95% CI: 1.04 - 1.62; p = .02), and median overall survival was 15.5 months versus 19.3 months, respectively (HR, 1.24; 95% CI: 0.98 - 1.57; p = .068).

In the phase 1/2 clinical trial NCT03037385, one arm assessed the therapeutic benefit of the selective RET inhibitor pralsetinib across a range RET fusion positive solid tumors, excluding NSCLC and thyroid cancer. 26% of these harbored KIF5B as the fusion partner. 3 of 5 cancers harboring RET::KIF5B fusions yielded an overall response to pralsetinib including 1 unknown primary (CR), 1 SCLC (PR), and 1 neuroendocrine (PR).

In the phase 1/2 clinical trial NCT03037385, one arm assessed the therapeutic benefit of the selective RET inhibitor pralsetinib across a range RET fusion positive solid tumors, excluding NSCLC and thyroid cancer. Efficacy was seen in 4 of 4 pancreatic (1CR, 3PR), 2 of 3 cholangiocarcinoma (2PR), 2 of 2 neuroendocrine (2PR), 2 of 3 sarcoma (1CR, 1PR), 1 of 1 unknown primary (CR), 1 of 2 head and neck (PR), and 1 of 2 SCLC (PR). Of 23 evaluable patients, the overall response rate was 57% (95% CI 35-77) with a median duration of response of 12 months, median progression-free survival of 7 months, and median overall survival of 14 months. The most common RET fusion partners were CCDC6 (26%), KIF5B (26%), and NCOA4 (13%). Responses were seen regardless fusion partner or tumor type.

In this multi-cohort, open-label, phase 1/2 study, 122 patients with RET-mutant medullary and 20 with RET fusion-positive thyroid cancers were started on pralsetinib dosed at 400 mg once daily. Overall response rates were 15/21 (95% CI: 48 - 89) in patients with treatment-naive RET-mutant medullary thyroid cancer, 33/55 (95% CI: 46 - 73) in patients who had previously received cabozantinib and/or vandetanib, and 8/9 (95% CI: 52 - 100) in patients with RET fusion-positive thyroid cancer.

In this double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial, 117 patients with tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) and at least one lesion with a diameter of 1 cm or greater, and either serial growth of a subependymal giant cell astrocytoma, a new lesion of 1 cm or greater, or new or worsening hydrocephalus. They were randomly assigned 2:1 to oral everolimus 4.5 mg/m(2) per day (n = 78) or placebo (n = 39). The primary endpoint was the proportion of patients with a confirmed response which was defined as a 50% or greater reduction in target to baseline in subependymal giant cell astrocytomas. 27 patients in the everolimus cohort had at least 50% reduction in the volume of subependymal giant cell astrocytomas versus none of the patients in the placebo cohort (95% CI: 15 - 52; one-sided exact Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel test, p < 0·0001). ). By week 24, 31/74 patients in the everolimus cohort had a reduction in tumour volume of at least 50% versus 1/34 in the placebo cohort. Lastly, the response to everolimus occurred in patients with TSC1 or TSC2 mutations, however, the rate was lower in patients with a TSC2 mutation: 5/10 individuals with a mutation in TSC1 compared with 16/55 with a TSC2 mutation.

In this phase III, randomized, open-label trial, 377 patients with wild-type KRAS exon two were randomized 1:1 to receive panitumumab 6 mg/kg IV on day 1 of each 14-day cycle plus BSC or BSC alone. The median overall survival was 10.0 months in the panitumumab plus BSC cohort versus 7.4 months in the BSC-only cohort (HR, 0.73; 95% CI: 0.57 - 0.93; p = 0.0096). Progression-free survival was also improved in the panitumumab group with median PFS being 3.6 (95% CI: 3.4 - 5.3) months for panitumumab plus BSC versus 1.7 (95% CI: 1.6 - 1.9) months for BSC alone (HR, 0.51; 95% CI: 0.41 - 0.64; p < 0.0001). Patients with wildtype RAS tumours (KRAS + NRAS) also benefited from panitumumab with a median overall survival of 10.0 (95% CI: 8.7 - 11.6) months versus 6.9 (95% CI: 5.2 - 7.9) months (HR, 0.70; 95% CI: 0.53 - 0.93; p = 0.0135). Lastly, the overall response rate for the panitumumab plus BSC cohort was 31.0% (95% CI: 23.5 - 39.3) versus 2.3% (95% CI: 0.5 - 6.7) for BSC alone (OR = 20.0; 95% CI: 5.9 - 101.6; p < 0.0001.

In this phase II, open-label, single-arm trial, 106 patients with 40 different malignancies were enrolled (78.5% solid tumors, 21.5% hematologic malignancies), including 12 with COL1A1-PDGFB fusion-positive dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans. In patients with solid tumours, the initial dose of imatinib was 400 mg twice daily, with escalation to 500 mg twice daily if no significant disease improvement occurred after the first 4 to 8 weeks. For patients with hematologic malignancies, the initial dose of imatinib was 400 mg/day, with escalation to 300 or 400 mg twice daily if no significant disease improvement occurred after the first 4 to 8 weeks. Notable activity of imatinib was observed in only five tumour types as follows: aggressive fibromatosis, dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans, hypereosinophilic syndrome, myeloproliferative disorders, and systemic mastocytosis. Of the 12 patients with dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans, four had a complete response, six had a partial response, one had progressive disease, and one had an unknown response, and the median time to progression was 23.9 (95% CI: 7.7 – infinite) months. Of the 9 patients that had a 17;22 translocation, all nine had either a complete or partial response, however, the one patient without the translocation had disease progression in one month.

In this phase II, open-label, single-arm trial, 106 patients with 40 different malignancies were enrolled (78.5% solid tumours, 21.5% hematologic malignancies), including seven with myeloproliferative disorders associated with PDGFRB. In patients with solid tumours, the initial dose of imatinib was 400 mg twice daily, with escalation to 500 mg twice daily if no significant disease improvement occurred after the first 4 to 8 weeks. For patients with hematologic malignancies, the initial dose of imatinib was 400 mg/day, with escalation to 300 or 400 mg twice daily if no significant disease improvement occurred after the first 4 to 8 weeks. Notable activity of imatinib was observed in only five tumour types as follows: aggressive fibromatosis, dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans, hypereosinophilic syndrome, myeloproliferative disorders, and systemic mastocytosis. Of the patients with myeloproliferative disorders, three had a complete response, one had a partial response, two had disease progression, and one had an unknown response.

In this phase II, open-label, non-randomized trial, 36 patients with the myeloproliferative neoplasms chronic eosinophilic leukemia, CEL (n = 23) and hypereosinophilic syndrome, HES (n = 13) were enrolled. FIP1L1-PDGFRA fusion-positive patients were treated initially with 100 mg/day imatinib whereas patients with a PDGFRB fusion gene and patients with HES or CEL without known molecular aberration were treated with 400 mg/day imatinib. The dose was adjusted according to the standard criteria for dose adjustment used in CML. In FIP1L1-PDGFRA positive CEL, complete histological remission (CHR) was achieved in 16/16 patients after a median time of 0.8 months (range, 0.2 - 3.3). Complete molecular remission (CMR) was seen in 12/16 patients after 6 months. The dose of imatinib was increased up to 400 mg in four patients without CMR at month 6. After 12 months, 13/15 patients had achieved CMR (median 4.3 months, range, 1.0 – 15.3). One of the remaining patients achieved CMR at month 15.

In this phase I, open-label, dose-escalation trial, 86 patients (n = 69 had AdvSM n = 14 had indolent SM, n = 2 had smoldering SM, and n = 1 had chronic myelomonocytic leukemia) were enrolled. 36 patients with AdvSM had at least one mutation in the SRSF2, ASXL1, or RUNX1 genes, which are associated with poor disease prognosis. Part 1 of the study dosed patients at 30, 60, 100, 130, 200, 300 and 400mg daily of avapritinib, with doses of 200 mg and higher achieving exposures consistently above, and doses of 100mg and 130mg partly above, the xenograft 90% inhibitory concentration for KIT D816V inhibition at steady state. No maximum tolerated dose was determined, and the dose selected for part 2 was 200 mg daily. Of the 53 patients in the response-evaluable cohort, overall response rate was 75% (95% CI:, 62 - 86%), with 19/53 exhibiting complete remission with full hematologic recovery or complete remission with partial hematologic recovery, 18/53 achieved a partial remission, and 3/53 showed clinical improvement. The overall response rate was 83% (30/36; 95% CI: 67 - 94%) in midostaurin-naïve patients, and 59% (10/17; 95% CI: 33 - 82%) in patients with prior midostaurin exposure. The median time to achieve partial remission or better was two months (range, 2 - 27 months), and nine months to achieve complete remission or complete remission with partial hematologic recovery.

In this randomized, phase III trial, 572 patients with HR-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer who had received endocrine therapy previously underwent randomization, including 341 patients with confirmed tumour-tissue PIK3CA mutations. Patients were enrolled into two cohorts based on tumour-tissue PIK3CA mutation status. The comparison was between 300 mg daily alpelisib plus 500 mg fulvestrant every 28 days and once on day 15 versus placebo plus fulvestrant dosed the same. In the PIK3CA-mutated cohort, progression-free survival (PFS) was 11.0 months (95% CI: 7.5 - 14.5) in the alpelisib–fulvestrant group compared to 5.7 months (95% CI: 3.7 - 7.4) in the placebo–fulvestrant group (HR, 0.65; 95% CI: 0.50 - 0.85; p < 0.001). Overall response in the PIK3CA-mutated cohort was greater with alpelisib–fulvestrant than with placebo–fulvestrant (26.6% vs. 12.8%).

In this study, a collection of pediatric spindle cell tumors were screened for the ETV6::NTRK3 fusion by RT-PCR. 10 of 11 (91%) cases diagnosed as congenital fibrosarcoma were found to harbor the ETV6::NTRK3 fusion while none of the 51 other malignant or benign spindle cell tumors (including adult-type fibrosarcoma, infantile fibromatosis, myofibromatosis, and more aggressive malignant spindle cell tumors) were positive for this fusion. The authors conclude ETV6::NTRK3 RT-PCR analysis is a reliable and specific modality to aid in the diagnosis of this disease.

In this study, the ETV6::NTRK3 fusion was detected in 7 of 10 (70%) of congenital fibrosarcomas by RT-PCR but absent in 38 other control spindle cell tumors, including adult-type fibrosarcomas, leiomyosarcomas, malignant fibrous histiocytomas, synovial sarcomas, MPNST, dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans, schwannomas, fibromatosis cases, and nodular fasciitis cases. This demonstrates utility of ETV6::NTRK3 fusion detection in diagnosis of this disease.

A 53 year old female patient had PTC treated with surgery and multiple brain metastases. TERT c.-124C.T mutation and ETV6::NTRK2 fusion was found in pleural biopsy and cerebellar resection specimens. The fusion preserved ETV6 PNT domain and NTRK2 kinase domain. After radiation and surgery, larotrectinib was given. This resulted in ongoing partial response (-39%) in pleural metastases with duration past 18 months and without evidence of recurrence in the brain.

In an analysis of 19 cases of mesoblastic nephroma, the ETV6::NTRK3 fusion was detected in 0 of 5 of the classic mesoblastic nephroma, 8 of 8 (100%) of the cellular mesoblastic nephroma and 5 of 6 (83%) of the mixed mesoblastic nephroma cohorts.

In an analysis of 22 cases of mesoblastic nephroma, 4 of 5 (80%) cellular mesoblastic nephromas harbored ETV6::NTRK3, 1 of 5 cellular mesoblastic nephromas harbored a KLHL7::BRAF fusion, 12 of 12 (100%) classic mesoblastic nephromas harbored EGFR ITD, 4 of 5 of mixed histology had EGFR ITD, and 1 of 5 of mixed histology had the ETV6::NTRK3 fusion.

In this phase II, randomized, open-label trial, 147 patients with histologically confirmed, unresectable or metastatic gastrointestinal stromal tumour that expressed CD117 were enrolled. Patients were randomly assigned to receive either 400 mg or 600 mg of imatinib orally. At 400 mg, 36 patients (95% CI: 37.4 – 61.3) had a partial response, at 600 mg, 43 patients (95% CI: 46.1 – 69.5) had a partial response, overall, 79 patients (95% CI: 45.3–62.0) had a partial response.

In this double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled, phase III trial, 154 patients with advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumours with progression on at least imatinib, sunitinib, and regorafenib. They were randomly assigned 2:1 to receive either oral ripretinib 150 mg once daily (ripretenib cohort) or placebo once daily (placebo cohort). The median progression-free survival was 6.3 months (95% CI: 4.6 – 6.9) with ripretinib compared with 1.0 months (0.9 – 1.7) with placebo (HR, 0.15, 95% CI: 0·09 – 0·25; p < 0·0001). Further, the median overall survival was 15.1 months (95% CI: 12.3 - 15.1).

In this phase III, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 312 patients were randomized in a 2:1 ratio to receive sunitinib or placebo. Median time to tumour progression was 27.3 weeks (95% CI: 16.0 – 32. 1) in patients receiving sunitinib and 6.4 weeks (95% CI: 4.4 – 10.0) in those on placebo (HR, 0·33; p < 0·0001). The median progression-free survival was 24.1 weeks (95% CI: 11.1 – 28.3] for sunitinib, 6.0 weeks (95% CI: 4.4 – 9.9) for placebo (HR, 0.33; 95% CI: 0.24 – 0.47; p < 0·0001).

In this phase II, open-label, single-arm trial, 276 patients with a histologically or cytologically confirmed diagnosis of metastatic non-small-cell lung cancer that carried either an ALK or ROS1 gene rearrangement were enrolled. 30 who were ALK-positive and treatment-naive (EXP1); 59 who were ALK-positive and received previous crizotinib without (n = 27; EXP2) or with (n=32; EXP3A) previous chemotherapy; 28 who were ALK-positive and received one previous non-crizotinib ALK tyrosine kinase inhibitor, with or without chemotherapy (EXP3B); 112 who were ALK-positive with two (n = 66; EXP4) or three (n = 46; EXP5) previous ALK tyrosine kinase inhibitors with or without chemotherapy; and 47 who were ROS1 positive with any previous treatment (EXP6). Lorlatinib was administered orally in a tablet form at a starting dose of 100 mg once daily. In treatment-naive patients (EXP1), an objective response was achieved in 27 ) of 30 patients (95% CI: 73.5 – 97.9). In ALK-positive patients with at least one previous ALK tyrosine kinase inhibitor (EXP2–5), objective responses were achieved in 93 of 198 patients (95% CI: 39.9 - 54.2). Objective response was achieved in 41 of 59 patients (95% CI: 56.1 – 80.8) who had only received previous crizotinib (EXP2–3A), nine of 28 patients (95% CI: 15.9 – 52.4) with one previous non-crizotinib ALK tyrosine kinase inhibitor (EXP3B), and 43 of 111 patients (95% CI: 29∙6–48∙5) with two or more previous ALK tyrosine kinase inhibitors (EXP4–5).

In a phase I/II, open-label trial, 570 patients with Philadelphia chromosome–positive CML were enrolled. Patient cohorts included second-line chronic phase (CP) CML (n = 286), third-/fourth-line CP CML (n = 118), and advanced leukemia (n = 166). Part 1 is a phase 1, dose-escalation study that determined a recommended dose of bosutinib 500 mg per day in primarily imatinib-resistant CP CML patients. The median duration of bosutinib treatment across cohorts was 11.1 (range, 0.03 - 83.4) months (Subgroups: CP2L, 24.8 [0.2 - 83.4] months; CP3L, 8.5 [0.2 - 78.1] months; advanced, 4.0 [0.03 - 77.9] months). Across cohorts, dose reductions and interruptions due to adverse events occurred in 45% and 65% of patients, respectively, and were more common in CP2L (49% and 72%) and CP3L (50% and 66%) cohorts versus the advanced disease cohort (34% and 51%). Lastly, The most frequently reported treatment-emergent adverse events were gastrointestinal events such as diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, and thrombocytopenia. The incidence rates did not substantially differ across the cohorts.

In this phase 1 dose-escalation study, 119 patients with imatinib-resistant, Ph-positive CML or acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) to receive nilotinib orally at doses of 50 mg, 100 mg, 200 mg, 400 mg, 600 mg, 800 mg, and 1200 mg once daily, as well as at 400 mg and 600 mg twice daily. No dose-limiting toxic effects were seen at doses of up to 600 mg daily. Dose-limiting toxic effects occurred among 18 patients at doses higher than 600 mg. Of 33 patients with the blastic phase, 13 had a hematologic response to nilotinib (39 percent) with 9 patients having a cytogenetic response. Of 46 patients with accelerated-phase CML (excluding those with clonal evolution only), 33 had a hematologic response, and 22 had a cytogenetic response. Among the 10 patients who had clonal evolution as the only feature of the accelerated phase of CML, 5 had active disease and 5 were in complete hematologic remission. All 5 patients with clonal evolution and hematologic disease had a complete hematologic response. Nilotinib was active in patients with and in those without mutations in the ABL gene, but there were no significant differences in the response rates between the two groups, however, Two patients with a T315I mutation (one with chronic-phase CML and one with blastic-phase CML) had no response to nilotinib.

evidence_statement: In this phase 1/2, open-label, 2-part study, 288 patients with imatinib-resistant (n = 200) or imatinib-intolerant (n = 88) CML were enrolled. Part 1 was a dose-escalation study of standard 3 + 3 design with successive cohorts of 3-6 patients with CP imatinib-resistant CML. Each cohort was evaluated for safety over the course of 28 days before enrollment of the next cohort to establish the maximum tolerated dose. Part 2 evaluated the efficacy and safety of bosutinib with the primary endpoint being major cellular response rate at 24 weeks. 31% of patients achieved major cytogenetic response by 24 weeks. After a median follow-up of 24.2 months, 86% of patients achieved complete hematologic remission, 53% had a major cytogenetic response, 41% had a complete cytogenetic response, and 64% of those achieving complete cytogenetic response had a major molecular response. At 2 years, progression-free survival was 79% and overall survival at 2 years was 92%. Lastly, responses were seen across Bcr-Abl mutants, except for the T315I mutation.

In this single-arm, open-label, phase 1/2 trial 137 patients who had advanced malignancies, including ALK-rearranged NSCLC and two patients with inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour (IMT) were enrolled and treated with brigatinib. The two patients enrolled with IMT had stable disease and partial response, respectively.

In this phase 1 study, oral ceritinib was administered to 59 patients in doses of 50 - 750 mg once daily to patients with advanced cancers harbouring genetic alterations in ALK. A total of 130 patients were enrolled: 59 patients in the dose-escalation phase and 71 in the expansion phase. A total of 83 of 122 patients with NSCLC (68%) had received crizotinib previously. Of the 8 patients with cancers other than NSCLC, 4 had breast cancer and 1 patient each had alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma, rectal adenocarcinoma, anaplastic large-cell lymphoma, and inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour. Among the eight patients with advanced cancers other than NSCLC, two had a response to ceritinib: one patient with anaplastic large-cell lymphoma, and one with inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour.

This case study was on a 43-year-old female patient with an FN1-ALK gene fusion. In several case reports and phase 1b/phase 2 studies, responses of ALK-positive IMTs to crizotinib have been shown. Crizotinib is therefore the standard of care for patients with unresectable ALK-mutated IMT. The tumour in this patient did not respond to neoadjuvant treatment with the first-generation ALK inhibitor crizotinib but reacted rapidly to the next-generation ALK inhibitor lorlatinib. This case indicates that ALK-positive IMTs, which do not respond to ALK inhibition by crizotinib, might not be refractory to ALK inhibition but can be successfully treated with newer agents. This could be of importance both in the neoadjuvant and in the palliative setting especially to prevent radical intervention and sustain bladder function.

This case study was on a 40-year-old male with dyspnea and a productive cough. He was found to have a right upper lobe opacity on a chest X-ray. Subsequent investigations, including CT and PET, showed a large right upper lobe mass with metastases to the hilar lymph nodes, right trapezius muscle, and left frontal lobe. Fluorescence in-situ hybridization analysis confirmed ALK rearrangement and the TPM4-ALK fusion gene was demonstrated by next-generation sequencing. Lorlatinib was administered orally at a dose of 100 mg daily. CT performed at 2 months showed an excellent partial response with a reduction in the size of the lung mass, trapezius, adrenal, and cerebral metastases. Lorlatinib was otherwise well tolerated with only mild toxicities of grade 1 oral stomatitis, insomnia, paronychia and grade 2 hyperlipidemia. Considering the positive response, lorlatinib was continued, with his dis- ease remaining stable for the following 6 months. 11 months after the start of lorlatinib, his disease progressed with enlarging lung and adrenal lesions in addition to a new left gluteal metastasis. He was given palliative radiotherapy to the gluteal mass for pain control and lorlatinib was discontinued. He was then treated with the ALK inhibitor brigatinib, but his disease continued to progress clinically with a worsening of his performance status after 1 month. Brigatinib was stopped and he died shortly afterwards.

This case study was on an 18-year-old Caucasian female presenting with severe headaches. Brain MRI revealed multiple brain masses with the largest (5 cm) found in the anterior left frontal lobe. A metastatic workup showed a 6 cm right middle lobe lung mass. Fluorescence in-situ hybridization confirmed ALK-1 gene rearrangement, however, DNA sequencing failed to reveal the fusion partner, likely due to intron interference. She was started on 250 mg of crizotinib twice daily. Serial laboratory and imaging studies were used to follow our patient’s disease regularly. Unfortunately, her CNS disease progressed on a follow-up brain MRI after being on crizotinib. Crizotinib was discontinued, and she was started on ceritinib at 750 mg daily, however, a grade 3 elevation of the patient’s transaminases required a dose reduction of this ALK inhibitor to 450 mg, and after eight months her CNS disease progressed again on brain MRI before being placed on alectinib daily at 600 mg. After eight months of alectinib treatment, she developed recurrent severe headaches and a brain MRI identified the rapid progression of several CNS lesions and the development of leptomeningeal disease in all spinal compartments. She was then given 100 mg daily lorlatinib and within a few weeks, the patient was able to discontinue IV opiate narcotics required to control her headaches. Follow-up brain MRI three months later revealed complete clearance of leptomeningeal disease in all spinal compartments and stable brain lesions without worsening signs. The patient was alive two and a half years after her initial diagnosis.

The authors assess the functional significance of the 55 ERBB2 mutations listed in COSMIC as of October 2018. A novel cell line model developed by the authors (MANO) was used, which allows the integration of barcoded individual genes into assay cells, with subsequent pooling and culturing to allow the evaluation of their oncogenic potential or drug sensitivity. The variant G776V was found to be an activating mutant, defined as having a statistically significant fold change in the ratio of ERBB2-mutant cell number on day 12 relative to day 0, as compared to the wild-type ERBB2 cell number.

evidence_statement: In an open-label, phase II trial, 18 patients with histiocytosis, including 12 patients with Erdheim-Chester disease, one patient with ARAF S225V, and one patient with ARAF P216A, of any mutational status were enrolled. The overall response rate was 89% (90% CI: 73 - 100). Responses were durable, with no acquired resistance at the time of publishing. At one year, 100% of responses were ongoing and 94% of patients remained progression-free. Cobimetinib treatment was efficacious regardless of genotype, and responses were observed in patients with ARAF, BRAF, RAF1, NRAS, KRAS, MEK1, and MEK2 mutations.

In this case series, 3 patients with Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH) were studied. Patient #1 was a 15-year-old male who has experienced five reactivations of LCH. He presented with left mastoid LCH at 3.5 years of age, confirmed by biopsy with CD1a and S-100 positivity, and has since been treated with multiple rounds of chemotherapy. Next-generation sequencing from the last biopsy showed BRAF p.N486_P490 deletion. He was treated with trametinib 0.5-1 mg daily and remains with no active disease on this dose at 18 months follow-up. Patient #2 is a 22-year-old male with LCH and two reactivations. He was diagnosed at age 18 years with biopsies confirming LCH with CD1a and S100 positivity. He was treated with cytarabine, but skin reactivation required hydroxyurea and methotrexate. He then had a second reactivation of pulmonary LCH. No biopsy was done but next-generation sequencing of a prior sample revealed BRAF p.N486_P490 deletion. Therapy with trametinib 2 mg daily produced a partial response with residual extensive cystic and nodular lung disease. He continues on monotherapy with trametinib 2 mg daily with stable lung disease after 12 months of therapy. Lastly, Patient #3 is a 2-year-old male child with multisystem disease with risk organ involvement LCH diagnosed at 2 weeks of age when skin biopsy demonstrated CD1a and CD207 positivity. At 2 months of age, he had systemic disease including bones, liver, pancreas, and lungs. Next-generation sequencing from the skin biopsy revealed a low level of MAP2K1 p.K57_G61del. He received a short corticosteroid pulse and trametinib 0.125 mg daily was started in parallel with prednisolone. His lesions rapidly responded, and he continues on trametinib monotherapy 0.25 mg daily with no active disease after 22 months of therapy.

In this open-label, non-randomized trial, 26 patients with BRAF V600–mutant Erdheim-Chester Disease or Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis (22 with Erdheim-Chester Disease, 4 with Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis) were enrolled and received 960 mg vemurafenib twice daily. The confirmed overall response rate was 61.5% (95% CI: 40.6% - 79.8%) in the overall cohort and 54.5% (95% CI: 32.2% - 75.6%) in patients with ECD. All evaluable patients achieved stable disease or better. The median progression-free survival and overall survival had not been reached in the overall cohort at study closure despite a median follow-up of 28.8 months, however, 2-year PFS was 86% (95% CI: 72% - 100%), and 2-year OS was 96% (95% CI: 87% - 100%).

In this case series, 11 patients with ECD or ECD/LCH (Seven had ECD and four had overlapped ECD/LCH) were treated with single-agent dabrafenib as initial histiocytosis therapy, following the failure of chemotherapy or radiation, or following discontinuation of vemurafenib therapy because of toxicity or intolerance were assessed. Dabrafenib monotherapy was initially dosed from 50mg BID to 150mg twice daily. FDG-PET/CT scans were performed prior to starting dabrafenib and in follow-up to measure disease response in nearly all cases. For the five patients treated with dabrafenib as initial therapy or following failure of conventional therapy, three had a partial metabolic response and two had a complete metabolic response by FDG-PET; all had a complete clinical response. In three of these six patients, dabrafenib maintained their clinical and metabolic response to vemurafenib; the sixth patient had been treated with interferon-a with poor clinical response, and dabrafenib achieved a sustained clinical and metabolic response. Two patients who stopped vemurafenib for arthralgia or fatigue stopped dabrafenib for similar intolerance after four and nine months, respectively.

In a randomized, double-blind, phase 3 trial, 553 patients with ovarian cancer, fallopian tube cancer, or primary peritoneal cancer with predominantly high-grade serous histologic features were enrolled. Of the 553 enrolled, 203 were assigned to the germline BRCA1/2 mutation cohort and 350 were assigned to the non-germline BRCA1/2 mutation cohort (including somatic BRCA1/2 mutations and wild-type BRCA1/2). BRCA1/2 mutation status and HRD status were determined by an NGS-based assay from Myriad Genetics. The patients were randomized in a 2:1 ratio to receive niraparib 300 mg or placebo once daily. Patients in the niraparib group had a significantly longer median duration of progression-free survival than the placebo group: 21.0 vs. 5.5 months in the gBRCA cohort (hazard ratio, 0.27; 95% CI: 0.17 - 0.41; p < 0.001) and 9.3 months vs. 3.9 months in the overall non-gBRCA cohort (hazard ratio, 0.45; 95% CI: 0.34 - 0.61; p < 0.001). Grade 3 or 4 adverse events reported in the niraparib group were managed with dose modification and included thrombocytopenia (in 33.8%), anemia (in 25.3%), and neutropenia (in 19.6%).
