In this phase II NCI-MATCH trial, a patient with extra-mammary Paget disease of the skin with ERBB2 D769Y mutation was treated with afatinib. A confirmed RECIST response was reported in the patient who progressed after cycle 6.

In this phase II NCI-MATCH trial, a patient with primary peritoneal carcinoma with ERBB2 D769Y mutation was treated with afatinib. A RECIST response was reported in the patient, however, it wasn't confirmed on follow-up radiological assessment.

In this phase II NCI-MATCH trial, a patient with ER+ invasive ductal breast cancer with ERBB2 V777L mutation was treated with afatinib. A RECIST response was reported in the patient, however, it wasn't confirmed on follow-up radiological assessment.

In this phase II NCI-MATCH trial, a patient with ER+ lobular breast cancer with ERBB2 S310F mutation was treated with afatinib. A 51% reduction of RECIST target lesions was reported after six cycles, however, the disease progressed because of a new nontarget lesion.

The goal of this study was to assess the efficacy and safety of larotrectinib in patients with TRK fusion–positive lung cancers. This was achieved by reviewing data from two global, multicenter clinical trials of patients treated with larotrectinib: a phase II adult and young adult basket trial (NCT02576431) and a phase I adult trial (NCT02122913). The total of 20 patients with TRK fusion–positive lung cancer were treated on these trials (tumor histology was adenocarcinoma in 19 and neuroendocrine carcinoma in one patient), of which 15 were evaluable. The objective response rate (ORR) among those 15 patients was 73%: one patient had a complete response, 10 had a partial response, 3 had stable disease, and 1 had progressive disease as best response. The median duration of response, progression-free survival, and overall survival were 33.9 months, 35.4 months, and 40.7 months, respectively. Of the total of 20 NTRK-fusions positive lung cancer cases, 6 had TPM3::NTRK1 fusion, but detailed response information was only provided for one TPM3::NTRK1 positive case. This patient was a 46-year-old man diagnosed with stage IV non–small-cell lung cancer which previously progressed on platinum-based chemotherapy after 9 months and on the PD-1 inhibitor dostarlimab after 2 months. A TPM3::NTRK1 fusion was identified on molecular profiling, and larotrectinib was initiated on a trial. A brisk and sustained partial response was achieved. The patient discontinued treatment because of progressive disease after a durable 39 months of disease control. The authors concluded that larotrectinib was highly active with rapid and durable responses, extended survival benefit, and a favorable long-term safety profile in patients with advanced lung cancer harboring NTRK gene fusions, including the TPM3::NTRK1 fusion.

molecular_profile: EGFR T790M AND EGFR Exon 19 Deletion AND MET Splice Site (c.3027_3028+21delAGGTATATTTCAGTTTATTGTTC
evidence_statement: A 53-year old man (non-smoker) presented with chest tightness and pain and was revealed to have stage IV lung adenocarcinoma with EGFR exon 19 deletion. The patient started first-line Erlotinib at 150 mg daily dose with partial response. After 28 months, new bone metastases formed and it was revealed to have developed a EGFR T790M mutation along with EGFR exon 19 deletion. Treatment was modified to Osimertinib at 80 mg daily which led to partial response for 15.4 months until progression of new bone metastases. Next-generation sequencing revealed a MET exon 14 skipping mutation (c.3027_3028+21delAGGTATATTTCAGTTTATTGTTC) and MET fusion (EX13:EX15) combined with the original EGFR exon 19 deletion. Combination therapy was started with Osimertinib (80 mg daily) + Capamatinib (400 mg, twice daily). This yielded parietal response and progression-free survival for 7 months. Upon examinations, there was disappearance of MET exon 14 skipping mutation and improvement of symptoms. There was also maintenance of bone metastasis as well.

molecular_profile: EZH2 Mutation OR SMARCA4 Loss OR SMARCB1 Loss
evidence_statement: In this NCI-COG pediatric MATCH trial, 20 patients (aged 1-21 years) harboring tumors with EZH2 mutations or SMARCB1 or SMARCA4 loss were treated with tazemetostat. The most frequent tumor types were atypical teratoid rhabdoid tumor (n=8) and malignant rhabdoid tumor (n=4). The six-month PFS was 35% (95% CI; 15.7-55.2) and the six-month overall survival was 45% (95% CI; 23.1 - 64.7). 30% of the patients (n=6) experienced grade 3 or higher adverse effects, likely associated with tazemetostat.

molecular_profile: MET Exon 14 Skipping Mutation AND CD274 Overexpression
evidence_statement: A 86-year old male (former smoker) presented to the hospital after an accidental fall. PET/CT confirmed lung adenocarcinoma with sarcomatoid transformation. Immunohistochemical evaluation and next-generation sequencing showed high PD-L1 expression and MET exon 14 skipping mutation, respectively. First-line tepotinib was administered at 500 mg daily, and yielded in partial response for the first year of treatment and stable disease afterwards until the patient was also diagnosed with a prostate carcinoma and was started on androgen deprivation therapy without any side effect concerns. After 6 months of tepotinib treatment, G2 peripheral edema was reported and treatment was temporarily discontinued until regression of edema. Tepotinib was restarted at 250 mg daily for 16 months until edema returned and was put on diuretics and physical therapy. Tepotinib was restarted again at 250 mg daily for 23 months until edema worsened and tepotinib treatment was lowered to 250 mg every other day. This treatment plan is ongoing for 31 months without worsening edema.

molecular_profile: BRAF V600E OR NRAS Mutation OR HRAS Mutation OR KRAS Mutation OR NF1 Inactivating Mutation
evidence_statement: In this Phase II study, 20 patients harboring activating RAS gene mutations (KRAS = 8, NRAS = 3. HRAS = 1), BRAF V600E mutations, and NF1 inactivating mutations (n=7) were treated with Selumetinib. No objected response was reported in these patients, and the six-month PFS was 15% (95% CI; 4-34). 25% (n=5) of the patients experienced a grade 3 or higher adverse effects, likely associated with selumetinib. Overall, selumetinib had limited efficacy in this cohort.

Using next-generation DNA and RNA sequencing, three cases harboring NTRK fusions were identified in a cohort of 113 osteosarcomas (including both primary tumors and metastases). Each of the three cases exhibited heavily recombined genomes. The fusions were validated by split-read analysis in the genome sequencing data and confirmed by RT-PCR. A novel UFD1::NTRK2 fusion (e6::e7) was detected in a 23-year-old patient with lung metastases. This fusion contained a frameshift preceding the NTRK2 tyrosine kinase domain, introducing a premature stop codon. Consistently, pan-NTRK immunohistochemistry was negative, confirming the lack of Trk protein expression in the tumor The authors conclud this NTRK fusion is non-functional and can be excluded as oncogenic or a driver. They emphasized the importance of functional validation of NTRK fusions, particularly in tumors with highly rearranged genomes, before initiating targeted therapy with pan-NTRK tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs).

Using next-generation DNA and RNA sequencing, three cases harboring NTRK fusions were identified in a cohort of 113 osteosarcomas (including primary tumors and metastases). Each of the three cases had heavily recombined genomes. The fusions were validated by split-read analysis in the genome sequencing data and RT-PCR. An intrachromosomal VPS18::NTRK3 fusion (e4::e1) was detected in a local recurrence of osteosarcoma in a 22-year-old female; however, the fusion transcript was found to be not fully transcribed. This fusion contained a premature stop codon, preventing the translation of NTRK3 domains, including the tyrosine kinase domain. Pan-TRK immunohistochemistry staining was negative in the tumor sample. The authors concluded that this non-functional NTRK fusion can be excluded as a driver/oncogenic event and recommended sequencing-based confirmation of fusions, especially in highly rearranged tumors, before initiating targeted therapy.

Using next-generation DNA and RNA sequencing, three cases harboring NTRK fusions were identified in a cohort of 113 osteosarcomas, including primary tumors and metastases. All three cases exhibited highly rearranged genomes, and the fusions were validated by split-read analysis and RT-PCR. A RALGPS2::NTRK3 fusion (5’UTR::e4) was detected in a locally recurrent osteosarcoma in a 51-year-old female. This fusion lacked an endogenous start codon, and although an alternative in-frame start codon was present just downstream of the breakpoint, it was insufficient to drive transcription of the NTRK3 functional domains, including the tyrosine kinase domain. Pan-NTRK immunohistochemistry was negative, confirming the absence of protein expression. The authors concluded that this fusion is non-functional and represents a passenger alteration rather than an oncogenic driver. They emphasize the importance of functional validation of NTRK fusions, particularly in tumors with highly rearranged genomes, before considering targeted therapy with pan-NTRK inhibitors.

A692V was shown to lead to increased H3K27 trimethylation in a breast cancer cell line (MCF-7) with induced transient expression and a B-cell ALL cell line (SUP-B8) with endogenous expression of the variant. This effect was intermediate and not accompanied by a corresponding decrease in H3K27 dimethylation as seen in some other EZH2 activating mutations. The SUP-B8 cell line also showed a program of transcriptional activation for genes associated with lymphocyte activation and cell death.

disease: Renal Cell Carcinoma With MiT Translocations
evidence_statement: Bakouny, et al. (2022) performed a comprehensive study of the molecular and clinical features of 90 translocation renal cell carcinomas (tRCCs), defined as subtype of kidney cancer driven by MiT/TFE gene fusions. Across the combined tRCC cohort, the majority of cases (88.6%) harbored TFE3 fusions with 12 different fusion partners identified. ASPSCR1 (13), SFPQ (13), PRCC (13), NONO (5), MED15 (4), RBM10 (4) were recurrent partners while U2AF2, MATR3, LUC7L3, KHSRP, FUBP1, and DVL2 were each seen in 1 case. All fusions analyzed preserve the helix-loop-helix/leucine zipper domain of the TFE3 transcription factor, which is critical for dimerization and DNA binding.

disease: Renal Cell Carcinoma With MiT Translocations
evidence_statement: Bakouny, et al. (2022) performed a comprehensive study of the molecular and clinical features of 90 translocation renal cell carcinomas (tRCCs), defined as subtype of kidney cancer driven by MiT/TFE gene fusions. Although the majority of cases (78 cases; 88.6%) harbored TFE3 fusions or TFEB fusions (8 cases; 9.1%), 2 cases harbored MITF fusions (ACTG1::MITF and PRCC::MITF).

This was a Phase 1/2 study in which 55 patients between 4 months and 76 years of age with TRK-fusion positive tumors were given NTRK inhibitor Larotrectinib. Patients had 17 unique NTRK fusion types. There were 9 patients with tumors of different histologies which were positive for the TPM3::NTRK1 fusion. Overall response rate in the study was 75% according to independent review and 80% according to investigator assessment. 7 out of 9 patients with TPM3::NTRK1 positive tumors showed response, of which 2 had pathologic remission. Authors stated that Larotrectinib had durable antitumor activity for tumors positive for NTRK-fusions (including TPM3::NTRK1) regardless of age or tumor type.

An intra-chromosomal TPR::NTRK1 fusion was found in a superficial soft tissue tumor located on the hand of a 7-year-old girl. The tumor had a prominently infiltrative growth pattern reminiscent of lipofibromatosis, but by immunohistochemistry, the tumor was multifocal S100 positive and positive for CD34, suggestive of neural differentiation. The tumor was therefore classified as LPF-like. Exon 10 of TPR fused to exon 9 of NTRK1, preserving the in-frame NTRK1 tyrosine kinase domain. This translocation required a break and inversion of the NTRK1 gene in order to achieve fusion to the 5’ portion of the TPR gene. The TPR and NTRK1 gene rearrangement was confirmed by FISH break-apart. A FISH fusion assay detected TPR::NTRK1, which was confirmed by RT-PCR. Staining of the tumor demonstrated diffuse NTRK1 immunoreactivity. At follow-up of 85 months, no evidence of disease was seen.

A male child (1 year old) presented with a rapidly growing tumor in the cervical region that had been present for 2 months. It was a firm to hard soft-tissue mass. Radiologic imaging disclosed a tumor measuring 11 cm. Biopsy showed spindle cells arranged in sheets and fascicles, with interspersed collagenous strands. Immunohistochemically, the tumor cells were diffusely positive for CD34 and S100 protein. Initial diagnoses from different laboratories included infantile fibrosarcoma, low-grade malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor, and solitary fibrous tumor. On review of the morphological and immunohistochemical results, including STAT6 negativity, the diagnosis of NTRK-positive spindle cell neoplasm was considered. The tumor sample was positive for a TPR::NTRK1 fusion. By FISH, 50% of the cells were positive for the fusion. Chemotherapy was given with no significant response, and there was rapid local progression. Due to lack of availability, an NTRK inhibitor was not given.

A female patient, 43 presented with right lower quadrant pain, and was surgically treated for perforated appendicitis including segmental small-bowel resection. Invasive adenocarcinoma stage IIB (pT4aN0) of the cecum was identified in the pathology, with intact MMR. The patient declined adjuvant chemotherapy. A year later the patient showed recurrence of the tumor mass consistent with stage IV recurrent/metastatic colorectal cancer. Testing revealed the tumor to be MSI-High. TPR-NTRK1 was found in the tumor by NGS and high tumor mutational burden (TMB) was found (39 mutations/Mb). Pembrolizumab was given (four cycles), but patient progressed. Combination immunotherapy of ipilimumab and nivolumab was then given, followed by further progression. Patient was then given NTRK inhibitor larotrectinib and after 5 weeks a considerable decrease in the size of peritoneal metastasis was seen, accompanied by other tumor shrinkage and remarkable improvement of symptoms. Curative-intent surgical resection of the tumor mass was performed, and adjuvant larotrectinib was declined. No evidence of tumor was apparent after 26 months.

The A687V EZH2-mutant SUP-B8 B-ALL cell line exhibited the greatest sensitivity to EZH2 inhibitor (GSK126) compared to 7 other EZH2 wild-type B-ALL cell lines by cell proliferation assay. The increased sensitivity was comparable with that seen with A677G- and Y641N/F-mutant DLBCL cell lines.

In this study, 331 patients with IDH-mutant grade 2 gliomas were either given vorasidenib (n = 168) or a placebo (n = 163). A median PFS of 27.7 months was reported in the vorasidenib group, compared to 11.1 months in the group given a placebo. The hazard ratio for disease progression or death was 0.39 (95% CI, 0.27-0.56; p<0.001). Additionally, a lower time to the next intervention was noted in the vorasidenib group compared to the placebo group. Grade 3 or higher adverse effects were noted in 22.8% of the patients in the treatment group, which may likely be related to the vorasidenib treatment. Overall, vorasidenib significantly improved PFS and delayed the time to the next intervention in the treatment group, compared to the control group (placebo group).

In this trial involving 500 patients, 188 individuals received treatment with VEGF/VEGFR inhibitors. Among them, 106 patients had tumors containing TP53 mutations. The analysis revealed a higher rate of overall improvement, encompassing stable disease (SD), partial remission (PR), and complete remission (CR), at 31% for those treated with VEGF/VEGFR inhibitors compared to 7% for those who didn't receive such treatment. Among patients treated with VEGF/VEGFR inhibitors, those with TP53 mutations (compared to wildtype TP53) exhibited a notably higher rate of improvement, suggesting a sensitivity to this treatment regimen.

molecular_profile: KRAS G12D AND KRAS G12R AND CDKN2A Loss AND CDKN2B Loss AND TP53 R267W
evidence_statement: In this clinical trial, 18 patients with pancreatic cancer were recruited. In this case, the patient (69 y/M) with pancreatic cancer harboring, CDKN2A exons 1-2 loss, CDKN2B loss, KRAS G12D, KRAS G12R, and, TP53 R267W, was treated with Palbociclib, Trametinib, and, Bevacizumab. The trial reported a progression-free survival (PFS) of 6 months and an overall survival (OS) of 6.5 months for this individual. The study concluded that the patient derived clinical benefit, defined as stable disease (SD) lasting at least 6 months, partial remission (PR), or complete remission (CR).

In this study, the sensitivity to Cisplatin (a platinum-based drug) was studied in XRCC3 knockout, and ORC1 mutant PDX models. A role of XRCC3 loss in cisplatin sensitivity was reported in the study. The study also reported increased cisplatin sensitivity in ORC1 mutant PDX models, compared to wildtype cells.

This study from 1991 (before the advent of next-generation sequencing) aimed to decipher molecular basis and oncogenic mechanisms of the t(1;19)(q23;p13), which was already known at the time as a recurrent, relatively common translocation in pediatric B-lymphoblastic leukemias. In this study, fusion transcripts of TCF3 (known at the time as E2A) and PBX1 were detected via RT-PCR in 97% (37 of 38) cases where t(1;19)(q23;p13) was found with cytogenetic approaches. The study confirms that the t(1;19) consistently correlates with the TCF3::PBX1 fusion and B-lymphoblastic leukemia.

Clinical trials conducted at St Jude Children's Research Hospital revealed that patients with pre-B acute lymphoblastic leukemia who have the TCF3::PBX1 fusion exhibit a favorable overall outcome when treated with contemporary treatment.

In an earlier study of 15 patients with TCF3::PBX1 B-ALL, 2 of the 15 had neonatal blood spots found to be positive for the TCF3::PBX1 fusion breakpoint using polymerase chain reaction (PCR). In this study, screening of umbilical cord blood samples from 340 healthy newborns, the TCF3::PBX1 fusion was found in 2 cases (0.6%) using a method that is called GIPFEL(genomic inverse PCR for ligated breakpoints). Although no followup on these children was conducted, the study suggest that B-lymphoblastic leukemia with TCF3::PBX1 fusion at least in some cases may have prenatal origin.

While it is not common in adult acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), the t(1;19)(q23;p13) rearrangement is still a hallmark for favorable prognosis in a retrospective cohort study with 427 adult patients(from 1992-2017) treated at The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center. 16(4%) patients were positive with the rearrangement and all achieved complete remission after treatment with HyperCVAD (n = 14) or Augmented BFM (n = 2). With a median of 7-year followup, the 5-year overall survival rate for patients with this rearrangement is 82%, better than other groups(p=0.001).

560 of 37,056 patients from hospitals across China were found to contain RET mutations with the prevalence highest in thyroid cancer (6.45%), mediastinal tumor (7.69%), uterine cancer (3.94%), urinary system cancer (3.85%), ovarian cancer (3.81%) and colorectal cancer (3.39%). After filtering out mutations found with other co-occuring well-known driver mutations (in order to reduce potential passenger mutations), 315 out of 560 (56%) patients with 252 distinct RET mutations were identified. 55 of these mutations were found in at least 2 tumors and were enriched in the cadherin-like domain 1 (CLD1) (approximate position: residues 1 to 150) and the C-terminal lobe of tyrosine kinase domain (TKD) (approximate position: residues 810 to 1010), indicating that mutations in these two domains might be largely involved in RET activation. Recurrent mutations at specific residues of the C-terminal lobe of the tyrosine kinase domain include L812Q/R (2), G814A/V (2), R820S/H (3), G830R (2), E884A/K (2), G885R/W (2), E901K (2), S904F/P (2), M918T (7), T930K/M/P (4), and P992L (2). (The number in parentheses indicates the number of patients with a RET mutation at that specific residue and no other driver genomic alterations identified.) In addition a G792E mutation in the N-terminal lobe of the tyrosine kinase domain occurred in 2 patients. Further functional assessment would be needed to confirm oncogenicity which was done for a few mutations.

Recurrent somatic mutations within or near the RET kinase domain (T930K/M/P and D898_E901del) were identified in a large study of 37,056 East Asian cancer patients. After excluding RET mutations with co-existing driver mutations and predicted benign variants, M918T was the most frequent mutation, observed in 3 lung cancers, 3 thyroid cancers and 1 neuroendocrine tumor. In vitro functional tests were run with RET M918T as a positive control and RET WT as a negative control. Ba/F3 cells expressing full length RET harboring M918T, T930P, T930K and D898_E901del, but not T930M, vector control, or RET WT grew in the absence of IL-3 supporting oncogenicity of these 4 variants. When expressed in NIH3T3 cells, both RET M918T and D898_E901del induced ERK phosphorylation, whereas other RET mutants did not, suggesting these 2 mutations have more potent gain-of-function properties.

An experimental study with conditional knockin mice demonstrated that TCF3::PBX1 fusion gene by itself is not sufficient for leukemogenesis and the participation of additional genetic aberrations was required

28 yo with acute B-lymphoblastic leukemia. RNA seq showed KIF5B::FGFR1 fusion. Fusion was reported to be in-frame. The FGFR1 fusion and its protein expression were validated by Sanger sequencing and Western blot. Flow cytometry showed a B cell phenotype. No myeloid component. Cytogenetic analysis reported a normal karyotype and targeted DNA sequencing identified no driver mutations. Despite the fact that he achieved complete remission after induction regimen, a relapse occurred and he became refractory to chemotherapy, and salvage haploidentical hematopoietic stem cell transplantation failed to control the progressive disease. According to the authors, while the FGFR1 fusions are in general associated with myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with eosinophilia, this KIF5B::FGFR1 fusion in this patient was identified in the context of B-ALL with no evidence for myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with eosinophilia. The authors commented that the patient's clinical characteristics (young male, absence of eosinophilia, no MPN history, poor outcome) support a diagnosis of BCR-ABL1 like ALL rather than typical myeloid/lymphoid neoplasia

70 yo with t(8;22)(p11;q11) and BCR::FGFR1 rearrangement presenting as pre-B ALL with complex cytogenetic abnormalities. Flow cytometric analysis at diagnosis showed B cell immunophenotype. BCR-FGFR1 fusion transcript between BCR exon 4 and FGFR1 exon 9 was found by RT-PCR and confirmed by direct sequencing of the amplified fragment. 8 months after diagnosis, while ongoing maintenance therapy, the patient developed progressive thrombocytosis (PLT 1.035 × 109/l) and neutrophilic leukocytosis (WBC 14.1 × 109/l) with 60% granulocytes. BM biopsy documented an initial relapse within a trilineage myelodysplasia. According to the authors, the patient developed progression in the context of 8p11 eosinophilic myeloproliferative syndrome (EMS). They speculate that the additional chromosomal abnormalities could be linked to the B-lymphoid transformation since they affected genes such as IKZF1, PAX5, MLLT3, regulating B-lymphoid development. the authors conclude that this case supports a multi-step model for EMS evolution: a first event involving a tyrosine-kinase gene (FGFR1) and subsequent events that affected transcription factors and other genes leading to loss of differentiation and consequently to disease progression. It is likely that BCR contributes to the peculiar features of EMS with t(8;22) and cooperates with specific secondary genetic lesions in influencing the transformation which may involve lymphoid or myeloid lineage.

This study investigates the relation between TP53 mutation status and VEGFA expression by analyzing data from 7,525 distinct tumor samples sourced from the TCGA database. The findings reveal a significant increase in VEGFA mRNA tissue expression specifically in TP53 mutated adenocarcinomas, contrasting with the absence of such increase in squamous cell cancers. This correlation also sheds light on the mechanisms underlying the observed sensitivity to anti-angiogenic therapies in certain TP53-mutated tumors.

molecular_profile: NBN Loss OR ATM Loss OR MUS81 Loss OR RAD51B Loss OR BRCA2 Loss
evidence_statement: To test for genes associated with PARPi response, a literature review of 79 publications was done, followed by CRISPR-Cas9 cell competition assays in combination with olaparib treatment in six EOC cell lines. Additional cell proliferation and survival assays were also used to confirm the data collected from the CRISPR-Cas9 competition assays. The study reported that only ATM, MUS81, NBN, BRCA2, and RAD51B are predictive markers for response to olaparib.

In this 2022 study by Peng et al., the authors performed whole-genome sequencing on 53 tumor-normal pairs from patients with Dermatofibrosarcoma Protuberans (DFSP) to define its comprehensive genomic landscape. The diagnostic role of the COL1A1::PDGFB fusion was a central focus, and its presence was investigated using fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) on 43 of the samples. The COL1A1::PDGFB fusion was identified in 74% (32/43) of the DFSP cases, confirming its status as a primary diagnostic driver. The authors noted that the breakpoint in the PDGFB gene was consistently stable, occurring between exon 1 and exon 2, while the breakpoints in the COL1A1 gene were highly variable, occurring between exons 5 and 48. The study also identified that cases harboring this fusion gene presented with significantly higher Ki67 expression, a marker of cellular proliferation, and were associated with a significantly longer disease duration compared to fusion-negative cases. The authors concluded that the COL1A1::PDGFB fusion is a fundamental diagnostic marker in DFSP, and its detection is critical for confirming the diagnosis, especially in a cohort where its prevalence may be influenced by factors such as patient age.

COL1A1::PDGFB fusion is typically found in dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans, but this study revealed it could appear in uterine sarcoma, and the presence of this fusion was suggested as a feature for a subgroup of uterine sarcoma with a morphology resembling fibrosarcoma.

In a phase 2 trial, 152 previously-treated metastatic NSCLC patients harboring mutations in ERBB2 (HER2) were treated with 2 different doses of the HER2 ADC trastuzumab deruxtecan (5.4 mg/kg and 6.4 mg/kg) once every 3 weeks. Both cohorts received clinical benefit with an ORR of 49% (95% CI, 39 to 59) and a median duration of response of 16.8 months (95% CI, 6.4 to not estimable [NE]) in the 5.4 mg/kg cohort and an ORR of 56% (95% CI, 41 to 70) and median duration of response of NE (95% CI, 8.3 to NE) in the 6.4 mg/kg cohort. Authors noted that deep and durable responses were seen regardless of HER2 mutation type, HER2 amplification status, baseline CNS metastasis, or prior treatment at both dose levels, but 5.4 mg/kg was associated with a more favorable safety profile.

In a cohort of 20 patients with dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans that were previously negative for COL1A1::PDGFB fusion with fluorescence in situ hybridization, RNA-sequencing was applied. novel and recurrent PDGFD rearrangements, including COL6A3::PDGFD and EMILIN2::PDGFD fusions, were found in 11 of them. Among the remaining 9 cases, 8 were positive with classical COL1A1::PDGFB fusion and the last one failed to show a fusion transcript by RNA-sequencing with all the algorithms the authors used.

This phase 3 study evaluated the PARP inhibitor talazoparib in combination with the androgen receptor inhibitor enzalutamide as a first-line treatment in patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer harboring mutations in homologous recombination repair (HRR) genes. 399 patients harboring mutations in BRCA2 (33.8%), ATM (21.6%), CDK12 (18.8%), CHEK2 (17.8%), BRCA1 (5.8%), PALB2 (4.3%), ATR (3.8%), NBN (2.8%), MLH1 (2.5%), FANCA (2.3%), RAD51C (1.0%), or MRE11A (0.8%) were randomized to receive talazoparib + enzalutamide or placebo + enzalutamide. Patients with BRCA1/BRCA2 alterations were found to have an 80% lower risk of radiographic progression or death (HR, 0.20; 95% CI, 0.11-0.36; P < 0.0001). A statistically significant improvement in progression-free survival was observed in patients with BRCA2 mutations who received talazoparib compared to placebo (hazard ratio 0.19, 95% CI: 0.10-0.38, p < 0.0001). The median progression-free survival was not reached (NR) in the talazoparib arm compared to 11 months in the placebo arm. Statistical significance was reached in part due to the high number of evaluable BRCA2 mutant patients with 55 patients in the talazoparib arm and 60 in the placebo arm.

The median progression-free survival was 21.9 months in the talazoparib arm compared to 13.8 months in the placebo arm in CDK12 mutant patients (28 in the talazoparib arm, 30 in the placebo arm).

There were 35 evaluable patients in the talazoparib arm and 22 in the placebo arm.

The median progression-free survival was 22.1 months in the talazoparib arm and not reached (NR) in the placebo arm.

A phase 3 trial (NCT03748641) evaluated the clinical benefit of the PARP inhibitor niraparib in combination with abiraterone acetate plus prednisone (AAP) in metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer patients with or without homologous recombination repair (HRR) gene alterations as determined by tissue/plasma-based assays. Of 423 patients with HRR mutations, 41.1% (174) has a single gene alteration in BRCA2, 3.8% (16) in BRCA1, 20.1% (85) in ATM, 9.0% (38) in CHEK2, 3.1% (13) in CDK12, 2.8% (12) in PALB2, 2.6% (11) in FANCA, 1.9% (8) in BRIP1, 1.2% (5) in HDAC2, and the remaining 14.4% (61) patients had more than one HRR gene mutated in their tumor. Median rPFS (radiographic progression free survival) in the BRCA1/2 subgroup was longer in the niraparib + AAP arm (16.6 months) than the placebo + AAP arm (10.9 months) with HR of 0.53 (95%CI, 0.36 to 0.79, P= 0.001). In this phase 2a clinical trial, 26 patients with either BRCA1-deficient or BAP1-deficient mesotheliomas were treated with Rucaparib. 38% of the patients were BAP1 and BRCA1 negative, 89% were BAP1 negative, and 50% were BRCA1 negative. The disease control rate at 24 weeks was 23% (95% CI 9-44). Overall, the study reported positive clinical activity of Rucaparib in the patients with minimal adverse effects.

In this study, 23 patients with refractory mesothelioma harbouring germline or somatic BAP1 mutations were treated with olaparib. The median PFS was 3.6 months (95% CI, 2.7-4.2), and the median OS was 8.7 months (95% CI 4.7 - not estimable). The study reported limited activity of olaparib in somatic BAP1 mutations.

56-year-old women was diagnosed with a stage IV ovarian cancer. Debulking surgery, and chemotherapy was given for 10 months. In the clinical trial NCT01775072, one patient had TPR::NTRK1 positive non-small cell lung cancer, and had a partial response with larotrectinib treatment before eventual progression.

A six month old M infant had a left upper extremity mass. The histology indicated mesenchymal neoplasm and no ETV6 rearrangement was found with FISH. Copy number aberrations were found together with The novel fusion SPECC1L-NTRK3. Since surgical resection would have caused extensive damage to the infant's musculature, neoadjuvant larotrectinib was given. After six cycles there was considerable tumor shrinkage. Limited surgical resection was performed and showed no residual tumor.

A 9-month-old boy with no family history of cancer presented with increased head circumference, and MRI demonstrated a solid lesion in the left frontal lobe. A subtotal surgical resection was performed, and 90% of the tumor volume was removed. Afterwards, a second surgery was performed. The tumor was diagnosed as gliosarcoma, WHO grade IV. Chemotherapy was given using the BABY POG protocol for 8 months, resulting in a stable lesion. Ki-67 was positive in 30% of neoplastic cells. INI1 expression was retained, and p53 showed focal positivity. A final diagnosis of infant-type hemispheric glioma was made. A solid tumor panel revealed a TPR (exon 33)–NTRK1 (exon 12) fusion. The patient was treated with larotrectinib at 100 mg/m²/day, given twice daily. At 3 months, stable residual disease was seen, and at 8 months, the characteristics of the tumor had changed, suggesting necrosis. The patient showed improved quality of life and age-appropriate neuropsychomotor development with no side effects.

FFPE samples from 351 primary thyroid carcinomas were subjected to targeted gene rearrangement next-generation sequencing, and 11 NTRK rearrangements were found, all with intact kinase domains, and including two with TPR-NTRK1 ((e20::e11) and (e21::e12)). One of them was a 54 year old male with history of radiotherapy in adolescence for acne, and had stage T3N1b thyroid carcinoma with lung metastasis at recurrence. After two cycles of larotrectinib disease burden decreased by 33% and remained stable for the subsequent 15 months leading to the study endpoint.

A 4.3-year-old girl had I-131–refractory papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC). There was lymph node involvement and lung metastases. She underwent thyroidectomy and neck dissection, and administration of I-131. After the second dose of I-131, there was no further uptake, and progressive lung disease was seen. The cancer was BRAF wild-type, and a TPR-NTRK1 rearrangement was found. Larotrectinib was started at 100 mg twice daily. After 4 weeks, considerable improvement was seen on CT. Radioiodine uptake was restored in the neck and lungs.

In this study, an EZH2 inhibitor was tested for effectiveness against KDM6A-null cancer in mouse and patient-derived xenografts. The growth of KDM6A null tumours was significantly inhibited in the in vivo models treated with EZH2 inhibitors. In this pre-clinical study, RAF inhibition and RAF inhibition in combination with MEK inhibition was tested in vivo in RAF1-amplified tumors (in both mice and PDX tumor models). The models were treated with either RAF265 alone or in combination with trametinib. Monitoring the tumor growth revealed that treated tumors were significantly smaller than untreated tumors. Additionally, tumors from treated mice were significantly smaller than those from untreated mice (0.34g vs 1.6g; P = 0.0008). Overall, it was reported that tumors with RAF1 amplifications may be sensitive to RAF plus MEK inhibition.

The effect of the MCL-1 inhibitor was tested in 21 human myeloma cell lies and bone marrow aspirates from 47 patients newly diagnosed with multiple myeloma. It was reported that patients with 1q21 amplifications are sensitive to MCL-1 inhibition.

evidence_statement: Comprehensive molecular studies through whole genome, whole exome, transcriptome sequencing, genome-wide copy number analysis, clustering analysis by DNA methylation profiling, as well as mutation hotspot analysis by Sanger sequencing and FISH were performed in a cohort of 91 low-grade neuroepithelial tumors (LGNTs) in 2016. Molecular alterations were detected in 31/32 (97%) of LGNTs with an astrocytic morphology, including 17 diffuse astrocytomas and 15 angiocentric gliomas, and the dominant lesions were MYB fusions (21/32; 66%). A MYB::QKI fusion characterized almost all angiocentric gliomas (13/15; 87%) with the reamining two tumors harborting a MYB::ESR1 fusion (1/15) or QKI rearrangement (1/15). The last case with QKI rearrangement had no apparent involvement of MYB or MYBL1, only showing split signals using FISH break-apart probes across QKI. However, the study did not have sufficient derivatives from this tumor for FFPE RNA-seq, so it was unable to determine whether a cryptic MYB::QKI aberration was present in this case, or whether QKI was fused to another gene partner. Most MYB::QKI fusions (78%) were between MYB exon 15 and QKI exon 5. Fusions were also identified between MYB exon 9 and QKI exon 5. These fusions removed the 3'UTR regulatory site or the entire inhibitory C-terminal domain of MYB, leading to its overexpression. Two tumors with a MYB::QKI fusion also harbored a BRAF p.V600E mutation.

In this trial, 19 patients with pediatric brain tumours (1 patient with Astrocytoma, 1 with Fibrillary Astrocytoma, 10 with Pilocytic Astrocytoma, 5 with Ganglioglioma and 2 with Pleomorphic Xanthoastrocytoma) harbouring BRAF V600E were treated with vemurafenib. The study reported a positive response to the treatment, with 1 complete response, 5 partial responses, and 13 patients with stable disease.

From 1101 patients enrolled in 4 consecutive acute lymphoblastic leukemia clinical trials at St Jude Children's Research Hospital (1979-1994), 45 of them were identified to bear t(1;19)(q23;p13) or der(19)t(1;19)(q23;p13) translocation [now known to correspond to TCF3::PBX1 fusion]. The t(1;19) and der(19)t(1;19) cases were characterized by CD19+/CD10+/CD34-/CD20+ or - immunophenotye, as opposed to CD19+/CD10+ or -/CD34+/CD20+ or - immunophenotype observed in translocation negative cases. The prognosis was intermediate regardless of whether the translocation was present in a balanced or unbalanced form. The overall evaluation of immunologic, cytogenetic and clinical features suggested that patients with the t(1;19) or der(19)t(1;19) abnormalities constituted a distinctive subgroup.

The study compiled clinicopathologic and molecular features of 46 gliomas with a MYB or MYBL1 alteration diagnosed at a single center. The tumors showed low-grade histopathologic features and were broadly classified as diffuse astrocytoma (n = 11) or angiocentric glioma (n=35). Molecular alterations interrogated by immunohistochemistry (n=46), RNA sequencing (n=29), FISH (n=24), or PCR-based sequencing (n=11) revealed MYB (n=44) or MYBL1 (n=2) alterations in all tumors. MYB and MYBL1 were fused with various gene partners. None had alterations in IDH1, IDH2, TP53, ATRX, or histone H3 genes. Regardless of histopathologic diagnosis or anatomic location, DNA methylome profiling on 35 MYB/MYBL1-altered gliomas formed a single cluster, supporting that MYB/MYBL1-altered gliomas represent a single disease entity with a range of clinical and pathologic characteristics. Only MYB rearrangements were detected in angiocentric gliomas. Of the 35 angiocentric gliomas, 22 had identified gene partners, primarily QKI (n=19), PCDHGA1 (n=1), LOC105378099 (n=1) and ESR1 (n=1).

Copy-number analysis was performed on 44 diffuse pediatric low-grade gliomas (PLGGs) to identify recurrent alterations. The most significant event, focal 8q13.1 gain, was observed in 28% (5/18) of diffuse astrocytoma grade IIs (DA2), resulting in partial duplication of the transcription factor MYBL1 with truncation of its C-terminal negative-regulatory domain. A recurrent deletion-truncation breakpoint between exons 10 and 11 of MYB on 6q23.3 was identified in two of four angiocentric gliomas (AGs). This study did not mention the partner genes involved in the MYB rearrangements in the two AGs. The results define clinically relevant molecular subclasses of diffuse PLGGs and highlight a potential role for the MYB family in the biology of low-grade gliomas.

A research study performed in 2010 involved 57 pediatric low-grade gliomas (LGGs) and a comparison group of 59 pediatric high-grade gliomas (HGGs). Among the LGG group, there were 34 cases of pilocytic astrocytomas (PAs) and 23 cases of diffuse gliomas, which included fibrillary astrocytomas (DAs, n=14), oligodendroglial tumors (n=7), and angiocentric gliomas (AGs, n=2). The study utilized SNP arrays and FISH to detect MYB rearrangements, and quantitative RT-PCR and immunohistochemistry (IMHC) to analyze MYB expression levels. Results revealed increased MYB expression in both AGs, with one AG showing a focal deletion in the 3' terminal region of MYB. Overall, increased MYB expression by RT-PCR was seen in 8 LGGs, including 5 DAs, 2 AGs, and 1 oligodendroglioma, and all three cases with MYB copy number aberrations. IMHC revealed an increase in MYB expression at the protein level in 60% of LGGs) including 41% of PAs, and 19% of HGGs. Notably, genomic abnormalities were exclusively observed in diffuse gliomas.The findings suggest that MYB dysregulation may contribute to pediatric gliomas through various mechanisms beyond amplification and deletion.

evidence_statement: In this 2012 study O’Meara et al. included 51 clear cell sarcoma of kidney (CCSK). Using an index CCSK with the t(10;17)(q22;p13) identified by cytogenetics, they were able to map the breakpoints and identified the gene fusion transcript YHWAE::FAM22, currently known as YHWAE::NUTM2. Using RT-PCR they screened an additional 50 samples. Overall, fusion positive transcripts of YHWAE::NUTM2 were detected in 7/51 (14%) cases. Ages of the patients ranged from 0 to 6 years. This rearrangement produces an in-frame YWHAE::NUTM2 fusion transcript, comprising exons 1–5 of YWHAE and exons 2–7 of NUTM2. Of the 3 cases with RNA sufficient to sequence the entire coding region, the YWHAE fusion partner was identified as either NUTM2B (FAM22B) or NUTM2E (FAM22E). None of the transcript-positive cases presented with stage I disease, suggesting the fusion may be associated with poorer outcome. Tumor cellularity was significantly higher in the cases that were transcript-positive.

molecular_profile: YWHAE::NUTM2A Fusion OR YWHAE::NUTM2B Fusion OR YWHAE::NUTM2E Fusion
evidence_statement: In this 2020 study Kenny et al. included 68 cases of clear cell sarcoma of the kidney (CCSK). Using RT-PCR with RNA extracted from FFPE tumour tissue they detected a YWHAE::NUTM2 fusion transcript in 1/68 (1.5%) of cases. The majority of cases (54/68, 79%) had a BCOR ITD which is mutually exclusive with the YWHAE::NUTM2 fusion. The group generated a cell line model system in which inducible expression of YWHAE::NUTM2 could be used to identify reliable immunohistochemical markers. The study concluded that reliance on a single marker in CCSK is not ideal and suggested BCOR, TLE1 and CCND1 could be useful as a group of markers, with the YWHAE::NUTM2 case as well as BCOR-ITD cases staining strongly for all three of these markers, while 63 control samples from tumor types often considered in the differential diagnosis were negative or weakly staining.

molecular_profile: YWHAE::NUTM2A Fusion OR YWHAE::NUTM2B Fusion OR YWHAE::NUTM2E Fusion
evidence_statement: In this 2016 study Kenny et al. included 159 cases of clear cell sarcoma of the kidney (CCSK). RNA was extracted from either snap-frozen or FFPE tumour tissue samples and real-time PCR used to identify YWHAE::NUTM2 fusions. Of the 102 cases tested, 2 (2%) were positive for the YWHAE::NUTM2 fusion transcript. The two cases were both aged less than a year (mean of 9 months), both male, and disease stage II or III/IV. The YWHAE::NUTM2 fusion transcript is present in only a minority of CCSKs, however the observation of the same rearrangement in high-grade endometrial stromal sarcoma, suggests this translocation is oncogenic.

In this study, the authors analyzed two index cases of pseudomyogenic haemangioendothelioma and 10 additional cases by interphase FISH. Both index cases showed a balanced t(7;19)(q22;q13) translocation. Interphase FISH confirmed recurrent rearrangement involving chromosomes 7q22 and 19q13 in the majority of additional cases. Using mRNA sequencing and RT–PCR, the authors identified and confirmed recurrent in-frame fusions between SERPINE1 and FOSB in both index tumors. Quantitative real-time PCR demonstrated significantly increased FOSB mRNA expression compared with other soft tissue tumors. The authors conclude that SERPINE1::FOSB is a recurrent fusion in pseudomyogenic haemangioendothelioma and that FOSB overexpression may serve as a useful diagnostic marker for this tumor.

The study evaluated FOS and FOSB immunohistochemistry (IHC) in osteoid osteoma (n=23), osteoblastoma (n=22), and other bone tumor types to gauge the specificity of FOS/FOSB IHC for diagnosing these tumor types. Control groups included reactive bone lesions, proliferative bone lesions, giant cell tumor of bone, aneurysmal bone cyst, chondromyxoid fibroma, osteosarcoma, chondroblastoma, and clear cell chondrosarcoma. Strong nuclear expression of FOS was observed in all osteoid osteomas (22 of 22) and 57% of osteoblastomas (12 of 21), but was rare in the control cases (3/197). FOS rearrangements were present in 94% of osteoid osteomas and osteoblastomas, with an 86% concordance between FISH and IHC. Two osteoblastomas (5%) were positive for FOSB, but FISH did not reveal any FOSB rearrangements in these cases. The study concluded that FOS IHC can be used to diagnose osteoid osteoma and osteoblastoma. FISH could be employed in cases where low-level or focal FOS expression causes diagnostic challenges.

This study investigated two cases of osteoblastoma to identify genetic aberrations using cytogenetic analysis, RNA sequencing, and molecular analyses. In the first case, a FOS::ANKH fusion transcript was identified, where exon 4 of the FOS gene was fused with sequences from intron 1 of the ANKH gene. In the second case, a FOS::RUNX2 fusion transcript was detected, involving the fusion of exon 4 of FOS with sequences from intron 5 of the RUNX2 gene. In both fusion events, the fusion introduced a stop codon and removed sequences involved in the regulation of FOS expression.

disease: Acute Myeloid Leukemia With Inv(16)(p13.1q22) Or T(16;16)(p13.1;q22)
evidence_statement: This study evaluated the independent prognostic significance of pretreatment cytogenetics based on the large Medical Research Council (MRC) AML 10 trial which enrolled a total of 1,966 patients (364 children and 1,602 adults). All patients diagnosed with de novo AML (337 children and 1,460 adults) or secondary AML (22 children and 119 adults) received comparable therapy. The study concluded that patients with different cytogenetics abnormalities can be divided into 3 prognostic subgroups with favorable, intermediate, and adverse outcomes solely based on the results of cytogenetics. AML with inv(16) [which results in CBFB::MYH11 fusion] were grouped together with AML with t(8;21) [RUNX1::RUNX1T1 fusion] and t(15;17) [PML::RARA fusion] in the favorable group.

In this phase 2 clinical study, 28 patients with recurrent Clear Cell Carcinoma of the Ovary, Fallopian Tube, Peritoneum, or Endometrium, harboring either wild-type ARID1A or ARID1A loss were recruited, and treated with Dasatinib. Of the 28 patients, 15 patients had retained BAF250a, while 13 had a loss of BAF250a. In this cohort, 53.6% of the patients had disease progression, 28% had stable disease, however, only one patient had a partial response. The median duration of stable disease was 5.67 months (3.55 - 20.73) in the loss of BAF250a group, and it was 4.65 months (1.58 - 17.84) in the retained BAF250a group. Overall, the study reported that Dasatinib was not effective as a single-agent treatment for recurrent Clear Cell Carcinoma.

A research study performed in 2010 involved 57 pediatric low-grade gliomas (LGGs) and a comparison group of 59 pediatric high-grade gliomas (HGGs). Among the LGG group, there were 34 cases of pilocytic astrocytomas (PAs) and 23 cases of diffuse gliomas, which included fibrillary astrocytomas (DA, n=14), oligodendroglial tumors (n=7), and angiocentric gliomas (AG, n=2). The study utilized SNP arrays and FISH to detect MYB rearrangements and quantitative RT-PCR and immunohistochemistry (IMHC) to analyze MYB expression levels. Gains involving MYB and MYB amplifications that upregulate MYB RNA and protein expression were demonstrated in 2/14 diffuse astrocytomas (DAs). No MYB fusions were detected in the two DAs, but the sequence from one DA was found to terminate within MYB exon 9. In addition, the study revealed increased MYB expression in both AGs, with one AG showing a focal deletion in the 3' terminal region of MYB. Overall, increased MYB expression by RT-PCR was seen in 8 LGGs, including 5 DAs, 2 AGs, and 1 oligodendroglioma, and in all three cases with MYB copy number aberrations. IMHC revealed an increase in MYB expression at the protein level in 60% of LGGs including 41% of PAs, and 19% of HGGs. Notably, genomic abnormalities were exclusively observed in diffuse gliomas. The findings suggest that MYB dysregulation may contribute to pediatric gliomas, particularly in diffuse gliomas, through various mechanisms beyond amplification and deletion.

disease: Acute Myeloid Leukemia With Inv(16)(p13.1q22) Or T(16;16)(p13.1;q22)
evidence_statement: This is a Cancer and Leukemia Group B study on core binding factor (CBF) AML (2005): AML with RUNX1::RUNX1T1 (303 adult patients who received treatment) vs AML with CBFB::MYH11 (164 patients who received treatment). The authors showed that AML-CBF should not be seen as one entity and consists of two distinct entities with AML with CBFB::MYH11 having better overall survival (OS) in general and after relapse despite of similar treatment. Additional abnormality (trisomy 22) in AML with CBFB::MYH11 was linked to longer relapse-free survival in adult patients with AML with CBFB::MYH11 younger than 60years.

disease: Acute Myeloid Leukemia With Inv(16)(p13.1q22) Or T(16;16)(p13.1;q22)
evidence_statement: A metanalysis study from the German AML Intergroup (2004) on AML-CBF included 8 German multicenter treatment trials enrolling patients with AML with RUNX1::RUNX1T1 (191 adult patients) and CBFB::MYH11 (201 patients). Patients with AML with CBFB::MYH11 had much higher rate of achieving complete remission (CR) after reinduction therapy compared to AML with RUNX1::RUNX1T1 group. Trisomy 22 emerged as the sole independent prognostic marker associated with superior progression-free survival in the CBFB::MYH11 group, underscoring the diagnostic and prognostic value of CBFB::MYH11 in risk stratification and clinical management of AML.

disease: Acute Myeloid Leukemia With Inv(16)(p13.1q22) Or T(16;16)(p13.1;q22)
evidence_statement: A small study on 18 patients of AML with inv(16)(p13q22) [now known to correspond to CBFB::MYH11 fusion] identified abnormal eosinophils as a unique morphologic characteristic of this entity. 76.5% achieved complete remission and 59% remained in first remission. The main conclusion was that AML with inv(16) represents a unique subtype of AML with distinct morphology, cytogenetics, and favorable prognosis.

The PLCG1 S345F mutation has been reported as a hotspot mutation in adult T-cell Leukemia/Lymphoma (ATL). This study performed in vitro characterization of the mutation by identifying an ATL cell line (KK1) that harbored a heterozygous copy of the variant. The authors report an increase of basal Phospholipase C (PLC) activity in vitro compared to wild type. By creating a KK1 derivative cell line with a reversion of the S345F mutation, the authors show reduced PLC activity, lower rates of proliferation and aggregation, and reduction in chemotaxis.

This study used micropatterned surfaces to enrich fluorophore-tagged FGFR3 in specific areas of the plasma membrane. Researchers quantified receptor activation by capturing cellular activity using total internal reflection fluorescence microscopy (recruitment of downstream signal transducer growth factor receptor-bound 2 or GRB2 tagged with mScarlet). They tested the activation of FGFR3 upon ligand addition (fgf1 and fgf2) for WT and four FGFR3 mutations (G380R, Y373C, K650Q, and K650E). Ligand addition increased GRB2 recruitment to WT FGFR3. Cells expressing K508M were used as a negative control as it inhibits the transautophosphorylation of the FGFR3 kinase domain and variant almost completely abolished GRB2-mScarlet colocalization (mean CmScarlet = 0.05 ± 0.01). Ligand addition did not induce GRB2 recruitment in cells expressing K508M (mean CmScarlet = 0.05 ± 0.01), indicating a kinase dead variant.

Paper analysing FGFR3-TACC3 frequency and oncogenicity in nasopharyngeal carcinoma. FGFR3-TACC3-K508M in HNE1 and HK1 NPC cell lines showed a significant reduction of cellular proliferation in the colony formation assay and anchorage-independent assay compared with FGFR3-TACC3. The author suggests the kinase activity of FGFR3 is essential for cell proliferation and transformation ability in the fusion context (Fig. 4).

The study analysed the expression of the two splice variants of FGFR3 (FGFR3-IIIb and FGFR3-IIIc/FGFR3-IIIc-KD) in two pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma cell lines (Capan-2 and BxPC-3). The FGFR3-IIIc-KD variant corresponds to the K508M variant. While the cells were able to form clones in both splice variants, this ability was decreased when the cells were transduced with the IIIc splice variant lacking the tyrosine kinase activity (K508M). Based on the study, the author suggests that variant K508M may have tumor suppressive properties, and the negative impact on tumor progression was related to FGFR3 tyrosine kinase activity.

A study that aims to analyse the biological significance of the FGFR3-TACC3 fusion. They transfected K508M (also referred to as KD or kinase-dead) variant FGFR3-TACC3 fusion transcript into cervical epithelial cell lines. FGFR3-TACC3 fusion transcript led to activation of the MAPK pathway via increased phosphorylation of ERK. However, overexpression of the FGFR-TACC3 KD fusion induced neither phosphorylation of downstream ERK nor phosphorylation of AKT in any of the four cell lines (SiHa, ME180, HeLa, and Ca Ski) (Fig. 2). Colony-forming ability was reduced compared to the FGFR3-TACC3 fusion-transfected cell lines (Fig. 3).

cDNAs encoding wild-type FGFR3 and other variants such as the kinse dead K508M (F3-B-KD) were inserted into the pCXND3 vector and used to transfect cells. No phosphorylation of the K508M variant was detected (Fig. 3).

HeLa, 293T and RCS cells were transfected with N540K, G380R, R248C, Y373C, K650M, K650E and K508M to test STAT1(Y701) activation. The assay showed no activation in cells transfected with the kinase-inactive K508M-FGFR3 (Figure 2).

Study show that the FGFR3-TACC3 (F3-T3) fusion triggers peroxisome biogenesis and new protein synthesis, enabling mitochondrial respiration and tumor growth. They expressed F3-T3 fusion in immortalized human astrocytes and compared gene expression profiles of cells treated with an inhibitor of FGFR TK or vector. HA-F3-T3 were also compared with the astrocytes expressing the kinase-dead F3-T3-K508M and HA transduced with an empty vector. They found that F3-T3-K508M did not activate mitochondrial biogenesis and had similar transcriptional activities to the empty vector. (See Fig.1)

The study found that TGFβ-activated kinase 1 (TAK1) is a novel protein that interacts and is targeted by FGFR3 kinase activity. Activating mutations in FGFR3 modulate expression of genes that regulate NFkB signaling. Experiments showed that TAK1 was tyrosine phosphorylated in HEK293 cells transiently expressing constitutively active K650E, but not the kinase-dead K508M (Fig. 1-2).

The study found that FGFR3 interacts with a regulatory subunit of PI3K, and this interaction negatively regulates the Ras/ERK/MAPK pathway in response to FGFR3 activity. This interaction could be a potential therapeutic target for multiple myeloma. The researchers used three FGFR3 plasmids to demonstrate this interaction. The plasmid with the K605E variant showed that FGFR3 can interact with multiple PI3K regulatory proteins. However, for the plasmid carrying the K508M variant, there was no FGFR3 activation, which disrupted the interaction with p85, resulting in no activation of downstream ERK (Fig.2).

Authors wanted to determine Ship2 role in FGF-mediated cell migration. They used the CRISPR/Cas9 system to disrupt the Ship2 gene in RCS cells. They found that loss of SHIP2 converted FGF-mediated sustained ERK activation into a transient signal and rescued phenotypes triggered by pathologic FGFR-ERK signaling. Wild-type SHIP2 did not coimmunoprecipitate with the catalytically inactive K508M mutant form of FGFR3. Wild-type FGFR3 and activating FGFR3-K650M co-immunopreciptated with human SHIP2 when expressed in 293T cells, suggesting that SHIP2 associates preferentially with active FGFR3 which leads to FGFR-ERK signaling. With the kinase-dead K508M mutant, there is no SHIP2 interaction to activate downstream ERK signaling (Fig. 2F).

Rat1A astrocytes cells expressing the FGFR3-TACC3-K508M were tested to evaluate anchorage-independent growth in soft agar (Fig. 2A and table S5) and did not show an ability to grow evidenced by no colony formation (Fig. 2A). FGFR3-TACC3-K508M behaved similarly to the specific FGFR inhibitor PD173074 (Fig. S6, D and E) avoiding constitutive phosphorylation.

A study was conducted to analyze the impact of mutations in the transmembrane and kinase domains that cause skeletal dysplasias. The study used PC12 cells with FGFR3 variants that were introduced by site-directed mutagenesis into the PFR3 chimera. The kinase-inactive K508M was used as a control. The analysis of autophosphorylation was carried out by anti-phosphotyrosine immunoblotting. The cells expressing the variant did not show any signs of ligand dependent or independent phosphorylation (Fig. 2). There were no morphological responses observed in cells containing the variant (Neurite growth, Fig. 3).

A RET c.1894_1899del p.E632_L633del mutation was identified in a 32-year-old patient with a particularly aggressive medullary thyroid cancer. This mutation removes 2 amino acids adjacent to the cysteine 634. To assess the oncogenicity of this mutation, it was introduced into NIH-3T3 cells and cellular transformation activity was assessed in a focus formation assay. RET E632_L633del induced colony formation even more potently (~200 colonies/100 ng DNA) than well-established oncogenic mutations RET C634R (~90 colonies/100 ng DNA) and RET M918T (~20 colonies/100 ng DNA) while RET WT formed few/no colonies. The authors note that the exceptionally strong transforming activity of RET E632_L633del correlates well with the clinical severity of the corresponding tumor with aggressive progression and multiple recurring metastases.

In a colony formation assay with NIH3T3 cells, RET C634R was used as a positive control (called MEN2A after its association with that disease). Cells transformed with C634R showed significant colony formation in comparison to cells expressing wild type RET. C634R cells developed more colonies (9.1x10^2) than the other positive control M918T (1.8x10^2), but less than the tested RET deletion Glu632_Leu633del (2x10^3).

Among 319 medullary thyroid cancer patients enrolled in the LIBRETTO-001 trial, 9 patients harbored the RET p.E632_L633del mutation (c.1894_1899delGAGCTG) in their tumor. After treatment with the selective RET inhibitor selpercatinib, 7 of the 9 patients had a PR (78%) and 2 maintained SD for 44 and 144 weeks, respectively. Median duration of response was 28 months and median progression-free survival was 31 months. These clinical observations were supported by preclinical data showing Ba/F3 cells transformed with RET p.E632_L633del were sensitive to selpercatinib with an IC50 of 16nM.

Preclinical data demonstrated Ba/F3 cells transformed with RET p.M918T were sensitive to selpercatinib with an IC50 of 5nM. M918T was included as a positive control for other variants that were being tested for sensitivity to selpercatinib.

disease: Acute Myeloid Leukemia With T(8;21); (q22; Q22.1)
evidence_statement: In this 1992 study, the authors isolated a clone containing the junction region of the (8;21)(q22;q22) translocation characteristic for acute myeloid leukemia with t(8;21). Using probes from the junction clone, the presence of this consistent junction region was confirmed in 9 independent cases of AML with t(8;21). The authors also isolated cDNA clones from a t(8;21) AML cDNA library that contained fused sequences from chromosomes 8 and 21. This allowed them to identify the chromosome 8 partner gene which they named ETO (currently known as RUNX1T1) and confirm the chromosome 21 partner as AML1 (currently RUNX1), which showed similarity with the Drosophila segmentation gene, runt. The consequence of the t(8;21) was determined to be the juxtaposition of 5' sequences of AML1 (RUNX1) to 3' sequences of ETO (RUNX1T1), oriented telomere to centromere on the der(8) chromosome. The study confirms that t(8;21) consistently results in an oncogenic fusion between specific partner genes, confirming its role as a defining oncogenic abnormality in a subtype of AML.

disease: Acute Myeloid Leukemia With T(8;21); (q22; Q22.1)
phenotypes: Pediatric onset,Intermediate young adult onset,Early young adult onset
evidence_statement: The researchers analyzed immunophenotype in 30 cases of newly diagnosed pediatric acute myeloid leukemia (AML) exhibiting M2 morphology per French-American-British classification. They correlated these findings with cytogenetic data. In 16 out of the 30 cases, the t(8;21)(q22;q22) translocation or its variants were detected. The leukemias harboring t(8;21) did not significantly vary from other M2 cases regarding expression of various cell surface markers like CD11b, CD13, CD14, CD15, CD33, CD34, CD36, CD41a, CD42b, CDw65, TdT, or HLA-DR. However, the B-cell antigen CD19 expression was observed in 81% of t(8;21) cases compared to only 7% of non-t(8;21) M2 cases. Moreover, 63% of t(8;21) cases exhibited the NK-cell antigen CD56 expression versus 14% of non-t(8;21) M2 leukemias. Coexpression of CD19 and CD56 was exclusively found in the t(8;21) group. This coexpression pattern was absent in 48 cases of other AML subtypes lacking t(8;21). Additionally, non-t(8;21) M2 cases frequently expressed CD2 or CD7, while none of the t(8;21) cases did. The authors deduced that t(8;21) defines a biologically unique pediatric M2 AML subgroup with distinct immunophenotypic features differentiating it from other de novo AML types.

phenotypes: Pediatric onset,Middle age onset,Young adult onset
evidence_statement: This study evaluated the independent prognostic significance of pretreatment cytogenetics based on the large Medical Research Council (MRC) AML 10 trial which enrolled a total of 1,966 patients (364 children and 1,602 adults). All patients diagnosed with de novo AML (337 children and 1,460 adults) or secondary AML (22 children and 119 adults) received comparable therapy. The study concluded that patients with different cytogenetic abnormalities can be divided into 3 prognostic subgroups with favorable, intermediate, and adverse outcomes solely based on the results of cytogenetics. AML with t(8;21) [which results in RUNX1::RUNX1T1 fusion] was grouped together with AML with inv(16) [CBFB::MYH11 fusion] and t(15;17) [PML::RARA fusion] in the favorable group. The 122 patients with AML with t(8;21) had a 98% CR (complete remission) rate and 2% induction deaths. The observed prognostic associations further support that these abnormalities define clinically and biologically distinct AML subtypes.

disease: Acute Myeloid Leukemia With T(8;21); (q22; Q22.1)
evidence_statement: The authors of this 1997 paper compared morphologic and cytochemical features between 30 acute myeloid leukemia subtype M2 (AML-M2) patients with t(8;21) and 50 AML-M2 patients without t(8;21). Morphologic characteristics highly enriched in cases positive for t(8;21) included irregular nuclear shape, Auer bodies, at least 90% myeloperoxidase positivity in blast cells, pseudo-Pelger-Huët anomaly of the nuclei, and homogeneous pink-colored cytoplasm of mature neutrophils. These features were observed in 90-100% of the t(8;21) positive cases and were rare in the t(8;21) negative group. Homogeneous pink-colored cytoplasm of mature neutrophils was the most characteristic of t(8;21)positive AML-M2, while pale-colored cytoplasm without any granules in mature neutrophils or dyserythropoietic features was never observed in association with t(8;21). The study suggests association of the t(8;21) with a subtype of AML that has morphologically recognizable features in a high proportion of cases. Of note, AML with t(8;21) translocation is now known to result in a RUNX1::RUNX1T fusion.

In this phase II clinical trial, 40 patients with breast cancer harboring either FGFR1 or FGFR2 alterations (amplifications or mutations) were recruited. Of the 40 patients, 30 had FGFR1 alterations (amplifications in n=26, mutations in n=1, both in n=3), while 10 had FGFR2 alterations (amplifications in n=2, mutations in n=6, both in n = 2). The objective response and disease control rate reported were 7% (95% CI; 1-24) and 27% (90% CI; 13 - 100) respectively. 34% of the patients experienced grade 3 or 4 adverse effects, and of these patients 62% had to permanently discontinue this treatment, while 31% received a dose adjustment. Overall, sunitinib did not meet predetermined criteria to declare clinical activity.

disease: Acute Myeloid Leukemia With CBFA2T3::GLIS2 Fusion
evidence_statement: In this 2012 study they included 14 patients diagnosed with non-down syndrome acute megakaryoblastic leukemia (AMKL), a subtype of pediatric acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Transcriptome sequencing was performed on diagnostic leukemia cells. In 7 of 14 cases a cryptic inversion on chromosome 16 [inv(16)(p13.3q24.3)] was detected that results in the joining of CBFA2T3, a member of the ETO family of nuclear corepressors, to GLIS2, a member of the GLI family of transcription factors. In 6/7 cases exon 10 of CBFA2T3 was fused to exon 3 of GLIS2, while in the remaining case exon 11 of CBFA2T3 was fused to exon 1 of GLIS2. Analysis of a validation cohort consisting of diagnostic leukemia cells from 62 AMKL cases (34 pediatric and 28 adult) revealed 6 additional pediatric samples carrying CBFA2T3::GLIS2 for an overall frequency of 27% (13/48) in pediatric AMKL. Patients found to have the CBFA2T3::GLIS2 gene fusion were aged from 0 - 4 years. Overall the presence of CBFA2T3::GLIS2 identified a subgroup of patients with a significantly worse overall survival. CBFA2T3::GLIS2 functions, in part, as a gain-of-function GLIS2 allele, with enhanced BMP2/4 signaling, however the fusion likely requires cooperating lesions for leukemogenesis.

disease: Acute Myeloid Leukemia With CBFA2T3::GLIS2 Fusion
evidence_statement: In this 2012 study the authors performed high-throughput sequencing of RNA (RNA-seq) of leukemic cells obtained after engraftment in immunodeficient mice from 5 patients with Acute megakaryoblastic leukemia (AMKL). A novel in-frame fusion transcript CBFA2T3::GLIS2 was detected in one sample. They then performed RT-PCR analysis on an independent validation cohort of 22 non-down syndrome (DS) pediatric AMKL, 9 DS AMKL, and 8 adult AMKL samples. They detected the CBFA2T3::GLIS2 fusion in 7/22 non-DS pediatric AMKL samples, but not in DS AMKL or adult AMKL samples. CBFA2T3::GLIS2 fusion results from a chromosomal inversion of chromosome 16 and leads to a fusion between exon 11 of CBFA2T3 and exon 3 of GLIS2. GLIS2 expression was only detected in AMKL samples with the CBFA2T3::GLIS2 fusion, where as CBFA2T3 was expressed in all AMKL samples. Analysis of global gene expression found the fusion was associated with a distinct molecular signature, including up-regulation of NCAM1 and of several target genes of the Hedgehog signaling pathway such as BMP2, BMP4, GATA3, and CCND2.

disease: Acute Myeloid Leukemia With CBFA2T3::GLIS2 Fusion
evidence_statement: In this 2017 study the authors included 74 pediatric patients diagnosed with non-down syndrome acute megakaryoblastic leukemia (AMKL). RNASeq was performed on 62 patients, where sufficient RNA was available, and the other cases underwent RT-PCR, FISH, or southern blotting. The CBFA2T3::GLIS2 fusion was detected in 9 (12%) of pediatric patients diagnosed with non-down syndrome AMKL. The patients were aged 0- 2 years. Patients carrying CBFA2T3::GLIS2 had inferior outcomes.

disease: Acute Myeloid Leukemia With CBFA2T3::GLIS2 Fusion
phenotypes: Juvenile onset,Early young adult onset,Childhood onset,Infantile onset
evidence_statement: This 2013 study included 7 pediatric acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) patients defined as cytogenetically normal (CN). They performed whole-transcriptome massively parallel sequencing and identified a chimeric transcript involving CBFA2T3 and GLIS2, resulting from a cryptic inversion of the telomeric region of chromosome 16 in 3/7 patients. Two patients showed the fusion between exon 11 of CBFA2T3 and exon 3 of GLIS2, while the third showed CBFA2T3 exon 10 fused to exon 2 of GLIS2. Using RT-PCR the authors then examined a validation cohort of 230 children with newly diagnosed de novo CN-AML and identified CBFA2T3::GLIS2 in a further 19 cases with CBFA2T3 exon 11 fused to GLIS2 exon 3. CN-AML patients harboring the CBFA2T3::GLIS2 fusion gene were aged from 0 - 17 years. These results indicate that the CBFA2T3::GLIS2 fusion transcript is not just seen in non-down syndrome AMKL and should be more broadly considered as a genetic abnormality that is shared with pediatric CN-AML where it is also associated with significantly worse event free survival.

A total of 15 pediatric patients with supratentorial ependymomas harboring YAP1::MAMLD1 fusions were reported. In all 15 cases, YAP1::MAMLD1 fusions were confirmed by RT-PCR and sequencing. In the majority of cases (14 of 15), the fusion joined exon 5 of YAP1 with exon 3 of MAMLD1. In 1 case, the fusion occurred between YAP1 exon 5 and MAMLD1 exon 2. Patients tended to be female (13 of 15) and less than 3 years old at diagnosis (12 of 15). All cases exhibited similar histopathological features including moderate to high cellularity with small to medium-sized nuclei, perivascular pseudo-rosettes, and strikingly dot-like epithelial membrane antigen (EMA) positivity. The authors suggest the characteristic histopathological, cytogenetic, and molecular features of this tumor type occurring mostly in young girls less than 3 years of age should be considered a distinct disease entity.

This is a case report of a 26-year-old male patient who sufferred 3 grand mal seizures and was found to have a left frontal lobe ependymoma with a YAP1::FAM118B fusion. No other genetic alterations were identified in the tumor. The authors mention that this is the second case report of an ependymoma with this fusion.

DNA methylation profiling of 500 ependymal tumors identified 9 molecular profiles with 3 occurring in the supratentorial compartment (designated ST EPN). RNA sequencing performed in 7 of the 13 cases that clustered with one of the non-RELA subgroups of supratentorial ependymoma (and had sufficient high-quality RNA) identified YAP1::MAMLD1 fusions in 6 of 7 tumors and a YAP1::FAM118B fusion in the remaining tumor. The YAP1::MAMLD1 fusions consisted of YAP1 exons 1–5 or 1–6 fused in-frame to MAMLD1 exons 2–7 or 3–7. In the YAP1::FAM118B fusion, YAP1 exons 1–7 is fused in-frame to FAM118B exons 3–9. No YAP1 fusions were identified by RNA sequencing in any of the 48 additional ependymal tumors of the other molecular subgroups of the posterior fossa or supratentorial regions. The authors conclude that this demonstrates YAP1 fusion-positive cases characterize another molecular subgroup of ST EPNs distinct from RELA fusion-positive ST EPNs.
