Genomic DNA from liver metastases of four different colorectal cancer patients who had previously undergone 5-FU-based adjuvant chemotherapy was evaluated using digital karyotyping. TYMS amplification was exclusively found in cancer lesions of patients who had been treated with 5-FU. Patients previously treated with 5-FU were separated based on TYMS amplification status, and it was found that overall survival in patients with TYMS gene amplification was significantly lower than patients without TYMS gene amplification (p < 0.01, 329 days v/s 1021 days). Additionally, patients with TYMS amplification also showed a relative risk of death that was 3.5x higher than those without the TYMS amplification (1.06 - 11.4, 95% CI; p < 0.05). These results suggest significant association between presence of TYMS amplification and resistance to 5-FU.

The TYMS DNA copy number was analyzed in 111 patient samples, divided into two groups: those exposed to 5-FU (n = 62) and those not exposed to 5-FU (n = 49). It was found that the 5-FU exposed group had a significantly higher frequency of TYMS amplification compared to the non-exposed group (19% vs. 4%; p = 0.036). No overall survival difference was observed between patients with low or high TYMS copy numbers. However, among patients who underwent chemotherapy following surgical resection of their metastases (n = 54), those with TYMS amplification (n = 8) had a poorer median survival post-resection (2.11 years vs. 3.61 years; p = 0.027). These findings suggest that TYMS amplification might be a mechanism of clinical resistance to 5-FU-based chemotherapy in colorectal cancer patients.

BRD4-NUT fusion was found to be associated with globally decreased histone acetylation and transcriptional repression in gain-of-expression and loss-of-expression assays. Following these results, it was postulated that chromatin acetylation would be restored by treatment of the cell lines with HDACi. In vivo efficacy of HDACi (LBH-589) was tested in 2 luciferized NMC cell line xenograft models (TC-797, PER-403) and significant suppression of tumour growth was noted in both models.

A 10-year-old male patient with NUT Midline Carcinoma (NMC) harbouring the BRD4-NUT fusion gene was treated with vorinostat, an HDAC inhibitor, at a daily dose of 400 mg. In patient-derived NMC cells, vorinostat induced significant squamous differentiation and growth arrest, as evidenced by Ki-67 staining and cell counts, with 8,645 cells showing these effects. After 5 weeks of treatment, PET imaging revealed a notable decrease in tumour uptake of F-fluorodeoxyglucose. When xenografted patient tumour cells were treated with LBH-589, another HDAC inhibitor, there was a substantial growth inhibition (p=0.0003). However, vorinostat was discontinued due to severe grade 3 toxicities, including nausea and vomiting. Additionally, tumour recurrence was observed after 5 weeks of treatment. The patient passed due to recurrent and metastatic disease 11 months after initial diagnosis.

Ba/F3 mouse lymphoid cells expressing wild-type or V777L mutant HER2 were treated with afatinib, neratinib, osimertinib or DMSO (vehicle) for 72 hours, at which time viable cells were measured using the Alamar Blue cell viability assay. Comparison of IC50 values demonstrated that cells expressing V777L mutant HER2 were sensitive to all three drugs. A separate experiment assessing the relative growth of V777L HER2-transduced Ba/F3 cells in the presence of inhibitors indicated that compared to wild-type the cells expressing the mutant protein were also sensitive to lapatinib and sapatinib but resistant to trastuzumab.

Ba/F3 mouse lymphoid cells expressing wild-type or V777L mutant HER2 were treated with afatinib, neratinib, osimertinib or DMSO (vehicle) for 72 hours, at which time viable cells were measured using the Alamar Blue cell viability assay. Comparison of IC50 values demonstrated that cells expressing V777L mutant HER2 were sensitive to all three drugs. A separate experiment assessing the relative growth of V777L HER2-transduced Ba/F3 cells in the presence of inhibitors indicated that compared to wild-type the cells expressing the mutant protein were sensitive to lapatinib and sapatinib but resistant to trastuzumab.

The V777L variant is located in the tyrosine kinase domain. In vitro kinase assays were conducted using recombinant expression of the isolated HER2 kinase domain. In this system wild-type (WT) HER2 showed a 2.3-fold increase in kinase activity upon in vitro dimerization. In monomer form the V777L variant had 22-fold greater activity than WT, which increased to 33-fold upon in vitro dimerization. To assess the effect on signal transduction pathways, retroviral vectors were used to transduce mutant V777L or wild-type HER2 into MCF10A, MCF7 and NIH 3T3 cells. In all three cell lines the variant form exhibited increased HER2 autophosphorylation, increased phosphorylation of HER2 dimerization partners (EGFR), and increased phosphorylation of downstream signaling proteins (MAPK or PLCgamma). When seeded into soft agar, MCF10A cells transduced with V777L formed colonies with a mean colony count of 2000, compared with a count of 500 for cells transduced with WT HER2. Both MCF10A and NIH 3T3 cells transduced with V777L formed tumors more rapidly upon injection into nude mice than cells transduced with the WT control.

Wild-type and V777L mutant HER2 proteins were ectopically expressed in NIH3T3 cells. The variant form of HER2 supported anchorage-independent growth in soft agar while the wild-type form did not and also exhibited increased autophosphorylation compared to wild-type.

To model HER2 missense mutations found in tumors without HER amplification, a targeted gene knock-in method was used to create isogenic MCF-10A and MCF7 human breast epithelial cell lines with a single copy of wild-type HER2 and a single integrated copy of either the V777L variant or the empty targeting vector; the heterozygous cells were verified to have equivalent expression of the variant and wild-type alleles by RT-PCR. Compared to the controls, the cells with HER2 V777L exhibited increased phosphorylation of HER2, EGFR and ERK but not AKT. The cells with HER2 V777L did not exhibit anchorage independent growth, in contrast to the behavior of MCF-10A and MCF7 cells in which the variant protein was overexpressed. MCF7 cells with heterozygous HER2 V777L did not form tumors as xenografts in nude mice. Enhanced phosphorylation of signal transduction pathway components ERK, AKT and EGFR was observed in double-knock-in cell lines containing an activating PIK3CA mutation in addition to V777L. The authors suggest that in the non-amplified/non-overexpressed context HER2 V777L may require additional genetic alterations to promote features of transformation.

In the SUMMIT basket trial (NCT01953926) patients with solid tumors of various histologies harboring mutations of either HER2 or HER3 were enrolled and treated with the pan-HER kinase inhibitor neratinib. Patients on the trial tended to be heavily pre-treated. Fifteen patients with the ERBB2 V777L variant were enrolled. Among these fifteen, two RECIST partial responses were observed, one in breast cancer and one in biliary tract cancer. Three instances of stable disease were observed; progressive disease was noted in the rest of the cases.

Osimertinib was effective in achieving a partial response in a patient with stage IV non-small cell lung cancer metastasis in the brain harboring ERBB2 exon 19 c.2262_2264delinsTCC, p.(L755P) variant.

In an analysis of 20 solid-pseudopapillary tumors, 95% (19 of 20) had nuclear accumulation of beta-catenin protein and 90% (18 of 20) had activating CTNNB1 mutations, including D32N (n=2), D32Y (n=3), D32V (n=1), S33A (n=1), G34V (n=3), G34R (n=2), and S37F (n=6).

By IHC, all 18 solid-pseudopapillary neoplasm (SPN) samples had diffuse nuclear/cytoplasmic beta-catenin staining and 15 of 18 (83%) had missense mutations in exon 3 including at codons 32 (n=5), 33 (n=3), 34 (n=3), 37 (n=3), and 41 (n=1). This strongly suggests a significant role of Wnt signaling in the tumorigenesis of this cancer.

22158988 Exonic sequencing of 4 types of pancreatic cysts, including serous cystadenomas (SCAs), intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms (IPMNs), mucinous cystic neoplasms (MCNs), and solid pseudopapillary neoplasms (SPNs), revealed all SPNs have CTNNB1 mutations and few other genetic alterations unlike other types. CTNNB1 mutations included D32A, D32H, D32N, S33C, G34R (n=2), G34V, and S37F.

Assessment of beta-catenin mutations in a large collections of pituitary adenomas (n=60) and craniopharynangiomas (n=41), identified CTNNB1 exon 3 mutations in 77% of craniopharynangiomas, all of the adamantinous subtype. Immunohistochemistry also identified nuclear beta-catenin in 94% of the adamantinomatous craniopharyngiomas but not in other tumor entities. The authors conclude beta-catenin mutations and/or nuclear accumulation serve as diagnostic hallmarks of the adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma.

Whole-exome sequencing identified CTNNB1 mutations in 11 of 12 (92%) of adamantinomatous craniopharyngiomas examined. No other recurrent mutations or genomic aberrations were identified. Targeted sequencing of a larger collection of adamantinomatous craniopharyngiomas identified CTNNB1 mutation in 51 of 53 (96%) of samples. CTNNB1 mutations clustered in the degradation targeting motif of exon 3, including D32N (n=4), D32Y (n=1), D32V (n=3), D32H (n=2), D32Y(n=1), S33C (n=5), S33F (n=5), S33P (n=2), G34E (n=3), G34V (n=2), G34R (n=3), I35S (n=2), H36P (n=1), S37C (n=1), S37F (n=6), T41A (n=1), T41I (n=17), S45F (n=2) as well as an inframe-deletion W25_32del (n=1). CTNNB1 mutations were clonal and viewed as a defining genetic aberration for this tumor type.

CTNNB1 sequencing a cohort of 80 adamantinomatous craniopharyngiomas and 35 papillary craniopharyngiomas identified CTNNB1 activating mutations exclusively in the adamantinomatous subtype (in 79 or 80 samples). Most of the identified aberrations directly involved serine or threonine phosphorylation sites of β-catenin, being essential for its degradation and inhibition. These include positions S33 (n=28), T41 (n=16), and D32 (n=13). Consistent with this 96% (72/75) of adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma tumors had nuclear beta-catenin accumulation by IHC.

An analysis of 260 typical desmoid tumors and 191 cases of spindle cell lesions (which can be difficult to distinguish morphologically from desmoid tumors) identified CTNNB1 mutations in 88% of desmoid tumors and none in all other lesions. Thus, CTNNB1 sequencing can be a useful diagnostic tool for desmoid tumors.
Exon 3 sequencing of CTNNB1 in 101 extra-abdominal desmoid fibromatosis revealed mutation rates of 87% including T41A (39.5%), S45P (9%), S45F (36.5%), and deletion (2%).

A sequencing-based method was used to assess the sensitivity of this variant relative to wild-type to trastuzumab, lapatinib, sapatinib, afatinib, neratinib and osimertinib. Results indicated sensitivity to all six inhibitors.

The ERBB2 G292R variant was observed in 1/57 normal/tumor pairs of human gallbladder carcinoma profiled by next-generation sequencing. Human gallbladder cancer cell lines (GBC-SD and NOZ) were transiently transfected with vector expressing wild-type (WT) or G292R variant ERBB2. In an MTT assay cells expressing the variant exhibited cell proliferation at a level of 150% compared to control cells at 100%. This effect on cell proliferation was not observed when human non-malignant HEK293 cells were transduced with the variant, either singly or when cotransduced with wild-type ERBB3 to serve as a dimerization partner.

A computational prediction algorithm based on genomic and proteomic features deemed critical for oncogenicity was applied to the sequences of 820 mutations within the project GENIE dataset; this algorithm predicted the ERBB2 G292R variant to be an oncogenic driver. The variant form was transduced into Ba/F3 mouse lymphoid cells and supported IL-3 independent growth in these cells to a degree similar to the known oncogenic variant ERBB2 V777L.

In the SUMMIT basket trial (clinicaltrials.gov identifier NCT01953926) patients with solid tumors of various histologies harboring mutations of either HER2 or HER3 were enrolled and treated with the pan-HER kinase inhibitor neratinib. Patients on the trial tended to be heavily pre-treated. One patient with an ERBB2 G292R variant in a bladder cancer was enrolled and experienced progressive disease as best overall response.

A 71-year-old male with esophageal carcinoma harboring NTRK1 amplification, based on FoundationOne CDx profiling test, was treated with larotrectinib. Treatment with larotrectinib led to a shrinkage of the primary tumor, in addition to liver and lung metastases within 6 weeks based on RECIST criteria. This was also accompanied by tumor marker decrease (Squamous Cell Carcinoma [SCC]). An increase in SCC and disease progression was observed in patient 3 months after starting on larotrectinib, which could likely be associated with a drop in NTRK1 levels below the limit of detection. These results indicate that larotrectinib may be efficacious in cases with NTRK1 gene amplification.

ERCC6 was knocked down using shRNA in HCT116 and DLD1 human colorectal cancer (CRC) cell lines, which made both cell lines more sensitive to 5-FU. To assess whether ERCC6 influences chemosensitivity in vivo, xenograft mouse models were created using HCT116 cells expressing either nsi shRNA or ERCC6 shRNA-2. Tumor growth was significantly reduced in the 5-FU-treated groups, with an even greater reduction observed in the ERCC6 knockdown xenografts. Additionally, qPCR analysis of 38 CRC tumor samples revealed that ERCC6 mRNA levels were higher in patients resistant to 5-FU compared to those who responded to the treatment. Kaplan-Meier survival curves were generated for two patient cohorts—one treated with 5-FU and the other untreated. In both groups, patients with elevated ERCC6 expression had worse survival outcomes. These findings suggest that high ERCC6 expression may contribute to 5-FU chemoresistance in CRC cells.

This study used RT-PCR assays to screen tumor blocks for SS18::SSX1 fusion transcripts in 134 synovial sarcomas cases. 194 normal tissue and samples from unrelated tumor types were used as negative controls. Of the 134 synovial cases, cDNA was obtained from 131 and SS18-SSX fusions were found in 96% of these. The most common fusion was SS18-SSX1 (n=74 cases). Figure 1 of this publication depicts the most common structure of SS18::SSX1 fusion observed.

This retrospective study from five independent study sites gathered diagnostic and prognostic data regarding the t(6;9)(p23;q34), known to result in a DEK::NUP214 fusion. Data from 20 different treatment protocols spanning from 1987 to 2002 was analyzed for 7690 patients with available karyotype results. Sixty-nine cases had the (6;9)(p23;q34) (0.9 %). Several characteristics of the t(6;9)(p23;q34) cases were described. There was a difference in frequency between adult and pediatric patients with 38 / 5454 (0.7 %) in the adult group and 31 / 2236 (1.4%) in the pediatric cohort. The t(6;9)(p23;q34) was identified as the sole cytogenetic abnormality in 88 % of the cases, highlighting its potential utility as a diagnostic marker. A subset of cases (31) were analyzed for FLT3-ITD, with 11/16 (69 %) pediatric cases and 11/15 (73%) adult cases being positive. Prognosis was poor for all patients with the t(6;9)(p23;q34), regardless of additional karyotype abnormalities or FLT3-ITD status. The study showed association of the t(6;9)(p23;q34) and the resulting DEK::NUP214 fusion in AML with the following characteristics: consistent pathologic features including increased basophilia, single or multilineage dysplasia in adult patients, variable FAB morphology, a characteristic immunophenotype (CD13⁺, CD33⁺, CD38⁺, CD45⁺, HLA-DR⁺), high incidence of FLT3-ITD, low incidence of secondary aberrations and unfavorable outcome, underscoring the importance of DEK::NUP214 detection for AML diagnosis and risk stratification.

This retrospective study gathered diagnostic and prognostic data for acute myeloid leukemia (AML) with the t(6;9)(p23;q34), known to result in a DEK::NUP214 fusion from 20 different treatment protocols spanning from 1987 to 2002 and including 7690 patients with available karyotype results. Sixty-nine cases had the (6;9)(p23;q34) (0.9 %). Prognosis was poor for both pediatric and adult patients with the t(6;9)(p23;q34), regardless of additional karyotype abnormalities or FLT3-ITD status. The 5-year survival estimate was 28% (95% CI [12%, 44%]) for pediatric patients vs 9% (95% CI [0%, 19%]) for adult patients which was comparable to other high-risk AML cases in recently completed clinical trials. Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (SCT) was reported for 18 patients (27%); although the numbers were small the data suggested that SCT may improve outcome in AMl patients with the t(6;9)(p23;q34)/DEK::NUP214.

This study gathered diagnostic and prognostic data from pediatric AML patients enrolled in Children’s Oncology Group trials between 1988 and 2010. In total 2839 patients had karyotype data available, and 48 patients (1.7 %) had a t(6;9)(p23;q34) karyotype associated with the DEK::NUP214 fusion. There was no significant difference between t(6;9)(p23;q34) patients and non-t(6;9)(p23;q34) patient groups for gender, race, WBC count at diagnosis, and BM blast percentage. The following was found to characterize cases with the t(6;9)(p23;q34): a significantly higher age at onset (12.6 vs 8.9), spanning all classifications in the French–American–British (FAB) classification system except M3 and M5 and a higher likelihood to be M2 (41 % vs 27 %). There was also higher probability of co-occurring FLT3-ITD, with 24 of 36 patients with a diagnostic specimen available being FLT3-ITD positive (75 %). Finally, patients with t(6;9)(p23;q34) had poor outcomes regardless of FLT3 status. However, some data from newer studies indicate that patients had better outcomes when assigned to high-risk protocols that include stem cell transplant.

This study gathered prognostic data from pediatric AML patients enrolled in Children’s Oncology Group trials between 1988 and 2010. In total 2839 patients had karyotype data available and 48 patients (1.7 %) had a t(6;9)(p23;q34) karyotype associated with the DEK::NUP214 fusion. Multiple outcome measures were shown to be inferior in patients with the t(6;9) as compared to patients without this translocation, including: lower complete remission (CR) rate of 67% compared to 79% (p=0.04); lower overall survival (OS) of 39±15% compared to 57±2% (p=0.03); lower event-free survival (EFS) of 32±14% compared to 45±2% (p=0.2); higher relapse risk of 64±18% as compared to 42±2% (p=0.04); and lower disease free survival (DFS) of 33±17% compared to 50±2% (p=0.1). Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) data was available for 10 patients, who appeard to have better outcome than patients treated by chemotherapy alone.

phenotypes: Childhood onset,Juvenile onset,Early young adult onset
evidence_statement: This retrospective study from the International Berlin-Frankfurt-Munster study group with 24 participating sites was performed to collect characteristics of AML with the t(6;9)( p23;q34) resulting in the DEK::NUP214 fusion. All patients with either a t(6;9)(p23;q34) karyotype or a confirmed DEK::NUP214 fusion were included in the study regardless of disease status. 62 patients were included in total with 54 having a diagnosis of AML and 8 with a diagnosis of MDS. The calculated diagnostic rate for DEK::NUP214 was 0.6 % (45/7,363) when only study sites with complete karyotype data were included. FTL3-ITD analysis was performed on 33 cases and 14 cases (42 %) were FTL3-ITD positive. Gene expression profiling was performed on a subset of samples (8) and DEK::NUP214 fusion cases showed upregulation of several genes including HIST2H4, PRDM2/RIZ, SESN1 and EYA-3. Prognosis in this cohort was overall more favorable than previous cohorts with a 5-year overall survival of 53 %. Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation during the first complete remission showed an improved event free survival compared with chemotherapy alone (68% versus 18%).

disease: Acute Myeloid Leukemia With NPM1::MLF1 Fusion
evidence_statement: In this 2019 study the authors aimed to detect the driver genetic alterations in a cohort of Japanese pediatric AML patients. Gene fusions were detected in 53/139 patients with RNA sequencing. The NPM1::MLF1 fusion was detected in one individual diagnosed at age 12 with the RAEB-T subtype of AML. Exon 8 of NPM1 was fused to exon 4 of MLF1. Overall the authors emphasis the role of RNA sequencing in AML, as they detected 22 novel or rare gene fusions.

disease: Acute Myeloid Leukemia With NPM1::MLF1 Fusion
phenotypes: Juvenile onset,Childhood onset,Early young adult onset
evidence_statement: In this 2024 study the authors analyzed RNA sequencing data from 887 pediatric acute myeloid leukemia (AML) cases. The median age of the cohort was 9.3 years (range 0 to 24 years). Oncogenic driver fusions or structural variants were identified in 627 (71%) of patients. The NPM1::MLF1 fusion was detected in 3 (0.3%) cases diagnosed at 4, 13 and 16 years of age. Cases with NPM1 fusions were assigned to the NPM1 category of AML. Overall the authors categorized the pediatric AML cohort based on RNA sequencing data into 23 molecular categories defined by mutually exclusive driver alterations.

disease: Acute Myeloid Leukemia With NPM1::MLF1 Fusion
evidence_statement: In this 2010 study the authors included 5876 acute myeloid leukemia cases. The median age of the patients was 44 years (range 16 to 59 years). With cytogenetic analysis the t(3;5)(q21∼25;q31∼35) (likely to represent the NPM1::MLF1 gene fusion) was identified in 26 patients (0.4%). The median age of onset for patients with t(3;5) was 31 years (range 16 to 58 years). The authors found patients with a balanced rearrangement of t(3;5)(q21∼25;q31∼35) typically occurred at a younger age and was associated with an intermediate prognostic outcome. The authors emphasize the benefit of achieving greater consensus in cytogenetic classification and importance of establishing the outcome associated with rarer cytogenetic abnormalities.

molecular_profile: EGFR L858R OR EGFR Exon 19 Deletion
evidence_statement: In this trial (MARIPOSA), 1074 patients with Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer harbouring exon 19 deletion or exon 21 L858R substitution were randomized (2:2:1) to receive lazertinib-amivantamab (n=429), osimertinib monotherapy (n=429) or lazertininib monotherapy (n=216). Patients who received lazertinib-amivantamab combination therapy had a significantly higher median PFS compared to patients who received osimertinib monotherapy (23.7 months vs. 16.6 months; HR 0.70 [95% CI, 0.58-0.85; p < 0.001]). Additionally, amivantamab-lazertinib prolonged PFS vs. osimertinib in patients with a history of brain metastases (18.3 months vs. 13.0 months; HR 0.69 [95% CI, 0.53-0.92]). In 136 patients with liver metastases at baseline, the median PFS was significantly prolonged in patients treated with amivantamab-lazertinib (18.2 months, 95% CI, 13.1-NE) compared to patients treated with osimertinib (11.0 months, 95% CI, 7.4-12.8), while the HR for disease progression in the amivantamab-lazertinib versus osimertinib groups was 0.58 (95% CI, 0.37-0.91, p = 0.017).

Ninety patients (pre-treated with a median of 2 lines of therapy) with Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer harbouring HER2 exon 20 insertion mutations were treated with poziotinib. The ORR was 27.8% (95% CI, 18.9-38.2), and 74.4% of the patients had a tumour reduction. The median PFS was 5.5 months (95% CI, 3.9-5.8).

Eighty pre-treated patients with Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer harbouring HER2 exon 20 insertions were treated with poziotinib. The ORR Was 39% (95% CI, 28%-50%), and 80% of the patients had a tumour reduction. The median PFS was 5.6 months (95% CI, 5.4-7.3).

In this arm of the trial (LIBRETTO-001), the efficacy of selpercatinib was tested in 45 patients harbouring RET fusion-positive solid tumours (excluding lung or thyroid tumours). The objective response rate was 43.9% (95% CI, 28.5-60.3) as per both investigator assessment and independent review committee assessment. The median duration of response was 24.5 months (95% CI, 9.2 - NE) according to the independent review committee and 18.4 months (95% CI, 9.2-NE) according to the investigator assessment. Investigators report that selpercatinib showed clinically meaningful activity in RET fusion-positive tumour-agnostic population.

In this arm of the trial (NCT03157128), the intracranial objective response rate (iORR) was assessed in 80 patients with RET fusion-positive non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) treated with selpercatinib. Of these 80 patients, 58 had non-measurable baseline intracranial lesions, while 22 had at least one baseline measurable intracranial lesion. Among the 22 patients with measurable intracranial disease at baseline, the iORR was 82% (95% CI, 60-95). This included 5 patients who achieved a complete response and 13 who had a partial response. For the remaining 58 patients with non-measurable lesions, 34% achieved a complete intracranial response, characterized by the complete resolution of all non-measurable lesions. Only 9% of these patients were reported to have progressive disease (PD) as their best response. Across all 80 patients, the median intracranial progression-free survival (PFS) was 13.7 months (95% CI, 10.9-NE). The most common RET fusion partner was KIF5B, found in 70% of patients, and 91% of patients had received prior systemic therapy.

KRAS mutation G12D is a very frequently mutated KRAS subtype. Compared to KRAS G12C, which responds well to covalent inhibitors, KRAS G12D lacks a reactive residue near the switch-II-binding pocket, making it largely unresponsive to drugs. Zhou, C., et al. developed a novel KRAS G12D inhibitor that is both highly selective for (0.083 nM affinity constant) and effective against KRAS G12D in preclinical models. When HRS-4642 was injected intravenously into mouse models bearing AsPC-1 human pancreatic tumors, tumor growth was inhibited in a dose-dependent manner compared to controls.

Zhou, C., et al. developed a novel KRAS G12D inhibitor, HRS-4642, and found that in preclincial experiments, HRS-4642 effectively reduced tumor growth compared to controls. After preclinical success, HRS-4642 was administered intravenously to patients with solid tumors with KRAS G12D mutations. In the initial cohorts, there were 9 patients with NSCLC. After treatment, the disease remained stable in 7 patients and exhibited a reduction in tumor size in two patients. The two patients who responded well to treatment did not harbor any other common lung cancer drivers and had previously shown partial response to other systematic treatments ( carboplatin, pemetrexed, camrelizumab, bevacizumab, and anlotinib).

molecular_profile: MAGEA4 Expression AND ( HLA-A *02:01P OR HLA-A *02:02P OR HLA-A *02:03P OR HLA-A *02:06P )
evidence_statement: In cohort 1 of this non-randomised, phase 2 trial (SPEARHEAD-1), 52 patients, aged, 16-75, with synovial sarcoma (n = 44) and myxoid round cell liposarcoma (n=8) harboring HLA-A*02 and MAGE-A4 were treated with afamitresgene autoleucel. Additionally, most patients were heavily pre-treated, with a median of three previous lines of therapy. The ORR was 37% (19/52; 95% CI, 24-51) overall. In patients with synovial sarcoma the ORR was 39% (17/44, 24-55), and 25% (2/8, 95% CI, 3-65) in patients with myxoid round cell liposarcoma. The median duration of response was found to be 11.6 months (95% CI, 4.4-18.0) in patients with synovial sarcoma and 4.2 months (95% CI, 2.9-5.5) in patients with myxoid round cell liposarcoma.

NSCLC with EGFR activating alterations are frequently treated with the tyrosine kinase inhibitor, osimertinib. Though initially very effective, cancers cells often develop resistance to osimertinib through acquisition of additional alterations that maintains the proliferation capacity. Combinatorial treatment of osimertinib and BMVC-8C3O prevented acquisition of osimertinib resistance and inhibited the growth of osimertinib-resistant tumors. Treatment with BMVC-8C3O resulted in reduction of both mRNA and protein c-FOS levels and causes the osimertinib and BMVC-8C3O synergistic cytotoxicity. The synergist effect is mainly due to simultaneous suppression of the PI3K/AKT pathway and c-FOS, however this combination did not affect ERK activity.

Two phase I studies included 119 patients with advanced or metastatic solid tumors, which included 28 patients with ROS1 rearrangements (n=28) where the overall safety and antitumor activity of entrectinib was examined. Entrectinib was shown to be safe and well tolerated. For phase 2, 14 ROS1-rearranged solid tumors were eligible. One of these patients had melanoma with GOPC-ROS1 found via next generation sequencing. This patient responded to entrectinib within a month of treatment, and was ongoing on the study after 11 months, with no disease progression.

molecular_profile: MAP2K4 loss-of-function Mutation OR MAP3K1 Loss-of-Function Mutation
evidence_statement: In this study, sensitivity to MEK inhibitors was evaluated in multiple cancer models harbouring MAP3K1 and MAP2K4 loss-of-function mutations. In in-vitro experiments, two breast cancer cell lines, MDA-MB-134VI and MPE600, in addition to 6 other cancer cells lines (large intestine, ovary, endometrium, pancreas) with MAP3K4 mutations were found to be sensitive to selumetinib, while six wild type control cell lines were resistant to selumetinib. The breast cancer cell lines with MAP2K4 mutations were also found to be sensitive to MEK inhibitor trametinib and ERK inhibitor SCH772984. There was a marked increase in sensitivity in MAP3K1 or MAP2K4 knockout cell lines, including MDA-MB-468 breast cancer, H358 lung cancer, and HCT116 colon cancer cells. Increased sensitivity was also noted in MAP2K4 knockout LoVo and DLD1 colon cancer cells. Increased sensitivity in the MAP2K4 and MAP3K1 knockout cell lines was also noted after treatment with MEK inhibitors trametinib, binimetinib and ERK inhibitor SCH772984. Seven patient-derived xenograft models with MAP3K1 or MAP2K4 mutations were also found to be significantly more sensitive to MEK inhibitor binimetinib compared to wild type models. Overall, this study suggests that cancer cells with MAP3K1 or MAP2K4 inactivating mutations are sensitive to MEK inhibitor monotherapy.

C57BL/6 mice were inoculated with B16/BL6 tumour cells and treated with anti-CTLA-4 to assess in-vivo effects of IFNGR1 knockdown on tumour growth. All untreated mice with wildtype scramble shRNA-transduced, and IFNGR1 shRNA-transduced B16/BL16 cell lines proliferated and formed measurable tumours. After treatment with anti-CTLA-4, 4/22 mice with wildtype B16/BL6 tumours, and 4/25 mice with scramble shRNA-transduced B16/BL6 tumours had progressive tumour growth, however, 12/25 mice with IFNGR1 shRNA-transduced B16/BL6 tumours had progressive tumour growth. Additionally, tumours with IFNGR1 shRNA were significantly larger compared to control tumours (p < 0.05), and had an impaired response to anti-CTLA4 therapy.

The OncoBird framework utilizes data from the open-label, randomized phase III FIRE-3 trial, which involved patients with metastatic colorectal carcinoma who received either cetuximab or bevacizumab in combination with FOLFIRI. In this trial, TOP1 amplifications were found to be strong predictors of prolonged overall survival in patients treated with cetuximab (p = 0.005, HR = 0.50 [0.30-0.81]). Additionally, favorable OS was also noted in CMS2 patients treated with cetuximab if their tumors carried chr20q amplifications like TOP1 amplifications (p = 0.01, HR = 0.34 [0.15-0.74]).

molecular_profile: EGFR L858R OR EGFR Exon 19 Deletion
evidence_statement: The phase 3 randomized LAURA trial (NCT NCT03521154) evaluated osimertinib as consolidation therapy after definitive chemoradiation in 216 patients with unresectable stage 3 non-small cell lung cancer harboring an EGFR exon 19 deletion or L858R mutation. Patients were allocated 2:1 to treatment with osimertinib or placebo until disease progression. The primary endpoint of progression-free survival (PFS) favored the osimertinib arm with a hazard ratio of 0.16 (95% CI, 0.10 to 0.24, P<0.001). The median PFS was 39.1 months for osimertinib vs 5.6 months for placebo. Overall survival data were not mature at the time of publication; eighty-one percent of the patients in the placebo arm received osimertinib after progression.

A treatment-naive patient with uterine leiomyosarcoma was treated with pembrolizumab monotherapy as part of the phase II KEYNOTE-028 trial. The patient showed a near-complete response, with the tumour in full remission for over two years while on therapy. Despite this, both the primary and treatment-resistant tumours exhibited minimal PD-L1 staining and widespread cytoplasmic PD-L2 staining. Notably, PD-1+ expression was significantly reduced in the treatment-resistant tumour (p = 0.02). Whole-exome sequencing (WES) and RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) revealed a heterozygous large deletion on chromosome 10q, which included the tumour suppressor gene PTEN, in the tumours. Additionally, analysis of RNA-seq data from 241 untreated primary sarcomas in The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) found that tumours with biallelic PTEN loss had significantly lower mRNA expression of PDCD1 compared to PTEN-wildtype tumours (p < 0.05). Overall, the study suggests that PTEN mutations may contribute to resistance to immune checkpoint therapy.

25 tumors from individuals with lung adca who have <= 10 pack-year smoking history underwent whole exome sequencing and RNA-seq. 5 tumors did not identify an established oncogenic driver. In one (tumor 9), RNA-seq identified an OCLN-RASGRF1 fusion. RASGRF1 expression was 8.7 fold higher in this tumor than the mean of RASGRF1 expression in the other 24 tumors. Two additional RASGRF1 fusions (SLC4A4- and IQGAP1-) were identified through database searches. All three fusions were transfected into HEK 293T cells and showed increased levels of GTP-RAS expression. RAF-MEK-ERK signaling was also upregulated in the transfected cells. OCLN-RASGRF1 and SLC4A4-RASGRF1 fusions induced anchorage-indepdendent proliferation in NIH3T3 cells. IQGAP1-RASGRF1 did not induce anchorage-independent proliferation but did induce loss of contact inhibition. All three tested fusions activated the RAF-MEK-ERK and PI3K pathways in NIH3T3 cells. OLCN-RASGRF1 induced IL3-independent proliferation in Ba/F3 cells; and all three tested fusions formed tumors when NIH3T3 cells were implanted into immune-deficient mice. Ba/F3 cells with OCLN-RASGRF1 were sensitive to trametinib.

An 88-year-old male acral melanoma patient harbouring EMSY gene amplification without abnormal BRCA2 expression levels was treated with PARPi, talazoparib. The patient was treated with talazoparib at 1 mg daily, and a near-complete response was observed after 13 months.

Patients with high-grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSOC) and EMSY overexpression (n = 265) received platinum-based first-line chemotherapy. When comparing patients with high and low EMSY expression, using the top 14th percentile as the threshold for high EMSY, those with high EMSY demonstrated significantly prolonged overall survival (OS) compared to those with low EMSY (uniHR, 0.63 [95% CI; 0.43-0.93; p = 0.020]). Similarly, the high-EMSY group showed improved progression-free survival (PFS) compared to the low-EMSY group (multiHR, 0.62 [95% CI; 0.40-0.96; p = 0.030]). These findings were validated in the MRC ICON7 cohort, where high-EMSY patients again exhibited prolonged OS (multiHR, 0.46 [95% CI; 0.23-0.91; p = 0.025]), but there was no significant difference in PFS (multiHR, 0.89 [95% CI; 0.57-1.38; p = 0.599]). In the same cohort, patients with high EMSY who received a combination of bevacizumab, carboplatin, and paclitaxel (n = 14) had poorer survival compared to those treated with carboplatin and paclitaxel alone (n = 10) (multiHR, 11.78 [95% CI; 1.31-106.32; p = 0.027]), though the small sample size limits the power of this analysis.

molecular_profile: MSI High AND ( B2M Mutation OR JAK1 Mutation OR JAK2 Mutation )
evidence_statement: Thirty-five MSI-H/dMMR patients were treated with anti-PD-1 therapy. Of the 35 patients, 10 patients harboured B2M mutations, and 8 patients harboured JAK mutations. A low TMB score was noted in patients with JAK1/2 mutations (p=0.009). There was no significant difference in response to anti-PD1 therapy in patients with wild-type or mutated B2M status (p=0.53). A significant difference was noted in clinical response to anti-PD1 therapy in patients harbouring JAK1/2 mutations v/s those with wildtype JAK1/2. However, when looking at the combined group of patients with either JAK or B2M mutant status, better clinical response was noted in the group harbouring the mutations v/s the wildtype group (p=0.035). These results were further validated against a cohort from an MSKCC research on cBioPortal, and similar results in terms of overall survival were noted in all the B2M mutant (p=0.438), the JAK1/2 mutant group (p=0.0713), and the combined group with either B2M or JAK1/2 mutations (p=0.0836).

In a cohort of melanoma patients treated with PD-1 antibodies, higher B2M levels were observed in those who achieved a complete response compared to those with partial response or progressive disease. Additionally, tumours with high B2M levels had lower TMB scores than those with low B2M levels. In LUAD specimens, IHC staining for PD-L1, B2M, and CD8A revealed that tumours with high B2M expression contained more CD8+ T cells compared to those with low or moderate B2M expression. Furthermore, B2M knockout in otherwise sensitive MC38 mice tumours led to resistance to PD-1 inhibition and reduced the therapeutic efficacy of immunotherapy.

Whole exome sequencing (WES) was performed on 49 longitudinal tumour samples from 17 patients with metastatic melanoma, of whom 10 responded to ICIs/CPB, where 5 had durable responses, while 5 eventually progressed. Performing a focussed case study on a patient from the group that eventually progressed, showed that they exhibited frameshift mutations in B2M only during progression. Further, phylogenetic analysis of the tumour suggests that B2M loss provided a significant selective advantage, allowing the B2M-deficient tumour lineages to dominate after progressive disease and evade immune destruction. Results from immunohistochemistry performed on the patients' biopsies revealed a dramatic drop in tumour-specific B2M protein levels after the development of resistance. In the 5/17 patients exhibiting B2M defects, three patients initially responded and then progressed. No B2M alterations were detected in patients who had responded in this cohort. Additionally, B2M aberrations, including LOH and mutations, were significantly enriched in non-responders and associated with poorer survival in two independent cohorts of patients treated with anti-CTLA4 and anti-PD1 therapies. These findings collectively suggest that B2M loss contributes to a common mechanism of resistance to checkpoint blockade therapies.

This is an international retrospective study by International Berlin-Frankfurt-Munster (I-BFM) AML study group including 543 pediatric AML patients from 18 countries diagnosed between 1995-2005. The authors recorded 62 pediatric AML patients with t(8;16)(p11;p13) determined by karyotyping, FISH and/or RT-PCR. Complete karyotypes were available for 57/62 cases, of which 22 (38.6%) showed additional non-recurrent cytogenetic aberrations. The t(8;16)(p11;p13) results in a fusion of exons 15 or 16 of KAT6A (also known as MOZ or MYST3, located to chromosome 8p11) to exon 3-8 of CREBBP (located to chromosome 16p13). Both proteins encoded by the KAT6A and CREBBP fusion partners have histone methyltransferase activity and are involved in cell cycle and transcriptional regulation. Pediatric AML cases with the KAT6A::CREBBP fusion showed specific clinical manifestations, including young age at diagnosis (median of 1.2 years), considerable frequency of leukemia cutis, disseminated intravascular coagulation, erythrophagocytosis and intermediate survival rate. Interestingly, seven neonatal AML cases with t(8;16)(p11;p13) showed spontaneous remission. The study also included gene expression analysis for 297 pediatric AML patients; differentially expressed genes were validated for 30 cases by quantitative RT-PCR. Gene expression signature of pediatric AML with t(8;16) showed similar clustering pattern as KMT2A (MLL)- rearranged AML cases with HOXA and RET genes up-regulation. The overexpression of HOXA and RET genes have been reported in adult AML with t(8;16) as well, indicating similarities in the expression profile between pediatric and adult AML with t(8;16).

This manuscript is the first report of a unique expression profile in pediatric AML with KAT6A::CREBBP gene fusion (known also as MOZ::CBP or MYST3::CREBBP). Genomic studies and gene expression profile analysis were performed for a de novo AML M5b diagnosed in a 10-year-old girl. Pathology evaluation showed 23% blast in peripheral blood and 80% blasts in bone marrow. Karyotype and FISH confirmed the t(8;16)(p11;p13), resulting in the KAT6A::CREBBP fusion, as the sole chromosome abnormality. Gene expression analysis results for this case were compared with five non-t(8;16) pediatric AML cases (two M1, one M4, two M5), and adult cases with t(8;16)(p11;p13). The gene expression profile of adult and pediatric AMLs with KAT6A::CREBBP fusion were similar, and shared features with the AML or T-ALL with KMT2A-rearrangements. The expression signature was characterized by upregulation of HOXA9, HOXA10, HOXA11, LMO2, PTPN6 and GFI1 genes. It was proposed that overexpression of HOXA genes confers self-renewal capacity and stem-cell properties to blasts, and is responsible for poor outcome, in AML with t(8;16).

The authors reported a congenital AML case with leukemia cutis and a cryptic insertional t(8;16)(p11.2;p13.3)/KAT6A::CREBBP fusion identified exclusively by FISH. They found KAT6A::CREBBP fusion in 11.4% of nuclei by Interphase FISH. The authors combined chromosome, interphase, and metaphase FISH results. FISH analysis showed a cryptic, insertional translocation event resulting in a KAT6A::CREBBP fusion on an apparently normal 16p. The authors discuss that pediatric AML cases with KAT6A::CREBBP fusion over 1 month of age have similar clinical manifestations, but with poorer clinical outcomes compared with congenital cases. Spontaneous remission has been reported in about 50% of congenital AML cases with t(8;16)(p11.2;p13.3) and in case of recurrence, patients would have favorable response to standard therapy. This case report illustrates several unique characteristics of AML with t(8;16)(p11.2;p13.3) including congenital onset, cryptic form of the rearrangement and manifestation as leukemia cutis.

molecular_profile: EGFR L858R OR EGFR Exon 19 Deletion
evidence_statement: In this phase III trial, 657 patients with locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC (Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer) harbouring EGFR mutations (exon 19 deletions or L858R) were treated with amivantamab plus carboplatin-pemetrexed (chemotherapy). These patients were then randomized 2:2:1 to receive amivantamab-lazertinib-chemotherapy (n=263), chemotherapy (n=263), or amivantamab-chemotherapy (n=131). PFS was significantly longer in the amivantamab-chemotherapy [median 6.3 months; HR 0.48, p <0.001] and the amivantamab-lazertinib-chemotherapy [median 8.3 months; HR 0.44, p <0.001] groups compared to chemotherapy alone [median 4.2 months]. Additionally, ORR was also significantly higher in the amivantamab-chemotherapy and amivantamab-lazertinib-chemotherapy groups at, 64% (95% CI 55-72) and 63% (95% CI 57-69) respectively, compared to the chemotherapy group alone at 36% (p < 0.001 for both).

In this phase III trial, 291 patients (12 years or older) with medullary thyroid cancer harbouring RET mutations were enrolled. Patients were randomized in a 2:1 ratio to receive selpercatinib (n=193) or cabozantinib/vandetanib (control group, n=98). Progression-free survival in the selpercatinib group was 86.8% (95% CI, 79.8-91.6) and 65.7% (95% CI, 51.9-76.4) in the control group at 12 months. Additionally, median treatment failure-free survival was not reached in the selpercatinib group and was 13.9 months in the control group (HR 0.25, 95% CI, 0.15-0.42, p <0.001), as assessed by blinded independent central review. Treatment failure-free survival at 12 months was 86.2% (95% CI 79.1-91.0) in the treatment group, and 62.1% (95% CI, 48.9-72.8) in the control group. Finally, the ORR in the treatment and control group was 69.4% (95% CI, 62.4-75.8) and 38.8% (95% CI, 29.1-49.2) respectively. Overall, treatment with selpercatinib resulted in significantly better PFS compared to cabozantinib/vandetanib treatment in patients with advanced RET-mutant medullary thyroid cancer.

In this phase 1 trial, 80 patients harbouring MTAP deletions/CDKN2A deletions received AMG 193 in a dose escalation study. The most common tumour types were PDAC (23.8%), NSCLC (17.5%), biliary tract cancer (BCT) (8.8%), GBM (6.3%) and gastric/esophageal cancer (2.5%). Of the 80 patients, 6 patients had MTAP-intact per central IHC and were therefore excluded from the efficacy analysis. The ORR was 21.4% (95% CI, 10.3-36.8), and the DCR was 54.8% (95% CI, 38.7-70.2). The median time to response (TTR) was 3.6 months (3.6-3.7) in the 800 mg QD cohort and 1.8 months in the 1200 mg QD cohort. The median DOR across all the cohorts was 8.3 months (95% CI, 2.7 - NE) with the longest being 12.9 months in a patient with RCC and 11.0 months in a patient with ovarian SLCT, and the median DoDC was 9.2 months (95% CI, 4.9-11.8). Finally, SDMA reduction (to near complete elimination) was noted in post-treatment biopsies from eight MTAP-deleted patients compared to pre-treatment biopsies at dose levels of 480 mg, 800 mg, and 1200 mg. Overall, encouraging anti-tumour activity of AMG 193 was noted in MTAP-deleted solid tumours between 800 mg and 1200 mg dose, with a manageable safety profile, and no dose-limiting cytopenia events reported.

A 55-year-old man with HNSCC harbouring PIK3CA Q75E (non-canonical) mutation was previously treated and responded to concurrent chemoradiation therapy (CRT) with cisplatin, however, experienced local recurrence after 6 months of completing CRT. His recurrent HNSCC was treated with 5-FU but he progressed after 2 cycles, so he was then enrolled in the TRIUMPH trial and received alpelisib monotherapy. The patient experienced a partial response with a 73% tumour reduction after 2 months of treatment. He remained on alpelisib for 12 months, before switching to durvalumab due to disease progression. The patient was alive on durvalumab after approximately 2 years of completing alpelisib monotherapy.

molecular_profile: PIK3CA N345K OR PIK3CA M1043V OR PIK3CA Q75E
evidence_statement: In this pre-clinical study, the role of the non-canonical PIK3CA mutation PIK3CA Q75E was evaluated. The expression of pKAT/total AKT was compared across canonical PIK3CA E545K mutation, non-canonical PIK3CA Q75E mutation, and WT PIK3CA. The E545K mutation showed a 2.73-fold increase, and the Q75E mutation showed a 2.34-fold increase in relative pAKT/total AKT level compared to WT PIK3CA cells. Additionally, colony formation was assessed in the WT and mutation cells in the PCI-52-SD1 HNSCC cell line model. The WT cell line led to a 1.59-fold increase in colony compared to untreated cells, while the canonical E545K mutant led to a 4.52-fold increase, and the non-canonical mutant Q75E led to a 3.30-fold increase. These findings imply that the non-canonical Q75E mutation may have the properties of a 'driver' oncogene. Further, the oncogenic properties of all 32 non-canonical PIK3CA mutations were assessed, and it was found that 21 demonstrated activating phenotypes in colony formation assay, which included M1043V and N345K. Treatment with alpelisib in HNSCC cells engineered to express Q75E, M1043V, or N345K PIK3CA mutations, resulted in modest induction of apoptosis, and dose-dependent inhibition of colony formation. These findings support that patients with non-canonical PIK3CA mutations might benefit from treatment with drugs like alpelisib.

In this trial, patients with advanced rare tumours harbouring BRAF V600E mutations were treated with a combination of dabrafenib and trametinib. The study included eight distinct cohorts: anaplastic thyroid carcinoma (ATC) (n=36), biliary tract cancer (BTC)(n=43), gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST) (n=1), adenocarcinoma of the small intestine (ASI) (n=3), low-grade glioma (LGG) (n=13), high-grade glioma (HGG)(n=45), hairy cell leukemia(HCL) (n=55), and multiple myeloma (MM)(n=19). The overall response rates for these cohorts were 56%, 53%, 0%, 67%, 54%, 33%, 89%, and 50% respectively. The median duration of response varied, with 14.4 months for anaplastic thyroid carcinoma, 8.9 months for biliary tract cancer, 7.7 months for adenocarcinoma of the small intestine, 31.2 months for high-grade glioma, and 11.1 months in multiple myeloma. In the remaining cohorts, the duration of response was not reached. Progression-free survival was measured at 6.7 months for ATC, 9.0 months for BTC, 9.5 months for ASI, 5.5 months for HGG, and 6.3 months for MM. PFS could not be evaluated in the LGG and HCL groups due to small patient numbers. The overall survival was 14.5 months for ATC, 13.5 months for BTC, 17.6 months for HGG, 21.8 months for ASI, and 33.9 months for MM cohorts. OS could not be evaluated for the LGG and HCL groups due to a low number of deaths. Adverse events were reported in 97.6% of the patients (n=201), with 87.9% (n=181) of these being related to the study treatment. Serious adverse events occurred in 45.1% (n=93) of patients across all cohorts.

In this trial, patients with pediatric (age <18 years) low-grade gliomas harbouring BRAF V600E (n=49), were treated with either trametinib monotherapy (n=13) or dabrafenib + trametinib (n=36). In patients treated with trametinib monotherapy, 15% (95% CI, 1.9-45.4; n=2) had objective PRs, and 46% (n=6) had stable disease for 12 or more weeks after the first dose of therapy. The estimated 24-month duration of response (DOR) was 100%. The median PFS was 16.4 months (95% CI, 3.2 to NR). In patients treated with a combination of trametinib and dabrafenib 25% (95% CI, 12.1-42.2; n=9) had objective PRs and 64% (n=23) experienced stable disease. The median DOR was 33.6 months (95% CI, 11.2 - NR), while the 24-month DOR was 80% (95% CI, 30-100). The median PFS was 36.9 months (95% CI, 36.0 - NR).

ZEB1 is a key transcription factor that controls epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and may contribute to chemoresistance in cancer cells by enhancing DNA damage response (DDR) and repair mechanisms. However, functional experiments demonstrate how ZEB1 induces chemoresistance regardless of whether other EMT-related changes occur. Furthermore, ZEB1 forms a complex with p300/PCAF and interacts with ATM kinase, stabilizing its function and promoting radioresistance. Additionally, ZEB1 downregulation reduces CHK1 levels, impairing DDR. This evidence suggests that elevated ZEB1 expression may thus be associated with increased chemoresistance.

In a study of oncogenic signalling pathways, tumours and cultured cells from 15 patients with MYB-NFIB translocation-positive adenoid cystic carcinoma (ACC) were analyzed. Treatment with linsitinib, an IGF-1R inhibitor, decreased MYB-NFIB mRNA (% expression of control ± SD = 27.2 ± 1.3, P < .001) and protein. Additionally, the expression of wild-type MYB was not reduced by linsitinib treatment, in fact, the expression of the wild-type MYB allele increased slightly after treatment. IGF1R knockdown led to a 50-60% reduction in MYB-NFIB mRNA, complete loss of protein expression, and inhibited cell proliferation. Gene expression analysis following MYB-NFIB knockdown revealed significant overlap (p < 0.001) between genes affected by IGF1R inhibition and MYB-NFIB knockdown (374 genes), most of which were also overexpressed in ACC surgical samples (p < 0.001).

Monensin was investigated for its effect on adenoid cystic carcinoma (ACC) cells. Viability assays were conducted on short-term cultured tumour cells from two ACC patients harbouring MYB-NFIB fusion. These demonstrated high sensitivity to monensin compared to non-tumorigenic mammary epithelial cells (MCF10A) and primary pleomorphic adenoma cells used as controls. Ectopic expression of MYB reduced the inhibitory effect of monensin on ACC1 cells, indicating that monensin partially inhibits cell viability through MYB suppression. Additionally, monensin reduced the self-renewing capacity of ACC cells in a concentration-dependent manner and inhibited MYB-NFIB expression at both mRNA and protein levels. Gene expression studies showed significant overlap between genes suppressed by monensin and those activated by MYB-NFIB, suggesting monensin affects MYB-NFIB-dependent gene transcription.

This case describes the treatment of a patient with a malignant gastrointestinal neuroectodermal tumour (GNET) harbouring an EWSR1-ATF1 fusion, initially treated with chemotherapy and radiotherapy. After multiple lines of systemic therapy and tumour progression, the patient was started on trabectedin in May 2022 as a 5th line of treatment. Despite the slight growth in some implants, the patient experienced pain relief, and after five cycles, a CT scan in September 2022 revealed a partial response, which lasted 10 months until disease progression was confirmed.

Treatment of ACC cells with a combination of linsitinib, crizotinib, and gefitinib resulted in synergistic inhibition of cell proliferation (p = 0.004). This combination also significantly downregulated key cell cycle regulators (p < 0.01). In two ACC tumour models, ACCXM1 and ACCX6, the treatment markedly suppressed tumour growth by 34.9% ± 20.3 (p = 0.006) and 24.1% ± 17.5 (p = 0.04), respectively. Furthermore, the therapy reduced MYB expression by 44.2% ± 18.1 (p = 0.003) in TKI-treated tumours and by 19.3% ± 6.1 (p < 0.001) in TKI-treated cultured ACC cells.

KRAS A146P was tested in Novellus FACT assay to track MAPK pathway activation via foloursent tagged ERK2 translocation to the nucleus in cells transected with different mutant KRAS vectors. The amount of translocation was normalized, and measured in comparison to KRAS G13D and wild type transfections. A146P cells showed a similar amount of transaction to G13D. Next, the mutations were tested in Ba/F3 transformation assays where cells were transfected and cultured without IL3. Cell viability was normalized and compared. A146P cells showed a 2x fold change in viability over the wild type cells, while G13D showed a 4x change in viability over wildtype.

In this 2018 study the authors investigated B cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia (BCP ALL) RNA-seq data from 1,223 cases enrolled in various clinical trials across multiple centers. The patients were predominantly pediatric patients, aged 0-18 years old. Patient samples were collected from several groups, including the Lund University Hospital cohort (cohort 2), the Singapore and Malaysia MaSpore cohort (cohort 4), and the Japan Adult Leukemia Study Group cohort (cohort 3), providing a diverse representation of childhood BCP ALL cases. Six cases (0.5%) with a TCF3::HLF gene fusion were identified, all in female pediatric patients, and one case with a TCF4::HLF fusion. Both TCF3::HLF and TCF4::HLF retained part of the HLF bZIP_2 domain and displayed significant up-regulated expression of HLF. The authors found that TCF3::HLF is a rare fusion associated with high-risk B-ALL.

In this 2023 study the authors investigated the occurrence and spectrum of TCF3 gene rearrangements in 203 patients with B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia (BCP-ALL), aged 0-18. The study utilized fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) to screen for chromosomal abnormalities, revealing that 2.0% (4 out of 203) of cases harbored a t(17;19)(q21-q22;p13.3) rearrangement, which was confirmed through additional FISH analyses. Direct Sanger sequencing revealed the complex nature of t(17;19)(q21-q22;p13.3) in three cases, with the formation of a chimeric product involving TCF3 exon 16 and HLF exon 4 as well as non-template insertions by terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase. The reading frame was preserved in all cases and the bZIP motif of the HLF protein retained. TCF3::HLF was associated with significantly lower survival rates.

In this 2015 study the authors applied genome and RNA sequencing to analyze a cohort of five diagnostic pre-treatment samples from patients aged between 7 and 17 years, all diagnosed with TCF3::HLF positive acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). The samples were collected from pediatric oncology centers across the United States, ensuring a diverse representation of clinical cases. The study found that TCF3 breakpoints were clustered in two specific intronic regions of the TCF3 gene. Type 1 translocations were identified in two patients, involving intron 16, which connected TCF3 exon 16 to HLF exon 4. These translocations included inserted non-template and intronic sequences, as well as new splice acceptor sites. Conversely, Type 2 translocations, observed in three patients, involved intron 15, linking TCF3 exon 15 to HLF exon 4. Monoallelic PAX5 deletions were enriched in TCF3::HLF positive ALL, detected in 3/5 cases compared to being generally observed in 13% of ALL cases, and PAX5 expression was reduced in all TCF3::HLF positive cases. The authors concluded that the TCF3::HLF fusion likely occurs in B lymphoid progenitors within the context of PAX5 haploinsufficiency. This genetic background is associated with transcriptional reprogramming towards an immature, hybrid hematopoietic state, highlighting the importance of these genetic alterations in the pathogenesis and clinical behavior of TCF3::HLF positive ALL.

disease: Acute Myeloid Leukemia With Mutated CEBPA
evidence_statement: In this 2021 study, the authors investigated the role of CEBPA mutations in the diagnosis and prognosis of pediatric and young adult acute myeloid leukemia (AML) in 2958 patients enrolled in Children’s Oncology Group trials. Patients were aged 0-29 years old. CEBPA mutations were identified in 160/2958 cases (5.4%). 132 (82.5%) cases had two CEBPA mutations, one in the transactivation domain (TAD) and the other in the basic leucine zipper (bZip) domain (CEBPA-double-mutated [CEBPA-dm]). 28 cases (17.5%) had a single CEBPA mutation in the bZip region (CEBPA-bZip). CEBPA bZIP and CEBPA-dm AML cases were typically characterized by higher white blood cell counts and normal karyotypes, had a characteristic pattern of secondary mutations frequently involving CSF3R and GATA2, had a unique expression profile, and were associated with a favorable outcome. It was confirmed that both CEBPA-bZip and CEBPA-dm cases have shared clinical and molecular features and were both associated with a favorable prognosis, which had not been established for pediatric AML before this study. The key finding is thus that CEBPA-bZip mutation is sufficient to drive this leukemia and should be considered as the defining molecular lesion for CEBPA mutant AML. Isolated CEBPA-TAD mutations were rare. Overall, this study highlights the importance of CEBPA abnormalities (specifically CEBPA-bZip mutations) in defining a type of pediatric AML associated with a favorable outcome.

disease: Acute Myeloid Leukemia With Mutated CEBPA
evidence_statement: In this 2022 study, the authors highlighted the diagnostic significance of different types of CEBPA mutations in 4,708 adult AML patients, recruited into the Study Alliance Leukemia trials and spanning a broad age range from under 30 to over 70 years. The study differentiated patients with CEBPA mutant AML based on mutation type: among 240 CEBPA mutant AML cases (5.1% of all cases), 60 had a single mutation in the N-terminal transactivation domains (CEBPAsmTAD), 49 had a single mutation in the C-terminal DNA-binding basic leucine zipper region (CEBPAsmbZIP), and 131 had both N-terminal TAD and C-terminal bZIP mutations (biallelic CEBPA, or CEBPA bi). Patients with CEBPAbi or CEBPAsmbZIP mutations showed distinct clinical characteristics compared to CEBPAsmTAD and CEBPA wild-type cases, including younger age and higher white blood cell counts at diagnosis. The study underscores the value of detailed CEBPA mutation analysis in AML diagnosis, by showing that CEBPAsmbZIP and CEBPA-bi define molecular subtype of disease with unique biologic and clinical characteristics, while CEBPAsmTAD represent non-specific changes.

disease: Acute Myeloid Leukemia With Mutated CEBPA
phenotypes: Pediatric onset,Middle age onset,Young adult onset
evidence_statement: In this 2022 study, the authors investigated the diagnostic significance of CEBPA mutations in AML, focusing on data from a large cohort of 1,028 patients aged 70 years or younger from the Japanese Multi-center Collaborative Sequencing Program. The study underscores that the location of CEBPA mutations is crucial in identifying specific AML subtypes. Among the 1,028 patients, 59 had a CEBPA single mutation (CEBPAsm) and 103 had a CEBPA double mutation (CEBPAdm). Of the CEBPAdm cases, 91.3% (94 of 103) had one mutation in the basic leucine zipper (bZIP) domain, while 32.2% (19 of 59) of the CEBPAsm cases had a bZIP mutation. The study reinforces the role of CEBPA mutational analysis as an essential diagnostic tool in AML, particularly in differentiating between single and double mutations and their locations within the gene. The presence of bZIP mutations, whether single or double, provides unique diagnostic markers and refines risk stratification, aiding in developing more personalized treatment strategies for AML patients based on their specific CEBPA mutation profile.

In this 2019 study, the authors investigated how the order of CEBPA mutations influences AML progression in mice that phenocopies the human disease transcriptionally and morphologically. The study reveals that CEBPA mutations when occurring before CSF3R mutations, drive leukemogenesis by blocking differentiation, resulting in AML. Through enhancer and transcription factor motif analysis, the researchers demonstrate that wild-type CEBPA activates differentiation-related enhancers, while mutant CEBPA disrupts this process. RNA-seq data analysis shows that CSF3R mutations alone promote differentiation, while early CEBPA mutations lead to a stem/progenitor-like phenotype and increased cell cycle activity. In mouse models, cells with early CEBPA mutations develop aggressive, immature leukemia, while those with initial CSF3R mutations show slower disease progression and partial differentiation. These findings highlight the diagnostic significance of CEBPA mutations in AML, emphasizing that their early presence impairs myeloid differentiation and contributes to leukemogenesis. The study stresses the importance of understanding mutation order in diagnosing AML and predicting disease progression.

This international, multi-center retrospective analysis examined characteristics of 107 cases of B- lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL) with MEF2D gene rearrangements (MEF2D-r), gathering information from 14 different regional study groups. The strength of this study was the collection of a large, well-annotated cohort of MEF2D-positive cases, allowing a more comprehensive understanding of the clinical characteristics associated with MEF2D-r. Most patients in this study were classified as high-risk based on their clinical characteristics, with approximately 70% meeting the National Cancer Institute (NCI) high-risk criteria. The median age of patients was 10.67 years, and the most common fusion partners identified were BCL9 and HNRNPUL1, accounting for 85% of the cases. The study demonstrated that MEF2D fusions in B-ALL lead to shared specific features, and are associated with female sex, older age, an atypical immunophenotype (characterized by expression of cytoplasmic immunoglobulin u chain and CD5, along with less frequent expression of CD10), and an unfavorable outcome.

This study was an international, multi-center retrospective analysis of 107 patients with MEF2D rearrangements, with information collected from 14 different regional study groups. The aim was to assess the prognostic implications of MEF2D gene rearrangements in patients with B-lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL). Previous studies, although based on a small number of cases, have shown that outcomes of patients with MEF2D rearrangements are unfavorable. The current study confirms the findings of previous studies that suggest a high risk of relapse for patients with MEF2D::BCL9 fusions. However, it could not confirm that this poor outcome extended to patients with other MEF2D fusion partners, such as MEF2D::HNRNPUL1. Outcome data was available for 95 patients, all of whom achieved complete hematological remission, with 93% testing negative for minimal residual disease (MRD) at the end of induction therapy. Despite this favorable initial response, 39% of the patients were classified as high risk based on National Cancer Institute (NCI) criteria, which may reflect the underlying genetic complexities of their conditions. After a median follow-up of 6.73 years, the event-free survival (EFS) rate was 74%, and 24% of patients experienced a relapse. While the EFS rate indicates that the therapeutic outcomes for patients with MEF2D rearrangements are not extremely poor, it remains lower than expected for patients with intermediate-risk genetics. Notably, the majority of relapses involved bone marrow, and the cohort displayed distinctive features associated with MEF2D rearrangements, including a predominance of female patients, older age at diagnosis, and a unique antigen expression profile. Overall, the study underscores the need for careful monitoring and potentially tailored therapeutic strategies for patients with MEF2D rearrangements, especially for those with MEF2D::BCL9 fusions, to improve outcomes in this high-risk population.

This study gathered diagnostic and prognostic data from pediatric B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL) patients stored in the Tokyo Children’s Cancer Study Group (TCCSG) biobank. Among the 328 selected RNA samples from B-ALL patients, 16 cases of ALL and 1 case of lymphoblastic lymphoma (LBL) harboring MEF2D fusions were identified. The MEF2D fusions included MEF2D::BCL9 (n=10), MEF2D::HNRNPUL1 (n=6), and one novel MEF2D::HNRNPH1 fusion. MEF2D fusion B-ALL patients aged between 3 and 15 years. This study identified MEF2D fusions at an incidence of approximately 2% in the B-ALL cohort. MEF2D fusion cases had a gene expression signature significantly distinct from other genetic subtypes of B-ALL; they were mutually exclusive with other subtypes defining primary genetic drivers, further emphasizing the diagnostic relevance of MEF2D fusions in B-ALL classification.

This paper presents two case studies on patients with advanced solid tumours harbouring the KRAS G12V mutation, treated with a combination of an mRNA vaccine targeting KRAS G12V and pembrolizumab. Patient-001, an 86-year-old female with locally advanced pancreatic head cancer, showed partial response and regression of the pancreatic tumour after three treatment cycles, experiencing only manageable side effects. Patient-002, a 69-year-old male with advanced NSCLC, received nine cycles of therapy, achieving partial response with significant regression in lung and lymph node lesions, and experiencing only mild, manageable side effects, such as fever and injection site pain.

In a phase 3 trial (NCT04305496) of 708 patients with advanced HR+ HER2- breast cancer, the combination of the AKT inhibitor capivasertib and the estrogen receptor degrader fulvestrant resulted in significantly longer progression-free survival compared to fulvestrant alone. Among the 289 patients (40.8%) with alterations (including PIK3CA, AKT1, or PTEN alterations), the median progression-free survival was 7.3 months in the capivasertib–fulvestrant group compared to 3.1 months in the placebo–fulvestrant group with a hazard ratio of 0.50 (95% CI, 0.38 to 0.65, p<0.001). In the capivasertib–fulvestrant group, 110 patients had PIK3CA mutations, 18 had AKT mutations, 21 had PTEN alterations, 2 had PI3KCA and AKT1 double mutations, and 4 had both PIK3CA and PTEN alterations. A breakdown of response by individual mutation was not provided.

Among the 289 patients (40.8%) with alterations (including PIK3CA, AKT1, or PTEN alterations), the median progression-free survival was 7.3 months in the capivasertib–fulvestrant group compared to 3.1 months in the placebo–fulvestrant group with a hazard ratio of 0.50 (95% CI, 0.38 to 0.65, p<0.001). In the capivasertib–fulvestrant group, 110 patients had PIK3CA mutations, 18 had AKT mutations, 21 had PTEN alterations, 2 had PI3KCA and AKT1 double mutations, and 4 had both PIK3CA and PTEN alterations. A breakdown of response by individual mutation was not provided.

The paper explores the diagnostic significance of MEF2D gene fusions in B-lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL), identifying them as important markers for a specific subgroup of the disease. RNA sequencing of 560 B-ALL cases revealed MEF2D fusions in 22 instances, with MEF2D::BCL9 fusion being the most prevalent (16/22 cases), with other fusion partners including CSF1R, DAZAP1, HNRNPUL1, and SS18. The age range of patients with MEF2D fusions was as follows: 15 cases (4.1%) were children up to 15 years old, 4 cases (6.5%) were adolescents aged 16–20 years, 2 cases (2.7%) were young adults, and 1 case was identified among 56 older adults. Further analysis of an expanded cohort of 1,164 cases confirmed that MEF2D fusions were present in approximately 5.3% of B-ALL cases that do not have other known primary alterations; FOXJ2 was identified as an additional MEF2D partner gene in the extended cohort. The study showed that B-ALLs with MEF2D fusions had a distinct gene expression profile and immunophenotype, along with frequent copy number changes at breakpoint sites within MEF2D and its partner genes. These MEF2D fusion cases were associated with poorer outcomes, highlighting their potential as diagnostic markers for a high-risk B-ALL subtype.

disease: Acute Myeloid Leukemia With Mutated CEBPA
evidence_statement: In this 2019 study, the authors investigated the diagnostic significance of CEBPA mutations in AML by analyzing how the order of these mutations influences disease development in a mouse model that replicates human AML transcriptionally and morphologically. The study reveals that when CEBPA mutations occur before CSF3R mutations, they drive leukemogenesis by blocking myeloid differentiation, resulting in AML. Enhancer and transcription factor motif analysis demonstrated that wild-type CEBPA activates differentiation-related enhancers, while mutant CEBPA disrupts this pathway. Additionally, RNA-seq data show that CSF3R mutations alone promote differentiation, whereas early CEBPA mutations lead to a stem/progenitor-like phenotype with heightened cell cycle activity. In mouse models, cells with early CEBPA mutations progress to aggressive, immature leukemia, contrasting with the slower, partially differentiated progression seen with initial CSF3R mutations. These findings underscore the role of CEBPA mutations as primary oncogenic events in AML pathogenesis.

RT-PCR in 215 cases of Schwannomas in a diverse cohort resulted in 29 out of 215 harboring SH3PXD2A::HTRA1 fusion (in-frame fusion between SH3PXD2A (exon 6) and HTRA1 (exon 2)). Histological analysis of fusion-negative tumor and fusion-positive cases revealed that fusion-positive cases exhibited shorted nuclei in the Verocay body and “serpentine” nuclear palisading histology. To confirm this pattern for a cohort of 60 cases, comprised of 36 cases with serpentine palisading histology and 24 without noticeable serpentine palisades, were subjected to RT-PCR. 81% of the serpentine cases and 8% of the non-serpentine cases were fusion-positive, suggesting that serpentine palisading could be used as an identifier of SH3PXD2A::HTRA1 fusion during histological analysis. In addition to identification of the serpentine palisades, in general, fusion-positive Schwannomas were typically smaller in size, in younger patients, and found within peripheral somatic tissues. BaseScope RNA ISH correctly identified 100% of the SH3PXD2A::HTRA1 fusion, as confirmed by RT-PCR. Transcriptomic comparison of 9 SH3PXD2A::HTRA1 fusion-positive Schwannomas and 9 fusion-negative Schwannomas, revealed no difference in the abundance of SH3PXD2A mRNA between the fusion-positive and fusion-negative groups. However, the HTRA1 mRNA was significantly upregulated in the fusion-positive group, which could potentially serve as a biomarker.

The goal of this study was to assess the frequency, overall survival, and classifying actionability of EGFR mutations in NSCLC within the Dutch population from 2013-2017. This study found that despite an increase in the number of patients tested, still 12% of patients have EGFR mutations and the distribution of the EGFR variants remained constant. This study assessed common EGFR mutations, exon 19 deletion and L858R, as compared to non-actionable/unknown/uncommon variants. They found that overall survival improved for people with EGFR mutations from 2013 to 2017. Patients with either an exon 19 deletion or L858R variant were more likely to receive first-line treatment (either gefitinib, erlotinib, or afatinib), additionally they found that EGFR exon 19 deletions had superior outcomes compared to L858R. 8.4% of exon 19 deletion patients treated with first-line treatments developed EGFR T790M mutation as a mechanism of resistance. Further studies need to be conducted as to whether Osimertinib is more effective for patients who develop T790M resistance in an exon 19 deletion or L858R background.
