Deguelin inhibits EGFR signaling in wild-type NSCLC cells. It reduces EGFR phosphorylation and downstream signalling, as shown by decreased phosphorylation of Akt and ERK1/2. This effect was not observed in wild-type cells treated with gefitinib, indicating that deguelin inhibits EGFR signalling in WT NSCLC cells. In the mouse xenograft model with WT EGFR tumour cells, while gefitinib had no visible effect on tumour growth, cells treated with deguelin reduced tumour size at the treatment endpoint.

Deguelin exhibits a potent inhibitory effect in gefitinib-sensitive HCC827 cells with exon 19 deletion (EGFR E746-A750). Both deguelin and gefitinib significantly suppressed EGFR kinase activity, reducing it to less than 20%, as shown by in vitro kinase assays. Decreased phosphorylation of downstream targets Akt and ERK1/2 was also observed. In mouse xenograft models, deguelin treatment significantly inhibited tumour growth using HCC827 cells.

Deguelin exhibits a potent inhibitory effect in gefitinib-resistant H1975 cells with EGFR L858R/T790M mutation. Decreased phosphorylation was noted in cell lines treated with deguelin but not gefitinib, in in vitro kinase assays. Decreased phosphorylation of downstream targets Akt and ERK1/2 was also observed. In mouse xenograft models, deguelin treatment significantly inhibited tumour growth using H1975 cells.

ZNF217 was overexpressed in 60% of ovarian tumour samples (26/44) as demonstrated by immunohistochemistry (IHC). Patients with ZNF217 expression had significantly shorter disease-free survival compared to those without ZNF217 expression (p = 0.042). Overexpression of ZNF217 enhanced proliferation and invasion in ovarian cancer cell lines. In female nude mice, ovarian transplantation with tumour tissues derived from subcutaneous tumours showed significantly increased metastatic activity in cell lines overexpressing ZNF217. These results collectively suggest the importance of ZNF217 in promoting tumour metastasis in ovarian cancer.

ZNF217 overexpression is linked to reduced survival across multiple breast cancer subtypes. A meta-analysis of relapse-free survival across nine studies involving 858 patients revealed that higher ZNF217 expression was significantly associated with increased relapse rates at both 5 years (p = 0.012) and 10 years (p = 0.023). Additionally, ZNF217 drives aberrant differentiation and signalling, enhances self-renewal capacity, motility, and metastasis, and represses adult stem cell gene signatures downregulated in cancers, as observed in primary mammary epithelial cells.

Triciribine inhibits ZNF217-driven tumour growth and signalling both in vivo and in vitro. In mouse models, triciribine reduced tumour burden and levels of phospho-AKT and phospho-MAPK, while increasing cell death. Tumour cells overexpressing ZNF217 are typically resistant to doxorubicin-induced cell death; however, the combination of triciribine and doxorubicin generates synthetic lethality, reversing this resistance and promoting cell death in ZNF217-overexpressing cells.

In an orthotopic mouse model of osteosarcoma (OSA), triciribine (TCN) treatment significantly reduces tumour growth and weight in both SJSA-1 and HOS cell line injections, with 5.4- and 3.0-fold reductions in tumour volume, respectively. Additionally, TCN treatment also decreased ZNF217 expression and micro-metastatic nodule formation, which demonstrates its potential to inhibit ZNF217 + OSA tumour growth and metastasis.

To study the impact of FAAP20 loss on sensitivity to PARP inhibitors (PARPi), clonogenic survival assays in HeLa cells and cell proliferation assays in U2OS cells were conducted after FAAP20 knockdown (KD) and treatment with AZD2461, a PARP1/2 inhibitor. FAAP20 KD combined with PARPi treatment nearly abolished colony formation and proliferation in both cell lines. Comparison with DMSO-treated cells confirmed that the growth loss was not solely due to KD. Additionally, RAD52 inhibition with DI03 caused further growth loss in U2OS cells with FAAP20 KD.

To evaluate the radiosensitivity of tumours with FAAP20 loss, HeLa, MIA-PaCa-2, and U2OS cells underwent siRNA knockdown of FAAP20 followed by treatment with 0.5 Gy IR. While this dose had minimal effect on WT cells, it significantly reduced colony formation in HeLa and MIA-PaCa-2 cells. U2OS cells exhibited hypersensitivity to IR, resulting in near-complete loss of cell growth.

In the phase 3 ASC4FIRST trial (NCT04971226), patients with newly diagnosed Ph+ CML were randomized 1:1 to receive either asciminib (n=201) or an investigator-selected TKI (n=204). At week 48, major molecular response (MMR) rates were 67.7% in the asciminib group versus 49.0% in the TKI group (difference, 18.9 percentage points; 95% CI, 9.6-28.2; adjusted two-sided p < 0.001). Within the imatinib stratum, 69.3% of patients in the asciminib group achieved MMR compared to 40.2% in the imatinib group (difference, 29.6 percentage points; 95% CI, 16.9-42.2; adjusted two-sided p < 0.001). In the second-generation TKI stratum, MMR rates were 66.0% with asciminib versus 57.8% with second-generation TKIs (difference, 8.2 percentage points; 95% CI, -5.1 to 21.5).

In the phase I/II trial AUGMENT-101 (NCT04065399), 94 patients (71 adults and 23 children under 18 years) with KMT2A-rearranged acute leukemia received at least one dose of revumenib. Among them, 78 patients had AML, 14 had ALL, and two had acute leukemia of ambiguous lineage. The median patient age was 37 years (range: 1.3-75.0). The median age for adults was 44 years (18.0-75.0), and for pediatric patients, it was 4 years (1.3-17.0). Among efficacy-evaluable patients (n=57), the CR + CRh rate was 22.8% (95% CI: 12.7-35.8), significantly exceeding the null hypothesis of 10% (p=0.0036). The overall response rate (ORR) was 63.2% (95% CI: 49.3-75.6), with a median time to first OR of 0.95 months (range: 0.9-2.0) and a median time to CR + CRh of 1.9 months (range: 0.9-4.6). The median duration of CR + CRh was 6.4 months (95% CI: 3.4-NR), and the median overall survival (OS) was 8.0 months (95% CI: 4.1-10.9).

In the phase 3 SPOTLIGHT trial (NCT03504397), 565 patients with gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma were randomized to receive either zolbetuximab combined with mFOLFOX6 (n=283) or placebo with mFOLFOX6 (n=282). The zolbetuximab group showed a significant reduction in the risk of disease progression or death compared to the placebo group (HR 0.75; 95% CI: 0.60-0.94; p=0.0066). The median progression-free survival (PFS) was 10.61 months (95% CI: 8.90-12.48) in the zolbetuximab group versus 8.67 months (95% CI: 8.21-10.28) in the placebo group. At 12 months, the PFS rate was 49% (95% CI: 42-55) in the zolbetuximab group compared to 35% (95% CI: 28-42) in the placebo group. At 24 months, the PFS rates were 24% (95% CI: 17-32) for zolbetuximab and 15% (95% CI: 9-22) for placebo. The median overall survival (OS) was 18.23 months (95% CI: 16.43-22.90) in the zolbetuximab group versus 15.54 months (95% CI: 13.47-16.53) in the placebo group. The 12-month OS rate was 68% (95% CI: 61-73) in the zolbetuximab group versus 60% (95% CI: 54-66) in the placebo group. At 24 months, the OS rates were 39% (95% CI: 32-46) in the zolbetuximab group and 28% (95% CI: 22-35) in the placebo group. Treatment-emergent grade 3 or worse adverse events occurred in 87% of patients (242/279) in the zolbetuximab group versus 78% (216/278) in the placebo group. The most common grade 3 or worse adverse events were nausea, vomiting, and decreased appetite. Treatment-related deaths were reported in 2% (5/283) of patients in the zolbetuximab group compared to 1% (4/282) in the placebo group.

In the phase 3 GLOW trial (NCT03653507), 507 patients with CLDN18.2-positive gastric or gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma were randomized 1:1 to receive either zolbetuximab combined with CAPOX or placebo with CAPOX. The zolbetuximab group demonstrated improved outcomes compared to the placebo group. The median progression-free survival (PFS) was 8.21 months in the zolbetuximab group versus 6.80 months in the placebo group (HR: 0.687; 95% CI: 0.544-0.866; p=0.0007). At 12 months, the estimated PFS rates were 35% in the zolbetuximab group compared to 19% in the placebo group. At 24 months, the PFS rates were 14% and 7%, respectively, favouring zolbetuximab. The median overall survival (OS) was 14.39 months in the zolbetuximab group compared to 12.16 months in the placebo group (HR: 0.771; 95% CI: 0.615-0.965; p=0.0118). The estimated 12-month OS rates were 58% in the zolbetuximab group versus 51% in the placebo group, while the 24-month OS rates were 29% and 17%, respectively.

In the phase 3 TALAPRO-2 trial 805 patients with castration-resistant prostate cancer were enrolled and randomized to talazoparib or placebo plus enzalutamide treatment. Patients were tested for homologous recombination repair (HRR) gene alterations in BRCA1, BRCA2, PALB2, ATM, ATR, CHEK2, FANCA, RAD51C, NBN, MLH1, MRE11A, or CDK12 using FoundationOne CDx or liquid CDx. In the subgroup analysis the hazard ratio for radiographic PFS (rPFS) was 0.46 (95%CI 0.3-0.7, p<0.001) for patients with HRR deficiency and 0.7 (95%CI 0.54-0.89, p<0.01) for patients without HRR deficiency, in favor of the talazoparib plus enzalutamide regimen, suggesting benefit in both HRR-deficient and HRR-proficient patients. The talazoparib treated HRR deficient patients had superior outcomes even with BRCA-altered patients removed from the analysis. Note, none of the patients in the talazoparib arm had mutations in ATR.

A 15-year-old male was diagnosed with B-cell ALL with a normal male karyotype by microarray (no aberrations >5Mb), normal FISH (including BCR::ABL1 and ABL1 breakapart) and aberrant phenotype B-lymphoid cells in cerebrospinal fluid. Patient initially received ALLTogether protocol Induction B but was MRD positive Day 29 and given consolidation. Day 71 he was MRD positive with multiple treatment-related side-effects at which point targeted RNA sequencing was performed (TruSight Pan-Cancer). A NUP214::ABL1 (e33::e3) fusion was identified, the result of a 445 kb duplication (too small for cutoffs in initial microarray studies and cryptic by FISH), and confirmed by RT-PCR. No ABL1 TKI-resistant mutations were identified so the patient was treated with imatinib mesylate with conventional chemotherapy. Patient was in complete remission in 1 month which was ongoing at 24 months from diagnosis.

In the randomized, open-label, phase 3 EMERALD trial (NCT03778931), the selective ER-degrader (SERD) elacestrant was assessed in ER+/HER2- breast cancer patients who had previously been treated with endocrine therapy and CDK4/6 inhibitor therapy. The primary end-point was progression free survival (PFS). ESR1 mutations were detected using the Guardant360 CDx test, including the variant D538G. There were 477 patients randomly assigned, 239 received elacestrant and 238 received standard-of-care (SOC: fulvestrant or aromatase inhibitors), with almost half of all patients (228 of 477) harbouring ESR1 mutations. The median PFS was significantly longer in the elacestrant arm compared to SOC in ESR1-mutated patients (HR = 0.55; 95% CI, 0.39 to 0.77 P = .0005), as well as in the entire patient population (HR = 0.70; 95% CI, 0.55 to 0.88; P = .002). Similarly, elacestrant treatment resulted in significant improvement compared to SOC in 6-month PFS [40.8% (95% CI, 30.1 to 51.4) versus 19.1% (95% CI, 10.5 to 27.8)] and 12-month PFS [26.8% (95% CI, 16.2 to 37.4) versus 8.2% (95% CI, 1.3 to 15.1)] in ESR1-mutated patients. The authors conclude that elacestrant is the first oral SERD to demonstrate a significant improvement in PFS compared to SOC treatment in pretreated ER+/HER2- advanced breast cancer patients.

disease: Acute Myeloid Leukemia With Mutated CEBPA
evidence_statement: In this 2021 study, the authors examined the prognostic implications of CEBPA mutations in pediatric and young adult acute myeloid leukemia (AML) by analyzing 2958 patients enrolled in Children’s Oncology Group trials. CEBPA mutations were found in 160/2958 cases (5.4%), with 132 (82.5%) cases having biallelic mutations (CEBPA-dm) and 28 (17.5%) cases having a single mutation in the basic leucine zipper (bZip) region (CEBPA-bZip). Both CEBPA-bZip and CEBPA-dm mutations were associated with favorable outcomes, including event-free survival (EFS) of 64% and overall survival (OS) rates of 81% and 89%, respectively. These rates were significantly higher than those in patients with CEBPA wild-type AML (EFS of 46% and OS of 61%). The study highlighted that the prognosis for both CEBPA-bZip and CEBPA-dm cases was similarly favorable, emphasizing that the presence of a CEBPA-bZip mutation alone is sufficient to predict a positive outcome. This finding challenged previous assumptions and provided new insight into the prognostic significance of CEBPA mutations in AML. In conclusion, this study establishes the favorable prognostic significance of CEBPA-bZip mutations in AML and underscores the importance of these mutations in the prognosis of pediatric AML.

In the phase 2 DESTINY-Lung02 trial, 152 metastatic NSCLC patients harbouring mutations in ERBB2 (HER2) were treated with the HER2 antibody-drug-conjugate (ADC) trastuzumab deruxtecan (5.4 mg/kg or 6.4 mg/kg once every three weeks). There was clinical benefit at both dose levels, with overall response rates (ORR) of 49% (5.4 mg/kg) and 56% (6.4 mg/kg). The median duration of response was 16.8 months (95% CI, 6.4 to not estimable [NE]) and NE (95% CI, 8.3 to NE) with 5.4 mg/kg and 6.4 mg/kg doses, respectively. The S310Y variant is included in the set of eligible ERBB2 mutations, though no patients harboured this specific variant.

This phase 3 clinical trial was conducted to assess the progression-free survival in patients with IDH-mutant gliomas treated with Vorasidenib, an oral brain-penetrant inhibitor, which showed preliminary activity in mutant gliomas. In this double-blind study, participants having residual or recurrent IDH-mutated grade 2 gliomas were randomly selected to either receive vorasidenib or placebo in 28-day cycles. The Oncomine Dx TargetTest was used for central confirmation of IDH2 R172K/W/G/M/S, though no patients in this population harboured R172M/S. The results showed significant improvement in progression-free survival for patients treated with vorasidenib compared to placebo (median progression-free survival, 27.7 months vs. 11.1 months; hazard ratio for disease progression or death, 0.39; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.27 to 0.56; P<0.001). Vorasidenib treatment also delayed the time to the next intervention.

The TRUST-I study (NCT04395677) was a phase II, multicenter, single-arm, open-label trial conducted in China to evaluate taletrectinib for ROS1 fusion-positive, locally advanced, or metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Of the 173 patients enrolled, 106 were TKI-naive, while 67 had been previously treated with crizotinib but experienced treatment failure. Twenty eight patients who had failed crizotinib treatment underwent rebiopsy. Next-generation sequencing (NGS) of tissue or liquid samples identified ROS1:p.G2032R mutations in 12 patients, ROS1:p.L2026M in 1 patient, ROS1:p.S1986F in 1 patient, and both ROS1:p.G2032R and p.G2101A mutations in another patient. The remaining 13 patients did not have any of these ROS1-acquired mutations. In the subgroup with the ROS1:p.G2032R mutation, taletrectinib-treated patients achieved an overall response rate (ORR) of 66.7% (8 of 12 patients; 95% CI, 34.89–90.08). For patients without ROS1-acquired mutations, the ORR of patients treated with taletrectinib was 38.5% (5 of 13; 95% CI, 13.86–68.42).

In this 2019 study, the authors investigated the association between NUTM1 rearrangements and B-lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL) in a cohort of pediatric and infant patients, up to 14 years of age. NUTM1 fusions were identified in 5 pediatric cases and 2 infant cases, resulting in the expression of NUTM1, a gene typically not expressed in leukemic lymphoblasts. The fusion partners identified included SLC12A6, CUX1, IKZF1, and ACIN1. These fusion events were detected in B-ALL cases that did not harbor primary genetic aberrations typically associated with leukemia, such as ETV6::RUNX1 or BCR::ABL1 fusions. Furthermore, the study found that NUTM1 fusions were linked to high gene expression on chromosome band 10p12.31-12.2, including BMI1, suggesting that these fusions are associated with a unique expression profile. The study concluded that NUTM1 fusions were present in 2.4% of pediatric B-ALL cases without sentinel cytogenetic abnormalities and defined a new genetic subtype of B-ALL.

In this 2021 study, the authors examined the diagnostic features of NUTM1-rearranged B lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL) in a cohort of infants and children. Among 161 KMT2A-wildtype infants, 21.7% were identified with NUTM1 rearrangements, detected through RNA sequencing and other molecular diagnostic techniques. The study extended the analysis to a cohort of 85 cases, which included 35 infants under 1 year of age and 50 children aged 1–15 years, sourced from the Interfant and Ponte di Legno study groups. The median age at diagnosis was 5.6 months for infants and 4 years for children, with infants more frequently presenting with elevated white blood cell counts (≥50×10⁹/L). NUTM1-rearranged B-ALL was characterized by increased expression of the nearly complete open reading frame of NUTM1 fused to various partners, including BRD9, which was exclusively observed in pro-B ALL cases. These fusions were associated with unique gene expression profiles, including upregulation of BMI1 and, in some cases, HOXA cluster genes. Importantly, NUTM1 rearrangements were mutually exclusive with common leukemia-associated aberrations, such as KMT2A rearrangements, deletions in ETV6, PAX5, or CDKN2A/B, and other sentinel genetic changes, emphasizing their distinct role in the molecular landscape of B-ALL.

This 2021 study highlights the diagnostic significance of NUTM1 rearrangements in infants with B lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL) negative for KMT2A rearrangements. Among the 30 analyzed cases of KMT2A-negative B-ALL, fusion genes were detected in 73% of the cohort, with NUTM1 rearrangements being the most frequent, identified in 9 cases (30%). The fusion partners associated with NUTM1 included ACIN1 (n=5), CUX1 (n=2), BRD9 (n=1), and ZNF618 (n=1). Diagnostic molecular profiling was performed using techniques such as split-signal FISH, multiplex RT-PCR, whole transcriptome RNA sequencing, and a custom NGS panel targeting 95 leukemia-related genes. The analysis revealed a distinct immunophenotypic profile for cases with NUTM1 fusions. These cases predominantly exhibited a CD10-positive immunophenotype (93%) and had favorable clinical diagnostic features, including low white blood cell counts (<300×10⁹/L) and prednisone good response (PGR) during initial therapy. These findings emphasize the role of NUTM1 rearrangements as a diagnostic marker for a specific molecular subgroup enriched among KMT2A-negative infant B-ALL cases.

Of the 173 patients enrolled, 106 were TKI-naive, while 67 had been previously treated with crizotinib but experienced treatment failure. Among 106 TKI-naïve patients, the independent review committee-assessed confirmed overall response rate (cORR) was 90.6% (95% CI: 83.33–95.38), with 3.8% (n=4) achieving a complete response (CR) and 86.8% (n=92) achieving a partial response (PR). The disease control rate (DCR) was 95.3% (95% CI: 89.33–98.45). After a median follow-up of 22.1 and 23.5 months, the median duration of response (DOR) and progression-free survival (PFS) were not reached. The 24-month PFS rate was 70.5% (95% CI: 59.17–79.16). The 24-month DOR rate was 78.6% (95% CI: 66.86–86.56).

molecular_profile: ZMYM2::FGFR1 Fusion OR BCR::FGFR1 Fusion OR CEP43::FGFR1 Fusion OR TRIM24::FGFR1 Fusion OR FGFR1 Translocation
evidence_statement: In this phase 2, multicenter trial, 41 patients were enrolled who had myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms (MLNs) with fibroblast growth factor receptor 1 (FGFR1) rearrangements. Patients (pts) may present with chronic-phase (CP) myeloid disease or blast-phase (BP) disease (myeloid, lymphoid, or mixed lineage) in the bone marrow (BM), and/or BP disease in extramedullary (EMD) sites. For diagnosis, the patients must have an 8p11 translocation resulting in FGFR1 rearrangement. The starting dose of pemigatinib was 13.5 mg daily (2 weeks on; 1 week off). With amendments, patients without prior therapy were eligible for a starting dose of 13.5 mg daily on a continuous schedule. The endpoints examined in this analysis include rates of complete response (CR) and complete cytogenetic response (CCyR) by karyotyping or fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH). Among 40 patients with FGFR1-mutant MLN, the most common FGFR1 fusion partner gene was ZMYM2 (13q12) (n = 17). For previously treated patients, among the 33 patients with BM and/or EMD involvement, the CR rate was 75.8%. Among the 35 patients evaluable for cytogenetic response, the CCyR rate was 71.4%. For the 5 treatment-naive patients, 2 of 2 patients with CP disease achieved CR and CCyR, and 1 of 3 pts with BP disease achieved CR and CCyR.

evidence_statement: In this 2019 study, the authors included 8 patients with B-ALL presenting with t(5;14)(q31;q32) and reviewed another 16 patients from the literature. The median age at onset was 14.3 years (range of 4 to 60) and were predominately male (20 males versus 4 females). Eosinophilia-related symptoms frequently occurred. The IGH::IL3 fusion was assumed from karyotype or proven by PCR or next-generation sequencing. A deletion of IKZF1 was also detected in 5 of the 7 analyzed cases. The authors conclude there is a subset of IGH-rearranged B-ALL cases with t(5;14)(q31;q32) and clinical features that result from the associated eosinophilia.

In this 2021 study the authors include four B-ALL cases with an IGH::IL3 gene fusion that initially were unable to be fully characterized by conventional methods. Patients' ages ranged from 6 to 19 years and consisted of 3 males and 1 female. The patients presented with elevated eosinophils and had normal karyotypes. An IGH rearrangement was detected by utilizing an IGH break-apart FISH probe for 3 patients and the IGH::IL3 gene fusion was confirmed in all four patients with next-generation sequencing assay. The patient negative for an IGH rearrangement by FISH had an insertion of the IL3 gene into the IGH region. The authors conclude that there is significant utility of next-generation sequencing techniques for B-ALL with normal conventional chromosome studies and IGH::IL3 cases may be underreported in patients with B-ALL.

In this 1989 study the authors analyzed the bone marrow aspirate from a B-ALL patient presenting with eosinophilia in the peripheral blood and found to have the t(5;14)(q31;q32) chromosomal translocation. Using cloning and nucleic acid sequencing they were able to confirm the juxtaposition of the IL3 gene and the IgH gene. The authors conclude that there is a rare distinct clinical form of acute leukemia with the t(5;14)(q31;q32) that joins the promotor of the IL3 gene to the IgH gene that likely increases transcription of a structurally normal IL3 gene.

On December 4, 2024, the Food and Drug Administration granted accelerated approval to zenocutuzumab-zbco (Bizengri, Merus N.V.) for adults with advanced, unresectable, or metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) harboring a neuregulin 1 (NRG1) gene fusion with disease progression on or after prior systemic therapy, or advanced, unresectable, or metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma harboring a NRG1 gene fusion with disease progression on or after prior systemic therapy. This represents the first FDA approval of a systemic therapy for patients with NSCLC or pancreatic adenocarcinoma harboring an NRG1 gene fusion. Efficacy was evaluated in the eNRGy study (NCT02912949), a multicenter, open-label, multicohort trial. The trial enrolled 93 adults with advanced or metastatic NRG1 fusion-positive NSCLC. Identification of positive NRG1 gene fusion status was prospectively determined by next generation sequencing assays. The major efficacy outcome measures were confirmed overall response rate (ORR) and duration of response (DOR), determined by blinded independent central review according to RECIST v1.1. For NSCLC, ORR was 29% (95% CI: 20%, 39%) and median DOR was 12.7 months (95% CI: 7.4 - 20.4).

This study identifies DUX4 rearrangements, specifically IGH::DUX4 fusions, as diagnostic markers for a distinct molecular subtype of Philadelphia chromosome-negative (Ph−) B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma (B-ALL), particularly in adolescents and young adults (AYA). In an initial cohort of 73 Ph− ALL cases (54 B-ALL, 18 T-ALL, and 1 unknown lineage), RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) detected 26 fusion genes, with DUX4 fusions being the most frequent (n=10). A second cohort of 61 Ph-B-ALL cases revealed 12 additional DUX4 rearrangements, all within the AYA group. DUX4 rearrangements involved insertions into the IGH locus, replacing the 3′ end of DUX4 with IGH fragments, which resulted in the overexpression of DUX4 with an aberrant C terminus. RNA-seq and RT-PCR confirmed high DUX4 expression exclusively in fusion-positive cases, while normal blood cells showed no expression. Hierarchical clustering placed these cases in a distinct branch of non-Ph B-ALL. Functional studies demonstrated that IGH::DUX4 fusions confer leukemogenic potential, allowing immature B cells to self-renew and expand in mouse models. The results support that DUX4 rearrangements, significantly enriched in the AYA age group, define a unique molecular subtype of B-ALL and represent a critical diagnostic marker with implications for disease classification and treatment.

This study highlights the diagnostic significance of DUX4 gene rearrangements in a distinct molecular subtype of B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma (B-ALL). Among 1,913 B-ALL cases, including 1,347 children, 395 adolescents (16–20 years), and 171 young adults (21–39 years), 141 cases (7.6%) exhibited a unique gene expression profile universally characterized by DUX4 rearrangements. These rearrangements involve the translocation of DUX4 from its native location within D4Z4 repeats on chromosomes 4q or 10q to the IGH locus, placing it under the control of the IGH enhancer and resulting in markedly increased DUX4 expression. The study showed that the presence of DUX4 rearrangements was associated with a distinct expression signature and molecular profile which in addition to DUX4 overexpression (present in all the cases), typically also included transcriptional deregulation of ERG, expression of a novel ERG isoform and frequent ERG deletion. Associated abnormalities in addition to the frequent ERG deletions (55% of cases), also included recurrent deletions in IKZF1 and PAX5. The study shows that DUX4 rearrangements represent the underlying oncogenic drivers for a B-ALL subtype characterized by DUX4 and ERG deregulation, and provide crucial molecular markers for its diagnosis and classification.

In this study, the authors analyzed the fusion gene landscape in pediatric B-lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL) across 195 cases using RNA sequencing. Fusion genes were identified in 127 cases (65%), including 27 novel fusions. Among these, 8 cases (4%) were classified as harboring recurrent IGH::DUX4 or ERG::DUX4 rearrangements, a distinct subtype characterized by overexpression of DUX4 and frequent co-occurring ERG deletions (present in 63% of DUX4-positive discovery cohort cases and 50% of validation cohort cases). These cases were identified exclusively in the "B-other" category, which includes cases lacking other primary, subtype-defining genetic drivers. DUX4 rearrangements resulted from insertions of DUX4 into IGH or ERG loci, leading to its overexpression via the regulatory regions of the partner genes. These cases displayed a unique gene expression profile, previously associated with subtypes marked by ERG deletions. The median age of patients with DUX4-rearranged B-ALL was 8.5 years, suggesting an association with older age at diagnosis compared to the broader B-ALL population. The study further revealed the utility of RNA sequencing in identifying cryptic DUX4 rearrangements and highlighted this novel subtype's generally favorable prognosis, though relapses were observed in 20% of validation cohort cases. These findings underscore the importance of genomic tools in improving pediatric B-ALL's classification and risk stratification, offering new insights into its molecular pathogenesis.

evidence_statement: This study highlights the diagnostic significance of DUX4 rearrangements in identifying a distinct molecular subtype of B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma (B-ALL). Using transcriptome sequencing of 1,988 childhood and adult B-ALL cases, the study identified DUX4 rearrangements in 106 cases (5.3%). These rearrangements involve the insertion of DUX4 from subtelomeric D4Z4 repeats into the IGH locus, resulting in transcriptional activation of DUX4 under the control of the IGH enhancer. This molecular alteration defines a unique subtype of B-ALL with a distinct gene expression profile, characterized by high DUX4 expression and frequent co-occurrence of ERG deletions (observed in 55.6% of DUX4-rearranged cases). Additional genetic alterations commonly associated with this subtype include mutations in IKZF1, PAX5, transcription factors, Ras signaling pathways, and epigenetic regulators. Unlike subtypes identified through conventional cytogenetics, DUX4 rearrangements require transcriptome analysis for detection, emphasizing the importance of RNA-seq in diagnosing these cases. The findings demonstrate that DUX4 rearrangements serve as a reliable diagnostic marker for classifying this B-ALL subtype, distinguishing it from other genetic subtypes and aiding in the refinement of leukemia classification systems.

In this trial, 101 patients with solid tumours, including lung, prostate, sarcoma, melanoma, and breast cancer, harbouring LRP1B alterations were treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors. Most patients (91%) received anti-PD-1 or anti-PD-L1 therapy, such as pembrolizumab and nivolumab, while the remaining were treated with a combination of anti-PD-1/PD-L1 and anti-CTLA-4 therapy. The objective response rate (ORR) was 54% in patients with LRP1B pathogenic or likely pathogenic (P/LP) variants (n=46), compared to 13% in those with variants of unknown significance (VUS) (n=55). Median progression-free survival (PFS) was 8.4 months (95% CI: 5.2–23) in the P/LP group versus 3.4 months (95% CI: 2.8–4.3) in the VUS group. Similarly, median overall survival (OS) was 15.5 months (95% CI: 10.3–25.1) in the P/LP group compared to 9.5 months (95% CI: 7.6–21.3) in the VUS group. Overall, the study reported better outcomes with ICI therapy in patients with P/LP LRP1B alterations than in those with VUS, irrespective of tumour mutational burden (TMB) or microsatellite instability (MSI) status.

disease: Large B-cell Lymphoma With IRF4 Rearrangement
evidence_statement: In this 2011 study the authors screened B-cell lymphomas for a FISH pattern indicating an IGH break but lacking known common partners. After identifying the t(6;14)(p25;q32) with long distance inverse PCR the authors suspected IR4, a known B-cell regulator, may have been juxtaposed to the IGH locus leading to a deregulation of IRF4 expression. Overall in the study using FISH probes for IRF4, a total of 23 lymphomas with IRF4 breakpoints were identified (17 cases with IGH::IRF4, 2 with IGL::IRF4, 1 with IGK::IRF4 and 3 where the partner remained unproven or ambiguous). Ages of the patients diagnosed with an IG::IRF4-positive lymphoma ranged from 4 to 79 years, however these lymphomas were more frequent in children with a median age of 12 years. The IG::IRF4-positive lymphomas were mostly classified histopathologically as diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) but some were classified as follicular lymphoma (FL). By immunohistochemistry the IG::IRF4-positive lymphomas were mostly characterized by a MUM1+ (MUM1 protein encoded by the IRF4 gene)/BCL6+/BLIMP1− pattern. The authors conclude that there is a novel recurrent translocation that juxtaposes the IRF4 oncogene next to one of the immunoglobulin (IG) loci that activate the transcription factor IRF4 in a subset of mature B-cell lymphomas.

disease: Large B-cell Lymphoma With IRF4 Rearrangement
evidence_statement: In this 2020 study the authors included FFPE tumour tissue of patients <18 years of age with morphological follicular lymphoma (FL) and/or diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL). FISH studies with IRF4 break-apart probes identified 7/34 (21%) patients with a positive IRF4 chromosomal rearrangement, with 4/7 cases confirmed as an IGH::IRF4 fusion. The patients were aged from 5 to 14 years. All seven cases of IRF4 breakpoint-positive FL/DLBCL cases were positive for MUM1 (protein encoded by the IRF4 gene) expression by immunohistochemistry. The IRF4-positive lymphoma frequently present as localised disease and involvement of the tonsils or nasopharynx occurred in 5 of the 7 cases. The authors conclude that all cases of MUM1-positive FL or DLBCL in children and adolescents should be tested for an IRF4 rearrangement.

evidence_statement: In this 2020 study the authors included twenty cases classified as IRF4 positive Large B-cell lymphomas (LBCL-IRF4). The patients were aged from 5 to 22 years (median of 14 years). All cases showed positivity by immunohistochemistry for MUM1 (protein encoded by IRF4) and BCL6. The rearrangement of IRF4 was confirmed by FISH for 17 cases and IGH involvement was detected in 7 cases. Through a targeted genome sequencing approach IRF4 and NF-κB-related genes (CARD11, CD79B, and MYD88) were found to be the most frequently mutated in LBCL-IRF4 cases. Copy number analysis by single-nucleotide polymorphism array platforms detected that LBCL-IRF4 cases had frequent 17p deletions and gains of chromosome 7 and 11q. Using a nanostring assay an overexpression of the downstream target genes of the NF-κB pathway were detected. The authors conclude that LBCL-IRF4 tumors have a distinct molecular profile.

evidence_statement: JAK2 rerrangements were found to be one of genetic aberrations demonstrated in 15 cases of Ph-like ALL that were characterised using transcriptome and whole genome sequencing. As these are genetic alterations activating kinase or cytokine receptor signalling, these lesions could be sensitive to tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs). This paper documented the following JAK2 fusions: BCR::JAK2, STRN3::JAK2 and PAX5::JAK2. All JAK2 fusions identified in the study are in-frame and disrupt the pseudokinase domain of JAK2, which is thought to relieve autoinhibition of the kinase domain, resulting in a constitutively active fusion protein. The authors performed targeted analysis for these specific detected fusions in another 231 cases of high risk B-progenitor ALL from the COG AALL0232. They did not identify any othe cases with the same JAK2 fusions, however this does not rule out JAK2 fusions with other not targeted partners. JAK2 rearrangements were not identified in the MPN, CMML, and AML cohorts, and have not been detected in other childhood B-ALL subtypes studied by WGS and mRNA-seq, indicating they are highly enriched in Ph-like ALL. Flow cytometric phosphosignaling analysis on the cases with BCR::JAK2 and STRN3::JAK2 fusions demonstrated activation of downstream signaling pathways and tyrosine phosphorylation. This basal level of phosphorylation was then reduced with the JAK2 inhibitor XL019. Dasatinib was able to slightly inhibit tyrosine phosphorylation in the JAK2 cases. A BCR::JAK2 rearranged xenograft model was also tested to investigate the therapeutic efficacy of the JAK2 inhibitor ruxolitinib. There was a striking decrease in leukemic burden after 4 weeks of ruxolitinib treatment compared to vehicle-treated controls confirming the role of the BCR::JAK2 fusion as the key abnormality driving survival and proliferation of leukemia cells.

The authors describe the creation of a data portal containing over 20,000 gene fusions identified in 9,966 cancer samples and 648 normal samples from The Cancer Genome Atlas. The VPS18-NTRK3 e4::e18 fusion was detected in the colorectal tumor of a 71-year-old man (TCGA-A6-2674-01A).

Using a panel of three androgen-insensitive prostate cancer cell lines (C-81, CWR-R1 and 22Rv1), a novel AR protein isoform was identified. This protein was found to be encoded by three novel alternative splice AR isoforms. The isoforms were labeled AR3, AR4 and AR5. The AR3 isoform (commonly known as AR-V7) was found to be overexpressed in the androgen-insensitive prostate cancer cell lines used. Immunohistochemical cytoplasmic expression of AR3 was increased in androgen-insensitive prostate cancer cell lines as compared to their androgen-sensitive counterparts. Nuclear translocation of AR3 immunohistochemical staining was also noted in androgen-insensitive prostate cancer cell lines. Additionally, overexpression of AR3 in an androgen-sensitive prostate cancer cell line promoted tumour growth in androgen-depleted medium, while knockdown of AR3 expresssion in androgen-insensitive prostate cancer cell lines attenuated tumour growth in androgen-depleted medium.

Seven novel AR isoforms were identified through the examination of cryptic exon splicing at exon 3 of the AR gene. All seven isoforms encode truncated AR proteins, lacking the ligand binding domain. Two of these isoforms (AR-V1 and AR-V7) demonstrated overexpression in hormone refractory prostate cancer, as opposed to hormone naive prostate cancer, with associated immunohistochemical overexpression. In hormone refractory prostate cancer cell lines, nuclear localisation of prototypical AR protein was observed on androgen exposure, however, nuclear localisation of AR-V7 protein occurred in the absence of androgen exposure. AR-V7 was transfected into an AR-negative prostate cancer cell line, and induced PSA reporter gene and androgen responsive gene expression in an androgen-independent fashion.

evidence_statement: In this study, the authors investigated the association of the RBM15::MRTFA fusion with acute megakaryoblastic leukemia (AMKL, FAB-M7), particularly in non-Down syndrome infants and young children. AMKL is a rare and heterogeneous aggresive disease that progresses rapidly, having a median patient survival of only eight months.The analysis focused on five patients, all infants and young children, diagnosed with AMKL carrying the t(1;22) translocation. Using fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH)-based positional cloning, the study defined the genomic breakpoints associated with the t(1;22) translocation. The researchers mapped breakpoints to a 28-kb intron on chromosome 22q13 and a 6-kb interval on chromosome 1p13. Subsequent analyses revealed a novel fusion gene, RBM15::MRTFA, resulting from the translocation. The RBM15::MRTFA fusion transcript encodes a chimeric protein that incorporates functional motifs from both genes, including RNA-recognition motifs (RRMs) from RBM15 and the SAP domain from MRTFA, potentially driving leukemogenesis through deregulation of RNA processing and altered transcriptional activity. This study highlights the central pathogenic role of the RBM15::MRTFA fusion in AMKL and its diagnostic significance, drawing parallels with other fusion-driven leukemias such as PML::RARA in acute promyelocytic leukemia. The findings emphasize the value of molecular diagnostics in identifying rare but critical genetic markers, underscoring the RBM15::MRTFA fusion as a key diagnostic and potentially therapeutic target in AMKL.

In this study, the authors explored the genomic landscape of acute megakaryoblastic leukemia (AMKL) in patients without Down syndrome (non-DS-AMKL). AMKL is a rare and heterogeneous subtype of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) with poor outcomes. The analysis included 99 patients, comprising 75 pediatric cases (infants and children) and 24 adult cases, making it the largest cohort of non-DS-AMKL to undergo next-generation sequencing to date. Using RNA and exome sequencing, the study identified seven genomic subgroups in pediatric non-DS-AMKL, characterized by distinct chimeric oncogenes and cooperating mutations. Among these, the RBM15::MRTFA (also known as RBM15-MKL1) fusion was detected in 10.5% of pediatric cases. This fusion, resulting from the recurrent t(1;22) translocation, was predominantly observed in infants. The RBM15::MRTFA fusion encodes a chimeric protein that integrates functional motifs from both genes, leading to aberrant regulation of RNA processing, transcriptional activity, and megakaryoblast proliferation. The study emphasized the the clinical importance of stratifying non-DS-AMKL patients by genomic subtypes and underscored RBM15::MRTFA fusion and a defining oncogenic driver for one of the molecular subtypes of AMKL.

In this study, the authors performed an international retrospective analysis of 490 pediatric patients (≤18 years) with non–Down syndrome acute megakaryoblastic leukemia (non-DS-AMKL), a rare and aggressive subtype of acute myeloid leukemia (AML), diagnosed between 1989 and 2009. The cohort, with a median age of 1.53 years, represents one of the largest studies to date on this leukemia subtype. Cytogenetic analysis, available for 372 patients (75.9%), identified the t(1;22)(p13;q13) translocation, associated with the RBM15::MRTFA (RBM15-MKL1) fusion, in 13.7% of cases. This translocation was predominantly observed in infants, with a median age of 0.55 years, and was more common in females (64.7%). The RBM15::MRTFA fusion gene, restricted to AMKL, encodes a chimeric protein that disrupts normal transcriptional regulation, aiding in leukemogenesis. The study highlighted the diagnostic significance of identifying t(1;22) through cytogenetic and molecular methods, such as fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) and reverse-transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR). The findings underscore the critical role of the RBM15::MRTFA fusion as a diagnostic marker for a subtype of non-DS-AMKL.

Drug resistance to CDK4/6 inhibitors was analyzed in a genomic study of 348 estrogen receptor-positive (ER+) breast cancer cases. Among patients treated with CDK4/6 inhibitors, those with FAT1 mutations had a median progression-free survival (PFS) of 2.4 months (95% CI: 2.0 - NR), compared to 10.1 months (95% CI: 8.7 - 12.2) for patients without FAT1 mutations (log-rank p-value = 2.2 × 10⁻¹¹). The impact of FAT1 alterations on CDK4/6 inhibitor sensitivity was more apparent in cases with bi-allelic inactivation of FAT1. FAT1 knockout and knockdown cell lines were created from the ER+, CDK4/6 inhibitor-sensitive MCF7 model to investigate this further. When exposed to 50 nM abemaciclib (a CDK4/6 inhibitor), the growth of parental MCF7 cells was completely suppressed, while FAT1 knockout or knockdown cells displayed resistance to the drug.

In this phase 3 trial, patients with chemorefractory metastatic colorectal cancer harbouring KRAS G12C mutations were assigned to one of three groups. The first group received 960 mg of sotorasib (KRAS G12C inhibitor) once daily plus panitumumab (n = 53), the second group received 240 mg of sotorasib once daily plus panitumumab (n=53), and the third group received investigator's choice of trifluridine-tipiracil or regorafenib/standard-care (n=54). The median PFS was 5.6 months (95% CI, 4.2-6.3) in the 960-mg sotorasib-panitumumab, 3.9 months (95% CI, 3.6-5.7) in the 240-mg sotorasib-panitumumab, and 2.0 months (95% CI, 1.9-3.9) in the standard care group. The hazard ratio for disease progression or death compared to the standard care cohort was 0.48 (95% CI, 0.30-0.78, p=0.005) in the 960-mg sotorasib-panitumumab group and 0.59 (95% CI, 0.37-0.95, p=0.036) in the 240-mg sotorasib-panitumumab group. The ORR was 26.4% (95% CI, 15.3 to 40.3), 5.7% (95% CI, 1.2 to 15.7), and 0% (95% CI, 0.0 to 6.6) in the 960-mg sotorasib–panitumumab, 240-mg sotorasib–panitumumab, and standard-care groups, respectively. Grade 3 or higher treatment-related adverse effects occurred in 35.8% of the 960-mg sotorasib-panitumumab group, 30.2% of the 240-mg sotorasib-panitumumab group, and 43.1% in the standard care group. Overall, the study concluded that the 960-mg sotorasib-panitumumab group resulted in a longer PFS compared to the standard treatment, and toxic effects were expected with limited discontinuation.

TROP2 T256R mutation alters the plasma membrane localization and cell-surface binding of hRS7, the humanized antibody incorporated into Sacituzumab Govitecan (SG). The TROP2 T256R encoded protein was expressed in both TNBC cells (BT549) and non-transformed cells (NIH 3T3), which lack endogenous TROP2 expression. Equivalent expression of wild-type and mutant TROP2 was verified, and cell-surface binding of hRS7 to TROP2 was assayed in these cells. Reconstituted wild-type TROP2 exhibited robust cell-surface binding by hRS7; however, in cells reconstituted with the TROP2 mutant, the binding was reduced by over 80% compared to wild-type TROP2 TNBC cells, with similar results in 3T3 cells. Experiments were then conducted to determine whether the attenuated binding of the mutant TROP2 protein by hRS7 was associated with decreased sensitivity to SG. Although reconstitution of wild-type TROP2 in TROP2 negative cells (TNBC and 3T3) conferred highly significant increases in sensitivity to SG, reconstitution with the mutant TROP2 conferred only minimal sensitivity, marginally distinguishable from that of non-reconstituted cells. These results were further corroborated by confocal immunofluorescence testing, which showed decreased binding to hRS7 in these mutant cells. Therefore, through altered localization and decreased binding to hRS7, the TROP T256R mutation confers resistance to SG.

TOP1 E418K mutation and TOP1 122fs contribute to acquired resistance to Sacituzumab Govitecan (SG) therapy through alterations in the drug target TOP1. The patient, a 42-year-old female with metastatic TNBC (MGH-18), was treated with SG after standard chemotherapy and investigational therapies failed. After a brief period of radiologic partial response, disease progression occurred within eight months, and autopsy samples were used to explore the underlying mechanisms of resistance. Whole-exome sequencing (WES) of pre-SG treatment and post-progression tumour lesions revealed a missense mutation in TOP1 E418K, which has been previously implicated in resistance to clinical TOP1 inhibitors by altering the specificity of DNA cleavage by TOP1. This branch also contained a subclonal frameshift mutation (TOP1 -122fs), which arose from the same clone harbouring the TOP1 E418K mutation, which suggests it could act as a secondary mutation to further promote resistance to SG. These TOP1 mutations were expressed in metastatic lesions further suggesting their role in SG resistance.

evidence_statement: This study reported 47 neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) patients with biallelic inactivation of NF1 genes were detected in all glial tumors. Targeted capture-based next-generation sequencing (479 cancer-related genes for detection of sequence variants, also for structural variants and copy number analysis), and DNA methylation profiling were performed. DNA methylation analysis identified a molecular low-grade group classified as "pilocytic astrocytoma arising in the setting of neurofibromatosis type 1" (PA-NF1) of 30 patients (median age 12.4 years; 17 males, 13 females), and a molecular high-grade group of 17 patients (median age 28.3 years; 8 males, 9 females). The molecularly classified PA-NF1 tumors were histologically resembled pilocytic astrocytomas (73%, 22/30 cases), with smaller subsets resembling diffuse astrocytomas (20%, 6/30 cases) or gangliogliomas (7%, 2/30 cases). Both the histologic and epigenetic features distinguished PA-NF1 tumors from sporadic pilocytic astrocytomas. The PA-NF1 tumors were distributed across the neuroaxis: thalamus/brainstem (30%), cerebral hemispheres (27%), cerebellum (23%), optic pathway (17%), and spinal cord (3%). None of the molecular high-grade group tumors was located in the optic pathway or spinal cord. All PA-NF1 tumors lacked CDKN2A mutations/deletions (p < 0.0001), ATRX mutations (p < 0.0001), and TP53 mutations (p = 0.041) compared to the molecular high-grade group. All PA-NF1 patients had favorable outcomes, with no glioma-related deaths (median follow-up 49.5 months). In contrast, 47% (8/17) of NF1 patients with molecularly high-grade gliomas died due to glioma-related complications (p < 0.0001), with a median time to death of 12.7 months. Within the molecular high-grade group, three out of five patients were histologically low-grade and succumbed to progression at 4.4, 37.2, and 62.1 months, respectively. Additionally, the PA-NF1 group showed a significantly lower rate of glioma progression (23%, median 23.5 months) compared to the high-grade group (65%, median 7.4 months) (p = 0.011). In the PA-NF1 group, four patients on trametinib or selumetinib had stable disease, and one showed partial regression with trametinib followed by further regression with selumetinib. In the molecular high-grade group, three patients experienced progression with MEK inhibitors alone (trametinib or selumetinib), while one had stable disease with combined trametinib and everolimus.

CNV analysis identified gains on chromosomes 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 (4n), 6, 7 (4n), 8, 9, 10, 11 (4n), 12 (4n), 13q (4n), 14q (4n), 15q (4n), 17 (4n), 18, 19, 21q (4n), and 22q (4n). No focal gene amplifications or deletions were identified. DNA methylation profiling classified the tumor as PA-NF1. Over 59.2 months of follow-up, no tumor progression or recurrence has been observed, and the patient remains alive.

This study reported 47 neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) patients with biallelic inactivation of NF1 genes were detected in all glial tumors. Targeted capture-based next-generation sequencing (479 cancer-related genes for detection of sequence variants, also for structural variants and copy number analysis), and DNA methylation profiling were performed. DNA methylation analysis identified a molecular low-grade group classified as "pilocytic astrocytoma arising in the setting of neurofibromatosis type 1" (PA-NF1), and a molecular high-grade group. A 14.6-year-old male (ID: 17) with a paternal family history of neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) and a 7.9-year-old male (ID: 21) with unspecified NF1 clinical stigmata but no known family history were both harbored the same NF1 germline (presumed) stop-gain variant (c.3826C>T, p.R1276*) from tumor (pilocytic astrocytoma) sequencing, with variable allele frequencies (VAF: 48% in ID: 17, 87% in ID: 21). Patient ID: 17 presented with headaches and had a brainstem tumor, while patient ID: 21 had a thalamic tumor. Patient ID: 17 had two NF1 somatic mutations (splice donor variant c.730+1G>T, VAF=23%; and frameshift deletion c.2824delA, p.S942fs*12, VAF=9%) with CNV analysis showed chromosomal losses (1, 2, 3, 8, 9, 16, 18, 22q); whereas patient ID: 21 had a NF1 somatic frameshift deletion (c.952delG, p.E318fs*58, VAF=5%) with CNV analysis showed copy-neutral loss of heterozygosity of 17q (containing NF1 gene). Both patients were diagnosed with PA-NF1 based on DNA methylation profiling. Patient ID: 17 underwent biopsy alone without adjuvant therapy and showed no tumor progression and remains alive over 319.0 months. In contrast, ID: 21 received Carboplatin/Vincristine, experienced tumor progression, and switched to Everolimus, remains alive over 44.2 months.

evidence_statement: In this study, the authors characterized 77 pediatric Ph-like B-ALL cases from the Dutch Childhood Oncology Group trials and German Cooperative ALL trials, and identified 5 cases with activated JAK signaling pathway. Specifically, there were three cases of PAX5::JAK2, one each of BCR::JAK2 and TERF2::JAK2. As the TERF2::JAK2 fusion was novel, it was additionally characterized. The fusion breakpoint was found to occur in TERF2 exon 10-JAK2 exon 19 with a deletion of the last 11 coding nucleotides of TERF2 exon 10. Overall, the authors found that JAK2 fusions comprised 6.5% of their Ph-like ALL cohort (n=77). In terms of clinical response to induction therapy, two out of five of the cases with JAK2 fusions (BCR::JAK2 and TERF2::JAK2) resulted in relapsed disease.

In this study, researchers examined the diagnostic significance of the PML::RARA fusion in acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL, FAB-M3), a subtype of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) associated with the t(15;17)(q24.1;q21.2) translocation. This chromosomal rearrangement leads to the formation of the PML::RARA fusion gene, which disrupts myeloid differentiation and results in the accumulation of abnormal promyelocytes in the bone marrow. The study focused on a pediatric female patient with APL who uniquely exhibited all three known PML::RARA transcript variants (bcr1, bcr2, and bcr3) simultaneously—an extremely rare occurrence not previously documented. These transcript variants were identified using multiple molecular techniques, including reverse transcription-quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR), HemaVision-28N Multiplex RT-qPCR, HemaVision-28Q qualitative RT-qPCR, and the AmpliSeq RNA Myeloid Panel. Further molecular analysis, including gene expression profiling via microarray, revealed upregulation of genes such as CCL1 and α- and β-defensins—markers rarely observed in AML but with potential diagnostic relevance in APL. These findings underscore the pivotal role of PML::RARA fusion in APL diagnosis and highlight the importance of molecular diagnostics in enhancing diagnostic accuracy and prognostic assessment.

This study presents a rare case of acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) characterized by an atypical PML::RARA fusion transcript resulting from the t(15;17) translocation. The patient, a 44-year-old female, was diagnosed through morphological, cytogenetic, and molecular analyses, including fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH), which confirmed the presence of t(15;17). RT-PCR revealed bands of unusual sizes, distinct from the typical PML::RARA breakpoints (bcr1, bcr2, bcr3). Sequencing identified a rare bcr2 transcript with a breakpoint in PML exon 6, which is still expected to produce a functional chimeric protein. This case reinforces the diagnostic significance of PML::RARA fusion in APL.

Two phase II clinical trials examined mTOR inhibitors, everolimus (NCT00436618) or temsirolimus (NCT00290472) in relapsed/refractory FL. Tumour blocks were collected from these trials for 21 cases (15 everolimus and 6 temsirolimus cases). In this cohort, the overall response rate to therapy (mTOR inhibitor) was 48% (10/21), including a case of complete response with everolimus. Mutations in CREBBP were significantly enriched in the responding group (100%) compared to the non-responders (54%) (Fisher's exact test, p=0.04). Mutations in CREBBP HAT were more pronounced and were present in 100% of responders, compared to 27.3% of non-responders (p=0.001).

Lymphoma cell lines with CREBBP R1446C mutations demonstrated heightened sensitivity to the HDAC3 inhibitor BRD3308. Both CREBBP R1446C and CREBBP KO cell lines showed significantly greater inhibition of cell proliferation in response to increasing concentrations of BRD3308 compared to CREBBP WT cell lines. This trend was further validated using cells treated with shHDAC3 RNA, which similarly exhibited increased sensitivity in mutant lines.

In this study, the authors investigated the molecular characteristics of acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) in patients with atypical PML::RARA fusion transcripts. APL is a rare and aggressive leukemia subtype characterized by the t(15;17) translocation, which generates the PML::RARA fusion gene. The study focused on three adult patients diagnosed with APL, all carrying novel atypical PML::RARA fusion transcripts that were undetectable using standard molecular assays. Using reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) and direct sequencing, the researchers identified abnormal-sized PCR products in these patients, indicating the presence of atypical fusion transcripts. Additional molecular analysis, including patient-specific quantitative real-time PCR (Q-RT-PCR), was conducted to monitor minimal residual disease (MRD) and evaluate therapeutic response. The study found a range of PCR product sizes, including 180 bp, 649 bp, and 505 bp in one patient, with other variations observed in the remaining two cases. This research highlights the clinical and biological significance of atypical PML::RARA fusion transcripts in APL, emphasizing their potential impact on diagnosis and treatment. The findings demonstrate that these atypical isoforms can complicate molecular detection, posing challenges for standard diagnostic assays. However, the study reaffirms that APL diagnosis is always associated with the presence of a PML::RARA fusion transcript, which in some cases requires specialized techniques for accurate identification.

In this study, the authors investigated the role of the ETV6::RUNX1 fusion in the diagnosis of B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma. B-ALL is a heterogeneous disease, and identifying cytogenetic abnormalities allows accurate stratification into genetically defined subtypes. The analysis included 342 children diagnosed with B-ALL, among whom 99 cases (28.9%) were positive for the ETV6::RUNX1 fusion, detected using polymerase chain reaction (PCR)-based molecular screening. The translocation t(12;21)(p13;q22) results in the fusion of ETV6 (TEL) on chromosome 12 and RUNX1 (AML1) on chromosome 21, creating a chimeric protein that disrupts normal hematopoietic differentiation and contributes to leukemogenesis. The study findings indicate that patients with the ETV6::RUNX1 fusion have a better event-free survival (EFS) compared to those without the fusion. While only 3% of ETV6::RUNX1-positive patients relapsed, the relapse rate in ETV6::RUNX1-negative cases was significantly higher (11.1%). This study underscores the diagnostic significance of the ETV6::RUNX1 fusion, highlighting its role as a key molecular marker in pediatric B-ALL.

Multiple myeloma (MM) is a neoplastic disorder of clonal B cells characterised by uncontrolled and aberrant proliferation of plasma cells within bone marrow, monoclonal protein in the blood or urine, and associated organ dysfunction. Approximately, 15% of patients with MM exhibit t(4;14) which often results in FGFR3 expression. FGFR3 is receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) of the FGF family. MM patients harbouring t(4;14) have a worse prognosis and shorter survival compared with patients without this translocation. Outcome of patients with MM improved significantly with the development of immunomodulatory drugs and proteasome inhibitors, but nearly all patients with MM eventually relapse. Dovitinib, an RTK inhibitor, has demonstrated in vitro inhibitory activity against FGFR. In this pre-clinical study, the author studied the efficacy and safety of dovitinib in patients with relapse or refractory MM. The author studied the effect and safety of dovitinib in 43 patients (13 t(4;14) positive, 26 t(4;14) negative, and 4 t(4;14) status non-interpretable). The result indicted that no patients had ORR or extended ORR, 20 patients had stable disease (SD). During the study, 90.7% of patients had adverse events most commonly diarrhea, nausea, vomiting and fatigue. In conclusion, dovotinib showed no single-agent activity in relapsed or refractory MM but may stabilise disease in some t(4;14) positive patients.

Philadelphia chromosome-like (Ph-like) acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is a high-risk subtype characterised by genomic alterations that activate cytokine receptor and kinase signaling. The author examined the frequency and spectrum of targetable genetic lesions in a retrospective cohort of 1389 consecutively diagnosed patients with childhood B-lineage ALL with high-risk clinical features and/or elevated minimal residual disease at the end of remission induction therapy. The Ph-like gene expression profile was identified in 341 of 1389 patients, 57 of whom were excluded from additional analyses because of the presence of BCR-ABL1 (n = 46) or ETV6-RUNX1 (n = 11). Among the remaining 284 patients (20.4%), overexpression and rearrangement of CRLF2 (IGH-CRLF2 or P2RY8-CRLF2) were identified in 124 (43.7%), with concomitant genomic alterations activating the JAK-STAT pathway (JAK1, JAK2, IL7R) identified in 63 patients (50.8% of those with CRLF2 rearrangement). The author then conducted transcriptome sequencing on the remaining patients, and found 1 patient with ETV6::NTRK3 fusion. Although the occurrence of ETV6::NTRK3 is 0.3% in the studied patients with Ph-like B-ALL, the finding this fusion was associated with the disease.

Four TP53 reactivator compounds—PC09859, PC10709, PC14374, and rezatapopt (PC14586)—were tested for their ability to restore wild-type (WT) TP53 function in TP53 Y220C-mutated cells. ELISA assays in NUGC-3 cells pre-treated with cycloheximide demonstrated that these compounds could resynthesize WT TP53 from the Y220C mutant without requiring new protein synthesis. Additionally, they induced G1 cell cycle arrest in a dose-dependent manner, leading to diminished cell proliferation in Y220C-mutant, WT, and TP53 knockout (KO) cells. In NUGC-3 xenograft models harboring the TP53 Y220C mutation, rezatapopt treatment for four days resulted in decreased mutant p53 levels and a dose-proportional increase in restored WT p53, with similar findings observed in the T3M-4 model. Further investigations in humanized p53 knock-in mice with Y220C mutations, treated with PC14374 and infected with MT373 (a primary sarcoma cell line), showed an increase in WT p53 protein levels alongside a reduction in mutant p53 protein expression.

Rezatapopt demonstrated clinical efficacy in the PYNNACLE Phase 1 dose-escalation study (NCT04585750), showing promising responses in two heavily pre-treated patients with solid tumors. A patient with small cell lung carcinoma harboring the TP53 Y220C mutation was treated with 1150 mg of rezatapopt once daily and achieved a partial response, with respiratory symptoms improving after six weeks. CT scans revealed a 60.3% tumor reduction at week 6 and 65.4% by week 12, with treatment continuing for nearly 12 months before disease progression occurred in non-target lesions. Another patient with advanced serous endometrial cancer, previously treated with four lines of therapy, received 2000 mg of rezatapopt once daily. CT scans showed a 17.8% reduction in target lesions by week 6 and 55.8% by week 11, with a complete response in non-target lesions. Although the TP53 Y220C mutation was present in biopsy tissue, circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) for the mutation was undetectable at treatment initiation, preventing a direct correlation between response and mutation status. Treatment was discontinued after 16 months due to disease progression.

To investigate the role of ATP7B in cisplatin resistance, the IGROV-CP20 ovarian cancer cell line was compared to its parental cisplatin-sensitive IGROV line. IGROV-CP20 cells exhibited significantly higher viability across various cisplatin concentrations, confirming their resistance to Pt-based therapy. Western blot, qRT-PCR, and immunofluorescence assays revealed elevated ATP7B expression in IGROV-CP20 cells compared to IGROV cells. Notably, ATP7B silencing reduced IGROV-CP20 cell viability by 50% upon cisplatin treatment, demonstrating ATP7B’s key role in promoting cisplatin resistance.

A high-throughput screening (HTS) strategy based on synthetic lethality was used to identify drugs that reduce cisplatin resistance in IGROV-CP20 cells, assessed via an MTT colorimetric assay. Various drugs were tested with and without 50 µM cisplatin for 24 hours. Compounds toxic on their own were classified as negative hits, while those that enhanced cisplatin-induced cell death were considered positive hits, yielding eight candidates. Among them, only Tranilast, Telmisartan, and Amphotericin B demonstrated a dose-dependent correlation with cisplatin sensitivity. Co-treatment with cisplatin and any of these three drugs significantly increased sensitivity compared to cisplatin alone. Despite their similar effects on resistance, only Amphotericin B led to a substantial increase in intracellular Pt levels. This was accompanied by a marked reduction in ATP7B protein, whereas Tranilast and Telmisartan did not promote Pt accumulation. Therefore, Amphotericin B enhances cisplatin sensitivity by increasing intracellular Pt levels and reducing ATP7B protein expression.

Traniliast suppresses ATOX1, a transport protein that delivers Pt to ATP7B. This suppression indirectly inhibits ATP7B trafficking and function, leading to increased nuclear Pt accumulation.

evidence_statement: This study investigates the diagnostic importance of the translocation t(16;21)(p11;q22), resulting in the TLS/FUS::ERG fusion gene, in acute myeloid leukemia (AML). The authors utilized RT-PCR to detect the TLS/FUS::ERG chimeric transcripts in 19 AML cases with the t(16;21)(p11;q22) identified through karyotype analysis. The median age at diagnosis was 22 years (range 2 to 61 years ). The fusion transcript was consistently detected, even during remission, suggesting its role in identifying persistent leukemic cells and potential chemoresistance. The reliable detection of the TLS/FUS::ERG chimeric transcripts at diagnosis demonstrates their utility as a highly sensitive molecular marker for initial AML diagnosis and ongoing disease monitoring. The study also identified a novel transcript variant (Type D), characterized by an additional 138 nucleotides from TLS/FUS exon 8 and ERG exons 7 and 8, which highlights increased molecular heterogeneity in this genetic alteration. This research emphasizes the diagnostic relevance of the t(16;21) translocation across various French-American-British (FAB) subtypes of AML, providing valuable insight for improved diagnostic accuracy in AML patients.

evidence_statement: This international retrospective study investigates the diagnostic features of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) with the t(16;21) translocation resulting in the FUS::ERG fusion gene in pediatric patients. Data were gathered from 14 cohorts within the Berlin-Frankfurt-Münster (I-BFM) Study Group, encompassing 31 cases exhibiting the FUS::ERG with a median age of 9 years (range 2 to 18 years). AML with t(16;21) did not show a predominance in any specific FAB classification and was frequently associated with complex karyotypes, including trisomy 8 and trisomy 10. Notably, FUS::ERG AML often presented with eosinophilia, micromegakaryocytes, and hemophagocytosis. Standard karyotyping may fail to detect the translocation, necessitating the use of more sensitive diagnostic methods such as FISH, RT-PCR, or RNA sequencing. Although 87% of patients achieved remission, 74% experienced relapse, most within the first year, and minimal residual disease (MRD) negativity did not predict relapse-free survival, indicating the presence of chemoresistant leukemic stem cells. Gene expression profiling revealed a distinct molecular signature, with altered retinoic acid signaling, which may offer potential therapeutic targets. The study highlights the unique diagnostic characteristics of AML with t(16;21), reinforcing the need for specialized molecular testing and offering insight into its distinct biological and clinical features.

evidence_statement: This study focuses on the diagnostic characteristics of pediatric patients with the t(16;21)(p11;q22)/FUS::ERG translocation using advanced molecular methods. The authors studied four cases of pediatric AML with a median age of 3 years (range 2 to 5 years) in which karyotype analysis revealed the t(16;21)(p11;q22) resultig in the FUS::ERG fusion. They identified multiple FUS::ERG transcript variants, including a novel fusion where FUS exon 7 fuses with ERG exon 9, complicating minimal residual disease (MRD) detection. To improve diagnostic accuracy, next-generation sequencing and long-range PCR were used to precisely map breakpoints at the DNA level. Cytogenetic analysis revealed the t(16;21) translocation either as an isolated abnormality or in combination with trisomy 8 and del(9), accompanied by distinct immunophenotypic features such as high CD56 expression. Additionally, mutations in DNMT3A, ASXL1, BCOR, and RUNX1 were detected, suggesting clonal evolution prior to FUS::ERG transformation. These molecular findings highlight the complexity of diagnosing this specific AML subtype, underscoring the importance of utilizing sensitive techniques such as next-generation sequencing and long-range PCR for accurate detection of FUS::ERG and related genetic alterations.

Sanger sequencing identified DICER1 hotspot mutations in 20 of 32 (63%) ovarian Sertoli–Leydig cell tumors. These mutations were unrelated to tumor differentiation and mostly (16/20, 80%) were E1705K. However, one Sertoli–Leydig cell tumors had a DICER1 G1809R mutation. No DICER hotspot mutations were identified in 15 testicular sex cord-stromal tumors (8 classical Sertoli cell tumors, 3 Sertoli cell tumors-large cell calcifying variant, 4 sex cord-stromal tumors not otherwise specified).

This study investigated the role of TFCP2-related gene fusions in primary intraosseous rhabdomyosarcomas (PIOS), particularly within spindle cell and sclerosing rhabdomyosarcoma subtypes. The analysis included seven patients with tumors located in the iliac bone, femur, maxilla, and skull, all exhibiting spindle cell morphology. Among the five cases tested for TFCP2-related gene abnormalities, three harbored an EWSR1::TFCP2 fusion, one had a FUS::TFCP2 fusion, and another showed a FUS rearrangement without TFCP2 involvement. Morphologically, TFCP2 fusion-associated tumors were composed of spindle cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm, arranged in short fascicles or sheets, with some cases also displaying epithelioid cells. Immunohistochemically, these tumors were diffusely positive for desmin, focally positive for myogenin, cytokeratin, and ALK. These findings highlight the diagnostic significance of TFCP2-related fusions in spindle cell and sclerosing rhabdomyosarcomas, distinguishing them as a rare subtype of bone rhabdomyosarcoma.

This 2018 study highlighted the diagnostic role of the FUS::TFCP2 fusion in spindle cell/sclerosing rhabdomyosarcoma (sRMS) through a single-case study of a primary spindle cell rhabdomyosarcoma of bone. The tumor harbored an in-frame fusion joining exon 6 of FUS to exon 2 of TFCP2, resembling previously reported cases of aggressive rhabdomyosarcoma. The fusion was confirmed using FISH, RT-PCR, and Sanger sequencing, establishing it as a key molecular feature. RNA-sequencing analysis demonstrated overexpression of ALK, TERT, MYOD1, and multiple keratin genes, distinguishing the tumor from normal skeletal muscle. Chromosomal microarray revealed a tetraploid complement, an unbalanced 16p11.2 rearrangement disrupting FUS, and CDKN2A deletion, suggesting genomic instability. Histologically, the tumor showed monomorphic spindle cell morphology, strong MyoD1 and desmin expression, limited myogenin expression, and ALK positivity. These findings underscore the diagnostic value of the FUS::TFCP2 fusion in identifying a genetically distinct and aggressive subset of sRMS, reinforcing its role as a molecular marker.

molecular_profile: SMARCB1 LOSS OF NUCLEAR PROTEIN EXPRESSION
evidence_statement: This is the first case report of cribriform neuroepithelial tumor (CRINET), a rare brain cancer identified in a 26-month-old girl and a 10-month-old boy, affecting the third and fourth ventricles. Histologically, CRINET is a non-rhabdoid neoplasm with cribriform strands and a trabecular pattern, distinct from atypical teratoid/rhabdoid tumors (AT/RT). Immunohistochemistry revealed a loss of nuclear INI1 (encoded by SMARCB1) expression in tumor cells, while surrounding vascular cells and infiltrating lymphocytes demonstrated a normal pattern of retained staining. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) detected no structural alterations at the SMARCB1 locus in 22q11.2. However, sequencing of SMARCB1 identified a homozygous 4-bp duplication within exon 4 (492dupCCTT), causing a premature stop codon in one case, with no mutations found in the other. In conclusion, CRINET is a non-rhabdoid intraventricular and periventricular intracranial tumor characterized by loss of INI1 expression.

evidence_statement: This study explored the molecular features of cribriform neuroepithelial tumors (CRINET) using multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification (MLPA) and molecular inversion profiling (MIP) assays alongside targeted sequencing. The analysis included 3 cases that exhibited the characteristic CRINET feature of INI1 protein loss (encoded by SMARCB1 on 22q11.2). MLPA and SMARCB1 sequencing identified an allelic loss on 22q with an exon 4 CCTT duplication (492dupCCTT) in case 1 and a p.T381R mutation in case 3. A homozygous deletion of exons 7 and 8 of SMARCB1 was found in case 2. MIP analysis revealed a stable genomic profile, with no large chromosomal changes beyond 22q loss, though copy number gains were detected in several cancer genes in individual cases. Collectively, this study confirmed previous findings that identify SMARCB1 as the key gene in CRINET pathogenesis.

A drug screen of triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) cell lines found several therapies to be synthetically lethal with RB1 loss of function. Cell lines with endogenous expression of RB1 (BT20, MB453, MCF7, and MB231) were resistant to gemcitabine, while those with RB1 loss (MB468, BT549, AW23) or experimental knockdown had increased sensitivity. In addition, inhibition of CDK4/6 upstream of RB1 reduced sensitivity to gemcitabine in RB1-positive cells (MB231).

Cell cycle analysis indicated that CHK1 inhibition in RB deficient cells resulted in the appearance of fragmented nuclei and S phase collapse, which indicates irreparable DNA damage during S phase.

evidence_statement: This study compared cribriform neuroepithelial tumor (CRINET) and atypical teratoid/rhabdoid tumor (AT/RT) to determine whether CRINET is a distinct entity or a variant of AT/RT. The study contained 10 CRINET samples, including 6 previously reported cases, and 30 AT/RT samples, with 10 samples from each of the three AT/RT subgroups (ATRT-TYR, ATRT-SHH, and ATRT-MYC). Molecular profiling used Infinium HumanMethylation450 arrays, SMARCB1 fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification (MLPA), and sequencing. Additionally, the survival outcome of the CRINET cohort was compared to a larger cohort of 27 patients with ATRT-TYR. Anatomical sites of CRINETs included supratentorial, infratentorial and lateral ventricle locations. CRINET cases showed diverse SMARCB1 alterations in copy number and mutations. 9 of 10 cases of CRINET harboured large heterozygous chr22q deletions inclusive of the SMARCB1 gene, with SMARCB1 mutations in the other allele in 5 cases (2 of which were germline). Methylation profiling placed CRINET within the AT/RT-tyrosinase (TYR) subgroup. Histologically, CRINET exhibited distinct morphology from AT/RT-TYR, although all CRINET cases and 9/10 AT/RT-TYR cases showed immunohistochemical staining for tyrosinase. Clinically, CRINET patients (n=10) showed better survival than ATRT-TYR patients (n=27). Mean overall survival was 125 months (95% CI: 100–151) for CRINET and 53 months (95% CI: 33–74) for ATRT-TYR. This study highlights key histopathologic and prognostic differences between CRINET and AT/RT-TYR. The results show that CRINET should be considered a separate entity although SMARCB1 abnormalities play the key role in pathogenesis of both AT/RT and CRINET.

In this study, the authors explored the role of retinoic acid receptor alpha (RARα) gene rearrangements in acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) and their connection to the t(15;17) chromosomal translocation. Using molecular and cytogenetic analyses, they examined eight APL patients and the NB4 cell line, derived from an APL patient. The study identified a RARα fusion transcript, formed by the translocation of RARα from chromosome 17 to the partner gene on chromosome 15. Southern blot analysis detected RARα gene rearrangements in six of the eight APL patients, while these alterations were absent in normal and non-APL leukemic controls. These findings strongly implicate RARα in APL leukemogenesis and suggest that the t(15;17) translocation results in a fusion gene that disrupts normal RARα function, contributing to the disease. The study further highlights the importance of molecular testing for RARα rearrangements as a diagnostic marker for APL.

In this study, the authors investigated the role of retinoic acid receptor alpha (RARα) gene rearrangements in acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL), a distinct subtype of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) characterized by the t(15;17) chromosomal translocation. The study analyzed 20 APL cases, of which 18 exhibited the t(15;17) translocation, while 2 had a normal karyotype. Using Southern and Northern blot analyses, the authors identified RARα gene rearrangements and aberrant transcripts exclusively in APL cases, but not in other neoplastic conditions or normal controls. These findings suggest that RARα is directly involved in the APL chromosome 17 breakpoint and plays a crucial role in leukemogenesis. The study highlights the diagnostic significance of RARα gene alterations, as their presence can serve as a molecular marker for identifying leukemic promyelocytes in APL.

evidence_statement: In this study, the authors investigated the diagnostic role of TFCP2 fusions in spindle cell/sclerosing rhabdomyosarcoma (SC/S-RMS), a rare and aggressive subtype of rhabdomyosarcoma. While SC/S-RMS encompasses molecularly distinct subgroups, recent RNA sequencing studies have identified a novel subset defined by TFCP2 rearrangements. The analysis focused on 14 cases, highlighting their unique clinicopathological and molecular characteristics. Using fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), array-comparative genomic hybridization (array-CGH), RNA sequencing, and targeted next-generation sequencing, the study confirmed the presence of TFCP2 fusions with either EWSR1 (n=6) or FUS (n=8). These tumors predominantly arose in bone (12/14), with a striking predilection for the craniofacial skeleton, an unusual site for rhabdomyosarcoma. Morphologically, they displayed a spindle cell and epithelioid pattern, frequently expressing myogenic markers (MYF4 and/or MYOD1) and keratins. ALK over-expression was observed in most cases, often associated with internal deletions rather than gene fusions. Genomic profiling revealed complex rearrangements, including recurrent CDKN2A deletions and high genomic instability. This study establishes TFCP2 fusions as a defining feature of a distinct spindle cell/sclerosing rhabdomyosarcoma subtype. The findings underscore the diagnostic utility of TFCP2 rearrangement testing in distinguishing this entity from other rhabdomyosarcoma subtypes and suggest ALK over-expression as a potential therapeutic target.
