evidence_statement: Eight MVNT cases (6 pure MVNT and 2 with ganglioglioma-like features) were examined, comprising 4 males and 4 females aged 11–63 years (median 39). Tumors were localized to the temporal lobe (n=7) or frontal lobe (n=1). NGS targeting 479 cancer-associated genes identified mutually exclusive alterations: non-V600E BRAF missense mutations, MAP2K1 missense/in-frame indel mutations, or an FGFR2–INA in-frame fusion/inversion (preiced N-terminal FGFR2 [exons 1–17, aa 1–768; breakpoint chr10:123241081] fused to C-terminal INA [exons 2–3, aa 356–499; breakpoint chr10:105043061]). Identical mutations were detected in both the MVNT and ganglioglioma-like components. No chromosomal copy number alterations were identified. IHC for pERK demonstrated strong immunoreactivity in neoplastic neurons and admixed glial cells in 5 MAP2K1-mutated cases and 1 FGFR2-fusion case, consistent with MAPK pathway activation.
In a 54-year-old female with chronic headache and a right temporal lobe MVNT, NGS (479-gene panel) identified a BRAF p.L597R mutation (NM_004333.6:c.1790T>G; VAF 5%).

In an 11-year-old female presenting with seizures, a mixed MVNT with a ganglioglioma-like component located in the left temporal lobe revealed a BRAF p.G469S mutation (NM_004333.6:c.1405_1406delinsTC; VAF 14%) on NGS targeting 479 cancer-related genes.

NGS targeting 479 cancer-associated genes were performed on two MVNT cases: a 63-year-old female with left-hand paresthesia and a 54-year-old male with long-standing epilepsy, both located in the right temporal lobe. Both tumors harbored the MAP2K1 p.Q56P mutation (NM_002755.4:c.167A>C) with VAFs of 4% and 21%, respectively. IHC for pERK demonstrated immunoreactivity in neoplastic cells, consistent with MAPK pathway activation.

A 43-year-old male with chronic headache was found to have a left frontal multinodular and vacuolating neuronal tumor (MVNT). NGS targeting 479 cancer-associated genes identified a MAP2K1 in-frame indel (NM_002755.4:c.167_182delinsT; NP_002746.1:p.Q56_G61delinsL) at a variant allele frequency (VAF) of 6%. IHC for pERK demonstrated immunoreactivity in neoplastic cells, consistent with MAPK pathway activation.

A cross-sectional cohort study was performed in 161 men with metastatic prostate cancer undergoing a change in treatment to determine if pre-therapy AR-V7 nuclear protein expression in circulating tumor cells (CTCs) is a treatment-specific marker for outcomes between androgen receptor signaling (ARS) inhibitors and taxanes. A multivariable model adjusting for baseline factor associated with survival showed superior overall survival with taxanes relative to ARS inhibitors when AR-V7-positive CTCs were detected pre-therapy (hazard ratio , 0.24; 95% CI 0.10-0.57; P=0.035).

A blinded, multi-institutional cohort study was performed in 142 men with metastatic, castration-resistant prostate cancer to determine if pre-therapy nuclear-localized expression of AR-V7 protein in circulating tumor cells (CTCs) is a treatment-selective marker for outcome following treatment with either androgen receptor signaling (ARS) inhibitors or taxanes. Patients with AR-V7-positive CTCs had superior overall survival with taxanes vs ARS inhibitors (hazard ratio 0.62; 95% CI 0.28-1.39; P=.25). Patients with AR-V7-negative CTCs had superior overall survival with ARS inhibitors vs taxanes (hazard ratio 1.67; 95 CI 1.00-2.81); P=.05).

To compare the activity of AR-V7 with that of full-length AR (AR-FL) lentiviral stable cell lines of castrate-resistant prostate cancer were generated that expressed doxycycline-regulated AR-V7 or AR-FL using the cell line C4-2 PCa. These cells were injected into the tibias of castrated male mice. Compared to cells expressing or over-expressing AR-FL those expressing AR-V7 induced mixed osteoblastic/osteoclastic bone lesions and increased the area of bone lesions 4-6 weeks after injection. Expression of SOX9 protein, a known driver of metastasis, increased significantly in tumors expressing AR-V7 but remained low and unchanged in those expressing AR-FL.

disease: B-lymphoblastic Leukaemia/lymphoma With Other Defined Genetic Alterations
evidence_statement: In this 2017 study, the authors analyzed 91 pediatric B-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukemia (BCP-ALL) patients and an additional 122 classified as "B-others" lacking conventional genetic abnormalities. ZNF384 rearrangements were identified through whole transcriptome sequencing and PCR-based fusion detection. ZNF384-related fusions were detected in 4.1% of all BCP-ALL cases (9.2% of B-others), with TCF3::ZNF384 being most frequent (2.4% overall). The leukemic cells exhibited a characteristic immunophenotype of weak/absent CD10 and aberrant CD13/CD33 expression, distinct from ZNF384-fusion negative cases. Gene expression profiling revealed enrichment of hematopoietic stem cell features in TCF3::ZNF384 cases, differing from TCF3-PBX1-positive ALL. Clinically, TCF3-ZNF384 patients presented with higher leukocyte counts and poorer steroid response compared to EP300-ZNF384 cases, suggesting fusion partner-dependent heterogeneity. The study demonstrates that ZNF384 rearrangements define a molecularly distinct BCP-ALL subgroup with diagnostic immunophenotypic features, while clinical outcomes vary by fusion partner.

Patient-derived GIST-T1/829 cells with driver mutation KIT 560-578 deletion and secondary KIT A829P mutations were tested for TKI responsiveness. 560-578del and A829P cells (Sunitinib IC50: 1168 nM and Imatinib IC50:1201 nM) did show resistance towards Sunitinib and Imatinib compared to GIST-T1 cells with 560-578 deletion alone (Sunitinib IC50: 15 nM and Imatinib IC50: 30 nM). Sunitinib and Imatinib did not inhibit p-KIT, p-ERK, and p-AKT in GIST-T1/829 cells.

Fibroblast Growth Factor Receptor 1 (FGFR1) amplification is frequently observed in estrogen receptor-positive (ER+) breast cancer and is associated with poor prognosis and resistance to endocrine therapy. FGFR inhibitors have shown potential to overcome this resistance. A phase II study, the NCI-MATCH ECOG-ACRIN Trial (EAY131) Subprotocol K1 (NCT06308822), was an open-label, single-arm trial that required central confirmation of FGFR1–4 amplification in tumors. A total of 18 patients were enrolled, including 9 with breast cancer. FGFR amplifications were detected by the NCI-MATCH sequencing assay, with a minimum laboratory reported copy number of 7.0. All participants received oral erdafitinib at a starting dose of 8 mg once daily, with dose escalation to 9 mg permitted based on tolerability. The primary endpoint was the centrally assessed objective response rate (ORR). Key secondary endpoints included 6-month progression-free survival (PFS6), overall PFS, overall survival (OS), and safety. No confirmed responses to erdafitinib were observed. However, five patients achieved stable disease as their best response. Notably, one patient with FGFR1-amplified breast cancer experienced prolonged survival, with a PFS exceeding 168 days (5.5 months).

A 30 year old women with advanced acinic cell tumor of the right parotid gland had her disease progressed after initial systemic chemotherapy, followed by empirical erlotinib hydrochloride therapy. Progression biopsy of the right parotid gland mass was subjected to comprehensive genomic profiling revealing an intrachromosomal duplication event at 7q34 with a breakpoint at intron 9 resulting in duplication of the entire BRAF kinase domain and an additional breakpoint in the intergenic space downstream of the BRAF gene. No other oncogenic driver alterations were observed across the 315 genes assayed. Based on this finding, patient was treated with regorafenib monohydrate and achieved a considerable partial response in all disease sites. Patient continued to maintain a partial response lasting more than 12 months with regorafenib therapy.

Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) studies were performed using home brew probes targeting 3′ BRAF, 5′ BRAF, and a commercial CEP7 probe on 59 patients with optic nerve glioma. Duplication of the BRAF kinase domain (3′ portion of the gene) was the most frequent molecular alteration, present in 11 of 15 (73%) of the evaluable tumor samples. The main molecular cytogenetic finding in optic nerve gliomas was duplication of the 3′ region of the BRAF gene, leading to 3 red signals in neoplastic cells, with the signal of duplication overlapped with green yielding yellow signals.

A total of 23,396 patients with lung cancer and comprehensive genomic profiling were reviewed for BRAF alterations, and kinase domain duplication (KDD) mutations were observed in 0.75% of the cases. Four different types of KDD mutations with different breakpoints upstream of the kinase domain were illustrated in figure 2C. This study is considered the largest cohort study of BRAF alterations in lung cancer, and reveal the prevalence of all BRAF mutations types in lung cancer, including BRAF KDD.

In this study, the authors used long-distance inverse PCR and sequencing to comprehensively analyze KMT2A (MLL) gene rearrangements in 2,345 acute leukemia patients, including those with B-lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL). The findings reinforce the diagnostic significance of KMT2A rearrangements in B-ALL, particularly in infants and young children. The study identified 135 distinct KMT2A rearrangements involving 94 translocation partner genes (TPGs); of those, only 9 fusions accounted for over 90% of the cases, including KMT2A::AFF1, KMT2A::MLLT1, and KMT2A::MLLT3. Among B-ALL patients, the KMT2A::AFF1 (AF4) fusion was the most frequent, especially in infants, followed by KMT2A::MLLT1 (ENL) and KMT2A::MLLT3 (AF9). Importantly, the study highlighted an age-dependent breakpoint shift within the KMT2A locus, with intron 11 breakpoints associated more frequently with B-ALL in younger patients, and intron 9 breakpoints found more often in AML and older patients. This study supports the classification of B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma with KMT2A rearrangement as a distinct diagnostic entity independent of the fusion partner; this is recognized in the WHO 5th edition (2022) and the International Consensus Classification.

In this publication, the authors conducted a comprehensive genomic analysis of 2,754 pediatric acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) cases using integrated whole genome, exome, and transcriptome sequencing. Of the 2,288 B-ALL cases analyzed, KMT2A rearrangements were identified in approximately 4.5%, confirming their role as a recurrent driver in pediatric B-ALL. These KMT2A-rearranged cases were characterized by a low somatic mutational burden, distinct gene expression profiles, and unique biological features compared to other B-ALL subtypes. The study revealed multiple KMT2A fusion partners, with recurrent fusions involving genes such as MLLT1, MLLT3, AFF1, and others, reinforcing that the diagnostic significance lies in the presence of the KMT2A rearrangement itself, irrespective of the fusion partner. Further sub-classification based on transcriptome clustering identified two transcriptionally distinct KMT2A subgroups—one enriched for NFATC4 expression and the other for CEBPA/FLT3 expression—suggesting underlying differences in developmental origin and potential clinical implications. These findings support the recognition of B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma with KMT2A rearrangement as a distinct diagnostic entity, consistent with the updated 2022 International Consensus Classification (ICC) and the 2024 World Health Organization (WHO) classification.

In this publication, the diagnostic significance of KMT2A rearrangements in B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma (B-ALL) is explored. The study reveals that KMT2A fusions are not restricted to lymphoid lineages but may also involve myeloid compartments and hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells (HSPCs), supporting a multilineage origin in a substantial proportion of cases. Notably, 36% of patients with KMT2A-rearranged B-ALL exhibited evidence of multilineage involvement at diagnosis. This finding has important diagnostic implications, as conventional MRD assessment strategies—relying on flow cytometry or immunoglobulin gene rearrangement—may fail to detect residual disease in cases where leukemic clones persist in non-lymphoid compartments. RNA sequencing data further demonstrate a gene expression profile enriched for HSPC and myeloid programs in these patients, reinforcing the hybrid lineage biology of KMT2A-rearranged B-ALL. These findings highlight the importance of incorporating molecular techniques such as fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) or RNA-based assays to detect KMT2A fusions as key diagnostic markers in this B-ALL subtype.

disease: Glioneuronal Tumor With ATRX Alteration, Kinase Fusion And Anaplastic Features
evidence_statement: A novel group of tumors identified by DNA methylation data based on a separate cluster distinct from all other established CNS tumor types. This study proposed the term glioneuronal tumor with ATRX alteration, kinase fusion and anaplastic features (GTAKA) for this tumor group. RNAseq identified CLIP2(ex10, 7:73791152)::EGFR(ex18, 7:55241614) fusion in one of 20 cases. This fusion retains CAP-Gly domain of CLIP2 and protein kinase domain of EGFR. Copy number profile derived from DNA methylation data showed gains of chromosomes 2, 3, 7, and 11, and loss of 5q. No functional data.

Dovitinib, a pan-FGFR small molecular inhibitor, has shown activity in pre-clinical models against FGFR-expressing breast cancer model cell lines, as well as as in a single agent in a phase II clinical trial in HR+/HER2- FGFR1 amplified breast cancer patients. Notably, this is among patients with higher levels of FGFR amplification. A phase II, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial was designed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of dovitinib in combination with fulvestrant in postmenopausal women with HR+, HER2− locally advanced or metastatic breast cancer with disease progression. FGF pathway amplification was determined using TaqMan assay as described by (André F. et al, 2013). Positive amplification for each FGF pathway marker tested (i.e., FGFR1, FGFR2, or FGF3) was defined as a copy number ≥6. The primary endpoint was progression-free survival (PFS). However, the study had to be stopped early due to slow accrual of patients with FGF pathway amplification. The overall response rate (assessed at regular radiological assessment) in the dovitinib + fulvestrant arm (n=47) was 27.7%, as compared to 10% in the placebo + fulvestrant arm (n=50), irrespective of the presence of FGF pathway amplification. The FGFR-amplified subgroup (n=31) reached a median PFS of 10.9 months vs 5.5 months in the dovitinib + fulvestrant vs placebo + fulvestrant arms respectively. The final analysis showed limited benefit, with the authors' recommendation to exercise caution when interpreting the study results (particularly the PFS results), due to a fewer than expected number of PFS events (18 vs 50 planned events), as well as the study's small sample size.

The Targeted Agent and Profiling Utilizing Registry (TAPUR) study is a prospective, phase II, basket trial that aims to evaluate the antitumor activity of commercially available targeted therapies prescribed to patients with advanced cancer with actionable targets. In this study, sunitinib is evaluated in patients with breast cancer, with FGFR alterations. Patients eligible for the study include those age 12 years or older, who have BC with an FGFR1/2 amplification or mutation. Definitions of amplification were not prespecified in the protocol because of the variety of genomic tests that could qualify a patient for participating in the study. The primary endpoint was disease control (DC) based on the investigator assessment – this was defined as objective response (OR) or stable disease (SD) of at least 16 weeks duration (SD16+), measured from the initiation of study treatment, as determined by the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) version 1.1. Secondary endpoints were progression free survival (PFS), overall survival (OS), duration of response, duration of SD, and safety. Thirty patients with BC with FGFR1 alterations (amplification = 26, mutation = 1, both amp + mut = 3) were initially enrolled. Due to patient ineligibility and drop out, 27 patients were evaluable for sunitinib efficacy (amp=26, mut=1). With regards to DC, two patients were reported with partial response and four with SD16+ were observed for DC. The DC rate was calculated to be 27% (90% CI, 13 to 100) and OR to be 7% (95% CI, 1 to 24). The median PFS was 9 weeks in the FGFR1 cohort (95% CI, 8 to 16). Given the null hypothesis of a 15% DC rate was not rejected, sunitinib did not meet the study’s thresholds for demonstrating antitumor activity in patients with BC harboring FGFR1 amplifications. The study concludes that sunitinib is not recommended for off-label use in FGFR1-altered BC.

A male adolescent patient with study ID SJBALL267_D was reported by gene expression profile to have Ph-like non CRLF2 B-ALL. White blood count was 1.7. WGS and RNA-seq was performed. ZEB2::PDGFR joining exon 9 to exon 9 was reported. Other alterations were IKZF1 Deletion or mutation with focal homozygous deletion and flanking heterozygous alteration. RAG deletion was reported and other key lesions were CDKN2A/B, BLTA-CD200 deletion. From WGS results, the tumor was found to have what the study determined as 11 Tier 1 AA changes, 10 Tier 1 UTRs, and 1 Tier 1 Silent SNVs. ZEB2 and PDGFRB are described as in frame.

Xenograft models of 10 Ph-like ALL tumors including ZEB2-PDGFRB were generated from engrafting primary human leukemia cells into NOD-SCID IL2R gamma null mice. The authors state that the xenograft cells which expressed ABL1-class fusions showed activation of STAT5 that was inhibited with imatinib or dasatinib. PDGFRB is an ABL1 class fusion, suggesting that the ZEB2-PDGFRB cells may be sensitive to TKIs imatinib and dasatinib.

A patient is reported with karyotype 46,XX,del(12)(p13)[6]/46,XX[19] to have Ph-like other ALL of B-ALL Lineage by expression profiling. Age at diagnosis was 16.674, termed Adolescent and Young Adult, and White blood cell count at diagnosis (x10˄9/ml) was 2. Treatment protocol was AALL0232. RNA seq and SNP6 copy array was performed and ZEB2::PDGFRB and PAX5::BZW1 fusions were reported.

The SRSF2 P95L mutation, located in the RNA recognition motif domain, is a statistically significant hotspot in myeloid malignancies. In vitro studies using HeLa and K562 cells show that P95L disrupts splicing fidelity, leading to aberrant exon usage and genomic instability. The mutation is considered likely oncogenic. Clinical data support its role as a poor prognostic marker in MDS, as listed in NCCN Guidelines v2.2025. Additionally, promising early-phase trial results suggest that ATR inhibition with ceralasertib may be effective in SRSF2-mutant MDS and CMML, particularly after HMA failure.

The STAG2 p.His421Thrfs*4 mutation is a truncating frameshift variant located in exon 14 of the STAG2 gene, a core component of the cohesin complex. Truncating mutations in STAG2 are recurrent across various cancer types and lead to loss of protein expression, likely via nonsense-mediated mRNA decay. Functional studies show that STAG2 depletion causes chromosomal instability in solid tumors, although AML patients with STAG2 truncating mutations often retain a normal karyotype. Based on its location and predicted impact, this variant is likely oncogenic. The evidence supports its role in leukemogenesis and poor prognosis in AML.

Hormone-receptor positive HER2-negative (HR+) breast cancers can harbor alterations in fibroblast growth factor receptors (FGFRs), particularly FGFR1 amplification, which is associated with poor prognosis and resistance to endocrine and CDK4/6 therapies. Preclinical data suggest that simultaneous targeting of FGFR, estrogen receptor α (ERα), and CDK4/6 may overcome these challenges. In a phase Ib clinical trial (NCT03238196)—an open-label, multicenter, dose-escalation and expansion study—erdafitinib (a potent oral pan-FGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor), fulvestrant (an ERα degrader), and palbociclib (a CDK4/6 inhibitor) were evaluated in 35 patients with HR+/HER2– metastatic breast cancer. All patients had previously received both CDK4/6 inhibitors and endocrine therapy. 83% harbored FGFR1–4 amplifications as determined by NGS (Foundation One , Guardant 360, MSK-IMPACT) and FISH. Copy number thresholds were not specified for the NGS panels. Amplification by FISH was determined as 'FGFR1/CEN8 ratio ≥2.0; and/or average number of FGFR1 signals per tumor cell nucleus ≥6'. A 3+3 dose-escalation phase (n = 13) established the maximum tolerated dose (MTD), followed by an expansion phase (n = 22) to assess efficacy and safety. The maximum tolerated dose (MTD) of erdafitinib, when administered with palbociclib and fulvestrant, was determined to be 6 mg once daily; clinically manageable adverse events included neutropenia (likely due to palbociclib), oral mucositis, and hyperphosphatemia (attributed to erdafitinib). Of 35 patients, 31 patients were evaluated for antitumor efficacy (4 patients were excluded from evaluation due to adverse events [n=3] and lack of re-evaluation [n=1]). Three patients (3/31; 10%) achieved partial response and 17 (55%) had stable disease. The overall response rate was 10% and median progression-free survival (PFS) was 12 weeks. An exceptional responder was noted in the cohort (PFS 42 months), despite no detectable FGFR1–4 alterations. This patient was said to be 'heavily pretreated' and harboured other alterations (11q13 [includes FGF3 and FGF4] CRKL, ZNF217 and AURK amplifications, and BRCA1 p.Q687P). FGFR1 amplification showed no correlation with treatment response. High FGFR1 protein expression by IHC (determined as 2+ or 3+ using HER2 scoring criteria) correlated with longer progression-free survival in the FGFR1-amplified cohort, as compared to those with low FGFR1 protein expression. No definite association was found between FGFR1 copy number and protein levels, notably in metastatic samples. Furthermore, the response rates with this triplet regimen were not superior to those reported in prior trials of FGFR inhibitors alone or combined with endocrine therapy.

PALOMA-3, a phase III, multicenter, double-blind randomized controlled trial enrolled patients with advanced estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer receiving fulvestrant (estrogen receptor antagonist) therapy with either palbociclib (a CDK4/6 inhibitor) (N = 347) or placebo (N = 174). Of the total number of 459 patients, 401 patients had enough DNA in pretreatment plasma samples for a custom targeted sequencing panel to assess for mutations (17 genes), copy number alterations (14 genes), and circulating tumor fraction. The prevalence of copy number alterations was assessed only in samples with more than 10% circulating tumor fraction (N=156). Gain of copy number of FGFR1 was observed in 10% (15/156) as one of the most frequent finding, together with gains of MCL1, CCND1, and MYC. In univariable analysis gains in FGFR1 were associated with poorer progression-free survival (PFS) in both treatment groups [HR=3.40, 95% CI 1.91. to 6.04, log-rank Q<0.001 for the group treated with palbociclib plus fulvestrant, and HR = 3.61, 95% CI = 1.31 to 9.97; log-rank Q=0.047 for the group treated with fulvestrant with placebo]. Since an increased circulating tumor fraction was required to detect copy number changes in plasma and higher circulating tumor fraction was also associated with worse PFS, a multivariable analysis was performed. FGFR1 gain remained statistically significant in the model [HR=2.91, 95% CI 1.61 to 5.25, p<0.001]. The median PFS of patients on palbociclib and fulvestrant with detected FGFR1 gain was 3.9 months vs 12.0 months for those without it. In addition, PFS of patients with FGFR1 gain together with TP53 mutations was at 3.7 months. There was no statistically significant interaction for FGFR1 gain with treatment randomization.

This study aimed to determine the amplification rates of FGFR1, FGFR2, and FGFR3 in breast cancer and evaluate their impact on prognosis. In a cohort of 894 breast cancer patients, FGFR1 amplification was present in 6.6% (33/503) of assessable tumors and was enriched in the luminal B-like subtype (69.7% of FGFR1-amplified tumors vs. 32.6% of non-amplified tumors). Due to the very low frequency of FGFR2 (<1%) and FGFR3 (<1%) amplifications, outcome analyses focused only on FGFR1 amplification. The results showed that FGFR1 amplification was associated with a trend toward poorer outcomes, particularly shorter distant metastasis–free survival (DMFS; p=0.04, unadjusted analysis); however, this difference did not reach statistical significance in analysis adjusted for other well-known prognostic factors (P=0.05). No significant effect of FGFR1 amplification was observed on other secondary outcomes, including overall survival (OS) and local recurrence–free survival (LRFS). These findings indicate that FGFR1 amplification is disproportionately associated with luminal B-like breast cancers (luminal B-like enriched), which are typically more aggressive and have higher proliferation rates. The absence of a statistically significant prognostic association in this study is likely due to the small number of FGFR1-amplified cases (n = 33), limiting statistical power.

HR+/HER2– breast cancers frequently harbor fibroblast growth factor receptor (FGFR) alterations, and FGFR1 amplification has been linked to poor prognosis and resistance to both endocrine therapy and CDK4/6 inhibitors. Lucitanib, an oral inhibitor of VEGFR1–3, FGFR1–3 and PDGFRα/β, demonstrated a 50% objective response rate (ORR) and a median progression-free survival (PFS) of 40.4 weeks in a phase I trial of heavily pretreated, FGF-aberrant patients. In the phase II FINESSE study, 76 metastatic HR+/HER2– patients (ECOG ≤2, ≥1 prior line of anticancer therapy, ≤2 prior lines of chemotherapy) received single-agent lucitanib and were stratified into 1) an FGFR1-amplified cohort (n = 32), 2) an 11q13-amplified-only cohort (n = 18) and 3) a non-amplified cohort (n = 26). The primary endpoint was ORR by RECIST v1.1, with secondary endpoints including clinical benefit rate, PFS, duration of response, safety and pharmacokinetics. FGFR1 copy-number variation was assessed by FISH and droplet digital PCR, and protein expression by IHC. In the FGFR1-amplified cohort, lucitanib achieved an ORR of 19% (95% CI, 9–35%), versus 0% (95% CI, 0–18%) and 15% (95% CI, 6–34%) in the 11q13-only and non-amplified cohorts, respectively. Patients with high-level FGFR1 amplification (FISH ratio ≥4) achieved an ORR of 22% versus 9% with lower amplification, a finding confirmed by ddPCR, while tumors with high FGFR1 protein expression (IHC H-score ≥50) had a 25% ORR compared with 8% in low-expressing tumors. Common toxicities included hypertension (87%), hypothyroidism (45%), nausea (33%) and proteinuria (32%). Overall, lucitanib showed modest antitumor activity accompanied by high rates of hypertension, with the greatest benefit observed in tumors harboring stringent FGFR1 alterations.

The authors detail a phase 1 dose-expansion trial of a pan-FGFR inhibitor, fubatinib. Most FGFR inhibitors are reversible ATP-competitor inhibitors that tumors can acquire resistance to. Futibatinib, unlike the ATP-competitive inhibitors, binds covalently and irreversibly to a cystine within the P-loop of the FGFR kinase domain and showed preclinical success in cell lines from diverse tissues that harbored FGFR aberrations. This mechanism of action also resulted in fewer drug-resistance clones than ATP-competitive FGFR inhibitors in preclinical studies, likely due to the inhibition of FGFR2 mutations conferring resistance. The patient cohort enrolled in this trial (n=170) had a variety of cancer types, including cholangiocarcinoma (37.6%), primary CNS (21.2%), urothelial (11.2%), breast (6.5%), gastric (5.3%) and other solid tumors (18.2%). The tumors harboured a variety of FGF/FGFR aberrations, with FGFR2 fusions/rearrangements (28.2%) being the most common. All patients had been pretreated for disease, including some previously receiving FGFR inhibitors. Objective responses were recorded in 13.7% of patients, while over half of all patients across cohorts experienced tumour reduction. Notably, these responses were observed in tumors that were previously not characterized as being sensitive to FGFR inhibition. Of patients receiving 20mg futibanib daily, partial response was seen in 10.6% and stable disease in 38.2%. The most significant target-lesion shrinkage was seen: cholangiocarcinoma (by tumour type) and in tumors harboring FGFR2 fusions/rearrangements (by genomic alteration). Five patients had more treatment responses more than 6 months, all of whom had cholangiocarcinoma. At the time of data cut off, 87.6% of patients had discontinued treatment, primarily due to disease progression. The RP2D of futibatinib was shown to be 20 mg once daily. A small subset of the patients who enrolled in the study prior to the confirmation of R2PD received a lower dose (16 mg once daily); encouragingly of the patients who received 16 mg of futibatinib, the objective response rate was 33.3%.

A 54 year old woman was diagnosed with AML by morphology. 45% myeloblasts, 22% monoblasts, 30% eosinophils, and 3% plasma cells were detected and she was classified as AML-M4 with eosinophilia. RTPCR detected type A inv(16) CBFB::MYH11. After induction therapy complete hematological remission (CR) was achieved, with bone marrow (BM) relapse after six months. 2 courses of salvage therapy resulted in complete response, followed by second BM relapse after 4 months with CNS involvement, after with the patient died. Cytogenetic analysis at diagnosis showed t(1;12)(q25;p13) as the sole chromosomal abnormality. FISH demonstrated a breakpoint associated with ETV6. 3'-RACE analysis on RNA using ETV6 primers and cloning was performed, and sequencing found ETV6 fused to ABL2 (ARG). This fragment had a 1466 amino acid open reading frame starting at the ETV6 first ATG and ending at the ARG TAG stop codon. RTPCR on patient samples showed two isoforms of ETV6::ABL2, with ETV6 exon 5 fused with nucleotide 362 or 425 of ABL2 (ARG). Both splicing forms contained the HLH oligomerization domain of ETV6 and the complete SH3, SH2, and RTK domains of ABL2. Both CBFB::MYH11 and ETV6::ABL2 present at diagnosis. Reciprocal fusion ABL2::ETV6 was detected at low levels.

The HT93A cell line was established from a patient with acute myelogenous leukemia (AML-M3). The patient was a 66 yr old man and was successfully induced to first and second remission with combined chemotherapy. The cell line was established at the second relapse, and had karyotype 46,XY,t(1;12)(q25;p13),der(2)1(1;2)(q25;q33), t(4;6)(q12;q13), t(15;17)(q22;q11.1). FISH analysis suggested involvement of ETV6 in the t(1;12) translocation. Northern blot indicated presence of ETV6 exons 1 to 5 and a novel fusion sequence. 3'-RACE and search with BLAST indicated parter gene ABL2 (ARG). ETV6 exon 5 was fused in-frame to ABL2. Fusions with ETV6 exons 1A and 1B were both found in RTPCR. The 1A form contained the PNT domain, and the 1B form contained a truncated PNT domain. Fusions to ABL2 were found at nucleotide 362 and also at nucleotide 425, for a total of 4 different ETV6::ABL2 isoforms. All isoforms contained the SH2, SH3, and tyrosine kinase domains of ABL2. ABL2::ETV6 was not detected. The authors conclude that given simmilarities between ABL1 and ABL2, it is conceivable that this ETV6::ARG has transforming activity via similar mechanisms to ETV6::ABL1.

The patient derived MT-ALL cell line was established from a mature T-ALL in first relapse. Uncultured blasts had an immunophenotype of mature CD3+ TCRa/b+ T lymphocytes with a functional T-cell receptor. Myeloid cytokines caused differentiation to mature neutrophilic granulocytes IL-2 caused differentiation to lymphokine-activated killer cells. A growth factor-independent subline was derived after multiple passages in severe combined immunodeficient mice with karyotype 47,XY,+del(6)(q15q25),t(1;10;12)(q25;p13;p13). Further analysis found two isoforms of the ETV6::ABL2 fusion in the cells. Both contained ETV6 exons 1 to 5, and ABL2 at base pair 362 or 425. Both isoforms contained ETV6 pointed domain, and ABL2 SH3, SH2, and tyrosine kinase domains. The R399H mutation was also found on the intact ETV6 allele.

In a study of 176 ALL patients, consisting of 136 B- and 40 T-lineage, multiplex nested RT-PCR was used to look for ETV6 fusions. One patient had ETV6::ABL2 fusion. Patient was a 17 year old with karyotype 45,XY,t(1;12)(q25;p13),-1,-5,+11[2]/46,XY,t(1;12)(q25;p13),-1,+11[3]/46,XY[15]. The patient did not achieve a hematological or a molecular complete response, and did not get hematological stem cell transplantation, and did not have a favorable response to traditional chemotherapy.

disease: Acute Myeloid Leukemia With Mutated NPM1
evidence_statement: In this 2005 study, immunohistochemical staining was used to assess the subcellular localization of NPM in 1,835 paraffin-embedded tumor specimens, including 591 from primary AML patients (ages 15–60), 135 from secondary AML patients, and 980 from hematopoietic and non-hematopoietic neoplasms other than AML. Of the 591 specimens tested, 208 (35.2%) were found to have aberrant cytoplasmic NPM localization (NPMc+), while the remainder displayed normal nuclear localization (NPMc–). Subsequent RT-PCR and Sanger sequencing found 51/52 NPMc+ specimens harbored a NPM1 exon 11 (NM_002520) mutation that results in a distinct C-terminal sequence and is predicted to alter the NPM protein at its C-terminus (referred to in this study as NPM exon 12 mutations). Transfection of NIH-3T3 cells with the NPM1 mutant alleles showed aberrant cytoplasmic localization compared to wild type, demonstrating a causal relationship between NPM1 mutation status and aberrant subcellular localization. NPMc+ was found to be associated with a normal karyotype in approximately 60% of AML patients (142/230, 61.7%). FLT3 internal tandem duplications were found to be twice as frequent in NPMc+ vs. NPMc- specimens, suggesting these mutations may be mechanistically linked. The majority of NPMc+ AML specimens were CD34- (49/52) and had a wide morphologic spectrum, demonstrating multilineage involvement. Finally, the authors investigated the response to induction therapy in 126 patients with AML and a normal karyotype (79 NPMc+, 47 NPMc-) treated according to the GIMEMA LAM99P protocol. AML patients with a normal karyotype and NPMc+ were found to have a relatively good response to induction chemotherapy. The study illustrates that AML cases characterized by NPM1 mutations represent a unique disease subtype with shared morphologic features, immunophenotype and molecular and clinical characteristics.

disease: Acute Myeloid Leukemia With Mutated NPM1
evidence_statement: In this 2005 study, the authors investigated the prevalence and prognostic impact of NPM1 mutation status in 300 adult patients with AML (16-60 years of age) with normal cytogenetics. The diagnostic bone marrow or peripheral blood sample of these 300 patients were analyzed and included the following: 257 patients with de novo AML, 24 patients with t-AML/s-AML, and 19 patients with no available information. NPM1 exon 11 mutations (referred to in this study as NPM exon 12 mutations) were identified in 145/300 (48%) of the specimens tested, representing the most frequent molecular event that has been identified in AML patients with a normal karyotype to-date. The majority of identified NPM1 mutations resulted in a 4 base pair insertion. Universally all mutations resulted in protein elongation and replacement of the last 7 amino acids in NPM1. Mutation status for FLT3, CEPBA, and MLL were also assessed. FLT3 internal tandem duplications (ITDs) and tyrosine kinase domain mutations (TKDs) were more frequently identified in the NPM1-mutated group (41% and 15% respectively) compared to the NPM1 negative group (25% and 5% respectively). NPM1-mutated/FLT3 ITD-negative mutation status was significantly associated with induction success and arose as a prognostic marker for achievement of complete remission (odds ratio = 2.81, 95% CI = 1.39-5.69). In addition, NPM1-mutated/FLT3 ITD-negative patients had significantly better relapse-free survival and overall survival. In summary, NPM1 mutations were frequent in AML and were associated with specific clinical (favorable outcome) and genetic characteristics (normal cytogenetics and FLT3 mutations).

A RET fusion-positive NSCLC patient who had been treated with multiple lines of chemotherapy and targeted therapies received selpercatinib. The patient initially tolerated selpercatinib achieving a systemic and intracranial response but showed disease progression after 11 months of treatment. Sanger and NGS identified a G810S mutation in malignant pleural cells which was not present prior to selpercatinib treatment.

Amplification of FGFR1 is one molecular alteration associated with hormonal resistance and relapse in breast cancer. Using two different patient data cohorts (H12O - patients diagnosed at Hospital 12 de Octubre [n = 251] and METABRIC [n=98 patients]) with hormone-positive breast cancer (HRPBC), FISH studies demonstrated FGFR1 amplification in 11.8% of H12O patients. This was validated in the METABRIC cohort, where 7.6% of HRPBC demonstrated FGFR1 amplification. Furthermore, both studies found that FGFR1 amplification was more common in luminal B (16.3% H12O, 11.1% METABRIC) versus luminal A (6.6%, 5.5%) subtype. Using the H12O cohort, RNA expression analysis revealed 17% of cases had FGFR1 overexpression. Cumulatively, 24.5% of patients had altered FGFR1 expression as measured by FISH (amplification) and/or RNA expression (overexpression). From the H12O cohort, the median relapse-free survival time for patients with FGFR1-amplification was 9.3 years, which is significantly lower than the median relapse-free survival time for patients with non-FGFR1-amplified breast cancer (11.2 years). From the METABRIC cohort, the median relapse-free survival for patients with FGFR1-amplified breast cancer was 12.2 years, which is lower than patients without the FGFR1-amplication in which the median relapse-free survival was 21.1 years. The discrepancy between the median relapse-free survival rates between the cohorts, might be attributed to the demographic and clinical characteristics of the patients in each cohort, with the patients in the METABRIC being slightly older and having earlier stage breast cancer (T1/T2 and N0/N1 stages) than the H12O cohort. However, in both cohorts, when breast cancer was sub-classified by luminal type A or B, the difference in the relapse-free survival time between FGFR1-amplified and non-amplified was no longer significant. When median relapse-free survival included patients with FGFR1 amplification and/or FGFR1 overexpression, the average relapse free survival was 8.8 years for versus 11.2 from non-amplified/non-overexpressed. This analysis combining amplification and overexpression was not performed on the luminal subtypes. In conclusion, FGFR1 amplification is found in HRPBC, more often in the luminal B subtype, and is associated with worse prognosis in HRPBC, however the prognostic consequences of FGFR1 amplification are lost when HRPBC is classified by luminal subtypes.

In a clinical cohort of patients with HR+/HER2- metastatic breast cancer (n=110), FGFR1 amplification status was determined using FISH analysis (FGFR1/centromere 8 ratio ≥2). Among those receiving endocrine therapy alone, FGFR1 amplification (n=30) was associated with poorer outcomes based on time to progression (TTP) compared to those without FGFR1 amplification (n=80). FGFR1 amplification was not associated with a shorter TTP with chemotherapy, and the shorter TTP with endocrine therapy was not observed when combined with an mTOR inhibitor (everolimus). In patients treated with endocrine therapy and a CDK4/6 inhibitor, those with FGFR1 amplification had a shorter TTP, but the sample size was too small to determine statistical significance. A multivariate analysis supported FGFR1 as an independent predictive variable in shorter TTP with endocrine therapy alone but not when combined with mTOR inhibitors.

In a tissue micro array from 46 cases histologically classified as MCL according to WHO criteria, 50% were positive for ZEB1 expression. ZEB1 expression correlated with beta catenin (Spearman correlation 0.781, p<0.001). Kaplan Meier survival plot of MCL patients was done using two gene microarray datasets. One had survival data up to 8 years for 66 untreated cyclin D1 positive MCL patients, 63 who had ZEB1 expression data. The other, from NCI, contained 92 untreated MCL patients, 64 of whom were cyclin D1 positive. In these data sets, patients with the highest expression of ZEB1 (defined as upper quartile) had shorter survival than patients with lower ZEB1 expression (defined as second, third and fourth quartiles) Results were significant (n=63, Hazard rate 5.3, P=7.7 e-7 and n=64, Hazard rate 2.38, P=0.0075). The authors conclude ZEB1 may be a potential biomarker with clinical value for MCL.

In a tissue micro array from 46 cases histologically classified as MCL according to WHO criteria, 50% were positive for ZEB1 expression. ZEB1 expression correlated with beta catenin (Spearman correlation 0.781, p<0.001). Treatment of MCL cells (Granta-519 and Jeko-1) with salinomycin reduced ZEB1 protein and mRNA levels. Granta-519 cells were treated with increasing salinomycin concentrations up to 15 uM for 48 hours and tested for cell death via MTT assay, and showed reduced viability at all concentrations tested, up to approximately 50 percent at the highest concentration. In a mouse xenograft model with Granta-519 cells, mice treated daily with 2.0 mg/kg of salinomycin, after 30 days tumor volume was significantly reduced (p < 0.01) with treated vs untreated approximately 100 vs. 800 cubic mm, respectively. The authors conclude that ZEB1 expression could potentially become a predictive biomarker and therapeutic target in MCL

In a tissue micro array from 46 cases histologically classified as MCL according to WHO criteria, 50% were positive for ZEB1 expression. ZEB1 expression correlated with beta catenin (Spearman correlation 0.781, p<0.001). In MCL microarray, ZEB1 correlated significantly and positively with proliferation associated genes HMGB2, UHRF1, CENPF, MYC, and MKI67. In Granta-519 and Jeko MCL cells, mRNA levels for HMGB2, UHRF1, CENPF, MYC, MKI67, and CCND1 were significantly reduced with shZEB1 vs control shRNA. Knockdown of ZEB1 in In Granta-519 cells increased pro-apoptotic caspase 3/7 activity, and was associated with down regulation of anti-apoptotic genes (MCL1, BCL2 and BIRC5) and up regulation of pro-apoptotic genes (TP53, BBC3, PMAIP1 and BAX). In both MCL cell lines, ZEB1 knockdown also reduced proliferation measured by 3H-Thy incorporation, by approximately 50%. In CB17-SCID mice, Granta-519 shCtl or Granta-519 shZEB1 cells were injected subcutaneously. Tumor volume in control mice was significantly larger than in mice with shZEB1. The authors conclude that ZEB1 is a potential new biomarker for the pathogenesis of MCL by promoting enhanced viability and proliferation, and reduced apoptosis in MCL cells.

In ZEB1 positive MCL cell line Granta-519, cells were treated with control shRNA or shZEB1, and then incubated with varying concentrations of vincristine. No difference in cell viability was seen over a range of concentrations (0-1000nM), whereas significant differences indicating resistance in control cells were seen with different chemotherapy drugs doxorubicin, cytarabine and gemcitabine.

To determine if there is a causal relationship between hormonal blockade (a frequent treatment for tumors in the adjuvant setting) and FGFR1 amplification/overexpression, this study used two non-FGFR1 amplified (MCF7 and T-47D) and one FGFR1 amplified (HCC1428) cell lines and exposed them to prolonged hormonal deprivation to mimic hormonal blockade treatment. After prolonged hormonal deprivation, all three cell lines developed estrogen-deprivation resistance as well as resistance to the selective estrogen receptor degrader, Fulvestrant, a therapy typically used upon metastatic relapse. The two cell lines that came from non-FGFR1 amplified parental lines had increased FGFR1 mRNA and protein levels after prolonged hormonal deprivation. However, engineered overexpression of FGFR1 in the non-FGFR1 amplified parental cell lines did not confer resistance to estrogen deprivation but did confer resistance to Fulvestrant. Furthermore adding Palbociclib, a CDK4/6 inhibitor frequently used in combination with Fulvestrant, all hormone-resistant FGFR1 amplified or overexpressed cell lines were resistant to the Fulvestrant + Palbociclib combination. However, this resistance was lost after adding Rogaratinib, a pan-FGFR inhibitor, to the Fulvestrant + Palbociclib combination, as shown by drastic growth reduction/no growth in culture, suggesting high sensitivity to this triple combination. To further understand mechanisms of resistance and sensitivity, the amount of Rb phosphorylation, CCND1 protein, and BrdU incorporation were measured in the various treatment conditions, due to their role in cell cycle progression. While fulvestrant or palbociclib result in some reduction in Rb phosphorylation, treatment with a doublet combination of fulvestrant + rogaratinib, or triple combination of Fulvestrant, Palbociclib, and Rogaratinib resulted in suppression of Rb phosphorylation and cell cycle arrest. This suggests that the triple blockade of ER, CDK4/6, and FGFR1 might be an appropriate therapy for FGFR1 altered, hormonal resistant breast cancer.

ABL2-rearranged (ABL2r) acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is a high-risk subtype of Ph-like ALL, typically treated with intensive chemotherapy. The ZC3HAV1::ABL2 fusion is a rare mutation in ABL2r and has shown sensitivity to asciminib, a STAMP inhibitor targeting the ABL2 myristate pocket. This study builds on previous findings by demonstrating that TERN-701, a second-generation STAMP inhibitor, also effectively inhibits ZC3HAV1::ABL2-positive ALL cells in vitro. A homology model of Abl2 (residues p.N110–p.R558) was developed to compensate for the lack of a complete crystal structure, revealing that asciminib binds the Abl2 myristate pocket in a shifted orientation compared to Abl, interacting with distinct residues (αH, αF, αE helices), which may influence drug affinity and resistance. Functional domain analysis using Ba/F3 cells expressing truncated ZC3HAV1::ABL2 isoforms (Δ3 and Δ4) lacking SH3 and SH2 domains showed resistance to both asciminib and TERN-701, highlighting the essential role of the SH3 domain (ABL2 exon 3) in STAMP inhibitor efficacy. Kinase activity assays confirmed these findings, with full-length fusion cells showing strong pSTAT5 inhibition (asciminib: 98%, TERN-701: 85%), while truncated isoforms showed minimal inhibition (asciminib: 27–31%, TERN-701: 14–24%). In vivo, asciminib significantly prolonged survival in ZC3HAV1::ABL2 PDX mice and reduced spleen and liver weights, unlike dasatinib, which improved survival but did not reduce organ burden. Ex vivo treatment of primary patient cells (n = 3) further validated the efficacy of both STAMP inhibitors, with asciminib reducing pSTAT5 by 40–77% and TERN-701 by 84–86%, supporting their potential use in targeted therapy for ABL2r ALL. In summary, preclinical models support the clinical use of asciminib against ABL2 fusion genes with an SH3 domain. However, novel resistance mutations may occur due to the alternate asciminib binding orientation in Abl2.

FGFR1 amplification (FGFR1amp) is frequently detected in metastatic breast cancer (MBC), where it is recognized as a generic marker of poor prognosis and most notably, resistance to CDK4/6 inhibitors and endocrine therapy. This prompted development of multityrosine kinase inhibitors (MTKIs) and pan-selective FGFR inhibitors (FGFRis) to treat specifically FGFR1-altered breast cancer; however, not all patients with FGFR1amp responded to FGFRis, leading to the hypothesis that FGFR mRNA expression may be a more accurate predictor of treatment response than gene copy number alterations (CNAs). In addition, up to 30% of breast cancers reveal concurrent amplification of FGFR1 and amplification of 11q13 segment encompassing cyclin D1 (CCND1) and 3 FGF ligands (FGFR3/4/19). Thus, 17 breast cancer patient-derived xenografts (PDXs) harboring amplifications in FGFR1 or 4 and/or 11q13 amplification (7 PDXs and FGFR1amp without 11q13amp, 4 PDXs with co-amplification of FGFR1 and 11q13, 3 PDXs with FGFR4amp, and 3 PDXs with 11q13amp), and samples from 10 patients treated with either FGFRis or MTKIs, were evaluated for antitumor activity. FFPE tumor samples were used for mRNA levels measurement (using nCounter and HTG EdgeSeq methods), and treatment effects on proliferation and angiogenesis were assessed by immunofluorescence detection of Ki-67 and CD31. High FGFR1–4 mRNA expression, rather than CNAs, was a more accurate biomarker for FGFRi sensitivity, with responders showing MAPK pathway downregulation. Rogaratinib, a pan-FGFR1–4 inhibitor, achieved partial or stable responses in 53% of models, while lucitanib, an MTKI, showed superior efficacy (86%) across FGFRi-resistant and FGFR-independent models due to its dual antiproliferative and antiangiogenic effects. Amplification of the 11q13 locus, which includes FGF3/4/19 and CCND1, frequently co-occurred with FGFR1amp and enhanced FGFRi sensitivity, especially when FGF ligands were overexpressed. A composite biomarker based on FGFR1–4 mRNA levels predicted treatment response with high accuracy (ROC AUC = 0.94), and in a cohort of 339 breast cancer samples, FGFR1 CNA was frequent but only moderately correlated with mRNA expression. Attempts to mimic lucitanib’s dual mechanism by combining rogaratinib with anti-VEGF agents showed limited efficacy, underscoring the therapeutic advantage of MTKIs like lucitanib in FGFR-addicted and resistant breast cancers. In conclusion, FGFR inhibitors may offer effective treatment for metastatic breast cancer patients with high FGFR1–4 mRNA expression, especially those resistant to CDK4/6 inhibitors or lacking targeted options in triple-negative breast cancer, but this approach requires further clinical validation.

In 2 patients with AML, the novel N841I point mutation was detected by Sanger and Mass spectrometry genotyping. FLT3 N841I was placed into and expressed in Ba/F3 cells, which lead to IL-3 independent growth. Immunoblots demonstrated FLT3 N841I in Ba/F3 cells was constitutively activated as it was phosphorylated in the absence of IL-3. Additionally, downstream targets STAT5 and ERK tyrosine 204 were also constitutive phosphorylated. Treatment with the FLT3 inhbitor, midostaurin, inhibited cell growth and reduced phosphorylation of FLT3 N841I, STAT5, and ERK. Crystal structures of the inactive FLT3 kinase suggests that the N841 residue forms hydrogen bonds that stabilize the inactive confirmation. Changing N841 to I is proposed to make the inactive state less energetically favorable. According to the authors, these data strongly suggest N841I was able to induce growth and maintain the constitutive activation of itself and downstream targets.

In 65 hematologic cancer patient samples (53 AML, 9 ALL, and 3 MDS) partially enriched for lacking FLT3 ITD mutations, resequencing of 21/24 FLT3 exons was performed. In 2 patients with AML, the novel N841I point mutation was detected by Sanger and Mass spectrometry genotyping. Both patients experienced relapse after induction chemotherapy or bone marrow transplant.

disease: Acute Myeloid Leukemia With Mutated NPM1
evidence_statement: To study the mutational spectrum in older AML patients over, 22 cases of NPM1-mutated de novo AML in patients older than 75 were sequenced and 76 mutations (50 different variants) were found across 16 genes in these diagnostic samples. In one sample (15), the FLT3 N841I mutation was detected at a VAF of 38%.

Mutational profiling was performed with targeted NGS of 43 genes to analyze potential factors related to response and outcome in older patients with AML at the time of diagnosis enrolled in the FLUGAZA phase III clinical trial. Overall, 207 Diagnostic bone marrow samples were sequenced. In one sample, FLU017007, the FLT3 N841I mutation was observed at a VAF of 10.56%.

Ba/F3 cells were manipulated to express FLT3-ITD or the FLT3 Tyrosine Kinase Domain point mutation N841I. These cells were treated with the FLT3 inhibitor, gilteritinib, for 2 days and subsequently cell viability was measured with the CellTiter-Glo Assay. IC50 values and 95% confidence intervals were generated from 3 to 6 independent experiments performed in duplicate. FLT3 N841I Ba/F3 cells (IC50 .77nM) were almost 6 times more sensitive to gilteritinib treatment than FLT3 ITD Ba/F3 cells (4.5nM).

A 27-year-old male (Patient #17, Table 1) with B-ALL harbored a ZC3HAV1(exon 12)::ABL2(exon 2) fusion, concurrent CD200-BTLA and IKZF1 (exons 2–7) deletions, and a gain of chromosome X, presenting with a white blood cell count of 30 × 10⁹/L. He was enrolled in the GRAALL‑2014 frontline trial. After induction therapy, his minimal residual disease (MRD) level was 9 × 10⁻⁴. Imatinib (600 mg daily) was initiated 58 days after diagnosis in combination with chemotherapy, reducing MRD to 2 × 10⁻⁴ at day 44 and to undetectable levels by day 175. He subsequently underwent allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) in first complete remission (CR1) and, at last follow‑up, remained alive and in continuous remission with an ongoing survival of 8 months.
In a phase II trial of 49 NSCLC patients with STK11 mutation, the MTORC1/2 inhibitor vistusertib did not result in any responses.

evidence_statement: The cohort included 44 CIC-rearranged sarcomas (CIC-RS), comprising 18 central nervous system (CNS) and 26 extra-CNS tumors. RNA sequencing (n=27) identified CIC::DUX4 (n=15), CIC::NUTM1 (n=4), CIC::LEUTX (n=3), CIC::NUTM2B (n=1), ATXN1::NUTM1 (n=1), ATXN1::NUTM2B (n=1), CIC::DUX4 proximity (n=1), and DOCK1::DUX4 (n=1). Among fusion-positive cases, methylation array classified as EFT_CIC for the CIC::DUX4 (n=14), CIC::DUX4 proximity (n=1), CIC::NUTM1 (n=2), ATXN1::NUTM1 (n=1), and ATXN1::NUTM2B (n=1). CIC::LEUTX tumors (n=3) remained unclassified by methylation array. No tumor was reclassified as another entity. CD99 and WT1 immunohistochemistry (IHC) were positive in >80% of CIC-RS cases. False-negative rates for diagnosis were 20% for CIC dual-color break-apart FISH, 14% for RNA-sequencing, and 14% for methylation array.

Preclinical studies demonstrated that the LSD1 inhibitor HCI-2509 reduced proliferation and induced apoptosis in five EWSR1-FLI1 fusion-positive Ewing sarcoma cell lines (A673, TC32, TC71, SK-N-MC, CHLA-10) compared to DMSO controls (p < 0.05), whereas non-Ewing sarcoma lines were relatively resistant. In A673 cells, fusion dependence was confirmed as EWSR1-FLI1 fusion (EWS/FLI) knockdown reduced drug sensitivity (EC50 113nM, 95% CI 81.9 - 158nM, 95% CI 1,111 - 2,999). In xenograft models derived from A673, TC71, and SK-N-MC cells (n = 8-10 per arm), daily HCI-2509 treatment significantly delayed tumor growth compared with vehicle (two-way ANOVA P<0.0001) and improved survival (log-rank P<0.05), with histologic evidence of reduced Ki-67 and increased cleaved caspase-3.

In this 2017 study the author included 44 cellular myofibroblastic tumors previously diagnosed as cellular myofibroma, cellular myopericytoma, or cellular myofibroblastic neoplasms (NOS), and a control group of 34 various myofibroblastic lesions, including typical myofibromas (adult and infantile variants), myopericytomas, malignant myopericytomas, low grade myofibroblastic sarcomas, and myofibroblastomas. RT-PCR and FISH was utilised to investigate SRF gene abnormalities. SRF gene rearrangements were detected in 10 cases of cellular myofibroblastic tumors and not detected in any of the control group, including classic examples of both myofibroma and myopericytoma. SRF::RELA fusions were present in 7 tumours, while another case had a SRF::C3orf62 fusion and in two cases the partner was not identified. RT-PCR confirmed fusion of SRF exon 4 with RELA exon 11 in one case. The cohort was composed of 7 females and 3 males, with a wide age range at diagnosis, of 3 months to 63 years (mean 17; median 14), the majority under the age of 18 years. The anatomic distribution was quite broad. The authors concluded that they have identified a subset of cellular myofibroblastic tumors occurring mostly in children and young adults, with morphologic features in keeping with cellular variants of myofibroma and myopericytoma, and harboring recurrent gene rearrangements in the SRF gene which in the majority of these cases resulted in SRF::RELA gene fusions.

In this 2020 study, the authors include 13 perivascular myoid tumors belonging to the previously described SRF rearranged subtype of tumors (PMID:28248815), which share morphologic features with myopericytomas and myofibromas and express smooth muscle markers similarly to most perivascular myoid tumors. The cohort was composed of 6 males and 7 females, and all patients except 1 were pediatric, with a mean age of 11.8 years (ranging from 1 week to 73 years). RNA-sequencing was successfully performed on 12 samples and detected the SRF::RELA fusion in 6 tumors, SRF::NCOA2 in 3 tumors, while SRF::CITED1, SRF::NFKBIE, and CITED2::SRF were detected once. The breakpoints were located in exons (ENST00000265354) 2 to 5 of the SRF gene. The tumors occurred in different anatomic sites, although often tumors (n=8) were situated in the head. Follow-up data showed that tumors seem to be nonaggressive. The authors concluded that they have expanded the molecular spectrum of the perivascular tumors with SRF rearrangement by identifying 4 additional fusion genes and suggest naming the distinct clinicopathologic entity SRF-fused perivascular tumor.

In this 2023 study, the authors included 3 cases of SRF rearranged cellular myofibromas/perivascular myoid tumors diagnosed in children, aged 7 to 16 years. RNA sequencing was utilized to detect SRF::NCOA3, SRF::RELA, and SRF::NFKBIE gene fusions in the 3 tumors. All 3 cases occurred in the extremities. The authors concluded that they have described 3 cases of rare SRF rearranged cellular myofibromas/perivascular myoid tumors with a smooth muscle-like phenotype in children and expanded the molecular spectrum by identifying a new fusion gene, NCOA3.

In this 2024 case report, the authors included 2 cases of SRF rearranged cellular perivascular myoid tumors diagnosed in a 3-month-old male and a 3-year-old female. FISH and next-generation sequencing were utilised to detect an SRF::NCOA2 gene fusion in case 1 and a SRF::RELA gene fusion in case 2, respectively. The authors conclude that SRF rearranged cellular perivascular myoid tumors have a broad morphologic spectrum ranging from a pericytic pattern to a myoid pattern, and include hybrid tumors with a mixture of pericytic and myoid patterns, and can be misdiagnosed as myogenic sarcomas.

In this Swedish population-based study, the authors retrospectively re-evaluated 71 poorly differentiated supratentorial CNS tumors in children, previously diagnosed as CNS-PNETs, to assess their molecular features, including BCOR genetic alterations. The cohort included 39 males and 32 females, with a median age at diagnosis of 6.2 years. Using WHO 2021 histopathological guidelines and the Molecular Neuropathology (MNP) brain tumor classifier, 10% (n=7) of tumors were subclassified as CNS neuroblastoma with FOXR2 activation (CNS NB-FOXR2). All seven CNS NB-FOXR2 tumors showed complete concordance between histology-based diagnoses and DNA methylation-based classification, with a calibrated score (CS) ≥ 0.9. The median age at diagnosis of CNS NB-FOXR2 patients was 5.3 years (range 2.5–15.7), with 43% males (n=3) and 57% females (n=4). Copy number analysis predicted gain of chromosome 1q in all seven tumors, and whole or partial loss of chromosome 16q in 86% (6/7) of cases. While the overall CNS-PNET cohort demonstrated poor outcomes (5-year PFS 38% ±11%, 5-year OS 45% ±12%), CNS NB-FOXR2 patients had excellent prognosis, with both 5-year PFS and OS at 100%. These findings highlight that CNS NB-FOXR2 represents a rare, molecularly distinct entity within pediatric CNS-PNETs, and that DNA methylation profiling provides a reliable diagnostic tool to accurately identify this tumor type, which is associated with favorable long-term outcomes.

Phase II trial (NCT04484142) of Dato-DXd 6 mg/kg every 3 weeks in 137 heavily pretreated patients with advanced NSCLC harboring actionable genomic alterations (57% EGFR-mutant; 51% with prior brain metastases). The confirmed ORR was 35.8% (95% CI 27.8–44.4) with a median DOR of 7.0 months. In subgroup analyses, ORR was 43.6% (95% CI 32.9-54.8) in EGFR-mutant patients and 23.5% in those with ALK rearrangements, with corresponding median PFS of 5.8 and 4.3 months. All four complete responses occurred in patients with EGFR mutations. Grade ≥ 3 TRAEs occurred in 28.5% of patients, most commonly stomatitis (9.5%), with oral mucositis and anemia as notable AESIs.

TROPION-Lung01 (NCT04656652) was a global, randomized, open-label phase III trial of 604 patients with previously treated advanced NSCLC comparing datopotamab deruxtecan (Dato-DXd) with docetaxel. Dato-DXd significantly improved progression-free survival (4.4 vs 3.7 months; HR 0.75; P = 0.004) but not overall survival (12.9 vs 11.8 months; HR 0.94; P = 0.530), with greater benefit in nonsquamous disease (PFS HR 0.63; OS HR 0.84) and a higher objective response rate (26.4% vs 12.8%). Grade ≥3 treatment-related adverse events were less frequent with Dato-DXd (25.6% vs 42.1%), with stomatitis and interstitial lung disease (ILD) as notable adverse events of special interest (AESIs).

A 14-year old patient with bi-allelic PMS2 pathogenic germline variants (c.2 T>A, p.M1K and c.2521del, p.W841Gfs*10) and a diagnosis of constitutional mismatch repair deficiency (CMMRD) was diagnosed with colon adenocarcinoma at 14 years of age followed by pediatric-type diffuse high grade glioma at 18 years of age. Both tumors were hypermutated with MMR deficiency and loss of PMS2 on IHC. The glioma had a very high tumor burden (337.56 mut/Mb) and a somatic, established oncogenic POLE mutation in the exonuclease domain (p.E978G). Among the list of other variants in this tumor was the POLE c.3697C > T (p.R1233*) variant and a c.5278 G > A (p.V1760M) variant in the context of high TMB and other mismatch repair deficiencies.

Studies submitted to cBioPortal (including 164 TCGA studies) were evaluated for POLE variants co-occurring with features of POLE-mutated tumors and co-occurring B2M variants. A single individual with an endometriod endometrial carcinoma showed 3 missense and one nonsense variant (P286R, R2017C, R1386W, R1233*) in the background of 162 variants detected in that sample. POLE P286R, present in this sample, was the most common variant detected in cBioPortal, indicating that additional variants in the background of this high mutation burden may not be POLE driver variants and therefore does not support this variant is oncogenic.

evidence_statement: In this 2016 study, the authors analyzed 398 newly diagnosed Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML) patients, identifying 12 (3%) cases that lacked the Philadelphia (Ph) chromosome by conventional cytogenetic analysis but were positive for the BCR::ABL1 fusion by RT-PCR. Six Ph– cases were further characterized to investigate the cytogenetic mechanisms responsible for this rearrangement. FISH analysis revealed cryptic insertions between chromosomes 9 and 22 in five patients and a classic two-step translocation in one patient, demonstrating four distinct fusion signal patterns and highlighting significant genetic heterogeneity among Ph– CML cases. The study found that the BCR::ABL1 fusion most frequently localized to chromosome 9q34 rather than the typical 22q11.2 region, contrasting with prior reports. These findings established that even in the absence of the visible Philadelphia chromosome, the presence of the BCR::ABL1 fusion gene serves as a definitive diagnostic hallmark of CML. The authors concluded that detection of BCR::ABL1 by FISH or molecular analysis is essential for confirming the diagnosis of CML in patients with a normal karyotype, supporting its role as the primary molecular event defining the disease.

Plasma ctDNA analysis detected an ETV6:NTRK3 fusion (described by the authors as "ETV6 exon4:NTRK3 exon14" at a VAF of 35.3%) in a female patient with recurrent GIST. Entrectinib therapy (600 mg daily) was initiated. A partial response was observed by imaging (CT) at 4 weeks on this therapy. ctDNA profiling after four months on therapy suggested clearance of the fusion. The patient remained asymptomatic after 8 months on therapy without any reported adverse events.

The authors report a case series where two patients with lung adenocarcinoma tumors harbored ERBB2 variant V659E (exon 17). Both cases achieved partial response to Trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd). These tumors lacked the more common ERBB2 exon 19/20 variants. Case 1, a 57-year-old female received T-DXd (5.4 mg/kg once every 3 weeks) monotherapy after receiving other treatments earlier in disease course. An ongoing PR of 4 months was observed as of last followup. Case 3, a 75-year-old female received T-DXd (5.4 mg/kg once every 3 weeks) as first-line treatment. At three months on therapy, imaging CT indicated that she had a PR, which was sustained for 6 months as of the last follow-up date.

The authors report a case series where one patient with lung adenocarcinoma harbored ERBB2 variant H878Y (exon 21). Case 2, a 59-year-old male, received Trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd) (5.0 mg/kg once every 3 weeks) as first-line treatment. The patient also had a TP53 (S241C) variant. A PR was noted after 1 month on therapy and was sustained by the last follow-up date 6 months later.

The authors report evaluation of zongertinib in a multicohort, phase 1a/1b trial involving patients with advanced or metastatic HER2-mutant non-small cell lung cancer. Three cohorts of patients are reported. The cohorts differed in the type of ERBB2 mutation present, prior treatment, and in the treatment dose/timing with zongertinib. In cohort 1 (n=75), patients had a mutation in the tyrosine kinase domain of ERBB2, received zongertinib at a dose of 120 mg, and were NOT previously treated with a HER2-directed antibody-drug conjugate. 71% of these patients (95% [CI], 60 to 80; P<0.001 against a ≤30% benchmark) had a confirmed objective response. The median duration of response was 14.1 months (95% CI, 6.9 to not evaluable). The median progression-free survival was 12.4 months (95% CI, 8.2 to not evaluable).

In a cohort of 427 patients from the MONALEESA-2 study, which compared aramotase inhibitor letrozole plus CDK4/6 inhibitor ribociclib vs. letrozole plus placebo in patients with ER+/HER2− advanced breast cancer, 20 patients had FGFR1/ZNF703 amplification, which was found via investigation of region 8p11.23. In a subgroup (n=212) of these patients treated with letrozole plus ribociclib, Progression free survival (PFS) was 10.61 months for FGFR1/ZNF703 amplified patients (n=10), while for non-amplified patientes it was 24.84 months (n=202), which is comparable to the overall PFS for the letrozole plus ribociclib reported in the MONALEESA-2 study of 25.3 months.

In a cohort of 100 patients with metastatic breast cancer, FGFR1 Amplification was found in 20 cases via FISH, with 17 cases classified as amplified and three cases as low amplified using published criteria. Median age was 56 in FGFR1 the amplified and 60 in the non-amplified group. Disease free interval (DFI) was 35 months in the amplified and 31 in the non-amplified group. Approximately half of the patients in each group had more than two metastatic sites. In a univariate analysis, FGFR1 amplification associated with median overall survival (OS) of 32 months versus 54 months in the non-amplified group (log-rank p = 0.0018). In a multivariate analysis, independent factors for OS were FGFR1 amplification, triple-negative status, and shorter DFI.

evidence_statement: The phase III INAVO120 trial (NCT04191499) in 325 patients with endocrine-resistant, PIK3CA-mutated HR⁺/HER2⁻ locally advanced or metastatic breast cancer evaluated inavolisib plus palbociclib and fulvestrant (n=161) versus placebo plus palbociclib and fulvestrant (n=164). Median PFS was 15.0 months (95% CI 11.3–20.5) versus 7.3 months (95% CI 5.6–9.3; HR 0.43; 95% CI 0.32–0.59; P<.0001), with ORR of 58% (95% CI 50–66) and median DOR of 18.4 months compared to 25% (95% CI 19–32) and 9.6 months in the control arm. The most common adverse events (≥20%) included neutropenia, hyperglycemia, stomatitis, diarrhea, and rash, consistent with the PI3Kα inhibitor class. Efficacy outcomes were reported for all eligible PIK3CA mutations detected by the FoundationOne Liquid CDx assay, which covers hotspot mutations in exons 2 (R88, G106, K111, G118), 5 (N345), 8 (C420, E453), 10 (E542, E545, Q546), and 21 (M1043, H1047, G1049); individual patient numbers by mutation were not provided.

In preclinical models of FET fusion–positive cancers, suppression of ATM signaling by the EWSR1-FLI1 oncoprotein created dependence on ATR-mediated repair. The ATR inhibitor elimusertib showed potent in vitro activity in Ewing sarcoma cell lines A673 (IC50 = 28 nM) and TC-32 (IC50 = 34 nM), and in other FET fusion cell lines (IC50 range 20–60 nM). In patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models in vivo (n = 5; 2 ES, 2 CCS, 1 DSRCT), oral elimusertib (40 mg/kg twice daily, 3-days-on/4-days-off) significantly reduced tumor growth (p < 0.01, unpaired t-test) and delayed progression with minimal toxicity. These results support ATR inhibition as a therapeutic strategy for FET fusion cancers with partial ATM pathway defects.

The phase 2 FIGHT-207 basket study was designed to evaluate pemigatinib, a selective FGFR inhibitor, in patients with previously treated advanced solid tumors harboring FGFR alterations. Eligible patients were ≥18 years old with a histologically or cytologically confirmed advanced/metastatic or surgically unresectable solid tumor and radiographically measurable disease per RECIST v.1.1 or RANO criteria. Safety was consistent with previous reports. This study consisted of three cohorts defined by FGFR alteration category. Patients with in-frame FGFR1–FGFR3 fusions and rearrangements, including intact kinase domains, were assigned to cohort A (n=49). Cohort B (n=32) consisted of patients with FGFR actionable single-nucleotide variants (SNVs), excluding kinase domain SNVs, considered known or likely to be activating and actionable. This set included specific somatic missense mutations, insertions or deletions of FGFR1–FGFR3 that were known or likely activating. Cohort C (n=26) included the remaining patients with FGFR1–FGFR3 mutations in the kinase domain or FGFR1–3 VUS with potential pathogenicity. Most patients underwent local testing with the FoundationOne CDx assay (Foundation Medicine), which profiles 324 genes at high coverage (>500×), with some tested using alternative platforms. Six Breast Cancer patients were included in this study: One in cohort B and five in cohort C. FGFR amplification, defined as a copy number ≥6, was identified in nine patients. These included cases with concurrent FGFR mutations or fusions, as well as amplifications in alternative FGFR genes unrelated to the primary alteration. FGFR1 amplification was observed in five patients, including two breast cancer cases in cohort C. Exploratory endpoints included objective response rate (ORR) of cohort C and analysis of co-alterations associated with resistance and response. ORRs for cohorts A, B and C were 26.5% (13/49), 9.4% (3/32) and 3.8% (1/26), respectively. Although new therapeutic areas for FGFR inhibition and mechanisms of drug failure were identified across tumor types, the FIGHT-207 study was terminated early by the sponsor for business reasons. As a result, some tumor and molecular cohorts were underpowered, limiting the ability to draw definitive conclusions about FGFR dependency for specific alterations. Additionally, the small number of patients with concurrent FGFR gene amplification precluded evaluation of its potential impact on pemigatinib response.

In a randomized phase II trial (n = 73) of patients with advanced translocation-related sarcoma, trabectedin (1.2 mg/m² q3w) significantly improved progression-free survival compared with best supportive care (n = 36), with median PFS 5.6 months vs 0.9 months (HR 0.07; 95% CI 0.03–0.16; p < 0.0001). Median overall survival was not reached in the trabectedin arm versus 8.0 months for control (HR 0.42; p = 0.04). Disease control (CR + PR + SD) occurred in 65% versus 0% of patients, and partial responses were observed in 8% of the treated patients. Common grade ≥ 3 adverse events included neutropenia (67%), elevated ALT (47%), and febrile neutropenia (11%), all manageable. These findings support trabectedin as an effective and tolerable second-line therapy for patients with translocation-related sarcomas after anthracycline failure.

evidence_statement: In a pooled analysis of two phase II studies (n = 66) of advanced translocation-related sarcoma, trabectedin (1.2 mg/m² q3w) produced median PFS 5.6 months (95% CI 4.1–7.3) and median OS 17.5 months (95% CI 12.6–23.6), with ORR 12% and disease control 71%. The MRCL subgroup showed longer PFS 7.4 months (95% CI 5.6–11.1) and the highest response rate (PFS vs synovial sarcoma p = 0.025; vs other TRS p = 0.049).

In a sub-analysis of a randomized phase II trial in extraskeletal myxoid chondrosarcoma (EWSR1-NR4A3 and TAF15-NR4A3 fusions; n = 2) and mesenchymal chondrosarcoma (HEY1-NCOA2 fusion, n = 6)(trabectedin n = 5; BSC n = 3), the two EMCS patients treated with trabectedin 1.2 mg/m² q3w achieved stable disease with PFS 13.0 and 7.4 mo and OS 26.4 and 10.4 mo. Tumor shrinkage of 1% and 27 % was observed; both eventually progressed. Whereas the three MCS patients in the BSC arm all had PD (median PFS 1.0 mo, 95 % CI 0.3–1.0). No ≥ G4 or fatal AEs occurred.

In retrospective analyses of two large ICI-treated solid tumor cohorts (DFCI n = 789, MSKCC n = 1250), CDKN2A loss-of-function alterations were associated with significantly worse overall survival and shorter time-to-treatment failure in urothelial carcinoma (UC DFCI n = 109, UC MSKCC n = 206). In the DCFI cohort, median OS was 8.8 vs 25.2 months (HR 1.8, 95% CI 1.1–3.1; p = 0.019) and median TTF 4.2 vs 8.4 months (HR 2.0, 95% CI 1.3–3.1; p = 0.002), while in the MSKCC cohort median OS was 11 vs 19 months (HR 1.7; 95% CI 1.1–2.6; p = 0.017). These results support CDKN2A loss as a predictive marker of resistance to immune checkpoint inhibitors.

Futibatinib is a selective FGFR inhibitor. In this 2020 preclinical study, its antitumor activity was evaluated in cancer cell lines and xenograft models. The antiproliferative activity was assessed in cancer cell lines derived from various tissue origins, including the MFM-223 and MDA-MB-134-VI breast cancer cell lines, with or without FGFR genomic aberrations (amplifications, point mutations, fusions, or translocations), by measuring cell growth after three days of futibatinib exposure. Additionally, the antitumor activity of futibatinib was investigated in murine and rat xenograft models bearing tumors with FGFR genomic alterations. Mice received oral doses of futibatinib once daily for two weeks. Futibatinib demonstrated antiproliferative activity against the FGFR-deregulated MFM-223 breast cancer cell line, which harbors FGFR1/2 amplifications. Furthermore, robust tumor growth inhibition was observed in the FGFR1/2-amplified MFM-223 breast cancer xenograft model at daily doses ranging from 12.5 to 50 mg/kg. In summary, the results of this study demonstrate that futibatinib is a potent, irreversible, and highly selective inhibitor of FGFR1–4, exhibiting broad antiproliferative activity in FGFR-deregulated cancer cell lines and animal tumor models.

A 67 year old female with stage IIIA lung adenocarcinoma had right lobectomy followed by 4 cycles adjuvant chemotherapy with pemetrexed and cisplatin. Next generation sequencing found EGFR L858R mutation. Patient had liver, lung, and bone metastases. 2 years after initial surgery she was treated with tyrosine kinase inhibitor icotinib with partial response.

Next generation sequencing was performed on 35023 Chinese cases with 13 different solid tumor types. EGFR Fusions were detected in 106 samples. Two cases of EGFR::VOPP1 were reported, with EGFR containing exons 1-25, and VOPP1 reported as intergenic.
