A 63-year-old female patient presented with BRAF V600E-mutant anaplastic thyroid cancer (ATC). Following three surgical resections and a new chemotherapy regimen the patient was diagnosed with lung metastasis. On treatment with dabrafenib plus trametinib regimen, the patient achieved complete response till 32 months.

This is part of a multi-centred, randomised, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial, CHOICE-01, that examined therapeutic response to first-line chemotherapy plus PD-1 inhibitor in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients to explore ctDNA-based stratification strategies. 405 treatment-naïve patients with either locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC that do not carry EGFR or ALK driver mutations were randomly assigned to receive toripalimab (n=309) or placebo (n = 156) in combination with chemotherapy. 371 of the 405 patients with pre-treatment ctDNA present (maximal somatic allele frequency of >=0.5%). Blood-based TMB (bTMB) measured by the 520-gene OncoCompass Plus panel (Burning Rock Biotech) was calculated as the number of small single-nucleotide variations (SNVs) and indels detected at an allele frequency of >=0.2% per Mb of coding regions of target genes (1.003 Mb for the panel used). Using 13 mutations/ Mb (top 20%) as the cut off, patients with high bTMB achieved greater progression free survival from chemotherapy plus PD-1 inhibitor compare dot the bTMB-low group (interaction p = 0.027). However, no difference in overall survival benefits from the addition of PD-1 inhibitor was observed between the two groups.

This is part of a open-label phase 3 trial, NEPTUNE, that examined therapeutic response to first-line durvalumab plus tremelimumab in patients with metastatic non-small cel lung cancer (NSCLC). 823 patiehts with metastatic NSCLC that do not carry EGFR or ALK driver mutations were randomly assigned to receive first-line durvalumab (20 mg/kg every 4 weeks until progression) plus tremelimumab (1 mg/kg every 4 weeks for up to four doses) or standard platinum-based chemotherapy. Blood-based TMB (bTMB) was evaluated in 512 patients.bTMB measured by the 500 gene Guardant OMNI plasma next-generation sequencing (NGS) platform was calculated as the number of synonymous and non-synonymous small single-nucleotide variations (SNVs) and short indels detected at all allele fractions per Mb of coding regions of target genes. Among the bTMB-high patients (>= 20 mut/ Mb) (n = 129), no statistically significant overall survival (OS) (HR 0.71 [95% CI: 0.49–1.05]; median OS, 11.7 versus 9.1 months) or progression free survival (PFS) (HR 0.77 [95% CI: 0.51–1.15]) improvement was observed with durvalumab plus tremelimumab (n = 69) compared to chemotherapy (n = 60). In the exploratory analysis of bTMB with various cutoffs (8-28 mut/Mb), OS and PFS analysis demonstrated an association between higher bTMB and improved hazard ratios for durvalumab plus tremelimumab compared to chemotherapy. Tissue TMB (tTMB) was also evaluated in 369 of the patients. tTMB measured by the 324 gene FoundationOne CDx platform was calculated as the number of synonymous and non-synonymous small single-nucleotide variations (SNVs) and short indels per Mb of coding regions of target genes. In the exploratory analysis of tTMB with various cutoffs (4-18 mut/Mb), OS and PFS analysis demonstrated an association between higher bTMB and improved hazard ratios for durvalumab plus tremelimumab compared to chemotherapy. Among the 236 patients with matched plasma and tissue samples, moderate correlation was observed between bTMB and tTMB (Spearman’s rho = 0.64; Pearson’sr = 0.80). In conclusion, this study did not meet its primary end point of statistically significant improved OS with durvalumab plus tremelimumab compared to chemotherapy among bTMB-high mNSCLC patients. The authors noted that despite this study being limited by altered study design and therefore a small size of the primary analysis population, the therapeutic activity was consistent with observations in previous studies and aligned with expected outcomes based on underlying biological mechanisms.

In a study of 100 patients with sporadic medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), RET gene exons 10-11 and 13-16 were analyzed with tumor and matched normal samples. A somatic RET mutation was identified in 43% of cases and of these 79% (34/43) were M918T mutations.

In this 2017 study, the authors characterized 284 cases of Philadelphia chromosome-like acute lymphoblastic leukemia (Ph-like ALL) identified from a cohort of 1,389 pediatric patients with high-risk B-ALL. This subtype is defined by a gene expression profile similar to BCR::ABL1-positive ALL but lacks that canonical fusion, and is associated with a diverse array of genetic alterations activating cytokine receptor and tyrosine kinase signaling. The cohort showed a male predominance (57.4%) and was enriched for older age and high white blood cell counts. Comprehensive molecular profiling, including reverse transcriptase PCR and transcriptome sequencing, identified targetable kinase alterations in 83.8% of the Ph-like ALL cases. Among these, fusions involving the LYN kinase gene were identified as rare, recurrent oncogenic drivers within this high-risk subtype. The study reported one case harboring a novel GATAD2A::LYN fusion. This fusion retains the tyrosine kinase domain of LYN and is predicted to activate SRC-family kinase signaling. The expression profile of this LYN-fusion-positive case was classified as Ph-like, definitively supporting its biological and diagnostic classification within the BCR::ABL1-like disease spectrum.

This retrospective Japanese multicenter study investigated kinase-activating gene fusions in pediatric B-lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL) lacking recurrent cytogenetic abnormalities, with the goal of defining their clinical and biological significance. Among 373 children and adolescents (median age 8.8 years; range 1.9–16 years) analyzed using mRNA sequencing and/or multiplex RT-PCR, 29 patients were identified with kinase or cytokine receptor fusions involving CRLF2 (n=14), PDGFRB (n=8), ABL1 (n=3), JAK2 (n=2), EPOR (n=3), and LYN (n=1). There was only one fusion involving the LYN kinase gene, indicating LYN fusions as rare oncogenic drivers in pediatric B-ALL. The 5' partner for the LYN fusion was the NCOR1 gene, and the gene expression profile of the NCOR1::LYN positive case resembled BCR::ABL1–positive ALL, supporting its classification within the Ph-like ALL spectrum. The studied patients showed characteristic high-risk features, including male predominance, older age at diagnosis, high white blood cell counts, and enrichment for NCI high-risk disease, as well as a high frequency of IKZF1 deletions (~73%). Clinically, outcomes were poor with conventional therapy alone, with 5-year event-free and overall survival rates of 48.6% and 73.5%, respectively, and inferior survival compared with fusion-negative cases in the mRNA-seq cohort. The study supports that B-ALLs with fusions involving the LYN kinase gene are associated with the BCR::ABL1 like subtype of the disease.

In this 2022 study, the authors investigate the oncogenic role of the MYB::TYK2 fusion gene in high-risk B-lymphoblastic leukemia (HR B-ALL). TYK2 rearrangements are identified as recurrent events in the high-risk BCR::ABL1-like (Ph-like) ALL subtype. The study functionally characterizes the MYB::TYK2 fusion, which was initially isolated from a patient with this aggressive leukemia. Through in vitro and in vivo modeling, the authors demonstrate that the MYB::TYK2 fusion is a driver oncogene that confers cytokine-independent growth in vitro and leads to the development of B-ALL in mice . The authors propose that TYK2 fusions share similar breakpoints and likely lead to constitutive TYK activation by disrupting its auto-inhibitory domain. Importantly, the study shows that the MYB::TYK2 fusion constitutively activates the JAK/STAT signaling pathway in the studied model systems, consistent with its association with the BCR::ABL1-like (Ph-like) ALL subtype.

RET is a known oncogene that encodes a receptor tyrosine kinase with important roles in cell growth, differentiation, and survival. Germline M918T is strongly linked with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B (MEN 2B) and its associated medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC). Somatic M918T is strongly associated with sporadic MTC. This study sought to elucidate the functional mechanisms and molecular properties of M918T RET protein. Isothermal titration calorimetry showed that M918T had >10-fold greater affinity for ATP compared to wildtype. Stoichiometry calculations and analytic gel filtration also suggest that M918T molecules are more likely to form dimers that associate with two ATP molecules compared to the single binding site for wild-type. In vitro kinase assays suggest that M918T increased stability of enzyme-ATP complex, strengthening ATP-binding, and achieving increased kinase activity at lower ATP concentrations compared to wildtype. Immunoprecipitation and western blotting experiments showed that M918T was more highly auto-phosphorylated in the presence or absence of ligand stimulation. Differential scanning calorimetry suggested that M918T may have changes in intramolecular interactions and reduced conformational rigidity that might play a significant role in M918T protein function. In low-stringency nonreducing conditions they show that M918T RET can dimerize and become autophosphorylated even in the absence of ligand stimulation. Taken together, these experiments and others suggest multiple distinct but complementary molecular mechanisms by which M918T leads to functional activation of RET relative to wild-type.

In prostate cancer (PCa) cell models (PC-3 and DU145; shRNA/siRNA knockdown of KMT2D), loss of enhancer activity markers H3K4me1/H3K27ac reduced FOXO3 protein abundance and DNA binding and suppressed transcription of antioxidative genes (GPX1, PRDX2, SOD2, CAT). KMT2D loss was associated with increased intracellular ROS (1.45–2.61-fold, P < 0.001), ROS-mediated DNA damage, apoptosis (9.74–14.66-fold, P < 0.001), and senescence (SA-β-gal+; 1.53–1.91-fold, P < 0.001). Consistent with increased oxidative stress and DNA damage, KMT2D loss increased sensitivity to doxorubicin, carboplatin, and the PARP inhibitor olaparib compared with matched control cells (PC-3 shKMT2D vs control; DU145 siKMT2D vs control; MTT assay, 72 h).

molecular_profile: ERBB2 Y772_A775dup OR ERBB2 G778_P780dup OR ERBB2 G776delinsVC OR ERBB2 V659E OR ERBB2 S310F OR ERBB2 G776delinsLC
evidence_statement: In an open-label, multicenter, multicohort phase 1–2 study of non-small cell lung carcinoma (NCT05099172; total n = 209), single-agent sevabertinib 20 mg BID demonstrated clinically meaningful activity in ERBB2 (HER2)–mutant disease. This population predominantly involves HER2 tyrosine kinase domain (TKD) mutations (90–97% across cohorts), including exon 20 insertion - Y772_A775dupYVMA (60–79%). Confirmed ORR was 64% (95% CI 53 - 75; n = 81; CR 2%, PR 62%, SD 25%) in previously treated patients without prior HER2-targeted therapy, 38% (95% CI 25 - 52; n = 55; CR 5%, PR 33%, SD 42%) in patients previously treated with HER2-directed ADCs, and 71% (95% CI 59 - 81; n = 73; CR 4%, PR 67%, SD 22%) in treatment-naive locally advanced or metastatic disease. Corresponding mPFS 8.3 mo (95% CI 6.9 - 12.3), 5.5 mo (95% CI 4.3 - 8.3), and NE (95% CI 9.6 - NE), and mDoR 9.2 mo (95% CI 6.3 - 13.5), 8.5 mo (95% CI 5.6 - 16.4), and 11.0 mo (95% CI 8.1 -NE), respectively. Exploratory analyses showed higher response and longer PFS in HER2 TKD mutations vs non-TKD alterations (n = 73 vs 7), with ORR 70% (95% CI 58 - 80) vs 14% (95% CI <1 - 58) and mPFS 9.6 mo (95% CI 6.9 - 12.3) vs 6.9 mo (95% CI 2.5 - NE). In Y772_A775dupYVMA vs other HER2 TKD variants (n = 49 vs 23), with ORR 78% (95% CI 63 - 88) vs 57% (95% CI 35 - 77) and mPFS 12.2 mo (95% CI 6.9 - 16.4) vs 7.0 mo (95% CI 4.0 - NE). These findings support ERBB2 (HER2) mutation, particularly TKD exon 20 insertions, as predictive of response to sevabertinib.

In this 2020 case report, the authors present a pediatric patient with relapsed B-lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL), providing critical evidence for the diagnostic and therapeutic role of LYN fusions. The patient was a 6-year-old male who presented with high-risk features, including an initial white blood cell count of 883 × 10⁹/L and a relapsed disease that was refractory to re-induction chemotherapy. Comprehensive molecular diagnostics performed at relapse, including karyotyping and FISH, identified a balanced t(8;17)(q12;p11.2) translocation, which was subsequently confirmed by sequencing to generate an in-frame NCOR1::LYN fusion gene. This fusion joined exon 34 of NCOR1 to exon 8 of LYN, retaining the intact tyrosine kinase domain. Additional high-risk genetic lesions, including deletions of IKZF1 and CDKN2A, were also present. Upon identification of this ABL/SRC-family kinase fusion, the patient was treated with the tyrosine kinase inhibitor dasatinib (60 mg/m²/day) as monotherapy, achieving a complete morphologic and molecular remission within two weeks. This rapid response provided the first direct clinical evidence that leukemias driven by LYN fusions are exquisitely sensitive to dasatinib. The patient subsequently underwent haploidentical stem cell transplantation and remained in minimal residual disease-negative remission on dasatinib maintenance. The authors concluded that the NCOR1::LYN fusion is a recurrent, targetable oncogenic driver in high-risk pediatric B-ALL. Response of the described leukemia to treatment with a kinase inhibitor supports association of the NCOR1::LYN fusion with the Philadelphia chromosome-like (BCR::ABL1-like) subtype, in which activated kinase signaling is the defining molecular feature.

In this 2014 genomic profiling study of 1,725 patients with precursor B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL), the authors define the high-risk "Philadelphia chromosome-like" (Ph-like or BCR::ABL1-like) subgroup. This subgroup is characterized by a gene expression profile similar to BCR::ABL1-positive ALL, a high frequency of IKZF1 alterations, and a diverse spectrum of genetic alterations that constitutively activate kinase and cytokine receptor signaling pathways. The cohort included children, adolescents, and young adults up to age 39. RNA sequencing was performed on 136 patients with Ph-like ALL. The study identified kinase-activating alterations in 91% of Ph-like ALL cases. Among these, a novel MYB::TYK2 fusion was identified in one patient. The fusion retained an intact tyrosine kinase domain, and its identification classified this patient's leukemia within the "other JAK-STAT" activating alteration subgroup of Ph-like ALL. The authors concluded that Ph-like ALL is a common, high-risk subtype characterized by a range of genomic alterations activating a limited set of signaling pathways, nearly all of which are potentially amenable to inhibition with approved tyrosine kinase inhibitors. They propose that identifying these alterations, including rare fusions like MYB::TYK2, is critical for directing targeted therapy to improve patient outcomes.

A 78-year-old Chinese female patient presented with BRAF V600E-mutant metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma. The patient received two cycles of chemotherapy. Following the second incomplete cycle of chemotherapy, the patient was treated with low-dose dabrafenib and trametinib combination therapy. Following the combination therapy, the patient achieved 8 months of progression-free survival (PFS).

Ba/F3 cells expressing FLT3 D835Y were stably transfected, cultured for 48 hours and then cell viability was analyzed. Wild-type FLT3 cells grown with IL-3 or in the absence of IL-3 served as positive and negative controls, respectively. After cells were cultured in the absence or presence of FLT3 ligand and normalized against cell viability in the presence of IL-3, cells expressing FLT3 D835Y showed increased cell proliferation and survival compared to cells expressing wild-type FLT3. In addition, Ba/F3 cells expressing FLT3 D835Y showed constitutive activation of AKT (after starvation in serum- and IL-3 free media for 4 hours before stimulation with 100 ng/ml of FLT3 ligand).

Ba/F3 cells expressing FLT3 D835Y and treated with sorafenib demonstrated a dose-dependent inhibition of cell proliferation. Ba/F3 cells transformed with FLT3 D835Y showed a 50% inhibition of cell proliferation upon treatment with 500 nM concentration of sorafenib. Treatment of Ba/F3 cells with increasing concentrations of sorafenib also demonstrated a dose-dependent decrease in ERK1/2 phosphorylation.

Preclinical data demonstrated Ba/F3 cells transformed with KIF5B::RET were IL3 growth independent, and sensitive to selpercatinib with an IC50 of 17.5 +/- 0.7 nM, which the authors considered sensitive. KIF5B::RET was included as a positive control for other variants that were being tested for sensitivity to selpercatinib.

Ba/F3 cells transformed with E632_L633del showed IL-3 independent growth. Pralsetinib inhibited growth of the cells at IC50 14.9 +/- 1.8 nM. This was similar to the IC50 for selpercatinib, which the authors considered sensitive.

In this 2023 study, the authors evaluated the diagnostic utility of NR4A3 immunohistochemistry in acinic cell carcinoma (AciCC) of the salivary gland. The cohort included 128 AciCCs, comprising 85 classic low-grade, 36 with high-grade transformation (HGT), and 7 high-grade tumors. NR4A3 rearrangements were assessed using a custom dual-color break-apart FISH probe. NR4A3 immunoreactivity was observed in 105 of 128 cases (82%), with similar positivity rates across low-grade, HGT, and high-grade AciCCs (82%, 81%, and 86%, respectively). FISH analysis was performed in 57 cases, confirming NR4A3 rearrangements in 23 of 28 (82%) low-grade cases, 11 of 14 (79%) HGT cases, and 2 of 2 (100%) high-grade cases, resulting in an overall confirmation rate of 36 of 44 (82%) in analyzable immunopositive tumors. Eight immunopositive cases (18%) were FISH-negative, while among 10 immunonegative cases, 2 of 8 analyzable tumors (25%) demonstrated NR4A3 rearrangement. Five cases were not evaluable by FISH. The authors conclude that NR4A3 rearrangements are strongly associated with AciCC and that NR4A3 immunohistochemistry is a robust and reliable tool for the differential diagnosis of this tumor.

NIH3T3 lysates expressing RET E632_L633del were immunoprecipitated with an anti Ret antibody and tested for kinase activity using radiolabeled ATP. Significant RET autophosphorylation was seen in the lysates expressing RET mutant but not wild type RET. Immunopercipitated RET E632_L633del and wild type proteins were run on SDS PAGE under both reducing and non-reducing conditions. Under non reducing conditions dimer formation was observed in mutant but not wild type immunopercipitates.

In an open-label, multicenter phase II study of recurrent low-grade serous ovarian cancer (ENGOT-OV60/GOG-3052/RAMP 201; NCT04625270), patients were stratified by KRAS mutation status and treated with avutometinib monotherapy or avutometinib plus defactinib (n = 115 treated; efficacy-evaluable n = 109). In the go-forward combination cohort (avutometinib 3.2 mg BIW + defactinib 200 mg BID), confirmed ORR by BICR was higher in KRAS-mutant vs KRAS wild-type tumors (44%, n=25/57 vs 17%, n= 9/52), with CR 4%, PR 40%, SD 49%, progressive disease 4% in KRAS-mutant tumors. Median PFS favored KRAS-mutant tumors (22.0 mo [95% CI 11.1 - 36.6] vs 12.8 mo [95% CI 7.4 - 18.4]; overall 12.9 mo [95% CI 10.9 - 20.2]), with a 6-month PFS rate of 79% (95% CI 70 – 86). Median DOR among responders was 31.1 mo (95% CI 14.8 - 31.1), with durable disease control ≥6 mo more frequent in KRAS-mutant vs KRAS wild-type tumors (70% vs 50%). Earlier regimen selection cohorts showed higher ORR with the combination vs avutometinib monotherapy (39% vs 9%). In comparison, a lower-dose combination (avutometinib 1.6 mg BIW + defactinib) demonstrated higher early progression (22% vs 12%), supporting dose-dependent efficacy. AEs included increased CPK (24%), diarrhea (8%), anemia (5%), and dermatitis acneiform (4%), with 10% discontinuation due to AEs.

Expression of EGFRvIII in Ba/F3 cells induced IL–3–independent growth, activation of downstream signaling, including phosphorylated EGFR, AKT, and ERK, and robust proliferative capacity, demonstrating that the EGFRvIII mutation results in a gain-of-function phenotype. In vivo, inducible expression of EGFRvIII in mouse lung epithelium activated EGFR signaling. It led to the development of atypical adenomatous hyperplasia, progressing to adenomas and adenocarcinomas, further confirming that EGFRvIII is a functionally activating alteration that drives aberrant signaling and promotes proliferation.

Inducible expression of EGFRvIII in Tet op EGFRvIII; CCSP rtTA transgenic mice produced a clear oncogenic phenotype, with sequential development of atypical adenomatous hyperplasia, adenomas, and ultimately adenocarcinomas, demonstrating that EGFRvIII is sufficient to initiate lung tumorigenesis in vivo. Complete tumor regression following withdrawal of doxycycline confirmed that tumor maintenance depends on ongoing EGFRvIII expression (oncogene addiction). In complementary in vitro assays, expression of EGFRvIII in Ba/F3 murine pro B cells resulted in IL–3–independent transformation and strong activation of oncogenic signaling pathways, including phospho EGFR, phospho AKT, and phospho ERK. Together, these in vivo mouse tumor models and transformed Ba/F3 cell line systems demonstrate that EGFRvIII functions as a driver oncogene capable of initiating and sustaining tumor growth.

Tumors driven by EGFRvIII show clear differential sensitivity to EGFR-targeted therapies. In vivo, treatment with the irreversible EGFR/HER2 inhibitor HKI 272 (neratinib) produced an average 88% reduction in tumor volume after 7 days, whereas the reversible EGFR inhibitor erlotinib produced only a 45% reduction over the same period. In vitro, Ba/F3 cells expressing EGFRvIII were approximately 40-fold more resistant to gefitinib and erlotinib than cells expressing EGFR L858R, yet remained highly sensitive to HKI 272 (IC₅₀ ≈ 9.4 nM). Introduction of the C530S substitution abolished sensitivity to HKI 272, demonstrating that covalent engagement of Cys 530 is required for inhibitor activity. These data indicate that EGFRvIII predicts reduced response to reversible EGFR inhibitors and increased sensitivity to irreversible EGFR/HER2 inhibitors such as HKI 272 (neratinib).

The MYSTIC study compared response rates for immunotherapy verses chemotherapy. Specifically looking at the efficacy of the anti-PD-L1 therapy, durvalumab, with/without the anti-CTLA-4 therapy, tremelimumab, compared to platinum-based chemotherapy for overall survival (OS) and progress free survival (PFS). When considering implementation of immunotherapy (immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs)), there is a strong correlation between tumors that have high tumor mutational burden (TMB) and success of ICI. Tumor mutational burden can be calculated from both tumor sample (tTMB) and circulating tumor DNA that has been shed and is now collected in the blood (bTMB). This study showed that bTMB, which is less invasive and captures more of the tumor mutational heterogeneity, can be used for determining whether patients should use ICIs in the setting of metastatic NSCLC. From MYSTIC phase III trial, 1001 of the 1118 patients had adequate plasma samples available and of those, 809 samples had valid bTMB score (meaning above the variant allele frequency (VAF) needed for NGS assays; 809/1001 = 81%). Of those 809 patients, 735 of them had tumor samples available, however 275 samples did not meet criteria for “valid” tTMB due to insufficient tumor sample, insufficient DNA yield, or insufficient VAF to calculate TMB. Ultimately TMB scores from blood were more likely to be valid as compared to TMB scores from tumors. When comparing the shared mutations from matched tumor and blood sequencing assays, across a shared DNA region, 50% of mutations detected were found both in the blood and tumor samples. Furthermore, when matching the tumor and plasma samples, there was a positive correlation between the bTMB and tTMB. When comparing the discordance between bTMB and tTMB, multiple factors should be considered including assay-specific differences in genes tested and TMB algorithms, as well as sample differences, such as the intratumoral heterogeneity common in NSCLC. When considering bTMB scores in clinical outcomes, having greater than 20 mutations per megabase (mut/Mb) had the most favorable OS and PFS when treated with durvalumab plus tremelimumab compared to chemotherapy.

Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have been revolutionary in treating solid cancers, however the responses to these therapies can be quite variable. Though response rate to these immunotherapies is often correlated with tumor mutational burden (TMB), this might not be true across all cancer types. Within gastrointestinal tumors, the majority are microsatellite stable (MSS) which has mixed efficacy when treated with ICI compared to microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H) gastrointestinal tumors that respond well to ICIs. Previous studies were unsuccessful in showing a correlation between tumor mutational burden (TMB) status and MSS for predicting clinical response to ICI. This study found that the combination of TMB-H status with mutations in specific genes had increased response to ICIs, likely due to the quality of the neoantigens presented in these tumors. 48,606 samples with confirmed gastrointestinal cancer were binned into three groups 1) MSS-TMB-H (3.29%) 2) dMMR/MSI-H (4.67%) and 3) MSS-TMB-L (92.03%). These samples were sequenced using either NextSeq or NovaSeq, which used NGS for 592 or 700 genes respectively. Tumors were considered TMB-H if they had greater than or equal to 10 mutations per megabase (mut/Mb). Within the sequence analysis for the TMB-H/MSI-H groups, a subset of genes had a positive association with antitumor response, these genes are referred to as the modified TMB (mTMB) signature genes (CDC73, CTNNA1, ERBB4, EZH2, JAK2, MAP2K1, MAP2K4, PIK3R1, POLE, PPP2R1A, PPP2R2A, PTPN11, RAF1, RUNX1, STAG2 , and XPO1). Furthermore, within the MSS-TMB-H group, there was a significantly higher rate of amplification of CCND1 and FGF genes, most of which are located on 11q13. MSS tumors with a mutation in the mTMB genes had distinctive molecular profiles (high mutation counts, indels, SNVs) and immune response indicators (neoantigens and B-cell receptor richness, higher IFN gamma signatures, higher infiltration of NK cells, M1-like macrophages, and Th1 cells, but lower infiltration of M2-like macrophages). Patients with mTMB mutations treated with ICIs had longer overall survival compared to mTMB wildtype patients treated with ICIs within the CARIS and MSKCC cohorts. Importantly, for patients that did not receive ICIs, there was no difference between the OS and mTMB gene signature.

Imidazo [1,2-a]pyridine derivative 6-(7-(1-methyl-1H-pyrazol-4-yl)imidazo[1,2-a]pyridin-3-yl)-N-(4-(methylsulfonyl)phenyl)pyridin-2-amine showed inhibitory effects on cell proliferation in MOLM14 cell line (patient-derived AML cell line) with secondary FLT3 D835Y mutation, with an IC50 of 3.16 +/- 0.65 nM. This compound showed inhibition comparable to gilteritinib in MOLM14 cells, and a balanced inhibition on MOLM14 cells with FLT3 D835Y secondary mutation. Treatment of MOLM14-D835Y cells with 10X the IC50 of the compound resulted in inhibition of FLT3 and ERK phosphorylation (demonstrated by Western blot, with DMSO diluent as a treatment control in each experiment and GAPDH as a loading control).

This study presented clinicopathological and molecular findings of TFCP2-rearranged rhabdomyosarcomas with epithelioid and/or spindle cell morphology. The cohort comprised 14 cases, including 3 index cases published in 2018. Six males and 8 females were included, with an age range of 11-86 years at diagnosis (mean: 31 years). Tumors were located in the bones (n=12/14) or soft tissue (n=2/14). TFCP2 gene fusions from FFPE materials were identified by RNA-seq (n=10/10) or anchored multiplex PCR (n=4/4), showing that exons 5 or 6 of FUS (n=8) or EWSR1 (n=6) were fused to exon 2 of TFCP2. FISH analyses were performed in select cases using EWSR1, FUS, and TFCP2 break-apart probes, showing positivity in 2 of 3, 5 of 5, and 9 of 9 tested cases, respectively. Homozygous deletion of CDKN2A was detected by aCGH in all tested cases (n=9/9), and mutations in the exon 1 of MYOD1 were absent (DNA, n=0/8; RNA, n=0/10) by Sanger sequencing. ALK overexpression was found in most cases (n=11/14) without underlying ALK fusion identified by either break-apart FISH (n=0/5) or NGS (n=0/14). Seven EWSR1/FUS::TFCP2 cases were subjected to unsupervised consensus clustering analyses, showing distinct segregation from the other rhabdomyosarcomas that include embryonal rhabdomyosarcomas (n=6), alveolar rhabdomyosarcomas (n=8), MYOD1-mutated rhabdomyosarcomas (n=4), and VGLL2-fused rhabdomyosarcomas (n=5). Collectively, this study showed that TFCP2-rearranged rhabdomyosarcomas exhibit recurrent EWSR1/FUS::TFCP2 gene fusions and are distinct from other rhabdomyosarcoma subtypes.

This study presented clinicopathological and molecular features of 11 cases of head and neck rhabdomyosarcomas (HNRMSs). The median age of the cohort was 29 years, ranging 16-74 years with no sex bias. All cases but one were intraosseous, involving the mandible (n=4), maxilla (n=3), and skull (n=3). The remaining case occurred in the superficial cervical soft tissue. Molecularly, FUS::TFCP2 (n=7) and EWSR1::TFCP2 (n=4) gene fusions were identified by FISH analyses and/or targeted DNA/RNA sequencing. ALK expression was detected in most cases by IHC (n=9/10), with an intragenic deletion identified in 43% of tested cases (n=3/7). CDKN2A loss was identified in all 5 tested cases. The lesions displayed characteristic spindle and epithelioid morphology. The authors also performed a literature review and included 27 TFCP2-rearranged HNRMS cases, showing that this disease mostly affects young adults and pediatric patients. In summary, HNRMSs with spindle cell and epitheloid phenotype exhibit recurrent EWSR1/FUS::TFCP2 gene fusions and preferentially arise in the skeleton.

This study reported clinicopathologic and molecular features of 25 cases of fusion-driven spindle cell/sclerosing rhabdomyosarcoma (SCSRMS). The tumors occurred in bone (n=19) and soft tissue (n=6). The bone tumor cohort included 6 male and 13 female patients, with an age range of 13-74 years (median age: 41 years), whereas the soft tissue tumors occurred in 4 men and 2 women, with an age range of 28-71 years (median age: 50 years ). In bone tumor cases, 17 of 19 cases were analyzed by NGS with the remaining 2 cases only studied by FISH. NGS analyses revealed the following gene fusions: FUS::TFCP2 (n=12/17), EWSR1::TFCP2 (n=3/17), and MEIS1::NCOA2 (n=2/17), with exon breakpoints identified. Specifically, exon 5 of EWSR1 was joined to exon 2 of TFCP2 in all 3 EWSR1::TFCP2 cases. FISH also successfully identified EWSR1 rearrangements (n=2/2). Among the studied soft tissue tumor cases 1 of 6 showed exon 5 of EWSR1 fused to exon 2 of TFCP2 by NGS, whereas the remaining 5 cases exhibited non-TFCP2 gene fusions. The study confirms EWSR1::TFCP2 as one of the primary oncogenic drivers in bone and soft tissue SCSRMS.

In this 2019 study, the authors aimed to evaluate the usefulness of NR4A3 immunostaining and compare it with NR4A3 Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) for the differential diagnosis of acinic cell carcinoma (AciCC). The study included 64 AciCC cases (53 low-grade tumors and 11 with high-grade transformation), 29 mammary analogue secretory carcinoma (MASC), and 70 other salivary gland carcinomas, evaluated by NR4A3 immunostaining. NR4A3 immunostaining was considered positive when moderate to strong nuclear staining was observed, while cytoplasmic staining was regarded as nonspecific. Moderate to strong nuclear NR4A3 expression was detected in 63 of 64 AciCCs (98%), including all high-grade transformed cases; only one case was negative. In contrast, none of the MASCs or other salivary gland carcinomas showed nuclear NR4A3 staining. These findings confirmed specific association of the NR4A3 rearrangement and upregulation with AciCC. FISH analysis was successfully performed in 58 AciCCs, of which 49 cases (84%) showed abnormal NR4A3 signals consistent with gene translocation (44 with split signals and 5 with single red signals). Nine cases (16%) showed normal FISH results. Samples were classified as positive when more than 20% of 50 counted nuclei displayed abnormal signals. The authors concluded that NR4A3 rearrangement is highly associated with AciCC and the immunostaining is sensitive and specific marker for AciCC, including high-grade cases. The studies shows utility of confirming NR4A3 rearrangement by immunostaining and FISH in distinguishing AciCC from MASC.

In this 2018 study by Keiko Segawa et al., the authors analyzed 22 tumors, including 16 clear cell sarcomas of soft tissue (CCSST) and 6 clear cell sarcoma–like gastrointestinal tumors (CCSLGT), to characterize EWSR1-related gene rearrangements using FISH and RT-PCR. EWSR1 rearrangement was identified in 93.8% (15/16) of CCSSTs and 66.7% (4/6) of CCSLGTs. In CCSST, 68.8% of cases showed concurrent ATF1 rearrangement, supporting the presence of the EWSR1::ATF1 fusion as the predominant genetic alteration; this was confirmed by RT-PCR in tested cases. In contrast, CCSLGT demonstrated a more heterogeneous fusion pattern, with both EWSR1::ATF1 and EWSR1::CREB1 detected (each in 33.3% of cases). Rare CREM rearrangements were also observed in both tumor types. Overall, the study reinforces the strong association of EWSR1::ATF1 fusion with clear cell sarcoma of soft tissue, while EWSR1::CREB1 appears relatively more frequent in gastrointestinal counterparts, highlighting the diagnostic utility of identifying specific EWSR1 fusion partners in distinguishing these related entities.

In this 2002 study by Cristina R Antonescu et al., 12 histologically confirmed cases of clear cell sarcoma (CCS) arising in the deep soft tissues of the extremities were analyzed to assess the prevalence and diagnostic utility of the EWSR1::ATF1 fusion using RT-PCR on both frozen and formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue. Histologically, 10 of 12 cases exhibited the classic nested epithelioid morphology with clear to pale eosinophilic cytoplasm, central nuclei, and prominent nucleoli. Immunohistochemistry showed diffuse positivity for HMB45 and MITF in all cases, and S-100 in 10 cases, supporting melanocytic differentiation. Ultrastructural analysis revealed melanosomes in 6 of 7 examined tumors. Molecular analysis detected the EWSR1::ATF1 fusion transcript in 11 of 12 cases (91%), all demonstrating the in-frame fusion of EWSR1 exon 8 to ATF1 codon 65, with no variant structures identified. RT-PCR for MITF transcripts confirmed expression of the melanocyte-specific MITF-M isoform in all tested cases. These findings establish EWSR1::ATF1 as a highly sensitive and recurrent molecular marker for CCS. Its detection serves as a reliable diagnostic tool, differentiating CCS from morphologic mimics such as malignant melanoma, and confirms CCS as a genetically defined, melanocytic sarcoma driven by this characteristic fusion.

molecular_profile: MET Exon 14 Skipping Mutation AND ( MET Splice Site (c.3028+1G>T) OR MET Splice Site (c.3028+1G>A) OR MET Splice Site (c.3028+1G>C) )
evidence_statement: In this retrospective study, 564 NSCLC patients with somatic MET mutations were analyzed. There were 117 cases of METex14 skipping that were further sequenced. 75/117 cases (64.1%) affect the splicing donor site, with 63 of those cases having mutations in the canonical splicing site. 19 of the mutations affecting the canonical splicing site harbored MET c.3028+1G>A/T/C mutations, 22 cases harbored MET c.3028G>A/T/C, 11 harbored MET c.3028+2T>A/C/G, and 11 harbored insertion/deletion spanning the splicing site. This suggests that mutations affecting these mutations affecting the splicing donor site can lead to exon 14 skipping.

This study presents a series of 81 cases of diffuse hemispheric glioma, H3 G34-mutant (DHG G34m). Cases were noted to have either the histological appearance of a typical glioblastoma (73%) or as primitive neuroectodermal tumor (27%). Despite these divergent appearances, DNA methylation profiling revealed that GBM-like and PNET-like variants clustered as a single epigenetically defined entity. The genomic profile of DHGs G34m is also highly consistent across all cases, regardless of histological appearance. Key diagnostic markers include H3-3A G34 variants (95% G34R, 5% G34V), TP53 mutation in 89%, ATRX protein loss in 95%, and alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT) in 100% of tested cases. Strikingly, ATRX or DAXX mutations were found in 100% of G34-mutant tumors, representing a near-universal association. Copy number analysis revealed highly specific chromosomal alterations: 3q loss in 67% and 4q loss in 70% of cases, with combined 3q/4q losses affecting approximately 90% of tumors. MGMT promoter methylation was present in 74% of cases.

Anaplastic histology (AH) in Wilm's Tumor is characterized by abnormal mitoses, and associated with poor prognosis in comparison to favorable histology (FH). Array CGH was used on 53 AH samples, and a further set of 23 AH and 55 FH samples. Broad loss of 4q was seen in over 20% of AH samples, and authors stated that 17p, 4q, 14q, 7p, and 20p appeared to be the most AH-specific changes. Individual profiles of 4q from AH samples did not indicate focal deletions targeting a single gene such as FBXW7, which has been associated with AH, but instead indicated large scale loss of 4q Genes on 17p, 4q, 14q, and 22q were overrepresented in differentially expressed sets of genes between FH and AH tumors, with underexpression of genes in 4q.

40 diffuse anaplasia in Wilms tumours (DAWT) samples were tested using copy number (n = 32) and gene expression (n = 36) arrays. 22 had TP53 mutations and 20 of these also had 17p loss. An increased risk of recurrence as a first event was seen in tumors with TP53 mutations and/or 17p loss (p = 0.03, hazard ratio (HR), 3.89; 95% CI, 1.26–16.0) as well as death (p = 0.04, HR, 4.95; 95% CI, 1.36–31.7) in comparison to tumors lacking TP53 variants. Constituional DNA was not available for testing, and the authors note 10 of the TP53 mutations had been ovserved in Li-Fraumeni families.

Microarray-based comparative genomic hybridization (aCGH) analysis was carried out on 58 Wilms’ tumor samples. 38 tumors were untreated primary and 20 were recurrent. An increase in copy number changes was found in the recurrent tumors, with 33.0% of genomic clones, in comparison to the primary tumors with 21.2%. Loss of 17p was the most statistically significant genomic variation acquired between diagnosis and relapse. Different losses at 17p were observed, including cases which extended across the whole arm, and in one case it extended from 17p12 to 17pter

77 tumors from Wilms Tumor patients were tested with Illumina BeadChip arrays and genomic profiles were tested for association with relapse and other clinicopathological variables. Copy number gain at the cytoband location q21.2 effecting between 2 and 216 genes, and of varying lengths, was seen at higher frequencies in relapsing patients (average above 30%) than in non relapsing patients (average below 10%), and the result was significant across multiple region lengths.

The PAX5::AUTS2 represents a rare primary oncogenic driver in B-lymphoblastic Leukemia/lymphoma (B-ALL). An international cohort of 50 patients—including 16 previously reported cases—was assembled, with fusion status confirmed or predicted through a combination of conventional karyotyping, fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), SNP array analysis, optical genome mapping (OGM), RT PCR, whole genome sequencing, and whole exome sequencing. Cohort analyses consistently demonstrate that PAX5::AUTS2 is associated with high relapse rates, frequent central nervous system involvement, and poor event-free and overall survival, with particularly adverse outcomes observed in very young children. The study reported a 5-year cumulative incidence of relapse of approximately 48% and an event-free survival of roughly 48%, highlighting a prognosis inferior to most standard-risk B ALL groups. Infants and toddlers (<3 years) comprise the majority of cases and are most vulnerable. Collectively, these findings support the PAX5::AUTS2 as a primary driver in B-ALL in high-risk disease.

molecular_profile: MET Exon 14 Skipping Mutation AND MET Splice Site (c.3028+1G>T)
evidence_statement: 1141 patients with lung cancer were analyzed using NGS, to which MET exon 14 mutations were found in 28 (3.0%) of them. Of the 28, 24 samples had RNA available for qRT-PCR for MET splicing. 23/24 (96%) showed exon 14 skipping, with exception in this cohort being a patient with Y1003C substitution. Locations of MET exon 14 genomic alterations were found in these patients and three of them harbored c.3028+1G>T mutations, suggesting that this mutation leads to exon 14 skipping in these patients.

Human embryonic kidney 293T cells were used in far-Western analysis experiments, which showed that Y1003 binds directly to the c-Cbl TKB domain in MET. When Y1003 was replaced with a non-phosphorylatable phenylalanine, MET was able to evade binding with c-Cbl TKB domain (Fig 2A), which is needed for ubiquitination and subsequent degradation. They further show that D1002 and R1004, when mutated, also affect ubiquitination of MET (Fig 4A). The authors suggest that the DYR motif (Fig 7) that is conserved within MET exon 14, and various other receptors in the family, is necessary for negative regulation and leads to overexpression of MET.

The extracellular domain mutation R248C was tested in a series of assays for an evaluation of oncogenicity. R248C was stably transfected into 3T3 cells along with WT controls. TAS (Transformation Activity Score) was defined by logistic regression of four experimental batches of focus formation assays and four experimental batches of the low-serum cell proliferation assays using these cells, into a score of 1 to 4. R248C had a TAS score of 3. In parallel, mixed-all-nominated-in-one (MANO) method was used for evaluation of transforming potential. Barcoded R248C and other barcoded variants were stably transfected into 3T3 cells along with controls and grown together. Next generation sequencing was used to compare relative amounts of different barcodes for a measure of relative proliferation. Using this method, R248C had approximately 8 fold change compared to WT on a base 2 scale (~ 256 fold). The authors evaluated this result as oncogenic: higher TAS score and significantly faster growth compared with WT.

disease: Head And Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma
evidence_statement: This retrospective analysis of the Phase 3 EAGLE trial (NCT02369874) evaluated tissue tumor mutational burden (tTMB) and blood TMB (bTMB) as predictive biomarkers in platinum-refractory recurrent or metastatic head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC). Using WES, tTMB (n=153) was calculated from somatic SNVs and indels (<20,bp) at 5–80% allele frequency. bTMB (n=247) was determined using the GuardantOMNI assay (500 genes; 2,Mb), incorporating variants across all allele frequencies. In the tissue-evaluable cohort, cutoffs from 10 to 20 mut/Mb were assessed. For durvalumab monotherapy, a 10 mut/Mb threshold showed the best discrimination [HR: 0.72 (CI: 0.45–1.15)], though OS differences were not significant. For durvalumab plus tremelimumab, significant OS benefit was observed at 10 [HR: 0.52 (CI: 0.28–0.98)] and 12 mut/Mb [HR: 0.46 (CI: 0.24–0.86)] cutoffs. At 10 mut/Mb, median OS for high- vs. low-tTMB was 9.9 vs. 4.4 months (durvalumab) and 16.0 vs. 3.3 months (combination). In the blood-evaluable cohort, bTMB ≥ 16mut/Mb was the optimal predictive threshold. Patients with bTMB ≥ 16 achieved superior survival over chemotherapy for both durvalumab (OS HR: 0.39; PFS HR: 0.48) and combination therapy (OS HR: 0.38; PFS HR: 0.45). Median OS for bTMB ≥ 16 was 8.1 (durvalumab) and 7.6 (combination) vs. 4.0 months (SoC); benefits were absent in patients with bTMB < 16. These findings suggest tTMB ≥ 10 and bTMB ≥16 mut/Mb as robust predictive thresholds for identifying HNSCC patients benefiting from checkpoint inhibition.

This analysis of the Phase 2 KEYNOTE-782 trial (NCT03664024) evaluated the correlation of blood tumor mutational burden (bTMB) with the efficacy of first-line pembrolizumab plus platinum-based chemotherapy in patients with metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). The cfDNA assay utilized was GRAIL, comprising 654 genes (1.9 Mb). Paired white blood cells were sequenced to eliminate mutations related to clonal hematopoiesis and germline variants. bTMB was calculated as the total number of nonsynonymous mutations per megabase pair of the sequenced genome. In the bTMB-evaluable population (n=101), the distribution of bTMB scores was found to be similar among both responders and non-responders. Consequently, the study concluded that bTMB does not have predictive value for the efficacy of pembrolizumab combined with platinum-based chemotherapy in this clinical setting.

In this study, the authors analyzed 14 cases of angiomatoid fibrous histiocytoma (AFH). The EWSR1::CREB1 fusion associated with t(2;22)(q33;q12) was detected in 13 of 14 tumors by dual‑color and four‑color FISH, demonstrating rearrangement of the EWSR1 and CREB1 loci. In the case with available frozen tissue, RT‑PCR confirmed an in‑frame EWSR1::CREB1 transcript. Sequencing studies indicate that the fusion typically joins the EWSR1 N‑terminal activation domain (commonly exon 7) to the CREB1 bZIP DNA‑binding region (commonly exon 7), generating an intact chimeric transcription factor that drives aberrant CREB‑mediated transcription. Although exon‑specific breakpoints were not detailed in this study, the RT‑PCR–verified transcript is consistent with the canonical EWSR1‑exon‑7::CREB1‑exon‑7 configuration described in AFH. These findings establish EWSR1::CREB1 as a highly specific diagnostic biomarker that helps distinguish AFH from clear cell sarcoma and other histologic mimics with alternative EWSR1 fusion partners.

In this study, the authors report a 34‑year-old patient with angiomatoid fibrous histiocytoma (AFH) who initially presented with a pulmonary nodule and a 4th‑rib lesion and subsequently developed metastases to the iliac bone, subcutaneous tissue, pleura, lymph nodes, and brain. FISH confirmed an EWSR1::CREB1 rearrangement, and RNA-based next-generation sequencing identified an in-frame EWSR1 exon 7–CREB1 exon 7 fusion. This molecular finding established the AFH diagnosis across multiple lesions despite the tumor’s atypical and highly metastatic presentation. The disease progressed systemically, resulting in death 18 months after initial surgery, representing the first documented case of fatal, multi-organ metastatic EWSR1::CREB1–positive AFH and highlighting the rare but significant potential for aggressive behavior in tumors harboring this fusion.

In this study, the authors analyzed 9 cases of angiomatoid fibrous histiocytoma (AFH). The EWSR1::CREB1 fusion was identified as the predominant molecular alteration, detected in 8 of 9 tumors by RT‑PCR and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, which demonstrated an identical junction of EWSR1 exon 7 fused to CREB1 exon 7 in all positive cases. FISH analysis showed EWSR1 rearrangement in 7 of 8 evaluable tumors, and conventional cytogenetic analysis in one case revealed a t(2;22)(q33;q12) translocation. These complementary molecular techniques establish EWSR1::CREB1 as the most frequent and characteristic fusion in AFH, serving as a highly useful diagnostic marker that distinguishes AFH from other round/spindle cell sarcomas, including Ewing sarcoma and clear cell sarcoma.

Schwartzentruber et al. performed whole-exome sequencing (WES) on 48 paediatric GBM samples (patients aged 3–20 years, tumour cores containing >90% neoplastic tissue, median 61-fold coverage with 91% of bases covered by ≥10 reads), with matched germline DNA available for six cases. In the initial six-sample germline-matched analysis, two samples harboured heterozygous H3-3A G34R single-nucleotide variants. Extending WES to the full 48-sample cohort identified G34R in 5 samples, with H3-3A mutations overall present in 15/48 tumours (31%). Validation in the broader 784-sample multi-grade, multi-histology glioma cohort confirmed that G34R/G34V mutations were entirely restricted to GBM, highly prevalent in the paediatric setting (32/90 paediatric GBMs, 35.6%), and occurred rarely in young adults (11/318, 3.4%; p<0.0001 between paediatric and adult GBM groups). G34R-mutant tumours arose exclusively in the cerebral hemispheres with a median patient age of 20 years (range 9–42), significantly older than K27M-mutant cases (median 11 years). Critically, ATRX/DAXX mutations were found in 100% of G34R/G34V-mutant cases (13/13, p=1.4×10⁻⁸) in the larger GBM cohort where sufficient material was available. TP53 mutations co-occurred in 86% of samples harbouring H3-3A and/or ATRX mutations (18/21, p=1.1×10⁻⁴). Gene expression profiling of 27/48 WES samples by unsupervised hierarchical clustering revealed a clear transcriptional separation of G34R/V from K27M tumours, with differential expression of developmental genes including DLX2, SFRP2, FZD7, and MYT1. H3F3A and IDH1 mutations were mutually exclusive (p=1.6×10⁻⁴).

G34V is the rarer of the two G34 substitutions identified in this stud by Schwartzentruber et al, with only 1/48 tumours in the primary WES cohort harbouring this variant (sample PGBM16), compared to 5/48 for G34R. PGBM16 was confirmed by Sanger sequencing to be a non-synonymous SNV absent from dbSNP and the 1000 Genomes dataset (October 2011). Consistent with G34R, PGBM16 co-harboured an ATRX mutation (p.R2111X, a truncating stop-gain) and a TP53 mutation (p.R342X), demonstrating the canonical G34-associated triple-mutant genotype. In the larger 13-case G34R/V cohort assembled from the 784-sample validation screen, ATRX/DAXX mutations were confirmed in 100% of G34R/V cases (p=1.4×10⁻⁸). Gene expression profiling of 27 WES cohort samples with available RNA demonstrated by unsupervised hierarchical clustering that G34V clusters with G34R and is transcriptionally distinct from both K27M-mutant tumours and H3.3 wild-type GBMs. The authors noted elevated H3K36 trimethylation in the G34V-bearing sample PGBM16 relative to other samples on western blot, providing preliminary molecular evidence that G34V perturbs K36 methylation status in a manner distinct from but related to G34R. Across the full 784-sample validation cohort, G34V (like G34R) was absent from all lower-grade gliomas and from adult GBM, and was mutually exclusive with IDH1 mutations (p=1.6×10⁻⁴).

A pBABE expression vector with wild-type FLT3 was subjected to site-directed mutagenesis to introduce single amnio acid deletions across the juxtamembrane domain then transfected into Ba/F3 cells to create stable cell lines. The Ba/F3 cell line expressing the FLT3 Y572del variant showed sustained growth in the absence of IL-3 above the wild type expressing control but less than the FLT3 ITD positive control cell line (Figure 1D). The Y572del cell line showed reduced apoptosis in the absence of IL-3 compared to parental Ba/F3 cells but more apoptosis compared to FLT3 ITD cell line (Figure 3A). The Y572del cell line showed increased phosphorylation of FLT3 and downstream pathways including STAT5, AKT, and ERK1/2 (Figure 3B). This data supports the transforming potential of the FLT3 Y572del variant.
Ba/F3 cell lines expressing the variant FLT3 Y572del showed sensitivity to midostaurin and was 5 to 10-fold more sensitive than the FLT3-ITD construct.
Ba/F3 cell lines expressing the variant FLT3 Y572del showed sensitivity to quizartinib comparable to the FLT3-ITD construct.
Ba/F3 cell lines expressing the variant FLT3 Y572del showed sensitivity to lestaurtinib and was 5 to 10-fold more sensitive than the FLT3-ITD construct (Figure 4).
Ba/F3 cell lines expressing the variant FLT3 Y572del showed sensitivity to sorafenib comparable to the FLT3-ITD construct (Figure 4).
Ba/F3 cell lines expressing the variant FLT3 Y572del showed sensitivity to crenolanib comparable to the FLT3-ITD construct (Figure 4).
Ba/F3 cell lines expressing the variant FLT3 Y572del showed sensitivity to ponatinib comparable to the FLT3-ITD construct (Figure 4).

Two uncommon EGFR frameshift deletions (E701fs and L702fs; VAFs of 32.8% and 21.5%, respectively) were identified by NGS in a patient with NSCLC. The patient was enrolled in the OCELOT clinical trial and started first-line osimertinib 80 mg daily. Treatment was well tolerated, with significant improvement in symptoms. The patient remained active and independent, reporting good appetite and no gastrointestinal issues or new pain. Recent imaging showed decreased left perihilar and mid-lung opacity, and tumor markers CEA and CA125 improved. The latest CT scan demonstrated a partial response with residual left lung opacity of 2.2 cm per RECIST criteria.

H596 cells harboring mutant c-MET due to exon 14 deletion were shown to be sensitive to capmatinib (INCB28060) inhibiting phospho-c-MET in in vitro ELISA studies. IC50s were 0.4 nM for H596 cells. Capmatinib showed a greater than 10000 fold selectivity over 56 other human kinases that were tested. H596 cells were also shown to positively regulate EGFR and HER-3 signaling, with capmatinib showing dose-dependent anti-tumor activity, showing 35% and 76% tumor growth inhibition in 1 and 3 mg/kg dosages respectively in c-MET–dependent mouse tumor models.

This landmark study provided revised classification of B-lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL) based on integrated genomic findings from 1,988 childhood and adult B-ALLs. All cases were subjected to RNA-seq analysis, and a subset of them were further characterized by WGS (n=17), WES (n=73), and SNP array (n=1,141). Among 23 described subtypes, two were related to the alterations of B-lineage transcription factor gene PAX5 despite showing different gene expression patterns, and were designated as PAX5alt and PAX5 p.P80R groups. The first group included diverse PAX5 alterations, including gene fusions, non-p.P80R mutations, and/or intrachromosomal focal amplification (PAX5amp). PAX5 fusions were found in 57 cases (38.5% of the PAXalt group); they were in-frame and involved 24 partner genes, the most frequent of which were ETV6 (n=19), NOL4L (n=5), AUTS2 (n=4), and CBFA2T3 (n=4). Importantly, PAX5::JAK2 were observed exclusively in Ph-like B-ALL, and PAX5::ZCCHC7 were observed in B-ALL cases with other subtype-specific pathognomonic events. In summary, PAX5 fusions, except PAX5::JAK2 and PAX5::ZCCHC7, are subtype-defining alterations for the PAX5alt B-ALL.

This European population-based cohort study examined the genomic landscape of 110 consecutively diagnosed childhood (aged 1-18 years) “B-other” lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) cases, collected over 7 years in the Czech Republic. The B-other ALL was defined as B-ALL negative for ETV6::RUNX1, BCR::ABL1, TCF3::PBX1, KMT2A-rearrangements, hyperdiploidy (>50 chromosomes), and hypodiploidy (<44 chromosomes). Molecular alterations were characterized using a combination of SNP arrays (n=103), WES (n=109), and RNA-seq (n=69) as well as RT-PCR and flow cytometry for select alterations. In-frame PAX5 gene fusions were identified in 14 patients, involving 11 distinct fusion partners. Of those, ten fusion types retained a large 5’ portion of PAX5 (exons 1-5/6/7/8) joined to partner genes. The remaining PAX5::ZCCHC7 fusion (n=2 cases), generated by an intrachromosomal inversion joining PAX5 with its adjacent gene ZCCHC7, resulted in near-complete loss of PAX5. This finding suggests distinct biological characteristics of PAX5::ZCCHC7 in B-ALL leukemogenesis compared to other PAX5 fusions. In summary, PAX5 fusions, except PAX5::ZCCHC7, represent primary oncogenic drivers in 11% (12/110) of B-other ALL.

This large FISH-based screening study systematically identified PAX5 fusion partners in a cohort of 446 patients with childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). Interphase FISH was performed on all cases and revealed patterns suggestive of PAX5 rearrangements in 10 cases, corresponding to 2.2% of tested childhood ALLs and 2.6% of B-cell ALLs. Using a combination of RACE (rapid amplification of cDNA ends) with Sanger sequencing and fusion gene-specific RT-PCR, the authors identified PAX5 fusion partners in 9 of 10 cases. In addition to the previously reported PAX5 partners (PML, ETV6, and H20orf112), this study identified five novel gene partners, including transcription regulators (HIPK1 and DACH1), scaffold proteins (POM121C, BRD1), and a kinase (JAK2). The study showed that PAX5 fusions represent important class of primary oncogenic alterations in B-ALL.

In this 2020 study, the authors analyzed clinical, histopathologic, and RNA sequencing data from 37 infants with rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS) diagnosed before six months of age. The median age of the cohort was 2.8 months (range 0–5.8 months). Spindle cell RMS (SRMS) was identified in eight (22%) patients. Among these, VGLL2 fusions were detected in three cases, with NCOA2 (n = 2) or CITED2 (n = 1) as fusion partners. Histologically, these VGLL2-positive tumors displayed a fibromatous-like spindle cell pattern. Fusion-positive SRMS cases were associated with favorable outcomes and long-term survival. Overall, the authors highlighted VGLL2 fusions as a diagnostic biomarker for infantile SRMS, enabling molecular distinction from embryonal and alveolar RMS subtypes.

In this 2021 study, the authors analyzed clinical, pathologic, molecular, and radiologic features of 4 pediatric patients with VGLL2-rearranged infantile sclerosing and spindle-cell rhabdomyosarcoma (ssRMS). Three patients were diagnosed at birth and one at 12 months of age. All primary tumors were localized but considered unresectable, and initial management included chemotherapy or observation. RNA sequencing confirmed VGLL2::NCOA2 or VGLL2::CITED2 fusion transcripts in all cases. Three patients showed high-grade sarcomatous transformation at progression, whereas one retained low-grade morphology in a metastatic adrenal lesion. Metastatic spread occurred in 3 patients (lungs, bone, lymph nodes, adrenal), and 2 patients died of disease. Whole-exome sequencing revealed low mutational burden in primary tumors and increased genomic instability with patient-specific alterations at relapse, including TP53, CDKN2A/B, and FGFR4 mutations. Transcriptomic clustering confirmed that both low- and high-grade tumors retained VGLL2-rearranged RMS signatures. The study highlights that VGLL2-rearranged RMS, although often described as indolent, can progress aggressively, especially when initial surgical resection is not feasible.

In a study using whole genome, exome and transcriptome sequencing of 2,754 childhood ALL patients, one patient with Ph-like B-ALL had PAG1::ABL2 reported. Patient ID was SJBALL020980. RNAseq, WES, WGS, and SNP6 copy array was performed. Ph-like disease was defined by gene expression profile using PAM.

Ba/F3 cells transduced with PAG1::ABL2 Fusion were found to show IL3 independent growth. Phosphoflow cytometric analysis showed increased phospho-STAT5, phospho-CRKL, and phospho-S6 over control Ba/F3. In normal mouse and human hematopoietic cells, expression studies found that PAG1 had moderately high expression while ABL2 expression was low. The authors concluded that juxtaposition of kinases to stronger enhancers results in deregulation in the B-cell lineage.

Ba/F3 cells transduced with PAG1::ABL2 Fusion were IL3 growth independent, and treated with dasatinib for 48 hours at different concentrations up to 50 nM. IC50 for viable cells (as percentage of untreated cells) was 2 nM.

In this 2020 study, the authors analyzed four cases of follicular lymphoma using circulating tumor DNA and droplet digital PCR to monitor EZH2 hotspot mutations, including A682G. One patient with transformed follicular lymphoma carried the EZH2 A682G mutation with a variant allele frequency of 1.8% in a bone marrow biopsy; seven months later, after multiple failed lines of therapy, the mutation was detected concurrently at 38.2% in a lymph node biopsy and 74.0% in circulating tumor DNA shortly before the patient's death. In this patient, the A682G mutation persisted across multiple anatomical sites and coincided with immunochemotherapy resistance, aggressive transformation, and a fatal disease outcome. Furthermore, the patient's EZH2 mutation levels in circulating tumor DNA tracked with tumor burden and PET-CT findings, suggesting that monitoring the persistent A682G mutation may reflect disease progression and treatment failure. The authors note that activating EZH2 mutations, including A682G, are clinically relevant in follicular lymphoma (occurring in ~25% of patients) and suggest they can serve as biomarkers for tumor burden and disease aggressiveness, supporting an oncogenic association of EZH2 A682G in follicular lymphoma.

In this 2013 study, the authors analyzed 366 follicular lymphoma (FL) patients with additional paired samples from 33 cases of transformed FL. Patients harbored EZH2 mutations predominantly at codons Y646, A682, and A692, with variant allele frequencies (VAFs) ranging from 2% to 61%. In total, 9 A682G mutations were detected. Comparative analysis with other recurrently mutated genes (CREBBP, MLL2, TNFRSF14, and MEF2B) demonstrated that the majority of EZH2 mutations were clonal. Gene expression analysis of high tumor-content samples identified 106 differentially expressed genes associated with EZH2-mutant cases. The authors conclude that EZH2 mutations act as early events in follicular lymphoma and contribute to disease pathogenesis.

This 2014 preclinical study evaluated the EZH2 inhibitor EPZ-6438 (tazemetostat) in multiple EZH2-mutant non-Hodgkin lymphoma models, including the Pfeiffer lymphoma cell line harboring the EZH2 A682G variant. In proliferation assays, the Pfeiffer A682G-mutant cell line demonstrated the greatest sensitivity to EPZ-6438 among the tested lymphoma cell lines, with a proliferation IC50 of 0.00049 μmol/L and a lowest cytotoxic concentration (LCC) of 0.0005 μmol/L. The authors reported that the Pfeiffer cell line showed a 20- to 300-fold increase in sensitivity to EPZ-6438 compared with EZH2 Y646-mutant cell lines. In a saturation mutagenesis study, all possible point mutations in the FGFR 1-4 kinase domain (amino acids 472-807 for FGFR3) were tested. In this study, tumor and matched normal DNA and RNA from 127 cases of B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma were analyzed to identify recurrent somatic variants. EZH2 A692V was identified in one lymphoma case. RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) demonstrated preferential expression of the mutant EZH2 allele relative to the corresponding wild-type allele in the tumor harboring the A692V variant. In addition, EZH2 was among the genes demonstrating significant evidence of positive selection for nonsynonymous variants across the cohort.

In this study, biochemical and cellular assays were used to characterize the EZH2 A687V variant identified in non-Hodgkin lymphoma. EZH2 A687V exhibited increased catalytic activity toward histone H3 lysine 27 monomethylation (H3K27me1) and increased global H3K27 trimethylation (H3K27me3) following transient expression in cells. A B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia cell line harboring heterozygous EZH2 A687V demonstrated elevated H3K27me3 levels and was highly sensitive to the EZH2 inhibitor GSK126, which reduced H3K27me3 levels, induced apoptosis, increased gene expression, and inhibited cellular proliferation.

In the phase 3 AGILE trial enrolling patients with newly diagnosed IDH1-mutated AML who were ineligible for intensive induction chemotherapy, IDH1 R132 mutations (confirmed by FDA-approved Abbott RealTime IDH1 PCR assay) were required for trial entry and served as the driver alteration defining a distinct, therapeutically actionable disease subgroup. IDH1 R132L was tested for, however, the exact number of patients with this variant is not specified. The trial demonstrated that selective targeting of mutant IDH1 with ivosidenib resulted in significantly improved complete remission rates (47.2% vs 14.9%), event-free survival (HR 0.33; 95% CI 0.16–0.69; p=0.0011), and overall survival (median 24.0 vs 7.9 months; HR 0.44; 95% CI 0.27–0.73; p=0.001) compared to placebo plus azacitidine. Additionally, IDH1 mutation clearance was observed in 53% of patients achieving complete remission with ivosidenib-azacitidine, supporting the direct pathogenic and oncogenic role of the IDH1 R132 mutation in AML disease maintenance.

In the double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase III AGILE trial (NCT03173248), 146 patients with newly diagnosed IDH1-mutated acute myeloid leukemia (AML) who were ineligible for intensive induction chemotherapy were randomized to receive ivosidenib plus azacitidine or placebo plus azacitidine. Treatment with ivosidenib plus azacitidine significantly improved event-free survival (HR 0.33, 95% CI 0.16–0.69; p=0.002), overall survival (median 24.0 vs 7.9 months; HR 0.44, 95% CI 0.27–0.73; p=0.001), and complete remission rates (47% vs 15%). These results support IDH1 R132 mutations as predictive biomarkers of sensitivity to ivosidenib plus azacitidine in patients with newly diagnosed AML who are ineligible for intensive induction chemotherapy. Although multiple IDH1 R132 substitution variants were represented in the study population, variant-specific efficacy analyses were not reported.

In this post hoc long-term follow-up of the phase 3 AGILE trial (NCT03173248; median follow-up 28.6 months; n=148), IDH1 R132 mutations served as the obligate driver alteration defining patient eligibility in newly diagnosed AML unfit for intensive chemotherapy, 3 of which harboured IDH1 p.R132L variants. Sustained deep molecular responses were observed in patients treated with the IDH1-targeted agent ivosidenib: of 33 ivosidenib-treated patients in complete remission evaluable for molecular measurable residual disease (MRD), 10 (30%) converted to MRD negativity by the 0.1% VAF threshold, consistent with direct targeting of an oncogenic IDH1 neomorphic enzyme activity. Importantly, MRD response was not associated with specific IDH1 variant type, baseline VAF, inferred clonality, or number of co-occurring mutations, supporting the disease-driving oncogenic role of IDH1 R132 mutations independent of co-mutational context. The durable clinical benefit observed with selective inhibition of mutant IDH1 across extended follow-up further confirms the oncogenic dependency of this AML subtype on IDH1 R132 neomorphic activity.

This post hoc long-term follow-up analysis of the phase 3, double-blind, placebo-controlled AGILE trial (NCT03173248) reports updated outcomes for 148 patients with newly diagnosed IDH1-mutated AML ineligible for intensive induction chemotherapy (3 of whom harboured IDH1 p.R132L mutations), randomized 1:1 to ivosidenib (500 mg orally once daily) plus azacitidine (75 mg/m² SC/IV, 7 days per 28-day cycle) versus placebo plus azacitidine, at a median follow-up of 28.6 months. Median overall survival was significantly prolonged with ivosidenib-azacitidine (29.3 months; 95% CI, 13.2 to not reached) compared to placebo-azacitidine (7.9 months; 95% CI, 4.1–11.3; HR 0.42; 95% CI, 0.27–0.65; P<.0001). Transfusion independence was achieved in 53.8% versus 17.1% of patients (P=.0004), and hematologic recovery was faster and more durable in the ivosidenib arm. MRD negativity (0.1% VAF threshold) was achieved in 30% of evaluable ivosidenib-treated patients in CR. The safety profile remained consistent with the primary analysis. These extended follow-up data confirm sustained sensitivity of IDH1 R132-mutated AML to ivosidenib plus azacitidine, supporting this combination as standard of care for this population (FDA-approved indication).

Popovici-Muller et al. report that IDH1 R132 mutations are gain-of-function alterations that result in production of the oncometabolite D-2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG). The authors state that elevated 2-HG competitively inhibits α-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases, leading to epigenetic alterations, impaired cellular differentiation, and oncogenic transformation. In primary acute myeloid leukemia samples harboring IDH1 R132H or R132C mutations, ex vivo treatment with the mutant IDH1 inhibitor ivosidenib reduced intracellular 2-HG levels and induced myeloid differentiation. whereas 2-HG was not measurable in IDH1 wild-type samples. patient tumor cells with R132H or R132C showed restored differentiation with ivosidenib treatment, whereas IDH1 wild type patient tumor cells showed no response, supporting R132H or R132C as oncogenic mutations that drive oncogenicity via elevation of 2-HG.

Popovici-Muller et al. reported preliminary efficacy data from an ongoing phase 1 study of ivosidenib (AG-120) monotherapy in patients with IDH1-mutated malignancies. In patients with relapsed or refractory IDH1-mutated acute myeloid leukemia (AML), interim results demonstrated an overall response rate of 42% and a complete response rate of 22%, with a median duration of complete response of 9.3 months. Ex vivo treatment of primary AML samples harboring IDH1 R132H or IDH1 R132C mutations resulted in potent suppression of 2-hydroxyglutarate (2-HG) production and induction of myeloid differentiation, whereas IDH1 wild-type samples did not demonstrate these effects. These findings support sensitivity of IDH1 R132H- or IDH1 R132C-mutated AML to ivosidenib.

In this 2011 study, the authors analyzed tumor and matched normal DNA and RNA from 127 cases of B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma to identify recurrent somatic variants. EZH2 A682G and A638G were identified in one case of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) for which both tumor and matched normal tissue were sequenced, and A682G was reported as a novel variant (Table S4). RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) demonstrated preferential expression of the mutant alleles relative to the corresponding wild-type alleles in tumors harboring A638G and A682G. In the A682G-positive tumor, 582 sequencing reads supported the mutant allele compared with 20 reads supporting the reference allele (Table S7). In addition, EZH2 demonstrated significant evidence of positive selection for nonsynonymous variants across the cohort. These findings support preferential expression of the mutant EZH2 allele and positive selection of EZH2 variants in lymphoma.
