In a retrospective cohort of stage III NSCLC treated with definitive radiotherapy with or without concurrent chemotherapy (n = 164), somatic STK11 (LKB1) mutations (n = 12) were associated with higher loco‑regional recurrence compared to STK11-WT (n = 152) (1‑year LRR 25.0%, 95% CI 4.8 - 53.1 vs 10.8%, 95% CI 6.5 - 16.5; p = 0.0108). They also showed shorter DFS (HR 2.53, 95% CI 1.38 - 4.66; p = 0.0029) and OS (HR 2.198, 95% CI 1.10 - 4.41; p = 0.0263). 5‑year DFS and OS rates were significantly lower in the STK11‑mut group (DFS 0% vs 14.6%; p = 0.0020; OS 15.6% vs 42.0%; p = 0.0228), while distant metastasis rates were higher but not statistically significant (1‑year DM 66.7% vs 39.3%; p = 0.1129). STK11-mut status independently predicted inferior OS on multivariable analysis (HR 2.12, 95% CI 1.06 - 4.25; p = 0.0337), supporting resistance to radiotherapy.

In retrospective analyses of multiple non‑metastatic NSCLC cohorts (TCGA PanCancer n = 736, MSK‑IMPACT n = 961, TRACERx n = 100), pathogenic STK11 mutations were associated with worse outcomes only in radiotherapy‑treated patients, but not in those who did not receive radiotherapy (RT). In the TCGA RT subgroup (n = 83), STK11 muts were associated with worse OS (HR 3.03, 95% CI 1.38 - 6.68; P = 0.006). The combined STK11 and KEAP1/NFE2L2 alterations showed stronger associations with lower OS (HR 3.78, 95% CI 1.85 - 7.74; P = <0.001), PFS (HR 3.80, 95% CI 1.87 - 7.72; P = <0.001), DFS (HR 4.46, 95% CI 0.94 - 21.1; P = 0.06), and disease‑specific survival (HR 4.83, 95% CI 2.20 - 10.6; P =<0.001). These findings support a predictive association with RT resistance. These findings were independently confirmed in additional cohorts, including MSK‑IMPACT, where the combined mutations were associated with lower OS in non‑resected tumors (n = 407; HR 2.04, 95% CI 1.36 - 3.04, P =<0.001). However, in resected tumors (n = 378), STK11 muts showed poorer OS (HR 1.96, 95% CI 1.02 - 3.78). In TRACERx, the combined alterations were prognostic only in lymph node‑positive patients after resection surgery (n = 24; HR 5.82, 95% CI 1.36 - 24.4; P = 0.02).

In this study, the authors investigated pediatric mastocytosis and compared the functional properties of KIT extracellular domain (ECD) variants with phosphotransferase domain (PTD) variants, including KIT D816V. KIT variants were introduced into murine Ba/F3, EML, and Rat2 cells, as well as human TF1 cells, to evaluate their biological effects. Both ECD and PTD variants induced constitutive KIT autophosphorylation and cytokine-independent proliferation. In contrast, only PTD variants promoted cluster formation, upregulated mast cell differentiation markers (MC-CPA and CD25), and increased expression of adhesion-related genes, whereas ECD variants preferentially activated the AKT pathway, which was required for colony formation in Rat2 fibroblasts and erythropoietin-induced erythroid differentiation in EML cells. Whole-genome transcriptional profiling further demonstrated that KIT D816V upregulated mast cell function- and adhesion-related genes while suppressing erythroid-associated genes, consistent with enhanced mast cell differentiation and proliferation.

In this study, the authors analyzed the functional consequences of the KIT D816V variant in murine hematopoietic progenitor cells (MIHCs). MIHCs expressing KIT D816V exhibited factor-independent growth and constitutive tyrosine phosphorylation of multiple proteins, including KIT. The mutant receptor constitutively recruited the p85 regulatory subunit of phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K), resulting in activation of downstream JNK1 and JNK2 signaling, whereas Akt and ERK1/2 were not constitutively activated. Pharmacologic inhibition of PI3K or mutation of the PI3K-binding site reduced proliferation and colony formation of KIT D816V-expressing MIHCs. In addition, KIT D816V-expressing cells formed tumors in vivo in mice in the absence of exogenous growth factors, demonstrating autonomous proliferative and tumorigenic activity.

In this computational study, the authors analyzed the structural and dynamic effects of the KIT D816V variant in the cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase domain using molecular dynamics simulations, normal mode analysis, and free energy calculations. KIT D816V destabilized the inactive (autoinhibited) conformation by disrupting local hydrogen bonds within the activation loop (A-loop) and weakening electrostatic interactions, resulting in unfolding of the A-loop and long-range reorganization of the juxtamembrane region (JMR). These changes reduced JMR–kinase domain interactions and increased JMR flexibility, facilitating displacement of the JMR from its autoinhibitory position. Normal mode analysis further demonstrated that the mutant JMR exhibited more independent motions, increasing exposure of the catalytic and substrate-binding sites. Collectively, these structural changes shifted the conformational equilibrium toward the active state, providing a mechanistic basis for ligand-independent KIT activation.

In this study, the authors evaluated a panel of activating KIT variants, including KIT D816V, for their transforming capacity and downstream signaling in hematologic malignancies associated with systemic mastocytosis. KIT variants were expressed in the murine Ba/F3 cell line, and their ability to confer interleukin-3 (IL-3)-independent growth and constitutive signaling was evaluated. KIT D816V induced IL-3-independent proliferation, demonstrating transforming activity, and exhibited constitutive KIT autophosphorylation. Constitutive KIT activation resulted in persistent phosphorylation of downstream STAT3 and STAT5 in the absence of growth factors, consistent with ligand-independent activation of proliferative and survival signaling pathways. KIT D816V was resistant to imatinib but remained sensitive to PKC412.

In this study, the authors investigated the structural and functional effects of the KIT D816V variant using molecular modeling, molecular dynamics simulations, docking studies, and Ba/F3 cell-based assays. Structural analyses demonstrated that KIT D816V destabilized the inactive (autoinhibited) conformation of the kinase domain by disrupting formation of a short 3₁₀-helix near residue 816. This destabilization increased the flexibility of the activation loop (A-loop) and shifted the conformational equilibrium toward the active state without affecting the stability of the active conformation. Consistent with these structural findings, Ba/F3 cells expressing KIT D816V exhibited cytokine-independent growth, demonstrating constitutive kinase activation. The study further showed that the inactive conformation-selective inhibitor STI-571 (imatinib) was ineffective against KIT D816V, whereas ATP-competitive ellipticine derivatives inhibited both wild-type KIT and KIT D816V by targeting the active kinase conformation.

This is part of a randomised phase 3 trial, CheckpOiNt Blockade For the Inihibition of Relapsed Mesothelioma (CONFIRM), that examined therapeutic response to the anti-PD1 inhibitor, nivolumab, in patients with relapsed mesothelioma. Patients were randomised to receive nivolumab (221 patients, 6 cycles without dose reduction) or placebo (111 patients, 4 cycles). As part of the exploratory multi-omic analysis, tumour mutational burden (TMB) was measured via whole transcriptome sequencing on the archival formalin fixed tumour blocks of a subset of patients who achieved a partial response (R group, n = 12) or no response (NR group, n = 9) to nivolumab. No significant difference in TMB was observed between these two groups of patients (both approximately 5 mutations/ Mb).

This is part of the randomised double-blind phase 3 trial, CameL-sq, a study that assessed the therapeutic effectiveness of the PD-1 blockade, camrelizumab plus chemotherapy as first-line treatment in advanced lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC) patients. 389 treatment naïve state IIIB-IV LUSC patients negative of sensitising EGFR or ALK genetic alterations were randomised 1:1 to receive either camrelizumab (200mg) or placebo in combination with chemotherapy (5 mg/mL*min carboplatin and 175 mg/m2 paclitaxel). Part of this study explores the value of blood TMB (bTMB) as a predictive biomarker in this setting. For this analysis, baseline tissue and peripheral blood samples were collected prior to initial treatment and an on-treatment peripheral blood sample collected after two cycles of treatment for 270 patients (134 from the combination group, 136 from the chemo only group). Pre-treatment tissue TMB (tTMB), bTMB, and on-treatment bTMB were measured using next-generation sequencing on a pre-designed 543-gene panel. TMB was calculated as the number of nonsynonymous mutations (SNVs and InDels) in coding regions that met a certain sequencing depth (100x for tissue and 500x for plasma) and an allele frequency (5% for tissue and 0.7% for plasma) per Mg of the exonic region. Driver gene mutations and hotspot mutations included in the dbSNP138/COSMIC database were removed from the TMB calculation. The tTMB or bTMB-High groups were defined as those with a TMB value ≥ 75% level. Among patients that received the combination treatment, pre-treatment tTMB or bTMB showed no predictive or prognostic value. Conversely, on-treatment bTMB and the bTMB dynamics, measured by ∆bTMB (the difference between on-treatment and pretreatment bTMB levels), showed complementary and non-redundant predictive value for the therapeutic benefit of the combination treatment. Specifically, patients with low on-treatment bTMB achieved longer PFS (median PFS, 9.1 vs 4.1 months; HR = 0.190, P < 0.001) and OS (median, not reached vs 8.0 months; HR = 0.144, P < 0.001). Patients with increased or unchanged bTMB compared to pretreatment (∆bTMB ≥ 0) had shorter PFS (median, 4.5 vs 8.5 months; HR = 2.545, P < 0.001) and OS (median, 9.0 months vs not reached; HR = 4.199, P = 0.201) compared to those with reduced bTMB following treatment (∆bTMB < 0). Patients with low on-treatment bTMB and ∆bTMB < 0 had the longest PFS and OS, while those with high on-treatment bTMB and ∆bTMB ≥ 0 the worst PFS and OS. Notably, on-treatment bTMB predicts long-term benefit from camrelizumab plus chemotherapy among patients achieving initial radiologic stable disease. Among the 48 patients with initial SD from the combination treatment, those with high on-treatment bTMB had significantly poorer PFS (median, 4.1 vs 5.6 months; HR = 2.861, P = 0.002) and OS (median, 7.8 vs 18.2 months; HR = 3.546, P = 0.001) compared to patients with low on-treatment bTMB. In conclusion, the combination of on-treatment bTMB and its dynamics is predictive for the therapeutic benefit of camrelizumab in combination with chemotherapy in advanced LUSC patients.
BRAF p.Lys601Glu (NM_004333.6:c.1801A>G) causes increased pERK/ERK ratio.
BRAF p.Lys601Glu (NM_004333.6:c.1801A>G) causes increased phosphorylation of substrate of BRAF.

In this study, the authors evaluated the functional effects of the EGFR T790M variant in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) by expressing wild-type and mutant EGFR in HEK293T, COS-7, and human bronchial epithelial (HBEC3-KT) cells. EGFR T790M exhibited increased autophosphorylation at Y992 and Y1068 compared with wild-type EGFR, indicating enhanced kinase activity. In overexpression systems, EGFR T790M also resulted in increased mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) phosphorylation relative to wild-type EGFR. In HBEC3-KT cells, EGFR T790M significantly increased colony formation compared with wild-type EGFR, demonstrating a proliferative advantage in vitro, although the effect was less pronounced than that of classical activating EGFR exon 19 deletion variants. Screening of 237 familial lung cancer probands, 45 bronchioloalveolar carcinoma tumors, and 60 sporadic lung tumors did not identify the EGFR T790M variant.

In this study, the authors evaluated the catalytic activity of epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) variants associated with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) using purified recombinant EGFR intracellular domains. In addition to activating EGFR variants, including L858R and exon 19 deletions, the study evaluated the T790M variant in combination with activating EGFR alleles. Biochemical kinase assays demonstrated that EGFR variants harboring T790M exhibited greater autophosphorylation activity than wild-type EGFR. Kinetic analyses further showed that mutant EGFR proteins exhibited altered enzymatic properties and increased affinity for gefitinib compared with wild-type EGFR. The study also notes that EGFR T790M has been identified as a secondary mutation in relapsed NSCLC and has been reported at low frequency in untreated tumors and in the germline in families with lung adenocarcinoma.

In this study, the authors evaluated the oncogenic and signaling effects of the EGFR T790M variant in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), both alone and in cis with activating EGFR variants, including L858R and exon 19 deletions. Using stable expression models in fibroblasts and human airway epithelial cells, EGFR T790M alone produced a modest increase in EGFR autophosphorylation and weak transforming activity. In contrast, EGFR T790M in combination with activating EGFR variants markedly increased ligand-independent EGFR kinase activity and receptor autophosphorylation. Double-mutant EGFR variants (T790M/L858R and T790M/del746–750) induced strong transforming phenotypes, including morphologic changes, anchorage-independent growth, and robust tumor formation in mouse xenograft models, whereas the corresponding single-mutant variants exhibited limited oncogenic activity. The double-mutant variants also demonstrated constitutive signaling and enhanced downstream activation of Src compared with activating EGFR variants alone. The study further notes that EGFR T790M has been identified not only in drug-resistant tumors but also in untreated tumors and in rare germline cases.

In this study, the authors investigated the role of the EGFR T790M mutation using inducible mouse lung tumor models expressing T790M alone or in combination with the activating L858R mutation. They demonstrated that expression of T790M alone is sufficient to induce lung adenocarcinoma formation in vivo in the absence of additional activating EGFR kinase domain mutations. Importantly, both T790M-only and T790M/L858R tumors were dependent on continued mutant EGFR expression for tumor maintenance and were resistant to the EGFR inhibitor erlotinib. The double mutant exhibited a more aggressive tumor phenotype, with earlier onset, higher tumor burden, and stronger oncogenic signaling compared with T790M alone. These findings demonstrate that EGFR T790M is sufficient to drive lung adenocarcinoma formation in vivo and can further enhance tumorigenicity when combined with activating EGFR mutations such as L858R.

phenotypes: Adult onset,Juvenile onset,Late young adult onset
evidence_statement: The authors performed retrospective analysis of 66 myoepithelial (ME) tumors arising outside the salivary glands, including soft tissue, bone, and visceral lesions. The cohort included 36 females and 30 males, with a wide age range of 1 to 75 years (median 26 years). EWSR1 gene rearrangement was detected by fluorescence in situ hybridization in 30 (45%) cases. More than half of the cases (n=16) occurred in children and young adults (less than 30 years of age). Among cases positive for EWSR1 rearrangement, POU5F1 rearrangement was identified by FISH in 5 tumors (8%), all arising in the deep soft tissues of the extremities, typically showing a clear cell, nested morphology. An PBX1 rearrangement was found in 5 EWSR1 positive tumors, occurring in deep soft tissue, bone, and lung, often displaying bland spindle cell or clear epithelioid morphology. A single ZNF444 rearrangement was observed in an EWSR1 positive tumor occurring in a 64-year-old female in the lung. Tumors without identified fusion partners but harboring EWSR1 rearrangements (n=19) exhibited variable morphologies, including small blue cell, epithelioid, and spindle patterns. EWSR1-negative tumors (n=36, 55%) were more often benign, superficially located, or cutaneous, and sometimes showed ductal or glandular differentiation. Overall, the authors concluded that EWSR1 rearrangement is a common molecular event in ME tumors in soft tissues and is absent in myoepithelial carcinomas of the salivary gland and other related tumors.

phenotypes: Pediatric onset,Early young adult onset,Intermediate young adult onset
evidence_statement: In this 2024 study, the authors analyzed 40 myoepithelial tumors of soft tissue and bone arising in patients ≤21 years of age. The cohort included 22 females and 18 males, with ages ranging from 3 months to 21 years (median 11.5 years). Molecular testing demonstrated evidence of gene fusions in 9 of 21 (43%) tested cases. Rearrangements involving the EWSR1 gene were detected by FISH in 6 of 18 (33%) cases. Among cases analyzed by next-generation sequencing, an EWSR1::POU5F1 fusion was identified in one tumor, while additional non-EWSR1 fusions included FUS::KLF17 and BRD4::CITED1. Tumors harboring EWSR1 rearrangements did not show a single uniform morphology but were seen across both benign and malignant lesions with variable histologic patterns, including epithelioid, spindle, and mixed cell types in myxoid or chondroid backgrounds. EWSR1-negative tumors comprised a substantial proportion of cases and included tumors lacking both EWSR1 and FUS rearrangements, highlighting genetic heterogeneity in this entity. Overall, the authors concluded that while EWSR1 rearrangement represents a recurrent and diagnostically useful molecular alteration in a subset of pediatric myoepithelial tumors, it is not universally present, and its absence does not exclude the diagnosis. Therefore, integration of morphology, immunohistochemistry, and molecular testing is required for accurate diagnosis, with EWSR1 fusions serving as supportive but not definitive diagnostic markers.

This clinical study focuses on 105 participants included in the CHRYSALIS-2 Cohort (Cohort C), examining the treatment outcome of atypical EGFR mutation non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) to a combined treatment of amivantamab and lazertinib, excluding coexisting exon 20 insertions, exon 19 deletions, or exon 21 L858R mutations from the patient cohort. Patients had received at most 2 other lines of treatment to qualify for the trial, excluding those who had received any form of third generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs). Treated CNS metastases were permitted if patient was stable. Participants were treated with 1,050 mg intravenous amivantamab once a week for the first 4 weeks and then once every 2 weeks as well as 240 mg oral lazertinib once daily. In atypical EGFR mutation patients (n=38) a second generation EGFR-TKI, afatinib, had a median progression-free survival rate of 10.7 months (PMID: 26051236). In this study the overall median progression-free survival rate was 11.1 months (95% CI, 7.8 to 17.8), the treatment-naive subgroup (n=49) saw a median progression-free survival rate of 19.5 months (95% CI, 11.2 to Not Estimable), and previously-treated group (n=56) had a median progression-free survival rate of 7.8 months (95% CI, 5.4 to 11.1).

phenotypes: Late onset,Middle age onset,Late young adult onset
evidence_statement: In this 2011 study the authors analyzed 18 cutaneous myoepithelial tumors arising in 7 female and 11 male patients, with a median age of 56 years (range 34–86 years). Tumors included 9 mixed tumors, 8 myoepitheliomas, and 1 myoepithelial carcinoma. Tumor size ranged from 0.3 to 1.7 cm (mean 1.0 cm). Mixed tumors were mostly located on the head (n=8), while myoepitheliomas arose mainly in the extremities (n=6). One myoepithelial carcinoma occurred on the cheek. Histologically, mixed tumors displayed ductal structures with epithelioid, spindle, and plasmacytoid myoepithelial cells, whereas the myoepithelial carcinoma exhibited infiltrative atypical spindle cells with pleomorphic nuclei and 5 mitoses per 10 HPF. Immunohistochemistry showed universal positivity for EMA and calponin, with variable expression of S100 (90%), cytokeratin (80%), ASMA (78%), and GFAP (50%). By FISH analysis, 7 of 16 cases (44%) exhibited EWSR1 rearrangement: 4 mixed tumors, 2 myoepitheliomas, and 1 myoepithelial carcinoma. The identification of EWSR1 rearrangements across different histologic subtypes further supports a shared molecular pathogenesis. No FUS rearrangements were detected. Follow-up data, available for 5 patients including the carcinoma case, showed no evidence of disease over 6–72 months. Overall, the authors concluded that cutaneous myoepithelial tumors form a spectrum from benign mixed tumor to myoepithelioma and myoepithelial carcinoma and that a subset harbors EWSR1 rearrangements, linking them genetically to their soft tissue, bone, and visceral counterparts.

In this case report the authors described a myoepithelial carcinoma of soft tissue in a 7-week-old female infant. The tumor was located ventral to the right shoulder and measured 25 mm in diameter. Histologically, the tumor exhibited heterogeneous cytology including epithelioid, spindle, and small round cell components, embedded in a fibromyxoid stroma, with necrosis and high mitotic activity. Immunohistochemistry showed co-expression of cytokeratin (AE1/AE3), S100, and calponin, with retained INI1. Genetic analysis using FISH with EWSR1 break-apart probe and NGS panel (Archer FusionPlex Sarcoma Panel) showed the presence of the EWSR1::KLF15 fusion. Pre- and postoperative chemotherapy was administered, followed by surgical resection and proton therapy after local relapse. The patient remained disease-free two years after initial diagnosis. Overall, the authors noted that EWSR1::KLF15 is a rare fusion associated with myoepithelial tumors. It has been previously reported in only six pediatric and adolescent cases, and is associated with heterogeneous morphology and sometimes aggressive clinical behavior.

In this report the authors described a 9-year-old boy with a myoepithelioma arising in the right posterior mediastinum. The tumor’s deep location is exceptionally rare, with only four well-documented cases reported in the literature. Histologically, the tumor exhibited features consistent with myoepithelioma, and molecular testing using next-generation sequencing revealed an EWSR1::ZNF444 fusion involving exon 7 of EWSR1 and exon 5 of ZNF444. EWSR1 fusions are a common molecular feature in soft tissue myoepitheliomas and have been reported with diverse fusion partners including PBX1, ZNF444, POU5F1, ATF1, and PBX3. Other rare alterations such as PLAG1, FUS, SRF, OGT fusions, and SMARCB1/INI1 deficiency are more frequently observed in malignant cases. This case underscores the importance of integrating histopathology with molecular genetics, particularly EWSR1 fusion status, to ensure accurate diagnosis and inform prognostic assessment.

molecular_profile: STK11 Rearrangement exon 1 AND KEAP1 G417W
evidence_statement: In a case report of KRAS wild‑type NSCLC (n = 1, age 53 male) a tumor harbored concurrent STK11 (rearrangement exon 1) and KEAP1 (G417W) mutations, along with additional somatic alterations (including RET R77H, TP53 R158L and APC N732fs*58). It demonstrated primary resistance to palliative radiotherapy and immunotherapy + chemotherapy, suggesting treatment resistance associated with STK11/KEAP1 co‑mutation regardless of the KRAS mutation status.

molecular_profile: ESR1 D538G OR ESR1 Y537C OR ESR1 Y537N OR ESR1 Y537S OR ESR1 E380Q OR ESR1 Mutation
evidence_statement: In the randomized, open-label Phase II ELAINE-1 trial (n = 103), patients with ESR1‑mutated ER⁺/HER2⁻ mBC progressing after aromatase inhibitor plus CDK4/6 inhibitor therapy received either lasofoxifene (LAS, n = 52) or fulvestrant (Fulv, n = 51). LAS did not significantly improve mPFS with Fulv (24.2 weeks [95% CI 11.3 - 32.1] vs 16.2 weeks [95% CI 11.7 - 24.1]; HR 0.699, 95% CI 0.434 - 1.125; p = 0.138). It showed numerically higher ORR (13.2% [5/38; 1 CR, 4 PR] vs 2.9% [1/35; 1 PR]) and a clinical benefit rate of 36.5% vs 21.6% (P = 0.117). The 6-mo PFS rates was 53.4% [95% CI 38.6 - 66.2] vs 37.9% [95% CI 23.9 - 51.8], and the 12-mo PFS rates was 30.7% (95% CI 18.0 - 44.3) vs 14.1% (95% CI 4.6 - 28.5). Among responders, mTOR was 15.8 weeks with LAS vs 36.6 weeks with Fulv, and mDOR was 52.4 weeks (CR DoR 72 weeks) vs 55 weeks. Common baseline ESR1 mutations included D538G (34 vs 24), Y537S (21 vs 22), Y537N (14 vs 16), E380Q (9 vs 14), and Y537C (7 vs 4), with polyclonal ESR1 mutations in 29 vs 27 and visceral metastases in 31 vs 33 patients, respectively.

Gastrointestinal stromal tumor patients with KIT exon 11 mutations were stratified based on the location of their pathogenic variant in exon 11 and those with a deletion or deletion/insertion of codon 557 and/or 558 (n=25) saw a reduced progression free survival compared to patients with any other exon 11 mutation (n=35) when treated with first-line imatinib. The median PFS for 557/558 codon effected patients was 24 months ((95% CI: 21.3, 26.7), and for non-557/558 effected patients it was 49 months (95% CI: 39.4, 58.6), p<0.001. Univariate (p=0.002) and multivariate (p<0.002) Cox regression tests showed significant impact on PFS for 557/558 codon effected group, but overall survival was not significant.

molecular_profile: KDM5C Loss-of-function AND ( PIK3CA E545K OR PIK3CA H1047R OR PTEN Loss )
evidence_statement: In ER+ breast cancer cell line models with PI3K-AKT pathway alterations (MCF7 with PIK3CA E545K, T47D with PIK3CA H1047R, CAMA‑1 with PTEN deletion), CRISPR knockout screens identified KDM5C as a modifier of sensitivity to the AKT inhibitor capivasertib. Genetic knockout or pharmacological inhibition of KDM5C resulted in increased anti‑proliferative effects of capivasertib compared to wild‑type controls. Sensitization was selective to KDM5C loss and not observed with knockout of other KDM5 family members, and was reversed by re‑expression of wild-type KDM5C. Analysis of cell cycle and DNA damage markers indicated that, in the presence of capivasertib, KDM5C loss increased markers of DNA damage, cell death, and compromised cell cycle progression.

A phase 1 dose‑escalation and dose‑expansion study in patients with previously treated advanced KRAS p.G12D mutant NSCLC (NCT05382559; n = 203 overall; n = 45 NSCLC treated at the recommended phase 2 dose) found weekly setidegrasib (600mg) had anti-tumour activity with an objective response rate of 36% (95% CI 22–51), median progression‑free survival of 8.3 months (95% CI 4.1–NR), and an estimated 12‑month overall survival of 59% (95% CI 40–74). Treatment‑related adverse events of grade ≥3 occurred in 9% of patients (n = 76; NSCLC and PDAC) at this dose, with no treatment‑related discontinuations or deaths reported.

A phase 1 dose‑escalation and dose‑expansion study in patients with previously treated advanced KRAS p.G12D mutant pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (NCT05382559; n = 203 overall; n = 21 PDAC treated at the recommended phase 2 dose) found weekly setidegrasib (600mg) had anti-tumour activity with an objective response rate of 24% (95% CI 8–47), median progression‑free survival of 3.0 months (95% CI 1.4–6.9), and an estimated median overall survival of 10.3 (95% CI 4.2–13.0). Treatment‑related adverse events of grade ≥3 occurred in 9% of patients (n = 76; NSCLC and PDAC) at this dose, with no treatment‑related discontinuations or deaths reported.

In the open‑label phase II AVATAR trial (NCT01130519), patients with HLRCC‑associated papillary RCC harboring germline FH pathogenic variants (n = 43) received erlotinib plus bevacizumab, with ORR as the primary endpoint. A confirmed OR occurred in 31 patients (72%; 95% CI 57 - 83; CR n = 2), with mTOR 1.8 months (range 1.7 - 18.3). The mDOR was 19.3 months (95% CI 12.9 - 35.9), mPFS 21.1 months (95% CI 15.6 - 26.6), and mOS 44.6 months (95% CI 32.7 - NE). The remaining patients achieved SD as the best response (12/43), including 9 with SD >6 months. Grade ≥3 treatment‑related AEs across cohorts were most commonly hypertension (34%) and proteinuria (17%), supporting a predictive association between FH deficiency and sensitivity to combined EGFR and VEGF inhibition with erlotinib and bevacizumab.

In the open‑label phase II AVATAR trial (NCT01130519), patients with sporadic papillary RCC (n = 40) received erlotinib plus bevacizumab, with ORR as the primary endpoint. They demonstrated a lower ORR of 35% (n = 14; 95% CI 22 - 51), median PFS 8.9 months (95% CI 5.5 - 18.3), mDOR 18.4 months (95% CI 13.8 - 49.7), and median OS 18.2 months (95% CI 12.6 - 29.3). SD was observed as best response in 21 patients, including 12 with stable disease > 6 months. Grade ≥3 treatment‑related AEs across cohorts were most commonly hypertension (34%) and proteinuria (17%), supporting a predictive association between FH deficiency and sensitivity to combined EGFR and VEGF inhibition with erlotinib and bevacizumab.

In the BRCA‑altered cohort (n = 160; BRCA1/2 alterations) of the global, randomized, open‑label phase III PROfound trial (NCT02987543) in metastatic castration‑resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC), patients treated with olaparib (300 mg twice/day; n = 102) supported sensitivity/response vs control treated patients (CTP; n = 58) of abiraterone (1,000 mg once/day + prednisone 5 mg twice/day; n = 33) or enzalutamide (160 mg once/day; n = 25). They experienced a longer median radiographic PFS of 9.8 mo vs 3.0 mo (HR 0.22, 95% CI 0.15 to 0.32), a longer OS of 20.1 mo vs 14.4 mo (HR 0.63, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.95), and a confirmed ORR of 43.9% (n = 25/57) vs 0% (n = 0/23). PSA response was 61.7% (n = 58/94; 95% CI, 51.1 - 71.5) vs 0% (0/54), and CTC conversion of 69.0% (n = 20/29; 95% CI, 49.2 to 84.7) versus 23.5% (n = 4/17; 95% CI, 6.8 to 49.9).

In the post hoc exploratory BRCA2-only subgroup (n = 128; olaparib, n = 81; control, n = 47) of the phase III randomized open-label PROfound trial (NCT02987543), olaparib monotherapy supported Sensitivity/Response versus the physician’s choice of abiraterone or enzalutamide in mCRPC after prior NHA. They showed longer rPFS (10.8 vs 3.5 mo) and improved OS (HR 0.59; 95% CI, 0.37 - 0.95).

In the post hoc exploratory BRCA1-only subgroup (n = 13; olaparib, n = 8; control, n = 5) of the phase III randomized open-label PROfound trial (NCT02987543), olaparib monotherapy supported Sensitivity/Response versus the physician’s choice of abiraterone or enzalutamide in mCRPC after prior NHA. They showed a slightly longer rPFS (2.1 vs 1.8 mo) and a favourable OS (HR, 0.42; 95% CI, 0.12 - 1.53).

In the BRCA-altered cohort (n = 302; deleterious BRCA1/2 alterations) of the global, randomized, open-label phase III TRITON3 trial (NCT02975934) in mCRPC, pts treated with rucaparib (600 mg twice/day; n = 201) after progression on 1 prior second-generation ARPI and no prior chemotherapy for castration-resistant disease supported Sensitivity/Response versus physician’s choice control (CTP; n = 101; docetaxel, n = 60; second-generation ARPI, n = 41). Patients showed longer independently reviewed imaging-based PFS of 11.2 mo (95% CI, 9.2-13.8) vs 6.4 mo (95% CI, 5.4-8.3) with HR 0.50 (95% CI, 0.36-0.69; P<0.001). In BRCA pts with measurable disease at baseline, confirmed ORR was 45% (n = 37/82) vs 17% (n = 7/41). The interim OS was not significantly improved (24.3 mo; 95% CI, 19.9-25.7 vs 20.8 mo; 95% CI, 16.3-23.1) with HR 0.81 (95% CI, 0.58-1.12; P = 0.21). In contrast, the exploratory ATM cohort [n = 103; rucaparib, n = 69; CTP, n = 34] did not show a benefit with rucaparib. The imaging-based mPFS was 8.1 mo (95% CI, 5.5-8.3) vs 6.8 mo (95% CI, 4.0-10.4) with HR 0.95 (95% CI, 0.59-1.52) and had no confirmed objective responses [0/24 vs 2/14], supporting that the treatment benefit was driven primarily by BRCA-altered disease.

A 53-year-old Chinese man and lifelong non-smoker presented with chest tightness and pain. CT scans revealed multiple small lung nodules in the right lower lobe were seen with CT scan. Biopsy confirmed stage IV lung adenocarcinoma with EGFR exon 19 deletion. First-line treatment with Erlotinib at a daily dose of 150 mg resulted in a partial response and tumors regressed. After 28 months, there was primary tumor enlargement and the emergence of new bone metastases. Biopsy confirmed the presence of both EGFR exon 19 deletion and T790M mutation.

molecular_profile: EGFR T790M AND EGFR Exon 19 del
evidence_statement: A 53-year-old Chinese man, a lifelong non-smoker, presented with chest tightness and pain. CT imaging revealed multiple small nodules in the right lower lobe of the lung. A biopsy confirmed stage IV lung adenocarcinoma with an EGFR exon 19 deletion. First-line treatment with Erlotinib (150 mg daily) resulted in a partial response, with regression of the tumors. After 28 months, disease progression was observed, characterized by enlargement of the primary tumor and the development of new bone metastases. Repeat biopsy confirmed the persistence of the EGFR exon 19 deletion along with the acquisition of a T790M mutation. The patient was subsequently treated with second-line Osimertinib (80 mg daily), achieving another partial response that lasted 15.4 months.

This study provides robust preclinical evidence, supported by genomic data from human tumors, demonstrating that exon 4 mutations in KRAS (particularly at codon 146) represent functionally oncogenic variants. Specifically, experimental assays show that these variants increase the active, GTP-bound fraction of KRAS, promote activation of proliferative signaling pathways, and are capable of inducing cellular transformation. In parallel, tumor-derived data indicate that these mutations recur in specific cancer types and display patterns consistent with driver events. However, compared to classical KRAS mutations (codons 12 and 13), these variants exhibit lower levels of activation and reduced transforming capacity, suggesting a distinct mechanism of activation and a more moderate oncogenic potential.

LITESPARK-004 (NCT03401788) is a Phase II, open-label study. The 61 study patients were diagnosed with a VHL disease that exclusively was resulting from a germline VHL alteration, and had at least one measurable RCC tumour. PFS in 96% of patients at 24 months. RCC PR in 49% of patients, and another 49% of patients with RCC SD (noted as the best response). In addition, non-RCC neoplasms in trial patients also showed results, with confirmed responses in 77% of patients. At least one adverse event related to the belzutifan treatment was reported in all patients, however, the highest level of adverse effects deemed treatment-related were grade 3, and reported in 15% of patients. The results of this clinical trial show potential for treatment of VHL-associated RCC tumours and non-RCC neoplasms through administration of belzutifan therapy through its mechanism of HIF-2α inhibition.

molecular_profile: KIT Exon 11 Mutation AND KIT Exon 9 Mutation
evidence_statement: This study describes a case report of a patient with a gastrointestinal stromal tumor who was prescribed neoadjuvant imatinib and had a pathogenic complete response. A 41-year-old female patient with a family history of breast cancer came in with abdominal pain and a CT scan showed a gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) of 9x10cm. 5 genomic sequences were amplified and sequenced with Sanger sequencing. KIT exons 9, 11, and 17, and PDGFR exons 12 and 18. PDGFR and KIT exon 17 showed only SNPs with neutral effects. The mutations seen in KIT 9 were p.Ala502Asp (previously undocumented) and c.1540+8T>A, which was predicted to be a splice donor variant by mutation taster. Exon 11 contained 5, Gln575Pro, Thr574Pro (which were predicted missense variants) and c.1731T>C; Pro577Pro (silencing variant) which were all unknown previously, as well as Leu576Pro and Pro577Ser. The predicted structure and kinetics of the mutated KIT molecule showed little to no impact on imatinib's binding. Surgery was deemed unlikely to succeed and patient was perscribed 400mg of imatinib per day as a neoadjuvant treatment. After four months the tumor reduced 40% in size and at least 15% in density, after a further 3 months there was an additional 10% decrease in tumor size. Patient underwent a subtotal gastrectomy with Finsterer gastro‐jejunal anastomosis and three weeks after surgery the patient resumed imatinib for 3 years. After 2 years of follow-up the patient showed no recurrence and good tolerance.

This review synthesizes current preclinical, translational, and clinical evidence evaluating tumor mutational burden (TMB) as a predictive biomarker for immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) response in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC). Across the literature, TMB is biologically supported as a marker of tumor immunogenicity due to its association with increased somatic mutation load, neoantigen generation, and potential enhancement of T-cell–mediated anti-tumor immune responses. However, clinical studies in TNBC demonstrate highly variable and often inconsistent associations between TMB-high status and improved outcomes following ICI therapy, including objective response rate (ORR), progression-free survival (PFS), and overall survival (OS). The review emphasizes that the predictive signal is not uniformly reproducible across cohorts, with several studies failing to show statistically significant enrichment of responders in TMB-high populations. Additionally, TNBC shows a relatively low frequency of TMB-high tumors compared to other immunotherapy-responsive malignancies, limiting its practical clinical utility and statistical robustness in trials. A major limitation identified is the lack of harmonization in TMB assessment, including variability in sequencing platforms (whole exome sequencing versus targeted gene panels), bioinformatic pipelines, mutation inclusion criteria, and absence of universally accepted TMB thresholds for defining “TMB-high” status. Furthermore, TMB does not capture critical qualitative and spatial features of tumor immunobiology, such as neoantigen quality, antigen presentation efficiency, immune exclusion, or suppressive tumor microenvironment states, and shows inconsistent correlation with established immune biomarkers including PD-L1 expression and tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs). Collectively, these limitations reduce its predictive reliability as a standalone biomarker in TNBC. The authors conclude that while TMB has biological and exploratory clinical relevance, it is not currently suitable as an independent predictive biomarker for ICI response in TNBC, but may hold utility when integrated into multi-parameter biomarker frameworks incorporating immune, genomic, and microenvironmental features pending further prospective validation and standardization efforts.

In a functional study investigating the role of DDX41 in erythropoiesis and myeloid neoplasms, DDX41 p.G530D was identified in a patient with myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) who also carried a somatic PRPF8 mutation. The authors reported that the DDX41 c.1673G>A (p.G530D) variant is located in the helicase domain and was indicated to potentially disrupt the ATP binding to DDX41. Sanger sequencing demonstrated that the DDX41 mutation was present in CD34+ hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells but only at noise background level in CD71+ erythroid progenitor cells, whereas the PRPF8 mutation was present at equal allele frequency in both populations. The authors stated that these findings suggest that DDX41 mutation may impair erythroid differentiation or survival, resulting in the selective depletion of DDX41-mutant clones in the erythroid lineage. Functional assays showed that recombinant DDX41 p.G530D protein had markedly reduced G4 binding capacity in pull-down assays and that the mutant lost G4 resolving activity in fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET) assays. The study further demonstrated that DDX41 deficiency led to G-quadruplex accumulation, genome instability, impaired ribosomal biogenesis, p53 upregulation, and activation of the cGAS-STING pathway in erythroid cells. The authors concluded that DDX41 is a G4 resolvase, which is compromised by its loss-of-function mutations, and that DDX41 deficiency contributes to myeloid neoplasm pathogenesis through genome instability and cGAS-mediated cell death.

In CRISPR/Cas9-engineered MCF-7 breast cancer cells, ESR1 L370F reduced sensitivity to fulvestrant by decreasing fulvestrant-induced ERα degradation, suppressing inhibition of ERα transcriptional activity and cell proliferation, and reducing fulvestrant binding affinity compared with ESR1 wild-type cells. Molecular dynamics simulations suggested that L370F alters ERα structural conformation, providing a potential mechanism for resistance. These findings support ESR1 L370F-mediated resistance to fulvestrant.

In a retrospective cohort of 32 patients with metastatic urothelial carcinoma harboring FGFR2/3 alterations treated with erdafitinib, FGFR3 S249C was the most common alteration (19/32, 59%). The overall objective response rate was 40% (12/30 evaluable patients), with a median progression-free survival of 2.8 months and median overall survival of 6.6 months. Responses were observed across multiple FGFR3 mutation subtypes, including FGFR3 S249C.

This preclinical study evaluated the combination of erdafitinib and quisinostat in bladder cancer models harboring FGFR3 alterations, including the FGFR3 S249C bladder cancer cell line UM-UC-14. Compared with either agent alone, combination treatment produced synergistic inhibition of cell viability and clonogenic growth. Quisinostat also reduced FGFR3 protein expression, inhibited FGFR signaling, and enhanced the antitumor effects of erdafitinib in FGFR3-altered bladder cancer models.

This report describes a patient with metastatic urothelial bladder cancer harboring an FGFR3 S249C mutation who developed disease progression after platinum-based chemotherapy and avelumab maintenance therapy. The patient subsequently received erdafitinib and achieved a partial response by RECIST at 10 weeks, including reduction of metastatic bone lesions, despite treatment interruptions and dose reduction due to adverse events.

A 47-year-old woman with advanced metastatic anaplastic thyroid carcinoma (ATC) harboring a BRAF V600E mutation, identified by comprehensive genomic profiling of a resected lung metastasis, received combination therapy with dabrafenib (150 mg twice daily) and trametinib (2 mg once daily) administered via a gastrostomy tube. Prior treatments included thyroidectomy, left neck dissection, adjuvant chemotherapy with carboplatin and paclitaxel, radiation therapy (63 Gy in 35 fractions), and cisplatin plus doxorubicin for recurrent disease. Following initiation of dabrafenib plus trametinib, the patient experienced marked clinical improvement and healing of a malignant pharyngocutaneous fistula. Radiologic imaging demonstrated regression of pulmonary metastases at 2 months, with continued response at 4 and 6 months. Local progression in the paraesophageal region was treated with palliative radiation while the systemic response was maintained. The patient continued treatment for 9 months until systemic disease progression led to treatment discontinuation, after which rapid tumor progression was observed within 15 days.

In this retrospective, single-center, real-world study conducted between May 2018 and April 2022, 27 patients with anaplastic thyroid carcinoma (ATC) were stratified into three groups: patients with BRAF p.V600E-mutated tumors treated with dabrafenib plus trametinib (DT; n = 9), patients with BRAF wild-type tumors receiving multimodal therapy (n = 8), and patients with BRAF wild-type tumors receiving compassionate care (n = 10). BRAF status was assessed by real-time polymerase chain reaction and confirmed by next-generation sequencing in the DT group. All patients in the DT group received dabrafenib (150 mg twice daily) plus trametinib (2 mg once daily), and treatment response was evaluated according to RECIST version 1.1 using serial computed tomography. In the DT group, objective responses were observed in 7 of 9 patients at the initial assessment, with median tumor size reductions of 33% after 1 month (P = .012) and 50% at the time of best response (P = .028); the median time to symptom improvement was 3.5 days. Median overall survival was 475 days in the DT group, compared with 156 days in the multimodal therapy group and 39 days in the compassionate care group (P < .001). Median progression-free survival was 270 days in the DT group versus 32 days in the multimodal therapy group, and the 12-month overall survival rate was 71% in the DT group, whereas no patients in the comparator groups survived to 12 months. Molecular profiling confirmed BRAF p.V600E in all patients in the DT group, with frequent co-alterations in the TERT promoter (100%) and TP53 (55.5%), and an acquired NRAS p.Q61K mutation identified at disease progression in one patient. No severe treatment-related adverse events were reported. These findings support an association between BRAF p.V600E and improved clinical response and survival following treatment with dabrafenib plus trametinib compared with standard therapeutic approaches in this retrospective cohort.

This single-patient case report describes a 63-year-old woman diagnosed with BRAF V600E-mutated anaplastic thyroid carcinoma (ATC). Following multiple surgical resections, the patient developed recurrent metastatic disease, including a pulmonary nodule, and was treated with the combination of dabrafenib plus trametinib. After treatment, the pulmonary nodule completely resolved on follow-up chest computed tomography, and the patient achieved a complete response that was maintained through 32 months of follow-up. Reported adverse events included nausea, constipation, and indigestion, all of which improved with symptomatic management. Serial serum thyroglobulin measurements were 0.14 and 0.21 ng/mL at 3 and 6 months after surgery, respectively, and 0.07 and 0.28 ng/mL after 5 and 16 months of targeted therapy, respectively. The reported diagnosis was recurrent metastatic BRAF V600E-mutated ATC.

This multi-institutional retrospective study analyzed 44 patients with anaplastic thyroid carcinoma (ATC) treated across three hospitals in Taiwan. BRAF mutation testing was performed in 24 patients (55.4%) using immunohistochemistry (VE1 antibody), polymerase chain reaction, next-generation sequencing, or a combination of these methods; among those tested, 12 patients harbored the BRAF V600E variant. Eleven patients with BRAF V600E-mutated ATC received targeted therapy with dabrafenib plus trametinib. In this treated subgroup, the objective response rate was 81.8%, including one complete response and eight partial responses, with a median progression-free survival of 7.4 months and a median overall survival of approximately 10.4 months. Compared with patients who did not receive dabrafenib plus trametinib, treated patients had longer overall survival (10.4 vs. 3.3 months), and multivariable analysis demonstrated that treatment with dabrafenib plus trametinib was associated with improved overall survival (hazard ratio [HR] 0.25, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.09–0.67). These findings support an association between the presence of the BRAF V600E variant and clinical response to combined BRAF/MEK inhibition with dabrafenib plus trametinib in ATC based on real-world retrospective data.

In this systematic review and meta-analysis, the authors evaluated the predictive relevance of the BRAF V600E variant in patients with anaplastic thyroid carcinoma (ATC) treated with MAPK pathway-targeted therapy, specifically the combination of dabrafenib (a BRAF inhibitor) and trametinib (a MEK inhibitor). The study pooled data from nine clinical studies comprising 168 patients with BRAF V600E-mutated ATC, including both clinical trials and observational cohorts. The included studies used molecular diagnostic methods, including next-generation sequencing, polymerase chain reaction-based assays, and immunohistochemistry, to confirm the presence of the BRAF V600E mutation before treatment. Across the pooled population, treatment with dabrafenib plus trametinib was associated with an objective response rate of 68.15%, a disease control rate of 85.39%, a median progression-free survival of 6.7 months, and a median overall survival of 14.5 months, with approximately 65% of patients alive at one year. Collectively, these findings support an association between the presence of the BRAF V600E variant and clinical response to dabrafenib plus trametinib in ATC. However, the evidence is derived from pooled non-comparative studies rather than randomized comparative analyses.

FLT3 M737I variant was found in patient at diagnosis but absent in the remission sample. BaF3 cells was transformed to express M737I and these cells were unable to grow in the absence of IL-3 similar to wildtype negative control. Cell proliferation experiments were performed in triplicate. Predictive algorithms (SIFT and PMut) predicted M737I to be tolerated.

A 10-year-old female (Case #62) with B-ALL harbored a ZC3HAV1::ABL2 fusion and a PAX5 deletion. The fusion was identified by RNA sequencing and confirmed by RT-PCR and Sanger sequencing; breakpoints were not determined. The PAX5 deletion was detected by SNP array. Cytogenetic analysis failed to yield a karyotype. The patient presented with a white blood cell count of 55 × 10⁹/L. Findings are consistent with a Philadelphia-like ALL subtype and a kinase-driven mechanism.

A 16.6-year-old Taiwanese male (Case #299) with B-ALL harbored a ZC3HAV1(exon 12)::ABL2(exon 2) fusion and concurrent deletions of CDKN2A/2B, PAX5 (exons 2–5), and IKZF1 (exons 2–8). The fusion was detected by RT-PCR and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, while deletions were identified by MLPA. The patient presented with hyperleukocytosis (WBC 310 × 10⁹/L), achieved remission, subsequently relapsed, and died without receiving tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy or bone marrow transplantation.

In an exploratory analysis of the phase III CheckMate 026 trial in previously untreated stage IV or recurrent non-small-cell lung cancer, patients with high tumor mutational burden (≥243 missense mutations by whole-exome sequencing) demonstrated improved outcomes with nivolumab compared to platinum-based chemotherapy. High-TMB patients treated with nivolumab had a higher response rate (47% vs. 28%) and longer median progression-free survival (9.7 vs. 5.8 months; HR 0.62, 95% CI 0.38–1.00). The association between high TMB and improved nivolumab response was exploratory and hypothesis-generating.

Introduction of FGFR3 carrying the p.Arg805Gln (R805Q) variant did not alter growth-factor independent proliferation in either of two cell lines (murine Ba/F3, human MCF10A) compared to introduction of wild-type FGFR3.

A 38-year-old male with Ph-negative B ALL was found to harbor a ZC3HAV1 ABL2 rearrangement identified by massively parallel DNA sequencing (MPDS), consistent with a Philadelphia-like genotype. The leukemia cells were CD25-positive (30%). Cerebrospinal fluid involvement was detected at diagnosis. The patient was treated with dasatinib in combination with chemotherapy (CALGB 10403 regimen) and achieved complete remission with undetectable minimal residual disease (MRD) on day 29.

This study examined ovarian cancer patients from The Cancer Genomics Atlas totaling 432 patient profiles. Patients were grouped into low and high tumor mutational burden (TMB) groups to examine the prognostic value of TMB in ovarian cancer. The threshold for high/low TMB (n=214/218 respectively) was set to the median TMB of all patients profiles (1.974 mutations/MB). Using this threshold. the researchers examined the Overall Survival (OS) and Progression Free Survival (PFS) between the two groups. In the TCGA patients, the OS (P = 0.038) and PFS (P = 0.007) in patients with high TMB were better than those with low TMB. When examining the same metrics in OC patients in a cohort from the International Cancer Genomics Consortium (ICGC) they found a similar result for OS and that high TMB was associated with a lower stage and tumor-free status. The evidence in the paper shows an increased immune infiltration of CD8+ T cells, Th1 cells, Th2 cells, and Th17 cells in the high TMB population compared to the low TMB population, and the authors point to this as the possible mechanism behind the better outcome.

Whole genome sequencing and staining of anti-CD3 and anti-CD8 antibodies were performed on fresh-frozen tissue from 6 Lynch syndrome associated microsatellite (MSI) colorectal cancer patients and 20 MSI colorectal cancer patients to obtain tumor mutational burden (TMB) and immune cell scoring. A higher immune cell score suggests a strong infiltration of T cells into the tumor and has been shown to be a strong prognostic factor in colorectal cancer (Galon et al., 2014; PMID: 24122236). The study found a similar TMB distribution between Lynch syndrome associated MSI colorectal cancer tumors and sporadic MSI colorectal cancer tumors. Furthermore, the study found no significant differences in TMB between MSI colorectal cancer tumors with a high or low immune cell score.

The molecular differences between MSI-H/dMMR and TMB-H/MSS prostate cancer were studied for the impact of these differences on immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) sensitivity. MSI and TMB were studied together, since while MSI-H leads to higher TMB, TMB-H can also have multiple causes. 3,244 tumors from 2,257 prostate cancer patients were sequenced. 63 (2.8%) patients had MSI-H/dMMR, and 33 (1.5%) had TMB-H/MSS (microsatellite stable) prostate cancers. TMB-H was defined as greater of equal to 10 mutations/megabase. MSI-H was defined using MSIsensor score ≥10 or MSIsensor score ≥3 and <10 with a deleterious MMR alteration. MSIsensor is a program which computes length distributions of microsatellites per site in paired tumor and normal sequence data. Of 27 patients with MSI-H/dMMR given ICB, 45% of patients had a RECIST response, 65% had a PSA50 response. Of 8 patients with TMB-H/MSS given ICB, 0% of patients had a RECIST response, and 50% had a PSA50 response. The authors conclude that MSI-H/dMMR prostate cancers have greater TMB, indel and neoantigen burden compared with prostate cancer that are TMB-H/MSS, and in addition these differences could contribute to improved responses to ICB.

In a targeted sequencing study of 28 patients with sarcomatoid hepatocellular carcinoma (SHC), a single case harboring an NTRK1 fusion involving downstream CRABP2 joined to intron 9 of NTRK1 was identified. This alteration represents a potentially actionable oncogenic driver. NTRK fusions encode constitutively active TRK fusion proteins that are known to be sensitive to TRK inhibitors. Based on prior clinical evidence across tumor types, patients with NTRK fusion-positive tumors may benefit from TRK-targeted therapies such as Larotrectinib or Entrectinib. These findings support the clinical relevance of screening for rare NTRK1 fusions in SHC to identify patients eligible for targeted therapy.

Ziegler et al. evaluated FGFR1 R189C in NIH/3T3 mouse fibroblast models engineered with pMIGR1 retroviral constructs to express FGFR1 R189C or FGFR1 wild-type. FGFR variant constructs were generated by site-directed mutagenesis using the Q5 Site-Directed Mutagenesis Kit, verified by sequencing, and construct-positive cells were purified based on linked enhanced green fluorescent protein expression. In low-serum proliferation assays, FGFR1 R189C-expressing NIH/3T3 cells showed reduced serum/growth factor dependency compared with FGFR1 wild-type controls, supporting an activating effect (Figure 2A). FGFR1 R189C increased colony formation in soft agar, and colony formation was suppressed by 50 nM erdafitinib, supporting sensitivity to FGFR inhibition (Figure 3A, 3E). The authors concluded that newly identified activating non-kinase domain FGFR variants, including FGFR1 R189C, are generally targetable by FGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors.

In a 56-year-old female diagnosed with B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma (B-ALL), transcriptome sequencing (RNA-seq) identified a CNTRL::ABL1 fusion. At diagnosis, the patient had a white blood cell count of 32.26 × 10⁹/L, 82.5% blasts by morphology, a deletion in the long arm of chromosome 13 as the only abnormality detected by karyotype analysis, and negative fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) studies for a BCR::ABL1 fusion. The CNTRL::ABL1 fusion was presumed to result from an interstitial 9q deletion, since the two genes map approximately 10 Mb apart in the 9q33–q34 region, with CNTRL localized upstream (centromeric) of ABL1, and both genes transcribed in the same orientation. The fusion was confirmed by Sanger sequencing, which showed that the junction occurred between exon 7 of the CNTRL NM_007018.6 transcript (hg38) and exon 4 of the ABL1 NM_005157.6 transcript (hg38); the reading frame was preserved, and the fusion contained the entire ABL1 kinase domain. Additional genomic alterations included SETD2 p.Asn2071fs, PRKCB p.Ser85Phe, and UNC13D p.Val91Met. The patient was refractory to conventional chemotherapy, with 21% blasts by morphology (31.4% by flow cytometry) at the end of induction. Following detection of the CNTRL::ABL1 fusion by RNA-seq, dasatinib was added to the treatment regimen, resulting in a dramatic decrease in residual disease after one month and minimal residual disease (MRD)-negative remission at the end of consolidation. The patient continued on dasatinib and remained in remission at the time of reporting. The dramatic response to therapy with an ABL1 inhibitor supports the conclusion that CNTRL::ABL1 was the critical oncogenic driver in this patient’s leukemia.

In a 15-year-old male with B-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma (B-ALL), a novel CNTRL::ABL1 was identified during screening of 212 childhood B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia cases. Samples lacking known genetic alterations were analyzed using multiplex RT-PCR and next-generation sequencing-based kinome capture analysis. The CNTRL::ABL1 fusion was detected by kinome capture sequencing and confirmed by bidirectional Sanger sequencing. Additional genomic alterations included CDKN2A/CDKN2B deletion and IKZF1 exon 2–3 deletion. Sequencing showed that the fusion occurred between the exon 37 of the CNTRL NM_007018.6 transcript (hg38) and exon 4 of the ABL1 NM_005157.6 transcript (hg38); the reading frame was preserved, and the fusion contained the entire ABL1 kinase domain, showing all structural characteristics of established oncogenic ABL1 fusions.

A 4 yr old boy presented with a history of 1 week with fatigue, weakness, fever and vomiting. Physical examination showed prominent hepatosplenomegaly and white blood cell count of 622.8x109/L with 88% blasts, and indicated T-ALL. Cytogenetic work on bone marrow aspirate showed added material of uncertain origin (46,XY,add(3) (q21),add(5) (q11)[9]/46,XY[11]). BCR-ABL1 was negative. Induction therapy was given, and after progression, augmented Berlin-Frankfurt-Münster consolidation therapy was initiated. Persistent disease remained evident. On day 83 after diagnosis, targeted RNA sequencing identified AGGF1::PDGFRb fusion and was confirmed by sequencing of the entire coding region. The fusion was subsequently also verified in a sample from day 1. The in frame fusion yielded an 1124-residue protein with exons 1-10 of AGGF1, an alanine encoded by one AGGF1 and two PDGFRb nucleotides, and exons 11-23 of PDGFRb without additional mutations. Patient bone marrow mononuclear cells responded to a set of tyrosine kinase inhibitors, and therefore dasatinib was added to patient chemotherapy regimen on day 87, and continued to day 166. Differing chemotherapy regimens were given over the course of this time which included vincristine, pegaspargase, dexamethasone, cyclophosphamide, and others. dasatinib was chosen due to superior penetration into the central nervous system. Dasatinib well tolerated and the patient had stabilization of disease with a 3 month improvement in splenomegaly and clinical symptoms. AGGF1::PDGFRb positive blast cells decreased from 71.5 percent to 8 percent at end of treatment. There was then rapid progression followed by patient death. The authors conclude that While the patient failed to achieve durable response to a dasatinib, disease stabilization for 3 months was seen, and relapse suggests additional genetic alterations as well as the potential that AGGF1::PDGFRb fusion was only part of a major subclone.

In frame AGGF1:PDGFRb (exons 1-10 and exons 11-23) containing the PDGFRb tyrosine kinase domain, with no additional mutations, was observed in a 4 year old patient with T-ALL, found by RNAseq and confirmed by sequencing. The authors concluded the fusion played a driver mutation role. AGGF1:PDGFRb caused IL3 independent growth in Ba/F3 cells, matching the growth of parental Ba/F3 in the presence of IL3. Parental cells with no IL3 added did not proliferate. Inclubation of Ba/F3 AGGF1:PDGFRb with tyrosine kinase inhibitors reduced AGGF1:PDGFRb autophosphorylation of PDGFRb in western blots, indicating an intact kinase domain and aberrant activation. The authors conclude that AGGF1 coiled-coil dimerization domain likely promotes constitutive autoactivation of the PDGFRb kinase.

Primary mononuclear cells from a 4 year old patient with AGGF1:PDGFRb were treated with PDGFRb inhibitors, which resulted in cell death. IC50 for reduction in cell viability were approximately Ponatinib: 1.5 nM, Dasatinib: 2 nM, Crenolanib: 11 nM, Sunitinib: 12 nM, Sorafenib: 13 nM, Nilotinib: 15 nM, and Imatinib: 15 nM. Ba/F3 cells with AGGF1:PDGFRb showed IL3 independent growth, and were also incubated in PDGFRb inhibitors, with resulting IC50s ranging from approximately 8 to 45 nM. Treatment of both cell types with non-PDGFRb inhibitors (erlotinib, gefitinib, ibrutinib, and vandetanib) did not result in cell death.

Ba/F3 cells with AGGF1:PDGFRb showed IL3 independent growth. Patient derived cells and Ba/F3, both with AGGF1:PDGFRb, were treated with erlotinib, gefitinib, ibrutinib, and vandetanib. IC50 for inhibition of cell viability was over 10,000 nM, whereas for sensitizing inhibitors it was below 10 nM

A 4 yr old boy was diagnosed with precursor B-cell ALL. Patient had normal karyotype. The patient was refractory to prolonged induction therapy. Presence of PDGFRB rearrangement was indicated by FISH and RNA-seq showed AGGF1::PDGFRb, in frame, consisting of AGGF1 exons 1-6 and PDGFRb exons 11-23. Saliva was used for normal control sequencing. In Ba/F3 cells, AGGF1::PDGFRb induced IL3 independent growth. Additionally, AGGF1::PDGFRb also induced cytokine independent growth in primary bone marrow cells from Arf -/- C57/BL6 mice. In Ba/F3 cells, AGGF1::PDGFRb localized to the cytoplasm in staining, and in western blots with Ba/F3 lysates, IL3 independent activation of Stat5, Erk, and Akt via phosphorylation was seen in AGGF1::PDGFRb vs controls. Authors indicate the patient had Ph-Like B-ALL, and that AGGF1::PDGFRb was likely the driver the leukemia pathogenesis.

A 4 yr old boy with AGGF1::PDGFRB Fusion, and Ph-Like B-ALL was refractory to chemotherapy and did not respond to induction therapy. The patient was given imatinib, and within 8 weeks leukemia clearance was apparent, with blast percentage drop from 51 percent to 3 percent. The authors characterized this as complete remission. Relapse occurred 5 months later, when a potential resistance mutation PDGFRb(C843G) became the dominant clone. Ba/F3 cells with AGGF1::PDGFRb showed IL3 independent growth and showed sensitivity to imatinib treatment (IC50 0.23nM).

In the phase II cohort of the KRYSTAL-1 trial, 112 evaluable patients with previously treated advanced KRASG12C-mutated NSCLC were treated with adagrasib monotherapy (600-mg in capsule form twice daily, with the patient in a fasted state). The treatment led to a confirmed objective response rate of 42.9%, a median duration of response of 8.5 months (95% CI, 6.2 to 13.8), a median progression-free survival of 6.5 months (95% CI, 4.7 to 8.4), and a median overall survival of 12.6 months (95% CI, 9.2 to 19.2) in patients . The estimated overall survival at 1 year was 50.8% (95% CI, 40.9 to 60.0).

In a retrospective cohort of 16 patients treated with primary debulking surgery followed by platinum-taxane chemotherapy (carboplatin and paclitaxel), patients classified as platinum-resistant exhibited significantly higher tumor mutational burden (TMB-High) than platinum-sensitive patients (P = 0.0321). TMB demonstrated predictive value for platinum resistance (AUC = 0.7778). Additionally, patients with higher TMB experienced significantly shorter progression-free survival (PFS) compared with those with lower TMB (P = 0.0083), supporting elevated TMB as a predictive biomarker of resistance to platinum-based chemotherapy and poorer clinical outcome.

In BRAF V600E-positive murine anaplastic thyroid carcinoma (ATC) cell lines (TBP-3743, TBPt-3403, and TBPt-3610R), treatment with the BRAF inhibitor PLX4720 decreased ERK phosphorylation and significantly reduced cellular migration. In an immunocompetent orthotopic mouse model generated using BRAF V600E-positive TBP-3743 ATC cells, PLX4720 treatment significantly reduced mean tumor volume compared with control mice after one week of treatment (92 ± 68 mm³ versus 231 ± 52 mm³; *P* < 0.01) and increased cleaved caspase-3 staining in tumor tissue, supporting a role for BRAF V600E signaling in ATC growth and survival.

In an orthotopic mouse model generated using BRAF V600E-positive 8505c anaplastic thyroid carcinoma cells, treatment with the selective BRAF V600E inhibitor PLX4720 decreased phospho-ERK1/2 expression, reduced Ki67 expression from 71.7% +/- 6% to 15.0% +/- 2.9% (p < 0.01), and reduced tumor volume from 57 mm3 at treatment initiation to 14 mm3 after 3 weeks of treatment. PLX4720 treatment also reduced lung metastatic burden from 624 +/- 92 GFP metastases/cm2 in control mice to 223 +/- 51 GFP metastases/cm2 after 3 weeks of treatment.

In transgenic mice with thyroid-specific expression of BRAF V600E, Tg-BRAF2 mice developed papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) in 14 of 15 animals at 12 weeks and 13 of 14 animals at 22 weeks. These tumors frequently exhibited tall-cell features, capsular invasion, vascular invasion, skeletal muscle invasion, and foci of poorly differentiated carcinoma. Tg-BRAF2 mice also demonstrated increased ERK phosphorylation and a 30% reduction in survival at 5 months.

A systematic review and meta-analysis of 34 studies comprising 978 patients with anaplastic thyroid carcinoma (ATC) reported a pooled prevalence of BRAF V600E of 33% (95% CI, 26%–40%). When cases with coexisting differentiated thyroid carcinoma were excluded, the pooled prevalence was 20% (95% CI, 6%–40%), supporting that BRAF V600E is a recurrent somatic alteration in ATC.

Targeted next-generation sequencing of 11 anaplastic thyroid carcinomas (ATCs) with matched normal tissue identified BRAF V600E in 10 of 11 tumors (91%), making BRAF the most frequently mutated gene in the cohort. The remaining tumor harbored a KRAS G12V mutation, resulting in BRAF or RAS mutations being present in all 11 ATC analyzed. Additional recurrent alterations included TP53 mutations in 8 tumors (73%), PIK3CA mutations in 2 tumors (18%), and a PTEN frameshift mutation in 1 tumor (9%).

In a retrospective study of patients with irinotecan-refractory metastatic colorectal cancer whose tumors were wild type for KRAS codons 12 and 13, one patient whose tumor harbored a KRAS A146 mutation did not respond to combined cetuximab and irinotecan therapy. In the BRAF-wild-type subgroup, none of the 8 patients with mutations in KRAS codon 61 or 146 responded, compared with 22 of 60 patients whose tumors were wild type at both codons (0% versus 37%; p=0.047). The pooled KRAS codon 61/146-mutant group also had shorter median progression-free survival than the corresponding wild-type group (3.8 versus 5.3 months; p=0.023), while the difference in overall survival was not statistically significant (9.7 versus 14.8 months; p=0.320). These results are consistent with KRAS A146P as a predictive marker of resistance to cetuximab plus irinotecan in colorectal cancer.

Park et al. evaluated the transforming potential of 169 KRAS variants by introducing sequence-confirmed variant constructs into NIH 3T3 fibroblasts and performing focus-formation assays in triplicate. KRAS A146P received a focus-formation score of 4, the highest assay category, corresponding to severe formation of diffuse, round-shaped foci. The authors classified variants with scores of 3 or 4 as oncogenic because they exhibited markedly greater transforming activity than wild-type KRAS. These results provide direct functional evidence that KRAS A146P is oncogenic.

Edkins et al. identified KRAS c.436G>C (p.A146P) in one primary colorectal cancer, PD1978a, during sequencing of two independent colorectal cancer cohorts. Normal DNA from the same individuals was analyzed, confirming that the codon 146 mutations detected in the primary tumors were somatic. Across primary tumors, xenografts, and colorectal cancer cell lines, KRAS A146 mutations were detected in 11 of 260 cases, including A146T, A146V, and A146P, establishing codon 146 as a recurrent mutation site in colorectal cancer. These findings support KRAS A146P as a likely oncogenic somatic variant, although A146P-specific transforming activity was not directly tested.

In a systematic analysis of KRAS mutations across 2,280 KRAS-mutant colorectal cancer samples from three large clinical sequencing cohorts (DFCI, TCGA, MSKCC), KRAS A146P was confirmed as one of three recurrent activating substitutions at codon 146 (frequency order A146T > A146V > A146P), accounting for 7.4% of all KRAS mutations collectively. Codon 146 resides in a densely packed hydrophobic region near the guanine moiety of the GTP/GDP nucleotide, and mutations at this site, along with G12, G13, Q61, and K117, disrupt GAP-mediated GTP hydrolysis, leading to constitutive KRAS activation.

In the PRIME trial, patients with KRAS exon 3/4 or NRAS mutations beyond exon 2 (n=108) had worse outcomes with panitumumab-FOLFOX4 vs. FOLFOX4 alone (PFS HR 1.28, 95% CI 0.79–2.07; updated OS HR 1.39, 95% CI 0.91–2.13), and the full "any RAS mutation" population (n=548) showed a significant detriment (PFS HR 1.31, P=0.008; OS HR 1.21, P=0.04). The published supplementary Table S1 confirms two patients in this cohort carried the specific A146P genotype.

In a prospective-retrospective analysis of the second-line phase III 20050181 trial, patients with metastatic colorectal cancer received panitumumab plus FOLFIRI or FOLFIRI alone. Extended RAS testing was methodologically identical to the PRIME trial, covering KRAS exon 4 codons 117 and 146. Among the sub-cohort of patients whose tumors were wild-type for KRAS exon 2 but harbored an actionable extended RAS mutation, the addition of panitumumab yielded no significant progression-free survival benefit (HR, 0.89; 95% CI, 0.56-1.42; p=0.63). These findings support resistance to anti-EGFR therapies in tumors with KRAS codon 146 alterations, though outcomes were not isolated for the specific KRAS A146P genotype.

In a pooled analysis of the CAVE (cetuximab + avelumab) and VELO (panitumumab + trifluridine/tipiracil) anti-EGFR rechallenge trials in tissue RAS-wild-type mCRC, pretreatment plasma ctDNA genotyping via the Idylla platform identified KRAS A146P in 2 of 32 RAS/BRAF-mutant patients. An additional 2 patients showed A146P co-detected with a second codon-146 allele (A146T or A146V), likely reflecting polyclonal, heterogeneous resistant populations. This highlights KRAS A146P as a marker of acquired resistance detected before rechallenge, although the study did not isolate individual treatment outcomes or specify patient distribution between the two trials.

In this study, the authors identified a somatic EGFR L858R mutation in two patients with gefitinib-responsive non-small cell lung cancer. Functional analysis of EGFR L858R expressed in Cos-7 cells demonstrated enhanced EGF-induced receptor autophosphorylation compared with wild-type EGFR and sustained receptor activation for up to 3 hours following EGF stimulation, indicating increased EGFR kinase activity associated with the L858R variant.

In this preclinical study, expression of EGFR L858R in Ba/F3 cells induced interleukin-3-independent proliferation, demonstrating ligand-independent cellular transformation. EGFR L858R was constitutively autophosphorylated in the absence of EGF stimulation and resulted in constitutive activation of STAT5, ERK1/2, ERK5, and AKT signaling pathways compared with wild-type EGFR. These findings demonstrate that EGFR L858R confers constitutive kinase activity and transforming potential.

In this preclinical study, biochemical and structural analyses demonstrated that the EGFR L858R kinase exhibited approximately 50-fold greater catalytic activity than wild-type EGFR and adopted a constitutively active conformation through disruption of autoinhibitory interactions. Crystal structures and kinetic analyses showed that the L858R substitution destabilized the inactive kinase conformation, thereby promoting constitutive kinase activation.

In this study, EGFR L858R was identified in multiple lung non-small cell carcinoma (NSCLC) cohorts, including 1 of 10 gefitinib-sensitive tumors, 3 of 7 erlotinib-sensitive tumors, 5 of 15 untreated lung adenocarcinomas from never smokers, and 4 of 81 untreated NSCLCs from former or current smokers. Matched normal tissue confirmed the somatic origin of the mutations when available. Functional characterization in transiently transfected 293T cells demonstrated that EGFR L858R induced a phosphorylation pattern distinct from wild-type EGFR, supporting altered EGFR kinase signaling associated with this variant.

In a moderate-throughput functional genomic screen, FGFR3 p.S187Y demonstrated cell proliferation and viability comparable to wild-type FGFR3 in growth factor-dependent Ba/F3 and/or MCF10A cellular assays and was therefore classified as having no detectable functional impact on FGFR3-mediated cellular transformation. These findings do not support FGFR3 p.S187Y as an activating oncogenic variant.

Expression of EGFR L858R in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) cell lines (H1299 and CL1-0) significantly increased cell invasion compared with wild-type EGFR, whereas EGFR L858R-specific knockdown reduced this invasive phenotype. Mechanistic studies demonstrated that EGFR L858R activated EGFR/ERK signaling, resulting in increased CXCR4 expression, and inhibition of CXCR4 by small interfering RNA (siRNA), a neutralizing antibody, or the CXCR4 antagonist AMD3100 significantly suppressed EGFR L858R-dependent cell invasion. In an intrapleural xenograft model, EGFR L858R-expressing cells promoted malignant pleural effusion formation, whereas wild-type EGFR-expressing cells did not. These findings support that EGFR L858R enhances invasive behavior and malignant pleural effusion formation through activation of the CXCL12-CXCR4 signaling axis, consistent with an oncogenic role in NSCLC.

Expression of EGFR L858R in stable cell models resulted in increased phosphorylation of EGFR tyrosine residues Y845, Y992, and Y1068 compared with wild-type EGFR following EGF stimulation. In both stable cell models and human non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) cell lines harboring endogenous EGFR L858R, the variant was associated with increased phosphorylation of Akt and STAT5, whereas ERK1/2 phosphorylation was comparable to that observed with wild-type EGFR. Mutation-specific siRNA-mediated knockdown of endogenous EGFR L858R in NSCLC cells induced extensive apoptosis, and EGFR L858R-expressing cells exhibited increased resistance to apoptosis induced by cisplatin, doxorubicin, and Fas ligand compared with NSCLC cells expressing wild-type EGFR.

The FLT3 V592G variant was found in a patient with AML. BaF3 cells transformed to express V592G demonstrated proliferation in the absence of IL-3 similar to D835Y positive control. Cell proliferation experiments were performed in triplicate. Western blotting with a FLT3 anti-phosphotyrosine antibody from BaF3 cells expression V592G showed constitutive FLT3 autophosphorylation, similar to the FLT3 D835Y positive control.

A retrospective cohort study was performed with advanced NSCLC patients who had prior immunotherapy with available genomic testing, and TMB determined by NGS via the Foundation Medicine assay. 87 patients with greater than six months follow up were included. Patients who had received ICI in a clinical trial were also excluded. Patients were assessed for Durable Clinical Benefit (DCB - no progression or ongoing treatment for ≥12 months) or No Durable Benefit (NDB). In patients with DCB, median TMB was 11.35. In patients with NDB, median TMB was 6.3. ROC curve analysis of patient response rate indicated that 9.24 out/Mb was an optimal cutoff for TMB. Overall Survival and Time To Progression were increased significantly in patients with TMB > 10. When higher TMB was combined with higher PDL-1 expression and lower neutrophil-lymphocyte ratio, predictive results were improved over TMB alone.

Temozolomide (TMZ), the principal alkylating agent used in PanNET, drives acquisition of a hypermutator phenotype through direct mutagenesis. In a paired pre/post-TMZ cohort (23 patients), a hypermutator phenotype (TMB >30 mut/Mb) was detected in 26% of patients, predominantly those with G3 disease; this was validated in an independent 1,079-PanNET cohort, where 2.3% were TMB-high and 67% of those carried an alkylating agent-associated mutational signature. A multicenter NGS study found TMB-high tumours had significantly higher rates of DNA damage repair (DDR) alterations (60% vs. 18%; p=0.05) and mismatch repair (MMR) gene mutations (60% vs. 0%; p=0.0004), with longer TMZ exposure and prior radioligand therapy associated with higher TMB-high frequency; an updated analysis showed post-TMZ DDR alterations rising from 15% to 36%, TMB-high (>15 mut/Mb) in 36% of post-treatment samples, and 3 of 6 matched patients acquiring hypermutation after treatment. In a separate multinational cohort of 53 alkylating-pretreated patients, 55% (29/53) of NGS-evaluable patients were TMB-high (>10 mut/Mb) post-alkylating therapy, and 14 of 35 patients assessed for MMR status showed MMR alterations. Overall, TMZ-based therapy induces a hypermutated molecular phenotype in approximately one-third of PanNET patients, with TMB-high status frequently co-occurring with DDR/MMR gene alterations; treatment sequences combining alkylating agents with radioligand therapy may further increase TMB-high incidence.

Functional analysis of 106 PTEN mutations associated with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), somatic cancer or PTEN hamartoma syndrome was performed using 18 assays in 5 model systems to measure PTEN activity and stability. The ASD associated variant PTEN Y68H, which resides in the phosphatase domain, showed loss-of-function characteristics relative to wild-type PTEN in multiple functional assays including: decreased PTEN function and abundance in yeast, and decreased protein stability and activation in HEK293 cells.
