Functional analysis of 106 PTEN mutations associated with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), somatic cancer or PTEN hamartoma syndrome was performed using 18 assays in 5 model systems to measure PTEN activity and stability. The ASD associated variant PTEN Y68N, which resides in the phosphatase domain, showed loss-of-function characteristics relative to wild-type PTEN in multiple functional assays including: decreased PTEN function and abundance in yeast, and decreased protein stability and activation in HEK293 cells.

Functional analysis of 106 PTEN mutations associated with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), somatic cancer or PTEN hamartoma syndrome was performed using 18 assays in 5 model systems to measure PTEN activity and stability. The ASD associated variant PTEN D107V, which resides in the phosphatase domain, showed loss-of-function characteristics relative to wild-type PTEN in multiple functional assays including: decreased PTEN function and abundance in yeast, and decreased protein stability and activation in HEK293 cells.

Functional analysis of 106 PTEN mutations associated with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), somatic cancer or PTEN hamartoma syndrome was performed using 18 assays in 5 model systems to measure PTEN activity and stability. The ASD associated variant PTEN D107G, which resides in the phosphatase domain, showed loss-of-function or partial loss-of-function characteristics relative to wild-type PTEN in multiple functional assays including: decreased PTEN function and abundance in yeast, and decreased protein stability and activation in HEK293 cells.

Functional analysis of 106 PTEN mutations associated with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), somatic cancer or PTEN hamartoma syndrome was performed using 18 assays in 5 model systems to measure PTEN activity and stability. The ASD associated variant PTEN F241S, which resides in the phosphatase domain, showed loss-of-function characteristics relative to wild-type PTEN in multiple functional assays including: decreased PTEN function and abundance in yeast, and decreased protein stability and activation in HEK293 cells.

Functional analysis of 106 PTEN mutations associated with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), somatic cancer or PTEN hamartoma syndrome was performed using 18 assays in 5 model systems to measure PTEN activity and stability. The ASD associated variant PTEN R130L, which resides in the phosphatase domain, showed loss-of-function characteristics relative to wild-type PTEN in multiple functional assays including: decreased PTEN function in yeast and decreased activation in HEK293 cells. While PTEN R130L stability and abundance levels were similar to wild-type levels, results from several other assays led to a loss-of-function classification.

The paper includes 1660 newly diagnosed de novo AML cases on frontline CALGB and a total of 37 point mutations and deletions were identified in the juxtamembrane domain of the FLT3 gene. Three patients had mutations at codon Y572 and changed the amino acid to C or S. The patient specific mutations are not documented, so it is unclear how many patients had each amino acid substitution.

The paper sequenced FLT3 in 222 adult patients with AML and no known FLT3 ITD, KIT, and NRAS mutations. Nine nonsynonmyous changes were identified including one patient with the Y572C amino acid substitution.

In the multicenter, open-label phase Ib/II trial NCT01543698, 55 patients with BRAF V600-mutant metastatic melanoma who had not previously received a BRAF inhibitor were treated with encorafenib plus binimetinib across the phase Ib and phase II portions of the study. BRAF V600E was present in 49/55 patients (89%), BRAF V600K in 5/55 (9%), and another BRAF subtype in 1/55 (2%). A confirmed objective response was observed in 40/55 patients (73%; 95% CI, 59–84), including 6 complete responses and 34 partial responses. The disease control rate was 96% (53/55; 95% CI, 88–100), and median progression-free survival was 11.0 months (95% CI, 6.8–14.6). These findings support sensitivity of BRAF V600-mutant melanoma, predominantly BRAF V600E, to encorafenib plus binimetinib.

In a multicenter, open-label phase Ib dose-escalation and cohort-expansion study (NCT01656642), 39 checkpoint inhibitor-naive patients with previously untreated, unresectable stage IIIC or metastatic BRAF V600-mutated melanoma received a 28-day run-in with cobimetinib plus vemurafenib followed by combination therapy with atezolizumab, cobimetinib, and vemurafenib. The confirmed investigator-assessed objective response rate was 71.8% (95% CI, 55.1–85.0), including complete responses in 20.5% of patients. At a median follow-up of 29.9 months, the estimated median duration of response was 17.4 months (95% CI, 10.6–25.3), with ongoing responses in 39.3% of responders, and the estimated median progression-free survival was 12.9 months (95% CI, 8.7–21.4). Grade 3–4 treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 66.7% of patients, and adverse events led to discontinuation of at least one study drug in 28.2%. These findings support sensitivity of BRAF V600-mutated metastatic melanoma to combination therapy with atezolizumab, cobimetinib, and vemurafenib, although interpretation is limited by the small sample size and single-arm phase Ib study design.

In the multicenter, open-label, single-arm phase II TRICOTEL study (NCT03625141), 65 patients with previously untreated BRAF V600 mutation-positive metastatic melanoma and CNS metastases received vemurafenib plus cobimetinib during cycle 1, followed by atezolizumab, vemurafenib, and cobimetinib from cycle 2 onward; 54 patients (83%) harbored BRAF V600E. At a median follow-up of 9.7 months, the independently assessed intracranial objective response rate was 42% (95% CI, 29–54), including complete responses in 6% of patients. Median intracranial duration of response was 7.4 months (95% CI, 5.7–11.0), and median intracranial progression-free survival was 5.3 months (95% CI, 3.8–7.2). Investigator-assessed extracranial and overall objective response rates were 57% and 52%, respectively. Treatment-related grade 3 or worse adverse events occurred in 68% of the 60 patients who received the triplet combination, and no treatment-related deaths occurred. These findings support sensitivity of BRAF V600-mutated melanoma with CNS metastases to atezolizumab, vemurafenib, and cobimetinib; however, interpretation is limited by the single-arm phase II study design.

In an exploratory biomarker analysis of the randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase III IMspire150 trial (NCT02908672), 379 patients with centrally confirmed BRAF V600E-mutated, previously untreated unresectable stage IIIC or stage IV melanoma received atezolizumab plus vemurafenib and cobimetinib (n=197) or placebo plus vemurafenib and cobimetinib (n=182). At a median follow-up of 18.9 months, median progression-free survival was 16.2 months with the atezolizumab-containing triplet compared with 10.0 months in the control group, and median duration of response was 20.4 versus 12.6 months, respectively. These outcomes were consistent with those observed in the overall BRAF V600-mutated intention-to-treat population and support sensitivity of BRAF V600E-mutated advanced melanoma to combination therapy with atezolizumab, vemurafenib, and cobimetinib. Exploratory analyses further suggested that treatment benefit was influenced by baseline immune and tumor biomarkers, with greater progression-free survival or duration-of-response benefit observed in subgroups with high tumor mutational burden, strong interferon-γ gene signature, or high CD8-positive tumor infiltration.

In the second interim analysis of the randomized phase III IMspire150 trial (NCT02908672), 514 patients with previously untreated unresectable stage IIIc or stage IV BRAF V600 mutation-positive melanoma were randomized to receive atezolizumab plus cobimetinib and vemurafenib (n=256) or placebo plus cobimetinib and vemurafenib (n=258). After a median follow-up of 29.1 months in the atezolizumab group and 22.8 months in the control group, median overall survival was 39.0 months (95% CI, 29.9–not estimable) with atezolizumab plus cobimetinib and vemurafenib versus 25.8 months (95% CI, 22.0–34.6) with placebo plus cobimetinib and vemurafenib (HR 0.84, 95% CI 0.66–1.06; p=0.14). Although median overall survival was numerically longer, the difference was not statistically significant. Progression-free survival and duration-of-response benefits reported in the primary analysis were maintained with longer follow-up, and no new safety signals were identified.

A 68-year-old woman presented with a painful left facial mass that was excised and pathologically diagnosed as malignant melanoma. Following surgery, she received adjuvant radiotherapy combined with temozolomide and initially experienced a favorable clinical course; however, she developed recurrent disease approximately four years later with a left parotid gland mass and regional lymph node involvement. DNA-based hybrid-capture next-generation sequencing of formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded recurrent tumor tissue identified a novel DPP10 (intergenic)::NTRK3 fusion. The report describes the breakpoint as occurring downstream of DPP10 and involving NTRK3 exon 14, although the exact fusion breakpoint is not clearly defined because the figure and text are not fully consistent. The fusion retained the NTRK3 kinase domain. Rearrangement of the NTRK3 locus was confirmed by break-apart fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH). RNA-based validation was not performed because of insufficient specimen, TRK protein expression was not evaluated by immunohistochemistry, and the patient was not treated with a TRK inhibitor.

A retrospective study of tumors sequenced through the Veterans Health Administration National Precision Oncology Program identified NTRK rearrangements in 25 of 22,450 solid tumors. Twelve patients with NTRK fusions or rearrangements received TRK inhibitor therapy, and none achieved an objective response. A LRRC71::NTRK1 fusion was identified in one patient with lung squamous cell carcinoma who experienced progressive disease during TRK inhibitor treatment. The publication did not report the fusion breakpoint, exon structure, reading frame, retention of the NTRK1 kinase domain, RNA or protein expression, or functional characterization of this fusion.

This case study reports a 78 year old patient with pancreatic adenocarcinoma harboring a GP2::NTRK1 gene fusion characterized by an in-frame rearrangement involving exon 2 of GP2 and exon 8 of NTRK1. The fusion is predicted to be in-frame and retain the kinase domain of NTRK1. The patient was treated with both entrectinib and larotrectinib (sequentially - see Figure 5 for detailed timeline). Partial response or stable disease were observed for both therapies. Liver metastases were stable for 18 months after initiation of larotrectinib therapy and the patient remained alive for 34 months since initiation of TRK inhibitor therapy.

In a pan-institutional cohort of 10,294 gliomas, the authors identified hypermutated tumors and evaluated 25 patients treated with PD-1 inhibitors. Hypermutated gliomas, including temozolomide-associated hypermutated lower-grade gliomas, did not demonstrate consistent clinical benefit from PD-1 inhibitor therapy despite high tumor mutational burden and predicted neoantigen load. These findings suggest that the association between high TMB and response to PD-1 blockade observed in other cancers may not extend to glioma.

This GWAS study identified a structural variant of FGFR1. Duplication of the tyrosine kinase domain (TKD) of FGFR1 was found in 11 of 149 patients (13/151 tumor samples, including 2 recurrent tumors, aged 1-17) with pediatric low-grade gliomas (PLGGs) and related low-grade glioneuronal tumors (LGGNTs). This alteration resulted in autophosphorylation of FGFR1 and subsequent activation of downstream PI3K and MAPK/ERK pathways as measured by AKT and ERK1/2 phosphorylation levels in 293T cells and in mouse xenograft tumours. Also, transfection of Tp53-null astrocytes with TDK duplicated FGFR1 and implantation into the brains of nude mice results in high-grade astrocytic tumours with short latency and complete penetrance.

In this study, immunofluorescence analysis of treatment-naive melanoma biopsies from 6 patients with BRAF-mutant tumors and 7 patients with BRAF wild-type tumors demonstrated significantly more cortactin foci in BRAF-mutant tumors. Paired biopsies from 3 BRAF V600E-positive melanoma patients obtained before and after 2 weeks of vemurafenib treatment showed significantly reduced cortactin foci following therapy. Complementary functional analyses in melanoma cell lines and a genetically engineered BRAF V600E-driven mouse melanoma model demonstrated that BRAF V600E promotes melanoma cell migration, extracellular matrix degradation, invadopodia formation, MMP2 secretion, and ERK-dependent phosphorylation of cortactin and Exo70, supporting a role for BRAF V600E in melanoma invasion.

In this study, BRAF V600E, reported as V599E, was identified as a recurrent somatic variant in melanoma. When transiently expressed in COS cells, BRAF V600E demonstrated approximately 10.7-fold greater basal kinase activity than wild-type BRAF and increased ERK phosphorylation. In NIH3T3 cells, BRAF V600E transformed cells approximately 138-fold more efficiently than wild-type BRAF, whereas introduction of a kinase-inactivating substitution abolished transforming activity. These findings support BRAF V600E as an activating oncogenic variant in melanoma.

In this study, conditional melanocyte-specific expression of BRAF V600E in mice induced benign melanocytic hyperplasia that did not progress to melanoma during 15–20 months of follow-up. In contrast, combined BRAF V600E expression and Pten silencing induced melanoma with 100% penetrance, short latency, and metastases to regional lymph nodes and lungs.

In this study, myc-tagged BRAF V600E (reported as V599E) transiently expressed in COS cells exhibited approximately 478-fold greater basal kinase activity than wild-type BRAF, constitutively activated ERK signaling, and transformed NIH3T3 cells (254 +/- 43 foci/ng DNA), whereas wild-type BRAF lacked transforming activity. Crystal structures of wild-type and V599E BRAF kinase domains identified disruption of the inactive kinase conformation associated with the V599E substitution.

In this study, sustained expression of BRAF V600E in primary human melanocytes initially increased proliferation but subsequently induced stable cell-cycle arrest accompanied by senescence-associated β-galactosidase activity and increased p16INK4a expression. Human congenital nevi harboring BRAF V600E similarly demonstrated senescence-associated markers, supporting oncogene-induced senescence as a physiological response that limits BRAF V600E-driven melanocyte transformation.

Hartmaier et al. performed targeted hybrid-capture next-generation sequencing of 18,004 adult solid tumors and identified a novel LRRC71::NTRK1 fusion in one uterine corpus endometrial carcinoma. The fusion joined LRRC71 exon 1 to NTRK1 exons 8–17. Available evidence supporting the oncogenicity of the fusion was limited and consisted primarily of the 3′ location of NTRK1 as the fusion partner (F1) and the retention of the exons encoding the tyrosine kinase domain (F2). The study reported the detection of the fusion but did not provide functional characterization, recurrence data, or therapeutic response data for this case.

Xu et al. retrospectively analyzed paired pre- and post-EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor samples from 3,873 patients with EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma and identified an acquired LRRC71::NTRK1 fusion in one patient after gefitinib treatment. The fusion was absent in the pretreatment sample and co-occurred with EGFR and MET amplifications in the post-treatment sample. Available evidence supporting the oncogenicity of the fusion was limited and consisted primarily of the 3′ location of NTRK1 as the fusion partner (F1) and the retention of the exons encoding the tyrosine kinase domain (F2). No functional validation or evidence of response to TRK inhibitor therapy for this fusion was reported.

Dufresne et al. identified a CCDC171::NTRK1 fusion by whole-exome RNA sequencing in one undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma from an ambispective cohort of NTRK-rearranged mesenchymal tumors. The fusion consisted of CCDC171 as the 5′ partner and NTRK1 as the 3′ partner. However, the exact exon-level breakpoint, reading frame, and fusion-specific functional validation were not reported. The authors concluded that the biological relevance of NTRK fusions in complex-genomic sarcomas remains uncertain.

A KHDRBS1::NTRK1 fusion was identified in a 33-year-old man with an unclassified mesenchymal sarcoma by next-generation sequencing, demonstrating fusion of KHDRBS1 exons 1–8 to NTRK1 exons 12–17. Fluorescence in situ hybridization confirmed the NTRK1 rearrangement. The patient was treated with crizotinib, resulting in regression of metastatic lesions after 1 month, complete disappearance of the remaining lesions after 3 months, and an ongoing complete response without disease progression during approximately 45 months of follow-up. These findings support the oncogenic relevance of the KHDRBS1::NTRK1 fusion in this tumor.

This retrospective study evaluated the predictive value of tumor mutational burden (TMB) for immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) outcomes in 97 patients with stage IV non-small cell lung cancer who had multiple TMB assessments before ICI initiation. Using the oldest pre-treatment TMB assessment and a cutoff of 10 mutations/Mb, no significant differences were observed between patients with TMB ≥10 mutations/Mb (n=43) and those with TMB <10 mutations/Mb (n=54) in objective response rate (ORR) (28% vs. 17%, p=0.18), median progression-free survival (PFS) (4.5 vs. 2.8 months, p=0.06), or median overall survival (OS) (15.6 vs. 16.0 months, p=0.24). When the most recent TMB assessment before ICI initiation was used, patients with TMB ≥10 mutations/Mb (n=43), compared with those with TMB <10 mutations/Mb (n=54), had no significant difference in ORR (30% vs. 15%, p=0.07), but had significantly longer median PFS (5.3 vs. 2.5 months, p=0.003) and median OS (34.8 vs. 15.6 months, p=0.02). Despite unchanged overall group sizes, 20 patients switched TMB categories between the two assessments: 10 patients from <10 to ≥10 mutations/Mb and 10 patients from ≥10 to <10 mutations/Mb. The authors suggested that a TMB assessment obtained closer to ICI initiation may be more reliable for predicting ICI outcomes.

In patients with initially low-grade IDH-mutant gliomas previously treated with temozolomide, a high tumor mutational burden (TMB-high)/temozolomide-associated hypermutator phenotype was associated with high-grade transformation, increased risk of discontiguous or distant recurrence, and reduced survival after transformation. Among patients with anaplastic/grade III transformation, TMB-high/hypermutated tumors were associated with shorter survival after transformation (HR 3.4, 95% CI 1.2–9.9, P = .024) after adjustment for grade, molecular subtype, age, and prior radiotherapy. Hypermutated tumors were also more likely to develop discontiguous disease in the brain and spine (P = .003). These findings should not be used to guide upfront treatment decisions for newly diagnosed IDH-mutant low-grade gliomas, since only patients who underwent surgical resection of recurrent tumors were included. However, these findings suggest that TMB-high/hypermutation status may have prognostic relevance after high-grade transformation and should be considered in future clinical trials of recurrent glioma.

A male patient older than 10 years with B-ALL harbored a ZC3HAV1(exon 12)::ABL2(exon 3) fusion and a concomitant IKZF1 deletion, presenting with a white blood cell count >50 × 10⁹/L. He was enrolled on the DFCI ALL Consortium Protocol 05-001, which included NCI high-risk, Ph-negative B-ALL patients between 2005 and 2011. The fusion was identified by multiplex RT-PCR, and IKZF1 deletion was detected by MLPA. After induction therapy, his minimal residual disease (MRD) level was >10⁻³. He belonged to a fusion-positive subgroup lacking favorable cytogenetic abnormalities such as hyperdiploidy and ETV6::RUNX1. The patient experienced an event and therefore did not remain event-free. IKZF1 deletion was an independent predictor of poor outcome, and patients with both a kinase-activating fusion and IKZF1 deletion had 5-year overall survival and event-free survival rates of 62% and 44%, respectively.

An adult patient (>18 years old) with B-ALL harbored an in-frame ZC3HAV1::ABL2 fusion, identified by targeted RNA sequencing, with no IKZF1 deletion, and presented with a white blood cell count of 72 × 10⁹/L. The patient was treated according to the NOPHO ALL-2008 MRD-directed protocol and received prednisolone during induction therapy. MRD assessment demonstrated a poor early response, with 30.5% blasts on day 15, 6.5% on day 29, and 0.01% on day 79, resulting in classification as intermediate risk (IR). The patient subsequently underwent allogeneic stem cell transplantation (alloSCT) in first complete remission (CR1). Despite achieving MRD negativity prior to transplantation, the patient experienced an event and died from sepsis following alloSCT.

CRISPR-mediated correction of endogenous BRAF p.V600E to wild type in patient-derived colorectal cancer organoids abolished constitutive MEK/ERK signaling, restored epidermal growth factor dependence, suppressed WNT target gene expression, promoted epithelial differentiation, and eliminated tumorigenicity in xenograft models. CRISPR-mediated knock-in of BRAF p.V600E into normal human colon organoids induced constitutive MEK/ERK signaling, increased WNT target gene expression, and altered DNA methylation patterns.

Intestinal induction of the murine BrafV637E allele (human equivalent BRAF p.V600E) resulted in persistent intestinal hyperplasia, followed by development of murine serrated precursor lesions, serrated adenomas, and invasive carcinoma over time. DNA methylation profiling demonstrated progressive, gene-specific increases in DNA methylation in Braf mutant intestinal tissue compared with age-matched controls.

Exosomes derived from BRAF p.V600E colorectal cancer cells promoted endothelial cell proliferation, migration, and tube formation, increased angiogenic factor expression, enhanced M2 macrophage polarization, and altered exosomal lncRNA and mRNA profiles compared with exosomes from BRAF-silenced cells, supporting a gain-of-function effect on remodeling of the colorectal cancer tumor microenvironment.

BRAF p.Val600Glu (V600E) increased glutamate-cysteine ligase (GCLC) expression and intracellular glutathione levels in colorectal cancer patient-derived organoids. CRISPR-mediated GCLC deletion reduced liver and lung metastasis formation and increased sensitivity to oxidative stress, while pharmacologic BRAF inhibition decreased GCLC expression and enhanced oxidative stress sensitivity in BRAF p.Val600Glu (V600E) organoids.

In Villin-Cre;BRAF p.V600E mice, dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced colitis cooperated with BRAF p.V600E to induce cecal tumor formation, with cecal adenomas developing in 83% of mice 3 months after treatment and progressing to carcinomas with longer follow-up. Neither DSS treatment alone nor BRAF p.V600E expression alone induced cecal tumors in this model.

Expression of BRAF p.V600E in HCT116 colorectal cancer cells increased cell proliferation, colony formation, migration, and invasion compared with wild-type BRAF or vector controls and was associated with decreased E-cadherin and increased vimentin and Snail expression, consistent with induction of epithelial-mesenchymal transition. In mouse xenograft models, BRAF p.V600E-expressing cells formed larger tumors and exhibited reduced sensitivity to 5-fluorouracil treatment compared with control tumors.

In murine colonic organoids, BRAF p.V600E induced transient proliferation, disrupted epithelial organization, and activated a fetal-like dedifferentiation transcriptional program. Co-expression of TP53 p.R172H promoted anchorage-independent growth and invasive properties, while Apc deletion prevented BRAF p.V600E-induced organoid disintegration and conferred long-term growth and niche-factor independence, demonstrating cooperative effects of these alterations during colorectal transformation.

In an inducible mouse model, intestinal expression of BRAF p.V600E induced persistent crypt hyperplasia, altered epithelial differentiation, and transcriptional programs associated with proliferation, dedifferentiation, and poor-prognosis BRAF-mutant colorectal cancer. BRAF p.V600E also increased expression of cholesterol biosynthesis genes, and treatment with atorvastatin prevented the establishment of crypt hyperplasia, while human serrated colorectal lesions exhibited enrichment of the same cholesterol biosynthesis signature.

Two adult patients with diffuse midline glioma (DMG) harboring a somatic H3F3B K27I mutation were reported. Next-generation sequencing on postoperative tissue was performed using a 539-gene panel (Simceredx). One patient, 36 F, had a pons tumor in the brainstem. (WHO Grade II) Astrocytoma was seen in postoperative pathology. H3F3B exon2 p.K27I was found at allele frequency (AF) 57.64%, and TP53 exon7 p.M237I at AF 80.27%. The second patient, 44 M, had spinal cord glioma, WHO grade III, and had H3F3B p.K27I (AF 30.46%), ATRX p.S1173* (AF 75.23%), KRAS p.G12A(AF 38.11%), and NF1 intron42 c.6580-1G > A(AF 36.44%). The authors conclude that the type of histone H3 mutated could have potential predictive value for outcome and diagnosis, and also glioma grading of DMG patients.

Mariet et al. identified a somatic H3C4 (HIST1H3D) p.Lys28Met (K27M) mutation in a pediatric posterior fossa group A ependymoma (EPN_PFA). The tumor demonstrated diffuse H3K27M immunoreactivity, loss of H3K27me3, and clustered within the EPN_PFA-1f DNA methylation subclass (calibrated score 0.99). The authors noted that H3 K27M mutations inhibit PRC2 activity and reduce H3K27 trimethylation, although no variant-specific functional experiments were performed in this study.

In a multicenter phase I dose-escalation and expansion study, 125 patients with relapsed or refractory IDH1-mutated acute myeloid leukemia (AML) received ivosidenib 500 mg once daily. The complete remission plus complete remission with partial hematologic recovery (CR+CRh) rate was 30.4%, the complete remission rate was 21.6%, and the overall response rate was 41.6%. Median durations of CR+CRh, complete remission, and overall response were 8.2, 9.3, and 6.5 months, respectively. Among patients achieving CR/CRh, 21% had clearance of detectable IDH1 mutations by digital PCR. These findings support the sensitivity of IDH1-mutated AML, including tumors harboring IDH1 R132H, to ivosidenib, although outcomes were not reported separately for individual IDH1 mutation subtypes.

In a subgroup analysis of a multicenter phase I study, 17 patients with relapsed or refractory IDH1 R132-mutated acute myeloid leukemia who responded to ivosidenib 500 mg once daily subsequently underwent allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. Before transplantation, the CR+CRh rate was 71% (12/17), the overall response rate was 100% (17/17), and 11 patients (65%) achieved a complete remission. Median overall survival from initiation of ivosidenib was 14.5 months (95% CI, 9.1 months to not estimable), and median overall survival after transplantation was 7.7 months (95% CI, 4.5 months to not estimable).

In a multicenter phase I study, 33 patients with newly diagnosed IDH1 R132-mutated acute myeloid leukemia who were ineligible for standard therapy received ivosidenib 500 mg once daily. The CR+CRh rate was 42.4% (14/33), the complete remission rate was 30.3% (10/33), and the overall response rate was 54.5% (18/33). With a median follow-up of 23.5 months, the median overall survival was 12.6 months, and IDH1 mutation clearance in bone marrow mononuclear cells was observed in 9 of 14 patients (64.3%) who achieved CR or CRh, whereas no mutation clearance was observed among patients with other responses (P < 0.001).

In a preplanned interim analysis of the pivotal phase 2 cohort of an open-label, multicenter phase 1/2 trial, 153 patients with relapsed or refractory IDH1 R132-mutated acute myeloid leukemia received olutasidenib monotherapy at 150 mg twice daily in continuous 28-day cycles. Among 147 efficacy-evaluable patients, 51 (35%; 95% CI, 27.0%–43.0%) achieved complete remission or complete remission with partial hematologic recovery, including 47 (32%; 95% CI, 24.5%–40.2%) who achieved complete remission. The overall response rate was 48% (71/147; 95% CI, 40.0%–56.7%), the median duration of CR/CRh was 25.9 months (95% CI, 13.5 months–not evaluable), the median duration of overall response was 11.7 months (95% CI, 6.9–25.9 months), and the median overall survival was 11.6 months (95% CI, 8.9–15.5 months). Of 86 patients who were red blood cell and/or platelet transfusion-dependent at baseline, 29 (34%) achieved transfusion independence for at least 56 days. IDH1 mutation subtypes included R132C in 90 patients, R132H in 34, R132G in 10, R132S in 10, and R132L in three.

In a final five-year analysis of a multicenter phase 2 trial, 35 patients with relapsed/refractory IDH1 R132H-mutated acute myeloid leukemia (AML) received olutasidenib monotherapy. The overall response rate was 26% (9/35), including a CR/CRh rate of 17% (6/35), with a median CR/CRh duration of 13.5 months. These results support the sensitivity of IDH1 R132H-mutated AML to olutasidenib, although response rates were lower than those observed for other IDH1 R132 substitutions and may have been influenced by concurrent NPM1, FLT3, or TP53 mutations.

In a multicenter, open-label phase 1 study, 22 response-evaluable patients with relapsed or refractory IDH1-mutated acute myeloid leukemia received olutasidenib monotherapy. Nine patients achieved an overall response, corresponding to an overall response rate of 41% (95% CI, 21%–64%). Responses included complete remission in 4 patients, complete remission with partial hematologic recovery in 3, and complete remission with incomplete blood-count recovery in 2. Olutasidenib 150 mg twice daily was selected as the recommended phase 2 dose based on safety, pharmacokinetic, pharmacodynamic, and clinical activity findings.

In this phase II basket trial (TAPUR), response to olaparib treatment was examined in four cohorts with ATM mutations. In the histology pooled cohort (36 evaluable patients) comprised of 19 different solid tumour types there were two PRs and seven patients with prolonged stable disease (SD16+). The DC rate was 25% (90% CI, 16 to 100) and the OR rate was 6% (95% CI, <1 to 19), which exceeded the prespecified DC rate of 15% to indicate clinical activity in this cohort. While five patients had co-mutation in BRCA1/2, none of these patients had DC. The authors note that the small sample size and heterogeneity of tumour types in the HP cohort make it difficult to draw conclusions about individual tumour types, while the DC rate was close to the prespecified lower limit, suggesting that ATM alterations alone may be insufficient as a predictor of benefit from olaparib.

In this phase II basket trial (TAPUR), response to olaparib treatment was examined in four cohorts with ATM mutations. In the colorectal cancer cohort (27 evaluable patients) there was one PR and three patients with prolonged stable disease (SD16+). The DC rate was 23% (90% CI, 8 to 100) and the OR rate was 4% (95% CI, <1 to 19), which did not exceed the prespecified DC rate of 15% to indicate clinical activity in this cohort. Six patients had co-mutation in BRCA1/2, but none of these patients had DC.

In this phase II basket trial (TAPUR), response to olaparib treatment was examined in four cohorts with ATM mutations. In the pancreatic cancer cohort (25 evaluable patients) there was one PR and five patients with prolonged stable disease (SD16+). The DC rate was 28% (90% CI, 14 to 100) and the OR rate was 4% (95% CI, <1 to 20), which did not exceed the prespecified DC rate of 15% (P = 0.14) to indicate clinical activity in this cohort. Nine patients had co-mutation in BRCA1/2, including the patient with PR (BRCA1-altered) and two of the patients with SD16+ (BRCA1/2 alterations).

In this phase II basket trial (TAPUR), response to olaparib treatment was examined in four cohorts with ATM mutations. In the lung cancer cohort (20 evaluable patients) there were four PRs and five patients with prolonged stable disease (SD16+). The DC rate was 45% (90% CI, 32 to 100) and the OR rate was 20% (95% CI, 6 to 44), which exceeded the prespecified DC rate of 15% to indicate clinical activity in this cohort. Two patients had co-mutation in BRCA2, and one of these patients had DC.

Targeted NGS of 17 genes was utilized to assess alterations in pre-treatment tumour biopsy samples of HER2+ breast cancers from the prospective GeparSepto (G7) trial of combination trastuzumab plus pertuzumab therapy in addition to a taxane/anthracycline regimen. In the G7 cohort 65/293 tumours (22.2%) had a PIK3CA mutation, while 56.9% (37/65) of the tumours with a PIK3CA mutation also had a TP53 mutation. The pathologic complete response (pCR) rate was significantly lower in the PIK3CA mutant tumours (47.7%; 95%CI 35.1%-60.5%, 31/65) compared to the wild-type group (66.7%; 95%CI 60.1–72.8%, 152/228) in the G7 cohort that was treated with anti-HER2 therapies (univariate Odds Ratio 0.46, p = 0.009; multivariate analysis Odds Ratio 0.41, p = 0.003), but not in the G3 cohort that received chemotherapy without anti-HER2 therapy (univariate Odds Ratio 1.92, p = 0.339; multivariate Odds Ratio 0.92, p = 0.935).

Targeted NGS of 17 genes was utilized to assess alterations in pre-treatment tumour biopsy samples of HER2+ breast cancers from the prospective GeparSepto (G7) trial of anti-HER2 therapy (trastuzumab/pertuzumab) in addition to a taxane/anthracycline regimen that included randomization to nab-paclitaxel or solvent-based paclitaxel. In the G7 cohort 65/293 tumours (22.2%) had a PIK3CA mutation, while 56.9% (37/65) of the tumours with a PIK3CA mutation also had a TP53 mutation. In the nab-paclitaxel group the pathologic complete response (pCR) rate was significantly lower in the PIK3CA mutant tumours (38.7%; 95%CI 21.8%-57.8%) compared to the wild-type group (72.0%; 95%CI 63.0%-79.9%; p = 0.001), whereas in the paclitaxel group there was no significant difference between PIK3CA mutated vs wild-type (p = 0.690).

disease: Myeloid And Lymphoid Neoplasms With Eosinophilia And Abnormalities Of PDGFRA, PDGFRB, And FGFR1
evidence_statement: Ba/F3 cells expressing two clinically relevant, imatinib-resistant, mutant forms of FIP1L1-PDGFRA, namely T674I and D842V were tested for growth inhibition by 8 PDGFR-blocking TKIs. Cells expressing D842V were resistant to sunitinib (IC50 >1000nM), nilotinib (IC50 4093nM), sorafenib (IC50 >1000nM), imatinib (IC50 >1000nM), dasatinib (IC50 1000nM) and masitinib (IC50 >1000nM).

In a Phase 3 trial (NCT03390504), patients with metastatic or surgically unresectable urothelial carcinoma, who had FGFR2 or FGFR3 alterations erdafitinib was tested against chemotherapy (docetaxel or vinflunine) in a 1:1 ratio. Patients had previous systemic therapy with anti–PD-1 or anti–PD-L1 agent and had received no more than two previous lines of therapy. Patient tumors were positive for FGFR3 R248C, S249C, G370C, or Y373C, or FGFR2–BICC1, FGFR2–CASP7, FGFR3–TACC3_V1, FGFR3–TACC3_V3, or FGFR3–BAIAP2L1. Of 266 patients, 136 were given erdafitinib (17 with R248C mutation and 2 with R248C co-mutation) and 130 chemotherapy (8 with R248C mutation and 2 with R248C co-mutation). Overall Survival was longer with erdafitinib (12.1 months vs. 7.8 months; HR for death 0.64; 95% CI 0.47 to 0.88; P = 0.005). Median progression-free survival was longer in erdafitinib group than in chemotherapy (5.6 months vs. 2.7 months; HR for progression or death 0.58; 95% CI 0.44 to 0.78; P<0.001). Grade 3 or 4 adverse event incidence was similar in the two groups (approximately 46%).

High-throughput screening. Used Ba/F4 cells - murine pro-B cell line, which is dependent on IL-3 for survival. ED50WT/ED50 variant ratio to measure the relative sensitivity of Ba/F3 cells expressing FGFR3 variants to IL-3 withdrawal relative to wild-type FGFR3 (see Figure 2). A ratio <1 would indicate the variant is less active than wild-type (loss-of-function/inactivating). Results showed P449S as inactivating (no oncogenic effect). That is, cells expressing the variant are more IL-3-dependent than wild-type.

FGFR3 variant, A500T was assessed among a panel of 26 FGFR3 kinase domain variants using purified protein in vitro auto-phosphorylation assays (Figure 2A). Compared to wild type, A500T showed only a small increase in auto-phosphorylation, falling well below the authors' threshold for presumed functional impact, consistent with the majority of tested variants that showed little to no effect on kinase activity. Variants that did lead to increased auto-phosphorylation in this assay included: I538V, N540K, N540S, K650E, K650N, R669G, R669Q.

In a phase 2 subgroup analysis of patients with IDH1 R132-mutated acute myeloid leukemia (AML) previously treated with venetoclax-based therapy, 16 patients received olutasidenib monotherapy at 150 mg twice daily. Eight of 16 patients (50%) achieved a composite complete remission (CRc). Olutasidenib demonstrated clinical activity in this previously treated IDH1 R132-mutated AML population.

In a saturation mutagenesis study, all possible point mutations in the FGFR 1-4 kinase domain (amino acids 472-807 for FGFR3) were tested. Lentiviral plasmids were infected at MOI < 0.3 into the growth factor-dependent cell line MCF10A, so that that majority of cells contained no more than one distinct stably transduced FGFR point mutation after selection was performed. Cells were then cultured in medium lacking growth factors and with serum reduced to 2% for 17-20 days, and then assayed with next generation sequencing to determine which FGFR constructs were present and enriched. All replicates of synonymous mutations were used as control, and activation was calculated as enriched FGFR construct frequency divided by control, then log transformed, and then classified as follows: potentially activating (1.5- to 2.5-fold), weakly activating (>2.5- to 5-fold), activating (>5- to 10-fold), strongly activating (>10-fold). 5 percent of activating mutations found were in FGFR3. A500T was classified as Neutral with median activation of 0.9745 reported for 1 distinct nucleotide change (G1498A).

Two patients with advanced lung adenocarcinoma harboring the EGFR L833V/H835L compound mutation received first-line furmonertinib (80 mg once daily), and both achieved partial responses according to RECIST 1.1. One patient had a progression-free survival of 29 months, while the other remained progression-free for >12 months at the time of reporting.

A 48-year-old man with stage IVB lung adenocarcinoma harboring an EGFR S768_D770dup exon 20 insertion and high PD-L1 expression (TPS 50%) received third-line paclitaxel plus tislelizumab after progression on prior chemotherapy and intolerance to afatinib. After six cycles of paclitaxel plus tislelizumab, tislelizumab maintenance was continued, and the patient maintained stable disease through June 26, 2026.

A patient with stage IVA lung adenocarcinoma harboring an EGFR exon 19 deletion developed acquired resistance to osimertinib without an identified molecular resistance mechanism. The patient subsequently received antigen-specific cytotoxic T-lymphocyte therapy and achieved a clinical complete response that was maintained for six years of follow-up. This single case supports sensitivity to adoptive cellular immunotherapy in EGFR exon 19 deletion-positive, EGFR-TKI-resistant lung adenocarcinoma.

A patient with stage IV lung squamous cell carcinoma harboring an EGFR G719C mutation and high PD-L1 expression (tumor proportion score of 90%) experienced disease progression after 1.5 months of afatinib treatment. The patient subsequently received sintilimab in combination with nab-paclitaxel and cisplatin. Imaging after three months demonstrated substantial tumor regression. The patient then received sintilimab maintenance therapy for one year, during which imaging showed stable disease with slight additional tumor shrinkage.

molecular_profile: EGFR L858R OR EGFR Exon 19 Deletion
evidence_statement: In the randomized, double-blind phase III KEYNOTE-789 trial, 492 patients with EGFR exon 19 deletion- or L858R-positive, TKI-resistant metastatic nonsquamous non-small-cell lung cancer received pemetrexed and platinum chemotherapy with either pembrolizumab or placebo. Median progression-free survival was 5.6 months with pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy versus 5.5 months with chemotherapy alone (HR 0.80, 95% CI 0.65–0.97; P=0.0122), which did not meet the prespecified efficacy boundary. Median overall survival was 15.9 versus 14.7 months, respectively (HR 0.84, 95% CI 0.69–1.02; P=0.0362), which also did not meet the prespecified efficacy boundary. The addition of pembrolizumab to chemotherapy therefore did not significantly improve progression-free or overall survival.

In the randomized, double-blind phase III ORIENT-31 trial, patients with EGFR-mutated, nonsquamous non-small-cell lung cancer that had progressed following EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy were assigned to receive sintilimab plus pemetrexed and cisplatin (n=158) or pemetrexed and cisplatin alone (n=160). Sintilimab plus chemotherapy significantly improved median progression-free survival compared with chemotherapy alone (5.5 versus 4.3 months; HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.55–0.94; P=0.016). The confirmed objective response rates were 35% and 29%, respectively. Median overall survival was 20.5 months with sintilimab plus chemotherapy versus 19.2 months with chemotherapy alone (HR 0.97, 95% CI 0.71–1.32). These results support improved progression-free survival with the addition of sintilimab to chemotherapy in this patient population.

This study highlights the potential efficacy of allogeneic stem-cell transplantation (allo-SCT) in ETV6::FLT3-positive myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with eosinophilia. A 33-year-old man presented with lymphadenopathy, leukocytosis, eosinophilia, T-lymphoblasts in lymph nodes, and bone marrow myeloid hyperplasia with eosinophilia. Cytogenetic, FISH, and RT-PCR analyses confirmed t(12;13)(p13;q12) and an ETV6::FLT3 fusion in both tissues. Hyper-CVAD chemotherapy resolved lymphadenopathy, but residual molecular disease persisted in the bone marrow. The patient subsequently underwent matched unrelated-donor allo-SCT, with transient reappearance of t(12;13)(p13;q12) on day +60. Following tacrolimus tapering, the cytogenetic abnormality disappeared, and the patient remained in complete molecular remission for six years after transplantation.

disease: Atypical Chronic Myeloid Leukemia, BCR-ABL1 Negative
evidence_statement: This study describes a 32-year-old female with atypical chronic myeloid leukemia (aCML) and a complex translocation [(t(2;13;2;21)(p13;q12;q33;q11.2)] resulting in a novel in frame SPTBN1::FLT3 fusion. Functional studies showed constitutive FLT3 signaling and growth-factor-independent transformation, which was sensitive to several FLT3 inhibitors but not imatinib. The patient underwent unrelated-donor allogeneic transplantation but experienced cytogenetic relapse four years later. She achieved sustained cytogenetic and molecular remission following donor lymphocyte infusion. These findings identify SPTBN1::FLT3 as a rare but potentially targetable driver in aCML.

This study describes a 71-year-old woman with myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with eosinophilia and T-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma associated with a novel GOLGB1::FLT3 fusion from t(3;13)(q13;q12). Despite tyrosine kinase inhibitor and CHOP (Cyclophosphamide, Hydroxydaunorubicin, Oncovin and Prednisolone) chemotherapy, the disease progressed rapidly, and the patient died. In invitro functional studies, the fusion caused constitutive FLT3 activation and growth-factor-independent cell growth, with sensitivity to midostaurin, sorafenib, and ponatinib, particularly sorafenib. This case highlights the aggressive nature of FLT3-rearranged disease and the potential importance of early allogeneic transplantation.

A 62-year-old man presented with chronic eosinophilic leukemia and systemic mastocytosis. Cytogenetic analysis revealed t(13;14)(q12;q32), with genome and RNA sequencing confirming a novel TRIP11::FLT3 fusion and a KIT D816V mutation. The patient was treated with hydroxyurea with no response. The patient rapidly progressed to T-lymphoblastic leukemia/lymphoma and died of sepsis shortly after diagnosis. This case represents a novel FLT3 fusion and aggressive nature of FLT3-rearranged disease.

Whole-exome sequencing-derived tumor mutational burden (TMB) was obtained from 75 patients recruited as part of the the CheckMate-012 trial (phase 1, open label, multicenter clincal trial of nivolumab + ipilimumab) with advanced (stage IIIB/IV) non-small cell lung carcinoma (79% non-squamous, 21% squamous) TMB was defined as the total number of nonsynonymous SNVs and indels, with high TMB classified as >158 nonsynonymous mutations (median). The primary clinical outcomes evaluated were objective response rate (ORR), durable clinical benefit (DCB), and progression-free survival (PFS). Patients with high TMB had significantly higher ORR (51% vs. 13%, p=0.0005), higher DCB (65% vs 34%, p-0.0011) and longer PFS (hazard ratio 0.41, log rank p=0.0024) compared with patients with low TMB. The authors concluded that high TMB was associated with improved clinical benefit from combined nivolumab and ipilimumab therapy in advanced NSCLC and may serve as a predictive biomarker independent of PD-L1 expression.

This study reported two cases of myeloproliferative neoplasm with eosinophilia harboring a ZMYM2::FLT3 fusion, which was cytogenetically cryptic and resulted from an approximately 8-Mb inversion. Case 1, a 48-year-old woman, rapidly progressed to myeloid blast phase, was refractory to AML induction chemotherapy, and died following allogeneic transplantation. Case 2, a 47-year-old man, failed to respond to steroids or hydroxyurea but achieved sustained complete hematologic remission with sunitinib. These cases highlight the diagnostic challenges of FLT3-rearranged neoplasms, the poor prognosis associated with ZMYM2::FLT3, and the potential efficacy of FLT3-targeted therapy.

Tumor mutational burden (TMB) derived from MSK-IMPACT targeted next-generation sequencing was evaluated in 7,894 breast cancers, from which 527 TMB-high tumors from 462 patients were identified. Tumor samples were predominantly metastatic (77%), with both primary and metastatic breast cancers included. MSK-IMPACT, a hybrid-capture sequencing assay targeting 505 cancer-associated genes (~1.2 Mb), was performed on paired tumor-normal samples with at least 10% tumor content. TMB-high was defined as ≥10 mutations/Mb. Genomic characterization of TMB-high breast cancers included hotspot missense SNVs, truncating/loss-of-function mutations, small indels, and gene amplifications. The authors characterized the genomic landscape of TMB-high breast cancers and identified TMB-high tumors as a distinct subset of breast cancers based on tumor genomic profiling.

disease: Atypical Chronic Myeloid Leukemia, BCR-ABL1 Negative
evidence_statement: This study describes a novel MYO18A::FLT3 fusion in a 47-year-old male with mixed myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative features. He presented with leukocytosis, splenomegaly, and atypical chronic myeloid leukemia with megakaryocytic dysplasia and a plasma cell population in the bone marrow. Cytogenetic analysis revealed t(13;17)(q12;q12), and RNA sequencing and RT-PCR confirmed the MYO18A::FLT3 fusion. He initially responded to hydroxyurea but subsequently developed extramedullary acute myeloid leukemia and underwent allogeneic stem-cell transplantation. The patient died one year later from relapsed disease and GVHD, describing poor prognosis associated with FLT3-rearrangement disease. Ex vivo drug sensitivity screening assay on the patient cells demonstrated FLT3 inhibitor (quizartinib and sorafenib) sensitivity, but not sensitive to imatinib.

This study describes a 50-year-old woman with peripheral eosinophilia and lymphadenopathy who was diagnosed with myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with eosinophilia (MLN-eo) and T-lymphoblastic lymphoma. Both bone marrow and tonsil biopsies showed t(13;14)(q12;q32), which was restricted to the myeloid lineage by single-cell analysis. The patient was refractory to chemotherapy but achieved complete remission following allogeneic hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation, without requiring tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy.

A 64-year-old man presented with splenomegaly, peripheral eosinophilia, and bone marrow findings consistent with myeloproliferative neoplasm with eosinophilia. Cytogenetic analysis identified a balanced t(11;13)(q24;q12) translocation. Although a targeted RNA-NGS panel was negative for known rearrangements, mate-pair DNA sequencing detected FLT3 and ZBTB44 sequences, and RT-PCR confirmed a ZBTB44::FLT3 fusion, showing the diagnostic challenges in FLT3-rarranged neoplasms. The patient was treated with hydroxycarbamide, resulting in normalization of the white blood cell count.

A 37-year-old male presented with a persistent sore throat, tonsillitis and cervical lymphadenopathy. Lymph node biopsy showed a T-lymphoblastic leukemia and bone marrow showed hypercellular marrow with marked myeloid predominance and 3% blasts. Cytogenetics revealed t(5;13)(q13;q12), and RNA sequencing identified a novel SSBP2::FLT3 fusion. The patient achieved only partial response with chemotherapy (CALGB 10403), however achieved complete metabolic response with introduction to gilteritinib during consolidation. The patient subsequently underwent allogeneic stem-cell transplantation and remained in complete remission for two years post-transplant.

This study showed that when HLH domain of ETV6 (also known as TEL) fused to the cytoplasmic domain of the wild-type FLT3 receptor, the fusion caused oligomerization and activation of FLT3. The constitutively activated ETV6::FLT3 (aka TEL::ETV6) fusion promoted IL-3-independent growth and proliferation of Ba/F3 cells through activation of the JAK/STAT pathway. In mice, ETV6::FLT3-expressing cells caused rapid leukemia-like disease with extensive infiltration of the liver, spleen, and bone marrow. These findings demonstrate the oncogenic potential of activated FLT3 and its role in leukemic transformation.

In this study ETV6::FLT3 (also known as TEL-ETV6) construct mimicking this fusion protein was used to generate transgenic mice. This study showed that constitutively active ETV6::FLT3 expression in transgenic mice caused myeloproliferative disease with splenomegaly and extramedullary hematopoiesis. ETV6::FLT3 also promoted expansion of hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells, supporting its oncogenic role in myeloid neoplasms.

This study investigated the rare ZMYM2::FLT3 fusion in myeloid/lymphoid neoplasm with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene fusions. Here lentiviral vectors containing the fusion gene and negative control were constructed and transfected into the mouse Ba/F3 (BF) cell line to establish stable cell lines. The fusion promoted IL-3-independent growth, proliferation, and chromosomal instability in Ba/F3 cells. Three tyrosine kinase inhibitors (sorafenib, sunitinib and midostaurine) suppressed proliferation and promoted apoptosis by reducing STAT3 and ERK phosphorylation. These findings support the oncogenic role of ZMYM2::FLT3 and its potential sensitivity to targeted FLT3 inhibition.

In the PORTEC-3 trial cohort, POLE-ultramutated (POLEmut) endometrial carcinomas had a 98% five-year recurrence-free survival, independent of the adjuvant treatment arm. Variant P286R is the most common among the pathogenic exonuclease-domain variants that classify tumors as POLEmut.

EFTX-G12V is an EGFR-directed, chemically modified siRNA designed to selectively target KRAS G12V. EFTX-G12V utilizes EGFR-mediated delivery to target tumor cells, taking advantage of the elevated EGFR expression observed in many KRAS-mutant cancer cells. In an A431 isogenic KRAS HA-tagged cell model, EFTX-G12V selectively reduced KRAS G12V mRNA and protein expression in a time- and dose-dependent manner while largely sparing wild-type KRAS. RNA sequencing further demonstrated that EFTX-G12V selectively altered the expression of differentially expressed genes in KRAS G12V lung cancer cell lines (H441 and H727) and the colorectal cancer cell line SK-CO-1. In vivo, EFTX-G12V demonstrated significant antitumor activity in KRAS G12V lung and colorectal cancer models. Tumors in mice treated with EFTX-G12V were significantly smaller than those in mice treated with control siRNA, demonstrating substantial inhibition of tumor growth. EFTX-G12V also significantly suppressed several cancer-associated pathways, including epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT), myogenesis, TGF-β, TNF-α/NF-κB, and WNT/β-catenin signaling, compared with pan-KRAS siRNA in a mouse tumor microenvironment (TME) model. In addition, EFTX-G12V significantly reduced microvessel density (MVD) in lung cancer models. These preclinical findings support KRAS G12V as a predictive biomarker of sensitivity to EFTX-G12V.

A BRAF V600E-positive melanoma cell line (M262) with AKT E17K mutation was found to have a similar level of sensitivity to combination dabrafenib plus AKT inhibitor GSK2141795B (IC50 < 1nM) as to dabrafenib alone, as measured by a cell viability assay.

Several BRAF V600E mutant melanoma cell lines (M249, M399, M397AR)) with PTEN mutation or loss of expression were among those sensitive to combination dabrafenib plus AKT inhibitor GSK2141795B, as measured by a cell viability assay. Two other PTEN null cell lines (M411, M397) had such high sensitivity (IC50 < 1nM) to dabrafenib alone that it was difficult to calculate the benefit of AKT inhibitor addition, however, the authors note that they showed synergism when measuring IC75 rather than IC50.

SOLO2/ENGOT-Ov21 was a randomized phase 3 maintenance study enrolling 295 women with recurrent, platinum-sensitive high-grade serous or endometrioid malignancies of the ovary, fallopian tube, or peritoneum who carried a germline pathogenic BRCA1 or BRCA2 alteration and had achieved an objective response to their latest platinum regimen. Participants were allocated in a 2:1 ratio to oral olaparib at 300 mg twice daily (196 patients) or placebo (99 patients). By investigator assessment, olaparib substantially prolonged median progression-free survival, from 5.5 months in the placebo arm to 19.1 months in the treatment arm, corresponding to a hazard ratio of 0.30 (95% CI, 0.22–0.41; p<0.0001). The study population was defined exclusively by germline BRCA1/2 alterations; no somatic BRCA1/2-mutated cases were included. Treatment efficacy was analyzed across the pooled BRCA1/2-mutated cohort, without separate outcome estimates for BRCA1- and BRCA2-mutated subgroups.

ENGOT-OV16/NOVA was a phase 3, placebo-controlled maintenance trial conducted in patients with recurrent, platinum-sensitive ovarian, fallopian tube, or primary peritoneal cancer, the majority of whom had high-grade serous histology and had achieved a response to their most recent platinum-containing regimen. Enrollment was stratified into separate cohorts according to germline BRCA mutation status, with participants in each cohort assigned 2:1 to receive niraparib 300 mg orally once daily or placebo. Among the 203 patients comprising the germline BRCA-mutated cohort, 138 received niraparib and 65 received placebo. Maintenance niraparib produced a marked improvement in progression-free survival, extending the median from 5.5 months with placebo to 21.0 months with niraparib (HR 0.27; 95% CI, 0.17–0.41; P<0.001). Membership in this cohort required detection of a germline BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation by BRACAnalysis. Clinical benefit was evaluated across the combined germline BRCA1/2-mutated group, and the publication did not provide distinct efficacy estimates for BRCA1-mutated and BRCA2-mutated patients.

PRIMA/ENGOT-OV26/GOG-3012 was a phase 3 randomized maintenance trial involving 733 patients with newly diagnosed, advanced FIGO stage III or IV high-grade serous or endometrioid cancer of the ovary, fallopian tube, or primary peritoneum who were considered at elevated risk for recurrence and had achieved either a complete or partial response after first-line platinum chemotherapy. Enrollment was not restricted according to BRCA status, and participants were assigned 2:1 to once-daily niraparib or placebo. Homologous-recombination deficiency and tumour BRCA alterations were assessed centrally using the myChoice tumour-based assay. Niraparib significantly improved progression-free survival in both primary analysis populations: among patients with HRD-positive tumours, median progression-free survival was 21.9 months versus 10.4 months with placebo (HR 0.43; 95% CI, 0.31–0.59; P<0.001), while the corresponding values in the entire study population were 13.8 and 8.2 months (HR 0.62; 95% CI, 0.50–0.76; P<0.001). A prespecified exploratory analysis of patients whose tumours contained a BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation likewise showed a substantial benefit, with median progression-free survival of 22.1 months on niraparib compared with 10.9 months on placebo (HR 0.40; 95% CI, 0.27–0.62). Because BRCA status in this subgroup was established from tumour tissue rather than germline testing, the reported alterations could not be classified specifically as germline or somatic. The publication also presented BRCA1- and BRCA2-mutated cases together rather than providing gene-specific efficacy estimates.

PRIMA/ENGOT-OV26/GOG-3012 was a phase 3 placebo-controlled maintenance trial that included 733 patients with newly diagnosed, advanced FIGO stage III–IV high-grade serous or endometrioid malignancies arising from the ovary, fallopian tube, or primary peritoneum. Eligible patients were considered at increased risk of recurrence and had achieved either a complete or partial response following first-line platinum-based chemotherapy. Participants were assigned in a 2:1 ratio to once-daily oral niraparib or placebo, irrespective of BRCA mutation status. Central molecular testing with the myChoice tumour assay was used to establish homologous-recombination deficiency and tumour BRCA status. The coprimary progression-free survival analyses demonstrated benefit with niraparib both in the HRD-positive population, with a median of 21.9 versus 10.4 months (HR 0.43; 95% CI, 0.31–0.59; P<0.001), and in the overall trial population, with a median of 13.8 versus 8.2 months (HR 0.62; 95% CI, 0.50–0.76; P<0.001). A prespecified exploratory analysis of patients whose tumours harboured a BRCA1 or BRCA2 alteration showed median progression-free survival of 22.1 months with niraparib and 10.9 months with placebo, corresponding to an HR of 0.40 (95% CI, 0.27–0.62). Because BRCA status was derived from tumour sequencing, the assay did not establish whether individual alterations were inherited or somatically acquired. The reported efficacy estimate also combined BRCA1- and BRCA2-mutated cases, with no separate gene-specific outcomes provided.

molecular_profile: ALK H694R AND ALK G881D AND ALK E1384K AND ALK V597A
evidence_statement: Analysis of 48 lung adenocarcinomas identified novel ALK mutations in six tumours, including S413N in the MAM1 domain, V597A in the MAM2, H694R in an undefined region, G881D in the glycine-rich domain, and Y1239H and E1384K in the kinase domain. Expression of four of these variants (V597A, H694R, G881D, and E1384K) in the lung cancer cell line H1299 resulted in increased activation of ALK, as measured by phospho-Y1604. These results were corroborated by IHC of patient tumour tissue. In addition, these four mutations caused varying levels of downstream activation of STAT3, AKT, and ERK. The variants S413N and Y1239H showed negligible activation of ALK and downstream pathways compared to wild-type ALK. In vivo tumour formation assays showed that all six mutations resulted in significantly increased tumour size compared to wild-type ALK and mock controls, suggesting all six mutations may be oncogenic in vivo. Further experiments examining the H694R and E1384K mutations showed that H1299 or NIH3T3 cells expressing these mutations resulted in increases in ALK activation, cell migration, anchorage-independent growth, and tumour formation, indicative of oncogenicity.
