In the GOG-281/LOGS study, 260 patients with relapsed low-grade serous ovarian or peritoneal carcinoma were enrolled in an international, open-label, randomised phase 2/3 trial and allocated equally to trametinib, given orally at 2 mg once daily, or to an investigator-selected conventional treatment comprising paclitaxel, pegylated liposomal doxorubicin, topotecan, letrozole, or tamoxifen. In the intention-to-treat analysis, trametinib substantially improved investigator-assessed progression-free survival, with a median of 13.0 months compared with 7.2 months for standard therapy (HR 0.48, 95% CI 0.36–0.64; p<0.0001), while objective responses occurred in 26% and 6% of patients, respectively. A prospectively defined molecular analysis was possible in 134 participants; 44 patients (33%) carried an activating alteration in KRAS, BRAF, or NRAS. Within this mutation-positive subgroup, median progression-free survival was 13.2 months (95% CI 9.4–20.8) with trametinib and 11.4 months (95% CI 3.7–13.3) with standard treatment (HR 0.55, 95% CI 0.28–1.07). The corresponding objective response rates were 50.0% (11/22) and 9.1% (2/22). Among patients receiving trametinib, tumours harbouring KRAS, BRAF, or NRAS mutations were associated with longer median progression-free survival than wild-type tumours (13.2 versus 7.3 months) and a markedly higher response rate (50.0% versus 8.3%). However, formal interaction testing did not demonstrate a statistically significant differential treatment effect according to mutation status, either for progression-free survival (adjusted p=0.72) or objective response (p=0.11). Consistent with this finding, a treatment advantage was also observed in the mutation-negative subgroup (HR 0.64, 95% CI 0.39–1.03).

GOG-281/LOGS was a multinational, open-label, randomised phase 2/3 study evaluating trametinib against conventional therapy in recurrent low-grade serous ovarian or peritoneal carcinoma. A total of 260 patients were assigned in equal proportions to trametinib 2 mg orally once daily or to one of five physician-selected treatments: paclitaxel, pegylated liposomal doxorubicin, topotecan, letrozole, or tamoxifen. In the overall intention-to-treat cohort, trametinib prolonged investigator-assessed progression-free survival from 7.2 months with standard therapy to 13.0 months (HR 0.48, 95% CI 0.36–0.64; p<0.0001). Objective responses were also more frequent with trametinib, occurring in 26% of patients compared with 6% in the control group. Sequence information was available for 134 participants included in the prospectively planned biomarker analysis, and 44 (33%) harboured an activating alteration in KRAS, BRAF, or NRAS. In this molecularly defined subgroup, median progression-free survival was 13.2 months (95% CI 9.4–20.8) with trametinib and 11.4 months (95% CI 3.7–13.3) with standard treatment, corresponding to an HR of 0.55 (95% CI 0.28–1.07). Responses were observed in 11 of 22 mutation-positive patients treated with trametinib (50.0%), compared with 2 of 22 receiving standard therapy (9.1%). Exploratory comparison within the trametinib group further showed more favourable outcomes for mutation-positive than mutation-negative disease, with median progression-free survival of 13.2 versus 7.3 months and response rates of 50.0% versus 8.3%. Nevertheless, mutation status did not significantly interact with treatment effect for either progression-free survival (adjusted interaction p=0.72) or objective response (p=0.11). Consistent with the absence of a statistically established mutation-selective effect, trametinib also showed activity in patients whose tumours lacked KRAS, BRAF, or NRAS mutations (HR 0.64, 95% CI 0.39–1.03).

GOG-281/LOGS was a multinational, open-label, randomised phase 2/3 study comparing trametinib with established systemic therapies in patients with recurrent low-grade serous carcinoma arising from the ovary or peritoneum. The trial enrolled 260 patients, who were allocated 1:1 to receive trametinib at 2 mg orally once daily or physician-selected treatment with paclitaxel, pegylated liposomal doxorubicin, topotecan, letrozole, or tamoxifen. In the intention-to-treat population, investigator-determined median progression-free survival was nearly doubled with trametinib, reaching 13.0 months compared with 7.2 months in the standard-treatment group (HR 0.48, 95% CI 0.36–0.64; p<0.0001). The objective response rate likewise favoured trametinib, at 26% versus 6%. Tumour sequencing was available for 134 participants included in the prospectively specified biomarker analysis. Activating alterations in KRAS, BRAF, or NRAS were identified in 44 patients, representing 33% of the sequenced cohort. Among patients whose tumours carried one of these mutations, median progression-free survival was 13.2 months with trametinib (95% CI 9.4–20.8) and 11.4 months with standard therapy (95% CI 3.7–13.3), yielding an HR of 0.55 (95% CI 0.28–1.07). The difference in tumour response was more pronounced: 11 of 22 mutation-positive patients treated with trametinib achieved an objective response (50.0%), compared with 2 of 22 patients assigned to standard treatment (9.1%). Within the trametinib-treated population, mutation-positive disease was also associated with more favourable outcomes than mutation-negative disease, with median progression-free survival of 13.2 versus 7.3 months and objective response rates of 50.0% versus 8.3%. However, formal treatment-by-biomarker interaction analyses were not statistically significant for progression-free survival (adjusted p=0.72) or objective response (p=0.11). Moreover, trametinib retained evidence of benefit in the mutation-negative subgroup (HR 0.64, 95% CI 0.39–1.03), indicating that its therapeutic activity was not confined to tumours harbouring activating KRAS, BRAF, or NRAS mutations.

A sequencing analysis of the DICER1 RNase IIIb region in nonepithelial ovarian neoplasms revealed a striking concentration of somatic mutations at residues required for metal binding within the catalytic domain. The initial discovery series comprised 14 tumours analysed by whole-transcriptome or whole-exome sequencing, with subsequent Sanger sequencing of 101 additional ovarian tumours. Recurrent heterozygous missense substitutions involving E1705, D1709, D1810, or E1813 were detected in 26 of 43 Sertoli-Leydig cell tumours (60%), making this tumour type by far the most frequently affected in the cohort. Comparable RNase IIIb hotspot alterations were considerably less common in other histologies, occurring in 1 of 14 juvenile granulosa-cell tumours (7%), 2 of 15 yolk-sac primitive germ-cell tumours (13%), and 1 of 8 mature teratomas (12%), while none of 15 adult granulosa-cell tumours harboured these changes. The mutant alleles were retained in a heterozygous state without accompanying loss of heterozygosity. In all 16 mutation-positive cases for which paired constitutional DNA was available, the alterations were verified as somatically acquired. Furthermore, these specific RNase IIIb hotspot positions were not represented in COSMIC or in a comparison set exceeding 1,000 cancer-sequencing libraries. Among the recurrent substitutions, D1709N was observed most frequently.

Somatic missense alterations repeatedly affecting the metal-coordinating residues of the DICER1 RNase IIIb domain, particularly E1705, D1709, D1810, and E1813, were found across nonepithelial ovarian tumours. Functional studies demonstrated that these substitutions do not simply inactivate DICER1 globally. When recombinant hotspot-mutant proteins carrying E1705K, D1709N, or D1709E were compared with wild-type DICER1 in RNA-cleavage assays, production of the approximately 22-nucleotide fragment generated by RNase IIIb was strongly diminished. In contrast, formation of the approximately 18-nucleotide RNase IIIa product remained relatively well preserved. This selective biochemical defect indicates that the hotspot mutations specifically compromise RNase IIIb-mediated cleavage while leaving much of RNase IIIa catalytic function intact. The genetic pattern was also notable: the mutations were recurrent and highly localized, remained heterozygous, were not accompanied by loss of the wild-type allele, and still permitted production of stable mutant protein. Taken together, these findings argue against a conventional biallelic tumour-suppressor mechanism. Instead, the authors proposed that altered microRNA maturation caused by RNase IIIb hotspot mutation represents an oncogenic driver, with the recurrent mutant allele exerting a dominant effect analogous in principle to activating oncogenic lesions in genes such as KRAS or BRAF.

disease: Small Cell Carcinoma Of The Ovary, Hypercalcaemic Type
evidence_statement: Small cell carcinoma of the ovary, hypercalcaemic type (SCCOHT) is a rare, poorly differentiated ovarian cancer that predominantly affects younger women and can be particularly challenging to recognize histologically because its appearance overlaps with several epithelial and nonepithelial ovarian neoplasms. At the time of this study, no reliable immunohistochemical marker was available to distinguish SCCOHT from these mimics. Genetic analysis provided a strong link to SMARCA4. Whole-exome sequencing in three affected families identified damaging germline SMARCA4 variants that segregated with disease, and an additional family was found to carry another inherited pathogenic SMARCA4 alteration. In every familial tumour examined, the remaining wild-type allele had been disrupted either by a second somatic SMARCA4 mutation or by loss of heterozygosity, establishing a pattern of biallelic gene inactivation. The broader tumour series reinforced this association. Among 43 collected cases, 35 were confirmed as SCCOHT following blinded central pathological review. Of the 32 tumours with sufficient material for sequencing, 30 contained at least one deleterious germline or somatic SMARCA4 alteration. The SCCOHT-derived BIN-67 cell line likewise carried two damaging SMARCA4 mutations in trans and lacked detectable normal SMARCA4 protein. Most of the identified variants were predicted to truncate the encoded protein and were scattered throughout the gene rather than concentrated at recurrent hotspots, a pattern consistent with loss of tumour-suppressor function. Recurrent loss of heterozygosity was confined to the SMARCA4 region on chromosome 19p. Moreover, whole-genome interrogation of a matched tumour-normal pair revealed only eight somatic mutations, suggesting that SCCOHT can develop against a relatively quiet genomic background in which SMARCA4 disruption represents a dominant molecular event. The genetic findings were closely mirrored at the protein level. Immunohistochemical loss of SMARCA4, also known as BRG1, was observed in 38 of 40 evaluable tumours and in 38 of 43 cases when the entire collected series was considered. Importantly, this staining pattern was highly uncommon among potential histological mimics. Of 139 additional ovarian tumours examined, including 50 clear cell carcinomas, 47 endometrioid carcinomas, 25 granulosa-cell tumours, and 5 Sertoli-Leydig cell tumours, only one clear cell carcinoma lacked SMARCA4 expression. These findings established SMARCA4 loss as a highly specific diagnostic feature of SCCOHT. The study also demonstrated an important hereditary component: among 12 apparently sporadic patients for whom constitutional DNA was available, 6 carried a deleterious germline SMARCA4 variant, indicating that inherited susceptibility accounts for a substantial fraction of SCCOHT even when there is no obvious family history.

disease: Small Cell Carcinoma Of The Ovary, Hypercalcaemic Type
evidence_statement: Pathogenic germline alterations in SMARCA4 were shown to underlie inherited susceptibility to small cell carcinoma of the ovary, hypercalcaemic type (SCCOHT). Across four affected families, distinct constitutional variants co-segregated with the disease: c.4071+1G>A in family 1, the truncating variant c.643C>T (p.Gln215*) in family 2, the splice-altering intronic change c.2617−3C>G in family 3, and c.3239G>A (p.Gly1080Asp) in family 4. Tumour development was consistently accompanied by disruption of the remaining wild-type SMARCA4 allele, either through an acquired second mutation or loss of heterozygosity, supporting a classical two-hit tumour-suppressor model of inherited cancer predisposition. Functional experiments further established the deleterious nature of the splice-associated germline variants: after inhibition of nonsense-mediated decay with cycloheximide in lymphoblastoid cells, aberrant transcripts derived from the splice-site and intronic alleles became detectable, indicating that these mutant transcripts are normally degraded. Corresponding tumours showed complete absence of SMARCA4 protein by immunohistochemistry. Importantly, hereditary involvement was not confined to multiplex families. Among 12 patients initially considered to have sporadic SCCOHT and for whom constitutional DNA could be examined, 6 carried damaging germline SMARCA4 variants. These findings establish germline SMARCA4 loss-of-function as a major predisposition mechanism for SCCOHT and indicate that inherited susceptibility accounts for a substantial fraction of cases lacking an obvious family history.

disease: Small Cell Carcinoma Of The Ovary, Hypercalcaemic Type
evidence_statement: SMARCA4, which encodes the BRG1 catalytic ATPase subunit of the SWI/SNF chromatin-remodelling machinery, was recurrently disrupted through biallelic loss-of-function events in small cell carcinoma of the ovary, hypercalcaemic type (SCCOHT). The mutational spectrum was characteristic of tumour-suppressor inactivation: most alterations were predicted to truncate the protein and were dispersed throughout the coding sequence rather than concentrated at recurrent hotspots. In hereditary cases, the constitutional SMARCA4 defect was consistently followed by loss of the remaining functional allele in the tumour, either through an acquired second mutation or loss of heterozygosity. Additional mechanistic support came from the SCCOHT-derived BIN-67 cell line, which contained two damaging SMARCA4 alterations on opposite alleles. One produced aberrant splicing with exclusion of two exons and deletion of part of the ATPase domain, whereas the second caused intron retention; consequently, no normal SMARCA4 protein was detectable. Genomic analyses further showed recurrent loss of heterozygosity specifically involving the SMARCA4 region on chromosome 19p. Strikingly, sequencing of a matched tumour-normal pair revealed only eight acquired mutations across the tumour genome. Together, these observations identify complete functional loss of SMARCA4 as a central driver of SCCOHT, arising against an otherwise remarkably low-mutational-burden genomic background.

disease: Adult-type Granulosa Cell Tumour Of The Ovary
evidence_statement: Adult-type granulosa-cell tumour (GCT), the predominant malignant sex cord-stromal neoplasm of the ovary, has historically posed a diagnostic challenge because its morphology can overlap substantially with both epithelial and nonepithelial ovarian tumours and no highly specific molecular discriminator was previously available. In this study, paired-end whole-transcriptome sequencing was performed on four adult-type GCTs, comprising one primary and three recurrent tumours, and compared with eleven non-GCT ovarian tumour transcriptomes as well as publicly available sequence datasets. This analysis identified FOXL2 c.402C>G, resulting in p.C134W, as the only recurrent sequence alteration present in all four discovery tumours. Two additional apparent recurrent variants involving ZNF141 and RBBP6 could not be independently validated and were ultimately attributed to alignment artefacts. The physicochemical impact of the FOXL2 substitution was unusually large: C134W had a Grantham score of 215, the highest among 6,410 nonsynonymous variants identified across the fifteen ovarian cancers analysed. Where matched constitutional material was available, the alteration was confirmed to be somatically acquired. The association was subsequently tested in two independent validation cohorts using several orthogonal genotyping approaches, including restriction-fragment-length polymorphism analysis, TaqMan allelic discrimination and direct sequencing. A mutation was accepted only when supported by at least two assays. Using these stringent criteria, FOXL2 c.402C>G was detected in 86 of 89 adult-type GCTs, corresponding to a prevalence of 97%. In all 48 mutation-positive patients for whom paired normal tissue was examined, the variant was absent from the germline, further establishing its somatic origin. The alteration was also strikingly specific for the adult-type granulosa-cell lineage. It was not detected in 149 epithelial ovarian tumours, 180 breast cancers, 14 Sertoli-Leydig cell tumours, 23 fibromas or 10 steroid-cell tumours. Outside adult-type GCT, it was found only occasionally in closely related ovarian sex cord-stromal entities, occurring in 3 of 14 thecomas (21%) and 1 of 10 juvenile-type GCTs (10%), both of which share morphological or differentiation features with adult granulosa-cell tumours. Closer review of the three adult-type GCTs lacking FOXL2 c.402C>G further strengthened the genotype-phenotype association. Two failed to express inhibin and calretinin, markers present in nearly all mutation-positive tumours, and were considered likely histological mimics rather than authentic adult-type GCTs. The third mutation-negative tumour contained a substantial fibrothecomatous component. FOXL2 itself encodes a forkhead transcription factor essential for granulosa-cell differentiation and ovarian development. Before this report, pathogenic FOXL2 alterations had principally been described as germline loss-of-function variants underlying blepharophimosis-ptosis-epicanthus inversus syndrome. In contrast, p.C134W represents a highly recurrent, tumour-acquired missense alteration tightly associated with granulosa-cell neoplasia, a molecular pattern the authors likened to recurrent driver mutations such as JAK2 V617F in polycythaemia vera. These data establish FOXL2 c.402C>G (p.C134W) as a highly sensitive and highly specific molecular marker for adult-type GCT and as a useful tool for distinguishing this tumour from its histopathological mimics.

Ovarian clear cell carcinoma is a relatively chemotherapy-refractory ovarian cancer subtype with a comparatively stable genome and a well-recognized association with endometriosis, but the somatic alterations responsible for its development were not clearly established before this study. Transcriptome sequencing of 18 primary ovarian clear cell carcinomas together with a clear cell carcinoma cell line uncovered recurrent mutations in ARID1A, the gene encoding BAF250a, a regulatory component of the SWI/SNF chromatin-remodelling complex involved in directing the complex to specific genomic targets. The finding was subsequently examined in a substantially larger tumour series by targeted exon sequencing and Sanger validation. Across 119 clear cell carcinomas, 33 endometrioid carcinomas and 76 high-grade serous carcinomas, ARID1A alterations were found in 55 clear cell tumours (46%) and 10 endometrioid tumours (30%), whereas none were detected in the high-grade serous group. This marked histotype-associated distribution was statistically significant (P<0.001). The nature of the mutations strongly supported loss of tumour-suppressor function. Most were nonsense or frameshift alterations predicted to truncate BAF250a, and they were dispersed throughout ARID1A rather than concentrated at a recurrent hotspot. One tumour contained a homozygous deletion associated with genomic rearrangement, while 17 cancers harboured two separate ARID1A mutations, providing evidence for biallelic disruption in a substantial subset. Constitutional DNA was available from 55 mutation-positive patients, and every evaluable ARID1A alteration was confirmed to be tumour acquired. Thus, unlike ovarian cancer susceptibility genes such as BRCA1, BRCA2 and TP53, the ARID1A lesions identified in this series represented somatic rather than inherited events.Genotype was also closely associated with loss of the encoded protein. Nuclear BAF250a staining was absent in 73% of ARID1A-mutant clear cell carcinomas but in only 11% of tumours without a detectable ARID1A mutation. At the histological level, BAF250a loss showed a distribution similar to that of the mutations themselves, occurring frequently in clear cell carcinoma and in a subset of endometrioid carcinomas, but only rarely in high-grade serous disease. This concordance between truncating mutation and protein loss provided additional functional evidence that the detected alterations impair ARID1A activity. Analysis of endometriosis-associated lesions further placed ARID1A disruption early in tumour evolution. In two patients, the same ARID1A mutation identified in the carcinoma was already present in directly adjacent atypical endometriosis, together with loss of BAF250a expression, whereas anatomically separate endometriotic foci retained wild-type ARID1A and protein expression. In one of these cases, the truncating ARID1A alteration could be detected before the lesion acquired the full immunophenotypic features of malignancy. Collectively, the genetic, protein-expression and precursor-lesion data identify ARID1A as a recurrently inactivated tumour suppressor and support its somatic loss as an early driver in the development of endometriosis-associated ovarian clear cell carcinoma.

Ovarian clear cell carcinoma is an aggressive and relatively chemotherapy-resistant form of ovarian cancer with a molecular landscape distinct from that of the more common epithelial subtypes. Earlier attempts to define its recurrent genetic drivers had been constrained by limited cohort sizes. In this study, hotspot regions of KRAS, BRAF, PIK3CA, TP53, PTEN, and CTNNB1 were sequenced across 97 ovarian clear cell carcinomas, including 18 affinity-purified fresh tumours, 69 microdissected formalin-fixed tumours, and 10 clear cell carcinoma cell lines. Among the genes examined, PIK3CA was altered most often, with mutations detected in 33% of the entire series and in 46% of the affinity-purified tumours and cell lines. By comparison, mutations in TP53, KRAS, PTEN, CTNNB1, and BRAF occurred in 15%, 7%, 5%, 3%, and 1% of cases, respectively. The PIK3CA alterations were concentrated predominantly within the established exon 9 helical-domain and exon 20 kinase-domain hotspots. These regions contain well-characterized activating substitutions that enhance the activity of the p110α catalytic subunit of phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase and promote downstream signalling involved in tumour-cell survival, growth, and invasive behaviour. Consistent with functional activation of this pathway, all 18 PIK3CA-mutant tumours examined by immunohistochemistry displayed strong phosphorylated AKT staining. However, intense AKT phosphorylation was also observed in 34 of 40 tumours lacking detectable PIK3CA hotspot mutations, indicating that PI3K-AKT signalling can be activated through additional mechanisms in ovarian clear cell carcinoma and is not restricted to PIK3CA-mutant disease. The investigators also examined whether increased PIK3CA copy number might provide an alternative mechanism of pathway activation. Genome-wide copy-number profiling of 12 purified tumours, together with quantitative PCR analysis of 10 cell lines, found no evidence of PIK3CA amplification. Thus, within this series, recurrent activating sequence mutations rather than gene amplification represented the principal genomic alteration affecting PIK3CA. At the time of publication, the observed PIK3CA mutation prevalence in ovarian clear cell carcinoma was higher than that reported for other tumour types. Because sequencing was restricted to known recurrently mutated exons rather than the entire gene, the measured frequency likely represented a minimum estimate of the true mutation burden. PIK3CA status was not significantly associated with tumour morphology, clinical stage, patient age, disease-free interval, or overall survival, arguing against a prognostic role in this cohort. Taken together, the high mutation frequency, concentration of alterations within canonical activating domains, and uniform AKT phosphorylation among mutation-positive tumours identify activating PIK3CA mutation as a major recurrent oncogenic event driving PI3K-AKT pathway signalling in ovarian clear cell carcinoma.

Ovarian mucinous carcinoma responds poorly to paclitaxel and carboplatin, prompting interest in targeted therapy, and it resembles gastro-oesophageal adenocarcinoma, a tumour type in which HER2 (ERBB2) amplification predicts benefit from the anti-HER2 antibody trastuzumab. HER2 status was assessed by immunohistochemistry and fluorescence in situ hybridization in 33 mucinous carcinomas and 16 mucinous borderline ovarian tumours, using a scoring system adapted from breast cancer. HER2 was amplified in 6 of 33 carcinomas (18.2%) and 3 of 16 borderline tumours (18.8%), a frequency higher than previously reported for epithelial ovarian cancer analysed across all histological subtypes. Immunohistochemistry and FISH agreed in 47 of 49 cases (96%), the two discordant cases both immunohistochemistry-negative and FISH-amplified. Amplification did not associate with recurrence (log-rank P=0.09), and none of the retrospectively identified amplified or overexpressing cases recurred, so HER2 amplification carried no prognostic weight in this cohort. Three prospectively identified patients with recurrent, HER2-amplified and HER2-overexpressing mucinous carcinoma received trastuzumab with chemotherapy. In the first, whose disease had progressed through prior carboplatin and paclitaxel, trastuzumab combined with carboplatin produced a dramatic response after three cycles, with resolution of ascites and omental nodules on imaging and a fall in CA125 that remained stable during subsequent trastuzumab monotherapy. In the second, trastuzumab produced clinical remission, after which the patient developed an isolated central nervous system recurrence while disease resolved at all other sites, a sanctuary-site pattern consistent with the inability of trastuzumab to cross the blood-brain barrier rather than loss of HER2 dependence. The third patient presented with a tumour classified as a mucinous borderline tumour that contained a discrete HER2-positive, amplified focus within predominantly HER2-negative tissue, demonstrating intratumoural HER2 heterogeneity. These data identify HER2 amplification as a recurrent, targetable alteration in a defined subset of mucinous ovarian carcinoma and provide preliminary clinical evidence that such tumours respond to trastuzumab-based therapy.

In a retrospective cohort of gastric or gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma (n = 3116; ERBB2 R678Q n = 40), ERBB2 R678Q was associated with reduced response to oxaliplatin-based regimens compared with ERBB2 WT tumors (ORR 19.0%, 95% CI 7.2 - 30.9 vs 38.0%, 95% CI 36.0 - 40.3; p = 0.03), supporting resistance to oxaliplatin-based therapy. Other ERBB2 mutations did not show reduced response (ORR 40.6%, 95% CI 29.4 - 52.9; p = 0.71 vs WT), supporting specificity of the association for R678Q.

In a retrospective cohort of gastric or gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma (n = 3116; ERBB2 R678Q n = 40), ERBB2 R678Q did not show a significant association with resistance to ramucirumab-containing regimens, with ORR 9.1% (95% CI 2.5 - 26.4) compared with 13.7% (95% CI 6.8 - 25.8) for other ERBB2 mutations and 22.8% (95% CI 21.0 - 24.7) for ERBB2 WT tumors.

In a retrospective cohort of gastric or gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma (n = 3116; ERBB2 R678Q n = 40), ERBB2 R678Q did not show a significant association with resistance to nivolumab-containing therapy, with ORR 20.0% (95% CI 8.9 - 39.3) compared with 18.9% (95% CI 10.5 - 31.9) for other ERBB2 mutations and 25.3% (95% CI 23.5 - 27.2) for ERBB2 WT tumors.

FGFR3 G370C was functionally evaluated in 293T, L8, and RCJ cells using chemical cross-linking, Western blotting, and c-fos luciferase assays. Compared with WT FGFR3, G370C demonstrated spontaneous ligand-independent receptor dimerization and increased basal receptor phosphorylation, as well as constitutive MAPK activation and c-fos transcriptional activity.

In a pan-cancer analysis of 10,967 TCGA tumor samples across 32 cancer types, FGFR3 G370C was identified in 5 bladder urothelial carcinoma samples and was classified as an oncogenic, activating FGFR3 mutation. G370C was additionally annotated as an OncoKB Level 1 alteration in bladder urothelial carcinoma.

In a targeted next-generation sequencing analysis of 4,853 solid tumors, FGFR3 G370C was identified as a somatic mutation in 4 cases across multiple cancer types, including 2 urothelial cancers. G370C was classified as an activating FGFR3 mutation; prior functional evidence cited by the authors demonstrated ligand-independent dimerization and phosphorylation, although its ability to transform cells in vitro was reported as unknown.

In an analysis of TCGA bladder urothelial carcinoma, somatic FGFR3 G370C was recurrently identified in 3 independent tumor samples, all within the non–T-cell-inflamed subgroup. The authors described G370C as an activating FGFR3 mutation and found FGFR3 mutations significantly enriched in non–T-cell-inflamed tumors (P < 0.0001).

In ex vivo human tumor slice models of mucinous cancers, GNAS-mutant tumors showed greater sensitivity to palbociclib than GNAS wild-type (WT) tumors, with significantly reduced proliferation following treatment (p = 0.028); a GNAS-mutant mucinous colorectal cancer was a notable responder, whereas most mucinous colorectal cancers did not respond. In appendiceal peritoneal mucinous carcinomatosis (PMC) slices from three independent donors, palbociclib produced dose-dependent reductions in 5-ethynyl-2′-deoxyuridine (EdU) incorporation (200 nM, p = 0.006; 2 μM, p = 0.0002), including a 37.3-fold reduction in PanCK-positive epithelial-cell EdU incorporation in donor 229 at 2 μM (p < 0.001), supporting sensitivity to CDK4/6 inhibition.

This paper details a prospective single-arm personalized cancer therapy study with n = 16 patients. The disease type was peritoneal mucinous carcinomatosis, predominantly of appendiceal origin. Palbociclib showed clinical activity in GNAS mutated tumors, with stable disease in 12/16 patients at 6 months and 8/10 evaluable patients at 12 months, 1-year PFS 56.2% (95% CI 36.5 - 86.7), and 1-year OS 81.2% (95% CI 64.2 - 100); median OS was NR. CEA decreased >10% in 13/16 (81%) and >50% in 6/16 (38%), while 6/11 (55%) previously treated evaluable patients had a PFS2/PFS1 ratio ≥1.3, supporting sensitivity to palbociclib.
